paragraphs.text: (1.) WHAT TOOK PLACE BETWEEN THE BISHOPS LIBERIUS AND FELIX.

In the time of the emperor Constantius, son of Constantine, a harsher persecution of Christians arose at the hands of the impious Arian heretics, with the support of Constantius. He persecuted Bishop Athanasius, who was resisting the heretics, and ordered that he be condemned by all the bishops. Out of fear of the emperor, bishops everywhere tried to do this, condemning an innocent man without a hearing. But Liberius, bishop of Rome, Eusebius of Vercelli, Lucifer of Cagliari and Hilary of Poitiers refused to give their verdict. So these men were sent into exile for keeping the faith.

Damasus, his deacon, pretended to set out with Liberius. But he deserted on the way and returned to Rome, corrupted by ambition. On the very day that Liberius was leaving for exile, however, the whole clergy, that is, the presbyters, the archdeacon Felix, Damasus the deacon himself and all the officers of the church, together swore an oath in the presence of the Roman people that, as long as Liberius lived, they would on no account have another bishop. Yet against all right and propriety, and with the gravest crime of perjury, the clergy ordained the archdeacon Felix and accepted him as bishop in Liberius' place. This deed displeased the whole people, and they kept away from his processions.

Two years later the emperor Constantius came to Rome, and the people petitioned him on behalf of Liberius. He soon agreed, saying, 'You shall have Liberius, and he will come back to you better than he left.' By this he was hinting at Liberius' consent, by which he had given way to the faithless. In the third year Liberius returned, and the Roman people went out joyfully to meet him. Felix, censured by the senate and people, was driven from the city. A little while later, urged on by the clergy who had perjured themselves, he burst back into the city and presumed to hold a station in the Basilica of Julius across the Tiber. The whole multitude of the faithful and the leading men of the city threw him out again in great disgrace.

Eight years later, in the consulship of Valentinian and Valens, Felix died on 22 November. Liberius showed mercy to the clergy who had perjured themselves and received them back into their own positions. Then, on 24 September, in the consulship of Gratian and Dagalaifus, Liberius departed this life.

Then the presbyters and the deacons Ursinus, Amantius and Lupus, together with the holy people who had kept faith with Liberius while he was in exile, began to assemble in the Basilica of Julius, and they asked that the deacon Ursinus be ordained bishop for them in Liberius' place. The perjurers, for their part, demanded Damasus as their bishop in the Lucina in place of Felix. Ursinus was consecrated by Paul, bishop of Tibur. When Damasus, who had always coveted the episcopate, learned of this, he stirred up with bribes all the charioteers and the ignorant mob, and, armed with clubs, broke into the Basilica of Julius and ran riot there for three days with a great slaughter of the faithful.

Seven days later, with all the perjurers and the arena fighters whom he had corrupted with huge bribes, he seized the Lateran basilica and was ordained bishop there. Then, by buying off Viventius, the judge of the city, and Julian, the prefect of the grain supply, he arranged for Ursinus, a venerable man who had been ordained bishop first, to be sent into exile along with the deacons Amantius and Lupus. Once this was done, Damasus began to harass the Roman people, who refused to attend his services, with clubs and all kinds of bloodshed. He also had seven presbyters arrested and tried to have them expelled from the city by the officials, but the faithful people ran to meet them, rescued the presbyters and took them without delay to the Basilica of Liberius.

Then Damasus, together with the faithless, summoned arena fighters, charioteers and gravediggers, and the whole clergy, armed with axes, swords and clubs, and he besieged the basilica at the second hour of the day on 26 October, in the consulship of Gratian and Dagalaifus, and stirred up a fierce battle. They broke down the doors and set fires, looking for a way to force an entry; some of his followers also tore apart the roof of the basilica and killed the faithful people with the tiles. Then all the followers of Damasus burst into the basilica and killed one hundred and sixty of the people, men and women alike; they also wounded a great many, of whom many died. On Damasus' side, however, no one was killed.

Three days later the holy people gathered together and began to recite against him the commands of the Lord, who says: 'Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul.' They also sang psalms of praise, saying: 'They have given the dead bodies of your servants as food to the birds of the sky, the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth; they have poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.'

So the same people, gathered in the Basilica of Liberius, often cried out, saying, 'Christian emperor, nothing is hidden from you. Let all the bishops come to Rome! Let the case be tried! Damasus has now waged war five times. Murderers out of Peter's see!' And the people of God begged with many prayers for the bishops to assemble and pass a just sentence on the man, stained as he was with such great wickedness. The matrons were so fond of him that he was called 'the ladies' ear-tickler'.

The cries of the people were therefore brought to the emperor Valentinian, who, moved by compassion, allowed the exiles to return. Then Ursinus, with the deacons Amantius and Lupus, returned to the city on 15 September, in the consulship of Lupicinus and Jovinus. The holy people joyfully came out to meet him.

But Damasus, conscious of his many crimes and shaken by no small fear, bribed the whole palace so that his deeds would not be revealed to the emperor. The emperor, not knowing what Damasus had done, issued an edict that Ursinus should be banished into exile, so that no further wicked strife would set the people against one another. Then Bishop Ursinus, a holy and blameless man, out of concern for the people, gave himself up into the hands of the wicked, and on 16 November, at the emperor's command, went willingly into exile.

But the God-fearing people, worn out by many persecutions, feared neither the emperor nor the judges, nor Damasus himself, the author of these crimes and a murderer, but went on holding stations without clergy in the cemeteries of the martyrs. So when many of the faithful had gathered at Saint Agnes', Damasus burst in with his armed henchmen and struck down a great many in a ruinous slaughter.

This most cruel deed greatly displeased the bishops of Italy. When he had solemnly invited them to his anniversary and some of them had come, he tried with entreaties and bribes to get them to pronounce sentence against the holy Ursinus. They replied, 'We have come for the anniversary, not to condemn a man unheard.'
So his wicked purpose failed to achieve what it was striving for.

AFTER THIS THE PRESBYTERS WERE AFFLICTED IN VARIOUS WAYS AND SCATTERED IN EXILE AND IN FOREIGN PLACES. AMONG THEM, THE PRESBYTERS MARCELLINUS AND FAUSTINUS PRESENTED A PETITION TO THE EMPERORS VALENTINIAN, THEODOSIUS AND ARCADIUS CONCERNING THEIR CONFESSION OF THE TRUE FAITH, THEIR DEMONSTRATION OF THE HOLY COMMUNION AND THE PERSECUTION BY THOSE WHO OPPOSE THE TRUTH, AS FOLLOWS:

We beseech your clemency, most pious emperors Valentinian, Theodosius and Arcadius, that, with your eyes on Christ the Son of God, who upholds your empire, you would deign to read this through without tiring. Your exalted reign rises to still higher things, with the help of God the Father almighty and of Christ his only-begotten Son, when you neither despise the truth in humble men nor strengthen a lie in the many or the powerful. For this is most just and most wholesome in a kingdom of justice: that persons be judged by the merit of the truth, and that truth not be presumed from the power of persons. Indeed, the very reason the law of this world was written down is that neither power nor numbers should prevail against what is true and fair, even when it is the humble who claim it.

If your serenity and foresight must take such great care even in the affairs of the state, so that the right of truth may prevail against all force and power even in the smallest matters, and the state entrusted to your rule by the will of God may flourish, how is it that in divine matters the truth of the holy faith is darkened and crushed by a crowd of the ungodly and their most deceitful schemes? This is all the more so since you, the princes of the Roman Empire, defend the pious faith and purity of the Christian religion in so many of your constitutions. You do this wholly as worshippers of Christ the Son of God: you make decrees on behalf of the catholic faith and with every effort write against heretics and the faithless by the authority of your empire. You do not attempt anything new out of a judgment of your own, as certain earlier princes tried to do, to their own ruin and that of others, but you show that your judgments and your pious faith agree with the sacred teachings of the divine Scriptures and with pious confessions of faith.

Yet although this ought to have helped the holy Church all the more after the most savage persecutions of former times, it afflicts her all the more. For the very same distinguished bishops who earlier persecuted her while asserting or assenting to heresy now persecute her under the authority of the catholic name. The more deceitfully they do this now under a false profession of the pious faith, the more destructively they rage, and the more painfully the truth is tormented, since even now, under you emperors who defend the pious faith, it is not allowed to breathe.

But so that we may not seem to be stirring up ill will without proof, we will set out the case as best we can. We beg you, we humbly beg you, to lend your royal ears to us, the least of men, while we show that we are not heretics and yet are grievously afflicted as though we were heretics. For neither those who grievously afflict us nor their associates can now say or prove that we are heretics. Nor can they even deny of themselves that in earlier times they either championed heresy most fiercely, inflicting unbearable punishment on the faithful, or at least surrendered to it, condemning the catholic faith they had previously maintained, because they were afraid to suffer exile for Christ the Son of God. Yet for him even a faithful layman ought to undergo any death, however cruel, since, as the apostle says, it has been granted to us for Christ's sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him. For such a death or suffering is the occasion of blessed immortality.

Your clemency and your religion devoted to God know well how ungodly and pestilential the Arian heresy is. Against it our fathers at Nicaea wrote with spiritual vigour, so that the pious confession of the apostolic faith might be preserved, and the condemnation of that heresy also preserved forever, so that no one in later times could be deceived.

But Arius, like Pharaoh in his heart, did not believe that the divine sentence had then been passed on him. By some means or other he crept into the favour of Constantine, hoping that with his support the sentence of the spiritual bishops could be rescinded and he could be received into the Church. And so this same Constantine ordered that the holy bishop Alexander of blessed memory should admit him to communion. This was not the Alexander who was bishop of the divine faith in Alexandria (who, full of wisdom and fervent in the Holy Spirit, was the first to expose Arius, expel him, and condemn him forever), but the Alexander who was in this city of Constantinople, himself also an admirable bishop.

When he saw that Arius was relying on the king of this world, he stood in the sanctuary and cried out from the depths of his grieving heart to Christ, the true and eternal King and Lord of all kings, not to allow that stain to enter the Church. How steadfast and faithful his prayer was is proved by this: before Arius could enter the church, he paid a new and most grievous penalty, ending in a shameful death. On the day before the impious man expected to enter the holy church with the emperor's help, though he suffered no illness or pain in his body, but, what is more serious, was incurably sick with a disease of the soul alone, he went off to the privy, as people do. As he sat there, he was suddenly tortured by a most violent pain and poured out all his bowels, and the very heart which was the treasury of his ungodliness, into the excrement. And so (wonderful to tell!) with all his insides emptied he became so thin, as if in a moment dissolved by the decay of a livid body, that his whole person slipped through the narrow opening of the seat.

This was a fitting punishment for an ungodly man, a fitting shameful death for a pestilential heretic, and a fitting burial for limbs made utterly foul by the spirit of the devil. For he who had devised new impieties against the only-begotten Son of God had to be tortured and to perish in a new way. He had said that the Son was not truly born of the Father, that there was a time when he was not, and that he was brought into being out of nothing, so that he would not be believed to be of the same substance, divinity, eternity and omnipotence as the Father. We have told this to your august clemency for this reason:

that your wisdom may attentively observe how venerable is the faith written at Nicaea against Arius, to which God bore witness not only through the authority of the divine Scriptures but also through the most sacred prayer of holy Alexander; and how accursed is the ungodly teaching of Arius, which the divine sentence condemned in Arius himself by a new kind of punishment, not waiting for the day of judgment in his case, so that others, terrified by the example of his punishment, might take care.

From this example there can certainly be no doubt that those who believed that Arius's ungodly teaching should be revived or adopted are also condemned before God. For how could eternal punishment separate those whom ungodly teaching does not separate? Even under your laws, those equally guilty are shut in one prison and struck by one sentence. Nor can it be doubted that those are truly catholics who, through exiles, through all kinds of punishments, through cruel deaths, defend without guile the faith that was written at Nicaea in accordance with the Gospels and the apostles. God most plainly approved that faith by the punishment of Arius, who attacked it.

If, then, those things are true in your eyes which are confirmed as true in the divine Scriptures, consider, most pious and most religious emperors, of what those people are guilty who, under these divine rules and professions, have consecrated their faith and devotion to Christ God, setting no fear above the fear of God.

But although Arius was buried in excrement, he nevertheless left heirs of his ungodliness; indeed, there was no lack of worms born from his rotting corpse. What the devil, the architect of error, accomplished through them would take long to recount, even if we were able to recount it; for these things are countless and incredible, yet not false. But we will now set out what bears on the present case: that through deceitful argument they made the emperor Constantius a sharer in the Arian ungodliness. These men too would have paid the penalty in this present life, were it not necessary, according to the apostle's saying, that there be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest.

These worms of Arius, then, of whom we have spoken, having the royal power on their side, at first strove one by one to overthrow the catholic faith and destroy the sacred religion for the sake of the Arian ungodliness, so that they assailed those who resisted with false accusations, or tormented and killed them with punishments or exile. But when they had raged further in their fury and made themselves feared everywhere, they were no longer content to go after people one at a time, and at last they forced the bishops from everywhere to meet together. A place was assigned for a synod: for the Easterners, Seleucia in Isauria, and for the Westerners, the city of Ariminum.

There the bishops who had come on behalf of the holy faith first confirmed the statement written at Nicaea, so that nothing was taken away from it, since it set forth the faith of the Gospel in unassailable words and condemned the ungodly teaching of Arius by divine authority. Then a written statement of faith was presented by Ursacius, Valens, Germinius and Gaius, of such a kind that it rejected the catholic faith and acquitted Arius, indeed even introduced his pestilential teaching. The bishops cursed and condemned both their ungodly faith and the men themselves, judging that it would be an inexpiable crime against those who violate the venerable faith of the fathers if the Church tolerated men so ungodly and their ungodly statement.

They also sent ten envoys to the emperor Constantius, writing to him about what had been done and urging him at the same time to keep inviolate the decrees of the fathers on behalf of the venerable faith against the heretics.

The heretics too, of course, sent envoys, and Constantius received them most warmly, as his own. But the envoys who had come on behalf of the catholic faith against the heretics he rejected. Through his agents he now enticed them with favour, now terrified them with threats, and meanwhile tormented them with mere delay, until at last, fearing the king's anger, unwilling to suffer exile for Christ the Son of God, and delighting in their own sees and in the most ruinous possessions of the churches, they rescinded what they had piously defended and accepted what they had condemned as ungodly.

Allow us here, before you religious emperors, to lament more grievously in the cause of God: bishops feared the anger of an earthly king more than Christ, the true God and eternal King; they thought temporal exile heavier than the eternal punishment, spoken of by Isaiah, of the worm that never sleeps and the fire that is never quenched; they found their own homes and possessions sweeter than a blessed and everlasting dwelling in the kingdom of Christ.

But Constantius, not content with the downfall and disgrace of the ten envoys, sent them to Ariminum so that all the bishops there might likewise be turned. And they too, following that evil example of their envoys, rejected the pious faith of the fathers which they had defended, subscribing to that faith of the Arians which they had condemned with sound and free judgment.

Your wisdom observes that the Synod of Ariminum began most piously but ended most impiously. And the same ungodliness was committed by the bishops at Seleucia in Isauria. Judge, most pious and most religious emperors, of what those are guilty, and for what they deserve to be afflicted, who refuse to associate with such bishops: bishops who at first defended the faith whole and rejected the ungodly faith, but afterwards, fearing exile and delighting in their property and sees, changed their judgment, condemning at the nod of a heretical emperor the apostolic faith they had defended and accepting the ungodliness of Arius which they had rejected.

If they really believed in God's coming judgment, should they not have been glad to suffer every evil rather than betray the venerable faith, whose power had been proved by the prayers of holy Alexander and by the punishment of Arius? All the more so since there had already been the example of glorious suffering, albeit of very few bishops, who, so as not to violate the faith of the Gospels and the apostles and not to yield to the ungodly, refused neither exile nor punishment nor any cruel death.
Indeed, before the Synod of Ariminum, Paulinus of Trier, a most steadfast bishop, was sent into exile for defending the pious faith and abhorring fellowship with the Arians.

Then too the apostolic man Lucifer of Sardinia, bishop of the city of Cagliari, was sent by the Roman Church as envoy to Constantius, because he was well known for his contempt of the world, his study of the sacred Scriptures, the purity of his life, the steadfastness of his faith, and divine grace. And because he defended the venerable faith and exposed and refuted the heretics, he was led into exile with every kind of cruel outrage.

Likewise Eusebius of Vercelli, and also Dionysius of Milan, who was at first on familiar terms with King Constantius, while he did not yet know that he was a patron of heretics. But after he learned and found it proved that the king was defending heretics, he spurned the king's ungodly friendship, preferring exile rather than lose the friendship of Christ God or be deprived of the fellowship of the saints.

Rhodanius too was sent into exile, and also Hilary, who even published writings against the heretics and the apostates, though afterwards he broke off [?], showing favour to the apostates, not to say for the moment that he [?] also to the heretics, against whom he had argued with all the power of his eloquence.

Maximus of Naples in Campania, too, because he had a weak stomach and a rather delicate body, was first afflicted for a long time with ill-treatment so that he would give way. Then, when the weakness of his flesh did not overcome the steadfastness of his mind and the strength of his faith, he was led into exile, and there as a martyr he rested in the peace of the Lord.

Rufinianus too, a man of remarkable simplicity but still more admirable in guarding the faith, anticipated exile by shedding his own blood. For when he persisted in the integrity of the faith, Epictetus, the savage and dreadful bishop of Centumcellae, forced him to run in front of his carriage; and after running a long way he burst his vital organs and died on the road, pouring out his blood. The people of Naples in Campania know this, where the relics of his blood torment the demons in possessed bodies, surely through the grace of that faith for which he shed his blood.

There were also other bishops from Egypt, though only a very few, some of whom were put to flight and others sent into exile, because they would not associate with ungodly and cruel bishops. How salutary, how fine, how glorious it would have been if all those bishops, with equal courage and like-minded agreement, had kept to the end the faith they had always rightly defended, fearing neither exiles nor punishments, so as to win the everlasting blessedness to come in the kingdom of Christ God!

And we say nothing of the fact that the united steadfastness of so many bishops might perhaps have confounded and broken Constantius himself, however terrible he was in royal power, and might perhaps have made him understand how great the worth of this faith was, for which not one of the bishops would refuse exile, proscription, torture and death. But at the slightest fright so great a number of bishops surrendered in droves to ungodliness, and ungodliness, hardened by so easy a slaughter of the multitude, grew into still greater madness.

This is no lesser sacrilege, no lesser ungodliness, than if one had sacrificed to an idol under a pagan persecutor. For to subscribe to heresy out of fear is to sacrifice to demons, since, as the divine Scriptures teach, heresy is a doctrine of demons, just as idolatry is.

Meanwhile, since with some people numbers are preferred to truth, because truth has very few followers, and we are afflicted because we follow the inviolable faith among the few and shun the many on account of their ungodly heresies and the sacrilegious subscriptions of the apostates: what is your judgment in this case, most just emperors and defenders of the catholic faith? To which of these two parties do you give your vote? One party is where there are many bishops; but where there are many, there the sacred faith of Christ, always defended before, has been violated through apostasy; there, out of fear of the king, the ungodliness of Arius, always condemned before, has been accepted. But where there are very few, there the faith of Christ is defended through exiles, through tortures, through the shedding of blood, through death itself, and the ungodliness of Arius and every heresy are abhorred as the supreme evil.

There need be no doubt that the few bishops are precious because of the merit of their confession and their inviolable faith, while the many are made worthless because of heresy or apostasy. For in a question of truth, and above all in a question of religion and the sacred faith, number is not to be weighed against number; rather, that pure apostolic faith, proved by exiles and proved by tortures, even if of only one person, is to be preferred to the faithlessness of many. Even so, it is necessary to bring forward a present divine proof of the condemnation of apostasy as well. Just as in Arius his ungodly sect, punished by divine judgment, foreshadows the fate of his followers, that the same punishment awaits them by which Arius is tormented, so too nothing else should be thought of the apostates from the sacred faith than what has been determined by divine judgment, through present punishments, in the case of one or two apostates.

Potamius, bishop of the city of Lisbon, at first defended the catholic faith, but afterwards, for the reward of an imperial estate that he had coveted, betrayed the faith. Ossius of Córdoba exposed him among the churches of Spain and rejected him as an ungodly heretic. But Ossius himself, summoned to King Constantius on Potamius's complaint, terrified by threats and afraid that, being old and rich, he might suffer exile or proscription, surrendered to ungodliness and after so many years betrayed the faith. He returned to Spain with greater authority, carrying a fearsome order from the king that any bishop who refused to communicate with him, now that he had become an apostate, should be sent into exile.

But a faithful messenger brought news of Ossius's ungodly apostasy to holy Gregory, the most steadfast bishop of the city of Elvira; and so, mindful of the sacred faith and of divine judgment, he did not consent to communion with that wicked man. But Ossius, who was all the more tormented if anyone, now that he himself had fallen, stood firm with unfaltering step and defended the faith whole, had Gregory, a man of most resolute mind, brought before the public authorities, hoping that he too could be made to give way by the same terror to which he himself had yielded. At that time Clementinus was vicar, and at Ossius's instigation and by the king's general order he had holy Gregory brought to Córdoba by his officials.

Meanwhile, as the affair became known, the news stirred everyone, and the common talk among the people was: 'Who is this Gregory who dares to resist Ossius?' For many still did not know of Ossius's apostasy, nor had they yet properly learned who holy Gregory was. Even among those who happened to know him he was still a new bishop, though before Christ, by the merit of his holiness, he was no novice as a defender of the faith.

And so they came before the vicar, and many officials were present. Ossius sat as judge, or rather above the judge, relying on the royal command, and holy Gregory, after the example of his Lord, stood as a defendant, not because of a guilty conscience but because of the nature of the trial, yet free in his faith. Everyone waited eagerly to see to which side victory would incline. Ossius relied on the authority of his age, Gregory on the authority of the truth; the one trusted in an earthly king, the other in the eternal King. Ossius made use of the emperor's letter, but Gregory prevailed by the written word of the divine voice.

When Ossius was refuted on every point, so that Gregory was vindicated by Ossius's own words, which he had formerly written on behalf of the faith and the truth, Ossius grew angry and said to the vicar Clementinus: 'It is not the hearing of the case that has been entrusted to you, but its execution. You see how he resists the royal commands. So carry out what you have been ordered and send him into exile.' But Clementinus, though he was not a Christian, showed reverence for the name of the episcopate, especially in a man whom he saw prevailing by reason and with faith, and answered Ossius: 'I do not dare to send a bishop into exile as long as he still holds the name of bishop. But you first pronounce sentence deposing him from the honour of the episcopate, and then I will carry out against him, as against a private person, what you wish done by the emperor's order.'

When holy Gregory saw that Ossius meant to pronounce sentence so that he would be seen as deposed, he appealed to the true and mighty Judge, Christ, crying out with all the strength of his faith: 'Christ God, who will come to judge the living and the dead, do not allow a human sentence to be pronounced today against me, the least of your servants, who stand here as a defendant and a spectacle for the faith of your name. Rather, I beg you, judge in your own cause today; deign to pronounce sentence yourself by taking vengeance. I do not desire this out of fear of exile, since no punishment for your name is anything but sweet to me, but so that many may be set free from the error of apostasy when they see a present and immediate vengeance.'

And as he appealed to God in words of faith, with all the more indignation and holiness, suddenly Hosius, as he tried to pronounce sentence, twisted his mouth and wrenched his neck along with it. He was hurled from his seat to the ground and expired there, or, as some would have it, was struck dumb. In any case he was carried out from there as though dead. Then, while everyone was amazed, even Clementinus, that pagan, was terrified. Though he was the judge, he feared that he too might be judged with a similar punishment. He threw himself at the feet of so great a man, begging him to spare him, since he had sinned against him in ignorance of the divine law, and not so much of his own will as by the command of the one who had given him orders.

Then everyone was stunned and marveled at the divine power, for in that man the whole spectacle appeared reversed. The one who had wanted to pronounce a human sentence at once suffered a heavier, divine one. The judge who had come to judge now turned pale and feared to be judged like a defendant. And the one who had stood there like a defendant about to be sent into exile was begged by the prostrate judge to spare him, as though he were the judge.
That is why Gregory alone, of all those who defended the faith whole, was neither driven to flight nor suffered exile, since everyone was afraid to pass any further judgment on him.

Do you see the remarkable proofs that God has condemned this betrayal? All Spain knows better than we do that we are not inventing these things. Nor did Potamius go unpunished for betraying the sacred faith. As he was hurrying to the estate that he had earned the right to obtain from the emperor in return for his impious subscription against the faith, he paid a strange penalty in his tongue, the tongue with which he had blasphemed, and died on the road, without reaping any fruit of the estate, not even the sight of it.

This was no light torment for a greedy man. The one who had violated the sacred faith out of desire for an estate from the imperial treasury died. As he hurried toward that estate, a penal death overtook him, so that he did not enjoy even the consolation of seeing it. In the holy Gospel we read the words of reproach to the rich man who boasted so vainly of what he had stored up: "Fool," he says, "this night your soul will be taken from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?" Anyone who considers that this text also fits Potamius will understand that he was judged with no light judgment, above all since he suffered punishment in his tongue, the very part in which that rich man too is most fiercely tormented in the underworld.

Florentius too, who knowingly held communion with Hosius and Potamius in a certain place when they were already traitors, himself paid strange penalties. As he sat on his throne in an assembly of the people, he was suddenly thrown down and went into convulsions. He was carried outside and recovered his strength. Then on another occasion, when he had gone in and sat down, he suffered the same thing, and still did not understand that this was the punishment for his defiled communion. Nevertheless, when he persisted in going in afterward, he was thrown from the throne a third time in such a way that he seemed to be driven off it as unworthy of it. Dashed to the ground, he was twisted with convulsions until his breath was wrung out of him with a kind of violence and great agony. This time he was carried out not to recover, as before, but to be buried.

The great city of Emerita knows what we are reporting, for the people in its church saw this very thing with their own eyes. And this too must be considered: Florentius suffered these things although he had not yet subscribed to the impiety. He had only held communion with those who had betrayed the faith, knowing full well that they had betrayed it.

We have added this so that those who have not subscribed as traitors, yet are joined by communion with men they know to be traitors, may see what they ought to do. And I think they understand what they should fear from the example of Florentius.

But it would take too long to report the other proofs as well, in which divine judgment in various places condemned this betrayal with immediate punishments. The purpose, clearly, was that anyone who for some reason pays no regard to the divine Scriptures might at least understand from the present chastisement of divine vengeance what he ought to pursue and what to avoid. Without doubt God chose to take vengeance at least on a few for this reason too: so that what he threatens through the divine Scripture about the future punishments of traitors should not be thought a fable, as it might be if he took vengeance on no one now in this world.

Let all the bishops who have betrayed the faith now understand for what grievous punishments they are reserved, since vengeance has been taken on their companions even in this world, to the astonishment of all. For this is why we have also set out the present punishments of betrayal: so that what has been avenged on a few may be believed to be avenged on all who are like them, especially since the divine Scripture asserts the very thing that has also been shown by present proofs. And let it be considered, most pious emperors, what those men are guilty of who refuse to join in the divine sacraments with such people, whose eternal punishments are read of in the sacred books and examples of whose punishments are seen in this world.

But we beg your wonderful kindness to lend us, for the sake of Christ God, your tireless patience in listening a little longer, while we set out, if only in summary, how far the impiety has grown. In the regions of the East, and above all in Egypt, the accursed Arians were not content merely with getting bishops to condemn the whole faith and turn to their impious opinion. When these very men, who had first been ordained by catholic bishops, subscribed as the Arians wished, they reduced them to the ranks of the laity. Afterward the same heretics ordained them bishops again, so that they might be seen to condemn not only the catholic faith but also ordination performed by catholic bishops.

Consider in this what was, as it were, a triumph of the heretics over the catholics, and the wretched, almost final and most shameful captivity of these bishops. Having condemned the pious faith and the catholic bishops, they handed themselves over to the heretics' domination and mockery, out of fear of exile and so that they might appear to keep the name of bishop among men, a name which in God's sight they certainly no longer had after their impious subscriptions. The authority of that name was sought even at the cost of every disgrace so that the church's properties would not be taken from them. Would that the church had never possessed them, so that, living in the apostolic way, it might possess the whole faith inviolate! And now it is called the height of impiety not to hold communion with such men, and this under you emperors who, as your decrees declare, defend the divine holiness of the venerable church. (Yet it is no wonder if, occupied with providing for the state, you do not know of these atrocious deeds of theirs.)

The bishops who were suffering the penalty of exile for the faith, or who had taken to flight, abhorred these impieties of theirs. Though separated in body by the distances between regions, they were united in spirit, and through letters to one another they decreed with apostolic vigor that there could be no communion of any kind with such bishops, who had betrayed the faith in the way we have described above, unless they sought lay communion and grieved over their impieties.

But when Constantius, the patron of the heretics, died, Julian held the empire alone, and by his order all the catholic bishops were released from exile. This is how the Godhead often works: it looks after its Christian religion even through its enemies, so that those who worship Christ may labor all the more on behalf of the faithful.

But not long afterward Julian was cut off, and Jovian became emperor. He defended the catholic faith and gave his support to the catholic bishops. Then those fine bishops, who under Constantius had condemned by heretical subscription the whole faith they had once defended, seeing that the emperor had intervened on behalf of the catholic bishops, crossed over once again to confessing the catholic faith. Where, then, is faith and reverence for Christ, when at the will of an earthly emperor bishops now turn from catholics into heretics, and the very same men turn back from heretics to the catholic faith?

Even if certain confessors, worn out at the last, came to believe they should join in communion with such men, overturning the decrees they had earlier made against them on prophetic, evangelical and apostolic authority, can this overthrow the divine truth? Can it prejudice the teachings of the Gospel? Can it shake the apostles' pronouncements, and above all that word of God, who says: "Whoever endures to the end will be saved"?

And there is also the apostle Paul, declared by Christ the Lord to be a chosen vessel, whose words in writing to the Galatians are these: "But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach a gospel to you other than the one we preached to you, let him be accursed!" Further on in the same letter he goes on to say: "For if I build up again the things I tore down, I make myself a transgressor." A man has surely been made a confessor by the Gospels, by the words of the prophets, by the teachings of the apostles. Which of the faithful would doubt that he loses the merit of his confession if he overturns the laws of the divine Scriptures and begins to build what the Gospels tear down?

Or are the divine Scriptures not assailed when the church's peace is joined with bishops who deny the Son of God? For who, considering the force of divine religion, could be confident that the peace of the faithless pleases God, unless, as the fathers decreed, they submit to being counted among the laity and grieve over their faithlessness?

But suppose they do have peace with the unbelievers. How, then, do those give offense, how do they wrong the emperors, how do they trouble the state, who in view of God's judgment reject a peace of this kind? It is a peace that takes in the sacrilegious, honors those who have betrayed the faith, favors hypocrites, despises the truth, sets up as lords of the church those who deny Christ, the true Son of God, stains the people with the blot of faithlessness, and overturns the Gospels. This is why we are counted guilty. This is why, under the authority of your name, we suffer persecution from those bishops who, at the nod of the previous emperor, defended heresy and spoke out against the catholic faith. Alas, what grief! The same bishops who once brandished the decrees of a heretical emperor against the faithful and the defenders of the catholic faith now brandish the laws of catholic emperors against the faithful and the defenders of the catholic faith!

We say these things weeping, with grief in our very hearts. It is not that the faithful find no glory in suffering for the truth under any ruler whatever. It is that so great a stupor lies on the world that their impiety, wrapped in so many deceptions, goes unrecognized, and no one understands how they keep deceiving even the ears of kings to harass Christians and faithful priests. Their impiety is covered under the word "peace," and the fine name of "unity" is put forward to protect the faithless.

But it is well that the Savior himself explained the nature of his peace, so that no one would be taken in by the bare word "peace" and join it to any of the world's impieties. He said: "My peace I leave with you, my peace I give to you; not as this world gives do I give to you." He distinguished his peace from the peace of the world. For if this peace that has received faithless bishops into the church is pleasing to God, what need is there to endure the heat of persecution, to bear prison, to go out to meet the sword, and to suffer every kind of torment and death? For after denial, after sacrilegious faithlessness, every one of the faithless is received in safety, as though unblemished, with his episcopal rank intact, for the sake of this peace which they are confident pleases God.

Indeed, by this reasoning the martyrs too must be condemned. For to what profit did they choose to bear punishment and death? If those who denied the Son of God for fear of persecution suffer no penalty, but are rather honored, then the martyrs should not have hoped for the crown of their suffering; rather, they are paying the penalty for their own rashness. This must follow in every case, for it cannot be that opposites are not judged [?] in opposite ways. Is it not plain what statement they are driven to under the name of this peace, or what they are forced to declare: that if those who denied the Son of God are rightly confirmed in their rank, we must believe the martyrs are being punished for their rashness?

But far be it, far be it from Christian conscience to admit this! For we believe the Son of God when he declares: "Whoever denies me before men, I too will deny him before my Father; and whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father."

Yet learn that in this matter too a divine judgment has been delivered through present proofs, so that no one should think the peace of such bishops is to be accepted, even if they returned to confessing the true faith after their impious subscriptions or their wicked communion with heretics, to which they knowingly yielded so as not to lose either the church's properties or their honors. The holy man Maximus, a bishop whom we mentioned above,

was led into exile for defending the right faith and rejecting fellowship with heretics. In his place the traitors ordained a man named Zosimus, who himself had previously defended the catholic position. This took place in Naples, a city of Campania. Saint Maximus learned of it, and writing from exile he pronounced sentence against him, not only by episcopal authority but also burning with the zeal and power of martyrdom for the glory of God.

Some years later, the blessed Lucifer, on his way to Rome from his fourth place of exile, entered Naples, the city of Campania we have mentioned. Zosimus tried to come to him, perhaps relying on the fact that he now seemed to have corrected himself from his impiety. But Lucifer the confessor refused to receive him, knowing what he had done. Indeed, in the fervor of the Holy Spirit he carried out more forcefully the sentence of the bishop and martyr Maximus, saying that by the judgment of God, who takes note of such things, Zosimus would not keep the very episcopate he was claiming for himself as a spiritual adulterer, and that here too he would feel the punishment for his impiety.

Not long afterward, when this same Zosimus wished to perform the duties of a priest in an assembly of the people, in the midst of the very words of the priestly rite his tongue stuck out, and he could not draw it back inside his mouth, because it hung out of his mouth against the course of nature, like a panting ox's. When he saw that he had lost the use of his tongue, he left the basilica, and (a wonderful thing!) outside, his tongue was restored to its use. At first it was not understood that the sentence of the martyr and the confessor was being fulfilled on him. But since this happened to him every time he tried to enter the basilica on different days, he at last recognized for himself that his tongue was denied him in the solemn words of the pontifical rite so that the sentence duly pronounced against him by the holy bishops might be proved. In the end he gave up the episcopate, so that his tongue, which had given up on him, might be given back.

We are not reporting ancient events, which for one reason or another tend to come into doubt. These present proofs are still alive. Zosimus is still in the body today and no longer loses the use of his tongue, now that he has chosen to live without his episcopate, grieving over his impieties. Has not judgment been passed in advance on those like him, too, that it does them no good to remain bishops on the grounds that they have, so to speak, corrected themselves? For this is not correction but mockery: to change one's faith according to the times of the emperors.

This, this is what deceived the emperor Valens as well, when he saw firmness in defense among the heretics but fickleness of faith among these fine catholics. For it was certainly proved to him that those who claimed to be catholics had previously subscribed with the heretics, condemning the faith they had first defended. And the heretics said: "If our faith is bad, why did those who now call themselves catholics subscribe in favor of it under Constantius? They are defending this faith now, though when they first defended it under Constantius they were refuted by argument and condemned it." Moved by these things, and not knowing the power of the true faith, Valens compared constancy with inconstancy and defended the impiety of the heretics with a certain show of justice.

And we pass over the fact that under Valens, too, certain men again surrendered themselves to the heretics, whom we nonetheless now see counted among the catholics. This is also why the heretical congregations have been strengthened in their impious faith: the heretics persist in evil, while those who are thought to be catholics again and again abandon the good and give way to the heretics. For with what authority do such bishops preach against a heresy to which they cannot deny they have subscribed? And with what confidence can they try to persuade the people of the catholic faith, when it is well known that they rejected it by impious subscriptions?

Do you see that even in your own times, though without your knowledge, as we believe, the pious faith is indeed being defended (and would that it were even truly defended!), but, even if truly, still with a certain injustice? For it is defended by unworthy bishops, to the affliction of the priests who defend the pious faith and to the ruin of faithful lay people. But it is thought a crime to depose so many traitors and to reject a crowd that is complicit in injustice. And where is the justice of true religion, if it must be handed over to an impious multitude, and that under most pious and most religious emperors?

Judgment was not given in the Flood in such a way that the crowd of unbelievers prevailed. On the contrary, the most righteous Noah pleased God all the more because in that destruction of the world he alone was found righteous. Likewise in Sodom and Gomorrah the impious multitude paid a heavy penalty, while the most hospitable Lot was delivered for his righteousness along with his two daughters only. Nor was Elijah, who was zealous for God, crushed, though he stood alone when four hundred and fifty false priests strove against him. Instead that whole impious crowd of priests paid the penalty at the hand of one faithful man, and this while King Ahab looked on, who impiously defended the false priests.

Nor did Jehu, king of Israel, defer to the impious multitude of priests. In the end he called together, by a pious deception, all the false priests who had been at the height of power under King Ahab, gathering them into the house of their impious religion as though he meant to reward them after the rites of the cult, and he ordered them to be killed, so that none of them survived. And we read that because of this deed he so pleased the Lord that the sons of that king sat on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation.

There are many other very similar examples. We do not cite them as though we wanted anyone's blood to be shed: far be that from our wishes, for whoever wants this to happen now strays from the laws of Christ. It was done then because at that time the divine law permitted it, when everything was still carried out in a bodily way, until spiritual instruction should grow. But although it is not now lawful for the good and faithful to desire the blood of false priests, it does not follow that the faithful must be handed over to false priests and afflicted with their most grievous persecutions.

Let what we say be thought false, if in various places the churches of faithful priests have not been seized in some places and destroyed in others; if at these men's instigation holy people have not been arrested, kept shut up for a long time to be abused, and finally sent into exile; if still others have not given up their souls, some in prison, others after being dragged about and beaten, for no other reason than that, fearing God's judgment, they would not hold communion with the faithless or with the companions of the faithless.

In Spain, what atrocities did the presbyter Vincent, a leader of the true faith, not suffer at the hands of the traitors, because he would not be a partner in their impious betrayal and because he held communion with the most blessed Gregory, that Gregory whose faith and courage we described above as best we could? First they lodged a complaint against him with the consular governor of the province of Baetica. Then, under the pretext of an intervention they had requested, a crowd of common people was gathered from other places, and they burst into the church on the Lord's Day. They did not find Vincent, because he had been forewarned and had told the people beforehand not to come out that day, since these men were coming to do slaughter. He thought it better to do so and give place to wrath.

But those who had come ready for slaughter, so that their fury should not seem to have come for nothing, beat with clubs certain ministers devoted to Christ God who were found there, so savagely that they died not long afterward. And because the holy congregation of the presbyter Vincent loathed them all the more after the killings they had committed in the Lord's house, these fine bishops, to terrify the whole congregation, began with the leading men themselves. They demanded that the town councillors of that city be brought before the court and shut up in prison. One of them, a leading man of his native city, was put in chains along with the rest because he held firmly to the faith in God as a believer and abhorred the stain of betrayal, and he was killed by hunger and cold, amid the weeping and lamentation of that province, which knew his honorable life very well.

Those fine catholic bishops Luciosus and Hyginus were the authors of this cruelty. Meanwhile they did seize the basilica, but they could not seize the faith of the congregation. In the end the same congregation built itself a church building elsewhere, on a small plot of land, where it gathered with the holy Vincent. But Satan, who nowhere allows Christ to be worshipped in piety, inflamed these men, and once again, after a petition had been lodged, a crowd of town councillors and common people was gathered from various cities.

His priests also come to the place with them. They break down the doors of that church and carry off everything in it that belonged to the church's sacred ministry. Finally, and it is horrifying to say, to crown the sacrilege they had committed, they took the very altar of God from the Lord's house and set it in a temple beneath the feet of an idol. And these are the men who were received as penitents into the catholic communion, after their impious subscription, for the sake of peace and unity! What worse could a pagan worshipper of idols do if he were given licence to persecute the Church?

At Trier, moreover, the priest Bonosus, an old man, was imprisoned and [?] and was long made to suffer punishment for keeping that undefiled faith for which Paulinus, the illustrious bishop of the same city, also gave up his life as a martyr in exile. And in the city of Rome itself, what grievous persecutions have been brought upon the faithful! There the blessed bishop Aurelius, who was in communion with the most blessed Gregory, was ill-treated a number of times; but this holy man, though often ill-treated, nonetheless died a natural death.

Against the priest Macarius, however, the ungodly committed many outrages. He was a priest in that same city of Rome, a man of remarkable self-restraint. He did not ease his stomach with wine or pamper his body with meat, but softened his rather coarse food with oil alone and gave himself to fasting and prayer. Indeed, as a reward for his faith and abstinence, he had the grace of the Holy Spirit to cast demons out of possessed bodies. We have recalled his life and merit so that those who do not allow such men to live within the Roman Empire may be judged all the more ungodly.

At that time a grievous persecution had broken out against our people, stirred up by Damasus, that illustrious archbishop, so that faithful priests were not free to call together the holy assemblies of the people by day for the service of Christ God. But since, as circumstances demand, the sacraments of our salvation must be celebrated at any time, even in secret, this same holy priest Macarius held vigils in a certain house, calling the brethren together, so that the holy people might strengthen their faith with the divine readings, if only by night.

But the devil, who favours the ungodly because the ungodly favour the devil, will not allow the divine sacraments to be celebrated even in secret. So the clergy of Damasus lay a trap, and when they learned that the priest Macarius was celebrating the sacred vigils with the people, they burst into that house with officials and scattered the people, who offered no resistance. They seized the priest himself, and no longer deigning to lead him, they dragged him over the paving stones, so that he received a dangerous wound in his hip. The next day they brought him before the judge as though he were guilty of a great crime.

The judge, as if acting under an imperial rescript, tried with threats to force him to enter into communion with Damasus. But the priest, mindful of the divine judgement and unafraid of the judge before him, rejected communion with the faithless man. For this he was sent into exile, and while at Ostia he died of the severity of that wound.

So great was his holiness that even the bishop of that place, Florentius by name, who was in communion with Damasus, looked upon him with a kind of reverence. For when the brethren had buried him in an old tomb, Florentius would not allow him to lie there, where the burial seemed unworthy of him; he moved him from there and buried him in the basilica of the martyr Asterius, where in the place of the presbytery [?] next to the tomb. By this pious act of respect he strove, as far as he could, to distance himself from the crime of Damasus.

Let Your Serenities consider: if you want such things to be done in the Roman Empire against holy and faithful people by those who are betrayers of the faith, is there not reason to fear that the blood of the faithful may weigh heavily on the Roman Empire? For this same Damasus, having obtained royal authority, also hounded other catholic priests, and laymen too, and sent them into exile, pleading his case through pagan advocates with judges who favoured him, even though your decrees were issued against heretics, not against catholics, and certainly not against catholics such as these, who did not abandon the whole faith even under heretical emperors and in fact suffered many grievous things.

And recently he tried to persecute severely the most blessed bishop Ephesius, who burns with zeal for the holy faith and was ordained for the undefiled people of Rome by the most steadfast bishop Taorgius, himself a man of unblemished faith. Damasus tried to stir up ill will by a false nickname, appealing through his advocates to the judge Bassus as though against 'Luciferians'.

But Bassus, who had long revered the catholic faith, knew that there had been no perversity of heresy in Lucifer; indeed, he knew well that Lucifer had endured exile for ten years for the catholic faith. With the steadfastness of his own integrity he rejected the accusations of Damasus and refused to persecute catholic men and men of sound faith. Above all, he said that the very decrees of the emperors were clearly issued against heretics alone, not against those who keep the most holy faith without worldly ambition. And then for the first time Damasus was put to shame, because a judge was found who, alone interpreting the imperial rescripts most devoutly, upheld them.

For it is also necessary for us to dispel the odium of the false nickname with which they taunt us, calling us 'Luciferians'. Who does not know that a man's name is given to the followers of one who has handed down some new [?] doctrine to his disciples by the authority of his teaching? But Christ is our teacher; we follow his doctrine, and so we are reckoned by his holy name, so that by right we should be called nothing other than Christians, since we follow nothing other than what Christ taught through the apostles. Heresies, on the other hand, are marked by the names of men because they have handed down the inventions of men. For whoever does not follow the teaching of Christ loses for himself the right to the name of Christian.

Let them say now what new thing Lucifer taught that was not handed down from Christ's teaching, that was not transmitted to later generations by the apostles, the disciples of the Saviour. And it is a good thing that he wrote books to Constantius, not, like most writers, seeking glory for his talent, but, fired with divine zeal for love of the Son of God, very aptly gathering divine testimonies against the heretics and against the very patron of the heretics. Let them point out what in them is contrary to the Scriptures, what new thing he wrote as a heretic would. These books,

since he dealt with everything in complete soundness, Athanasius too admired as the work of a true champion, and he translated them into Greek so that the Greek language should not lack so great a good. Nor is that all: in letters of his own Athanasius also praises these same books as woven together from the teachings of the prophets, the Gospels and the apostles and from a pious confession. And although he extols him with abundant praise, he still does not match the full acclaim his merit deserves. Indeed, he could not praise him more: so far does the excellence of his deeds surpass any tongue that praises them.

Lucifer, though unskilled in artful eloquence, nonetheless had the grace of the Holy Spirit, as a reward for his right faith and most sincere conscience, to write in the manner of the prophets, the Gospels and the apostles, which is above all human eloquence. Through that Spirit he also worked divine miracles, not only in Sardinia but also in his four places of exile, so much so that his opponents called him a sorcerer, since they could not deny that apostolic miracles were being done through him.

Holy Gregory also came to him and marvelled at his great learning in the divine Scriptures and at his life, which was truly as if it were set in heaven. How great a man, then, must Lucifer have been, when he is admired even by Gregory, who is admired by all, not only for that clash with Hosius, but also for the divine miracles that he performs, having within him the grace of the Holy Spirit?

What then? In this too they are ungodly: although Lucifer believed, taught and lived according to the divine Scriptures and worked miracles in the name of Christ, they attach Lucifer's name to the champions of the true faith in order to crush them, not knowing, wretched men, that they commit the gravest sacrilege when they label the doctrine of Christ with the name of a man; just as they are ungodly in this too, that they defend sacrilegious ordinances, issued at the whim of men, under the authority of the Christian name. Is it not the height of impiety to defend one's own iniquities and sacrileges under the name of Christ? Is it not the height of impiety to brand with human names the holy doctrine consecrated under the name of Christ? Yet this fraud, this cruelty, is practised against the faithful in Spain, at Trier, at Rome and in various regions of Italy.

We must now of necessity set out what has been done in these parts, where illustrious bishops, clothed not in the truth of the faith but only in the name of 'catholic', scatter the faithful and true catholics not only through judges, nor only by military force, but at times also through their own clergy, committing atrocities while the judges are unaware or even turn a blind eye. And where would it end, if we were to relate everything that each of the faithful has suffered and still suffers? Yet one atrocious act of persecution must be related briefly, which was committed in Egypt, at Oxyrhynchus, with the whole city as witness.

There is at Oxyrhynchus a certain part of the holy people, and in that sacred company most, the more intently they have devoted their zeal and care to divine things, the more anxiously and diligently they strive to keep the catholic faith inviolate, so that they do not join themselves through the divine sacraments with any heretics or any betrayers of the faith. Many of them were trained in this observance by the example and influence of the most blessed Paul, who lived in the same times as the renowned Antony and was not inferior to holy Antony in life, zeal or divine grace. The city of Oxyrhynchus itself knows this, for to this day it most devoutly celebrates the holy memory of Paul.

But when this part of the people saw that the bishop of that city, Theodore by name, had fallen into impious betrayal of the faith, so far that he not only condemned the whole faith and not only subscribed impiously, but even allowed himself to be made a layman by the ungodly George and then ordained bishop again by that same heretic, they abhorred communion with him. They had with them priests and deacons of unblemished faith, through whom they enjoyed the divine sacraments together with the most blessed Paul mentioned above. Later they also had a bishop ordained for themselves by the catholic bishops of that time: holy Heraclidas, all the more suitable in that he had to be ordained to stand all the firmer against heretics and betrayers of the faith. He was a man of conspicuous life, who had served God from his earliest years, despising worldly goods, and who was perfect in faith and doctrine. For this reason, for his apostolic faith, his evangelical doctrine and his heavenly way of life, he is revered by everyone there, displeasing only the heretics and the betrayers of the faith; and so he is all the more pleasing to God, since he displeases such men.

This man, so great and of such character, began to exercise his episcopal office in such a way that, drawn by the reputation of his faith and doctrine and of his most holy way of life, many came even from very distant regions, abhorring the wicked fellowship of the betrayers and longing for his sacred communion.

But that illustrious twice-made bishop would not tolerate this. First he harassed him through the public authorities, so that several times he had him seized alone in the dead of night by soldiers and removed from the city. But when those authorities did not persist in what they had rashly begun (for what right could they have against a catholic bishop? So they rightly ceased from the persecution they had begun, especially as one of them had been warned by a blow from God), then this illustrious twice-made bishop relied on his own forces and sent a mob of clergy to the church of the blessed Heraclidas, the catholic bishop. He wrecked it, tearing down its walls on every side, so that he even hacked the very altar of God to pieces with axes, to the horror and grief of the whole city that that church should be overthrown whose bishop even people of the other party acknowledge to be of right and unblemished faith.

Consider, we beg you, most pious emperors and champions of the right faith: are you issuing edicts on behalf of such ungodly bishops, so that those who, by the merit of their faith and most holy life, are more precious than the world itself should be afflicted? Believe us, most religious emperors, the blessed Heraclidas is one of that number of saints of whom divine Scripture speaks, saying: 'They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted with tribulations and sorrows; of whom the world was not worthy.'

For how is the blessed Heraclidas not such a man? Rejecting all worldly pleasures, following the footsteps of the Lord through the very bitterness of this rugged life, he pursues, stripped and unencumbered, the saving path of virtue. He is so devoted to the love of the divine faith, just as we read the saints were devoted, having nothing from the world but tribulations and sorrows for the faith, living and walking just as those saints did of whom the testimony above was cited. Rightly, then, the blessed Gregory and the other holy bishops, amid the many evils of the afflicted Church, are refreshed by the venerable fellowship of this man's holiness as by divine consolations.

And Theodore has raged not only against so venerable a bishop but also against his most holy people, who have been formed by the doctrine and character of a most sincere and faithful priest. It would take long to relate what he has contrived against the modesty and the vows of the holy virgins, whose convents the city itself reveres for the merit of their holiness. He has also several times inflicted cruel injuries on the servants of God themselves, the more so the holier he found them to be. But what wonder is it if, like a wolf, he afflicts the sheep, when he so often afflicts their good shepherd?

See: here is a man who, under you, pious emperors who stand up for the catholic faith, boasts that he is a catholic, while overthrowing the church of the catholics, persecuting catholic priests and the servants of Christ, and impiously afflicting his holy virgins as well! This is that illustrious and most holy bishop who, having first been ordained bishop by catholic bishops, was later reduced to the rank of the laity by the ungodly George, and was nonetheless ordained bishop again by that same George for the harassment of the faithful. He sits in one and the same city and is in communion with Apollonius, bishop of the Melitians, who consented to George's impieties; and together with this same Apollonius, Theodore persecutes the blessed Heraclidas, champion of the catholic faith!

See: to him, as though he were a catholic, the basilica of Apollonius has now been handed over by the authority of your general edict, even though this same Theodore, who as a supposed catholic received the basilica of the heretic Apollonius, acted just as impiously as Apollonius did, except that Theodore acted more atrociously, since from being a catholic bishop he became a layman, condemning the holy faith and subscribing to the Arian impiety, so as to be ordained bishop again by a heretic! Indeed, he wants to appear catholic on this ground: that he himself now, by some persuasion, makes certain priests and deacons of Apollonius laymen and then ordains them again, so that he seems to be paying back in kind that most shameful ordination which he himself underwent. Does it not exceed every sacrilege to defend such mockeries under the name of catholic, to the affliction of faithful priests and laypeople?

In Palestine too, at Eleutheropolis, there is a holy virgin of Christ named Hermione, born of a noble family but made far nobler by faith and holiness. She adorns her very virginity with contempt for worldly things and for human glory, which many strive after, even among those who boast of having renounced the world and the desires of the flesh.

As much as she guards the chastity of her body with holy strictness, so much does she preserve the purity of her soul by chaste observance of the holy faith, holding no communion with heretics or with betrayers of the faith, because she understands that virginity of the body is of no profit unless she also guards the integrity of her soul by a holy confession, fleeing the stain of adulterous communion and seeking the saving sacraments of faithful priests. And so she pleaded in devout letters to the blessed Heraclidas that she might be helped by his holy visits.

In place of the blessed Heraclidas, holy Ephesius visited her, who at that time had come from the city of Rome to bishop Heraclidas on matters of Church business. This is the Ephesius who, as we said above, was ordained bishop for the unblemished people of Rome by the most steadfast bishop Taorgius. When he came to Eleutheropolis, not only were Hermione and her holy convent refreshed, but also certain most faithful servants of God, among them the noble household of Severus, a former tribune devoted to the catholic faith, who had long refused communion with heretics and betrayers of the faith but had not yet found the holy communion of catholics.

When he saw holy Ephesius, after testing him at length and proving him a catholic, he gave himself over to him in holy communion, judging himself blessed that divine mercy had unexpectedly visited his house through the coming of so holy a priest. He was moved to admiration of him not only by the purity of his life but also by certain heavenly signs. For the blessed Ephesius is a man of such faith and holiness that wherever he goes, divine grace accompanies him. The holy people at Oxyrhynchus, who are in communion with the blessed Heraclidas, also proved this; bound to him by devout love on account of the divine grace in him, they escorted him on his departure with many tears, as the people of Asia once did the apostle Paul.

We do not say these things out of eagerness to praise, but so that you may know what holy and faithful souls are being afflicted with the most grievous persecutions under the authority of your name by men who, without your knowledge, are even now evidently either heretics, or betrayers of the faith, or the associates of such.

Those in Palestine to whom the holy truth is a burden made some small attempt against holy Ephesius but afterwards desisted, fearing in him both the freedom of his faith and the steadfastness of his spirit, and considering this very thing: that their heresy and impiety might be exposed all the more if, under you, catholic emperors, they harassed too fiercely a bishop of sound and steadfast faith. But when the blessed Ephesius, invited by letters from the faithful, sailed to Africa, giving us a charge in the apostolic manner to devote ourselves to the divine and ecclesiastical offices for the holy brethren, as the holy brethren there themselves requested, the illustrious Turbo, bishop of the city of Eleutheropolis, despising our lowliness, began to want to carry out against us what he had not dared to carry out against holy Ephesius, not knowing that the grace of Christ God protects even his least servants, especially those who labour for the cause of the right faith.

For this Turbo, after he heard that certain people were joining themselves to the sound faith and that the cause of truth was growing by the grace of God, threatens us with destruction and with mobs. He also threatens to burn the house of Severus, [?] who defends the faith of God all the more because he served the Roman Empire faithfully as a soldier. He also tries to persecute the holy virgin Hermione, a woman whom anyone who has come to know her has admired as one of the women of the Gospel. And he lays traps for every single person who is joined with us in the fellowship of holy communion, charging us with a crime, as under that law of Babylon, because within our own dwellings, free of the stain of heresy and without communion with faithlessness, we celebrate the divine sacraments for the faithful who desire them, according to the traditions of the Gospels and the apostles. For with a like fury they once pursued holy Daniel in Babylon with hostile hatred, because he worshipped God in his own house in observance of the divine law.

This is the Turbo who was deacon to the heretic Eutychius, under whom the blessed Lucifer suffered exile in the city of Eleutheropolis, and who also severely afflicted Lucifer himself with many cruelties as he freely defended the faith. There are still people in Palestine today who at that time suffered the most grievous punishments at the hands of these persecutors because they were in communion with Lucifer, a bishop of the catholic faith. Let them deny, if they can, that among their other atrocities they broke down the locked door with axes; that, bursting in upon Lucifer, that most faithful priest, they also overthrew the divine sacraments, savagely beating each of the brethren who had gathered there; let them deny that to this day they keep in their possession the sacred vessels, together with the holy books, which they then impiously plundered from Lucifer.

At that time Turbo certainly kept company with the heretic Eutychius; since then he calls himself a catholic and persecutes catholics under the authority of your name. You defend the catholic faith out of regard for a holy authority: will you allow, most pious emperors, impiety to hold sway everywhere for so long against the faithful under the authority of your name? Is it of benefit to the Roman Empire (and we say this out of the devotion and faith of the reverence you show to Christ God) that those who devoutly preach Christ should suffer persecution and death, so that nowhere may they set up holy altars to God, or that, once they have been set up, they should be destroyed?

Under Ahab, the wicked king of Israel, when the prophets had been slain and the altars torn down, Elijah appealed to God against Israel, saying in the book of Kings: “Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have torn down your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life.” Will you allow every faithful priest to make this damning appeal to God in your times as well?

For even if they keep silent, is God unaware that these very things are being done? What? Do we suppose that God takes no offence when these things are committed against true Catholics and against his true Church, when the same things, once committed against the servants of God, were most severely avenged by divine punishment? And where else do so many plagues come from, by which the Roman world is shaken and oppressed?

There is no need for us now to list each of these plagues one by one, for Your Serenity knows them well amid the heat and anxiety of ruling your empire. Let us rather soften this common grief by keeping silent, so that we may not seem to inflame the wound rather than share the suffering. But this, we beg you, most pious emperors, be pleased to consider: from what causes these things arise. Is it because the faithful servants of Christ, fearing the divine laws, refuse to join in communion with unbelievers, or because true Catholics are being crushed by false priests?

For how are they not false priests? They are to be shunned not only on account of the betrayal of faith set out above, but also because a great many of them, even now, defend their own heresies under a false profession of the Catholic name before you. For who would now fear to preach the impieties of bishops, when impiety committed so often has been rewarded with honour, since no one is removed from the priesthood for it? Indeed, some of them are Origenists, others Anthropomorphites, others again uphold the sect of the impious Apollinaris; others, in a threefold faction [?], blaspheme against the Holy Spirit with their various zeal; and even those among them who are thought to believe piously maintain or look favourably upon the view that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are three substances. Yet all of these boast of your edicts and claim the churches for themselves, although our fathers always condemned these impious sects by apostolic and evangelical authority.
To examine these sects is not the purpose of the present little work; but we will say something that should move to horror your mind, intent as it is on the true faith. A single

heresy, we believe, was accepted at Ariminum under a heretical king, and now, under you, pious Catholic emperors, so many heresies are upheld that are no less impious than the impiety of Arius. And though each of them writes books or letters against the others, yet all of them hold communion with one another, either directly or through some indirect chain of connections. They quarrel only in debates, with the empty zeal of philosophers, and not, as Christians should, out of devotion to the sacrament, each shunning the other as impious. So it now seems that there is a contest of wits among them, as in the schools, and not a sacred defence of the true religion, since they do not separate their sacraments from one another, even though they are separated from one another by impious opinions.

They do this because some of them pursue human glory, and others greed; and that is why they collude with one another under an impious pretence, so that they lose neither the church's possessions nor its honours. Meanwhile, to cloak their many impieties, they make a show of what look like signs of a most kindly spirit, to deceive the unwary, and say that they join even those who think otherwise in the fellowship of church communion so that the good of peace may not perish in the Church—as if a peace of this kind, which admits such great impieties into his Church, could please Christ our God.
