But let those who think so hear what is written of them: “And the way of peace they have not known; there is no fear of God before their eyes.” And in Jeremiah we read still more plainly of that impious and unjust peace, as the following testimony sets out: “From the least of them to the greatest, all have done wickedness; from the priest to the false prophet, all have dealt falsely. And they plotted the crushing of my people, counting it as nothing and saying, ‘Peace, peace!’ And where is peace?” And we must note what dreadful things he goes on to say about those who boast of this most empty peace, for he continues: “They were put to shame because they failed, and even so they did not feel shame or blush, and they did not recognize their disgrace. Therefore they will fall in their ruin, and in the time of visitation they will be brought low.”

What evil are we committing, what impiety are we doing, if, keeping faith with Christ, we reject a peace of this kind, whose great shame and disgrace and most grievous end are so described? But these fine lovers of peace stir up war against faithful priests. For what does the devil want, but that the impious and the betrayers should boast of the world's peace? What does the devil want, but that those who are pious and faithful should be harassed by the persecution of their attackers?

We have set out these things so that the blood of Christians defending the most holy faith may not continue to be shed because you do not know of it. For what good is it that you are defenders of the Catholic faith, if you allow the followers of the Catholic faith to be tortured everywhere, driven out everywhere, and the holy faith to be freely preached nowhere?

Let them have basilicas gleaming with gold, clad in lavish displays of precious marble or raised up on magnificent columns; let them also have estates stretching far and wide, for whose sake the integrity of the faith has been endangered. But why do they also claim for their impieties the cities that are common to all Romans, so as to allow no one in them to live piously—cities in which even empty superstition is practised by many without danger and upheld without arousing their resentment? Let the truth at least be allowed to worship Christ our God piously and adore him faithfully, even among the meanest and most humble stables, where once that same Christ, born according to the flesh, deigned to lie as an infant.

We do not make this request as though we dreaded being killed for the truth. God is our witness, he who truly sees into the heart, that by the grace of God it would be for us the highest refreshment and a sure hope of future blessedness if we were slaughtered for this faithful confession. So we have not set out these things as men afraid to suffer, but so that the blood of faithful Christians, shed through the impieties and cruelties of others, may not long weigh upon the most pious empire of your rule.

Above all under you, most religious Augustus Theodosius, who with wonderful devotion stand united against all heretics in the holy confession of the Christian religion, we believed that a great punishment would await us before God if, in the presence of so religious, so pious an emperor, consecrated to Christ our God with a divine and perfect fear, one whom God Christ has truly chosen for the empire, we kept silent about the things that concern the true faith and the true Church. After this we have no doubt with what care you will act, as father of the empire, so that the purity of the faith professed and of communion may not be oppressed in the Roman world. The more holily you act in the cause of the sacred faith and the professed truth, the more gloriously you will reign, both here and for ever, by the favour of Christ.

I, Marcellinus, presbyter, wish for your most happy empire secure peace, and in the kingdom of Christ and God everlasting blessedness, most pious emperors. I, Faustinus, who cannot be worthily called a presbyter of God, wish that here you may reign happily for many years with the help of the most merciful Godhead, and that in the future kingdom of Christ the Son of God you may attain everlasting blessedness with the saints, most glorious emperors.
TO THIS PETITION THE IMPERIAL LAW REPLIED AS FOLLOWS:

Greetings, Cynegius, most dear to us. No reverence in human hearts ought to be greater than reverence for the divine law, and nothing can be added to it. Its sovereign excellence rules the world and the earth, and when it is propitiated it guards everything that the favor of almighty God has willed to be under us.

Nevertheless, our clemency has been petitioned through Faustinus and Marcellinus, priests most full of faith, and we were concerned [?] that if we gave the petitioners no reply, we might seem to agree with those who have added something to the divine law we serve, against our purpose. So we keep a balance between the two: we respect the petition that has been presented, but we neither wish nor order anything to be added to the faith by our own decision. For no one was ever so profane in mind that, when he ought to follow catholic teachers, he would himself lay down for the teachers what is to be followed.

The praise in the petition is certainly commendable and just, for it has covered almost the whole course and sequence of the heretical superstition that is contrary to the catholic faith. It has shown both where this superstition arose and under what author it advanced. Through the persuasion of certain persons the ancient tradition of the whole age was changed, and innocent men driven into exile for the faith laid down their lives with the highest praise.

But vengeance was not delayed for those who plotted against good morals and heavenly institutions. For a little while, out of contentiousness, and moved not by faith but by faction, they perverted the minds of many with detestable insinuations. The patience of almighty God was so far provoked that, as an example to all, they felt before death the punishment that is owed to criminals after death.

But not even this could convert them and turn them to God's precept. They harass, pursue and assail catholics with secret schemes. Their persistence in error is so great that they would rather sin daily with followers of other observances than think rightly with the catholics.

In this the petitioners' plea deserves praise. They are in communion with Gregory of Spain and Heraclida of the East, truly holy and praiseworthy bishops, and they desire to live in the catholic faith without attack or harassment from anyone, and without being troubled by the plots and confrontations of assailants, since it is their wish to keep the faith they have once received with all devotion forever.

Therefore let whatever has deserved to be eternal remain inviolate. Let no confrontation, no assault and no fraud of others make any attempt against it. Let them pursue their purpose in whatever place they wish, and let them hold to the catholic faith with divine love, Cynegius, father most dear and most beloved.

Let your Sublimity order that the precept of our Serenity be observed. By this precept we venerate with all favor the catholic faith, without which we cannot be saved. It is to be observed in such a way that it protects and defends Gregory and Heraclida, prelates of the sacred law, and other priests like them who have devoted themselves to the same observance, from the injuries of wicked men and heretics. And let all know that this is settled in our minds: we believe that the worshipers of almighty God are none other than the catholics.
(3.) ON THE CONSTRUCTION OF THE BASILICA OF THE HOLY APOSTLE PAUL.

VALENTINIAN, THEODOSIUS AND ARCADIUS, AUGUSTI, TO SALLUSTIUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY. Out of regard for a veneration hallowed since ancient times, we desire to adorn the basilica of Paul the apostle as the sanctity of religion deserves, to enlarge it to suit the size of the congregation, and to raise it up as the zeal of devotion requires. Your Sublimity's service has therefore been welcome to us. You undertook to inspect everything, as the matter required, and with careful and fitting words you informed the ears of our Serenity of the whole site and the appearance of the place. For it was fitting that we should be better informed when ordering what is to be ordered.

Therefore, after sharing the examination with the venerable bishop and making known what we order both to the most magnificent order and to the Christian people, let your Sublimity examine the matter with closer attention and a full inspection. Both the people and the senate may agree that the old road, which runs behind the back of the basilica and lies beside the bank of the river Tiber, should be altered so that the present road is added to the space of the future work. If so, you will have the architects lay out the plan of the future basilica as far as the level ground suitable for building extends, so that no unevenness spoils the splendor of the more spacious building. In every façade of walls beauty is the greatest thing, and the very design of great buildings shows at first glance that it must be preserved.

The matter itself now requires that a plan of the work to be built be drawn up with faithful scrutiny, and that a preliminary estimate of all the costs be set out in full, according to the prices of things in the most sacred city, and reported to our clemency at the proper time. In this way the assent of our Serenity may be added to the common counsel of all, so that what a devout mind has resolved may more readily be carried out as befits the merits of so great a religion. AND IN ANOTHER HAND, THE EMPEROR'S: May the Divinity preserve you for many years, father most dear and most beloved.
(4.) LETTER OF CONGRATULATION ON THE ORDINATION OF POPE SIRICIUS.

Hail, Pinianus, most dear to us. We see that it is in keeping with the custom of the Roman people that the people of the eternal city rejoice in concord and elect the best bishop, and we are glad that this has happened in our times.

They wished the religious Siricius, prelate of holiness, to preside over the priesthood, and in doing so they shouted down the wicked Ursinus with their acclamations. Let the said bishop therefore remain in office, to our joy, Pinianus most dear and most delightful. It is a great example of innocence and integrity that in one acclamation he himself should be elected and the others rejected. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, at Milan.
(5.) WHERE URSINUS AND THOSE WITH HIM ARE RELEASED FROM EXILE.

Hail, Praetextatus, most dear to us. The punishment may seem to have been just, since by coercion it quelled a faction that was rioting in the place where there ought to be the greatest concord: in the see and the affairs of the church, both of which demand moderation and reverence. Nevertheless, from the gentleness of our own nature and out of regard for religion itself and the law, we take pity on all who were recently condemned to deportation because of that disturbance, Praetextatus most dear and most delightful.

Your most exalted Sublimity will therefore set free, by the authority of our judgment, all who share that lot and that guilt. But for the future it will hold to this rule: if these same men, once restored to their former status, again do anything in a restless spirit that disturbs the restored tranquility, the severest sentence shall be pronounced against them. For those who do not stop sinning after pardon can merit no pardon.
(6.) WHERE THE BASILICA OF SICININUS IS RESTORED.

VALENTINIAN, VALENS AND GRATIAN TO PRAETEXTATUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY. Now that the author of the dissension has been removed, every cause of discord must be laid to rest. Otherwise, if any material for it remains, it will have done no good to remove the kindling of quarrels, Praetextatus, father most dear and most beloved.

Your most exalted Sublimity has considered the petition of the defensors of the church of the city of Rome, that is, of Damasus, prelate of the sacred law. It states that one of the churches of the catholic religion, and only one, is still being kept from its service by the dissenters. For the sake of public security it is to be feared that some tumult may arise again from this, since it would be no small image of separation if anything were thought to be shut off in this way. You will therefore order the church to be opened to Damasus, so that each and every one may know with what zeal unity is to be cherished and in what peace all must live. For once the churches are restored, assembly permitted everywhere calls for the fullest concord.
(7.) ON EXPELLING THE ASSOCIATES OF URSINUS FROM ROME.
THE SAME AUGUSTI TO PRAETEXTATUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY. Such moderation is innate in us that we desire to safeguard public discipline without bringing disaster on anyone.

Therefore, since we do not favor occasions for punishment, the associates and ministers of Ursinus, whom your most exalted Sublimity thought should be removed for the sake of the quiet of the eternal city, are to be permitted to live in their own right wherever they prefer, Rome alone excepted, since it is Rome's tranquility we are concerned for. They may do so without any injury to religion, so that they seem to be traveling abroad rather than exiled, Praetextatus, father most dear and most beloved. It does not matter to us where they choose to live, provided that the incitements to dissension are removed and concord is again firm among the people. Given on the day before the Ides of January, in the consulship of the three Augusti.

THE SAME AUGUSTI TO OLYBRIUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY. As you indicated in your recent letter, you have worked with the most strenuous zeal to ensure that there can be no discord in the city of Rome and that the Christian people may rejoice in security and deep peace. But as the letter of the clarissimus Aginatius, vicarius of the prefecture, has testified, some still delight in stirring up what has been calmed, and frequent uproar breaks out at assemblies outside the walls, Olybrius, father most dear and most beloved.

Therefore let your excellent Sublimity, by the authority of this precept, serve both the fatherland and the law by ensuring that the dissenting people have neither leave nor opportunity to assemble within the twentieth milestone. If this mad gathering will not stop, it must move away, as has been ordered. Only in this way, with all tumults banished far away, will sure peace be granted to the people for all time.

THE SAME AUGUSTI TO AGINATIUS, VICARIUS. As your Prudence has written, these dissensions are throwing the most sacred city into confusion while the Christian people waver. Desiring to remove every cause of them, we order by this letter that no assembly be held within the twentieth milestone by those who delight in turbulent separation, Aginatius most dear and most delightful. Let your proven Sincerity therefore carry out this most salutary precept, which leaves no room for interpretation through any ambiguity, with the spirit that both a judge and a citizen owe to the restoring of peace and tranquility. In this you also have the help of the urban prefecture. Our Serenity has instructed Olybrius, a clarissimus and illustrious man, with the same decision regarding the impious gatherings of the factious, that he should shut them out by a clearly marked boundary, so that a disturbance not allowed in the city should not arise even in its vicinity. And the two of you together will easily achieve what each of you could achieve alone.

THE SAME AUGUSTI TO OLYBRIUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY. Nothing can be more pleasing than abundance or quiet, and whenever the two are joined it is the height of happiness. Your Sublimity therefore doubtless perceives how welcome your letter was to us. It testified both that those who had disturbed the most holy law with tumult and sedition have been suppressed, and that the grain supply of the common fatherland of all has gradually begun to return to its former state.

But in a man so well known we are hardly astonished at this. When we conferred the prefecture on you for your merits, we presumed you would be just the man we found you to be at the very start of your administration. Accordingly we do not urge your illustrious Authority to keep the same efficiency and devotion and to heap upon the condition of the people both the glory of moderation and the blessings of security, by restoring the former discipline and providing the necessary goods, Olybrius, father most dear and most beloved. You see to this by your own nature; it is enough that what follows should match what has begun.

Nor should you weigh the origins of offenses in such a way as to think that our Clemency must be consulted about the correction of individuals. You anticipate of your own accord everything from which any confusion may arise, and you restrain it so carefully and modestly that what is left to us is not so much the need to urge you on as the pleasure of approving.

THE SAME AUGUSTI TO AMPELIUS, PREFECT OF THE CITY. It has rightly been given to the feelings of our Clemency, whether as a divine gift or from the tranquility of our nature, that we do not compete with the crimes of offenders through the severity of the laws. In the hope of future amendment we wish the harm of correction to be milder than the deserts of the guilty provoke, Ampelius, father most dear and most beloved.

Some time ago, provoked by the restlessness of Ursinus, and favoring the concord of the Christian people while also providing for the quiet of the most sacred city, we had decreed that this disturber of public tranquility be lawfully confined for the time being to one place, within the Gauls only, so that the harm of dissension would not be spread widely through contact with his ways. But softened by the clemency of our nature, we have now given the said man leave to depart, on condition that he not attempt to set foot in the city of Rome or the suburbicarian regions, or to pour in the contagion of his wickedness.

We decree the same concerning the other partners in his error, namely Gaudentius, Ursus, Rufus, Auxano, Auxanius, Adiectus, Leontius and Rufinus: those whom a likeness in wickedness unites are to be bound by the same condition of amendment. But if any of the aforesaid, with sacrilegious intent, thinks fit to transgress the statute of our Clemency, let him feel the severity of public punishment, no longer as a Christian but as one cut off by the reason of law and religion. We also wish your Censure to know that, concerning this same observance, to the clarissimus

Maximinus, vicarius of the city of Rome, we have given a suitable order. In this way those who govern our commonwealth will more readily carry out the statutes concerning the persons named, and those who perceive that the quality of their morals and actions lies under the watchful eyes of many will show greater restraint. AND IN THE EMPEROR'S HAND: Farewell, Ampelius, most dear and most beloved.

THE SAME AUGUSTI TO MAXIMINUS, VICARIUS OF THE CITY OF ROME. This has been divinely implanted in our Clemency: even when amendment of morals suffices in human life, we never cease from the zeal and the will to show indulgence, and we wish the harm of correction to be milder than the deserts of offenders provoke.

For this reason we have granted Ursinus freedom to move about. For the sake of the quiet of the Christian people and the discipline due to religion and the laws, we had ordered him to remain for the time being in one place within the Gauls. He is now free, on condition that he not dare to go either to the city of Rome or to the suburbicarian regions.

If with ungrateful obstinacy he thinks fit to transgress the statute of our Clemency, let the severity of the law pursue him, Maximinus most dear and most delightful. It will pursue him no longer as a Christian, since his restless mind cuts him off from the communion of religion, but as a factious man, a disturber of public tranquility and an enemy of the laws and of religion.

Let your Sincerity therefore display the text of our order with due veneration and address the leading men and inhabitants of the cities and regions over which it presides for the time being, in a letter of its own. They are to know that the aforesaid has been granted leave to go beyond the bounds lawfully prescribed, together with the partners of his restlessness or error, Gaudentius, Ursus, Rufus, Auxano, Auxanius, Adiectus, Leontius and also Rufinus, on such terms that they understand they must keep away from the forbidden places. For in this way we temper the indulgence of our Clemency, so that we do not, by giving the restless the opportunity of being near, perhaps provoke the feelings of the religious people to some outcry.
(13.) ON THE REBAPTIZERS.

GRATIAN AND VALENTINIAN, AUGUSTI, TO AQUILINUS, VICARIUS. The sentences of ordinary judges are confirmed by the lapse of time, by a pronouncement against a contumacious party, or by a hearing held in the presence of the parties. This modest authority has no fear of being shaken and overturned either by the more powerful or by the shameless. Then what patience will be able to bear the abandonment of our precepts through your negligence? Indeed, by despising that patience you rouse it, so that it takes on the tones of a long tolerance driven to despair and compels you through fear to acknowledge your duty.

Is what the madness of Ursinus branded into people still more vigorous than what our Serenity urged by mild edicts? We ordered that all who attempted impious assemblies, profaning religion, be driven out as far as the hundredth milestone from the city. There their stubborn fury, abandoned by its followers, would rush to the ruin only of the one who alone erred. We also ordered that those condemned by the judgment of right-thinking bishops should afterwards have no return to the churches they had defiled, and should beg us in vain, with shameless obstinacy, to reopen the judgment.

Let your praiseworthy and proven Sincerity recall the letter our Clemency once sent to the clarissimus Simplicius, formerly vicarius, and stop hoping for a repetition of the mandate, since having to renew a precept is a regrettable embarrassment to our Clemency.

Ursinus, indeed, is confined in Gaul, and his withdrawal to Agrippina restrains him from stirring up any restless disturbances. Yet we have heard that, through those who come to meet him, he has been importuning more often than lamenting, with the result that he has been repeatedly rebuffed [?].
Isaac has been shut away, under the title of condemnation, in a remote corner of Spain. He will have taken poor thought for his own head if in his madness he stirs up any disturbance.

The bishop of Parma is all the more dangerous because he is nearer to the illustrious city. Being close by, he stirs up the multitude of the ignorant and troubles the church from which he was cast out by the judgment of holy prelates, evidently hoping for the empty glory of a heavier sentence. If your predecessor had had any devoted vigor, he ought to have thrust him far beyond the borders.

And Florentius of Puteoli was rightly convicted and condemned, and when he tried to disturb our Clemency he received the reply his wicked offense deserved. Yet now, after the fifteenth year, he is again trying to defile the church from which he had been expelled. He strives to form illicit congregations and corrupts a multitude lacking counsel through the persuasions of his depraved mind. Evidently he is relying on the sloth of our judges, who sacrifice imperial precepts to private favor and patiently allow the religion we rightly venerate to be disturbed, perhaps because they themselves neglect it.

Claudianus too was summoned by those who, against the divine precepts, repeat the initiation of religion, by those, I say, whom we had ordered to be expelled. As if he had attempted too little crime by staying in Africa, he is said to have made his way into Rome. As a false teacher he strives either to profane those still uninitiated with a deviant mystery or to corrupt anew, with a greater outrage, those already initiated, although repetition does not increase the discipline of the most holy religion but overturns it. We pursued this Claudianus with a penalty unlike what he deserved, and our severity was moved only so far as to order him to return to his homeland. But he is said to be staying on even now. He solicits the ignorant and gathers empty names for a fee, and so destroys the souls of bodies that have been redeemed.

Hence those assailants of the most holy see did not fear to harass Bishop Damasus with the foulest calumnies, a man of most holy mind, proved so not only by the will of God, which was enough, but also by the scrutiny of the courts, as was also confirmed to our deified father Valentinian. After they despaired of being able to overthrow him, they began to harass the people for whom he stands as a hostage before the Divinity.

But let the idle connivance of the judges go this far and no further; nor is there any need to point out how far a sanction held in contempt can go. Thus far, I say, and no further, let the supine idleness of the officials go. Henceforth you must drive beyond the hundredth milestone from the city all those whom the substance of our order names, or whom the consensus of a holy council of bishops shows to be plotting disturbances of this kind. You must also order them banished from the territories of those cities whose people or churches they trouble, either in person or through a rabble like themselves. If you do not, then besides the injury to your reputation, which is no slight loss among good men, you will incur the guilt of neglecting this sanction.

It is our will that this apply to anyone who has been condemned by the judgment of Damasus, held with a council of five or seven bishops, or by the judgment and council of those who are catholics. If he wishes unjustly to keep hold of a church, or through contumacy refuses to appear when summoned to a priestly judgment, he is either to be sent back to the episcopal judgment by the illustrious praetorian prefects of Gaul and Italy using their authority, or to be summoned by the proconsuls or vicarii and brought to the city of Rome under escort.

Or if such ferocity arises in anyone in more distant parts, the whole hearing of his case shall be brought before the metropolitan bishop of the same province for examination. If he himself is a metropolitan, he must of necessity go to Rome, or to those whom the Roman bishop has assigned as judges, without further referral. This is to be done in such a way that those who have been deposed are banished only from the territory of the city in which they were bishops. For we restrain those who deserve severity more mildly, and punish sacrilegious obstinacy more leniently than they deserve.

But if the metropolitan bishop or any other bishop is suspected of injustice or favoritism, the one summoned may appeal to the Roman bishop or to a council of fifteen neighboring bishops, provided that once the hearing has been held, what has been decided is not reopened.

Furthermore, natural justice has implanted a principle in our minds even for matters of lesser business and trivial pleadings, and we wish it to prevail much more carefully in the weightiest cases: it must not be easy for any reprobate, marked by notorious depravity of morals or branded by infamous calumny, to take on the role of accuser or to give testimony in an accusation against a bishop.
ON THE PROCEEDINGS BETWEEN BONIFACE AND EULALIUS, WHEN, AFTER THE DEATH OF POPE ZOSIMUS, BOTH SEIZED THE EPISCOPATE OF THE CITY OF ROME THROUGH CONTENTIOUS AMBITION.
(14.) Copy of the report of Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to the Emperor Honorius, residing at Ravenna.
Whatever happens in the city of Rome, it is not right for me to keep silent about it, given the service I owe and always render to Your Majesty.
Bishop Zosimus had long been suffering from a serious illness, so much so that he was frequently reported dead, and it happened that he departed this life on the second day after I took office.

At once, as had been agreed, I addressed the people and warned them that everything should be settled quietly by deliberation of the clergy, and that popular disorder should not interfere in the arrangement of affairs, since it was certain that in electing a bishop the judgment of almighty God must be awaited, my lords Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, pious, fortunate, renowned victors, ever Augusti. I also warned the guilds, threatened my own staff as well, and deterred the heads of the districts, so that no one should attempt to disturb the peace of your city.

This was indeed observed so well that everything was concluded without uproar. But when the holy man Eulalius had been brought by the people and the clergy from the funeral of the previous bishop to the Lateran church, he remained there for two days with a very great crowd and with many priests, to await the customary day on which he could be solemnly ordained.

While matters stood thus, a number of presbyters suddenly hurried with Boniface, a man of the same order, to the church of Theodora, having gathered the people, and there, after deliberation, set about wishing to ordain him bishop.

When I learned of this, I demanded that all the presbyters who were gathered there come to me, and sitting with the most distinguished tribune Serenianus I warned them not to allow anything to be done rashly, nor to act against the order of the sacred law or against the principle of custom. But they resisted with such obstinacy that they did not hesitate in the least to do what they had threatened. For they even decided that the presbyter Boniface should be ordained in the church of Marcellus, and with him they proceeded to the basilica of the holy apostle Peter.

And since it belongs to Your Piety to pass judgment on this matter, I at once, with fitting concern, thought it right to consult Your Majesty, so that I might be clearly informed, by command of Your Divinity, what Your Piety decrees on this matter. For what has been done through the rashness of a few against reverence for the venerable law ought not to be long deferred, lest things be strengthened by delay which ought to be cut off at their beginning.

I have appended to my report the records of the acclamations of the people which were made on each day; whatever is done hereafter I shall not pass over in silence. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of January.
(15.) Copy of the imperial letter.

Once all the records had been reviewed, the commendable report of Your Sublimity made it plain that the insolence of a few had sought to assail the long-standing peace in the ordination to the venerable priesthood. For after the departure of the venerable man Zosimus the multitude had loudly agreed by common judgment on the merit of Eulalius to succeed him in due order, and the confirmation of the successor had fully preserved everything that the rule of catholic discipline required for it; so we are greatly astonished that some have appeared who, scorning the solemn procedure, hurried to ordain another.

Our clemency ought rightly to rise up to punish their deed, were it not that we nevertheless judge them deserving of pardon on this account: that, quickly recognizing their own lapse, they have fallen back on the resort of entreaty, asking to be forgiven for what they complained they had done under compulsion.

Let Your Sublimity therefore learn, by the authority of our clemency in this present letter, that our wish and our favor are agreed upon Eulalius as prelate of the sacred law, on whom the proper number of ordaining bishops, the solemnity of the lawful time and the fitness of the place have rightly conferred the summit of that venerable title. But since it is clear that Boniface lacked all of these, we consider that our verdict was awaited needlessly, since those who had presumed to make him bishop appear, by the petitions they have submitted, to have condemned their own act.

We therefore decree by an absolute command that, this extraordinary presumption being set aside, Boniface be at once barred from the city, which is forbidden to him. It will befit his modesty to comply with the heavenly decrees and depart of his own accord; if he resists too obstinately, we order him to be expelled against his will.

Your Sublimity, Symmachus, dearest and most beloved father, will of course see to it that the instigators of the popular sedition, together with their associates, are detained and fittingly punished, so that a rashly presumptuous deed may not pass unpunished. For this purpose our Clemency has seen fit to send Aphrodisius, a man of clarissimus rank, tribune and notary, so that in his presence our decrees may be carried out more speedily, in order that the peace of the people may not be troubled by any disturbance, and that the whole community, at peace, may revere the man whom the mysteries of the sacred law, observed according to ancient custom, have received. Given on the third day before the Nones of January, at Ravenna.
(16.) Copy of the report of Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to the emperor.

As soon as the sacred word of Your Piety outran the expectation of the people by its speed, it removed everything that conflicting wills had usurped for themselves in the election of bishops, and by divine foresight cut off at the outset what, had there been delay, would have been harder to remove as the partisan zeal of the ignorant multitude grew, my lords Emperors.

For this reason, with due service, I at once hastened to carry out what had been commanded; and—something to be ascribed to the good fortune of Your Clemency—an affair without precedent, of the greatest contention and great conflict, which had begun (not) without commotion among the people, has ended, with Your Clemency's authority unimpaired, in the quiet of the whole multitude.

For since the sacred authority had been delivered to me at the very time when the solemnity of the holy day was to be celebrated, I at once, as was proper, sent the chief of the record office and summoned Boniface to come to me, to learn what had been commanded and to refrain from the procession, which he had learned was forbidden to him. He, scorning the summons, went in procession and handed over the man I had sent to the people to be beaten.

When this was reported, after consulting with the clarissimus tribune Serenianus, I sent copies of the sacred letter, as a precaution, to the church of the holy apostle Paul, where he had gathered, so that the multitude, being incited, might not attempt anything against the commands to the public injury; and at the same time I dispatched part of my staff.

But he allowed neither to take effect, and when he wished to return to the city with the people, both the guards and the attendants at once met him at the gates to prevent him, as had been decreed, from entering your city. But he thought that they too could be disregarded, and having forced his way in, he was driven back from a certain part of the city by many who confronted him there, and was not allowed to carry out what he intended. When the crowd accompanying him saw this, it dispersed without any tumult.

He himself, having been led outside the wall, is staying not far from the city. Lest he should secretly enter the city by night, rush to the church and once again stir up the partisanship of the people, I have, by common deliberation and with fitting care, arranged for four guards and attendants to keep watch over him there without harming him, while I await what Your Piety decrees, so that the peace which has been kept so far may endure.

As for the party of the bishop Eulalius, a venerable man, who on that day was celebrating the solemnities at the basilica of the holy apostle Peter with almost the entire multitude, as soon as Your Piety's commands were published, the whole city rejoiced.

I have therefore appended to my report everything that the Roman people, giving thanks to Your Majesty in public joy with various acclamations, thought should be made public, so that Your Piety may know both with how great a calm, by your favor, those things have been set right which had been wrongly committed through the rashness of a few, and with how great gratitude those things have been received which Your Clemency thought should be decreed by divine judgment and out of reverence for venerable religion, and established for the perpetual preservation of the peace of the Roman people. Given on the sixth day before the Ides of January.
(17.) Copy of the petition of the presbyters on behalf of Boniface.
We petition your clemency, most pious and most clement emperors Honorius and Theodosius, ever Augusti.

After the departure of the holy Zosimus, pope of the catholic church of the city of Rome, many of us priests gathered together, as custom required and the very discipline of religion dictated, to deliberate by common judgment about appointing a successor. But the archdeacon Eulalius, impiously disregarding the funeral of the supreme priest, had occupied the Lateran church with the deacons, a very few presbyters and a crowd of disorderly common people, and had blocked nearly all its entrances. So on the next day, after conferring together, we hastened to the church where it had earlier been agreed by all that we should meet, and there, having taken counsel with the Christian people, we elected the man whom God commanded.

For we chose the venerable man Boniface, a presbyter of long standing, most learned in the law and proven by his good character, and—what adorned him still more—unwilling, by the acclamation of the whole people and the consent of the better citizens; and he was consecrated according to the order of divine institution. For it is established that, with some seventy presbyters subscribing and nine bishops from various provinces standing by, the blessing was celebrated at the proper time, and afterwards everything that the solemnity required was fulfilled.

But the aforesaid Eulalius had earlier been approached by three of our fellow priests, on the authority of many, and warned not to take anything rashly upon himself without the knowledge of the greater part of the clergy. Yet he got round a very few presbyters, mistreated those who had come with letters to forbid him and had them consigned to various places of custody, and also produced, along with others, the bishop of Ostia, who, it is clear, was summoned when he was nearly dead (for the old man's sickness testifies that he was dragged there against his will). And when he had thus rushed by intrigue into a place not owed to him, with no regard for the order of religion, he began to defend his act in an unseemly manner through men ignorant of discipline and unacquainted with religion, thinking that he could confound the unanimous judgment by human disturbances.

And since it is clear that your clemency was deceived by a false report into sanctioning something to the injury of divine judgment (for whatever the choice of so many confirms is divine), we petition your piety to order the earlier decrees to be revoked, and Eulalius, who has crept into another's place, to be brought with his supporters to the court of your Perpetuity. For we declare that the holy pope Boniface will be present together with our fellow priests. Leaving one presbyter in each titular church, all will attend to declare their will, that is, the judgment of God.

Let your clemency also order all whom the case concerns to be present, and those who are unwilling and will not allow themselves to be brought to be expelled even from the city. Once an inner inquiry begins to be conducted, you will find something that is not only abhorrent to divine laws but may also be displeasing to human ones; and when we have obtained this, we shall render the greatest and most abundant thanks to your eternal empire.
In response to the petition of the presbyters, the emperor sent the following sacred rescript to Symmachus, Prefect of the City:

After the report of Your Sublimity had been brought to the ears of our clemency, the submission of the presbyters has given us cause for deliberation that is not superfluous. Therefore, setting ambiguity aside, it is fitting to test the truth of the matter at first hand, and to establish, with many judging in person, which party is convicted by the neglect of proper procedure and which is supported by its observance, so that, the character of both acts being weighed together, an ordination properly determined may stand and one rashly assumed may not remain. Symmachus, dearest and most beloved father.

For this reason Your Illustrious and Exalted Magnitude, suspending everything decreed above, and with no prejudice established in the meantime, will by the authority of this present oracle summon with fitting urgency both men, that is, the most religious Boniface and Eulalius, so that they do not delay to hasten to the city of Ravenna in person before the sixth day before the Ides of February,

all those who are the authors of either ordination being likewise warned not to be absent, every excuse set aside, so that each may stand forth as defender of his own act against the other, citing precedents of ecclesiastical institution, and, having cleared himself, may prove that the other has offended more against catholic law by presumptuously electing an unworthy man. Anyone who neglects to attend will receive judgment on his standing, plainly giving it to be understood that he acted improvidently, indeed unlawfully, in a matter he dares not defend in person.

We too are summoning, by letters of our serenity, a fitting number of bishops from various provinces, so that the discussion of many in our presence may resolve for us the matter that has been brought into doubt.

Since, however, everything is reserved intact for the coming judgment, no one should flatter himself about what has already been done: the example of the present judgment will teach what ought to be observed in such affairs in future. Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, through Aphthonius.
(19.) Likewise a report of Symmachus, Prefect of the City.
When the clarissimus Aphthonius, decurion of your sacred palace, had arrived at the venerable city with the heavenly command, I made every haste to render obedience to the commands of Your Divinity.

For at once the leading men were assembled, the sacred order was published, and a summons was sent to the religious men Boniface and Eulalius, my lords Emperors. I also ordered their clergy to be notified likewise, so that nothing would be lacking for the coming examination before Your Piety. I have therefore appended all this below, set down in a series of records, for your full information.

But after both parties began stirring up the people with various seditions, I sent a warning to each of them not to assemble at the same church, lest the multitudes clash with one another, which was not permitted. But this, I believe, seemed suspicious to them, because I thought peace should be urged upon men who wished to disturb the city. For this reason both parties thought I should be attacked with slanderous protests, so as to excuse their own error with fabricated lies. Lest this should be in any way hidden from Your Clemency, I have sent the very documents they submitted, entered in the records, so that they cannot complain that anything has been suppressed.

It remains only that, before Your Clemency, your servant should not be assailed in his absence by the partisanship of either party—I who, having always been approved by Your Majesty for faithful service, believed, as was fitting, that I must keep myself apart from either attacking or favoring either party. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February.
(20.) Copy of the imperial letter to the synod.

Our clemency has indeed already given Your Beatitude every instruction in fitting order, that, with all else set aside, you should determine by your judgment what ought to be observed for the peace of the people.

We recall also that we commanded this above all, as equity required: that those bishops who are known to have taken part in their ordinations or to have subscribed afterwards should not sit as judges—without injury to themselves and with due respect preserved—nor be able to give any testimony, lest they should appear not so much to pronounce a fresh verdict as to uphold a past act. These, therefore, as we said above, must abstain from that hearing.

Let Your Beatitude know that this too is likewise to be upheld: that no prejudice has been created for either party by what we had earlier plainly decreed. For since the commands sent in haste for the peace of the people have been withdrawn by a subsequent authority of our piety, neither party can claim anything from them, nor the other fear anything.

Attending therefore to the judgment of God, which clearly sits together with you in such a case, you ought, after examining everything, to uphold that which, by the inspiration of the heavenly Spirit, may keep reverence for the Christian law intact.

This synod, divided among itself, could not bring the present case to a conclusion. The venerable emperor Honorius therefore judged that this matter should be deferred to a larger council, and meanwhile, because the days of holy Easter were approaching, he ordered both men, namely Boniface and Eulalius, to leave the city, and ordered the bishop of Spoleto, Achilleus by name, to celebrate the sacred mysteries, informing Symmachus, Prefect of the City, of this by his letter:
Judgment in great deliberations ought not to be hasty, nor should things be rashly pronounced which are decreed to be kept forever.

The inquiry concerning the bishops of the eternal city has often been shaken by the wrangling of the parties during the examination before the bishops. But so that nothing hasty may be pronounced through a speedy judgment, our clemency has decided as follows. Since the nearness of the holy days demanded the presence of a bishop, and it would not be right in the most sacred city to celebrate the days of Easter in particular without a bishop, let Your Illustrious Magnificence know, Symmachus, dearest and most beloved father, that we have chosen Achilleus, who is clearly a stranger to the partisanship of the parties, to perform the mysteries of the sacred observance. Once the feast days are over, we shall consider with more mature counsel, on the basis of the bishops' judgment, what ought to be upheld.

We certainly admonish you to summon the leading men of the districts and to provide for public order and peace; have the instructions of our decrees made known to them, namely that no one should dare to stir up any tumult or sedition. If anyone, through insane persuasion, provokes one, let them understand that punishment will fall not only on those caught in the disturbance but also on the heads of the districts. For we know that public peace is easily kept if the ambitions and incitements of instigators cease.
(22.) Copy of the imperial letter to Achilleus, bishop of Spoleto.

Since it is clear that judgment on the Roman episcopate has been deferred because of the shortness of time caused by the solemn days, which did not allow bishops to be absent from their churches, our serenity has rightly thought it should be arranged that Your Beatitude hasten with fitting reverence to the venerable City, so that you may present the days of holy Easter to the people with due peace and the customary solemnity, and so that custom may not be harmed by the fact that manifold necessity has caused the synod to be postponed.
Above all and especially we admonish you that no mention ever be made of those who are known to be suspended pending judgment.
(23.) The emperor's address to the Senate.

We know, Conscript Fathers, that our hesitation cannot be blamed by you, whose maturity of counsel and judgment is proven in every matter. Nor indeed should or could a verdict on matters of the highest importance be hasty, since it ought to be as credible and perfect in every respect as it is to be lasting.

We had ordered that the bishops whom the zeal of supporters or the will of factions had elected in the most sacred city be heard by all the bishops who were present, and the inquiry was repeated several times. But since the examination required for a just inquiry was causing longer delays, and the diligent investigation of the judges was uncovering more matters to which a quick end could not be put, and the celebration of the feast days demanded a speedy decision, we thought the whole matter should be deferred, lest we pronounce anything rash.

Accordingly Achilleus, a religious man, bishop of the city of Spoleto, has been sent to carry out the celebration of the holy days. It is the task of Your Amplitude to keep the minds of the populace calm by wholesome counsel, since you cannot doubt that our delay is reasonable and necessary. Given on the Ides of March.
(24.) Edict of the same emperor to the people.

Judging the care of the faith to be of the greatest importance, excellent citizens of Rome, we have thought that nothing hasty or premature should be pronounced. For we hold that in a matter of religion only such things should be decreed as all can approve without error and without reproach to the verdict.

Therefore, since in the inquiry into the bishops who had been appointed in the city the dispute remained undecided under the judgment of the bishops, and no end could be put to the issues that kept arising one after another while partisan passions contended, and our deliberation hung long upon various matters, we have decided that the whole business be deferred for a future hearing before a complete council with a fuller number of bishops, so that the case, weighed from every side, may receive after the days of Easter the conclusion that equity and religion demand. At the same time, since nothing could be determined about the bishop, we have temporarily chosen someone to celebrate the reverend mysteries on the holy days, so that you, citizens, for the honor of the sacred city, may have the solemn ministry of a bishop.

Therefore, following the example of our patience, accept with calm minds what we urge for the sake of public peace: let the worship of the holy days pass with due tranquility; let no sedition disturb the public peace. Let no personal favor toward anyone be displayed such as to attract notice. For it befits you to hold your feelings in suspense and reserve everything intact for our judgment, and, not in a kind of frenzy but with due uprightness, to wait for a bishop rather than demand one.

But if you follow wicked instigators and choose disorder and tumult rather than quiet and moderation, you will expose those whom you favor, and a danger to life, to which you are driving us, will hang over not only you but also your leaders, to whose counsels you cling. For he is not worthy of pardon who cannot be held back from wickedness by the warnings of our kindness. Given on the Ides of March.
(25.) Letter of the same emperor to Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola.

To the holy and venerable father, Bishop Paulinus. Even at that time we were firmly convinced that the bishops who had gathered for the synod could settle nothing, since your Blessedness, pleading bodily infirmity, was unable to endure the hardship of the journey. In the absence of a holy man, vices rejoice for the moment, though they will not in fact prevail; for a perverse and long-standing ambition wishes to keep up its contest with a blessed man of holy life, and believes that against these good things of apostolic institution it can rely on walls seized by force.

O cause truly worthy, which nothing but the blessed life of your Crown can resolve! We therefore announce that the judgment has been postponed, so that the divine precepts may be set forth by the mouth of your Reverence, who have followed and fulfilled them. Nor can anyone else be the bearer of those precepts than you, who are proven to be, in a special way, a worthy disciple of the Apostle.

Therefore, holy lord, deservedly venerable father, righteous servant of God, as you are about to render a divine service in disregard of toil, grant us this gift of your visitation, if it may be so called: set everything else aside, since the calm of temperate weather favours it, and deign to come to preside over the synod and, without delay, to present yourself also to our longings and to the blessing we desire.
(26.) Likewise from the same sovereign to the African bishops.
Our Serenity wishes to have a carefully weighed judgment in all matters, but above all in those that pertain to our venerable religion.

We believe that news of the dispute which has arisen over the episcopate of the eternal City has already reached you even across the seas. It could not be settled by a few, and therefore the judgment of many is clearly necessary.

Wherefore let your Holiness, whom goodness of life and learning in the law commend, deign to cut short all excuses and hasten to the city of Spoleto by the Ides of June, so that whatever truth or the rule of religion dictates may be decided by a common judgment, God likewise inspiring the minds of all, and the episcopate of the apostolic see may not be delayed any longer.
(27.) Letter of the same sovereign to Saint Aurelius, bishop of Carthage.

We would indeed have wished that some other occasion had arisen for seeing your Reverence, so that we might enjoy the longed-for sight of your Blessedness. But since a reprehensible ambition has declared war on the pope of the city of Rome and thinks that a holy life need not be looked for in a bishop, the judgment begun in this inquiry has been deferred by a smaller number of bishops than synodal custom requires to more numerous and very learned men, of whom your Holiness is the foremost. For it was not fitting that the rewards of chastity and merit, once the vices rejected by the sacrosanct precept of divine religion had been removed, should be made known by any but such men.

And although the letters of my lord brother, the Augustus and emperor, could have sufficed, I have nevertheless added my own as well, in which to entreat the coming of your Holiness. I beg you, therefore, holy lord, deservedly venerable father, that, to confer a twofold benefit—both your blessing, which we long for, and the judgment which must necessarily be pronounced on behalf of his Blessedness—you would set everything aside and, looking to God, for the confirming of whose bishop the labor of the journey ought not to be refused, deign to present yourself.
(28.) Letter of the same to the bishops Augustine, Alypius, Evodius, Donatian, Silvanus, Novatus and Deuterius, in identical terms.

Our Piety is certain that it has come to the attention of your Reverence that vices are fighting against chastity in opposition to the pope of the city of Rome, and that the conflict over this matter has lasted so long that, among the many bishops who had gathered for the synod, because some dissented, the life confirmed by apostolic precept has not yet been able to prevail.

Yet they confessed without hesitation—even the dissenting party agreeing—that they knew your [?] well, so that it was plainly evident that the judgment of your Holiness was being awaited, and that the sentence was being deferred to be pronounced in your presence; for you, preeminent by the merit of your life, are rightly summoned even from regions overseas so that you may judge.

But although the sacred authority of my lord brother, the Augustus and emperor, summoning you to the synod of Italy—an authority not to be neglected—has reached you, we judge that letters from our Serenity should also be specially added, in which I beg that you grant us without excuse the desirable sight of your blessing and judge this labor pleasing to almighty God; for, as you are to pronounce sentence both on behalf of an excellent bishop and for the merits of a holy life, you understand that the recompense for this trouble is laid up as a divine reward. Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, at Ravenna.
(29.) Report of Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to Constantius. To my lord, ever illustrious, in all things magnificent, deservedly

exalted and most eminent patron Constantius, Symmachus. Whatever happens suddenly and unexpectedly cannot be laid to the fault of the magistrate, and it throws a populace that does not reason into confusion by its unlooked-for novelty.

For the religious man Eulalius entered the city at midday on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April without my knowledge. I believed he had brought some order with him; but toward evening of the same day the bishop of Spoleto sent me a letter, thinking I should be informed that by a sacred rescript issued to him he had been commanded to celebrate the holy day of Easter in the city. Of this order I had previously been completely unaware, my lord ever illustrious, in all things magnificent, deservedly exalted and most eminent patron. When it became known to me after the arrival of the holy Eulalius, I at once thought that the commands of the most invincible emperor must be obeyed.

But when, a day later, the holy bishop Achilleus had entered the city, there arose such a commotion among the people that on one side an armed crowd, with swords and missiles and in military dress, assembled at the forum. When I had summoned the leading men and gone out to hold a discussion and calm the people by addressing them for the peace of the city, at first only a few came to the meeting; then, when the holy bishop Achilleus was expected to appear and publish what had been commanded, he could not come because the crowd resisted.

And when both I and the respectable vicar, under pressure from the people, had gone out to the Forum of Vespasian to urge peace upon the crowd of both parties, suddenly armed slaves with missiles and stones, some even with swords, attacked the people of Eulalius's party, who had gathered unarmed to learn what order had been given concerning the bishop of Spoleto. Those who had come prepared against the unprepared wounded them, and went so far as to think that I too and the respectable vicar should be attacked, since in their seditious fury they would listen to no reason at all.

Had divine power not been present to rescue us, and had we not escaped by a more secluded way, avoiding the hail of stones and the onslaught of the conspiring crowd, we could scarcely have got away. It is clear that most of them were slaves, some of whom have been recognized and are being held for a hearing.

Accordingly, as was my duty, I have hastened to report to your Excellency, so that, once you know what has taken place, your Magnitude may decide on a definite end to these affairs. For since the holy Eulalius had entered, and the bishop of Spoleto had followed two days later, and no orders from your Virtues had reached me for me to follow, a disturbance of the whole populace has arisen, raging both against itself and to the peril of the magistrates. Unless you command by a swift reply what is to be done before the venerable day of Easter, the people threaten to fight one another, each side supposing that it will be shut out of the Lateran basilica. Therefore, lest any misfortune occur (which may the good fortune of your Sublimity avert), I ask that by a clear order you decree that the dangerous stubbornness of this furious contention be excluded. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of April.
(30.) Letter of the illustrious Count Constantius to Symmachus, Prefect of the City.

So that we may learn everything with certainty, and the instigators of the factions may not escape a faithful messenger and inspector, we have dispatched our chancellor Vitulus to convey with all speed the address and judgment of our lord the most invincible emperor to your Excellency and to the people; and we give this warning:

that whatever is contained in the sacred enactments be violated by no rashness, and that what has been commanded be carried out with swift diligence, lest the August clemency, which, as is now recognized, has held back, be provoked to correct the matter without delay by the full vigor of his majesty.
(31.) Copy of the sacred letter [?] to Symmachus, Prefect of the City.

When our Clemency, desiring to restore peace, had devised this kind of plan to remedy the error of the first disturbance—namely, that until a definitive sentence should be issued on the confirmation of the bishop of the City, both of those on whose account the tumult had earlier grown up should be kept away from residence in the most sacred City and should await the coming judgment, the place in which each was to stay being clearly specified—

we cannot calmly overlook that something close to open war has been declared, by which the commands of our Clemency would be trampled underfoot, and that its ringleader has been Eulalius, who has overstepped our orders and has not been willing to stay away for a short while as the commands required, Symmachus, dearest kinsman.

Let your Sublimity therefore know that we have decided that both the salutary earlier order and the moderate arrangement of the synod must be upheld, which we judge cannot be done unless Eulalius is pressed in every way to leave the city with all speed, so that his presence may not provoke the insolent populace nor become a cause of death for the innocent.

He should be in no doubt that, if he persists in this obstinate presumption, not only has judgment already been passed on his status, but judgment will also be passed affecting his very life (for a fault that is not avoided when it has been forewarned deserves no pardon); nor will he have any excuse in claiming that he is being held back by the people against his will.

If any of the clergy decides to hold communion with Eulalius while judgment is pending, let him know that he is to be condemned by the same sentence. As for laymen who, after the prohibition of our Gentleness, think they should seek communion with Eulalius, those of more honorable rank will suffer the penalty of proscription, while slaves will undergo capital punishment, and their masters will not be exempt from this danger.

Let the chief men of the regions know that, unless they tame and curb the spirit of the unruly populace, they will be seized and subjected to the ultimate penalty. The bishop of Spoleto, as was determined earlier, will carry out the rite of the festal solemnity during the holy days of Easter. We decree that the Lateran church shall be open to him alone for celebrating the mysteries, and that all others who presume to do so shall be driven off. Indeed, if the aforesaid bishop of the city of Spoleto [?], we direct that someone should be received in his place to carry out the rite of the holy mysteries.

These our decrees shall be posted in all the titular churches and in the places frequented by large gatherings, so that it may be clear to everyone both that we did not wish anything turbulent to be done and that we are still waiting for the disturbances to be settled. Let your Sublimity know, moreover, that the chief of the bureau and the rest of the staff who assist you in your administration will not only be struck with the loss of a very heavy fine but will also incur capital punishment, unless they apply their utmost effort and hasten to give effect to the decrees of our Clemency. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, at Ravenna.
(32.) Copy of the report of Symmachus, Prefect of the City, to the illustrious Count Constantius, patrician.

To my lord, ever illustrious, in all things magnificent, deservedly exalted and most eminent patron Constantius, Symmachus. As soon as the sacred commands of our lord the most invincible emperor were delivered, I immediately rendered due obedience, as was fitting.

But Eulalius, with the same obstinacy with which he entered the city without a sacred order, refused with equal stubbornness to leave it, though compelled by all the authorities. For it is known that the command of the most invincible emperor was made known to him through the staff of the city prefecture in the evening hours of the very day on which it was delivered, my lord ever most illustrious and most sacred, magnificent, deservedly exalted and most eminent patron. When it had been read, he sent word that he would consider it more carefully; yet, though urgently admonished, he made no effort to leave.

The next day, having again been admonished by the whole body of attendants, even during the night, he gathered a crowd and with reckless daring decided to seize the Lateran basilica. But after a consultation with the leading men, all the official staffs were dispatched with orders that he be driven out. The respectable vicar too had resolved to go to that basilica, but at first could not approach it for sheer terror. I myself, having sent both the guildsmen and my entire staff, did not go there in person, lest some rival should stir up religious resentment against me.

Nevertheless, with all deference to your Excellency, when many guildsmen and the heads of the regions, who serve the imperial commands, had burst in, Eulalius was driven from that church and expelled from the city, and, with attendants assigned to him, was sent to the place where he had been ordered to reside.

Instructions were also given that the religious man, the holy bishop Achilleus, now that Eulalius had been ejected, should quietly celebrate what had been commanded, without any uproar from the people, out of reverence for the holy days. For I have stationed attendants to guard the Lateran basilica, so that it may not be handed over to anyone else. Some clergy of Eulalius's party, instigators of the sedition, have also been arrested; concerning them I await your orders.

And since I thought I should meanwhile report to your Virtues in general on what has been done, whatever is done in the following [?] days for the peace of the City, which your felicity governs, I shall report item by item, with fuller evidence, in keeping with the truth and order of events.
(33.) Copy of the sacred letter to Symmachus, Prefect of the City.

Our Serenity acted with particular moderation, so that presumption might find no opening. For the inquiry was deferred to the judgment of the venerable bishops precisely so that a calm discussion might decide, without any disturbance, whatever religion and truth required.

But the text of your report has informed us that, through Eulalius's usurpation, many unlawful acts were committed in defiance of the sentence of the venerable synod; by his presence he supplied the people with cause for fury and wished to destroy everything that our moderation preserves. For it had been determined by our arrangement and by the sentence of the bishops, the greater number of whom had assembled in the synod, and also with the consent and declaration of the parties, that whoever entered the city to incite the people should know that he would be specifically condemned. Yet he, forgetting himself, has shown by his present conduct what sort of beginning he appears to have had.

Since, then, after so many offenses he has rightly been driven from the City, which, as both our Clemency and the bishops evidently decided, he ought not to approach, let your Sublimity know, Symmachus, dearest and most beloved kinsman, that we have decreed that the venerable man Bishop Boniface, to whose moderation we have rightly judged our authority should be joined, is to enter the City, so that under his guidance reverence for the law of religion may be fulfilled with the customary moderation. Given on the third day before the Nones of April; received on the sixth day before the Ides of April.
(34.) Copy of the report of Symmachus, Prefect of the City, on the entry of Pope Boniface, to the emperor named above.

Whatever is established by God's authority is rightly brought forth by the divine judgment of your Piety. For recently, when the sacred authority of your Clemency had been sent to me, your servant, by which your Majesty, removing all doubt, confirmed the episcopate of the venerable man Bishop Boniface, what was commanded proved so welcome to everyone that both the most distinguished order and the Roman people approved it, my lords emperors Honorius and Theodosius, pious, fortunate, renowned, triumphant, ever Augusti.

For when I had read the heavenly decrees to the people and they had been published by edicts posted everywhere, as is customary, there was such approval and joy throughout the whole city that all bore witness with fitting rejoicing that religion had been restored to them and the security of peace granted.

Accordingly, two days later, the venerable bishop mentioned above entered the City, with all the people coming out to meet him, as your Serenity had ordained; nor was the attendance of my staff lacking. No dissension remains among the people any longer, since all have acquiesced in the divine judgment and in the will of your Majesty.

So, with partisanship at an end, all have begun to be of one mind on what you, admonished by God's command, have decreed. The Roman people has testified to the reasons for its joy by the acclamations appended below, and does not cease to give thanks day by day to your Serenities, whose foresight, as it protects the peace of the world, has likewise restored quiet to the City and concord to the people.
(35.) Copy of the sacred letter to the Proconsul of Africa.

The victorious Honorius, renowned triumphant ever Augustus, to Largus, Proconsul. Among all our concerns, those that we judge to pertain to the episcopate trouble us no less. For when the dispute over confirming the bishop of the eternal City was being considered, and the bishops who had been gathered together judged themselves too few to pronounce sentence on so great a matter, it had been decided, as the sacred letters circulated, that a larger number of bishops should come from the African and Gallic provinces, on the understanding, namely, that in the meantime nothing should be presumed against what our sentence had ordained or what the sentence of the synod appeared to have decided.

But, disregarding all this, Eulalius thought he could seize the interval by sheer usurpation. It is established that, as was fitting, he has been expelled by our authority and the holy bishop Boniface confirmed.

And since the matter has been concluded, our Clemency has judged it unfitting that the bishops should suffer the hardships of a voyage or journey. Let your Respectability therefore know that the synod has been dissolved. Accordingly, after first publishing our sacred words, admonish each of the bishops by your authority, so that they may know that this ordinance must be observed, which provides that each should devote himself, as is fitting, to prayer in his own church, since the case is seen to have been already settled by the best of judgments. Given on the seventh day before the Ides of April.
(36.) Letter of Largus, Proconsul, to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage.

To my lord and honorable father Aurelius, bishop, Largus. The contest over the merit of the bishop whom God has proven fit for his people has ceased. The imperial clemency has confirmed the holy and venerable man Boniface as bishop of the city of Rome, for whose election it had some time ago ordered your Holiness to be summoned, as its sacred words, delivered with reverence, testify.

You should therefore make haste to visit your people and churches, since you have been relieved of the necessity of a voyage. AND IN ANOTHER HAND: May divine favor keep you safe for many years, my lord and deservedly honorable father.
(37.) Letter of the Emperor Honorius to Boniface, bishop of Rome, in which he decreed that if two bishops should again be ordained, both should be driven out of the city.

The victorious Honorius, renowned triumphant ever Augustus, to the holy and venerable Boniface, pope of the eternal City. We have received the letter of your Blessedness with the rejoicing due to reverence, giving the greatest thanks to almighty God that we have learned that your Holiness, after a long illness, has been restored to the health we prayed for; and therefore, as the venerable men return, we set our seal on our joy by the testimony of our sacred letter,

and we ask that your Apostleship deign to devote its zeal and prayers, in daily supplication, to our welfare and our empire. Know, moreover, that our Piety was well pleased that your Holiness is concerned about disturbance in the churches or among the people; our Clemency believes it has made sufficient provision that this cannot happen in any way.

Accordingly, we wish it to come to the notice of all the clergy, through the proclamation of your Blessedness, that if anything should happen to your Holiness by human lot—which we do not desire—all should know that they must refrain from ambitious intrigues; and if by chance two should be ordained, unlawfully and through the recklessness of rival parties, neither of them shall be bishop at all, but he alone shall remain in the apostolic see whom divine judgment and the consent of all shall choose from among the clergy by a new ordination.

This must therefore be observed: that all, in accordance with the admonition of our Serenity, keep a tranquil mind and peaceable spirits, and not attempt anything by seditious conspiracies, since it is certain that partisanship will benefit no one.
(38.) Copy of the sacred letter of Honorius Augustus sent to Arcadius, emperor of the East, concerning the person of Saint John, bishop of Constantinople.

In another letter I have already warned you about the image of a woman that has been carried around the provinces in an unprecedented way, and about the talk of detractors that has spread through the whole world. I hoped that by repenting of such a deed and abandoning the plan you would let the hostile rumour die of old age, so that public gossip would have nothing in the morals of the age to carp at. I have also told you, out of dutiful affection, that we grieve over the ruin of perishing Illyricum, and grieve that you were unwilling to acknowledge these losses to the state, so that they were reported to us by other informants rather than by letters from your Piety.

Nevertheless, it is not right for us to hide from your Serenity this further matter either. Something has very recently happened in divine affairs that raises fear of public danger, and rumour, always the swift herald of evils, has not kept silent about it. Human nature, as it always does, is stirred by new events to find fault, and now that it has been given an occasion for carping, it exercises its malice against the times with a zeal for perverse chatter.

For it has recently been reported that at Constantinople, on the venerable and most holy day of Easter, when religion had gathered almost all the peoples of the neighbouring cities into one place to celebrate the feast with a more solemn rite in the presence of the emperors, the catholic churches were suddenly closed and the priests thrust into custody. So at the very season when the emperor's indulgence unbars the grim prisons of the guilty, a cruel jail shut up the ministers of the holy law and of peace. All the mysteries were thrown into confusion as if in war; some people were killed in the very sanctuaries of the church; and such violence raged around the altars that venerable bishops were driven into exile and human blood (dreadful to say) was spilled over the heavenly sacraments.

I confess that we were shaken when we suddenly learned of this. For who would not fear the displeasure of almighty God at so bloody a crime? Or how could anyone think the Roman world and all mankind were out of the gravest danger, when almighty God himself, the author of our empire and the governor of the state he has entrusted to us, was believed to be angry at such deadly and abominable deeds, my holy lords, brother and nephew, venerable Augusti? If some question of religion was being disputed among the bishops, the judgment ought to have been an episcopal one. For the interpretation of divine things belongs to them; to us belongs obedience in religion.

But suppose that imperial concern did presume to take somewhat more upon itself in mystical and catholic questions. Did the indignation it stirred up have to go as far as the exile of priests and the slaughter of men, so that where pure prayers, sincere vows and unblemished sacrifices are offered, the sword should be drawn there, a sword not lightly to be bared even against the throats of the guilty?

Finally, events themselves teach us what the divine majesty thought of these things. This was the first sign of the present upheaval, and would that it were the only one! For human anxiety, conscious of so great a crime, makes us fear something worse after experiencing so terrible a vengeance (may almighty God avert it). I hear that the most holy church, adorned by the wealth of so many emperors, renowned for its precious furnishings, made splendid by the [?] of so many emperors in prayer, has burned, and that this unique light of the city of Constantinople has collapsed into ashes and smoked, with God not preventing it. For he seems to have cursed the defiled mysteries and turned his eyes away from the place that blood had already stained, so that no one could beseech the heavenly mercy beneath bloodstained altars. I hear too that sacred buildings no less splendid were consumed as the flames of the raging fire spread more widely, and that the ornaments our ancestors had worked so hard on to grace the public face of the city were burned up, as though at a kind of funeral of the city.

Provoked as I have been by repeated injuries, I ought perhaps to have kept silent about these things and not warned my dearest brother and partners in rule so faithfully. Yet putting the bond of blood ahead of the sting of my silent grief, I urge and advise that, if it can be done, these things be corrected by amending conduct in the future, and that the divine anger, which events show has been aroused, be appeased by earnest prayers. Accept from me the clearest proof of my sincerity: I thought this should be brought to your Clemency's attention so that my silence itself would not make anyone suspect me of secret rejoicing, and so that no one would believe I consent to such deeds or that, having often warned against them beforehand, I did not grieve once they were committed. For who that remembers he is a Christian could be free of grief that so great a disturbance of religion has suddenly been brought about that the whole state of the catholic faith must waver?

There was a case among bishops that ought to have been settled by holding a council and deliberating. Envoys from both sides were sent to the priests of the eternal city and of Italy. A verdict, backed by the authority of all, was awaited to set the rule of discipline. Until that considered decision came, of course, everything should have been left untouched and nothing changed. Meanwhile, however, a strange and headlong haste flared up.
