Without waiting for the letters of the priests whom both parties had consulted by their embassies, and without examining the matter, bishops were thrust into exile, handed over to punishment before they had been tried by an episcopal court. Events have shown how premature that condemnation was. For those whose authority was awaited allowed Bishop John peaceful communion, decreed that concord should be confirmed, and held that no one should be driven from fellowship before judgment.

What is left now but for schisms, pulling in different directions, to tear the catholic faith apart, and for heresies, always enemies of communion, to spring from so much confusion in what has been done? It can hardly be blamed on the people now if they split into discordant parties through a variety of sects, since public authority has supplied the material for discord in advance and kindled, as it were, a spark to feed sedition.

So that this does not break out again into some great destruction of the human race, prayers must be offered that God, patient with human failings, may make a badly handled affair turn out well and prosper. For as far as we are concerned, we have reason to fear what has been done. But as for the goodness of God, who can always be appeased, any exemption from punishment that is granted will be a matter of pardon, not of desert.
(39.) Letter of the usurper Maximus to Valentinian the Younger, Augustus, against the Arians and Manichaeans.

If our Clemency did not have sincere good faith toward your Serenity and the goodwill of full concord, I am sure that what is now said to be going on in the regions under your Tranquillity could even be to my advantage: the disturbance and upheaval of the catholic law. For what could anyone who was your enemy [?] desire more than that you should attempt something against the churches of God, that is, against God himself, and choose to sin where error has no excuse?

But our Serenity has too great a reverence for God to think it desirable for him to be outraged even by our worst enemy [?]. And our concern for your most serene youth is so close and so earnest that your right actions please us more than your errors would. For that reason we have thought it right to warn your Perpetuity to consider the nature of the supreme deity and to reflect on the power of his majesty, and so to weigh carefully in your mind what you ought to do.

For I hear (rumour does not allow things to stay hidden, especially what is done to whole peoples) that violence has been done to the catholic churches by new edicts of your Clemency: priests are besieged in their basilicas, a fine has been imposed, the death penalty added, and the most holy law overturned under the name of some law or other. You will be able to see how serious this is if you are willing to consider the greatness of God. I would blush if your Serenity believed that I wanted to build some argument and plead God's case. For what if this were the only point? If you were changing what has grown together and been confirmed over so many centuries, would you not seem to be stirring up no small discord? Even under human laws in this mortal life, custom has our reverence, and to introduce something new in a matter long established and familiar is open to reproach.

All Italy and Africa believe in this mystery. Gaul, Aquitaine and all Spain glory in this faith, and so does venerable Rome herself, whose primacy shows itself in this respect too, that she acknowledged God in the way she chose to follow him. I will confess (and I say it not without sorrow) that Illyricum alone dissented. Would that there were no surviving example of its error! Would that the town of Mursa, of the Arian law, had remained unharmed and had not once fallen in judgment on its wretched error, so that, because it had taught the very authors of that error, it lay prostrate under a special vengeance of the angry deity! Believe me, it is dangerous to tamper with divine things.

The divine Valentinian of venerable memory, your Clemency's father, ruled faithfully in this faith. He was unwilling to touch anything he saw had been well established. These men were certainly bishops already in his time. What great change has happened, that those who were formerly judged priests are now judged sacrilegious? They are certainly consecrated by the same precepts and the same sacraments, and they believe with the same faith they believed before.

Or does your venerable Serenity really think that a religion once implanted in human minds, a religion God himself established, can be torn up? How much discord will be stirred up by this? How much strife will arise? How frequent and how deadly the riots will be! How many prayers of the righteous, and how surely they reach God, when among Christians (dreadful to say) something like a persecution arises!

It is up to you how you interpret this zeal of ours. Certainly I could prove [?] my care for your Clemency in no better way than by urging you to stop. For I think you recognize that no enemy would give such advice. I want you to understand that we have said these things in a friendly spirit.

I hope you believe it. It is therefore entirely fair that you should not tear up what is dedicated to the holy deity, that you should give back to all Italy, to venerable Rome and to the other provinces their churches and their priests, and that you should not put yourself in the middle. For it is more just that those who have left the catholic church for the Arian interpretation should exchange their error for the true religion than that they should force their depravity on those who think rightly.
(40.) The victorious Magnus Maximus, perpetual triumpher, ever

Augustus, to Siricius, his father. We have received your Holiness's letter, which was most welcome to us and was entirely worthy both of the name of a priest and of the dignity of a most splendid city. As for the catholic faith, about which you wished to consult our Clemency, I confess that the greater the special favour of God I experience toward myself, the greater my care for it. For I came up to the empire straight from the very font of salvation, and in all my efforts and successes God has always stood by me as my helper, and today, and I hope forever, he deigns to be my protector and guardian, dearest father. As for Agroecius,

who, you report, rose to the rank of presbyter improperly: what could I do more reverent toward our catholic religion than to let catholic priests judge this very matter, whatever it turns out to be? I will convene an assembly of them, from Gaul and from the Five Provinces, at whatever time suits all of them and in whatever city they choose, so that the case may be judged with them sitting and examining what custom holds and what the law is. For these things, which must be established from books and from the most religious ordinances of our forefathers, are better set out by those who know them.

For the rest, we declare that it is our mind and will that the catholic faith, with all dissension removed far away and all the priests in agreement and serving God with one heart, should continue unharmed and inviolable. For when we arrived we found and discovered certain things so defiled and polluted by the stain of wicked men that, had our foresight and remedy, which came from the fear of the supreme God, not quickly brought help, a huge rupture and ruin would surely have arisen, and the evils would have grown so firm that they could hardly have been healed afterward.

Moreover, as to what crimes it has very recently come out that the Manichaeans commit, crimes proved not by arguments or by doubtful or uncertain suspicions but by their own confessions given in court, I would rather your Holiness learn of them from the official record than from our lips. For such things are not only shameful to do but foul to speak of, and we cannot utter them without blushing. And in the emperor's hand: May the Godhead preserve you for many years.
(41.) Third letter of St Innocent to five bishops.

Innocent to his most beloved brothers Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Evodius and Possidius. We have received with great pleasure the letter of your Fraternity, full of faith and shaped with all the vigour of the catholic religion, which was sent together with [?] both councils through our brother and fellow bishop Julius. For its whole tenor and argument rest, with sound reasoning, on the consideration of God's daily grace and on the correction of those who think otherwise, so that it can both remove all error from them and, by giving whatever suitable example from our law they ought to follow, provide them with a worthy teacher.

But I think we have already said enough about these matters above, when, in reply to your reports, we wrote back what we thought both of their faithlessness and of your judgment. Yet there is always plenty to say against them, and there can never be a lack of what will defeat them, since what is so wretched and impious is all the more thoroughly defeated by the strength of our faith and by the truth itself. For a man who has rejected and despised every hope of life, confusing his heart with a hostile and damnable argument, believes that there is nothing he receives from God and nothing left for him to ask in order to be healed. Once he has taken this away from himself, what has he left beyond it?

If, then, there are some whom such perversity has bound to its defence, who give and join themselves to this doctrine, hoping that it belongs to catholic teaching when it is shown to be far removed from it and utterly opposed to it, and who were led into falling by those men's tainted advice and words, they will hasten to return to the right path, so that error does not besiege their minds any longer and take hold of them as if it fed on their senses.

For if Pelagius, wherever he stayed, deceived by this assertion the minds of those who readily or naively believed his arguments, then whether those people are here in the city (which we can neither confirm nor deny, since we do not know; even if they exist, they keep hidden, and never dare either to defend those views when he preaches them or to air such things when any of us is present, and in so great a crowd of people no one can easily be caught or recognized anywhere) or whether they live in some other part of the world, we trust in the mercy and grace of our God that they will easily be corrected once they hear of the condemnation of the man who has been found to be the obstinate and defiant author of this doctrine. Nor does it matter where they are, so long as they are healed wherever they can be found.

Yet we cannot be persuaded that he has been cleared, even though certain laymen, I know not who, have brought us proceedings by which he would have us believe he was heard and acquitted. We doubt whether these are genuine, since they did not come with any covering letter from that council, nor have we received any letter on this matter from those before whom he answered the charges in this case. If he had been able to feel confident about his acquittal, we believe he would rather have done what would have been far more genuine: he would have urged those who had judged him to inform us by their letters.

But there are certain things set down in these very proceedings in which, of the charges brought against him, he suppressed some by evading them, and confused others in total obscurity by twisting many words back on himself. Some he cleared, as it could seem for the moment, by false arguments rather than true reasoning, denying some things and turning others by false interpretation.

But would that (and this is more to be wished) he would now turn from the error of his own path to the true way of the catholic faith, so that he might desire and be willing to be cleared, considering God's daily grace and acknowledging his help, and so be seen to be truly corrected and be approved by all on clear grounds, not on the evidence of proceedings but with his heart turned to the catholic faith! So we can neither approve nor blame their judgment, since we do not know whether the proceedings are genuine or, if they are, whether he evaded the charges rather than cleared himself in full truth.

If he is confident and knows that what he says does not deserve our condemnation, or that he has already refuted everything he once said, he ought not to be summoned by us; he ought rather to hasten here himself so that he may be acquitted. For if he still thinks as he did, when would he submit himself to our judgment, whatever letter summoned him, knowing that he must be condemned?

And if he had to be summoned, it would be better done by those who are nearer and not separated from him by a great distance. But care will not be lacking if he gives us anything to heal. For he can condemn what he believed, and by sending a letter he can ask pardon for his error, as befits one returning to us, dearest brothers.

We have indeed read through the book said to be his, which your Charity sent us. In it we found many things written against the grace of God, many blasphemous things, and nothing that pleased us, nothing that did not thoroughly displease us and that anyone ought not to condemn and trample underfoot. No one except the man who wrote such things would ever entertain or think anything like them.

For we did not think it necessary at this point to argue at greater length about the law, as though Pelagius were present and contradicting us, since we are talking with you who know the whole matter and rejoice in the same agreement with us. Such examples are better set out when we are dealing with people known to be ignorant of these things. For on the capacity of nature, on free will, and on the whole daily grace of God, who that thinks rightly does not have the most abundant matter for argument?

Let him therefore anathematize what he has believed, so that those who fell through his words and teachings may learn at last what the true faith holds. For they can be called back more easily when they see these things condemned by their own author. But if he chooses to persist stubbornly in this impiety, we must act so that help may at least be brought to those led astray not by their own error but by his, lest they too lose this remedy because he neither accepts nor asks for such a cure. And in another hand: May God keep you safe, dearest brothers. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, after the consulship of Theodosius Augustus and Junius Quartus Palladius, of clarissimus rank.

Innocent to his most beloved son Jerome, presbyter. The apostle testifies that contention has never done any good in the church, and therefore he commands that heretics be rebuked at the outset rather than drawn into long debate. When this rule is carelessly regarded, the evil that should be guarded against is not avoided but increased.

Yet since your grief and lamentation so shake our heart that there is no [?] for deliberating and taking counsel, I first address the faith of your constancy. You have often told many people that whoever is struck down by injury, or, as you say, by danger for the sake of truth, may expect blessedness, and we remind you to remember your own preaching well.

Likewise, roused by so great a spectacle of evils, we hastened to take up the authority of the apostolic see to suppress all this wickedness. But we did not read the name of anyone we might move against, nor any charge assessed against him. So we do what we can: we share your grief.

But if you lodge an open and clear accusation against particular persons, I will either assign competent judges or, if something more urgent and careful can be done by us, I will not delay it, most beloved son.

Even so, I have written to my brother Bishop John that he should act more circumspectly, so that nothing more of this kind happens in connection with the church entrusted to him; for it would later be most troublesome to him too that he had to foresee and prevent such a thing from happening.

Innocent to his most beloved brother John. The most noble holy virgins Eustochium and Paula have lamented that the devil has committed plunder, slaughter, arson and every crime of utter madness in places belonging to your church; for they kept silent about the name of any man and about the cause.

Although there is no doubt who committed it, your Brotherliness ought nevertheless to have taken more careful measures to guard that flock, so that nothing of this kind would arise that, while endangering others, calls your negligence into question.

Add to this: the Lord's flock, and such lambs, [?] to fire, arms and persecutions? We have heard that they are barely alive, stripped, weakened, after the slaughter and death of their people. Is the piety of your priesthood not moved at all by so great a power granted to the devil against you and yours? Against you, I say: for it utterly condemns a priest's dignity that so great a crime was carried out in the church. Where were your precautions? Or at least, if such things had happened, where was help or comfort, when they say they still fear more than they complain of having suffered?

I would decide more strictly if they had spoken with me more openly about this matter. See, brother, the snares of the ancient enemy, and keep watch with the spirit of a good ruler, so that these things, which have been brought to us more as rumour than as a clear accusation, may be either corrected or repressed, lest the law of the church compel the one who failed to defend to answer for the damage done.
To his most beloved brother Aurelius, Innocent. Our fellow presbyter Jerome did well to believe that your affection offered the most devoted route by which to reach us.

We share the suffering of this member of our flock, and what we judged we ought to do, or were able to do, we have quickly carried out. Let your brotherliness, dearest brother, make haste to deliver the letter to the man we have mentioned as soon as possible.
(45.) Here begins a copy of the first letter of Pope Zosimus in defense of Caelestius against the African bishops.

Zosimus to Aurelius and all the bishops established throughout Africa, his most beloved brothers in the Lord, greeting. Great matters require a great weight of examination, so that the scale of judgment may not fall short of the matters themselves that are being dealt with. To this is added the authority of the apostolic see, to which the decrees of the fathers, in honor of the most blessed Peter, have assigned a particular reverence. We must pray, therefore, and pray unceasingly, that by the continual grace and perpetual help of God peace may be sent from this fountain into the whole world of faith and catholic holiness, darkened by no clouds. For charity, which, as it is written, is God, rejoices in the perfect abundance of its fullness when whatever suspicion an anxious [?] concern for the faith may have held, or whatever dispute has been drawn out at length, is corrected either by [?] or by amendment.

The presbyter Caelestius presented himself for our examination, asking that the things which had been pressed upon the apostolic see about him, otherwise than they should have been, be cleared away. And although many occupations, binding us with the stronger ties of church business, were drawing away our attention and concern, nevertheless, so that your fraternity's expectation about the arrival and examination of the aforesaid man should not be kept in suspense any longer, we set everything else aside and on the day of the hearing took our seat in the basilica of Saint Clement. Imbued with the teachings of the blessed apostle Peter, he had amended old errors under so great a master and had made such progress that he consecrated by martyrdom the faith he had learned and taught; our purpose, namely, was that the authority of so great a bishop might stand as an example to the present hearing for a salutary correction.

We therefore examined everything that had been done before, as you will learn from the record of the proceedings attached to this letter, and, having brought Caelestius in, we had the statement he had submitted read aloud. Not content with this, we repeatedly probed whether he spoke what he had written from the heart or only with the lips, although judgment of the secrets of souls can belong to our God alone, to whom not only what has been thought but also what is yet to be thought is already present. What his words contain, we thought it more expedient for your holiness to learn by reading them.

One thing indeed troubled us: that although you had Caelestius there in person, nothing was clearly judged, and the report was sent afterwards on the strength of the letters of Heros and Lazarus. Certainly it is quite evident that this was hastened by fervor of faith. But when he was questioned about these men, he asserted that he had never had any conversation with them about such disputes, and had not known them even by sight before they wrote about him; Lazarus he had indeed met in passing, while Heros, after offering an apology for having thought ill of a man who was unknown to him and absent, had parted from him on good terms.

With so frail a foundation, indeed none at all, for an unknown charge, it was undoubtedly right that inquiry be made into the character of such men, which had proved so windy and light: whether at least their standing in their own place and their manner of life were sound, so that credit ought to be given to absent men speaking against an absent man, and whether their letters carried such weight as to merit the authority of testimony. It became clear that they, unknown foreigners, had laid claim to bishoprics within Gaul through ordinations made in disregard of the rules, with the people and clergy objecting. From these they deposed themselves by their own decision; and we, following, among other things, especially their own repentance and confession about themselves, removed them from priestly rank and from all communion. It weighs heavily enough that the case originated with such men, by letter, in accusation of an absent man who, when present, defends himself, sets out his faith, and challenges his accuser.

No one has ever regretted turning a judgment toward the better. A young man, the agent of the Holy Spirit, found Susanna innocent after she had been condemned by the falsehood of the elders: the chaste woman, whom aged men falsely made out to be unchaste, is brought back from punishment by a boy. Not every spirit, therefore, is to be believed, as we have been warned, but each must be examined long and carefully, especially concerning a man's faith, where his standing and eternal life are at stake.

Nor did the search for truth fail Solomon in the quarrel over the child: he did not immediately award the child to one of the two women wrangling with each other, but as judge, after hesitating, he found the truth where he perceived the feeling of true devotion. It must be very rare indeed for long and disciplined deliberation not to reach truth's lair. It is the sign of an excellent mind to be slow to believe evil; for very often those whose good confession about themselves is believed too slowly are driven by necessity over the precipice of that very error, and an incurable wound is made, which there is no hope of healing.

Hence in the present case we have decided nothing premature or hasty, but have resolved to make known to your holiness our examination concerning Caelestius's faith, which is complete. His earlier statement, given in Africa, ought also to have served you as testimony, and things unexamined and tossed about by rumor should not have been so readily believed. Therefore, within two months, either let those come who can refute him to his face, showing that he thinks otherwise than he set out in his statements and profession, or let your holiness know that, after the things he has put forward, so open and manifest, no doubt remains.

Caelestius himself, indeed, and whatever bishops from various regions were present at the time, were admonished that these snares of questions and foolish disputes, which do not build up but rather destroy, flow from that contagion of curiosity, while each man abuses the Scriptures with his own cleverness and intemperate eloquence; for in this way even the writings of great men, along with their very authors, are sometimes endangered, after much time has wretchedly passed, at the whim of an interpreter. So it was divinely said that in much speaking sin is not avoided, and holy David rightly asked for a guard set about his lips and a watch on his mouth.

I admonish your charity, both by the authority of the apostolic see and by the mutual affection of love. Would that our minds were equal to the precepts and observances of all the holy Scriptures that have been received according to the tradition of the fathers and our forebears! What is not abundant there, what is not full of the Spirit of God and of his words? Unless each one prefers to trust himself more and to rely on his own judgment about himself. Given [?] copies of the authors held [?], in the consulship of Honorius Augustus for the eleventh [?] time and Flavius Constantius.
(46.) Bishop Zosimus to Aurelius and all the bishops established throughout Africa, his most beloved brothers in the Lord, greeting.

After the presbyter Caelestius had been heard by us and had clearly expressed what he thought about the faith, and had confirmed by frequently repeated professions the same things he had set out in his statement (concerning his case we have sent a fuller letter to your love), behold, we received a letter from Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, who was ordained bishop in place of the late holy John.

He intervened as a very earnest supporter of Pelagius's cause. Pelagius himself also sent a letter containing a very full defense, in which he set out at length the faith of his profession, what he followed and what he condemned, without any disguise, so that all the snares of interpretation might cease.

These were read publicly: they contained everything that Caelestius had put forward earlier, entirely matching and framed in the same sense and statements. Would that any of you, dearest brothers, could have been present at the reading of the letter! What joy there was among the holy men who were present! What admiration in each of them! Some could scarcely restrain their weeping and tears that men of such perfect faith could have been defamed. Is there any place in which the grace or help of God has been passed over? Whoever can conceive even in his mind anything apart from it, has he not subjected himself to that penalty and sentence pronounced concerning the Holy Spirit, that he will be granted neither pardon nor remission, either here or in the world to come?

I see that this Pelagius too is defamed by the letters of Heros and Lazarus. Is it really so, dearest brothers, that not even rumor has reached your ears of what whirlwinds and storms of the church these men are? Were the lives and condemnation of these men so hidden from you? And although a special authority of the apostolic see has removed them from all communion, learn in this letter too, if only briefly, the character of these men.

Lazarus has an old habit of accusing the innocent: through many councils he was found to be a diabolical accuser of holy Brice, our fellow bishop of the city of Tours; at the synod of the town of Turin he received from Proculus of Marseilles the sentence of a slanderer. By that same Proculus, after many years, he was made bishop by a tyrant's decision: when the defender of the city of Aix had been struck down for opposing it, he burst into the very sanctuary and onto the episcopal throne, almost spattered with innocent blood, and remained there as the shadow of a bishop for just as long as the tyrant's semblance of empire stood. After the slaughter of his patron he stripped himself of that place of his own accord and condemned himself by his own resignation.

With Heros, likewise, everything is similar: the same tyrant as patron, killings, riots, chains and imprisonment for the presbyters who opposed him, the handing over of the whole city, and a similar repentance in the resignation of his bishopric. Is it any wonder if these men wished to strike down with false letters a layman striving toward good fruit through long service to God, when they contrived such things against their brothers and fellow bishops and have stirred up so many storms for the church?

It does not befit episcopal authority, and especially your prudence, to hang upon the writings of frivolous whisperers. Behold, Pelagius and Caelestius present themselves to the apostolic see in their letters and confessions: where is Heros, where is Lazarus, names to be blushed at for their deeds and their many condemnations? Where are those young men, namely Timasius and James, who, as was asserted, [?] certain writings? Judge for yourselves whether, when men confess such things in the apostolic see, the things spread about them by depraved and frivolous authors and by uncertain rumor ought to be believed.

Love peace, cherish charity, strive for concord! For it is written: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. Who are more truly neighbors to one another than all of us, who ought to be one in Christ? Not every wind that enters our ears is a messenger of truth, and so there is always need of a mind that presides and keeps watch, lest everything be left to rumor and everything to witnesses.

Look through the sacred writings and the divine records: false witnesses take up the greatest part wherever we find accusations against the saints or dangers to them. The greatest part, do I say? Rather the whole, since false witnesses rose up against our Lord and Savior himself, the sacrifice for the whole world and the saving high priest, pretending that they had heard him blaspheme. Consider what deceit can now let pass, when with perjuries it made an assault on the God of faith, indeed on faith and truth itself.

We have written these things so that henceforth, if any persons who are absent and little known tell such wanton lies about anyone, your feet may stand firm against the battering ram of deceit. That is why so great a man prays for a lamp for his feet and a light for his paths, namely, so that our steps may not be blind and wandering amid deceptive darkness. And in the Gospel: Does our law judge a man unless it first hears from him and knows what he does?

And already in the Old Testament: You shall not give credence to an idle report, and you shall not join with the wicked to become an unjust witness. And lest the multitude of detractors should be believed before judicial examination, he added: You shall not side with the majority in wickedness, and you shall not incur sin through them. And again elsewhere: Do not find fault with anyone before you inquire, and when you have inquired, rebuke justly. And again: What your eyes have seen, speak of.

And in the Acts of the Apostles, when the chief priests and elders of the Jews demanded the condemnation of the apostle Paul in his absence, Festus, a Gentile and a tribune, pronounced a most just sentence, which it is fitting for us too to set before the shame of those who believe too easily: It is not the custom of the Romans to condemn any man before the accused has his accusers face to face and receives an opportunity to defend himself and clear himself of the charges. If, then, a man placed outside the fold of our faith kept to this moderation, a credulity too ready to accept what absent men say against the absent burdens the honor of bishops; for how few will be found free from wounds, if a credulous breast is laid open to every blow of whoever strikes?

Let earthly moderation teach us how things are done in secular judgments and cases, first in choosing and rejecting the judges themselves. And how much hesitation, how many delays are interposed! How often is adjournment granted, and judgments extended even at the very end of the contest! When an innocent defendant is involved, recourse is had to the sea and to evidence from overseas, so that proof, which on the spot is often strangled by tighter constraints, may at least come from afar. I am lying about all this if these things were not devised as a protection for innocence. For it is more tolerable that an innocent man be found innocent late than that he be quickly condemned as guilty.

It was too burdensome for Lazarus and Heros to follow in the footsteps of their own letters. Or did they not know that your love would refer the matter to the apostolic see? Surely they should have sailed here, without the shortcut of slander! When it is a matter of seeking a bishopric, seas and lands are traversed and no vote of support is overlooked; but when the reputation of the innocent is to be struck down, these idle and pampered men, whether as accusers or as witnesses (for in deceivers either name is infamous), misuse letters from their bedrooms and couches, and these two plagues cloud over all Africa and the whole tranquility of catholic serenity at their whim. We shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ; no one will be able to be absent there, nor anywhere escape the judgment of God, whose immensity pervades all places and things.

If it pleased our God, for the sake of the lost sheep, that the Word should become flesh and that, being Lord, he should take on the form of a servant, in order to restore the freedom long taken away, let it be a joy for us to recognize that those whom false informers accused have never been torn away from our body and from catholic charity. Certainly what your expectation desired has shone forth: that they should condemn what is to be condemned and follow what is to be followed.

If the father of the household rejoiced at the return of his son, who had been dead and came to life again, had been lost and was found, and ordered a clean robe, that is, the emblem of a pure mind, to be brought for him, along with the fatted calf, how much more abundant is the rejoicing of faith that those about whom falsehoods were spread were neither dead nor lost?

We have therefore sent to your love copies of the writings that Pelagius sent, and we do not doubt that reading them will give you the same joy in the Lord at his perfect faith. Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October.
(47.) The statement of the deacon Paulinus against Caelestius, submitted to Bishop Zosimus.

I appeal to the justice of your beatitude, my lord Zosimus, venerable pope. The true faith is never disturbed, and above all in the apostolic church, in which teachers of corrupt faith are as easily detected as they are truly punished, so that in them, if they correct themselves, there dies what they had wickedly conceived and still more wickedly brought forth, and in them [?] the true faith, which the apostles taught and which the Roman church holds together with all teachers of the catholic faith.

But if, like the other authors of heresy, who long ago were judged by the apostolic see or by the fathers and, cast out of the bosom of mother catholic church, perished in everlasting death, these too who have now been detected or are being detected persist in their faithlessness, let them be handed over to the spiritual sword, to be slain by it; as now Pelagius and Caelestius have been condemned by your beatitude's predecessor of blessed memory, Pope Innocent, should they reject the right faith and persist in their perverse teaching.

Following his sentence, your beatitude, when Caelestius was being heard by the apostolic see, among other things instructed him in these words: 'Do you then condemn all the things contained in the statement of Paulinus, that is, concerning the questions?' And in another place: 'Do you know what letter the see sent to our brothers and fellow bishops of the African province?' And it was added: 'Do you condemn all the things we have condemned, and do you hold what we hold?' And again: 'Do you condemn all the things that have been spread abroad in your name?' And again: 'Or the things that Paulinus set out in his statement?'

And when he said that I could be proved a heretic from the things that had been objected against him, you, filled with the Holy Spirit, by apostolic authority rejected and checked the words of this raving slanderer, pronouncing a sentence by which I would be approved as a catholic and he would be healed by your care, if he wished to be healed. It runs thus: 'I would not have you lead us around in circles; condemn all these things that have been objected against you by Paulinus or spread about by rumor.' Who would not be satisfied with this sentence?

Who else would reject a sentence so wholesome, so worthy to be embraced, so devout, except one who has strayed from the faith? And he who had earlier professed that he would condemn whatever had been objected against him, if you judged it contrary to the faith, hears 'Condemn!' and not only does not condemn, but goes so far as to insult so great a see. Hence the Roman church is no longer unaware of its defendant, who with so bold a spirit dared to contradict and not condemn what your beatitude decreed should be condemned. I, however, give thanks to God and to Christ our Lord,

who willed that the cause of his church be conducted in such a way that the apostolic see, through the mouth of two of its pontiffs, by whom the heresy had to be condemned, also commanded the condemnation of the things I had objected against Caelestius, whose condemnation I have never desired; I have always desired, and still desire, his correction.

His dispute is now no longer with me but with the whole church of God, as the letters of the African bishops sent to your beatitude testify, since he strives to go against the apostle's statement by denying original sin, which passed to all men and, until the end of the world, keeps hold of the inheritance of that Adam who sinned first; and unless it is remitted in infants through the sacrament of baptism, they cannot have eternal life and the kingdom of heaven.

Even his master Pelagius contends against him, since he condemned at the Eastern hearing the very things this man tries to maintain in the assembly of the apostolic see. He also has against him a great many ancient catholic teachers of the churches, of the East and the West, of the south and the north, who in their books could teach him about original sin, if he wishes to be healed; he has the blessed martyr Cyprian, the blessed confessor Ambrose, Gregory Nazianzen, the blessed Pope Innocent; he has also those still living in the body who would contend with him, if indeed he judges himself fit for so great a contest, or at any rate whom he ought to follow, if he wishes rather to learn what is right than to teach what is perverse; he has, and this comes first, your beatitude, whose sentence he ought to have obeyed when he heard 'Condemn!'; finally, he has the nursing infants themselves, on whom he ought to have mercy if he will not have it on himself, and to whom, to use the martyr's words, not their own sins but another's are forgiven.

Therefore I beg your blessed apostleship to order this statement of mine to be received, by which I return thanks to so great a see and for the most just sentences pronounced on my behalf. I have sent it because Basiliscus the subdeacon, sent by your beatitude with the proceedings of the apostolic see, met me at Carthage on the fourth day before the Nones of November, though only by word of mouth, summoning me to appear before the apostolic see and the judgment of your holiness, to which it had been suggested I had fled, and to promise that I would not fail to appear, if a sentence had been pronounced against me and not in my favor.

At that time I could do nothing in the matter, because the one who had appealed to the apostolic see was absent, though he certainly ought to have established the merits of his appeal, especially since, when the appellant takes no action, even under human laws the one who has won always prevails. For what concern was it of mine any longer to come forward, even before your reverence, as a party in the matter of his perverse doctrine? I could have rejoiced over him if, by condemning the things I had objected against him, as the judgment of the apostolic see has confirmed, he had already deserved to be absolved, and so had not let himself be ordained before he was cleared.

But the little fox was always given to tricks; he does not know how to change his nature. He did not believe he could be caught, since he always puts his confidence in holes, in which he tries to hide the sunken head of his conscience. This could no longer stay hidden, but, now more plainly made public, it is cut off through your beatitude by the spiritual sword, so that the Lord's flock may no longer be torn apart by wild beasts' teeth, the flock which you, the good shepherd, guard with anxious and watchful care.
I have sent this statement to your beatitude by Marcellinus, subdeacon of the church of Carthage. Given on the sixth day before the Ides of November.
(48.) Likewise, a copy of the letters of Saint Augustine, replying to what is written above, sent by Albinus the acolyte and Firmus the presbyter.

TO MY LORD SIXTUS THE PRESBYTER, MY VENERABLE AND HOLY BROTHER, WHO IS TO BE WELCOMED IN THE LOVE OF CHRIST, AUGUSTINE SENDS GREETING IN THE LORD. Your kind letter, sent by our holy brother Firmus the presbyter, arrived at Hippo while I was away. I was able to read it after I came back, although by then its bearer had already left. This is the first chance I have had to reply, and also the most welcome one: it comes through our dearly beloved son Albinus the acolyte.

You wrote to the two of us together, but at that time we were not together. That is why you are receiving a separate letter from each of us and not one letter from both. The bearer of this letter left me intending to go by way of my venerable brother and fellow bishop Alypius, who will write back to your holiness about other matters. He also took to Alypius the very letter of yours that I had read.

How can anyone try to say how great a joy it filled us with, when it cannot be put into words? I do not think even you fully know it, but believe us when we tell you how much good you have done by sending us such a letter. You are the witness of your own mind, and in the same way we are witnesses of ours, and we know how it was moved by the shining sincerity of that letter.

You sent a very short letter on this same matter to the most blessed old man Aurelius through Leo the acolyte. In it you set out for us what you think of that most pernicious doctrine, and on the other side what you think of the grace of God, which he bestows on small and great alike and to which that doctrine is utterly hostile. We copied that letter with joyful eagerness and read it with great enthusiasm to everyone we could. So with how much greater joy do you think we read this longer letter? And how carefully do you think we offered it to as many as we could, so that they might read it, and how eagerly are we still pressing [?] it on as many as we can?

For what could be more welcome to read or to hear than so pure a defense of the grace of God against its enemies, and from the lips of a man who was once boasted of as an influential patron of those same enemies? And for what should we give God more abundant thanks than that his grace is defended in this way by those to whom it is given, against those to whom it is not given, or to whom what is given is unwelcome? For by the hidden and just judgment of God it is not given to them to welcome it.

Therefore, venerable lord and holy brother, to be welcomed in the grace of Christ, you do very well to write about this matter to the brothers among whom those people are in the habit of boasting of your friendship. Yet a greater task still remains for you. Those who dare to chatter quite openly about that error, so deeply hostile to the Christian name, must be punished with wholesome severity.

But you must also guard most carefully, with pastoral vigilance, against those who never stop whispering it, for the sake of the Lord's weaker and simpler sheep. They whisper more covertly and more timidly, it is true, but they still do it, "making their way into houses," as the apostle says, and doing the rest of what follows there, with practiced impiety. AND SO ON.
(49.) TO THE HOLY LORD, WORTHY OF ALL HONOR, THE MOST BLESSED POPE CYRIL, FROM EUSEBIUS.

I have given thanks in Christ that I was granted a letter from your blessedness in words sweeter than honey, and that you deigned to ring out in answer to the one who struck, holy lord, worthy of all honor, most blessed pope. So I ask you to deign to receive kindly what my humble self has to say, and not to regard as pride the freedom we seem to have in the faith of Christ.

Ever since the name of Christ became known to the whole world, the see of Alexandria is known to have held fast, by the bond of Christ, to the provinces of Italy more than the others have. How is it, then, that the church of Alexandria alone has received the Pelagian and Caelestian heresy into communion? Innocent of blessed memory condemned that heresy together with its leaders, and all the Easterners reject them. Yet the church that has received them is the very one that ought to have been the only one and the first among its fellow provinces to refute such men.

The pestilent man behind this is the one I wrote to your holiness about a year ago: Valerian the ventriloquist, their standard-bearer and ally. He is a slave to his stomach, and whatever idle flatterers he finds there he proclaims to be saints and most faithful men. But your blessedness should not take him for a free man. He is a slave belonging to the estate at Ariminum of the most illustrious Count Valerius. Out of reverence for our love for you, we have so far said nothing about having him reclaimed from you.

Rather, deign to pray for us and to cast such men out of fellowship, remembering what is written in the prophet: holy flesh bound up in a priest's garment does not make holy what it touches [?] when that is unclean; such things are threatened by what is unclean. This law is a question put to the priests. But please deign to forgive my humble boldness, as I asked above. May the inviolable Trinity deign to keep your blessedness safe and mindful of me, holy pope.

ZOSIMUS TO AURELIUS AND THE OTHERS WHO WERE PRESENT AT THE COUNCIL OF CARTHAGE, HIS DEARLY BELOVED BROTHERS, GREETING IN THE LORD. The tradition of the fathers has given the apostolic see such great authority that no one would dare to dispute its judgment, and it has always preserved that authority through canons and rules. Church discipline, still running its course according to its laws, pays due reverence to the name of Peter, from whom that discipline itself also descends.

(For the antiquity of the canons, by the judgment of all, willed that this apostle should have such great power, from the very promise of Christ our God that he should loose what was bound and bind what was loosed. An equal measure of power was given to those who, with his consent, had earned the inheritance of his see. For he has the care of all the churches, and above all of this one, where he had sat. He does not allow any part of its privilege to be [?], or any of its judgments to waver in any breeze. He himself laid its foundations in his own name, firm and unshaken by any upheaval, and no one may rashly attack it without danger to himself.)

So Peter is the head of such great authority, and the later statutes of all our forebears have confirmed it. By every law and discipline, human and divine, it has now been settled that the Roman church,

whose place he governs, also holds the power of that very name. This is not hidden from you; you know it, dearest brothers, and as priests you ought to know it. Yet although we had so much authority that no one could reopen our sentence, we have done nothing that we did not report to you of our own accord in our letters. We granted this out of brotherhood and took counsel in common. It was not that we did not know what ought to be done, or that we would do anything that harmed the church's interest and would therefore displease you. Rather, we wished to deliberate together with you about that man who, as you yourselves say in your letters, had been accused among you. Asserting his innocence and not shrinking from judgment, he had come to our see on the basis of an earlier appeal. He demanded of his own accord that his accusers appear, and he condemned the charges that he said had been falsely brought against him through rumor.

We think, and in fact know, that his whole petition was set out in the earlier letter we sent you, and we believed it had been sufficiently answered in the letter you wrote back. But afterwards we unrolled the whole volume of the letter sent to us by your subdeacon Marcellinus. When we had finally read it through, we found that you had taken the whole text of our letter as if we had trusted Caelestius in everything and, without examining his words, had agreed with every syllable, so to speak.

Matters that require long deliberation are never settled rashly, and what has to be decided by the highest judgment must not be determined without careful deliberation. Your brotherhood should therefore know that since we wrote that letter to you, or received yours, we have changed nothing. We have left everything in the same state it was in before, when we informed your holiness in our letter of this decision: that the solemn protest you had sent us would be upheld. AND THE SUBSCRIPTION: Farewell, brothers. Given on 18 March, in the twelfth consulship of Honorius Augustus. Received on 29 April.

BISHOP LEO TO LEO AUGUSTUS. We would like to honor your piety's glorious resolve in defending the faith with all the praise the greatness of the matter demands. But if we celebrate the joy of the universal church only within the narrow limits of our own speech, we will find ourselves unequal to the task of giving thanks. A worthier reward for your deeds and merits will be kept for you by him in whose cause you excel in singular devotion and triumph in the glorious outcome you desired.

Let your clemency know, then, that all the churches of God are rejoicing and glad together as they praise you. The wicked parricide has been driven from his yoke over the church of Alexandria. The people of God, whom an infamous robber was oppressing, have been brought back to the ancient freedom of the faith. They can now be called back to the way of salvation by the preaching of faithful priests, since they see the whole seedbed of poisons thrown out together with its author.

You have done all this with steadfast resolve and great spirit. So now add this to the work of faith you have completed: decide, as will please God, on a catholic bishop for that city, one who has not been stained by the slightest touch of the impiety so often condemned. Otherwise a hidden wound may grow beneath what looks like a healed scar, and the Christian people, whom your action has openly freed from the perversity of heretics, may again be exposed to deadly poisons.

You see, venerable emperor, and you clearly recognize, that in the case of the person whose removal is at issue, soundness of faith is not the only thing to consider. Even if his faith could be purged by some corrections and professions and fully restored on whatever terms, plausible declarations could never wipe out what he did so wickedly and with so much bloodshed. In a bishop of God, and above all in the priest of so great a church, the sound of the tongue and the words of the lips are not enough. It is no use if God is proclaimed with the voice while the mind stands convicted of impiety.

For the Holy Spirit speaks of such people through the apostle: "having the appearance of godliness but denying its power"; and again elsewhere: "they profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds." In every member of the church we look for both the truth of sound faith and the fullness of good works. How much more should both excel in the chief bishop, since one without the other cannot be joined to the body of Christ?

Nor is there any need now to list everything that makes Timothy detestable. What was done by him and because of him has become fully and plainly known to the whole world. And if the unruly mob did anything against justice, all of it comes back onto his head, since the hands of the rioters were serving his wishes.

So even if he neglected nothing and falsified nothing in his profession of faith, the course best befitting your glory is to shut him out completely from what he is seeking. In the bishop of so great a city, the universal church ought to be able to rejoice with holy gladness, so that the true peace of the Lord may shine out not only through the preaching of the faith but also through the example of his life. Given on 17 June, in the consulship of Magnus and Apollonius. Delivered by Philoxenus, imperial agent.
(52.) BISHOP LEO TO GENNADIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.

From your love's letter, and from what our brothers and fellow bishops Domitian and Geminian have told me, I have learned that Timothy, after being expelled from the church of the city of Alexandria, has been allowed to come to Constantinople through the efforts of certain enemies of the faith. As far as one can tell, the aim is this. Since he is hemmed in by the judgments of all the Lord's priests, he is to turn to catholic doctrine, at least against his will. Then, as if this were the only reason he had been thrown out, he is to condemn the error of heretical perversity and accept the apostolic teaching, so that he may return to Alexandria. But even if he were shown to be catholic, one thing stands firmly against him: he seized so great a see while its bishop was still alive, and he has shown himself responsible for a cruelty never heard of before.

Therefore, with the diligence for which you are renowned, your love must strive and labor to make sure that no one speaks with so wicked a man, privately or publicly. Nor must a meeting of certain persons give him an opening, under the pretext of correcting him, to gain full freedom to return. The most Christian prince has already passed judgment on him in his edicts.

Strive, therefore, dearest brother, with all your effort and watchful care, to serve the unity of the church. Make sure that his supporters lose all hope, and that orthodox Egyptians consecrate a catholic bishop for the Alexandrians from their own clergy, according to the ancient custom. For that parricide will not be abandoned by his defenders unless the church of Alexandria, which must be restored to the honor of the fathers and to its own freedom, gains a ruler of proven worth to heal all the harm that has been done. Given on 17 June, in the consulship of Magnus and Apollonius. Delivered by Philoxenus, imperial agent.

BISHOP LEO TO TIMOTHY, CATHOLIC BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF ALEXANDRIA. The apostle's shining words make it plain that "for those who love God all things work together for good." By the dispensation of divine goodness, prosperity is granted in the very place where adversity is endured.

The experience of the church of Alexandria shows this. There the suffering and endurance of the humble have stored up great treasures of patience for it, because "the Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart, and he will save the humble in spirit." It has now been glorified in every way by the faith of the renowned prince, through whom "the right hand of the Lord has done mighty things," so that the disgrace of antichrist should sit no longer on the throne of the blessed fathers. His impiety harmed no one more than himself. Though he drove some into partnership in his crime, it was he who stained himself with blood beyond any atonement.

So I write in reply that the whole church of the Lord rejoices with me over the election of you, my brother, which the clergy, the people and all the faithful made at the prompting of faith. I pray that the kindness of God's goodness may confirm it with ever greater grace, and that your devotion may serve it in all things. In this way you may earnestly win back, through the prayers of the church, even those who have resisted the truth to some degree, so that they are reconciled to God. As a caring ruler, join them to the sacrament of the catholic faith, whose solidity admits no division. Imitate that true and loving shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep, and who did not restrain the one stray sheep with whips but carried it back to his own fold on his shoulders.

Let your love therefore see to it, dearest brother, that no trace either of the Nestorian doctrine or of the Eutychian error can be found among the people of God. For "no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus." He would not have reconciled the whole world to God the Father unless, through the regeneration of faith, he had taken all people up into the reality of our flesh.

You rightly sent us, as custom requires, the documents of your ordination through our sons Daniel the presbyter and Timothy the deacon. In the same way, whenever opportunities to write come your way, my brother, keep up this duty at all times. Send us reports as often as possible on the progress of peace, for we are anxious to hear. Then through our letters to each other we may feel that "the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us." Given on 18 August, in the consulship of Magnus and Apollonius.

BISHOP LEO TO THE PRESBYTERS AND DEACONS OF THE CHURCH OF ALEXANDRIA, HIS DEARLY BELOVED SONS, GREETING IN THE LORD. I rejoice exultantly in the Lord at the devoted affection you have among yourselves. As your letter shows, the shepherd loves the flock and the flock loves the shepherd.

So, as the apostle says, be eager for one another "to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace," and hasten to reach the fruit of your patience. With the help of God's grace, use the faith of our most glorious prince to build up the firmest peace, now that the beast has been driven far away which, as the prophetic psalm sings, was laying waste the vineyard of the Lord's planting with singular savagery. What could you more worthily wish for or do than this?

Since thieves' snares and robbers' raids are no longer feared in the Lord's sheepfold, let your whole community return to harmony. Under the teaching of the Holy Spirit, seek unity in all things, the unity for whose sake the apostle says: "not seeking what benefits me, but what benefits many, so that they may be saved." Let all say and think the same thing. Let there be no conflicts of opinions or disputes. What the disciples of truth in the church of Alexandria learned and taught down to the time of its catholic bishops, let all the faithful bring forward in the same confession. For truth is simple and one, and admits no variety.

If the impious lies of heretics have unsettled any Christians, of whatever rank, call them to the remedy of making amends, and correct them kindly in a spirit of gentleness. For, as the blessed apostle Peter says, "the Lord is not slow about his promise but is patient for your sake, not wanting any to perish but all to turn to repentance." We must therefore take care that making pardon hard to obtain does not delay the cure. Given on 18 August, in the consulship of Magnus and Apollonius.

BISHOP LEO TO THEOPHILUS, JOHN, ATHANASIUS, ABRAHAM, DANIEL, JOHA [?], PAPHNUTIUS, MUSAEUS, PANULVIUS [?] AND PETER, EGYPTIAN BISHOPS. Our sons Daniel the presbyter and Timothy the deacon brought me your letter, my brothers, and I rejoice to have learned from it that the faith of our glorious and venerable prince, joined to the teachings of the prophets and the gospel, has brought his measures to a holy and God-pleasing outcome. The most bloodthirsty usurper of the church of Alexandria has been thrown out and sent far away, and the election by the whole city has won a ruler worthy to govern it. No ambition drew you to his consecration, no sedition drove you, no wrongdoing spurred you on. Instead, the merit of the holiness evident to all did not hesitate to set above everyone the man the whole community wanted to preside over it.

So, rejoicing that God's peace has been restored to the Christian peoples, we commend to you the dignity of your shared work. The bishop, ordained in a religious manner in every respect, should find himself supported by your brotherly agreement, and should have the joy of your cooperation in removing the scandals that heretical error had stirred up.

Now that the man who imitated the devil, who "did not stand in the truth," and who abused the semblance of a stolen office and title has been thrown out, it is fitting that the church of Alexandria should revere and love the man it has found worthy of so great a priesthood for both his upright conduct and his firm catholic faith. We offer him the full affection of our heart in mutual love. We urge you, dearest brothers, and confidently require of you that in preaching the word and teaching its precepts you keep to that pattern of love without which no virtues can be of any benefit.

You know what was written to our brother and fellow bishop Timothy about calling back those who strayed from the path of truth and behaved rashly and violently. Let your love understand that this is your concern as well. Since that pestilent disease has spread widely, the same medicine must be applied to all the wounds everywhere. Then through pastoral diligence the Lord's sheepfold will be restored in all the churches, and through the care of love and teaching all Christ's sheep will know that they have one shepherd. Given on 18 August, in the consulship of Magnus and Apollonius.

Bishop Simplicius to Zeno Augustus. For my part, given the devotion with which I look up to Christian princes in unceasing reverence, I would gladly pay Your Piety the duties I owe in constant correspondence. But since concern for our sacred religion adds to that wish, I have a weightier matter to attend to: I must both render you honour with a willing mind and confidently put before you the causes of the faith. I am drawn to both, partly by my abiding devotion to Your Clemency and partly by the demands of my office and my responsibility for apostolic government.

Having therefore discharged the duty of greeting you, most glorious and most clement son, Emperor Augustus, I neither ought to nor can keep silent about the scandals that are said to be breaking out again in the churches of the East through the robberies of heretics. For, as the letters of monks who burn with zeal for the catholic faith have informed me, I have learned that Timothy the parricide has been at it again. Long ago he laid waste the church of Egypt. Like Cain, as Holy Scripture testifies, he was cast out from the face of God, that is, shut out from the dignity of the Church, and, as though to wander through the desert and long suffer the torments of a guilty conscience, he was led away into the exile of his own error. Yet now he has rekindled the flames of his former fury, gathered together bands of reprobates, and once more forced his way into the church of the city of Alexandria, which he had earlier stained with priestly blood, himself stained with blood anew by driving out its lawful bishop.

So the humiliation of his banishment, which ought to have pricked him to repent of his impious deeds, seems instead to have given him leisure to nurse a still more savage madness. Without doubt this proves him far more detestable than Cain himself: Cain, once condemned, refrained from crime after committing it once, whereas this man goes on to greater crimes after his punishment.

Yet not content even with this extent of wickedness, this destroyer of human salvation, so as to leave nothing undefiled, is said to have boldly entered the city of Constantinople as well, which has always burned with love for right doctrine, and to have listened with pleasure as the partners of his depravity hailed him with words due to Christ alone. By this he was plainly shown to be, not one blessed who comes in the name of the Lord, but evidently an antichrist who usurps the divine majesty.

Although he had been so commendably excluded from catholic communion, it is reported that, with hands spattered with human blood, he celebrated in certain private houses not divine sacrifices but sacrileges. This did nothing to confirm his acceptance; rather, it exposed the treachery of his accomplices, who, unless they come to their senses, will fall utterly with him from that seat of iniquity which, like the devil his father who made himself like the Most High, the faithless man never ceases to build up as an eternal one for himself, to his ruin.

Venerable emperor, though the mind shudders that such a gladiator should even have attempted these things, I confess that I am held in the greatest astonishment that they could have been done under the eyes of Your Piety. For who does not know, or who doubts, that Your Clemency's mind is always devoted to God and given over to orthodox rules? By the disposition of heavenly providence you were trained in the virtues of Marcian and Leo of august memory for the public good, and you were equally formed by their convictions in catholic truth. No one at all doubts that Your Piety follows the faith of those whose empire you have inherited.

Since everyone holds these things about Your Serenity's mind as certain and settled, far be it that in your times the integrity of divine worship and the long-established purity of the catholic faith should be thought open to alteration. Look, I beg you, at God's benefits and weigh what has been bestowed on you; and, so that this prosperity may endure, resolve that the author of the gift must be propitiated, not offended. Amid all his public business a religious prince must above all take care of what protects his rule, and the [?] of heavenly observance must be preferred to all things, for without it nothing stands aright.

If Your Clemency orders the archives [?] of your palace to be searched, abundant documents agreeing with the definition of our forebears will be readily at hand. For we must not suppose that Your Majesty is unaware of what was spread through all the provinces of the East from the very citadel of your empire: namely, the replies that my predecessor of blessed memory, Leo, sent to Marcian and Leo of august memory and to the Council of Chalcedon, in which he set out the mystery of the Lord's incarnation so fully and so clearly that anyone who does not plainly recognize there the grounds of his own redemption cannot be called a catholic, nor even a Christian. Indeed, so that you may more easily have the instruction you need, I have sent copies of those same letters to my brother and fellow bishop Acacius, to be presented to Your Majesty.

If, then, Your Piety deigns to review these, or what the bishops of the whole East wrote back in agreement with this teaching, you will surely see that they were both carefully examined and truthfully promulgated, and therefore must in no way be shaken by the twists and turns of pestilent falsehood. For truly, what has flowed pure and clear from the most pure fountain of the Scriptures cannot be disturbed by any arguments of murky cunning. This same rule of apostolic doctrine endures in the successors of him to whom the Lord entrusted the care of the whole flock, to whom he promised that he would never fail him to the end of the age, against whom he promised that the gates of hell would never prevail, and by whose sentence, he declared, what was bound on earth could not be loosed even in heaven.

Wherefore I pray and beseech Your Clemency, before whom my brother and fellow bishop Acacius will plead the more earnestly in my place, that you imitate the deeds of such great predecessors, reject with a catholic heart the workers of this wicked presumption, and resolve that they be restrained by your royal power. Whoever tries to sow anything other than what we have received, as the Apostle foretold, let him be anathema. Let no access be opened for pernicious minds to creep into your ears; let no confidence be granted for reopening anything of the ancient decrees. For, as must often be repeated, what has deservedly been cut off by apostolic hands with the edge of the gospel sickle, with the assent of the universal Church, cannot gain the strength to grow again, nor can what is known to be consigned to eternal fire return as a fruitful shoot of the Lord's vine. Thus, in the end, the contrivances of all heresies, once struck down by the decrees of the Church, are never allowed to renew their crushed assaults.

Above all, however, I beg that the see of the blessed evangelist Mark (I mean the church of Alexandria) be freed from the occupation of this most bloodthirsty robber and restored to a catholic bishop, and that it recover its freedom and its peace together. As for the wicked parricide, who is guilty under both divine and human laws, let him be sent back to where he was rightly thrust before, and so be kept from the slaughter of innocent souls. Let the poisons of that deadly head be removed far from the realm of Your Piety; and since, with ears stopped against the saving preaching, they could not take in the healing words, let them be carried away from the bane of human company to waste away in a solitude fitting for their virulence.

All the more, then, do I, the minister, such as I am, of the see of the blessed apostle Peter, adjure Your Piety in his voice: as you wish to have your enemies subdued, do not allow the enemies of the ancient faith to rampage unpunished; as you desire to keep the world of your empire at peace, decree that all the Lord's churches keep the peace of the true confession; as you long to have God favourable to your reign and to your salvation, do not suffer the one hope of salvation, which leads the human race to the heavenly kingdom and to eternal life, to be violated in any part.

May almighty God preserve your reign and your well-being with his perpetual protection, most glorious and most clement emperor. Given on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the consulship of Basiliscus Augustus.
(57.) Bishop Simplicius to Acacius, Bishop of Constantinople.

As our sons, the illustrious patrician Latinus and the honourable Madusius, were being sent on a public embassy, we could not neglect what we are pursuing with all our energy. Recently, when a complaint came from priests and monks about Timothy, long since separated from the universal Church, we wrote both to the most Christian prince and to Your Charity, dearest brother, that he should be resisted by every means, so that the audacity of the heretics might attempt nothing against the Council of Chalcedon. And in praising Your Charity's steadfastness, we said that it greatly pleased us, or rather the Lord himself, that you did not permit a man condemned not only for his faith but also for parricide to enter any church in Constantinople.

We now urge this again: when those same letters reach Your Charity, and indeed even before they arrive, do not cease to plead humbly with the most Christian prince, in our name as well, and to impress upon him that what has been so often and so well established should not be violated by any underhand trick. For the sure and singular bulwark of his reign before the true and eternal King is to preserve unimpaired the council of bishops gathered by the Holy Spirit in the cause of the faith.
(58.) Bishop Simplicius to Acacius, Bishop of Constantinople.

As has been disclosed by the report of priests and of monks serving the Lord in various monasteries, the devil is again disturbing the churches of the Lord. The bishop of Alexandria has been driven out, and a heretic condemned by the whole Church is said to have seized the very place from which he had been expelled. Moreover, with the help of certain people, he is said to have dared to press on to Constantinople, so that the city of Christian princes, which excels in devotion to the truth of the catholic faith, and the Christian people, stunned as they stand in defence of their religion, might be troubled by the depravity of heretics that had already been laid to rest.

But the mercy of God, whose cause this is, did not fail: Timothy, who was rightly separated from the universal Church by the sentences of bishops and the decrees of emperors, was not permitted to approach Your Charity's church or even the thresholds of the houses of the faithful.

We have learned that he is threatening to hold new assemblies on his own behalf, supposing that what universal authority has decreed against him can be undone. The teaching of our predecessors of holy memory stands, and it is wrong to dispute it; whoever is seen to think rightly needs no new assertions to instruct him, for everything by which one deceived by heretics can be taught, or one to be planted in the Lord's vineyard can be trained, is full and complete. Therefore, appealing to the faith of the most clement prince, see to it that the call for holding a synod is rejected, and let your counsel not be slow to reach the Christian ears of the emperor, for Christ is his salvation and the strength of his reign.

So, together with the aforesaid priests and monks, entreat His Piety in season and out of season in our name as well, and present this embassy to His Clemency on our behalf too, so that nothing may be slipped past him. Let him be instructed by the prayers of all alike, so that the enemy may not, amid public business, contrive any plots against the peace of the Church; let him restore the church of Alexandria to its integrity, drive the enemy and parricide from the see of the blessed evangelist Mark, and graciously inquire how the integrity of the catholic faith is kept within the inner chambers of his own palace.

Lest these documents perhaps be corrupted by some fraud of the faith's rivals, we have sent copies, although they can be found in the archives of your church, and you will hasten to present them to His Piety. Let him recognize what is well known and celebrated among all the authorities there: what my predecessor of holy memory, Leo, wrote in answer to the inquiry of Leo of august memory, and how reverently it was received. Let him show himself, as we trust, an imitator of the faith of the man whose empire, by God's favour, he has the more worthily inherited; and let him consider written to himself whatever was handed down to the princes before him in that holy reading. For this is the perpetuity of a kingdom: that through the line of succeeding posterity the successor finds what has come down from his predecessor.

I urge you, therefore, dearest brother, to resist by every means the attempts of perverse men to have a synod held. A synod has never been convened except when something new has arisen in wrong opinions or something doubtful in the statement of doctrine, so that, as men deliberated in common, the authority of episcopal counsel might shed light on any obscurity. This is what the impiety first of Arius, then of Nestorius, and lastly of Dioscorus and Eutyches compelled. And it must be made known — may the mercy of Christ our God and Saviour avert it — that it is abominable, against the sentences of the Lord's bishops throughout the world and of the princes who rule both realms, for the condemned to be restored, exiles brought back, and those banished for wicked conduct acquitted.

Therefore, as must often be repeated, humbly make all these things known to his most clement ears. God will surely come to our help, for the king, holding that his heart is placed in God's hand, knows no other source of his power. Given on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the consulship written above.

Bishop Simplicius to the priests and archimandrites residing at Constantinople. We received Your Charity's letter through our son, the praiseworthy Epiphanius, later than you wished, and we were deeply grieved that, within the Church of God there, the fires of scandal are springing up again, where they have so often been put out by the authority of the apostolic see and the sentence of a universal synod.

For who in the whole world does not know of the condemnation of Nestorius, Eutyches and Dioscorus together with their wicked and perverse doctrines? Who does not know of the deposition of Timothy, the usurper of the church of Alexandria, once again? The Council of Ephesus bears witness to it in earlier times, and the Council of Chalcedon recently; and whoever wishes it to be reopened declares that he does not count himself among the faithful. For the impiety of these men, at the instance of Christian princes too, was cut off not only from the body of the Church but from human society by various exiles, and was struck down by the condemnation of a unanimous verdict.

Nothing need be said now about their error, since, after the tradition of so many of the Lord's bishops who long before us refuted these heresies too in every part of the world, our predecessor of blessed memory, Leo, set out in many discourses of teaching what the integrity of catholic truth follows and what it abhors. With this teaching as a foundation, there is no need for contention, as though judgment were still to be passed on doubtful matters. Rather — and we rejoice that Your Charity is doing so — stand with firm steps against those who have been cast down; do not let the adversary frighten you, or think that victory from on high is slow in coming. He who rises up against you has learned to fall.

We have written these few words to Your Charity in reply to your inquiry, and indeed for your consolation. We would have wished to send some persons, as you desire, because of the needs of the case, were it not that what is required is fully supplied — not now for defending the faith, which is solidly founded, but for repelling heretics and condemned men — by what you remember he wrote to Flavian of holy memory, to the holy synod of Chalcedon, and to Marcian of august memory and to Leo, and by what the bishops of the whole East made known in their own replies to Leo, then emperor. Hence there is no doubt that it cannot be undone, whether what so many of the Lord's bishops decreed earlier when gathered together, or what they said individually, each settled in his own church, holding the same convictions and speaking with different voices but with one mind, condemning the authors and followers of these detestable errors alike.

Wherefore, among so many models of right preaching, we must strive not by new assertion but by a constancy already proven. What this has achieved through you with the Lord's help is shown by the fruit of your labour, which is pleasing to God: through your resistance the robber was not allowed to enter his house, and by the fact that some came out to meet him, he exposed others like himself who perhaps had until then lain hidden.

For good things are not joined to the worst, nor right to perverse. Wholesome things cannot unite with harmful ones, since light has no fellowship with darkness, nor has the believer a portion with the unbeliever.
