Hence those who have chosen the company of such men will necessarily share the fate of the condemned, unless perhaps they come to their senses — especially those who have recently been deceived — and, seeing into what precipices they have been led, scatter the cloud of falsehood and betake themselves to the splendour of the true faith. Out of the apostolic see's devotion we desire that this may come about, for we know that life lies in the Lord's will.

We have also sent suitable letters both to the most Christian prince and to my brother and fellow bishop Acacius. We do not think his silence in so great a matter is to be blamed, for, knowing the faith of this most approved bishop, we hold it certain that his silence was not his own doing. And so that Your Charity may know more fully the content of the letters we have sent to the most Christian prince, we have sent copies by the messenger you sent, on his return. Given on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the consulship written above.

Simplicius, bishop, to Zeno Augustus. Among the works of divine providence, which are always holy and just, hardly any human tongue will be equal to telling the mighty acts of the Lord in our own times as well. For who could either grasp in thought or put into words how, at the very crisis when both causes were in distress, he restored you to peace for the sake of the public prayers and of holy religion? We can only cry out with the prophet as we consider so great a miracle: This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High, which powerfully humbles those who exalt themselves and mercifully exalts those who humble themselves.

In these events too, if the measure of the heavenly dispensation is weighed more shrewdly, it plainly appears that the ruin brought by the faithless crept in for this reason: so that Your Clemency's faith might be proved even amid adversity, and the more you were believed to be pressed by hostile circumstances, the more clearly your magnanimity might shine out. It was for this reason that Your Mildness departed from the city of Constantinople, so that, sought after by the longing of all, you might return with greater glory, and from the dangers of adversity everyone might learn what in you was of benefit to all. This was surely after the example of David's virtue: yielding for a little while with singular patience to the fury of a parricide, he soon returned as victor, implored by the prayers of the peoples, to his kingdom at a loftier height.

Rejoice, then, venerable emperor. Rejoice that your enemies were the very men who proved to be enemies of God, and that you both labored together with the Church and were restored to the empire together with the freedom of the catholic faith. And so that you may show in all things that your cause is one with God's, rely manfully on his help and press on, so that he through whom the usurpers of the state were subdued may also drive out the tyrants of the Church. For just as Your Piety rightly and justly trusts that at that time we implored our God in supplication for nothing else than that rulers of the Roman Empire such as those we now speak of might be restored to us, so you see that it is expected that you show by the quality of your deeds that you are such.

Look, I pray, at the constancy in catholic devotion of Marcian and Leo of august memory, conspicuous to the whole world, and weigh with wholesome reflection that, since those who strayed from their uprightness were unable to stand in the same place, the lawful and divinely appointed successor to royal power will without doubt be the one who has persevered as an imitator of their faith. You owe, most glorious and most clement son and emperor, reverence to the august memory of such great and good men; you owe a return for the gifts of God. He brought you back to their empire: render to God a service like theirs. And since these things, taught by the blessed apostle Peter and lately preached by my lowliness, were rejected by those who were destined to fall, may they by God's favor profit those who are destined to remain in the firmness of the kingdom.

For my part, receiving in the letter which Your Clemency sent an immense pledge of venerable piety, I breathe again with great rejoicing, and I do not doubt at all that your mind will accomplish in divine matters far more than I desire. Yet, mindful of my office, I exhort Your Clemency on this point at greater length because, out of concern alike for your empire and for your salvation, I always long for you to hold fast to those causes by which alone the stability of the present reign is preserved and the glory of the eternal one is gained.

Therefore above all I beg you to decree that the church of Alexandria, freed by Your Clemency's arrangements from an invader no less deadly than heretical, be restored to its catholic and lawful bishop; that those whom he is said to have ordained with diabolical rashness for various churches be expelled, and bishops of the right faith be appointed in their place; and that, just as you have purged your commonwealth of tyrannical domination, so you strip the Church of God everywhere of the robberies and contagions of heretics. Do not allow the iniquity of the times of those whom a spirit rebellious not only against your empire but also against God stirred up to prevail over what so many great bishops, together with distinguished orthodox emperors—the consent of the universal Church—have decreed.

Command that the decrees of the Synod of Chalcedon, and what my predecessor Leo of blessed memory taught with apostolic learning, remain in force inviolate, since what has been laid to rest by their definition can in no way be reopened, nor can anything be received at all that has been condemned by the one voice of the whole catholic truth everywhere. For it is indeed the catholic faith, as you have experienced, that, when wronged, cast down the mighty from their seat, and, when guarded, preserved the humble to be exalted. Therefore Your Piety must take great care to spread abroad yourself the faith which is the source of this gift to you. Given on the seventh day before the Ides of October, after the consulship of Basiliscus and Armatus.
(61.) Simplicius, bishop, to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople.

How effective is the perseverance of priests who make supplication to the Lord, and with what joyful result the zeal shown with sincere minds in defense of the faith is rewarded, is learned from Your Charity's letter, since after such great struggles God's mercy, appointing servants and ministers of his own power in the cause of his own religion, has made those he most approved the victors. For you testify that the church of Alexandria, at last freed by divine judgment, calls us to share in the common joy, since he who had been driven out by the heretic has returned to his see.

Therefore with exultant spirits we pray to Christ our God for the peace of the universal Church, and first for the welfare of the most faithful emperor, to whom, in return for the devotion in which he surpasses all priests, divine goodness grants this peace, which allows us to stand freely as intercessors for the Christian peoples before the heavenly Almighty.

Just as, then, we rejoice at the return of our brother and fellow bishop Timothy, so we wish that, with Your Charity admonishing him, he may be found blameless; for you remember that some time ago he did not show the constancy of a faithful bishop when it was extorted from him that the name of the condemned Dioscorus be recited at the altar. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of the most distinguished Illus.

Simplicius, bishop, to Zeno Augustus. Delivered by the honorable Peter, count of the most noble lady Placidia. Some time ago, when the triumphant glory of your reign in the Lord had spread abroad amid exultation over divine gifts, I remember offering a letter from my lowliness together with the joy of the universal Church. Nor, among all the priests of the catholic faith, could I be the only one, still less the first, to keep silent about the works of our God; for, bearing the care of all the churches, as the blessed apostle Paul says, I claimed for myself in a special way the fullness of joy at the peace restored to them through Your Clemency. For by divine help, the enemies of religion and of the realm being cast down, we were found worthy to have you as victors, and in one and the same outcome, with Christ conquering everywhere in you, both the worship of the true faith and the condition of the empire were restored. Both had been thrown into confusion by the devil thrusting himself in for a time precisely so that, when the adversaries of each had been scattered, the praises of the victor might be the greater.

Hence, having gained the fruit of so splendid a victory, I cannot now either, together with the joy of the universal Church, keep silent about the thanks—which I give without ceasing and which are surely everlasting—that you have restored the church of Alexandria to the ancient and true faith in the person of my brother and fellow bishop Timothy. His letter, which recently reached me, reported that, the profanity of the condemned Eutyches and Dioscorus having been expelled, he had recovered the see of the blessed apostle and evangelist Mark to govern the orthodox, as had already been learned; and he urged us, who were willing in any case, to convey these very things to Your Piety's attention.

So, then, that the peace of your reign may be perpetual and firm, fortify with watchful protection the quiet which you have granted to all in that church, and protect with more devout zeal and more attentive diligence what you have done, with the Lord's help, for the salvation of innocent souls. For it is no less glorious to preserve what you have founded than to found it, and it is plain to all that as much divine favor has been bestowed on you as Your Piety has shown zeal for the Christian religion.

And although your providence does not fail to supply what will benefit the one worship in every part of your realm, and you put the peace of the Church before public concerns, I nevertheless beg—this is what is earnestly asked through us, or rather what we ourselves especially entreat—that you order by a most pious decree that Peter, the invader of the church of Alexandria and for that reason justly condemned, be removed to distant parts. For he is reported, as has been written to us, to be secretly plotting certain things in the city of Alexandria against what you have decreed; let him not infect any of little faith, as he is said to be doing, and draw them over to be instruments of his perversity. Let deadly contagions be far from the innocent, so that through you purity may enter within the fold of the Lord's flock, which imperial authority alone can maintain. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of the most distinguished Illus.

Simplicius, bishop, to Acacius. Delivered by the same bearer as above. How many and how rich are the fruits that constancy of faith and the fortitude of minds devoted to the catholic religion always bear is shown by the labor of Your Charity and of those who together were for some time suddenly troubled by the devil. For when the enemy of Christ and of the realm, soon to fall, invaded the ever-Christian court and shook the Lord's faithful and the people with impious persecution, you overcame his sacrilegious assaults with prayer and vigils, and the heavenly victory reached so far that, with the return of the most religious emperor, a catholic bishop was restored to the church of Alexandria too. Concerning this we promptly shared our joys, exulting in divine grace, and rejoiced together through an exchange of letters.

And although that joy never lacked its fullness, nevertheless our brother and fellow bishop Timothy, made more approved by persecution and not forgetful of his former practice, sent formal letters through our brother and fellow bishop Isaiah and our sons Nilus, presbyter, and Martyrius, deacon, of the church of Alexandria. In them he reported that he had undone what he had previously done out of fear regarding the name of Dioscorus, and he sought pardon for that error, and made us rejoice over the peace of the Church. He has learned in his own case, dearest brother, as Your Love sees together with us, that what we then reproved in him did not go unpunished, and that the tender mercy of God is now reconciled to him.

Since these men had been staying in the City from the moment they arrived, we seized the opportunity offered by our son Peter, the honorable count, who was setting out as though by design; and both of our own accord and at the request of our brother and fellow bishop Timothy and the entreaties of his envoys, we wished this very matter to come to your knowledge, so that even now you might become a sharer in the common joy and, in the peace of the aforesaid church, as we have said, reap with us the fruit of your labor. We also wished you to present our letter on this matter to the most Christian and most clement emperor, so that he too may rejoice, under God's protection, in the gifts of his own devotion and faith, and, at the urging of Your Love, may deign with greater zeal to fortify the churches by sending salutary writings in support of the catholic religion.

Lest, as we have experienced, that ancient serpent pour out in some region the venom of his head, so often cut off, and once again find, God forbid, an opportunity to infect some, let the emperor make provision by a farsighted ordering of his pious decrees. Let him enact religious laws which, as he has clearly proved, commend him to God, so that these men may not lurk in darkness and strike unexpectedly at those who walk in the light, nor, as the prophet testifies, lie in wait to seize those whom they find poor in faith. Above all, for the peace of the Church, let him decree by special order that Peter—who is harbored in the hiding places of certain houses and of men like himself, and whom, in zeal for the faith, he ordered removed from the episcopate—be cast out into foreign lands, as we too have written to His Piety; for it is again asserted that he is ceaselessly plotting something against the emperor's settlement of the faith.

Since, then, we needed to make these things known by the opportunity of a most trustworthy bearer—or rather to give a special admonition—we urge you, when the messenger sets out on his return, or if perhaps some other opportunity arises, to inform us as soon as possible and to hasten to relieve our concern. And so that we might rejoice with perfect joy, the same brother and fellow bishop Timothy also sent us a copy of the petition of satisfaction of those whom Timothy and Peter, both condemned, had led away from the truth of the catholic faith by the terror of their domination, and who now ask for pardon. He desires with priestly compassion to help the fallen, and in view of the divine mercy, which wills that no one should perish, we do not think this should be refused. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of the most distinguished Illus.

Simplicius, bishop, to Zeno Augustus. Recently, when Timothy, bishop of the city of Alexandria and brother and fellow bishop of my lowliness, sent envoys to the City according to the renewed custom, I learned of the victory of your faith in his restoration; for through Your Piety, supported by divine help, both the peace of the empire and the integrity of the catholic religion have returned in their own splendor, the cloud of scandals having been dispersed. For this I remember giving thanks, after God, to Your Clemency, and now too I could not keep silent the homage due to your reign, lest I seem in some way ungrateful if on any occasion I ceased to praise to you so many triumphs, both of the empire and of the churches.

Discharging therefore the duty of due veneration, I beg you to bestow the aid of your protection more zealously on all priests of the right faith, and especially on the bishop of Alexandria, of whose struggle you were both witness and judge; and to order by most pious decrees that Peter, the invader of that see, who could not even keep his own rank in the diaconate, be banished farther from so illustrious a city, lest he perhaps lead astray some of weaker faith and, God forbid, stir up again in that church the scandals you have laid to rest. You have proved in this work that he who, to the joy of the whole world and the exultation of the universal Church, preserves the Roman Empire in Your Clemency has given us the protection of his right hand. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of the most distinguished Illus. Delivered by the envoys of the Greeks.
(65.) Simplicius, bishop, to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople.

Recently, at the request of those who had been sent to us by our brother and fellow bishop Timothy, bishop of the church of Alexandria, I announced our common joy to Your Charity by letter, and declared that we rejoice together at the fruit of a most pious work, namely that a catholic bishop has been restored to that church. We have hastened to signify this again now, so that you may know that joy does not love silence.

Therefore, ever rejoicing in the Lord and desiring that the petitions of our common prayers be joined, I exhort you, dearest brother, now that matters have been settled by God's doing through the most clement and most Christian emperor, not to let careful diligence lapse. Peter, cast down from an honor that was not his due, must not be permitted to live in the region of Alexandria; rather, by repeated representations, ask that he be banished far beyond the borders of his homeland, as we too have requested, lest by the persuasion of his depravity he lead astray any of the unlearned and turn them from the path of catholic truth.

Whatever you obtain from the most religious emperor, let Your Charity take care to bring it to my knowledge and to make us sharers in the actions that concern the safeguarding of the gospel teaching. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of the most distinguished Illus. Delivered by the same bearers as above.

Simplicius, bishop, to Zeno Augustus. Concerning the church of Antioch. I received with joy Your Piety's letter, always venerable to me, in which we found that, with the zeal for the catholic religion innate in you, after defending the faith, which protects you because you have preserved it, you have restrained the audacity of impiety and the crimes committed at Antioch. We rejoice that there is in you the spirit of a most faithful priest and emperor, so that imperial authority joined to Christian devotion has become more acceptable to God and its integrity has been made manifest, since those who took part in the sacrilegious slaughter in the murder of bishops are ordered to perish by fitting punishments. In this you provide both for the peace of the Church and for your empire, since when an insult to God is avenged, the avenger gains favor, and the help of divine grace is won for those whose care has not left sacrilege unpunished.

But, to speak with confidence to a Christian emperor: if the course laid down in my earlier letter, which I remember writing long ago to my brother and fellow bishop Acacius concerning Peter and others by name, had been followed, things could not have come to this point, which has now rightly deserved punishment. For I had instructed that, by a representation made to Your Piety, the aforesaid man, like the others who had invaded the churches of God under cover of the tyrant's domination, be driven beyond the bounds of your empire, lest with his sacrilegious mouth he pour the poison of his pestilent ideas into any of the simpler folk and wound more innocent souls with impious words against the orthodox faith.

But, as it appears, since these things were neglected and thought trivial, it has come about that, as you report, at the altars it was no longer the people perishing by their persuasions, but the bishops themselves, preachers of the faith, priests, perishing by deadly swords. Therefore, if any remnants of such men are found under your rule, order them even now to be driven out into foreign lands, so that henceforth there may be no necessity or cause for punishing them; for it is better to have blocked the approach to sin than to have exacted its penalty.

And since, in your most religious purpose, you judged that the seditions at Antioch could be quelled in no other way than by having a bishop ordained at Constantinople, at the request of those same people, without prejudice to that venerable Council of Nicaea—a measure which you have stated was adopted in his case alone, so that hereafter, according to the definitions of the fathers, the creation of the bishop of Antioch is reserved to the Eastern synod—and since you do not wish what was done for the sake of removing dissension to be regarded as an injury, the blessed apostle Peter holds this pledge of Your Piety, and holds that the mind of a most Christian and most faithful emperor has sworn to these words: that henceforth in the city of Antioch, the ancient custom being observed, the bishop shall be ordained by his fellow bishops of the province. Otherwise, what my brother and fellow bishop Acacius has now carried out at your command might become a practice for posterity and throw into confusion the statutes of the fathers, which you above all keep unimpaired.

Therefore we cannot reject what you have ordained in a holy and religious manner out of love for peace, lest the state of the church of Antioch seem uncertain because of our hesitation, especially since the man who, we read, has been ordained is supported by such high commendation in Your Clemency's testimony that in him both the pain of past wounds can be suppressed and the church which has been found worthy of him can glory.

I have taken care to reply with these words, in discharge of the duty of answering and of veneration, so that you may order the great frauds and crimes of the heretics—which are to be prosecuted by divine and secular laws, and which you have so often proved to be so harmful—to be removed from the memory and company of men, for their impiety, as you see, cannot be restrained by any authority. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, after the consulship of the most distinguished Illus.

Simplicius, bishop, to Acacius, after Calendion had been ordained by him bishop of Antioch. Wounded by the letters of the most clement emperor and of Your Charity concerning the sacrilegious and most deadly slaughter that took place at Antioch, and overcome with grief, I reply and affirm this: if what I wrote long ago about Peter and his other accomplices, and asked you to represent to His Piety together with the other brothers who were present, had been carried out as it ought to have been, the rashness of the heretics would not have gone as far as so great a crime, nor would any necessity have arisen that the said church could be helped in no other way than by a remedy which itself diminished something of its rights.

For although it has contributed to peace that a bishop was ordained for the people of Antioch by Your Charity at the command of the most Christian emperor, and indeed without prejudice to the canons, yet it was not done without arousing ill will, and even he who gave the command testifies that it must not be taken as a precedent hereafter.

For this it is fitting that we give thanks to His Piety, since he so moderated the power of his glory as, with most faithful devotion, to submit what he commanded to the rules of the fathers, and not to allow to be received as authoritative what he has decreed shall be forbidden in the age to come: namely, that what was done out of necessity should suffice in this one person alone, whom you consecrated bishop for the people of Antioch by his command and for the sake of peace, not by any usurpation of your own. In this we recognize that your compliance was not unreasonable, since you testify that, out of regard for the rights of the churches, you held back for a long time, and not without cause, lest you seem to be seeking what you could not refuse so great an emperor in so grave a matter.

Wherefore, dearest brother, not forgetful of the ancient institutions which have been proved to be upheld in you, just as you see that we judge pardonable what was clearly commanded of you, so do you yourself, giving honor to the fathers, strive that there may never be any need to do what you now wish to be cleansed by satisfaction.

Bishop Simplicius to Acacius. Carried by Uranius. We are both astonished and grieved that your concern for charity and faith lies so neglected in your mind, beloved. The most Christian emperor, moved by piety and religion, sent faithful and capable envoys to greet me and to consult me on church matters. Yet you, forgetting both the courtesy we owe each other and your pastoral vigilance, neither chose to write to us nor thought we should be told about matters that concern the guarding of catholic truth. Therefore, dearest brother, understand that what you see being blamed, not undeservedly and with frank affection, must be made good by greater diligence. Devote yourself to the office entrusted to you, rouse your mind with prudence, and keep vigorous watch to protect the decrees of the synod of Chalcedon, so that deadly loss may not creep upon the Lord's flocks through our negligence and sloth.

Recently a report came to us in the customary way from the Egyptian synod, which is very numerous and upheld by communion in the catholic faith, and from almost the whole clergy of the see of Alexandria. It told us that our brother and fellow bishop Timothy, of holy memory, had died, and that John, who was believed to have every qualification for the priesthood, had been put in his place by the united will of the faithful. Nothing seemed to remain but this: as we gave thanks to our God and rejoiced that a catholic bishop had succeeded to the ministry of the deceased without disturbance, he should receive the confirmation he desired through the assent of apostolic moderation as well. But just as I was arranging this according to custom, letters from the most serene emperor were delivered to me. In them he declared that this man was unworthy of the priesthood because he was guilty of perjury, a matter said to be known to your fraternity as well.

At once I drew back and withdrew my decision on his confirmation, so that I would not be judged to have acted too hastily against such weighty testimony. But I was astonished, and not a little, that in the same letter the emperor thinks Peter should be raised to the government of that church. Peter is proved to have long been an associate and leader of heretics. We remember that this is not hidden from you, beloved, and we trust that you know the very instructions by which he was refuted. Beyond doubt he still remains outside catholic communion, and it is certain that we have often written that he should be expelled from that city. Yet the emperor promises that Peter agrees with the definitions of the right faith, though, as I said above, Peter lives as much a stranger to the fellowship of that faith as he is cut off from its communion.

If he now answers that he is returning to it, he cannot enter except by a satisfaction that befits the Christian rules. So he ought not to rise to the summit of priestly dignity. Once reconciled, he ought to be given the remedy that is granted after penitence, seeking help for his soul and not reaching for the rank of highest honor, since he has long been proven perverse. Otherwise, under the guise of one returning, he may seek not the remedy of sincere salvation but an opportunity to spread his depravity. If that were done, we would not so much draw such a man away from error as bring ruin upon the faithful. In this way we would violate the statutes of the synod of Chalcedon and, through a savage union, open the way for ravening wolves to rampage into the church.

Indeed, he is said to be demanded as bishop by the very people with whom he was once separated from catholic fellowship. So it is clear enough that they do not want the right faith. What they seek in a bishop of their own is power for their abominable doctrine. Nor can any trustworthy peace arise between them and those who hold the truth from a source that makes the deadly dominion of heretical minds grow and leads to the pitiable captivity of the catholics.

You are therefore bound on every side by the weightiest considerations, given the nature of your priesthood and your regard for catholic preaching, to resist such great evils and dangers wisely, by whatever means you can. Nor is it right for you, beloved, to act sluggishly in a matter that you do not doubt bears on the cause of your own soul, your honor and your reputation. So seize your opportunities. By ceaseless entreaty for the catholic faith, diligently call the will of the most clement emperor back from whatever harms Christian doctrine, inform it often according to what we instruct, and toward the side that is friendly to truth

do not cease to press it all the more. As the venerable apostle Paul instructed holy Timothy, in season and out of season, you will never stop urging these things, by suggesting, entreating and explaining. From time to time you will also report to us truthfully what is being done and what needs to be done. In this way you will show yourself a faithful servant who multiplies the talents entrusted to him by the Lord's dispensation, if you do not refuse to plead for catholic unity and for the definitions of the fathers, not only in the church over which you preside but wherever you can. Given on the Ides of July, in the consulship of the most illustrious Severinus.
(69.) Bishop Simplicius to Acacius, bishop of Constantinople.

We could hardly have failed to know why the beginning of the bishop of Antioch's tenure was reported rather late. Even so, he himself and his synod have explained it. We did not wish this to happen, but we have readily accepted the excuse that necessity created, since what is not voluntary cannot be charged as a fault. We have also received your letter, beloved, through our brother and fellow bishop Anastasius, who was sent from that region, and we now send you a reply in turn. Having of necessity embraced the episcopate of our brother and fellow bishop Calendion in the bosom of the apostolic see, we count the bishop of so great a city as our colleague in the unity of the college, through the grace of Christ our God.

We are surprised, however, that you have told us nothing about the state of the church of Alexandria. We have never known it to be in such a condition as it is now reported to be, with wicked men using the death of Timothy of holy memory as an occasion to try to hold that church captive. So you must take this up with the most clement emperor, beloved, so that what could be maintained even in the time of the tyrant is not overthrown under his rule. Given on the Ides of July, in the consulship of the most illustrious Severinus.

The holy synod assembled at the church of blessed Peter the apostle, to all the orthodox presbyters and archimandrites in Constantinople and Bithynia, our most beloved sons in the Lord, greeting. Long ago, and from the beginning, your holiness's faith was proven to us and to the apostolic see, the chief of us all. No one can doubt that you hold so steadfastly to true piety toward God that, by the gift of the divine Spirit, you also have the skill to tell the just from the impious, the faithful from the unfaithful, and catholics from heretics.

We glory in this in the Lord. And although we know that nothing in the cause of the faith escapes you, still, in case anyone should perhaps be faint of heart, our concern for our ministry leads us to set before you the words the Lord spoke specially through the prophet Ezekiel: "If the watchman sees the sword coming and does not sound the trumpet, and the people do not guard themselves, and the sword comes and takes a life from among them, that man is indeed taken in his iniquity, but his blood I will require at the watchman's hand." See, then, what care binds us and what commands fill us with fear, so that we may not keep silent about what must be guarded against, not even to peoples who are hostile. For it is more to be feared that we fall under divine punishment. Whoever guards himself on hearing the heavenly voice can without doubt be saved, so the watchman's guilt becomes heavier if his silence has caused anyone to be lost.

We therefore recount what was done when Vitalis and Misenus, placed under our judgment, gave an account of the embassy entrusted to them on behalf of the faith. Since the children of darkness are shrewder than the children of light, they were found to have betrayed the embassy entrusted to them, with Acacius outwitting them and, still more, overpowering them. As swift rumor had already made known, it was established that, contrary to the terms of their instructions, they had rendered forbidden service to that man:

They had been sent specifically to rebuke him in the church in your hearing, to see that Peter was removed from the city of Alexandria (holy Pope Simplicius had often demanded that he be banished into distant exile), and to come to the aid of the catholic bishops, clergy and peoples. Yet in your presence, among the venerable altars, they entered into communion not only with Acacius, who was acting against his instructions, which had been forbidden, but even with the very persons they had been sent to shun. They claimed they had done this unwittingly. Nor were they willing to help the catholic bishops and clergy whom Acacius was persecuting, for they had been won over by crafty seduction. They falsely claimed to have done everything as instructed. But when the letter of Acacius that they themselves had brought was read, it became clear, leaving them no excuse, that they had seen Peter and Acacius to be of one and the same mind. Yet this was the Acacius who had reported to holy Simplicius that Peter had been condemned even before his episcopate and had been driven from the honor of that very episcopate.

While these matters were being examined, it was further reported that Acacius had made John preside over the church of Tyre. This John had been ordained bishop of Apamea by Peter, the tyrant of the church of Antioch, but was not accepted there. Then, after his own ordainer had been driven out, he did not fear to seize that same see. At that time the hypocrite Acacius had them condemned by the apostolic see so severely that even the name of Christians was taken from them, as the records of the proceedings held before him show.

Having discovered these things and worse, we suspended Vitalis and Misenus from the priestly college and from holy communion. As for Acacius, who clings most perniciously to the members of Christ and is scattering the one catholic church of God through cities and provinces, we judged that he is not to be counted among the holy bishops nor among Christians. For how could one who tears the tunic of Christ, which even those who crucified him did not dare to divide, be reckoned among the faithful?

We have weighed and foreseen everything that befits us in the fear of God. The plague of the Eutychian heresy has been extinguished so often, and Acacius is its defender and patron. So that it might not creep like a cancer and destroy the members of Christ, we declare that he was even then cut off from the body of the church by the sentence of anathema, as a rotten part, in obedience to the Lord's words: "If your eye or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you."

We want your charity to know that we hold to the venerable synods of Nicaea, the first of Ephesus, and Chalcedon, against Nestorius and the most impious Eutyches. So, after the sentence that was pronounced against Acacius, the disturber of the church of the whole East, we have assembled again and now send you this letter as well. To it we append that sentence, which it was decided should be sent to Acacius through Tutus, defender of the church, so that no one who wishes to get around the truth may lead the simpler sort astray with most malicious flattery. For if ambushes were not laid for the orthodox by land and sea, many of us could have come to you bearing that same sentence against Acacius.

Now, gathered once more at the church of most blessed Peter the apostle because of the case of the church of Antioch, we have hastened to inform you, beloved, of the custom that has always prevailed among us. Whenever the Lord's priests assemble within Italy on church matters, especially matters of faith, the custom is kept that the successor of the bishops of the apostolic see decides everything on behalf of all the priests of the whole of Italy, in keeping with the care for all the churches that belongs to him. He is the head of all, for the Lord said to blessed Peter the apostle: "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it."

Following this word, the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers assembled at Nicaea conferred upon the holy Roman church the confirmation of decisions and authority. By the grace of Christ, all the successions down to our own time have preserved both. What the holy synod at the church of blessed Peter the apostle decided, as we said, the most blessed Felix, our head, pope and archbishop, has made known through Tutus, defender of the church, and it is contained below.

But Acacius has pushed the impiety of his pestilent domination so far that even when cast down he mocks, and even when cut off he does not stop raging. Though he is held to be wholly outside the body of the church, he still tears its members apart and proves that it was written of him: "When the wicked man has come into the depth of evils, he scorns." He adds worse things to the former ones, persecuting the living though he is himself already dead. By grievous sin his soul has incurred the condition of the second death. As we have learned, after the holy bishop Calendion was recently driven out, he sent into his church Peter, who had been condemned so many times, even by Acacius himself. As a result, if the report is true, a great many catholic priests have given way and left their sees, and our pearls have been thrown to swine and dogs.

Yet let no one be frightened because the condemned Acacius does not rest. Satan has been crushed, and yet he is at work. Christ has conquered his works and conquers them still, and yet the enemy has not withdrawn even now. And since we are certain that you also remember the prophetic reading and have no fear of camps pitched against you, we exhort you most fittingly to look to the Lord, as we do, to persevere to the end, and to hold with steadfast mind to the sentence you will find below.

So that nothing [?] in our letter can be altered by the most depraved minds or interpreted differently, we first made supplication to the most clement emperor, as was fitting. We then sent this same letter in three copies: to you, beloved, to the clergy and people, and to the most distinguished senate. Each and every one of us has signed it, asking God's help that he may cause this letter to reach you safely, escaping ambushes. Given on the third day before the Nones of October, in the consulship of the most illustrious Symmachus. AND IN ANOTHER HAND:

May God keep you safe, most beloved sons. AND THE SIGNATURES OF THE BISHOPS: I, Candidus, bishop of the city of Tibur, have signed, pronouncing anathema upon Peter, usurper of the church of Alexandria, upon Acacius, formerly of the church of Constantinople, and also upon Peter of Antioch, who have long since been rightly and deservedly separated from the episcopate and from the number of Christians, and upon all their followers. In this I follow the authority of the apostolic see, which was set forth by catholic deliberation according to our desire and in keeping with the state of the church. AND FORTY-TWO BISHOPS SIGNED LIKEWISE.

(71.) Here begins the letter of Felix, pope of the city of Rome, to Peter of Antioch, deposing him because he preached that the suffering of Christ's body belonged to the Trinity, saying: "Holy God, holy Mighty, holy Immortal, who were crucified for us."

You are steeped in pestilent doctrines in the impiety of your words, and you have not chosen to follow the holy fathers who went before you and adorned the see of Ignatius of blessed memory, the glorious martyr. (That see

you have somehow obtained to govern, unworthy as you are, I know not how. By your crimes and your profane and impious doctrines you have thought to bring novelty into the catholic church, so that you do not say that Christ was crucified for us. Instead you have most wickedly attributed suffering to the impassible God and presumed to assign death to the immortal Spirit. Nor were you afraid to build up with crafty fabrications things that were not handed down to you by the holy Gospels and the apostles and by the most blessed and approved fathers, and

to press upon the simpler sort the ideas of your own sickness and the scandal of this heresy, so that these things do not merely resemble the earlier heresies but surpass them many times over. You were unwilling either to walk in the truth or to lend an ear to our two letters.)

Now, therefore, I have begun to pronounce sentence against you, or rather Peter, the supreme prince of shepherds, who speaks the truth among the proclamations of the holy apostles, pronounces it. It is pronounced not only against you, who are known to be his equal in name but not in judgment or in faith, since you have strayed beyond all measure from his upright intention and inviolable faith. It is also pronounced against those who, without shame before the marks of the venerable Gospels or the words of the apostles who followed them and of perfect and learned men, cling with unstable judgment to your wicked traditions. They truly follow the bitterness of an evil sect with delight and do not turn away from such execrable impiety.

We therefore say to you, as also to them: "Because you have loved malice more than goodness, and iniquity rather than speaking what is just, you have loved all words of ruin, a deceitful tongue; therefore God will destroy you forever," not only from the see of the church of Antioch but from every city. Let this condemnation stand fixed upon you from me and from those under me who are known to govern episcopal sees, and from Acacius, pastor of the church of Constantinople, and the venerable bishops subject to his jurisdiction, since they too do not agree with your fabrications in any way.

For at one time you said that the Trinity was crucified for us, and not Christ. At another time you said it of the immortal Spirit, following the error of Mani. At yet another time, fleeing these positions after our words had rebuked you, you said that Christ suffered after the immortal Spirit, like Paul of Samosata and Nestorius, who divide the one Son into two sons.

And because you thought you should not stop there, you went on to worse. The hymns that the cherubim send forth unceasingly and with trembling to the Trinity would no longer be referred to the glory of the Trinity, but the whole hymn would be turned toward the Son. In this way you wished to confirm the opinion you had put forward against the simple, as a cancer creeps. And so, turning aside from the truth, you have been hurled into the snares of all the heresies, and you do not preach that Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who is glorified with reverence between the Father and the Holy Spirit, was crucified for us.

What could be more damnable than this? You rob the Father and the Holy Spirit of glory, and you slander the seraphim, as though they were believed not to glorify the Trinity when they say "Holy, holy, holy," but only the person of the Son. What hellish heresy was ever so cruelly shameless as you?

Still running on in these things, you have newly reached the very foundations of blasphemy by calling the Son of God the Father and the Holy Spirit. You follow Sabellius, you bring in confusion, and at the same time you deny the confession of the Trinity in which we were baptized and which we believe and confess.

Who then would not mourn for those who say such things about the holy and inviolable Trinity? It is very fitting for me to refuse [to be consoled] and to pour out my lament in full, since the souls of the simple have been taken captive by this. "They then spread abroad an impious thing as though it were pious. These too we judge to be strangers to the orthodox faith and to the catholic church," and to the communion of our glorious prince Peter, who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven from our Savior.

So let those who wish to be in communion with the apostle also follow his teaching, saying and believing that Christ was crucified for us, and not denying him as did Peter. Peter has lately been condemned because he wickedly and abominably introduced into the Trisagion hymn the new words "who were crucified for us." You know that you did not receive from the apostles that the Trinity was crucified, nor the Father, nor the Holy Spirit, but only the only-begotten Son of God, in the flesh.

Flee, therefore, from communion with him, for it is sacrilegious. Then I will be your companion and in communion with you, and you with me, once the deceitful plague has been driven far from your uprightness. Disciples of Christ and my sons, keep the traditions that you received from the sacred books. HERE ENDS THE LETTER OF POPE FELIX TO PETER OF ANTIOCH, CONDEMNING HIM. As far as its text shows, this letter [?] is found to have been written before the condemnation of Acacius. We found it in a Greek volume, together with letters of others addressed to the same Peter, translated there from Latin. Compelled by necessity, because of the snares of the heretics, we have now translated these letters back from Greek into Latin, copied them out, and attached them to the letters of the same pope written above.
(72.) Here begins the letter of Quintianus, bishop of Ascoli, written to the same Peter of Antioch.

In many ways and by many means you have turned aside from the truth, dearest brother, by doing things contrary to the Lord's mystery and by not following the Gospels, the apostles or the holy fathers. It is a grave matter that you have brought a novelty into the catholic Church against them. Yet you refused to give it up, even though many bishops warned you, above all the most holy Pope Felix, urging you to turn back from it and to remain upright and orthodox in the preaching that brings salvation. Instead, entangled in heresies, you hid the talent of divine Scripture in the ground and did not choose to set it out on the table, that is, to place sound doctrine in people's hearts.

On the contrary, you have sown tares. Who, then, will put up with you any longer as you overturn the gospel of Christ? You do not preach one Son from both, from two natures and in two, our Lord Jesus Christ, and him crucified for us. Instead, with perverse novelty, you go so far [?] as to say that God, the strong, the immortal, was crucified, as if the one essence of the Trinity had been crucified. And not only this: you have also said that there is one nature of God the Word and of the flesh.
But if there is one nature

of God the Word and of the flesh, and the nature of God the Word and of the Father is one, then in some way the Father, the body and the Word have the same nature. But if God the Father, human flesh and the Word do not have one nature, explain how the Father, the Word and the flesh have one nature. How can the created and the uncreated be one nature? And if this is impossible, how are the created flesh and the one who is not created one nature, and not two different ones? And if the Son is of one nature and not of two, what do you say? That Christ was made, as Arius says, or not made, as the Manichaean says?

Where, then, is the nature of Christ's birth in time, and the natural begetting of his divinity before the ages? Where is "Today I have begotten you," and "From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you," and "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and for ever"? And how can you speak of "two natures before the union of God the Word and the flesh," if the one who is from Mary according to substance did not exist beforehand? For if Christ's flesh did not exist before Mary, as the ungodly Valentinus taught, how did two natures exist beforehand?

And whose saying is this? Is it not that of Eutyches, most wretched of men, that one nature came about from two natures? But if you hold his views, how can you reject him while you take up his vile follies? For if this were truly your position, you would accept the holy fathers who assembled against him at Chalcedon.

But explain to me how the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit together are called a Trinity while God is one, if you do not accept that two natures are to be spoken of in the one Son. And if the Trinity is one God, how is it that God the Word, together with our body united to him, should not be called one Son in two natures? But if God the Word and the flesh are one nature, then clearly the Word has been changed and is no longer Word but flesh; and if the flesh has been changed and become Word, it will no longer be flesh. But if no change has taken place in them, how are there not two natures in Christ? For flesh is flesh, even if it is God's flesh, and the Word is the Word, even though he has taken on our flesh.

But if it has been changed, how is the flesh not consubstantial and coeternal with the Father, as the Word is? And if the flesh is of a different essence from the Father, since it is recent while the Father is timeless, how is the Word not recent too, since you affirm that the flesh and God the Word are one nature, and say that he is of a different essence from the Father? But if God the Word and the flesh are not the same nature, how are the flesh and the Word not two natures? If the whole Godhead became flesh, how did the Word remain what he was? But if part of it became flesh, the Word's Godhead has been divided. And if the Word, once incarnate, remained what he was, how is he not unchangeable even when incarnate? And if Christ is not in two natures, how did God the Word, once incarnate, remain what he was?

And if God the Word is passible while the Father is impassible, how is God one and only? And how is their nature one? But if the Trinity is impassible, how did God the Word suffer for us, if he did not suffer in the other nature, that of the flesh? And if everything that suffers is also a creature, how is God the Word not a creature by suffering in the flesh? And if God suffers in the flesh, how does he not suffer in his Godhead? But if he does not suffer in his Godhead, in what way does he suffer in the flesh? And if he suffers in the flesh, how does God himself not suffer too?

And if saying "God suffered in the flesh" is the same as saying "Christ suffered in the flesh," how will it not be the same to say "the Holy Spirit suffers in the flesh," since God is Spirit? But if saying "God suffered in the flesh" is not like saying "Christ suffered in the flesh," how is it possible for God the Word to make the things of the flesh his own any more than for the Father to make the things of the Word his own?

And if God the Word properly suffers in the flesh, how will the Father not also properly suffer in God the Word? And if God the Word died in the flesh, how will he be consubstantial with the Father in immortality? For he who died for us is not immortal, since he died, as it is written. And if one of the Trinity died, how has the Trinity not become a duality? And if the Trinity has never become a duality, how did one of the Trinity die, if the other nature of God the Word, that is, human nature, did not die? But if the Trinity of the thrice-holy cry does not subsist, it is plain that you assert the Trinity to be of one subsistence; and how are you not shown to be a Sabellian? But if there is one nature of the thrice-holy cry in three subsistences, how are you not saying that the Trinity was crucified, and how are you not declaring yourself to be without God in the world, like the Marcionites?
I. Therefore, whoever says that God the Word and the flesh are one nature, and not two natures united and undivided, let him be condemned.
II. If anyone confounds the two natures of Christ by saying that God suffered in the flesh, and not that Christ suffered in the flesh, as the apostle says, let him be condemned.
III. If anyone says that God the Word, impassible and immortal, was changed so as to suffer and die, and does not ascribe these things to his flesh, let him be condemned.
IV. If anyone says that the Trisagion, that is, the thrice-holy cry, was crucified for us, and not our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, let him be condemned.
V. If anyone, after the thrice-holy cry, says that God was crucified for us, and not rather the one Son, to whom the hymn is sung in the middle of the thrice-holy cry, let him be condemned.
VI. If anyone says that the one who was crucified for us is a man, or else God, dividing the natures instead of joining them in his crucifixion, let him be condemned.
VII. If anyone speaks of two persons or two subsistences, and not rather of two natures coming together into one person and one subsistence, let him be condemned.
VIII. If anyone says that the Lord's flesh is of a different essence from our flesh, and not rather consubstantial with us, apart from sin, let him be condemned.
IX. If anyone says "God-man" and not rather "God and man," let him be condemned.
X. If anyone says that the Father's Word was created, and not rather his flesh, let him be condemned.
XI. If anyone says that the Lord's flesh is consubstantial with God the Father, and not rather God the Word, let him be condemned.

XII. If anyone says that our Lord Jesus Christ was without mind and without soul, and had the Godhead in their place, and that it must therefore be said that God the Word suffered in the flesh; and does not rather say that God the Word became man with a mind together with a rational soul, and that the same one must be called impassible in his Godhead but passible in his humanity, let him be condemned.

I have sent you these twelve condemnations so that, fearing their judgments, you may turn back from your most crafty novelty, knowing that we must follow the revelation given to Proclus, the most holy bishop of the church of Constantinople. When the city was shaken by an earthquake and he had gone out to the Campus with all his people, and everyone was crying out in grief, a boy was suddenly lifted into the air by some power and was commanded that in the litany the Trisagion should be said, that is, "Holy God, holy Strong, holy Immortal, have mercy on us," and he was ordered to announce this to the bishop. After three hours he stood on the platform at the feet of that bishop and recounted these things, and when the people performed the litany in this way, those terrors ceased.

So you too must perform the litany in this way, and the wrath that has been brought against you will cease; otherwise the condemnation of our Pope Felix will come upon you. May God guard the world from scandals, <to whom be glory> now and always and for all ages of ages. Amen.
HERE ENDS THE LETTER OF QUINTIANUS, BISHOP OF ASCOLI, TO PETER OF ANTIOCH.
(73.) HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF BISHOP JUSTIN TO THE SAME PETER OF ANTIOCH ON THE SAME MATTER.

A soldier must be armed against enemies, and an athlete against opponents. Our contest, however, is not of the flesh, nor is it fought with oils rubbed on the surface of the body. No one who stays away from this contest will win the prizes of the Godhead if he neglects to take up the contest for the truth with toil. For an athlete is not crowned unless he has won lawfully, and our weapons are not fleshly but mighty through God for pulling down strongholds, demolishing arguments and every lofty thing raised up against the knowledge of God.

So I rouse you with this admonition as a brother, since it is good to obey the fathers and to renounce one's own novelty. Obey the exhortations of Felix, dearest brother, and do not add two sons to the Trisagion. Obey also the seraphim, who glorify the Trinity in the same way, and do not languish in novelty beyond this by devising wicked inventions. For by adding the cross to this hymn you have become a cause of blindness to many.

Why then do you gouge out the eyes of the ignorant by giving force to the assaults of the ungodly, arming Mani, Valentinus and Eutyches when you call the Godhead passible, and even more Paul of Samosata and Nestorius, since you add a quaternity to the Trinity? In whatever way you twist this impious idea, it carries no godliness at all but displays the shapes of many heresies.

For Arius calls the Son lesser, and so does Eutyches, in that he imposes suffering on the divine nature of the Son. So he does not call the Son consubstantial either, just as Eunomius does not. For if in their view the Father is impassible but the Son passible in his Godhead, how is he consubstantial? Macedonius cuts the Holy Spirit off from the Father. Likewise Nestorius divides the one Son into a pair of sons and delights, as you do, in speaking of a quaternity in the Trisagion, impiously adding the cross after the confession of the Trinity.

So cease from this most savage impiety. Do not add scandal to scandal, and do not become the cause of simple people's ruin, lest our pontiff Felix condemn you according to the canons. It will do you no good to say, "I did well to add this, since I confessed the Crucified in the thrice-holy cry." Remove this iniquity from the world, lest it quickly spread everywhere, for impiety is readily accepted, whereas what is better is not accepted at all.

Take this, then, as the admonition of your brother. Silence the roaring of the heretics, and be a shepherd of the sheep and not a wolf. Follow also the most blessed Proclus and the revelation given to him in the Campus at the time of the terrors, and sing the Trisagion plainly, so that the wrath may cease, and do not stir up fierce indignation again. Otherwise, see to it yourself; my brotherhood will be innocent, and I with them, as will those who are writing to you with me about these things.

Guard yourself from scandals, dearest brother. You have learned from Isaiah to say, "Holy, holy, holy." Did he tell you to speak of the cross? But you say, "At that time the Son had not been crucified, and that is why 'who were crucified' was not handed down then." What then? Have the seraphim now added "who were crucified" to the Trisagion, as you say? And you answer, "I do not think so." If you do not know, why do you act impiously? For even then the prophet spoke both of the sufferings of the Word's flesh and of the hymn to be sung in glorifying God with the Trisagion.

And how can you say that you accept the Council of Chalcedon, when you do not glorify the Trinity as it handed down to you, but disobey it, and did not fear it when it said, "Whoever does not think so, let him be anathema"? Give glory wholly and you will be whole; otherwise you alone will drain the cup of evils. HERE ENDS THE LETTER OF JUSTIN, BISHOP OF THE PROVINCE OF SICILY, TO PETER OF ANTIOCH.
(74.) HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF ANTHEON, BISHOP OF ARSINOE, TO THE SAME PETER OF ANTIOCH.

I am deeply grieved over you, dearest brother, because a great scandal has grown up through you, when you ought rather to have cut scandals away. I want to hold back my tears over this, but I am prevented by your heresy, which has been put forward with such malice, for by you the Gospels have been wounded, and the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apostle too. In departing from them you have evidently devised the false doctrine that Christ is not to be confessed simply as crucified for us, but that the cross is to be fitted to the Trisagion, as your earlier letter to Acacius, the shepherd of the church of Constantinople, indicates, in which it is written:

Since you have fallen into impiety, you keep twisting the opinion you put forward this way and that, to see whether you can somehow make it appear lasting and firm to everyone. But when the metropolitans blamed you for it, you did not come to be examined and make amends, nor did you take care to give glory rightly. You are refuted on every side. For we do not call the Godhead passible, as you do, nor do we say that the bare Word was crucified, but Christ Jesus. Wherever the cross is mentioned, there must be a body raised up on it; but in the Trisagion, what place is there for any reference to a body that would give room to speak of the cross?

For you say "Holy God": and who does not know that the Father comes first for all according to the order of the customary doxology, though not by any pre-eminence of divine dignity? Then you say "Holy Strong": and who does not know, according to the prophet Isaiah, that a child has been born to us, Christ Jesus, whose government is upon his shoulder, and who is called and is the Angel of great counsel, God, the Strong? For although he was crucified in weakness, he suffered this by taking on our weak body; but being the strong God, he confidently gave up his own body to the cross. That is why he also said, "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak." And for this reason the prophet himself says, "He took up our infirmities."

All confess Christ as God and man. But you, having spoken only of the strength of Christ's Godhead, and having passed beyond that as well, came to the Holy Spirit and confessed him as immortal, as he truly is.

Whom, then, are you bringing in afterwards as crucified for us? Do you mean Christ? Then you are plainly holding to a quaternity, naming someone other than Christ, the strong God. Or do you say that the Holy Spirit was crucified? What could be more impious than that? Or do you assert that the dispensation of the passion was an illusion? Then, according to the ungodly Manichaeans, our salvation is an illusion.

Do you see how you are falling headlong on every side? Are you ignorant, or do you knowingly and willingly do evil? Now that you have been warned, turn back from your waywardness and follow what you received from the prophet: glorify God with the Trisagion, that is, the thrice-holy hymn. Since it names God incorporeally, with no figure of the incarnation of the Only-begotten set forth, it ought to be sung purely, with no addition of the cross. For whatever anyone may devise, he falls headlong from the right faith.

Since you have received Christ, the Son of God, as crucified for us, according to blessed Paul, who says, "But we preach Christ Jesus, and him crucified," do not deny his name and his passion. Otherwise, as he already said beforehand, "If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than what you received, let him be anathema." "For I decided," he says, "to know nothing among you except Christ Jesus, and him crucified."

But if you deny that he is the Crucified and attach the passion to the Trisagion, how will you not fall under the anathema? It is Paul who pronounces the anathema, the chosen vessel. Put Christ forward and do not deny the cross, nor speak of one in place of the other; for many have been crucified, but only one for us.

So attach his name to the cross, lest you be thought to say that someone else was crucified; for you know the many snares of the deceiver. That is why the three hundred and eighteen and the hundred and fifty handed down the Lord Jesus Christ as crucified, and not the Trisagion. As for those who judge themselves more learned in the law than these fathers, how do they not rather show themselves to be strangers to them?

So the blessed assembly at Chalcedon followed them and confessed one Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. And when on another occasion they had to set forth the Godhead of the Trinity, they said, "Holy God, holy Strong, holy Immortal, have mercy on us." Did they add to the Trinity "who were crucified for us"? If, then, neither they nor those before them added it, how can you bring in this impious novelty? What good does it do anyone to say he accepts these councils if he does not think as they say? None at all. For they themselves declared that those who presume to compose another faith, if they are bishops or clerics, are to be removed, bishops from the episcopate and clerics from the clergy; and if they are monks or laypeople, they are to be anathematized. HERE ENDS THE LETTER OF BISHOP ANTHEON TO PETER OF ANTIOCH.
(75.) HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF FAUSTUS, BISHOP OF APOLLONIAS, TO THE SAME PETER.

Those who come first may be challenged by those who come after, to whom the mystery of Christ is revealed, and the former must then fall silent about their bad doctrine, since they are the worst of dogmatists. Now I have heard from many fellow bishops, dearest one, that you have strayed from the right faith, and this has caused discord everywhere. I therefore judged it necessary to ask you whether these things are so. For it seemed right to me to show you that you ought not to hold such views as to attach the cross to the Trisagion and subject the Godhead to suffering and death, but should simply glorify God as the seraphim do.

For how will [?] be Christian, and how will Christians themselves be faithful, if they do not attach the name of Christ to the cross? When unbelievers hear that the immortal God was crucified for us, they will say it is a scandal to believe in Christ. They will turn away and say: 'We declare our gods, whom the Christians call false, to be immortal. So how did their God, though immortal, die? Clearly this statement is false. For if he died, he is no longer immortal or mighty, but weak, having been changed from his immortality.'

And not only they, but also devout people who share our faith will say: 'These are theopaschites and not Christians, Manichees and not right preachers, worshippers of a quaternity and not of a Trinity, Eutychians and not orthodox, Nestorians and not lovers of Christ.'

But if anyone hears that he who hung on the cross is Christ Jesus, who is rightly called Christ because he was graciously anointed with our mortal flesh (and so they crucified him, the one of whom we hope that he is the one who is to redeem Israel), then he will fall on his face and say: 'I too am a Christian; I believe in him in whom these too have believed.' And the sufferings and death of his body will be believed.

It was for this very reason that the right faith of the six hundred and thirty fathers of Chalcedon was attacked with many curses by unbelievers: they said that there are two natures in Christ. One is passible, mortal, visible and tangible, and this is our flesh. The other is impassible, immortal, invisible and intangible, and this is the inviolable nature of God.

We must therefore confess both in Christ. Do not introduce separation into their unity or divide God from the flesh, and you will not be found to be a Nestorian. Do not deny the difference between Christ's natures, and you will give no grounds for suspecting that you are a Eutychian. Do not confound God with the sufferings of the flesh, and you will not be called an Apollinarian. Do not say that the impassible and immortal God was changed, and you will not be scorned as a Manichee. Do not add 'Christ crucified' in the Trisagion after God the Father, his mighty Son and the immortal Spirit, and you will not hold the heresy of the Samosatene or be charged with holding a quaternity

instead of a Trinity. Do not imagine a Trinity in Christ by holding that one and the same person is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and you will not incur the condemnation of Sabellius. Do not wish to be called a teacher rather than a follower of Christ and so introduce heresy through novelty of doctrine, and you will not defile your own soul. For you know that the apostles were not teachers of novelty; they sought only Christ as their teacher and lawgiver.

Take care, dearest one, not to carry through what is being rumored about you. Do not think of invoking the same Person twice in the Trisagion and the Father and the Holy Spirit only once, and you will not be an Arian by glorifying the Son more abundantly in like manner [?]. Do not make yourself a laughingstock along with those who say that God suffered or who hold a quaternity. If you have been captivated by some loftiness or wisdom in these sayings, turn quickly from evil and do good, so that, as we pray, you may rightly preach the word of truth. Confess Christ, the Son of the living God, who suffered in the flesh for us, and confess him in exactly this way, so that you are not tripped up by heresies. For many deceivers have gone out into the world who do not confess that Christ Jesus has come in the flesh. HERE ENDS THE LETTER OF FAUSTUS, BISHOP OF APOLLONIAS, TO PETER OF ANTIOCH.
(76.) HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF PAMPHILUS, BISHOP OF ABYDOS, TO THE SAME PETER OF ANTIOCH.

Great grief, dearest of my sons, stirs me to cry out in mourning. For you know that in whatever house someone dies, lamentation arises there. How then shall I not grieve over the death of my sons, poured out into error from your vessels? You ought to have been eager, like another brother, to gather them with me to God.

Instead you have done the opposite, beloved of God. You have become their ruin and not their life, bitterness and not sweetness, unripe fruit and not ripe food, tares and not wheat, stubble and not gold, a thorn and not a flower, turmoil and not calm.

Why do you not heed the creeds of our predecessors, so as not to add a quaternity to the Trinity when you say the Trisagion with the addition of the cross? For you wrote: 'In no way will I give up this mention of the cross. For I know that God was crucified, and I always carry the invocation of him over to the cross.'

This is the voice of dragons and poisonous heresies, the gate of hell and the eternal doorkeeper of death. It is a snare for Christians, a hunt for the innocent, a stain on the orthodox, the ruin of the faithful, a perversion of the chaste and a scandal to ascetics. You suppose you are sweet to them, while the statement you have put forward shoots beyond the apostolic boundary, beyond the Gospels, and beyond the creed of the three hundred and eighteen, who knew of no addition to the Trisagion, that is, of this poison of the mind.

Tell me, then: who says that the Godhead endured the cross? Why do you strip God the Word of his robe? Why do you use your own authority to divide the indivisible? Why do you wound the truth? Why do you divide Christ and submit to the rule of Nestorius and Eutyches? Why did you learn from the Samosatene to tear Christ's divine essence away from the flesh? And why, like Valentinus, have you wickedly vomited out the same words, saying that the Immortal was crucified and making the divine nature subject to suffering?

What should I keep silent about, and what should I say? Shall I not call you a Paulianist, when in your writings you have placed 'Christ crucified for us' after the words about the Trinity? Shall I not call you a Manichee, when you convict yourself by saying that God, and not Christ, was crucified? Shall I not name you a Nestorian, when you have shown that the one to whom the faithful sing their hymn, the mighty Son of God crucified in the flesh, is not to be confessed after the Father? Shall I not denounce you as a Eutychian, when you have shown yourself a preacher of a suffering God? Shall I not call you an Apollinarian, when in your invention you have confounded God with the sufferings of the flesh?

So, worn down by great sorrow, I add this to you together with Acacius, who invited me to confirm these things (as the Roman pontiff invited him, and Christ, the bishop of all, invites everyone): Why do you lay waste the Church? Why do you scatter the sheepfolds of Christ? If I speak wrongly, tell me. For I want you to surpass me and many others in the most correct doctrine.

What then shall we say? That Christ was crucified, as Paul says, or that the Immortal was crucified, as you say? That the Christ had to suffer these things, as the Lord says, or that the Trisagion is passible, as you say? What do we say? That the Son of Man had to suffer, as the Lord often said, or that the Godhead suffered, as you have newly introduced?

If, as you claim, the Gospels, the Acts and the Apostle do not speak as they ought, then these things are blameworthy in the eyes of you and of those who follow this folly of yours by saying that the Trisagion was crucified. For these are the approved ones, because they are with you in bringing in a quaternity. But if this is so, why are the divine Scriptures read, if they are not believed and you are? From top to bottom they hand down to you a Christ crucified for us, and not a crucified Trisagion, as you now say. Indeed, the divine Scriptures have even said that those who say God suffered are to be rejected.

Even before this letter I instructed you, as my lord and father and as one of right understanding, to correct and cut away this impious dogma that you have newly put forward, and you did not comply. That is why I now move against you as the first inventor of these impious words. Perhaps this will make you afraid, when your mouth is stopped by someone lower in rank. Then you may more quickly agree to preach rightly the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, adding nothing to them and taking nothing away, and you may keep the chief seat of the see above us.

But if you do not refrain even then, I will impose on you the refusal of communion. For the Apostle says: 'After a first and a second warning, avoid a heretic, knowing that such a man is perverted and sins, being condemned by himself.' Nevertheless we pray God that you may not be condemned by yourself, but may rightly preach the word of truth. HERE ENDS THE LETTER OF PAMPHILUS, BISHOP OF ABYDOS, TO PETER, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH.
(77.) HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF FLACCINUS, BISHOP OF RHODOPE, TO THE SAME PETER, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH.

Hunters of wild beasts are not frightened by their rage or unsettled by their bloodshot eyes. They provoke them instead, because they are confident, knowing they have their javelins with them. In the same way, those who search out the truth do not fear the rage of kings and of the princes of heresies, or their eyes inflamed for destruction. They approach them boldly, in case they can somehow hunt food for God from among them, by making them stop the fury that comes from their evil opinion. For these people resist the Holy Spirit.

When the swallow cannot hold out against the winter, it makes for places where the air is calm. So too devout men who cannot drive back the waves of the heretics take refuge where a temperate faith is found.

Who is it, then, who has stirred up the storms of heresy? Is it not you? You worked on the ears of an innocent emperor and crept by false letters into the heart of the pontiff, that is, Acacius, so that he would receive you into communion. You said: 'Let it not be for me any longer to attach the cross to the Trinity; I will preach Christ crucified. For to whom would a careless word not seem mistaken? Where, then, shall I stay, if I turn away from this and am not received by you? And where is the tender mercy of Christ toward Peter?' Saying these and similar things, once you had turned aside the rod of punishment, you held to your purpose, and now you spread it among everyone.

For you were sifted canonically by our prelates, that is, by Peter, the prince of the apostles, to whom the Lord said: 'Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven.' You did not even deserve to be released through fitting penance, since you resolved within yourself to persist in this condemnation. In this life your only hope is to hope in princes, so that you may return to the place from which you were justly cast down, the holy see. You are therefore altogether more miserable than all men, as one who has scarcely any desire for the living God and for his kingdom of heaven.

Do not, however, whitewash yourself with dust in vain by claiming that you seized the primacy of the priesthood according to the canons. And do not puff yourself up against us, the devout and right preachers, as though you were made of iron, when you are bursting with gall. Even if your fellow heretics are still held fast with you in this to this day, they too, like you, have left to this life such a memorial of folly, since you could not even stay hidden because of the heresies that defeated you.

Why, then, do you shrink from Arius and imagine that you do not hold his views? Where is consubstantiality to be found with you, when he does not accept it at all? For you said: 'I hold that one of the Trinity is passible, not the Father or his Spirit, but his Son.' You have become a follower of the Arian heresy, convicted by your own words, since Arius too had said this: 'If the Son is passible but the Father is not, how are they consubstantial?' So do not reject him in word while honoring him in deed. For you

not only speak his words but go even further. It was for this very reason that the fathers decided to say 'Trisagion' as the seraphim do, because it confirms consubstantiality. Through this venerable cry his blasphemy has been rebuked until now, and as a result many of his followers have chosen consubstantiality and flocked to our church.

Where, then, is consubstantiality with you? See, you have perverted the statement that the synod of the illustrious fathers gathered at Nicaea made against Arius. For he does not want to interpret the Trisagion as a wise utterance; he even [?] dreads its very sound, like a deaf asp stopping its ears, as if he were hearing something wicked.

Now you have opened your ears to him by adding the death of the cross to the Immortal. See, on this point he agrees with you, singing in the Trisagion 'who was crucified for us'. He knows that this removes the consubstantiality of the Trinity, and he takes it as proof that the Father is greater, who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up to death for us all.

But you say: 'Why, then, do you find fault with the Apostle?' Far from it! It is you I find fault with, together with your companion Arius, because you have corrupted things that were well said, not knowing what they mean. For in the same way that someone did not spare to hand over his eternal Word to death, he handed over himself [?]. 'But that is not what is written!' Far from it! But among you these things are said as by people who do not confess that Christ is of a twofold nature: the same one passible and mortal as man, and the same one impassible and indestructible as God.

As God, together with his own Father, he did not spare his own flesh, when he said to the wicked: 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.' It is as if he were saying: "Destroy by death the tabernacle of David, which had already fallen through disobedience, and in which I graciously dwell, so that I may raise it from death.
