You must not think, as you suppose, that I was crucified out of the power of God; I am crucified out of weakness. The weak flesh was hung up and pierced with nails, but this did not reach me, because my nature cannot receive it; it is impossible for such things to come near it. So I was not put to death in the divine spirit. I was put to death in the flesh, as my own body, and my spirit gives it life, because whatever I loose, I will also bring to life along with it.

Do not, then, attach to me what belongs to my created flesh, and do not bring creaturehood, being made, suffering or death into the One of the Trinity. For what was, both is and will be. Do not try to bring in anything beyond this, and do not deprive my flesh of the Godhead. For I am by nature his Word. I gave the flesh what is mine, not by transferring to it what is mine by nature, but by grace. And it gave me what is its own, not by transposing to me what is naturally its own; rather, I willed to come from it by grace, as though clothed round with it, an animate man.

So, although I am by nature the Son of God, I confess that I am also by nature the Son of Man. For this reason Paul, speaking of me as God, says that I am the creator of all things: 'whether principalities or powers, all things were created through him and in him.' But when he speaks of me as man, he says that I was made: 'Consider,' he says, 'Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who was faithful to the one who made him.' For the distinctive character of each nature is preserved in me.

Whoever, then, does not preserve these for me, but asserts that I am of one nature, is saying that God, having become man, is no longer God, neither uncreated nor impassible but passible. Such people leave me utterly stripped of what is mine. That is why I inspired the authors of the faith to call the Trisagion consubstantial, since it is proof of the Trinity and a display of divine reasoning, a refutation of Arius and a muzzle for Sabellius. And those who had been led astray by these men were instructed in the right faith of the fathers.

But now, through Peter, who has been justly condemned, the orthodox are becoming Arians and are made Sabellians. They deny that I am of equal honor with the Father, and make me lesser, as though girded as his subordinate. So the hymn in the Trisagion is not sung to me equally; instead the suffering of the cross is coupled with me, and the Trisagion is not sung to three subsistences, but the hymn of the Trinity is directed to me alone. For in the Trisagion these people apply the crucifixion to me, so as not to be caught saying that the Holy Spirit, the Immortal, was crucified for us.

Peter's evil opinion has gone beyond and surpassed every heresy. So at the examination of all that is to come, the Arians will make excuses for themselves, though in vain, as will the other heresies, saying: 'Lord, you said, The Father is greater than I, just as the apostle Peter taught when he said: This Jesus whom you crucified, God has made both Lord and Christ. That is why we too believe that you were made and are not consubstantial with the Father.' But this man we are speaking of,

what excuse will he give? By what Scripture will he say that a crucified Trisagion was handed down to him? For we know that Isaiah says the seraphim glorify the Trinity consubstantially in the Trisagion. He does not say that they cried, 'Immortal Father, but mortal Son'; they cried consubstantially, 'Holy, holy, holy.'

Did the Gospels hand this down? No, he is refuted by them, for they said: 'The Son of Man is going to be handed over to be crucified,' and: 'The Son of Man must suffer many things,' and: 'Everything that has been written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled,' and: 'They will hand him over to the Gentiles, and they will crucify him,' and: 'Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?' Not only the apostles preached these things; the angels did too, saying: 'Remember how he spoke to you in Galilee, saying that the Son of Man must suffer many things.'

These things are to be said not as though the Godhead were ever separated from him anywhere. They persuade you rather that the Godhead remained impassible and immortal, assigning the sufferings and death separately and distinctly to its own flesh. Where, then, does this dogma of 'the cross in the Trisagion' come from? From the fathers? No, they too will be his accusers, since they never asserted this. So, since he has no excuse, let him be silent!" Therefore come to your senses;

be watchful, so that you remain within the judgment of the fathers. For know that neither kings nor powers nor princes will be able to free you from the eternal bond unless, convicted, you give up your temporal dignity and sit like Job on the dunghill outside the city. This is my greeting to you, out of concern for you, according to God in Christ Jesus and not according to men. HERE ENDS THE LETTER OF FLACCINUS, BISHOP OF RHODOPE, TO PETER OF ANTIOCH.
(78.) HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF ASCLEPIADES, BISHOP OF TRALLES, TO THE SAME PETER.

See, dearest friend, the world is filled with the scandal of your exposition. The imperial court has grown anxious, and the shepherds have been roused to mourn over you, as is only right. I beg you, then, give one word of right preaching, so that you may establish the truth by confessing, together with all, the Son of God crucified for the world, and so that he and his name are not cast aside through you. Otherwise his cross is spoken of perversely in the Trisagion.

Do you come before the fathers who assembled at Nicaea, so that your definition should rank above theirs? But you say, 'I added the cross to the Trisagion because of Nestorius, since he separates the divinity in Christ's crucifixion.' And what of it?

Is Nestorius's idea something new? It had its beginning with Paul of Samosata, a man of unsound mind. The holy fathers at Nicaea did not find him still alive, but they condemned his doctrine, and it came to an end. They did not do this by writing 'crucified' into the Trisagion, since that would have seemed very grave indeed to them. Instead they laid down that the Trisagion should be sung only in the mysteries, just as the seraphim say it, and they made no addition to it and took nothing away.

Later, however, this impiety was revived and strengthened under the impious Photinus. The fathers of holy memory who gathered at Constantinople did not find him alive either, but they nevertheless condemned his doctrine, so that no one should believe in two sons. For this reason they confessed one Son in their definition. Did they say that the Trisagion was crucified for us? No, for they followed the definition of the earlier fathers and judged that their teachings must be followed, so that the Trisagion should be heard only in the mysteries, without reference to suffering, as the seraphim say it, and without 'crucified'.

Then, when Nestorius was pressing on and upholding the impious teachings of his predecessors, Paul of Samosata and Photinus, those who were assembled on his account at that time around the most blessed Celestine and Cyril checked impieties of this kind, and they did not add the cross to the Trisagion. Do you think you are wiser than all of these, or more full of the Holy Spirit than those who possessed knowledge? Your addition of the cross to the Trisagion, therefore, is an implacable blasphemy.

Moreover, after these holy fathers, when a very severe earthquake struck Constantinople, small and great, rich and poor, slave and free left the city and ran together into the Campus. They would rather perish there in the frost and winter than fall with the city. God in his mercy spared them and revealed to the most blessed Proclus that they should sing the Trisagion with a litany to appease his wrath. This was made plainly known not to one or two people but to the whole world. Did God add that the cross should be spoken in it? Not at all, for that would have been an insult to him. For he said that it should be sung: 'Holy God, holy Mighty, holy Immortal, have mercy on us.'

How then have you dared to add the cross, going beyond God and even beyond the fathers? By bringing the cross into the Trisagion you confuse the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit, so that for you the Father is not only Father but also Son, the Son is not only Son but also Father, and the Holy Spirit is not only Spirit but also Son.

Therefore, if anyone adds the cross to the Trisagion apart from the Son of God, let him be anathema. If anyone brings a quaternity into the Trisagion by adding Christ crucified after the Trinity, let him be anathema. If anyone confuses the Trinity, saying that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are the same, let him be anathema.

If anyone divides the one essence of the Trinity into two, let him be anathema. If anyone cuts the one Son into a duality of sons, let him be anathema. If anyone says that the Word of God and the flesh are one nature, ignoring the difference of the natures, let him be anathema.

If anyone confuses the divine nature of the Son with the sufferings of his flesh, and does not confess that he is impassible in spirit but suffered in the flesh, let him be anathema. If anyone speaks of God as passible, or says that God tasted death, as though he had come to these things by his own good will after undergoing a change, and does not confess that as God he was not under the dominion of death, but that he put death to death through the mortal flesh that he assumed, let him be anathema.

For we believe that Life is life and does not fall back into death. As for you, recognize the points on which you have spoken wrongly, and cut them away. Yet may the grace of God be, as indeed it is, with those who rightly preach the word of truth. HERE ENDS THE LETTER OF ASCLEPIADES, BISHOP OF TRALLES, TO PETER OF ANTIOCH.
(79.) GELASIUS TO THE BISHOPS THROUGHOUT DARDANIA.
TO HIS MOST BELOVED BROTHERS, ALL THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT DARDANIA, BISHOP GELASIUS. AS IT WAS ALSO SENT TO ALL THE BROTHERS THROUGHOUT

DALMATIA. Now that we are first able to breathe again after the storm of continual wars, which the conditions of the times have stirred up without ceasing both in those provinces and in these, we have thought it right to address all the Lord's priests throughout Dardania with the concern of brotherly love.

We write first because, when we took up the governance of the apostolic see, the public turmoil, as has been said, held us back, and we could not announce by a letter of our own, as was the custom, the office of the sacred stewardship entrusted to us, so that your fraternity might rejoice in the gift of the Lord's communion with us. Next, we write so that an exchange of letters might tell how each of us was faring after such great bitterness and worldly hardship. Finally, if any church matters need to be reported, matters that must always be watched with pastoral vigilance because of the snares of the perpetual enemy, we write so that we might make them known to one another.

Prompted by these reasons, we have taken care to send the present letter through our brother and fellow bishop Ursicinus. We greet you first and then urge that, while we bravely endure with the Lord's help the devastation of passing things, we should be more alarmed lest we suffer, God forbid, the loss of eternal life. Therefore let your love attend for a little while to the dangers that the good of catholic truth requires us to guard against.

Among the Greeks, among whom many heresies undoubtedly abound, a controversy arose about forty-five years ago concerning the incarnation of our Lord and Savior. Eutyches, formerly a presbyter of Constantinople, rushed headlong into blasphemies, saying that we ought to believe in only one nature or substance in the Lord Jesus Christ, namely the divinity alone, while the reality of the flesh he assumed was done away with entirely.

This impious and perverse invention, allied with the Marcionites and Manichaeans, would without doubt destroy the whole mystery of our salvation. For, as the authority of venerable Scripture declares and the teaching of our forebears testifies, it is certain that the Redeemer of the world, God, was born of the Virgin Mary at once wholly God and wholly man, and appeared visibly in this world. It is established that he suffered as such and rose from the dead, and so spent forty days with his disciples. It is clear as broad daylight that he ascended into heaven, and, as the angel testified, it was said that he will come to judgment in the same way, so that the Son of Man, whom the blessed martyr Stephen saw standing at the right hand of the power of God, may appear openly, and his persecutors may look on him whom they pierced. All this certainly cannot hold without the substance of human flesh. The flesh he assumed was glorified by the Godhead without being wholly absorbed into it.

Hence the blessed apostle John says: 'Whoever denies that Christ has come in the flesh is the antichrist.' And the glorious apostle Paul openly declared how we ought to believe in our Lord Jesus Christ even today, saying: 'In him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily.' With this short phrase, by heavenly preaching, he overthrew both the Arian plague and the Eutychian one we have mentioned. For nothing is lacking where all the fullness of the divinity is said to dwell, and the word 'bodily' proves that he remains truly in our body.

On these matters, moreover, it is certain that the Greeks have often been refuted by the apostolic see, both through the holy Leo of blessed memory and through his successors, as their own documents, which we have in our possession, show beyond doubt.

Now, however, although they do not dare to profess this pestilence itself, they defend with ruinous frenzy those who were in communion with such men, who were rightly condemned by the apostolic see in accordance with the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon and died obstinate under that same condemnation. And they are striving to force the recitation of their names on the catholic Church. If these men were received, God forbid, we would in consequence incur the contagion of the depravity with which they joined themselves in communion. In the same way, if the name of Arius or of any heretic were admitted to the Church's recitation, God forbid, a share in his detestable error would be taken on along with it.

These people admit the error itself, but they think catholic communion should be relaxed for them on this condition: that they be allowed to recite in church the names of those who betrayed the faith. They are striving not so much to correct themselves as to infect catholic purity with the contagion of the faithless. Therefore, with the affection of brotherly love, we have not ceased to warn your love that, if any who sow such things should happen to come into your regions, they must be shut out by every means, so that your communion with the see of the blessed apostle Peter, as our fathers handed it down, may continue unimpaired and wholly unshaken.

Certainly, if anyone thinks your ears should be assailed with this underhand scheme, hasten with pastoral concern to report it to us as quickly as possible. Then all catholic priests may confer with common zeal and in catholic deliberation for the house of the one Lord, so that what belongs to the orthodox definition may be kept inviolate, and so that reasoned deliberation may determine how far it is fitting to help those who err.

Let your love also take care to pass these things on to all the neighboring provinces and nearby bishops, so that all the heads of the churches may receive instruction in the truth and be able to avoid deadly falsehood. AND THE SUBSCRIPTION: May God keep you safe, dearest brothers.

TO THE HOLY LORD, THE APOSTOLIC AND MOST BLESSED FATHER OF FATHERS, GELASIUS, POPE OF THE CITY OF ROME, THE HUMBLE BISHOPS OF DARDANIA. With fitting devotion we have received the most salutary precepts of your apostleship, brought by the religious man Tryphon, our son. We give the greatest thanks to almighty God and to your blessedness that you deigned to visit us with pastoral admonition and gospel teaching, holy lord apostolic and most blessed father of fathers. For it is our desire and our prayer to obey your commands in all things and, as we have received from our fathers, to keep [?] inviolate toward the apostolic see, which has been entrusted to you for your life and merits. It is also our desire to guard the orthodox religion, of which you are the preachers, with faithful and blameless devotion, as far as our rustic understanding allows.

Even before your command we shunned the fellowship of Eutyches, and of Peter and Acacius and all their followers, as a kind of pestilential contagion. Much more now, after the admonition of the apostolic see, we must keep ourselves from that same pollution. And there may be others who have followed or will follow the sect of Eutyches or of Peter and Acacius, or who think they should mix with their accomplices and associates. We desire to serve the apostolic see blamelessly according to the divine precepts and the statutes of the fathers, and by us such people

are to be shunned in every way. And if any, perhaps with perverse intent, should think that they ought to separate themselves from the apostolic see, which we neither suppose nor wish, we declare that we have no part in their fellowship. For, as has been said, we keep the precepts of the fathers in all things and follow the inviolable institutions of the sacred canons, and so we strive to obey that apostolic and unique see of yours with common faith and devotion.

Your blessedness, in its innate kindness, has given us occasion to make requests. We have therefore entrusted certain requests to the aforementioned religious man Tryphon, our son, the bearer of your precepts. With earnest prayers we beg your apostleship to deign to receive gladly what he puts forward on our behalf, which we consider just and reasonable. If our petition deserves to be granted, order one of your angelic see to be sent to us along with the man of religion we have often mentioned, so that in his presence the things required by the orthodox faith and the integrity of your command may be set in order.

AND THE SUBSCRIPTION: I, John, bishop of the holy church of Scupi, a metropolitan city, consenting to this reply given by us and to everything contained above, have signed with my own hand. I, Samuel, bishop, have signed as above. I, Bonosus, bishop, have signed as above. I, Verianus, bishop, have signed as above through Valentinus the archdeacon. I, Faustinus, bishop, have signed as above. I, Ursicinus, bishop, have signed as above.
(81.) HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF POPE GELASIUS TO LAURENTIUS OF LYCHNIDUS.

Your love's long letter filled us with great joy in the part where it was reported that in the church of Thessalonica, and likewise in others, when our predecessor's letter about the excesses of Acacius was read, everyone pronounced anathema on him, and no one joined in the communion of the traitor.

You urge us with brotherly love to administer a kind of medicine of faith to the bishops throughout Illyricum and to others. This was already done most abundantly by our predecessor of blessed memory, but it is also the custom of the Roman church for a newly appointed bishop to send out the statement of his faith to the holy churches. I have therefore taken care to restate these same things very briefly, so that, because this letter of ours is short, the reader may learn without weariness the faith by which we must live according to the statutes of the fathers.

We confess, then, our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born of the Father before all ages, without beginning, according to the Godhead. In the last days the same was made flesh from the holy Virgin Mary and became perfect man, of a rational soul and an assumed body. He is homoousios with the Father according to the Godhead and homoousios with us according to the humanity. For a union of two perfect natures has come about in a way beyond words.

For this reason we confess one Christ, the same Son of God and of man, only-begotten from the Father and firstborn from the dead. We know that according to the divinity he is coeternal with his Father, and according to that divinity he is the maker of all things. After the holy Virgin gave her consent, when she said to the angel, 'Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word,' he deigned in a way beyond words to have a temple built for himself from her, and he united it to himself. For he did not bring down from heaven a body coeternal with him and of his own substance. He took it from the mass of our substance, that is, from the Virgin.

When God the Word received this body and united it to himself, he was not changed into flesh, nor did he appear as a phantom. He preserved his own essence unchangeably and immutably and united to himself the firstfruits of our nature. For God the Word, the Beginning, in his great goodness deigned to unite these firstfruits of our nature to himself. He is not mixed, but was seen to be one and the same in both substances, as it is written: 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.' For Christ Jesus is destroyed according to my substance, which he assumed, and he himself raises up his own temple once destroyed, according to the divine substance, by which he is also the maker of all things. After the resurrection he has never left his own temple and its union with our nature, nor can he leave it, because of his kindness beyond words. The Lord Jesus Christ himself is both passible and impassible: passible according to the humanity, impassible according to the divinity.

God the Word, then, raised up his temple and brought about in himself the resurrection and renewal of our nature. After he rose from the dead, the Lord Christ showed this to his disciples, saying: 'Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.' He did not say 'as you say that I am' but 'have,' so that by considering both the one who has and what is had, you may see that a union has come about, and not a mixing, a conversion or a change. For this reason he also showed the marks of the nails and the wound of the lance, and ate with his disciples, so as to teach in every way that the resurrection of our nature had been renewed in him. According to the blessed substance of the divinity he is unchangeable, immutable, impassible, immortal, lacking nothing, and he brings all sufferings to their fulfillment. For this reason he allowed sufferings to be inflicted on his own temple, which he raised up by his own power, and through the perfecting of his own temple he brought about the renewal of our nature.

There are those who say that Christ was a mere man, or that God was passible, or that he was changed into flesh. Some say he had a body that was not united with him, or that he brought it down from heaven, or that he was a phantom. Others say that God the Word was mortal and needed to be raised by the Father, or that he assumed a body without a soul or a man without a mind. Still others say that the two substances of Christ were mixed and confused and became one substance, and they do not confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is two natures unconfused but one person, since there is one Christ, one and the same Son. All these the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.

These, then, dearest brother, are the things you asked us to send as an antidote, so that no one may shun the bitter or regard the sweet as harmful [?]. We had also planned to send some members of our own assembly, if the circumstances of the time had allowed it. We believe it will be timely to do so when, with the Lord's help, the correction of those regions has been reported to us by a most complete

embassy, as we trust it will be. We also hope from the mercy of our God that the most clement and most Christian emperor will join his agreement and help to this preaching of ours. Then, for the sake of the faith in which he is strong, he may restrain in those regions those who, with new petty questions and according to the elements of the world, as the chosen vessel foretold, put together superfluous and empty things and refuse to be bound by sound teaching.

But you, as the same apostle says, did not learn Christ in this way, if indeed you have heard him and been taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus. That truth can surely be grasped by anyone who has kept the institutions of the orthodox fathers, as has often been said already. May God keep you safe, dearest brother.

Bishop Agapetus to Justinian Augustus. Venerable emperor, we rejoice that you burn with such zeal for the catholic faith. Throughout your most pious life you have graciously shown a devout concern to preserve and strengthen concord among the churches, and you desire that one faith, consistent and firm in every respect, be preached to all Christian peoples.

Nor is it surprising that your clemency holds fast to a purpose so pleasing to God, since nothing advances your empire more blessedly than the growth of religion. I will therefore gladly sing this in the prophet's words: "Our mouth is filled with joy and our tongue with gladness," because we see your most flourishing reign adorned every day with divine blessings.

For you desire, venerable emperor, that we too confirm with our authority the letter in which your piety set out your faith. That letter was recently sent through the bishops Hypatius and Demetrius to our predecessor of blessed memory, John, bishop of the Roman see, and the aforesaid prelate confirmed it. We praise it and we embrace it. We do so not because we grant laymen authority to preach, but because we confirm and strengthen your zeal for the faith, which agrees with the rules of our fathers. Through this zeal the church has already gained unity, and we trust that the steadfastness of your Christian faith will bring the remaining members of the catholic church back into its body.

We append below the text of this profession, that is, of your letter, and with our authority we confirm the zeal that you wholeheartedly show toward God. We declare that this faith agrees with all the rules of our fathers and accords with the teachings of the apostolic see. By the present definition we confirm that this faith is in harmony with the rules of the fathers, so that no suspicion of heresy may remain. We decree that anyone who attempts to oppose this, our catholic faith, shall be cut off from holy communion.

Accordingly, Cyrus and his followers were already suspended from the communion of the catholic church for this madness and have persisted in their faithlessness until now. Unless they make canonical satisfaction and come to follow the apostolic teaching, we will by no means allow them to be restored to holy communion. Indeed, we also subject them to anathema as heretics. For we judge it right that whoever has refused to obey our decrees should not stain the order and purity of the church. The text of the letter is as follows.

Bishop Vigilius to his most glorious and most clement son, Justinian Augustus. Among the countless cares that burden the imperial majesty, we recognize the praiseworthy purpose of your clemency. The enemy of the human race had scattered seeds of discord in the Lord's field, and you removed them all. You then hastened to restore all the Lord's priests to unity and concord, after they had first submitted professions as a testimony of their conscience. These professions showed that they adhere to the definitions and judgments of the holy fathers, of the four venerable synods, and of the prelates of the apostolic see.
So that the form of these professions may be handed down to posterity as an example of church peace to be embraced, we declare that it is inserted in the present document exactly as it stands.

Copy of the first profession, which they made at Saint Euphemia. All the faithful ought to pursue peace and holiness with everyone, and the priests of God most of all, for without these, as the apostle says, no one will see the Lord. We, therefore, follow the apostolic teaching and are eager to preserve concord among the churches, and so we make the present statement.

First, we receive the four holy synods and the fathers who sat in them. These are the synod of Nicaea, of the three hundred and eighteen; the synod of Constantinople, of the one hundred and fifty; and the first synod of Ephesus, of the two hundred. The most blessed Pope Celestine of elder Rome is known to have presided at Ephesus through his legates and representatives, namely the most blessed Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria, the bishops Arcadius and Projectus, and the presbyter Philip.

The fourth is the synod of Chalcedon, of the six hundred and thirty holy fathers. At these synods the most blessed popes of elder Rome, the predecessors of your holiness, each in his own time, presided through their legates and representatives. Whatever was defined, judged, established or arranged in all the acts of the council of Chalcedon and of the other synods named above, by common consent with those legates and representatives of the apostolic see, we promise to follow in all things and in every respect, as it is found written in those four synods. This applies whether the decisions concern the faith or any other matter, and whether they were made by judgment, by decree or by arrangement. We promise to follow them unshakably, inviolably, blamelessly and irrevocably, without any addition or alteration. We will not admit anything contrary to them, on any pretext or by any innovation, that would tend to censure, revise, alter or injure them, nor will we consent to those who presume to do anything of the kind.

On the contrary, whatever was declared orthodox there by common consent with the legates and representatives of the apostolic see, we revere and receive as orthodox. Whatever they anathematized or condemned, we too anathematize and condemn. Everything that is found recorded in those synods as judged, defined, established or arranged by common consent with the representatives of the apostolic see, we preserve irrevocably and unchangeably.

We also promise to follow and keep in every respect the letters of Pope Leo of blessed memory and the decrees of the apostolic see that have been issued both on the faith and on the authority of the four synods named above. We anathematize every person in the ecclesiastical orders and ranks who attempts, on any pretext or in any dispute, to go against what we have promised above.

As for a written statement on the matter of the Three Chapters, which is the subject of the dispute, I personally made none against the decree of the most pious emperor and of your beatitude. But I wish and consent that all such statements that have been made be handed back to your beatitude in accordance with this form.

As for whatever wrongs have been done to your beatitude and to your see, I did not commit them. But since we must hasten by every means toward the peace of the church, I ask pardon as though I had committed them. And because, in the time of discord, I received into communion people whom your beatitude had excommunicated or had not received, I likewise ask pardon.

This profession was made in this form by Menas, bishop of Constantinople; Theodore of Caesarea in Cappadocia; Andrew of Ephesus; Theodore of Antioch in Pisidia; and Peter of Tarsus. Many others also did the same.

Likewise, copy of the profession which the remaining bishops made to us on the day of the Theophany. We know how many good things are brought about by the peace of God. It guards the hearts and minds of the faithful and gathers them together, so that they think one and the same thing in the right confession of faith and in carrying out the divine commandments. It also makes God gracious to those who are in agreement about what is right.

Eager, therefore, to preserve unity, we make it known to the apostolic see of your beatitude that we have always kept, and still keep, the faith handed down from the beginning by our great God and Savior Jesus Christ to the holy apostles. They preached it throughout the whole world, and the holy fathers explained it, above all those who assembled in the four holy synods.

We follow and receive these fathers in all things and in every respect. First are the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers who assembled at Nicaea. They set forth the holy creed, or statement of faith, and anathematized the Arian impiety together with those who held or still hold it.

We also receive the one hundred and fifty holy fathers who assembled at Constantinople. They explained that same holy statement of faith and clarified the doctrine of the deity of the Holy Spirit. They condemned the Macedonian heresy, which attacks the Holy Spirit, and the impious Apollinaris, together with those who held or still hold the same views as they did.

We also receive the two hundred holy fathers gathered at the first synod of Ephesus. They followed that same holy creed, or statement of faith, in every respect. They condemned the impious Nestorius and his wicked doctrines, together with those who at any time held or still hold views like his.

In addition, we receive the six hundred and thirty holy fathers who assembled at Chalcedon. They agreed in every respect with the three holy synods named above. They followed the creed, or statement of faith, that the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers set forth and the one hundred and fifty holy fathers explained. They anathematized those who presume to teach, expound or hand down to the holy churches of God anything other than that creed. They also condemned and anathematized Eutyches and Nestorius, together with their impious doctrines and those who held or still hold views like theirs.

This being so, we affirm that we have kept and still keep everything judged and defined by the four holy synods named above. Although those four holy synods were held at different times, they kept and preached one and the same confession of faith. We also receive and embrace the letters of the prelates of the Roman apostolic see, both those of Leo of holy memory and those of others, which were written about the right faith and about the four holy councils, or about any one of them.

Since, then, we have kept and still keep all these things, and we agree with one another about them, it is necessary to hold a discussion about the Three Chapters, which some have called into question. We therefore ask that your beatitude preside over us, in calm and with priestly gentleness, with the holy Gospels set before us. We ask that these chapters be laid before us all, examined and discussed in common deliberation. We ask that the question then be brought to a conclusion that pleases God and agrees with what the four holy councils defined. This serves to increase peace and concord among the churches: once all dissension has been removed from our midst, what the four holy councils defined will be kept unshaken, and reverence for the holy synods will be preserved in all things. To this we have also signed our names.

In this manner our brothers and fellow bishops Eutychius of Constantinople, Apollinaris of Alexandria, Domninus of Antioch in Syria, and Elias of Thessalonica, along with the others who had not made the first profession, either signed this second profession or made the same profession separately.

With these matters thus arranged, venerable emperor, we did indeed wish, as we very often asked you in humble petition, to go to some place in Italy or at least to Sicily. There we would summon to us the Latin-speaking bishops of Africa and other provinces, or the sacred orders of our own church, and deliberate according to custom. After full deliberation we would then give your piety a reply on the questions concerning the Three Chapters.

Your serenity did not consent to this. In the meantime, therefore, it was decided that we would submit to your gentleness the names of bishops from the provinces mentioned above to be brought into the deliberation with us, and that your clemency would have them come. Out of love for the church's peace, we likewise consented to this arrangement.

Afterwards, however, shortly before the holy day of Easter, your piety decided on a different course, with the agreement of our brothers, the bishops of these regions. We were to have an equal number of members with the bishops present in the city of Constantinople, and we were to enter into deliberation with them on the Three Chapters, the subject of the dispute, according to the profession of our brother bishops described above.

We were hastening to carry out what, by your arrangement, had been agreed upon with our brothers for preserving the peace of the churches. The plan was that, after sound deliberation in common, everything done among us would be put in writing and laid out for the instruction of the universal church, and from this material our judgment on the Three Chapters under dispute would follow. But at once your piety acted. Following that volume

which you sent to us through our brother Benignus, bishop of Heraclea in Pelagonia, not many days before Easter, you sent yet another document after the holy day of Easter through the magnificent Theodore, decurion of the palace. In it you set out, for the time being, your own view of the Three Chapters and demanded that we give our reply on the same matter. Meanwhile our brothers would neither sit with us in equal numbers nor allow what we did or discussed to be put in writing. They acted as though we were saying things contrary to right belief that we were afraid to write down, which God forbid! On top of this, your clemency sent most glorious nobles to us and insisted that we deliver our reply on the matter of the Three Chapters as quickly as possible.

Even so, we did not stop wishing to obey your clemency. We asked only this: because of our bodily infirmity, which is unknown to no one, you should grant us a delay of twenty days. That way, after deliberating with God's help, we could pronounce our sentence in writing on a day fixed for our definition.

You said that you were likewise demanding a reply on the same matter from our brothers and fellow bishops. We sent our son, the deacon Pelagius, to them with this instruction. Since the agreed procedure for holding the conference had been set aside, they should at least wait twenty days for our definitive reply on the Three Chapters, because of the weakness of my body mentioned above, which they know of. In this way they would keep the ancient and regular order. They should not attempt to put forward anything before the sentence of ourselves, that is, of the apostolic see over which by God's grace we preside, had been promulgated. Otherwise, the occasion of scandal that had been laid to rest could arise again.

We therefore set before us the codices and acts of the synods and examined them carefully, as far as the nature of each disputed chapter required. We also produced other synodal letters of those same fathers who are shown to have sat in the four holy synods or in one of them. We likewise examined the decrees of our predecessors, the prelates of the apostolic see, and went through the other necessary instructions of approved fathers. Mindful of the professions described above, we took care to find out whether any of the matters now in dispute had been examined, settled and decided by our fathers.

We examined certain doctrines contained in the first part of the paper volume that your piety sent through our brother Benignus, bishop of Heraclea in Pelagonia. To exclude any error arising from ambiguity, their text is inserted in our present definition, together with an explanation of its meaning, which is set out below. We saw that these doctrines are full of abominable blasphemies. They are extremely hostile to the orthodox faith, which, as we read, the four holy synods of Nicaea, Constantinople, the first of Ephesus and Chalcedon defined soundly and blamelessly, according to the teaching of the Gospels and the apostles and with the Holy Spirit present and at work with them. We saw that these doctrines must be driven far from Christian minds. These doctrines are abominable, and the holy fathers condemned them long ago without hesitation. Therefore we too anathematize and condemn them by our sentence. The first chapter of them reads as follows:
Chapter 1.

"How then can you, who more than anyone need to be kept under restraint as a madman, say that he who was born of the virgin is God, from God, and should be considered consubstantial with the Father? Or perhaps you would have us attribute his creation to the Holy Spirit?

"He who is God, from God, and consubstantial with the Father was perhaps present in the one who had been born of the virgin, you marvel, who was formed by the Holy Spirit according to the divine Scriptures and was fashioned in a woman's womb. He was present because, as soon as that one was formed, he received him so that he might be a temple of God. [?] Yet we must not think that God was born of the virgin, unless perhaps we must also think that what was born, the temple within what was born, and God the Word who is in the temple are one and the same. Nor, then, should it be declared at all, as you say, that God, from God and consubstantial with the Father, was born of the virgin.

"For if, as you say, the one born of the virgin is not an assumed man but God incarnate, how could the one who was born be called God from God and consubstantial with the Father, when flesh cannot admit such a title? It is indeed madness to say that God was born of the virgin. To say that is nothing other than to say that he was begotten of the seed of David, from the substance of the virgin, and formed in her. For what is of the seed of David and from the substance of the virgin took shape in the mother's womb, and we say that what was formed by the power of the Holy Spirit was born of the virgin.

"Suppose someone grants them, on this basis, the right to say that God, from God and consubstantial with the Father, was born of the virgin because he is in the temple that was born. Still, it is not that God the Word was born in his own right; rather, he was 'incarnate,' as this wise man says. If, then, they say he was born together with the flesh, and that what was born is God from God and consubstantial with the Father, they must say the same of the flesh as well.

"But the flesh is not that. It is neither God, nor from God, nor consubstantial with the Father; it is of the seed of David and consubstantial with him whose seed it is. Therefore what was born of the virgin is not God, from God and consubstantial with the Father, unless perhaps as a part of the one born, just as he himself further on calls the Godhead a part of Christ. The divine nature was not born of the virgin.

"The one born of the virgin is the one who consists of the virgin's substance. God the Word was not born of Mary; the one born of Mary is the one who is of the seed of David. God the Word was not born of a woman; the one born of a woman is the one who was formed in her by the power of the Holy Spirit. The one consubstantial with the Father was not born of a mother, for, as blessed Paul says, he is without a mother. Rather, the one born of a mother is he who in later times was formed in the mother's womb by the power of the Holy Spirit, and who for this reason is said to be without a father."

The first chapter above seems to assert, by a roundabout route, that a mere man was born of the holy virgin Mary. It argues that if we confess that God the Word, who is consubstantial with the Father, was born in the flesh of that same virgin, we must consequently say that the flesh too is consubstantial with the Father. Therefore, whoever thinks, teaches, believes or preaches in this sense, and does not believe that the same Word and Son of God became incarnate and was born of the holy virgin in a second birth, let him be anathema.
Chapter 2.

"God the Word came to be in the one who was formed right from the start. He was present in him not only when he ascended into heaven, but also when he rose from the dead, since he was the one who raised him according to his promise. He was present not only when he rose, but also when he was crucified and baptized, and when he lived the gospel life after his baptism. He was present before his baptism too, when he fulfilled the requirements of the law, when he was presented according to the law, when he was circumcised, and when he was wrapped in swaddling clothes at birth. Perhaps he was in him also as he was being born, and while he was in his mother's womb, from the very first moment he was formed. For he gave order to the dispensation concerning him, leading him step by step to perfection."
Chapter 3.

"Over time he led him to baptism, and after that to death. Then, as he had declared, he raised him, led him into heaven, and set him at the right hand of God by virtue of his union with him. By virtue of that union he sits there, is worshipped by all, and will judge all. God the Word held the outcome of all these things in himself, since he was in him, and he accomplished everything in its order. He himself judged this order to be good, by predetermination and by the will he had fixed beforehand for the things that were to come. By the good pleasure he had toward him, he was likewise present in him from the beginning, and by an order pleasing to himself he led him to perfection."

The second and third chapters above seem to assert that God the Word was present in the man who was formed, as one being in another. They say that he gave order step by step to the dispensation concerning him, and that he led him on to advance toward perfection because of the good pleasure he had toward him and granted to the one who was assumed. Such words seem abominably to introduce a duality of persons in our one Lord and God Jesus Christ, and to suggest that, like any other man, he advanced over periods of time by the grace of God the Word. Therefore, whoever thinks, teaches, believes or preaches in this sense, let him be anathema.
Chapter 4.

"He provided his cooperation to the one who was assumed for the works set before him. How does this make the Godhead take the place of the mind in the one who was assumed? For it did not take the place of the mind in those to whom it gave its cooperation. And even if it gave some special cooperation to the one who was assumed, that did not make the Godhead occupy the place of the mind."

"But if, as you say, the Godhead took the place of a mind in the one who was assumed, how did he come to feel fear in his passion? Why did he need more fervent prayers in the face of what was about to befall him, prayers which, according to blessed Paul, he offered to God with a loud cry and with many tears? How was he gripped by such fear that in his overwhelming dread he poured out streams of sweat, as the evangelist plainly says that his sweat came down like drops of blood?

And why did he need the coming and visit of an angel to restore his soul in the trial of his sufferings, to strengthen his resolve, to rouse him to face the passion that was upon him, to urge him to bear his sufferings bravely, to anoint him for patience and endurance in suffering, to show him the fruit of his present sufferings, the change that would come from the passion, and the good glory that would be his after the passion? For the one who, as the evangelist says, strengthened him, that is, the angel, made him strong with these words, urged him to rise above the weakness of his nature, and made him strong by fortifying his thoughts."

The fourth chapter written above is understood to say that God gave his cooperation to the one who was assumed just as he gave it to other men; though it was given to him in a special degree, it is still said to have been given in the same way as to other men; and so a mere and weak man needed the help of an angel at the time of the passion, so that, to fortify his thoughts, future glory was promised to him for enduring the passion. If anyone thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter V.

"'Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, because you are not thinking of the things of God but of the things of men.' Death is no disgrace to me. I will not flee it as something unseemly out of regard for human glory. Rather, I will bear the trial of death with good courage for the sake of the many good things to come, in which I myself shall share and through me all men. Do not wound my spirit or trouble it by urging me to flee the trial of death as though it were something shameful."

The fifth chapter written above says that Jesus Christ rejected the words of the apostle Peter when he said to him, "Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, because you are not thinking of the things of God but of the things of men," so that his own spirit would not be shaken by Peter's dissuasion and shrink from the passion, and because he would profit by his passion and would undergo the trial of the coming death for the sake of the many good things he would gain from it. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not rather believe that his death, which he underwent in his own flesh, won for us the reward of eternal life, let him be anathema.
Chapter VI.

"The words 'he was led by the Spirit' plainly mean that he was guided by the Spirit, strengthened by him for the virtue he had set before himself, led by him to the things he had to do, taught by him what was fitting, and fortified by him in his thoughts so that he would be equal to so great a contest. As blessed Paul also says, 'For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God,' calling 'led by the Spirit' those who are governed by him, taught by him, set on a better course by him, and given by him instruction in what is fitting.

And when the evangelist said that he returned from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit, he plainly showed that he received the indwelling of the Holy Spirit at his baptism for this reason: to draw from it strength for what he had set before himself. Hence he was also led by the Spirit to that contest which he was to wage against the devil on our behalf."

In the sixth chapter mentioned above he is again said to have been led in all things, like a mere man, by the Spirit, whose presence he is said to have received after his baptism, and to have been strengthened and taught like other men, of whom, as this passage seems to claim, the Apostle says, "All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God." If anyone therefore thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not believe, confess and preach that God the Word incarnate is the one Christ, let him be anathema.
Chapter VII.

"Let these wisest of all men tell us, then: if, as they say, the Godhead had taken the place of a mind for the Lord Christ according to the flesh, why did Christ need the cooperation of the Holy Spirit for these things? For the Godhead of the Only-begotten did not need the Spirit for justification; it did not need the Spirit to conquer the devil, or to work miracles, or to be taught what it was fitting to do, or to appear without stain.

For if the Godhead served as his mind and its power was sufficient for everything, everything must have been accomplished by it, so that the indwelling of the Holy Spirit would have been superfluous. But in fact Scripture says that he was anointed with the Spirit, that the Spirit dwelt in him and helped him in all he set out to do, that he received teaching and power from the Spirit, that from the Spirit he obtained justification, and that by the Spirit he was made spotless."

The seventh chapter written above is understood to say that, like other men, he needed the indwelling of the Holy Spirit for his justification, to conquer the devil, to work miracles, to be taught what it was fitting for him to do, and to appear spotless, and that he was helped by that Spirit in all that he set out to do. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not believe that Christ, as true God, by his own Godhead accomplished all that he willed and accomplishes whatever he wills, but holds that like a mere man he needed the support of the Holy Spirit, let him be anathema.
Chapter VIII.

"He says that what existed before the ages came into being in the last times, as though certain people confessed this, although no one who cares for true religion suffers from such an illness of madness as to say that he who exists before the ages came into being in the last times. And from this he infers that it necessarily follows that what exists in the last times also exists before the ages; and he accuses those who do not say all things alike by way of interchange, as though those who confess that there is one Son were bound to say everything by interchange.

Who would not congratulate you on your madness? Who would not long to obtain such teachers, who bring such confusion into the doctrine of true religion as to say that 'what is before the ages came into being in the last times,' and so estrange it from its own nature and drag it down to something lower, and then turn it around and say that what is in the last times is also before the ages, when they ought rather to have said that he who was before the ages assumed the one who was in the last times, as blessed Paul says?

Come then, following your laws and accepting the interchange, or rather the subversion, devised by your wisdom, let us confound everything together, and let there no longer be any distinction between the form of God and the form of a servant, between the temple that was taken and him who dwelt in the temple, between the one who was destroyed and the one who raised him up, between the one who was made perfect through sufferings and the one who made him perfect,

between the one who was found worthy to be remembered and the one who was mindful of him, between the one who was visited and the one who visited, between the one who was made a little lower than the angels and the one who made him lower, between the one who was crowned with glory and honor and the one who crowned him, between the one who was set over the works of God's hands and the one who set him over them, between the one who received these things in subjection and the one who gave the subjection."

In the eighth chapter mentioned above a duality of persons seems to be introduced in various ways, through the claim that "he who was before the ages is not to be said to have come in the last times," as though the person of the one assuming the humanity were one and the person of the one assumed another. If anyone therefore thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not confess that the same God the Word, who was born of the Father before the ages, was in the last times made flesh and born of the blessed Virgin Mary, so that one and the same Christ exists in both natures, let him be anathema.
Chapter IX.

"This man, then, through whom he determined to judge all, for the assurance of things to come, after raising him from the dead and showing him to be judge of all, as blessed Paul says, he rightly deemed worthy of union with himself, and through the conjunction formed with himself he made him a sharer in such things that he even shares in worship: all render the worship due to the divine nature, but in that worship they include also the one whom it knows to be inseparably joined to itself. From this it is clear that he raised him to greater things."

In the ninth chapter written above, using the terms 'conjunction' and a kind of 'participation', as though made by God with the man Christ, it is asserted that Christ is adorned with divine works; and through these a duality of persons is again introduced. If anyone therefore thinks, teaches, believes or preaches in this way, and does not acknowledge and believe one and the same Christ, our God and Lord, with the difference of natures remaining in their own properties, let him be anathema.
Chapter X.

"'I whom you see can do nothing according to my own nature, since I am a man; but I work because the Father, abiding in me, does all things. For since I am in the Father and the Father in me, and God the Word, the Only-begotten of God, is in me, it is certain that the Father too abides in me together with him and does the works.'

Nor is it surprising that such things are thought of Christ, since he himself clearly says of other men, 'Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.' For if the Father and the Son make their dwelling with every such man, why be surprised if both are thought to abide together in the Lord Christ according to the flesh, since their communion in substance perhaps also entails a communion in indwelling?"
[?] ...of a man to dwell. Whoever therefore thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter XI.

"So too, having first received a soul, human and immortal by constitution and endowed with mind, and having established it in immutability through the resurrection, he has in the same way granted us a share in these same things through the resurrection.

That is why, before his resurrection from the dead, he rebukes Peter for causing him to stumble with his words, and, placed in great dread at the time of his passion, he needs the appearance of an angel to strengthen him for patience and endurance in the sufferings that were upon him. But after his resurrection from the dead and his ascension into heaven, having become wholly impassible and immutable and seated at the right hand of God, he is the judge of the whole world, since the divine nature exercises judgment in him."

In the eleventh chapter written above the same things seem to be repeated that were already said above in the fourth: that before the passion Christ was so weak that, placed in great dread at the time of the passion, he seemed to need the comfort of an angel. Since this seems to describe him as a mere man who needs such help, if anyone thinks, teaches, believes or preaches in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter XII.

"So then here too, O wisest of all men, you teach that we have the mind of Christ inasmuch as we have the Holy Spirit, who supplied a certain power to the mind of Christ, granting him wisdom for all that had to be done;

as we have also shown in what precedes, he was led by him into the wilderness for the contests against the devil, and by his anointing he received both the knowledge and the strength for what had to be done; and having become a sharer in him, he not only worked miracles but also knew with precision how miracles ought to be used, so as to make true religion known to the nations while also bearing the infirmities of the suffering, and so bring his will to fulfillment; and by him he was justified and shown to be spotless, whether by the correction of what was worse, or by the preservation of what was better, or by gradual advances toward what was better."

In the twelfth chapter written above the same things seem to be set out as in the seventh chapter, by asserting that our Lord Jesus Christ was formed in all things through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit and attained perfection over time with the help of his anointing. If anyone therefore, not believing that he was perfect by his own Godhead, but holding that like a mere man he needed the anointing of the Holy Spirit and was helped by it, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches this, let him be anathema.
Chapter XIII.

"How then does it follow, from the fact that God became man, that one should say that this man is God the Word? For if God the Word is man, as you yourself say, we must in every respect say of the man what the evangelist says of God the Word. And what does he say? 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made

that was made.' So if God the Word is man, we shall say of him: 'In the beginning was the man, and the man was with God, and the man was God. The man was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made.' For if God the Word is man, as you say, everything the evangelist says of God the Word will apply to him."

In the thirteenth chapter written above it seems to be denied that God the Word became man, and again that the man is God the Word, so that by this, as was said above, a duality of persons is introduced. If anyone therefore thinks, teaches, believes or preaches in this way, and does not rather believe that in our Lord God Jesus Christ, while the difference of natures remains without change and without division, there is one person or one subsistence, in such a way that God the Word is believed to be man without any change in his divine nature, and the humanity assumed is believed, because of the oneness of the person, to be God without change, let him be anathema.
Chapter XIV.

"As for the words 'to my Father and your Father, and my God and your God,' no one is so mad as to say that they apply to anyone other than the temple of God the Word, the man assumed for our salvation, who both died and rose again and was about to ascend into heaven. He claims the Father as his along with the disciples, having himself obtained adoption by grace; and he calls God his own God, because, like other men, he received his very existence.

Hence, because of their common nature, he says 'my Father and your Father' and 'my God and your God'; but again he set his own person apart from them, indicating the special grace on account of which, through his conjunction with God the Word, he is honored by all men in the place of the true Son."

In the fourteenth chapter written above, the words we read in the Gospel, "I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God," are interpreted to mean that Jesus Christ, our Lord and God, received, like other men, the grace of adoption so as to be called Son of God, and that, as it were through conjunction with God the Word, he is worshiped by all in the place of the true Son. If anyone thinks, teaches, believes or preaches this, and does not rather understand and believe that the one Jesus Christ, Son of God and our Lord, exists in two natures unconfused and inseparable, let him be anathema.
Chapter XV.

"When he said 'Receive,' he meant 'You will receive.' For if, when he breathed on them, he had given the Spirit to the disciples, as some have very foolishly supposed, it would have been superfluous for him to tell them later, and above all at the time of his ascension into heaven, not to depart from Jerusalem but to wait for the promise of the Spirit, and afterward, 'But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you.'

Moreover, Luke plainly says that the very coming of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples took place on the fiftieth day after the resurrection, after the ascension. And this too must be noted: if they had received the Spirit from the breathing, he would not have said 'Receive' but 'since you have received'; for the word 'Receive' suits those who have not yet received."

The fifteenth chapter written above says that when our Lord Jesus Christ breathed on the faces of his disciples after his resurrection, he did not give them the Holy Spirit but signified that it would be given, so that by this either the Truth himself, God forbid, would be thought to have lied, or else, like a mere man, he would be thought to have had nothing to give by that breath or to have been quite unable to give it. If anyone therefore thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter XVI.

"He says to Thomas, 'Put your finger here and see my hands, and reach out your hand and put it into my side, and do not be unbelieving but believing.' He means: 'Since you do not believe, and think that touch alone is enough to make you believe (for you did not escape my notice when you said this), touch with your hand, put it to the test, and learn to believe and not to doubt.' When Thomas had come to believe in this way, he says 'My Lord and my God,' not calling him Lord and God (for the knowledge of the resurrection did not teach him that the one who had risen was also God), but praising God, as it were, for the miracle that had taken place."

In the sixteenth chapter written above, concerning the passage of the Gospel where the apostle Thomas, feeling the marks of the nails, said "My Lord and my God," it is asserted that the apostle Thomas did not confess Christ himself [?] as Lord and God, because the knowledge of the resurrection did not teach this, nor that the one who had risen was God, but that the apostle Thomas rather praised God for the miracle that had taken place. If anyone therefore thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not rather believe that Thomas's confession declared both that Jesus Christ is true God and that he rose in true flesh, let him be anathema.
Chapter XVII.

"He said that they must repent of the wickedness of the cross, acknowledge Jesus Christ as Savior and Lord and author of all good things, since it was for this purpose that he came and was assumed by the divine nature, put their faith in him and become his disciples, and above all come to baptism, which he himself handed down to us, which contains a prefiguration of the hope of things to come, but is to be celebrated in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. For

when he says that each one should be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, he does not mean that they should abandon the invocation in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit and invoke Jesus Christ in baptism. Rather, it is like the saying that they were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, meaning that under the cloud and the sea they were separated from the Egyptians and freed from their slavery so that they might heed the laws of Moses. Such too is the meaning of 'let each one be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ':

that, having come to him as Savior, author of all good things and teacher of truth, they should be called after him as the author of good things and teacher of truth, just as it is customary for all men who follow any school to be called after the founder of its doctrine, as Platonists, Epicureans, Manichaeans, Marcionites, and any others so named.

In the same way the apostles judged that we should be named Christians, thereby making it certain that it is his teaching we must heed; and so too they were to receive the baptism given by him, first instituted in him, who was also the first to be baptized, and handed on by him to others, to be celebrated according to the prefiguration of things to come."

In the seventeenth chapter written above, from the words of blessed Peter in the Acts of the Apostles, "Let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ," it is maintained that Christ is not included in the invocation made in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and that when the apostle Peter said they should be baptized in the name of Christ, he does not seem to have signified the mystery of the Trinity. It follows from this that when someone is baptized in the name of the Trinity, he does not appear to be baptized in the name of Christ, so that on this understanding a quaternity is evidently introduced.

It is further added in the same chapter that we are called Christians after Christ in the same way that the followers of various sects or errors have taken their names from their founders and teachers, that is, Platonists from Plato, Marcionites from Marcion, and Manichaeans from Mani. If anyone therefore thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema. For we are called Christians, and are Christians, because in receiving baptism we have put on our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and with him as our head we all become one body in him.
Chapter XVIII.

"And he holds the place of an image for two reasons. Those who love certain people often set up images of them after their death and consider this a sufficient consolation for death; looking on the one who is not seen and not present as if in the image, they think they see him, and so soothe the flame and force of their longing. And those who keep images of the emperors in their cities likewise appear to honor those who are not present as though they were present and visible, by the veneration and worship of their images.

Both of these things are fulfilled through him. All who are with him, who pursue virtue and are ready to give God what they owe him, love him and greatly honor him. The divine nature, though it is not seen, fulfills the love owed to it in him who is seen by all, since everyone considers that through him they see it and are always in its presence. And they give it all honor as if to an imperial image, since the divine nature is, as it were, in him and is seen in him.

For even if it is the Son who is said to dwell in him, the Father is also with him, and all creation believes that he is inseparably and in every way with the Son. Nor is the Spirit absent, since he has become for him a kind of anointing, and he who was assumed always has the Spirit with him. This is not surprising, since even with any men who pursue virtue the Father is said to be present together with the Son: "For I and the Father will come and make our dwelling with him." And everyone knows that the Spirit too is inseparable from such men.

In the eighteenth chapter quoted above, Christ is said to be the image of the invisible Word of God in the same way that images of absent princes are venerated in their honor. If anyone thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 19.

For the words "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased" show an adoption in baptism, comparable to the adoption of the Jews, since it had been said to them as well: "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High," and: "I have begotten sons and raised them up." He shows the pre-eminence of this adoption by saying "beloved" and "in whom I am well pleased."

This is why the Father's voice also came, confirming the adoption. By the name "Son" it pointed out him who is truly Son, through an adoption according to grace, and union with the true Son established this one in a true and firm adoption. And the Holy Spirit, descending in the form of a dove, remained upon him, so that, held by the Spirit's cooperation in union with him who is truly Son, he might keep the firm dignity of adoption. In all these things, in which the baptism of adoption was first foreshadowed (I mean the baptism of the Lord Christ), what took place was completed by the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

The nineteenth chapter quoted above appears to expound the Gospel according to Luke on the baptism of Christ, and it deserves censure on two counts. First, it introduces two sons, since it seems to say that Christ is Son of God by adoption. Second, it asserts that Christ himself was baptized in the name of the Trinity, which plainly implies a fourfold Godhead. If anyone, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 20.

So the psalm shows us how great the difference is between God the Word and the man he assumed. In the New Testament these parts are found divided. The Lord applies to himself the opening of the psalm, which says that he is the maker of creation, that his majesty is raised above the heavens, and that he is marveled at in all the earth. The apostle applies to Jesus the second part, which concerns the man who was granted so great a benefit. How is it not obvious that divine Scripture clearly teaches us that one is God the Word and the other a man, and shows us that the difference between them is great? For the one remembers, while the other is granted to be remembered;

the one visits, while the other is called blessed because he is granted the visit; the one, in giving a benefit, made him a little lower than the angels, while the other received a benefit through that very lowering; the one crowns with glory and honor, while the other is crowned and is called blessed for it; the one set him over all the works of his hands and put all things under his feet, while the other was granted rule over things over which he had no power before.

In the twentieth chapter quoted above, which appears to expound the eighth psalm, Christ is asserted to be a mere man, as has already been said of other passages. He is shown as divided from God the Word, and two persons are introduced. If anyone thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not understand that in Christ, our Lord and God, two natures are united indivisibly and without confusion, so that, while the difference of those natures remains, he is one and the same, true Son of God and true Son of man, let him be anathema.
Chapter 21.

But since they do not wish to consider these things, they try to apply all the sayings to the Lord Christ. As a result they understand in the same way even what was said about the people, and they make themselves a laughingstock to the Jews, who show from the context of the scriptures that the sayings have nothing to do with the Lord Christ.
Chapter 22.

The same is true of "his soul was not left in hell, nor did his flesh see corruption." The prophet uses hyperbole here about the people. He is speaking of providence, and means that God preserved them untouched [?] by all evils. But since this became true and was fulfilled in actual events in the Lord Christ, blessed Peter, speaking of him, uses the saying most fittingly. He shows that what the prophet said hyperbolically about the people, using the expression for a particular reason, has now truly come about in actual events in the Lord Christ.

The twenty-first and twenty-second chapters quoted above appear to say that the prophecy spoken in the person of Christ, "You will not abandon my soul in hell, nor let your holy one see corruption," was not foretold of Christ himself but of the people of Israel, and that blessed Peter the apostle chose to apply this prophecy to Christ because of how events turned out. Therefore, whoever thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 23.

The same interpretation applies to "They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." It is certain that the psalm does not fit the Lord at all. It was not for the Lord Christ, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found, to say:

"The words of my transgressions are far from my salvation." But the Lord himself, according to the common lot of men, cried out when he was overwhelmed in his passion, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" And the apostles plainly applied "They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots" to him, because what David had earlier said hyperbolically about the evils inflicted on him actually happened to the Lord Christ, whose garments they divided and whose tunic they gave up to the lot.

The twenty-third chapter quoted above expounds certain words of the twenty-first psalm, which read: "They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." It denies that these words fit the Lord Jesus Christ and says instead that David spoke them about himself because of certain evils he had suffered, and that the evangelist applied them to Christ because of how events turned out. It adds that the Lord Jesus Christ, who committed no sin, could not have said:

"The words of my transgressions are far from my salvation." Therefore, whoever thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not understand that the words in which transgressions are mentioned refer to his body, which is the Church and cannot be without sin in this world, and does not believe that the words about dividing the garments were foretold specifically of the Head himself, that is, our Lord God Jesus Christ, and were fulfilled in him, let him be anathema.
Chapter 24.

"They dug my hands and feet": that is, they searched into everything, both what I was doing and what I was attempting. He said "dug" as a metaphor taken from those who dig to try to find what lies deep below.

"They numbered all my bones": they took possession of all my strength and all my property, so far as even to count up my belongings. He said this because of the custom of enemies, who, when they have conquered, make a precise count and inventory of what they find.

For this reason, after saying, "But they considered and looked upon me," he adds: "They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." By "considering me" he means "looking on," because everything they had desired had happened to them in me. ("Look upon" is used as it is among us, meaning "he saw happen to him what he wanted him to suffer.") He means that, as though I were now wholly given over to misfortune, they divided my belongings as enemies do after laying waste and taking captives, making the division by lot.

The evangelist, taking up the words because of the events, used them of the Lord, as we have said in other cases too; for we have clearly shown above that the psalm does not refer to the Lord. Blessed David, however, said these things hyperbolically, drawing rather on what was done by Absalom. When David had withdrawn, Absalom entered the capital by right of war and took possession of all the royal property, and was not even ashamed to defile his father's bed.

The twenty-fourth chapter quoted above concerns the words of that same twenty-first psalm where it says: "They dug my hands and my feet, they numbered all my bones; but they considered and looked upon me." It asserts that these words were not foretold of Christ, but that David said them about himself because of the tyranny of Absalom, who had seized the royal city and its wealth and had counted up all his father's possessions [?], and that the evangelist applied these words to the person of Christ because of how events turned out. Whoever, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 25.

Food and drink become pleasant in a time of joy, but unpleasant and bitter in sorrow. So he says: "What they did was such that, because of my sorrow and anger, food was like gall to me and drink was no different from vinegar." This happens above all in fits of anger that come with distress, which they were likely to suffer against their own. The evangelist applied this testimony to the Lord. The Lord himself also said of himself, "Zeal for your house has consumed me." Blessed Paul, speaking of the Jews, said, "Let their table become," and so on, and blessed Peter said of Judas, "Let his dwelling become desolate."
