Certainly, these are different matters. It is not that the psalm speaks about these people in one place, then about him, then about someone else. Rather, many things are said about the Jews who separated themselves from God and from the law, exposing their impiety. So the use of these testimonies is fitting, and at the same time it is drawn from the events, as in: "They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink."

The twenty-fifth chapter quoted above concerns the passage of the psalm that says: "They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink." It expounds it against the plain truth of the Gospel, saying that the Lord was not really given vinegar to drink. Rather, because of his sorrow and the anger of those who offered it, the drink was to him like vinegar and the food like gall. It also says that this was not foretold of him, but that the evangelist applied this testimony to the Lord because of how events turned out. Therefore, whoever thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 26.

A confession of this kind does not show that Nathanael had knowledge of the Godhead, for the Jews and Samaritans, who hoped for such things, were very far indeed from knowledge of God the Word. In the same way Martha's confession proves that she did not yet have knowledge of the Godhead, and clearly neither did blessed Peter.

For at that time it was still enough for them, as they received that revelation, to form some idea of something special and greater about him than about other men. But after the resurrection, led to knowledge by the Spirit, they then received perfect knowledge of the revelation as well. They came to know that what set him apart from other men did not come to him from God as some mere honor, as it does to other men, but through his union with God the Word, by which he shares in all honor with him after his ascension into heaven.

The twenty-sixth chapter quoted above denies that Peter had knowledge of Christ's Godhead before his resurrection, and says instead that he received only an idea of him above that of other men. It again introduces two sons when it says that the man became a sharer with God the Word after he ascended into heaven. Whoever, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not understand that Christ our Lord is one and the same, Son of God and Son of man, while the difference of the united natures remains in him, let him be anathema.
Chapter 27.

The evangelist Matthew says that after the temptations angels came and ministered to him. That is, they stood with him and worked together with him, serving God in all that concerned him, because through his contests with the devil he had already been shown to be more glorious. We also learn from the Gospels that angels were with him when he was about to suffer, and that when he rose they were seen at the tomb.

All these things showed the dignity of Christ, since angels were inseparably with him and ministered in all that concerned him. Just as they withdraw from sinners, so they come to the help of those honored for their merit. That is why the Lord rightly said: "You will see greater things: heaven will be opened to all through me, and all the angels will always be with me, now ascending, now descending, as to a member of God's household and his friend."

The twenty-seventh chapter quoted above expounds the evangelist Matthew's statement that, when the temptations were over, angels came to minister to Christ. It says that angels came to the help of Christ because he was honored for merit, as they do for others, and that angels ascended to Christ in heaven and descended in the same way as to a friend and member of God's household. Whoever, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not hold that the angels served and still serve him as their Creator and Lord, true God and Son of the true God, one and the same with the perfect humanity he assumed from the Virgin's womb, let him be anathema.
Chapter 28.

The Lord was more troubled by the passions of the soul than by those of the body, and had a greater struggle against them. With his better mind he overcame the desires, and the Godhead helped him toward perfection. This is why the Lord appears to have directed his struggle chiefly against these. He was not deceived by love of money or held by desire for glory, and he gave nothing to the flesh, for it was not in him to be overcome by such things.

But if he had not assumed a soul, and it was the Godhead that overcame these things, then nothing that was done brings any gain to us. (For what likeness is there between the Godhead and the human soul with respect to perfection of life?) The Lord's struggles would then seem to bring no gain to us, and to have been undertaken merely for show.

But if this cannot be said (for it is certain that those things were done for our sake), then he waged a greater struggle against the passions of the soul and a lesser one against those of the flesh, because the former troubled him far more, and it was the soul that needed the stronger medicine.

Clearly, having assumed both flesh and soul, he struggled through both and for both. In the flesh he put sin to death, tamed its desires, and made them easy to master by the better reason of the soul. The soul he trained and exercised both to overcome its own passions and to rein in the desires of the flesh. The indwelling Godhead worked these things, and the indwelling Godhead brought them about for each of the two.

The twenty-eighth chapter quoted above again presents Christ as a mere man. It says that by the reason of the soul he tamed the desires of the body, and trained and exercised the soul to overcome its own passions and rein in the desires of the flesh within itself. Yet it says that the soul brought these things about for both through the mediation of the Godhead. On this view we would no longer have one and the same Jesus Christ as mediator between God and men; rather, the Godhead would appear to have been the mediator for the flesh and the soul. Whoever, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 29.

"But if it was flesh that was crucified," he says, "how did the sun turn away its rays, darkness cover the whole earth, the earth quake, the rocks split, and the dead rise?" What, then, would they say about the darkness that came on Egypt in the time of Moses, not for three hours but for three days? What about the other miracles done through Moses? What about those done through Joshua son of Nun, who made the sun stand still, the same sun that turned back against nature in the time of King Hezekiah? And what about the bones of Elisha, which raised a dead man?

If the things that happened at the cross prove that God the Word suffered, and they will not grant that these things happened because of a man, then neither will the miracles in the time of Moses have happened because of Abraham's descendants, nor those in the time of Joshua son of Nun, nor those in the time of King Hezekiah. But if those were done miraculously for the Jewish people, how much more were the things that happened at the cross done for the temple of God the Word?

In the twenty-ninth chapter quoted above, while it seems to oppose Apollinaris, who involved the divine nature in sufferings, it turns aside from the right path and goes beyond due measure in its claims, so that a mere man is thought to have hung on the cross. Therefore, whoever thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not believe that Christ is true God and confess that, while his Godhead remained incapable of suffering, the same Christ suffered in his own flesh, let him be anathema.
Chapter 30.

It is clear that the union is fitting, for through it the natures brought together have produced one person by virtue of the union. Just as it is said of a man and a woman that they are no longer two but one flesh, we too may reasonably say, by the principle of union, that there are not two persons but one, the natures of course being distinct. For just as there it does no harm to the number two that they are called one flesh (since it is clear in what sense they are called one), so here the unity of the person does no harm to the difference of the natures.

For when we distinguish the natures, we say that the nature of God the Word is complete and his person complete (for one cannot speak of a subsistence without a person), and likewise that the nature and person of the man are complete. But when we look to the union, we then speak of one person.

The thirtieth chapter quoted above uses a very bad example in trying to show how the one person of Christ may be understood. It says that just as we read of a man and a woman who come together, so too in Christ there is, as it were, one person, with the natures distinct. It goes on to say that the nature of God the Word is complete and his person complete, and likewise the nature and person of the man. From this it is clear that two persons of the one Christ are introduced, both by the example of man and woman, where there are two persons, and by what follows, even though the number is not stated. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes or preaches this in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 31.

He calls Christ, according to the flesh, the form of a servant that was assumed, and calls him who assumed it God over all. Yet he joined these together in view of the union, so as to make a clear division of the natures through the meaning of the names. Let no one, therefore, call him who according to the flesh is from the Jews God, nor again say that God who is over all is from the Jews according to the flesh.

The thirty-first chapter quoted above occurs in what appears to be an exposition of the creed of the three hundred and eighteen fathers. It not only asserts a division of the natures. By saying without qualification that neither should he who according to the flesh is from the Jews be called God, nor should God who is over all be said to be from the Jews according to the flesh, it declares that there are two persons, each set apart from the other: a man stripped of Godhead, and God alone, without flesh. If anyone, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not confess that the natures are united in the one Christ in such a way that a single person or subsistence is acknowledged, let him be anathema.
Chapter 32.

For he speaks of "Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power." But whoever is anointed with the Spirit of God has in every case received something from it. Who would be mad enough to say that the divine nature received something from the Spirit, or that it has companions? For by "companions" he clearly means those who have themselves been anointed. And those who have been anointed and have rightly been made his companions in this could not be said to share the anointing with anyone other than him who was assumed.
And this very passage shows that he received a just reward: "Because," it says, "you loved righteousness and hated wickedness, for this you were granted a special anointing."

In the thirty-second chapter quoted above, in a commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews, the saying of blessed Peter is brought in: "Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power." It goes on: "But whoever is anointed with the Spirit of God has in every case received something from it," and adds: "Who would be mad enough to say that the divine nature received something from the Spirit?"

These words present Christ as a mere man, who by the anointing of the Holy Spirit was made a sharer in the divine nature, as others are, and who was granted a special anointing as a just reward for having loved righteousness and hated wickedness. Whoever, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 33.

"Rabbi, you are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel": that is, "You are the Christ foretold long ago." For these were clearly the things they hoped for from the Christ, as one who would belong to God's household more than anyone else.
Chapter 34.

He too was certain that he was the Son of God, meaning not according to the birth of the deity but in that he was intimate with God. On this ground men who had been made intimate with God through virtue were for a time called sons of God.

In the thirty-third and thirty-fourth chapters above, from the commentary on the Gospel according to John, the words of Nathanael are cited, saying to the Lord, "You are the Son of God, you are the King of Israel"; and it is inferred that this was said to Christ as to one intimate with God, so that Christ himself is not God but is more intimate with God than other men are. It is added that just as other holy men are called sons of God and yet are men, so Christ too was called God by Nathanael, with whom he was speaking, because of the familiarity he has with God.
If anyone thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not confess the same Christ to be true God and true man, one, perfect in each nature, let him be anathema.
Chapter 35.

For when he said, "concerning his Son, who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh," it is certain that here he calls Son the one who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh: not God the Word, but the form of a servant that was assumed. For God was not made according to the flesh, nor was God made of the seed of David; rather, the man assumed for us, whom the blessed apostle plainly calls Son.

In the thirty-fifth chapter above, where the passage of the apostle from the Epistle to the Romans is expounded, where he says, "concerning his Son, who was made to him of the seed of David according to the flesh," the bare form of a servant is set forth, by saying that here he calls Son the one who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh, not God the Word but the man assumed for us, whom the blessed apostle plainly calls Son. These words show that, as has been said, a bare man is being preached.

Whoever, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not believe that the very one who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh is also, in the words of the apostle Paul, God over all, let him be anathema.
Chapter 36.
Reborn, he has become one person in place of another: no longer a part of Adam, who was changeable and beset by sins, but of Christ, who through the resurrection was made wholly blameless.

In the thirty-sixth chapter above, where it is said to the baptized person that "reborn, he has become one person from another: no longer a part of Adam, who was changeable and beset by sins, but of Christ, who through the resurrection was made wholly blameless," by these words he wants Christ to appear to have been blameworthy before the resurrection, which God forbid. Whoever, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 37.

So that he showed him great care, and made all that was his his own and endured it, leading him through all the sufferings by which he made him perfect according to his own power; not departing from the dead man according to the law of his own nature, but by his presence, working and grace delivering him from death and from the evils that come from it, raising him from the dead and bringing him to a better end.

In the thirty-seventh chapter above it is said that God the Word was present to Christ in his sufferings and in death by presence, working and grace. If that is so, he will appear to have bestowed grace and working as one present to another. Whoever, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not say that God the Word himself, preserving the impassibility of his divinity, willingly endured all that is written of his passion in the flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul, which he united to himself from the virgin from the very moment of conception, let him be anathema.
Chapter 38.

Then, showing for whose sake he suffered, he adds the lessening: "so that apart from God he might taste death for all"; for, the divine nature so willing, he tasted death by himself, separated from it, for the benefit of all. He also shows that the deity was indeed separated from the one who suffered as regards the experience of death, since it was not possible for it to undergo the experience of death; yet it was not absent from the one who suffered as regards its care for him.

In the thirty-eighth chapter above we recognize also a falsified testimony of the apostle: where we read, "so that by the grace of God he might taste death for all," here is found, "so that without God he might taste death for all." And as though to support this it is said that, the divine nature being separated, he tasted death by himself, as a mere man, for the benefit of all. Whoever, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not confess that God the Word never abandoned, either in its sufferings or in death, the flesh that he united to himself according to subsistence from the very moment of conception, let him be anathema.
Chapter 39.

For he says, "Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Spirit and with power": having merited this anointing, he was made spotless in all things and merited conjunction with the divine nature. For he would not have received that conjunction had he not first been made spotless, so that he might thus be fit for union with it.

In the thirty-ninth chapter above, expounding again what blessed Peter said, "Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Spirit and with power," he says that through the anointing of the Spirit, which he merited, he was made spotless in all things and merited conjunction with the divine nature. These words plainly present Christ as a mere man. Whoever, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 40.

For as to the saying, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased," it is manifest madness to think that he says it of God the Word. For he who said, "This is my beloved Son," and added, "in whom I am well pleased," indicated that he says this plainly by comparison with other sons, who neither became beloved to him nor were able to please him greatly.

In the fortieth chapter above, from the commentary on the Gospel according to Matthew, where it says, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased," it is added and said: "It is manifest madness to think that he says it of God the Word. For he who said, 'This is my beloved Son,' and added, 'in whom I am well pleased,' indicated that he says this plainly by comparison with other sons, who neither became beloved to him nor were able to please him greatly."
These words once again plainly show Christ Jesus to be a mere man and an adopted son. Whoever, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 41.

And remaining with him until, loosing the pangs of death according to his own creative power, he freed him from those unspeakable bonds and, raising him from the dead, transferred him to immortal life; and making him incorruptible, immortal and unchangeable, he led him up into heaven.

In the forty-first chapter above it is said that, loosing the pangs of death, he freed Christ from those unspeakable bonds and, raising him from the dead, transferred him to immortal life, and making him incorruptible, immortal and unchangeable, led him up into heaven. By all these words it is made clear that Jesus Christ is asserted to be a bare man. Whoever, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 42.

Christ, justified and made spotless by the power of the Holy Spirit (as blessed Paul says in one place, "he was justified in the Spirit," and in another, "who through the eternal Spirit offered himself spotless to God"), he caused to die according to the law of men; but since he had been made sinless by the power of the Holy Spirit, he raised him from the dead and established him in a better life, making him unchangeable in the thoughts of his soul and incorruptible and indissoluble in his flesh as well.

In the forty-second chapter above it is said that Christ was justified and made spotless by the power of the Holy Spirit, and it is added: "he caused him to die according to the law of men; but since he had been made sinless by the power of the Holy Spirit, he raised him from the dead." By these words a man is suggested to be so separated from God the Word that he is asserted to have been made spotless and sinless by the power of the Holy Spirit, like some righteous man. Whoever, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 43.

"But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ": saying that the cause of these things for us was God, who has given us the victory against all our adversaries, whether death or sin or any evil arising from them; who, taking our Lord [?] Christ as a man for us, also transferred him through the resurrection from the dead to a better end, made him sit at his right hand, and granted us communion with him.

In the forty-third chapter above, in expounding the words of the apostle Paul in which he says, "But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ," after much else it is added: "[?] our Lord [?] Christ as a man for us, also transferred him through the resurrection from the dead to a better end." By these words a man, as though already existing, is indicated to have been assumed by God the Word, so that there appear to have been two, and the one to have conferred benefits on the other. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes or preaches this in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 44.

So when they ask whether Mary is mother of man or Mother of God, let us say: both, the one by the nature of the thing, the other by relation. She is mother of man by nature, because it was a man who was in Mary's womb and who also came forth from it; but Mother of God, because God was in the man who was born, not circumscribed in him by nature, but present in him by the disposition of his will.

In the forty-fourth chapter above it is said, "So when they ask whether Mary is to be called mother of man or Mother of God," and, as though in the person of one answering, it is said that she is called both, and it is added, "the one by the nature of the thing, the other by relation"; and further, "for she is mother of man by nature, because it was a man who was in Mary's womb and who also came forth from it; but Mother of God, because God was in the man who was born"; and it is added, "not circumscribed in him by nature, but present in him by the disposition of his will."

These words likewise show both that Christ is a bare man and that blessed Mary had two sons. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes or preaches this in this way, and does not acknowledge that God the Word, who was ineffably born of the Father before all ages, is the same one who, as we said in the first chapter, was by his second birth incarnate and born of the holy virgin Mary, one in both natures, unconfused and inseparable, let him be anathema.
Chapter 45.

The man born of Mary is Son by grace, but God the Word by nature. What is by grace is not by nature, and what is by nature is not by grace. There are not two sons. Let it suffice for the body that is from us to have sonship, glory and immortality by grace, because it became the temple of God the Word; let it not be exalted above its nature, and let God the Word not be wronged in return for the thanksgiving we owe him.

And what is the wrong? To compound him with the body and to think that he needs the body for perfect sonship. God the Word himself does not wish to be David's son, but his Lord; yet he did not begrudge that this body should be called David's son, and indeed it was for this that he came.

In the forty-fifth chapter above it is said that the man born of Mary is Son of God by grace, but God the Word by nature; and it argues, as it were, saying, "what is by grace is not by nature, and what is by nature is not by grace"; and it adds, "let it suffice for the body that is from us to have sonship by grace, and let it not be exalted above its nature, and let God the Word not be wronged in return for the thanksgiving we owe him." These words present a bare man born of the virgin Mary, who is called Son of God by grace. Whoever, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 46.

When the question concerns births according to nature, let God the Word not be thought to be the son of Mary. For a mortal begets a mortal according to nature, and a body like itself; and God the Word did not undergo two births, one before the ages and the other in later times.

In the forty-sixth chapter above it is said that God the Word should not be thought to be the son of Mary, with the addition that a mortal begets a mortal according to nature, and a body like itself. These words both present a mere man born of the holy virgin Mary and introduce two sons. Whoever, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 47.

So now let them cease from their shameless fighting and desist from their vain contention, blushing at the evidence of what has been said; for he speaks of him who leads many sons to glory. See, then: in the matter of sonship the apostle plainly counts the assumed man among the rest, not in that he shares in sonship in the same way as they do, but in that he, like them, received sonship by grace, while the deity alone possesses natural sonship.

In the forty-seventh chapter above, in expounding what the apostle says, "who had brought many sons to glory," it is said that the holy apostle counts the assumed man among the rest, in that he likewise received the grace of sonship, while the deity alone possesses natural sonship. These words too, as was said above, introduce two sons of God, one by grace and the other by nature. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes or preaches this in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 48.

But to this they say that the name Jesus means Savior: "But how," they say, "could that man be called Savior?" They forget that the son of Nun too was called Jesus, and, what is remarkable, he was not given that name by chance at birth but was renamed by Moses. And it is certain that Moses would not have allowed this name to be given to a man if it signified the divine nature in every respect.

In the forty-eighth chapter above, concerning the name of Jesus, it is denied by argument that it signifies Savior [in the divine sense], and it is said that if Savior signified the divine nature, such a name would never be given to a man. By these words Christ is shown to be simply a mere man, and two persons are understood. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes or preaches this in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 49.

Thus he is shown not only to call him Son while separating him from God the Word, but also, in the matter of sonship, to count him among the others who share in sonship; for he too shared in sonship by grace and was not born of the Father by nature. Yet he has a pre-eminence over the others, because he possesses sonship by union with him, which gives him a firmer share in the thing itself.

In the forty-ninth chapter above it is said that Christ shared in sonship by grace, yet had a pre-eminence over the others in that a firmer share in the thing itself was given to him. Whoever thinks, teaches, believes or preaches this in this way, and does not rather understand and believe that God the Word with the flesh he assumed is one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, both true Son of God and likewise true Son of Man, let him be anathema.
Chapter 50.

The man Jesus is like all men, differing in nothing from men of the same nature except in what grace gave him; and grace, once given, does not change nature. But after the destruction of death God gave him the name that is above every name.

In the fiftieth chapter above it is said that the man Jesus differs in nothing from all men of the same nature except in what grace gave him. These words make our Lord Jesus Christ be regarded as one of the righteous men, who is not understood to be exalted by his deity but is asserted to have obtained by grace something more than other men. If anyone thinks, teaches, believes or preaches this in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 51.

But my brothers, who are sons of the same mother as I, say to me, "Do not separate the man and God, but call them one and the same." When I say man, I mean one of the same nature as myself; if I say God, I mean one of the same nature as God. How are man and God one? Is the nature of man and of God, of master and servant, of maker and thing made, one and the same?

Man is consubstantial with man, and God is consubstantial with God. How then can man and God be one by union, the one who saves and the one who is saved, the one who is before the ages and the one who appeared from Mary?

In the fifty-first chapter above it is denied that God and man can be called one and the same, saying, "How can man and God be one by union, the one who saves and the one who is saved, the one who is before the ages and the one who appeared from Mary?" These words introduce two persons in Christ. If anyone, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches this in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 52.

He aptly added, "For I too am a man," as if to say: "It is no wonder if you can do this, since you are a man receiving it from God; for I too, being what I am, receive obedience, having once been given the power to command through the kindness of the one who gave it."
Chapter 53.

"Therefore it is not unfitting that you too, having received this power from God, should drive away diseases by a word of command alone." For the centurion did not approach him as the Son of God, existing before all creation and the creator of all that is.

In the fifty-second and fifty-third chapters above it is said that the centurion said to Christ: "It is no wonder if you can do this, since you are a man receiving it from God; for I too, being what I am, receive obedience, having once been given the power to command through the kindness of the one who gave it." And although, from what follows, namely that the centurion did not approach him as the Son of God who created all creation, he himself does seem to confess that he is the Son of God and the maker of all creation,

nevertheless he did not judge rightly of the centurion's understanding, for the Lord would not have praised his faith, saying, "I have not found such faith in Israel," unless he knew that the centurion had understood that he is God. Moreover, from the earlier chapters and from other statements, since Christ is said to be Son of God not by unity of subsistence but by grace, here too Christ appears to be presented as a mere man who received power for his merit through the kindness of the giver. If anyone, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 54.

In agreement with this the apostle also says, "And manifestly great is the mystery of godliness: he who was manifested in the flesh was justified in the Spirit." He says that he was justified in the Spirit either because before his baptism he kept the law with fitting exactness, or because after it too he fulfilled the way of life of grace with great exactness through the cooperation of the Spirit.

In the fifty-fourth chapter above, on what the apostle says, "what was manifested in the flesh was justified in the Spirit," Christ is asserted to have been justified either because before his baptism he kept the law with fitting exactness, or because after it too he fulfilled the way of life of grace with great exactness through the cooperation of the Spirit.

Since these words likewise show that Christ was a mere man who needed justification, if anyone thinks, teaches, believes or preaches this in this way, and does not rather believe that he himself, as true God consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit, justifies the ungodly through faith, let him be anathema.
Chapter 55.

We rightly say the same thing of the Lord too: that God the Word, knowing his virtue, was pleased by foreknowledge to dwell in him at the very beginning of his formation, and, uniting him to himself by the disposition of his will, granted him a certain greater grace, inasmuch as the grace that is in him was to be distributed to all men. Hence he also preserved his will intact in what is good.

For we will not say that that man had no will, but that he willed the good, and indeed that the desire for good and hatred of its contrary were present in him in the highest degree by his own will; yet his will was kept intact from the beginning by divine grace, since God knew precisely what kind of man he would be, and by his indwelling gave him great cooperation to strengthen him, for the salvation of us all. Hence no one should say it is unjust that something exceptional, beyond all others, was given to that man who was assumed by the Lord.

In the fifty-fifth chapter above it is said that God the Word, knowing by foreknowledge the virtue of the man Christ, was pleased to dwell in him at the very beginning of his formation, and, uniting him to himself by the disposition of his will, granted him a certain greater grace.

From these words and from others that follow, they are clearly judged to be two persons, and the Son of God appears to dwell in the son of man by disposition, grace and relation. If anyone, therefore, thinks, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not acknowledge and believe that one and the same Christ exists in two natures, perfect, undivided and unconfused, let him be anathema.
Chapter 56.

For it is proper to a rational being to discern good and evil. But if there were no contraries, it would not be possible for him to discern anything. First, therefore, he made a great contrariety in created things.

In the fifty-sixth chapter quoted above it is said that the power to tell good from evil is proper to a rational being, and a little later it follows: “First, then, he made a great opposition among the things that were created.” If these words are said with the intention of introducing a nature of evil as well as a nature of good, let him be anathema.
Chapter 57.

Since Adam did not obey, he was then made subject to death, and this came about through his disobedience. Yet even without disobedience it would have been brought about by the Creator for our benefit: we have all been taught sin.

In the fifty-seventh chapter quoted above it is said that even if Adam had not been disobedient, this would still have been brought about by the Creator for the benefit of human beings, and that we have been taught sin. Far be it from the catholic faith to believe that we could have been taught sin by God so that we might become sinners.

If anyone, then, holds, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, and does not rather confess that sin was brought in by the fault of the first man, against God's prohibition, and that by the just judgment of God he and his descendants underwent the penalty of death because of his disobedience, let him be anathema.
Chapter 58.

So God did not bring death upon human beings against his will or apart from his own judgment, nor did he give sin entry for no benefit (for it was not as though he could not have prevented it had he not wished it to happen). Rather, because he knew it would be useful for us, and indeed for all rational beings, that evil and worse things should first gain entry, and that afterward these should be done away with and better things brought in, God divided creation into two states, the present and the future. In the future state he will lead all things to immortality and immutability, while in the present creation he leaves us for the time being to death and mutability.

For if he had made us immortal and immutable right from the beginning, we would have no difference from irrational creatures, since we would not know our own good. Not knowing mutability, we would not have known the good of immutability; not knowing death, we would not have known the gain of immortality; ignorant of corruption, we would not have praised incorruption; not knowing the burden of the passions, we would not have marveled at freedom from passion. To put it briefly, and not make a long speech of it: without experience of evils we could not have merited knowledge of those goods.

In the fifty-eighth chapter quoted above it is said that God gave sin entry because he knew this to be useful for us, and indeed for all rational beings: namely, that evil and worse things should first gain entry, and that afterward, once these had been done away with, better things should be brought in. And it is added that if he had made us immortal and immutable right from the beginning, we would have no difference from irrational creatures, since we would not know our own good.

By these words, first, it is asserted against the rule of faith that God brought in sin as something useful to us. Second, since he includes all rational beings, he gives it to be understood that this applies also to the angels and to the whole heavenly host, which is endowed with reason. Third, what the devil persuaded the first human beings of in order to deceive them, namely that if they ate from the forbidden tree they would become like gods, knowing good and evil, is asserted to have done them good, as though it were a benefit. If anyone holds, teaches, believes or preaches these things in this way, let him be anathema.
Chapter 59.

It is necessary for all rational beings together—I mean the invisible ones and ourselves, whose body is mortal but whose soul is in every respect of the same kind as the invisible and rational substances—to undergo the present mutability here, so that we may be trained in the best teaching of religion and be established in goodwill.

In the fifty-ninth chapter quoted above it is said: “It is necessary for all rational beings together, the invisible ones and ourselves, whose body is mortal but whose soul is in every respect of the same kind as the invisible and rational substances, to undergo the present mutability here, so that we may be trained in the best teaching of religion and be established in goodwill.” If by these words it is asserted that the angels of light and all the heavenly and invisible powers are still subject to mutability in the same way as human souls, let him be anathema.
Chapter 60.

For he knew that they would certainly sin, but he allowed this to happen, knowing that it was to their advantage. For it was not possible that he who had made them when they did not exist, had shown them to be lords of so many things, and had set before them such great goods for them to enjoy, would not have prevented sin's entry, were it not that he knew this to be to their advantage.

"For it was not possible for us to learn otherwise about sin, the trouble of the passions and the things that are worse, or for our weakness to be shown in these, so as to reveal the greatness of the immutability he would later give us, unless God had arranged these things this way from the beginning, so that by comparison and experience we might know the greatness of those infinite goods. For this reason, letting sin enter as something that would benefit us, he found great help in the war against it."

In the sixtieth chapter quoted above, it is said that God, knowing that man would sin, allowed him to sin because he knew that this was good for him. It says that God did not block sin's entrance because he had arranged things this way from the beginning, so that by comparison and experience we might know the greatness of those infinite goods. For this reason, it says, God let sin enter as something that would benefit us, and man found great help in the war against that same sin.
These words are foreign to the meaning of divine Scripture, for they say that God brought sin in for our benefit. If anyone thinks, teaches, believes or preaches this, let him be anathema.

For the holy catholic Church holds and believes this as certain: God forbade the first man to sin and punished him with a just penalty when he sinned through disobedience. Yet God makes good use even of our evils, and he freed us from the bonds of all sins by a unique remedy, the incarnation, passion, death and resurrection of his only-begotten Son, our Lord God Jesus Christ.

We have now fittingly condemned these things, in keeping with the uprightness of the orthodox faith and by the authority of an apostolic sentence. In doing so we have held to the statutes and traditions of the fathers. We therefore decree that nothing we have condemned with apostolic authority may give anyone occasion to insult the fathers or doctors of the Church who went before us, for that would undoubtedly stir up scandal in the most holy Church. We anathematize any member of the ecclesiastical orders who tries in any way to attribute any of the impieties named above to the fathers and doctors of the Church, or to heap insult on them on that account.

We have condemned and anathematized the doctrines mentioned above in the sense explained for each. In the volume your Piety recently sent us through our brother Bishop Benignus, they are said to appear under the name of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia. For this reason we turned our careful attention to another question. We set out to search most diligently whether the fathers had ever inquired into the person or name of this Theodore, or whether they had established or arranged anything about his name according to the canons.

In this research we found that Cyril of blessed memory, bishop of the city of Alexandria, wrote about the person of Bishop Theodore, who had already died. Replying to a letter from John of revered memory, bishop of the city of Antioch, and to the Eastern synod, he said among other things: "At the holy synod of Ephesus a definition was put forward. Those who presented it said that Theodore had set it out, and it contained nothing sound. The holy synod rejected it as full of perverse ideas. But while it condemned those who think this way, the synod, by a wise act of discretion, made no mention of the man, and it did not anathematize him or anyone else by name."

We have also carefully reviewed the first synod of Ephesus itself. We found nothing in it about the person of Theodore of Mopsuestia. It records only the creed that the presbyter Charisius produced there, with the statement that it had been sent to the churches of the Philadelphians by Anastasius and Photius, who at that time adhered to the heretic Nestorius. It was sent through Antonius and James, who were presbyters in name only.

From this it is clear what blessed Cyril says in his letters: those who produced the creed had brought forward the name of Bishop Theodore, who had already died. With foresight and priestly wisdom, Cyril kept to ecclesiastical restraint toward the dead man. He did not want Theodore's name included even in the synodal records, because of the rule that the priesthood must observe toward the dead.

Blessed Cyril said above that the synod acted with discretion in not anathematizing the man's name. Further on in the same letter he showed that he meant this to extend to the Church's general rule, for he added: "Those who give rise to such disputes will rightly hear this, even if they do not want to: you forget yourselves when you bend your bows against ashes, for the man whose name you have written down no longer survives. Let no one blame me for going so far in these words, but let them give way, and give way greatly, to one who has gone before. It is a grave thing to insult the dead, even if they were laymen, and much more so those who ended this life as bishops. Prudent men see that it is entirely just to yield to him who foreknows each person's will and knows what each person will become."

It is also established that blessed Proclus, bishop of this imperial city, replied in a similar way to the letter of John, the bishop of Antioch mentioned above. Among other things he said: "When did I write to your Holiness that Theodore, or any others who died long ago, ought to be anathematized? When did I mention anyone by name?"

And shortly after: "I rejected the chapters that were attached, because they lacked the precision of true piety. But I did not write about Theodore, or about anyone else who has already died, that he should be anathematized or repudiated, most God-loving one. Nor did our dearest Theodotus, the deacon we sent, receive any such instructions."

In a letter to the deacon Maximus, the same blessed Proclus also says, among other things: "How is it, then, that I have now learned by letter that the names of Theodore of Mopsuestia and certain others have been placed at the head of chapters to be anathematized? They have already gone to God, and it is pointless to insult after death those who have left this life, when we never blamed them while they were alive." And shortly after: "Once the tome has been signed and the chapters have been rejected, though we do not know whose they are, have the deacon Theodotus ready at once to come to the imperial city."

Let your Piety's singular wisdom weigh this, then: Proclus was the most learned of bishops and lived not long after Theodore of Mopsuestia. He had readily condemned those evil teachings, yet even then he declared that he did not know whose they were.

Nor have we found anything decreed or said against the name of this Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, so often mentioned, in the holy and venerable Council of Chalcedon. That venerable synod sent a report to Marcian of pious memory, who was then emperor, and you too have laudably cited this report as testimony in your laws, where you affirm by orthodox confession that Christ our God and Lord is to be confessed as one of the holy Trinity. In that report the synod respectfully recalls the letters that John of Antioch and the Eastern synod sent to blessed Proclus and to Theodosius, then emperor, of most pious memory. In those letters the person of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, is defended against being condemned after his death.

After this we examined with even greater care whether our predecessors of holy memory had also decreed anything about people who had already died and were not found to have been condemned during their lifetime. Looking into this, we recognized that the venerable decrees of our predecessors, the bishops of the apostolic see, have handed down to us a very clear pattern for this caution and foresight.

Most blessed Pope Leo, writing to Theodore, bishop of Forum Livii, says among other things: "It is not necessary for us to examine the merits and deeds of those who have died in this way. The Lord our God, whose judgments cannot be comprehended, has reserved to his own justice what the priestly ministry could not accomplish."

Likewise blessed Pope Gelasius, in the letter he wrote to the bishops of Dardania on the case of Acacius, says among other things: "He fell back into fellowship with depravity and so rightly deserved to be cut off from apostolic communion. He died still under this condemnation. Now that he is dead he cannot obtain the absolution that he neither sought at all nor deserved while he lived. For it was to the apostles themselves that Christ's voice entrusted 'whatever you bind on earth' and 'whatever you loose on earth.' As for one who is now set under divine judgment, it is not lawful for us to decree anything other than the state in which his last day found him."

Likewise Pope Gelasius of blessed memory, mentioned above, taught this clearly in the synodal acts drawn up on the absolution of Misenus, bishop of Cumae: "Let us leave to divine judgment everything that lies beyond the measure of our power. They cannot hold it against us that we forgive the offense of betrayal to the living, for by God's gift the Church is able to do this. Nor let them demand that we grant pardon to those already dead, for it is plain that we cannot do this. It was said, 'whatever you bind and loose on earth.' Those who are clearly no longer on earth God has reserved not to human judgment but to his own. The Church does not dare to claim for itself what it sees was not granted even to the blessed apostles themselves, for the case of the living is one thing and the case of the dead is another."

This rule was also clearly observed in the case of the venerable memory of the saints John, bishop of Constantinople, whom they call Chrysostom, and Flavian, bishop of the same city. They were forcibly driven out, yet they were not regarded as condemned, because the Roman bishops always kept communion with them unbroken. They could not have been said, and cannot be said, to be cut off from the Church, since apostolic authority judged them to be firmly united with itself.

In the seventh book of the History of Eusebius, also called Pamphili, we read that Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, who lived long before, acted this way toward a certain Nepos, a bishop in Egypt. This Bishop Nepos is said to have written about the thousand years in which, as blessed John the apostle says in the Apocalypse, the saints will reign with Christ after the first resurrection, and he is reported to have understood them in a Jewish sense. After his death, word reached Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, that all Egypt regarded the books Nepos had left behind as some great and hidden mystery. Dionysius went to that place (Eusebius reports that the question had arisen in the district of Arsinoë), and by his writing he refuted those books and overturned them. But he did no injury to Nepos, who had written them, above all because Nepos had already died. Anyone who wants to learn more about this will find it in the seventh book of Eusebius's History mentioned above.

We have carefully examined all these things. Our fathers spoke in different words but with one and the same understanding, and they left unharmed the persons of bishops who died in the peace of the Church. The decrees of the apostolic see, which we cited above, lay down the same thing according to the canons: no one may pass any new judgment on the persons of the dead, but each must be left in the state in which his last day found him. And what our holy fathers decided specifically about the name of Theodore of Mopsuestia has been clearly set out above.

Therefore we do not dare to condemn him by our own sentence, nor do we allow anyone else to condemn him. Yet far be it from us to admit, not only into our minds but even into our ears, the doctrinal chapters written above, which we have condemned in the sense explained under each. The same holds for any sayings, under whatever name they are set down, that do not agree and harmonize with the teachings of the Gospels and the apostles, of the four synods of Nicaea, Constantinople, the first of Ephesus and Chalcedon, and of the apostolic see.

As for the writings put forward under the name of the venerable Theodoret, formerly a bishop, we are surprised, first of all, that anyone should feel it necessary to drag anything into reproach under that bishop's name. More than a hundred years ago he stood under the judgment of the holy and venerable synod of Chalcedon. There he signed without hesitation and agreed with ready devotion to the letter of most blessed Pope Leo.

At that time Dioscorus and the Egyptian bishops were there, and they said that Theodoret had anathematized holy Cyril and that he was a heretic. Our holy fathers heard this. They then examined Theodoret most diligently, questioning him in person before all present. Yet they are known to have demanded nothing of him except that he at once anathematize and condemn Nestorius and his impious doctrines. They judged it enough that he did this before the whole council, condemning Nestorius and all his doctrines in a clear voice while all the fathers listened.

From this it is plainly evident that whatever is or was put forward under anyone's name that seems to agree with the doctrines of the impious Nestorius was then condemned without doubt by the venerable Theodoret in that holy council. It would therefore be utterly contrary, and beyond doubt hostile, to the judgment of the synod of Chalcedon to condemn certain Nestorian doctrines now under the name of that bishop. As we have said, he then openly anathematized and condemned that same impious Nestorius and his detestable doctrines together with the holy fathers.

For to say that some of those fathers held views like those of Nestorius is nothing other than to make out that the fathers who sat in the holy synod of Chalcedon were liars or only pretended to profess the right faith. Yet you can see that Nestorius and his doctrines were condemned by their judgment.

Nor should anyone suppose that our most blessed fathers at the holy synod of Chalcedon overlooked the insults that the venerable Theodoret is thought to have heaped on Cyril of holy memory by criticizing his twelve chapters. These events had happened only recently and the fathers had everything before their eyes. Either they established that Bishop Theodoret had done nothing of the kind, or they judged that they should follow the example of Cyril of holy memory himself. The Easterners at Ephesus had done many grave things against Cyril in writing, but when he returned to concord with them, he left all of it in silence for the love of peace, as if it had never happened. He was fulfilling the apostle's saying when he writes to the Corinthians: "Anyone whom you have forgiven anything, I forgive too."

We must also believe that the holy synod of Chalcedon had this in mind. The teaching of holy Cyril, contained in his letters, was read out and accepted at that synod, and Bishop Theodoret received it so devoutly that he even used Cyril's teachings as testimonies in praise of the letter of most blessed Pope Leo. So even if it were established that he had insulted Cyril, he was seen to have made full amends by reverently embracing the faith of the man he had falsely suspected of error. It is therefore not fitting for us now to search for anything as if our fathers had overlooked it, or to reopen it. We utterly reject those who now take pleasure in criticism of holy Cyril, or who think that our holy fathers took pleasure in it.

Having weighed the truth of these matters, we therefore decree and determine that no one may do or put forward anything that injures or disparages a man most fully approved at the synod of Chalcedon, namely Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, by attaching a charge to his name. In every respect, reverence for his person must be preserved. But whatever writings or doctrines, put forward under anyone's name, are shown to agree with the errors of the wicked Nestorius and Eutyches, we anathematize and condemn.

This ought to be more than enough. We condemn and anathematize Nestorius together with Paul of Samosata and Bonosus, and, on the other side, Eutyches together with Valentinus and Apollinaris, along with their errors and all other heretics with their doctrines. And we likewise condemn those who, entangled in their errors and remaining incorrigible, departed from the life of this present age. In this way we leave no part of perverse doctrine that is not found to be shut out of God's holy Church by this sentence, which we have pronounced with apostolic authority. Nevertheless, we again add the following specifically:

1. If anyone, while upholding the unchangeableness of the divine nature, does not confess that the Word was made flesh and that from the very moment of conception in the Virgin's womb he united to himself, according to subsistence, the beginnings of human nature, but instead says that God the Word was with a man who already existed, so that the holy Virgin is not believed to be truly Mother of God but is called so in name only, let him be anathema.

2. If anyone denies that the union of the natures in Christ took place according to subsistence, but says that God the Word dwells in a man who exists separately, as in one of the righteous, and does not confess the union of the natures according to subsistence in such a way that God the Word, together with the flesh he assumed, remained and remains one subsistence or person, let him be anathema.
3. If anyone divides the sayings of the Gospels and the apostles concerning the one Christ in such a way that he also introduces a division of the natures united in him, let him be anathema.

4. If anyone says that the one Jesus Christ, true Son of God and the very same true Son of man, was ignorant of future things or of the day of the last judgment, and that he could know only as much as the deity revealed to him, dwelling in him as in someone else, let him be anathema.

5. The apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews that he learned obedience by experience, and that with a loud cry and tears he offered prayers and supplications to the one who was able to save him from death. If anyone applies this to a Christ stripped of deity, one who was perfected by the labors of virtue, so that he seems to introduce two Christs or two sons from it, and does not believe that one and the same Christ, Son of God and Son of man, is to be confessed and worshiped from two and in two natures that are inseparable and undivided, let him be anathema.

We have thus repudiated and condemned all these blasphemies and others like them. By the provisions of this present constitution, we take the greatest care that, as we said above, persons who rested in the peace and communion of the universal Church should not, on the pretext of the perverse doctrine we have condemned,

suffer any harm to their reputation. While the detestable doctrines of the heresiarchs Nestorius and Eutyches and of all their followers are condemned, no insult must be brought against the bishops who, as has been said, died in the peace of the catholic Church. Otherwise this would give rise to insults in the very place where reverence for the holy fathers ought rather to be preserved.

You also asked about the letter of the venerable Ibas, formerly bishop of the city of Edessa. We likewise searched diligently to find whether our fathers in earlier times had raised, debated, inquired into or decided anything concerning it. As everyone knows, and your Piety above all, we do not know the Greek language. So now, through our own people who appear to know that language, we have searched most diligently in the synodal books for the acts of the holy and venerable Council of Chalcedon, and we have clearly

and plainly found the following. The case of the venerable Ibas was examined in two sessions of that synod. There, from the acts drawn up before Photius, bishop of Tyre, and Eustathius, bishop of Berytus, his accusers produced against him, among other things, the letter in question. When the hearing of the case was complete, the venerable fathers were asked what should be decided about Ibas's case, and the following sentences were then given:

Paschasinus and Lucentius, most reverend bishops, and Boniface, a presbyter, holding the place of the apostolic see, said through Paschasinus: "Now that the documents have been read again, we recognize from the sentence of the most reverend bishops that the most reverend Ibas is shown to be innocent. For when his letter was read again, we recognized that he is catholic. We therefore decree that both the dignity of the episcopate and the church from which he was unjustly driven out in his absence be restored to him. As for the most holy bishop Nonnus, who was made bishop in his place a short time ago, the most reverend bishop of the church of Antioch must consider what ought to be determined about him."

Anatolius, most reverend archbishop of Constantinople, New Rome, said: "The good faith of the most reverend bishops and judges, and the reading of everything that followed, show that the most reverend Ibas is innocent of the accusations brought against him. I therefore set aside at present all suspicion concerning him, since he agrees to and signs both the definition of the faith now issued by the holy council and the letter of the most holy archbishop of Rome, Leo. I judge him worthy of the episcopate and of having the care of the church over which he formerly presided. As for the most reverend bishop Nonnus, who was made bishop in his place, Maximus, the most reverend bishop of Antioch, will give a ruling."

Maximus, the most reverend bishop of the city of Antioch, said: 'From what has just been read out it is clear that the most reverend Ibas has been found innocent of all the charges brought against him. And from the text of the letter that was read again, which his opponent produced, his writing has been shown to be catholic. Therefore I too decree that he should recover both the dignity of the episcopate and his own city, as the most holy archbishops have also judged: both those who hold the place of the most holy Archbishop Leo and the most holy Anatolius, archbishop of the imperial city. The most reverend Bishop Nonnus, however, who was made bishop in his place, is to keep the proper dignity of the episcopate, so that I may deliberate with the most holy bishops about his appointment.'

Juvenal, the most reverend bishop of Jerusalem, said: 'Divine Scripture commands that those who turn back be received. For this reason we receive even those who return from the heretics. So I judge that the most reverend Ibas deserves clemency, since he is an old man, and that he should hold the rank of the episcopate, being catholic.'

Thalassius, the most reverend bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, said: 'Since the most reverend bishops Photius and Eustathius approved Ibas's case and did not condemn him, I am persuaded by their judgement and I too wish him to hold the priesthood, as the most holy prelates have decided. This is especially so because he undertook in the proceedings to anathematize what his accusers had alleged against him in writing.'

Eusebius, the most reverend bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, said: 'The reading of the sentence pronounced at Tyre by the holy bishops Photius and Eustathius has shown that in that hearing the most reverend Ibas anathematized Nestorius and his impious doctrines and assented to right doctrine. For this reason the aforesaid most reverend bishops accepted this satisfaction and approved that he should hold the episcopate. Now, therefore, since the same most holy Ibas anathematizes Nestorius and his impious doctrines, I wish him to hold the priesthood.'

Stephen, the most reverend bishop of Ephesus, said: 'Since the most reverend Bishop Ibas anathematizes Nestorius and Eutyches and their impious doctrines, I too decree, as the holy fathers have, that he should be in the rank of the episcopate.'

Diogenes, the most reverend bishop of Cyzicus, said: 'I have decided that the definition pronounced by the most holy bishops Photius and Eustathius concerning the most reverend Ibas should stand. This is especially so because his accusers who were present there agreed, with their own signatures, to the definition set out on that occasion, and it has now been read again in the holy and universal council.'
Constantine, the most reverend bishop of Bostra, said: "I too agree with what the holy council has rightly decided about the most holy bishop Ibas."
Theodore, the most reverend bishop of Damascus, said: "I too agree with what the holy fathers have since defined, in accordance with the canons, concerning the venerable Ibas."

Meletius, the venerable bishop of Larissa, acting for Domnus, the most reverend bishop of Apamea in Syria, said: "I too agree with what the holy and reverend fathers have rightly decided about the most reverend Ibas."

Romanus, the most reverend bishop of Myra in Lycia, said: "As the evidence of the documents read to us has persuaded us, I too decree that the same most reverend bishop Ibas be kept in the priesthood, as the most holy archbishops have also decreed, provided of course that he anathematizes Nestorius and Eutyches and their impious opinions."

Eunomius, the most reverend bishop of Nicomedia, said: "From what has been read, the venerable Ibas has already been shown to be innocent. For where he seemed to censure the most blessed Cyril by speaking ill of him, in the end he made a correct confession and retracted what he had censured. Therefore I too decree that, since he anathematizes Nestorius and Eutyches and their impious doctrines and agrees with what was written by the most holy archbishop Leo and by this universal synod, he is worthy of the episcopate."

John, the venerable bishop of Sebastea; Seleucus, the venerable bishop of Amasea; Constantine, the venerable bishop of Melitene; Patricius, the venerable bishop of Tyana; Peter, the venerable bishop of Gangra; and Atarbius, the venerable bishop of Trebizond, who also acted for Dorotheus, the most reverend bishop of Neocaesarea, said: "The judgment of the most reverend bishops Photius and Eustathius shows that the most reverend Ibas is innocent. Likewise his denial makes us the more ready to receive him, for mercy is always dear to the Lord Christ. Therefore, in accordance with the sentence of the holy bishops and of the whole holy council, we too decree that it is just for him to receive the rank of bishop."

Frangion, the venerable bishop of Philippopolis, and Basil, the venerable bishop of Trajanopolis, said: "Since he was neither present at the trial nor summoned to it, we hold that he is in no way harmed by the sentence pronounced against him."
Nunechius, the most reverend bishop of Laodicea in Phrygia, said: "We agree with what the holy fathers have defined about the most holy Ibas."
Florentius, the most reverend bishop of Sardis in Lydia, said: "I too likewise agree with what has been said above about the most reverend Ibas."
Eusebius, the most reverend bishop of Dorylaeum, said: "Since so many most holy fathers are restoring the episcopate to the most reverend Ibas, I too agree."
All the most reverend bishops cried out: "We all say the same thing: let him anathematize Nestorius now, let him anathematize his teachings now, let him anathematize Eutyches and his teaching now."

The most reverend Ibas said: "I have already anathematized Nestorius and his teachings in writing, and now I anathematize him ten thousand times. For what is done once with satisfaction does no harm if it is done ten thousand times." And: "Anathema to Nestorius, and to Eutyches, and to anyone who says there is one nature." And: "I anathematize everyone who does not think as this holy synod thinks."
The most glorious judges said: "What the holy and venerable council has judged concerning the most reverend bishop Ibas shall keep its own force."

This, then, is how matters stand in the judgment and settlement of the holy synod of Chalcedon. The statements of the vicars of the apostolic see, who represented the presence of their venerable prelate, and of the other fathers have been made clear. From them we plainly observe that those known to have held the place of our most blessed predecessor Pope Leo at that same holy synod of Chalcedon said:

"Having had his letter read again, we have recognized that he is catholic." Anatolius of Constantinople said: "The reading of everything that followed shows that the most reverend Ibas is innocent of the charges his accusers brought against him." And Maximus of Antioch said: "From the reading of the copy of the letter produced by his adversary, what he wrote has been shown to be catholic." The other bishops are known not only not to have contradicted these statements but even to have given them their most open consent.

They say that in this same letter Ibas excused Nestorius by saying that, because Nestorius was unwilling to call holy Mary the mother of God, many thought he belonged to the heresy of Paul of Samosata, who said that Christ was a mere man. But no one doubts that our holy fathers examined this point in the letter carefully. Because Nestorius, by not calling the holy Virgin Mary the mother of God, deserved to be reckoned among the followers of Paul of Samosata's heresy, our holy fathers understood all the more clearly that Ibas's verdict made the charge against Nestorius heavier,

since Ibas is shown by these words to have said nothing else than this: that Nestorius, by denying that the blessed Virgin is the mother of God, appears to present our Lord God Jesus Christ as a mere man, and the Son of God as without real substance, after the impiety of Paul of Samosata, although Nestorius was the author of a heresy of his own.

So when the venerable man Ibas said that some thought Nestorius belonged to the heresy of Paul of Samosata, he said it rather to make the charge against him heavier, as if he were saying: "Although Nestorius had founded an error of his own, yet by not calling the holy Virgin Mary the mother of God he appeared so impious that many thought he taught the heresy of Paul of Samosata without any difference at all."

In his letter Ibas so magnified the guilt of this error as to make Nestorius quite like Paul of Samosata, whose baptism the universal church, following the sentence of the holy synod of Nicaea, judged must be rejected. Since the church receives those who return from the Nestorian heresy to the holy catholic church once they have merely condemned that heresy, Nestorius is without doubt found weighed down, through the letter of the venerable Ibas, by a heavier curse, since his error is compared to an error that has no valid baptism.

Nor should anyone accuse Ibas of using the words "he was thought" as though he were in doubt, since the blessed apostle Paul says affirmatively to the Corinthians: "For I think that I too have the Spirit of God." Nor did he doubt that he had the Spirit of God, for elsewhere he said: "Or are you seeking proof of Christ who speaks in me?" How could it be doubted that one in whom Christ speaks has the Spirit of God?

Our holy fathers sitting at the synod of Chalcedon also noted that in this same letter of Ibas, Apollinaris, with his teaching that asserts one nature of the divinity and humanity of our Lord God Jesus Christ, is condemned as impious and execrable. And they strongly approved what Ibas said in the same letter: "two natures, one power, one person, which is the one Son, our Lord Jesus Christ."

In saying "one power" he is recognized as following the teaching of the apostle Paul, who speaks of Christ in the singular as "the power of God and the wisdom of God," and says in another place: "For though he was crucified out of the weakness of the flesh, yet he lives by the power of God." We must believe that Ibas had this in mind when he composed his letter. He confessed the power of the Word who assumed the flesh, and recognized in him the assumed flesh as the Word's own; so by saying "one power" he expressed the supreme and inseparable unity of one person, under the name of the one Son, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ. By what he added afterward he showed that he had understood it in this way and persevered in confessing this orthodox faith, when the fathers at the holy synod of Chalcedon urged Ibas, so that he might be joined to their fellowship, to do as they themselves had done, namely to condemn Nestorius and Eutyches with their teachings.

Ibas did this devoutly, testifying that he had always done so, and said freely before all the fathers: "Anathema to Nestorius and Eutyches," adding: "and to anyone who says there is one nature." For he knew that he had been pronounced orthodox precisely for this rejection of one nature in favour of confessing two natures in one and the same Son.

We must also explain the following, so that no one may think that Ibas's letter excuses Nestorius from the heresy of which he is the author when it says: "But Nestorius, because he was hated by his city and by the greatest men in it, could not return there."

These words are rather understood to mean that Ibas called Nestorius, as a heretic, hateful to his city and to the greatest men in it at that time. We must believe that our fathers at Chalcedon understood it so, since earlier in the same letter Ibas had said that this Nestorius wrote harmful books that scandalized those who heard them, and denied that the blessed Virgin Mary is the mother of God. It is right, then, that we understand what our fathers accepted in this sense, and not suspect something else that the writer of the letter is nowhere read to have said.

By God's grace we could indeed give an account of every passage and sense of this letter one by one. But the rest can fittingly be read in the same way as the few passages we have explained, and even if any obscurity arose in them, we would yield to the authority of the fathers and their deeper understanding. So there is no need to dwell on these matters any longer.

For these reasons, then, which we have stated above, and on account of that profession of faith through which Cyril of venerable memory, bishop of Alexandria, and the most reverend John, bishop of Antioch, and all the Eastern bishops were reconciled through Paul, bishop of the city of Emesa (a profession which Ibas too praises and gladly embraces in this very letter), the fathers pronounced the letter of Bishop Ibas orthodox.

But the things said in this letter of the bishop Ibas against Cyril of blessed memory, through a misunderstanding, the fathers at the holy synod of Chalcedon by no means accepted when they pronounced the letter orthodox. Indeed, the venerable bishop himself, once he had gained a better understanding of Cyril's chapters, refuted these things in many ways, as is shown most clearly by the statement of Eunomius of venerable memory, bishop of the church of Nicomedia, who sat at that same holy synod of Chalcedon.

It runs as follows: Eunomius, bishop of Nicomedia, said: "From what has been read, the venerable Ibas has indeed been shown to be innocent. For in the passages where he seemed to speak ill and to blame the most blessed Cyril, he afterward made a right confession and refuted what he had blamed. Therefore I too decree that he is worthy of the episcopate, since he anathematizes Nestorius and Eutyches and their impious teachings and agrees with what was written by the most holy archbishop Leo and by this universal synod."

The statement of Juvenal of venerable memory also means the same thing. Bishop Ibas had disparaged saint Cyril because he misunderstood his chapters, but afterward he professed that, once Cyril had explained them and he had understood them, he had devoutly entered into communion with him and had changed his mind about what he had earlier understood differently. Juvenal therefore decreed that he should receive the episcopate, as being orthodox in his profession of faith, saying:

"Divine Scripture commands that those who turn back be received. That is why we receive even those who return from among heretics. So I consider that the most reverend Ibas deserves clemency, since he is also old, and should keep the rank of bishop, as he is orthodox." These words are understood to mean: "If we receive those who come to us from heretics, how can we not receive Ibas, who is orthodox and who, being uncertain about the meaning of blessed Cyril's chapters, seemed to speak against him, now that he has turned away from the understanding in which he was mistaken, since it is established that he is orthodox?" For Bishop Juvenal would not have said that Ibas was orthodox unless he had confirmed from the words of his letter that his confession of faith was orthodox.

To show that Juvenal's statement agrees with that of Eunomius, the very words of Eunomius's statement instruct us. Among other things they run: "For in the passages where he seemed to speak ill and to blame the most blessed Cyril, he afterward made a right confession and refuted what he had blamed." These words show most clearly that nothing was censured in Bishop Ibas regarding his confession of faith, which is known to have been praised, but that this same Ibas refuted the wrong opinion he had held about blessed Cyril because his understanding had misled him.

For in the earlier proceedings, as the sentence of Photius and Eustathius records, this same venerable bishop Ibas is stated most clearly to hold and accept everything done at the first synod of Ephesus, to judge it equal to what was established at Nicaea, and to consider that there is no difference between it and the other. And they declare that they greatly praised his holiness because Ibas readily saw fit to reassure those who, whether from suspicion or in any other way, were damaging the reputation of his teaching.

For after blessed Cyril's twelve chapters had been explained and the meaning saint Cyril had in those chapters had been made clear to him, he professed that he, together with all the Eastern bishops, held Cyril to be orthodox and remained in communion with him until his death. From this it is clear that the venerable Ibas, before he understood blessed Cyril's twelve chapters, when he suspected that one nature of Christ was being proclaimed in them, rejected with an orthodox mind what he had judged to be wrongly said; and after they were explained, he likewise with an orthodox mind reverently accepted what he had come to recognize as rightly said.

But this too is beyond doubt plain to the minds of all the faithful: that it was rather Dioscorus and Eutyches who, at the second synod of Ephesus, heaped insults on blessed Cyril and the first council of Ephesus by their heretical understanding. They believed that saint Cyril had proclaimed one nature in our Lord God Jesus Christ through his twelve chapters, and for this reason Dioscorus condemned some Eastern bishops who refused to accept the proclamation of one nature.

Among them he condemned Bishop Ibas as a heretic, specifically on account of this profession of his faith, in which he most openly confesses two natures, one power, one person, which is the one Son, our Lord Jesus Christ. At the same time he restored Eutyches as catholic because he proclaimed one nature, and he also condemned Flavian of holy memory for speaking of two natures. So Dioscorus himself was found to be the one trying to destroy the first synod of Ephesus, which he defended under the guise of an execrable interpretation; and Dioscorus and Eutyches, by praising blessed Cyril, accused him more than Ibas did by blaming him through the error of a false understanding.

For since both the praise and the blame were directed at one and the same interpretation, Dioscorus and Eutyches, who praised, were found to have praised in a heretical spirit, and were therefore condemned by the holy synod of Chalcedon.
