But Bishop Ibas, who through error, thinking that one nature was proclaimed in the chapters, at first blamed them, and after their meaning had been made clear to him professed that he, with all the Eastern bishops, was in communion with blessed Cyril, was judged by that same synod of Chalcedon to have remained in the right path of the catholic faith.

This same synod saw that Dioscorus and Eutyches, who strove to cover themselves falsely with the veil of blessed Cyril, were in fact shown to be opposed to blessed Cyril's teachings, since they proclaimed in a blasphemous spirit one nature after the union. So it condemned Dioscorus together with Eutyches by one and the same sentence, overthrowing the second synod of Ephesus and confirming the first.

Since the words of the prophet Ezekiel are thrown at us, which he spoke in the person of the Lord to the priests of Jerusalem who did not distinguish evil from good: "Her priests have despised my law and defiled my holy things; they did not distinguish between holy and profane, nor did they separate clean from unclean," your Piety, and together with you the hearts of all the faithful, ought to observe from these words

that this is why we do not dare to reopen the judgment of the synod of Chalcedon: lest the snares of heretics should fasten this stain (God forbid) on the bishops who sat there, so that they accuse them of having been unable to distinguish between good and evil, between holy and profane, between clean and unclean, if they see us now reopening, on any pretext whatever, cases of that holy synod which were concluded by its judgment with the consent of the apostolic see.

Therefore we preserve in all things the discernment and judgment of the holy fathers, and the settlement of every matter has been made clear from the judgment of the synod of Chalcedon according to the reasoning we have given. It shines out with plain truth, from the words of the letter of the venerable Ibas examined with a most correct and pious understanding, from the proceedings held before Photius and Eustathius, and from the charges against Bishop Ibas examined in his presence by those present, that our fathers sitting at Chalcedon most justly pronounced the faith of this venerable bishop Ibas orthodox, and that his censure of blessed Cyril, which they recognized as having arisen, as human failings do, from a misunderstanding, had been purged by fitting satisfaction.

By the authority of this our present sentence we therefore establish and decree that the judgment of the fathers who sat at Chalcedon remains inviolate, both in all things and also with respect to the often-mentioned letter of the venerable Ibas. By this our constitution we permit no one belonging to the ecclesiastical orders and dignities ever to presume to introduce any rash novelty, whether by addition, subtraction, alteration, or in any other way, either concerning the matter of this letter or concerning the other things judged, ordered, defined and settled at the council of Chalcedon with the consent of the vicars of the apostolic see, as though they were incomplete or open to blame.

On the same principle we decree that no one should think that the letter of blessed Cyril to which the twelve chapters are appended, or the chapters themselves, issued against the perfidy of Nestorius, should be disparaged, since it is established that the venerable man Ibas and all the Eastern bishops, after the meaning of these chapters had been explained to them, remained in communion with blessed Cyril for the whole of his life. And we reject and banish from the right path of our understanding anything, whether from the above-mentioned letter of the venerable bishop Ibas or from all that was judged, ordered, defined and settled at the holy synod of Chalcedon, that is twisted so as to make it appear that by the authority of that synod either the perverse teaching of Nestorius was upheld or Nestorius himself was excused.

Someone might perhaps think it doubtful whether the case of Ibas, bishop of the city of Edessa, was properly taken up before the holy fathers, on the grounds that the most blessed Pope Leo commissioned his aforesaid legates and vicars of the apostolic see only on the matter of faith, and not also on the restoration of bishops improperly deposed, and might regard that case as having been handled needlessly. Let him know that the most blessed Pope Leo wrote this, among other things, to the holy synod of Chalcedon: "But since we are aware that through wicked rivalries the state of many churches has been thrown into disorder, and that very many bishops who would not accept heresy were driven from their sees and deported into exile, and others put in their places while they were still living, the remedy of justice must first be applied to these wounds, so that no one is deprived of what is his own or makes use of what belongs to another."

And lest anyone doubt whether what was done at the synod of Chalcedon concerning the restoration of bishops was brought to the notice of the most blessed Leo and confirmed by him, let him not neglect to read with due care the synod's own report sent to the most blessed Leo our predecessor, which at the end, after other matters, contains these words: "We have taken care to make known to you the whole substance of the proceedings, for our support and for the confirmation and [?] of what we have done."

After learning of these things, the same most blessed Pope Leo, giving thanks to Pulcheria Augusta of pious memory for the restored bishops, writes as follows: "Let your Clemency know, then, that the whole Roman church greatly rejoices at all the works of your faith: both that you supported our legation with devoted affection in every way, and that you brought back the catholic bishops who had been driven from their churches by an unjust sentence." See, then: by the fact that all the proceedings were sent to the most blessed Pope Leo, knowledge of what had been done reached him; and by his returning thanks, his confirmation of what had been done is made plain.

We have no doubt, therefore, that it is plain to the minds of all the faithful what instructions for the handling of affairs blessed Pope Leo gave to his vicars who were present at the synod in his place, what courses of action they received to carry out, and what was established by that general council with the prelate of the apostolic see presiding and consenting through his vicars. It is not lawful for anyone to diminish these things, add to them, break them, or [?] reopen them.

That it is not lawful for the statutes of the venerable synod of Chalcedon to be torn up or reopened under any colour or pretext is taught us by the constitutions of our predecessors, a few of which, out of countless, we cite here, chiefly from the letters of our predecessor the blessed Leo, as whose supreme prelate, present through his vicars, the holy council of Chalcedon flourished.

For he says this in a letter to Leo Augustus of pious memory: "These gifts of God are bestowed on us from heaven only if we are not found ungrateful for what has been granted, and do not rather look for the contrary, as though what we have obtained were nothing. For to search into what has been made plain, to reopen what has been completed, and to overturn what has been defined: what else is this but failing to give thanks for what we have obtained, and stretching out the wicked appetites of deadly desire toward the food of the forbidden tree?"

And a little further on: "Let your Piety know in advance, then, venerable emperor, that those whom I promise to send will set out from the apostolic see not to do battle with the enemies of the faith nor to contend against anyone; for concerning the things defined, as it pleased God, both at Nicaea and at Chalcedon, we dare enter into no discussion, as though what so great an authority established through the Holy Spirit were doubtful or weak."

Likewise our same blessed predecessor Pope Leo, in another letter to the aforesaid venerable Augustus: "Do not allow," he says, "conflicts that were extinguished by the triumphs of the Almighty's right hand to rise up again in renewed commotions, especially since this is not at all lawful for the long-condemned audacities of the heretics, and since this fruit is owed to pious labours: that the whole fullness of the church should remain secure in the firmness of its unity, and nothing whatever that has been well settled should be reopened. For to want to fight on after lawful and divinely inspired decrees is the mark not of a peaceable spirit but of a rebellious one, as the apostle says: 'For to quarrel about words is useful for nothing but the ruin of those who hear.' For if people were always free to argue by human persuasions, there would never be lacking those who dare to resist the truth and trust in the glibness of worldly wisdom."

And again, a little later: “We must act devoutly and steadfastly, so that, by admitting a debate over such matters, we do not detract from the authority of what has been defined by God.” Likewise from the letter of Pope Leo to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople: “Let your diligence take care that this exhortation reaches the knowledge of all the brethren. For, as must often be said, the whole Christian religion is thrown into turmoil if anything that was established at Chalcedon is overturned, and if you allow what was composed by divine inspiration to be violated by any novelty.”

And our most blessed predecessor Pope Simplicius also says this, among other things, to the Emperor Zeno: “Let no one who is doubtful in his reasoning and fearful in mind expect that anything new will be reconsidered after the Council of Chalcedon against its definitions. For what was established by the whole body of bishops is maintained throughout the entire world with an observance that cannot be undone.”

Likewise the same Pope Simplicius to the Emperor Zeno: “Let no access to the ears of your piety be opened to pernicious minds. Let no confidence be granted for reconsidering things settled of old. For in this way the schemes of all heresies, once laid low by the decrees of the Church, are never allowed to renew the struggles of their crushed assault.”

Likewise the aforesaid most blessed Pope Simplicius to the same Emperor Zeno: “Command that the decrees of the Synod of Chalcedon, and what my predecessor Leo of blessed memory taught with apostolic learning, remain in force inviolate; for what has been laid to rest by their definition can in no way be reconsidered.”

It is clear, then, from the foregoing testimonies of the fathers, what caution we ought to keep for the sake of the integrity of the Apostolic See and out of regard for the universal Church. Mindful of this caution long ago, we too, in the letter we had then given to Menas, bishop of Constantinople (which, however, insofar as it concerns the matter of the Three Chapters, we have annulled, having received it back when Menas, the bishop of holy memory, offered it to your clemency in the presence of many bishops and of the glorious senate, and your piety returned it to us with his consent),

never departing from the circumspection proper to our office and purpose, took care to show in every way due reverence to the Synod of Chalcedon. This is attested by the text of that same letter, from which, to prove our caution, we have appended a few passages out of many; when these are carefully examined, it is plainly shown how the holy Synod of Chalcedon has remained, and remains, inviolate in our eyes. For it is certain that in that very letter of ours we wrote, among other things, the following about that synod:

“Since it is perfectly clear to us by plain reason that whoever attempts to do anything to the dishonor of the aforesaid synod will rather harm himself.” And again, after other things: “But even if it had been plainly shown to us that this was rather contained in the acts themselves, no one would dare to be the author of such presumption as to judge anything brought before that most holy tribunal to be doubtful, since we must believe that those who were then present, with the matters fresh in their memory, were able to inquire into some things more carefully, even beyond what was written, and to define more surely what now, after so long a time, seems doubtful to us as though the case were unknown; since this too is owed to the reverence due to synods, that even what is less understood should yield to their authority.”

And again, after other things: “All things being preserved and remaining in their perpetual firmness that are known to have been defined in the venerable councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, the first of Ephesus and Chalcedon, and confirmed by the authority of our predecessors and our own; all those condemned in the said holy councils being without doubt condemned, and those likewise absolved whose absolution was decreed by those same synods.”

And again, after other things: “Subjecting also to the sentence of anathema anyone, whoever he may be, who accepts as having any validity anything that is found against the aforesaid Synod of Chalcedon, whether the present document or anything done or written in this matter, whether by us or by anyone else; and let the holy Synod of Chalcedon, whose firmness is great and unshaken, perpetual and venerable, retain its firmness just as the councils of Nicaea, Constantinople and the first of Ephesus retain theirs.”

And again, after other things: “We also anathematize anyone who does not both faithfully follow and equally venerate the most holy synods of Nicaea, Constantinople, the first of Ephesus and Chalcedon, which agree with the apostles in one spotless faith and have been confirmed by the prelates of the Apostolic See; or who wishes either to correct, as if wrongly stated, or to supplement, as if incomplete, the things that were done in those holy councils we have named.”

See, venerable emperor, it is shown clearer than daylight that in our reverence for the four holy synods our will has always been this: that whatever was defined, established or judged by the holy fathers sitting in them should remain inviolate.

Therefore, all that is contained concerning the letter of Ibas and his person in the statements of the holy fathers and of the legates of the Apostolic See remaining in force, let that suffice for us and for all Catholics with one and the same will which the holy synod there proclaimed could suffice for it, saying: “Let him only anathematize Nestorius and his doctrines”; and by this anathema of the most wicked Nestorius and Eutyches, repeated so many times by Bishop Ibas, the will of the whole synod was satisfied.

These matters having therefore been settled by us with every caution and diligence on all sides, in order to preserve inviolate the reverence due to the above-mentioned synods and their venerable decrees, and mindful that it is written that we must not go beyond the boundaries set by our fathers, we establish and decree that no one belonging to the ecclesiastical orders and dignities may hold, write, put forward, compose or teach anything concerning the oft-mentioned Three Chapters contrary to what we have asserted or established in the present constitution, or after the present definition raise any further question.

But if anything has been or shall be done, said or written concerning the same Three Chapters contrary to what we have here asserted or established, in the name of anyone belonging to the ecclesiastical orders and dignities, and found by anyone anywhere, we reject [?] it in every way by the authority of the Apostolic See, over which we preside by the grace of God. I HAVE CORRECTED IT.

Given on the day before the Ides of May, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus, in the twelfth year after the consulship of Basilius, a man of clarissimus rank, in the city of Constantinople.
TO OUR MOST GLORIOUS AND MOST CLEMENT SON, JUSTINIAN AUGUSTUS

JOHN, BISHOP. Among the illustrious praises of Your Clemency's wisdom, most Christian of princes, one shines out with a purer light, like a star: that, out of love for the faith and zeal for charity, and instructed in the teachings of the Church, you preserve reverence for the Roman see, subject all things to it, and bring all things into its unity. To its founder, that is, the first of the apostles, the Lord gave the command: "Feed my sheep." That this see is truly the head of all the churches is declared both by the rules of the fathers and by the statutes of princes, and is attested by the most reverent words of Your Piety.

It is plain, then, that what the Scriptures say has been fulfilled in you: "By me kings reign, and the mighty decree justice." For nothing shines with a brighter light than right faith in a prince, and nothing is so incapable of setting as true religion. Since both look to the author of life and light, they rightly reject darkness and know no failing.

For this reason, most glorious of princes, the divine power will be entreated with every prayer to preserve Your Piety, without failing, for long ages to come in this ardor of faith, this devotion of mind, this zeal for undefiled religion; for we believe that this is also of benefit to the holy churches. For it is written: "The king rules by his lips"; and again: "The king's heart is in the hand of God, and he will turn it wherever he wills."

This is what makes your empire firm, this is what preserves your realms. For the peace of the Church and the unity of religion guard, with the tranquility so dear to them, the one who has brought this about and raised him on high.

Nor is it a small recompense that the divine power grants to him through whom the Church is not divided and sundered by any wrinkles, nor marred by any blemishes set upon it. For it is written that "when a just king sits upon the throne, nothing evil will stand against him."

Accordingly, we received with our customary reverence the letter of Your Serenity by the hands of the most holy men Hypatius and Demetrius, my brothers and fellow bishops. From their report we also learned that, out of love for the faith and to defeat the designs of the heretics, you had issued an edict to the faithful peoples in accordance with apostolic teaching, with the consent of our brothers and fellow bishops. Because this agrees with apostolic teaching, we confirm it by our authority. The text of the letter is as follows:

THE VICTOR JUSTINIAN, PIOUS, FORTUNATE, RENOWNED, TRIUMPHANT, EVER AUGUSTUS, TO JOHN, MOST HOLY ARCHBISHOP OF THE BOUNTEOUS CITY OF ROME AND PATRIARCH. Rendering honor to the apostolic see and to Your Holiness, as has always been and still is our wish, and honoring Your Beatitude as befits a father, we hasten to bring to Your Holiness's attention everything that concerns the state of the churches. For it has always been our great concern that the unity of your apostolic see should be preserved, and the state of God's holy churches, which has prevailed until now and remains unshaken, with nothing standing against it. For this reason we have made haste both to subject and to unite all the bishops of the entire East to the see of Your Holiness.

So, in the present case too, although the matters that have been stirred up here are clear and beyond doubt, and have always been firmly kept and preached by all the bishops in accordance with the teaching of your apostolic see, we have thought it necessary that they should come to Your Holiness's attention. For we do not allow anything that concerns the state of the churches, however clear and beyond doubt the question raised may be, to go unreported to Your Holiness, since you are the head of all the holy churches. For in all things, as has been said, we are eager to increase the honor and authority of your see.

We therefore make known to Your Holiness that a certain few unbelievers, strangers to the holy catholic and apostolic Church of God, have dared, in the manner of the Jews, to speak against what all the bishops, in accordance with your teaching, rightly hold, glorify and preach, denying

that our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God and our God, who was made flesh by the Holy Spirit and of the holy and glorious Virgin and Mother of God Mary, became man and was crucified, is one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity and, the very same, consubstantial with us according to his humanity, capable of suffering in the flesh, the very same incapable of suffering in his Godhead.

For in refusing to confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God and our God, is one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, they appear to follow the evil teaching of Nestorius, saying that he is Son of God by grace, and saying that God the Word is one and Christ another.

But all the bishops of the holy catholic and apostolic Church, and the most reverend archimandrites of the holy monasteries, following Your Holiness and preserving the state and unity of God's holy churches which they have with the apostolic see of Your Holiness, changing nothing whatever in the state of the Church which has prevailed until now and still prevails, with one accord confess and glorify, preaching our Lord Jesus Christ,

the only-begotten Son and Word of God and our God, born of the Father before the ages and outside time, who in the last days came down from heaven, was made flesh by the Holy Spirit, was born of the holy and glorious Virgin and Mother of God Mary, became man and was crucified, to be one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

For we do not acknowledge God the Word as one and Christ as another, but one and the very same, consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity and, the very same, consubstantial with us according to his humanity, capable of suffering in the flesh, the very same incapable of suffering in his Godhead. For as he is perfect in divinity, so the very same is also perfect in humanity; for we accept and confess the union in one subsistence, which the Greeks express as "we confess the union according to hypostasis."

And since the only-begotten Son and Word of God, born of the Father before the ages and outside time, the very same who in the last days came down from heaven, was made flesh by the Holy Spirit and of the holy and glorious Virgin and Mother of God Mary, and became man, our Lord Jesus Christ, is properly and truly God, we therefore also call the holy and glorious Virgin Mary properly and truly the Mother of God: not because God the Word took his beginning from her, but because in the last days he came down from heaven, was made flesh of her, became man, and was born.

Him we confess and believe, as has been said, to be consubstantial with the Father according to his Godhead and, the very same, consubstantial with us according to his humanity, acknowledging as his both the miracles and the sufferings which he willingly endured in the flesh.

We accept the four holy councils: that is, of the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers who assembled at Nicaea; of the hundred and fifty holy fathers who met in this royal city; of the holy fathers who first assembled at Ephesus; and of the holy fathers who met at Chalcedon, as your apostolic see teaches and preaches.

All the bishops, then, following the teaching of your apostolic see, so believe, confess and preach. We have therefore hastened to bring these matters to Your Holiness's attention through the most blessed bishops Hypatius and Demetrius, so that it may not escape Your Holiness what has been wickedly denied, in the manner of the Jews and after the perfidy of Nestorius, by a certain few monks.

We therefore ask your fatherly affection to make it clear to us, by letters sent both to us and to the most holy bishop and patriarch of this bounteous city, your brother (for he too, eager to follow in all things the apostolic see of Your Beatitude, has written to Your Holiness through the same men), that Your Holiness receives all who rightly confess what has been set out above, and condemns the perfidy of those who, in the manner of the Jews, have dared to deny the right faith.

For in this way the love of all for you will grow the more, and the authority of your see will increase, and the unity of the holy churches with you will be kept undisturbed, when all the most blessed bishops learn from you the pure teaching of Your Holiness on the matters reported to you. And we ask Your Beatitude to pray for us and to win for us the providence of God.

AND IN ANOTHER HAND: May the Divinity keep you for many years, holy and most religious father. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of June at Constantinople, in the third consulship of our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus.

It is clear, then, most glorious emperor, as the tenor of the letter we have read and the report of your envoys have shown, that you are devoted to apostolic teaching, since in matters of religion and the catholic faith you hold, write and have published to the faithful peoples what, as we have said, the apostolic see teaches, the venerable authority of the fathers has decreed, and we have confirmed in every respect. It is fitting, then, to cry out in the prophet's words: "Let the heavens rejoice from above, let the mountains pour forth gladness, and the hills shall rejoice with joy."

These things, then, the faithful should write on the tablets of their hearts; these things they should guard like the pupils of their eyes. For there is no one in whom the love of Christ burns who would oppose so right and so true a confession of your faith. For you plainly condemn the impiety of Nestorius and Eutyches and of all heretics, and with a mind devoted to God and pious you keep unshaken and inviolate the one true catholic faith, established by the teaching of our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ, spread everywhere by the preaching of prophets and apostles, strengthened by the confessions of the saints throughout the whole world, united in the judgments of the fathers and doctors, and in agreement with our teaching. Your professions are opposed only by those of whom the divine Scripture speaks, saying:

"They have made falsehood their hope, and hoped to be covered by falsehood"; and again, those who, according to the prophet, say to the Lord: "Depart from us; we do not wish to know your ways"; on account of which Solomon says: "They have strayed from the paths of their own husbandry, and gather fruitless things with their hands."

This, then, is your true faith, this is sure religion; this, as we have said, is what all the fathers and prelates of the Roman Church of blessed memory, whom we follow in all things, and what the apostolic see has preached until now and kept unshaken. Whoever stands up to contradict this confession, this faith, has judged himself a stranger to holy communion and a stranger to the catholic Church.

For we found in the city of Rome Cyrus, who was from the monastery of the Acoemetae, with his followers. With apostolic persuasion we strove to call them back to the right faith and, like sheep that had wandered and been lost, to the Lord's fold, so that, as the prophet says, stammering tongues might learn to speak the things that make for peace.

But to those who did not believe, the first of the apostles speaks through us the words of the prophet Isaiah: "Walk in the light of your fire and of the flame that you have kindled." But their heart was hardened, as it is written, so that they did not understand; and these sheep, which were not mine, would in no way hear the voice of the shepherd. In their case, observing what was laid down by their own pontiff, we have by no means received them into our communion, and we have ordered them to be estranged from the whole catholic Church, unless they condemn their error and, by making the regular profession, signify that they follow our teaching without delay. For it is just that those who refuse obedience to our decrees should be held outcasts from the churches.

But since the Church never closes her bosom to those who return, I implore Your Clemency that, if they lay aside their error, cast off their wicked doctrine and wish to return to the unity of the Church, you will, once they have been received into our communion, remove the sting of your indignation and, at our intercession, grant them the favor of your kind disposition.
And we beseech our God and Savior Jesus Christ to deign to keep you through long and peaceful times in this true religion and unity and in veneration of the apostolic see,

whose primacy you, as most Christian and pious, preserve in all things. Moreover, most serene of princes, we commend the persons of your envoys, Hypatius and Demetrius, our brothers and fellow bishops. Your very choice has shown how pleasing they are to Your Clemency: for you could not have entrusted the weight of so great a matter to any but those perfect in Christ, nor would you have deigned to send words so full of piety and reverence except by men who love you.

AND IN ANOTHER HAND: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God the Father, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be always with you. Amen, most pious son. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

TO OUR MOST BLESSED AND HONORABLE LORD, OUR HOLY BROTHER AND FELLOW BISHOP JOHN, FROM REPARATUS, FLORENTINIANUS, DATIANUS AND THE OTHER TWO HUNDRED AND SEVENTEEN BISHOPS WHO WERE PRESENT FROM ALL THE COUNCILS AT JUSTINIANA CARTHAGE. Desiring to keep once more the excellent custom of times past, which a violent captivity had taken from us for a hundred years, to the grief of all, we have assembled with faithful devotion for a general synod of all Africa, consecrating the first fruits of our gathering to the Lord in that basilica of Justiniana Carthage from which the tyrant Huneric had driven out our fathers. Among us this basilica is called the basilica of Faustus; it is distinguished by the bodies of many martyrs, whose prayers God has heard, so as to give the bishops confidence in this undertaking.

How much each of us was able to weep there with tearful joy we leave rather for Your Beatitude to imagine; for in all there was one feeling of spiritual gladness: to give thanks to almighty God, whose grace is given to sinners without the merit of works, and to offer the antidote of saving faith to the heretics recently reconciled.

When the definitions of the Council of Nicaea had been read through publicly, among other matters that were bound to give rise to debate the question had begun to be raised of how the priests of the Arians ought to be received into the catholic faith: whether in their own ranks or in lay communion. And so all of us at once unanimously agreed to inquire first of all into the judgment of Your Beatitude. For the apostolic see, as we hope, can give us such an answer to our inquiry as the truth, once examined, will lead us to approve with one accord.

From the unspoken feelings of all our colleagues we sensed, indeed, that no one was in favor of receiving the Arians in their own ranks; yet we believed it befitting charity that no one should make public what our view is until either the custom or the ruling of the Roman Church had been made known to us.

We have therefore at once dispatched this letter of greeting by our brothers and fellow bishops Gaius and Peter and by our son Liberatus the deacon, honoring both the authority and the grace of Your Beatitude with due respect. For you are such a man as the holy see of Peter deserved to have as its pontiff: worthy of veneration, full of love, speaking the truth without falsehood, doing nothing arrogantly. That is why the free charity of the whole brotherhood has thought it right to seek your counsel. Let that mind, fervent with the Holy Spirit, answer, I beg you, kindly and truthfully.

For we are consulting you not only about the priests but also about those who were baptized among them as little children: whether they are customarily admitted, or ought to be admitted, to the clergy if they ask for it. For by many such petitions are frequently made
[?] we neither grant nor refuse, until our embassy returns after a more thorough discussion with you.

We believe we should also inform Your Beatitude that a number of brothers from our college frequently abandon their congregations without cause and sail to lands overseas. The Church has long tolerated them, the violence of evil times serving as their excuse. We now ask that any bishop, presbyter, deacon or cleric of whatever lower order who may perhaps come without a letter from us, and cannot prove that he was sent for the benefit of the holy churches, be judged a mere vagrant and not be considered worthy of your communion, so that in all things and through all things the discipline of Your Beatitude may be praised.
AND IN ANOTHER HAND: May almighty God keep you in good health and mindful of us, lord brother.

Agapetus, bishop, to Reparatus, Florentinianus, Datianus and the other bishops established throughout Africa. Long ago indeed, most beloved brothers, our mouth was filled with joy at your good fortune, and our tongue with gladness; and now too, having received the letter your charity addressed to our predecessor, we renew the joys we felt before, blessing the everlasting Lord, who has delivered us from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us. We rightly say "us" together with you, for we were afflicted along with you. Since the Church is one body everywhere, its principal members here among us also suffered with it. Your grief was always our affliction, and at the groaning of all of you, as charity moved our hearts, we often heaved sigh upon sigh.

This being so, as our brothers and fellow bishops Gaius and Peter and our son the deacon Liberatus return, we commend the most sincere charity of your council. As befitted wise and learned men, you did not forget the apostolic primacy. Wishing to untie the knots of the question put before you, you sought access, as was fitting, from the see of him to whom the power of the keys was granted.

We therefore gladly open what the fathers laid down on such a matter in their inner counsels, and we append it, copied out, to this present letter, so that you may recognize beyond doubt that it is not lawful to cross boundaries set long ago. If, then, we wish to avoid the stumbling block of which our elders gave warning, let us follow this. Those who transgress after being warned have no excuse, and those whom ignorance does not shield only add to the bitterness of their transgressions.

Hence, since almighty God has so raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David that we are now dealing with the reconciliation of all those to whose wickedness we were subjected, we ought to apply remedies with such care that what is being healed does not harm our own soundness, and the medicine does not take on a stain from the wound to which it seeks to give health.

But let us perform this duty with regard to the clergy, as you yourselves most prudently judged, so that in wishing to gather what was lost we do not perish ourselves, and in granting absolution too loosely we do not become liable and fall into guilt, which may the Lord avert. This is all the more so since the judgment of our predecessors embraced in the faith, with great charity, those who returned to us from the Arians, in whatever way and at whatever age they had been polluted by the stain of that plague; it rebuked them with justice tempered by love, and with such reasoning shut them out from seeking honours that they would be ashamed to seek anything other than to return.

As to what you asked with most devout compunction, namely whether, even if they ought not to be received back into their office or ought not to be promoted at all, they might at least be helped with the benefit of maintenance: we praise this, we encourage it, we embrace it. Since promotion, or the office they once held, is in fact denied them, let all judge that you are seeking reverence for the canons rather than indulging a burning greed. Let kindness, therefore, nourish and console those who come to the most sincere faith; let mercy be ready for all, for of its reward it is said: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.

You also direct that Catholics who preside over or serve in the church should by no means be received by us without letters from their own bishops. We judge this both consistent with the canons and beneficial to discipline and to faith, for by remaining in the churches in which they serve, they will be able to grow fervent in the love of God our Saviour through diligence in their ministry, and to avoid the blameworthy things that come with wandering about. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of September.

Agapetus to Reparatus, bishop of Carthage. In your fraternity's letter you told us that after you had written the letter meant for my predecessor, during the delays in finding a ship caused by the harshness of a long winter, news of our ordination reached you by the kindness of almighty God, and you rejoiced with brotherly affection that the Godhead had granted me the office of the pontificate.

This did not surprise us, coming from one as sincere as you; the affection of the letter you sent brought you so vividly before us that as I reread your beloved letter I seemed to see you. Embracing you, then, with the same mind with which I saw you, I pray the mercy of the Godhead that the restored grace of peace may bear fruit among you, and that almighty God, who gave me the gift of the priesthood, may also grant me the merit for it.

Moreover, as to the matters which our brothers and fellow bishops Gaius and Peter, and also our son the deacon Liberatus, said your fraternity had charged them to raise with us by word of mouth, we thought it fitting to reply by word of mouth as well, and if it please the Lord we shall not delay to deliver that reply through our legates.

Further, as we restore to your charity the metropolitan rights over everything that the perversity of the enemies had seized, we urge you to make known to all what we have written in reply, whether in your name or in that of others. Supported as you are by the authority of a metropolitan, see that no one can plead ignorance as an excuse for not knowing what the primacy of the apostolic see has set down in accordance with the canons. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of September, after the consulship of the most distinguished Paulinus.

Agapetus, bishop, to Justinian Augustus. For the first fruits of my priesthood I was already bound in many ways to give thanks for the gifts of divine goodness. Yet, venerable emperor, now that I have received through our son Heraclius, the venerable presbyter, the words of your serenity, which you sent so full of the abundance of eternal fruit, the joys of my prayers have been doubled in the Lord. For as your felicity advances, you bring earthly kingdoms under your rule with such a glorious purpose of mind that you win heavenly ones at the same time.

Of this the proofs are not in doubt, since the light of Catholic profession so shines in the letters you have sent that it also gleams in blessed works. For that is a full and firm belief in our God which is commended by an abundance of spiritual fruits as well, as the vessel of election proclaims when he says: In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but faith working through love.

What greater work of your faith could there be than that you have raised up the apostolic see with such marks of charity and munificence that you surpassed even the hopes of those who looked to you? Indeed, by the grace of God, this disposition has always flourished in you, as I myself have also found: the greatness of your gifts showed the measure of your means, and you directed the weight of the power you had attained toward these advances, so that the kindness born in you either anticipated or outdid the wishes of those who petitioned you.

Hence it is that, up to the summit of the imperial crown and beyond, your tranquillity has until now gloried in prosperous success, and will never be deprived of heavenly help, for it is written: For those who love God all things work together for good. Therefore I too, with the devotion of a rejoicing church, have had the most pious words of your liberality written down and attached to the divine services, as you commanded, so that they may be presented with unwearied prayers before the eyes of the supreme Majesty, and that there may be an everlasting remembrance to obtain for you your rewards.

And so, most clement lord and son, as I reverently pay you the homage of a most abundant greeting, I embrace you in the bosom of spiritual charity. I hope that, as regards my devotion, so far as it lies in me, in the things you command for the unity of the Church's peace, you may rather promise yourself whatever is Catholic, according to what the apostle says: So, as far as it lies in me, I am ready for you too. Do not believe that we resist the exhortations of your gentleness in any of the matters in which we can lawfully obey, for, as the teacher of the Gentiles declared, I have hope, as your faith increases, to be magnified among you according to our rule. And so I give immense thanks to our God that you burn with such ardent charity for the increase of the Catholic people that wherever your empire spreads, the everlasting kingdom soon begins to advance.

Pressing still more urgently on the kindness of this zeal, you think that we too, in gaining those who, as you tell us, wish to shun the Arian perfidy, can set aside the censure of the fathers' tradition, namely so that they may both keep the honours they held among the heretics and be promoted to others. It is indeed good, and worthy of the highest praise, that you desire to gather all into the Lord's fold through the true faith; but we ought not to receive those who try to enter by a wrong way, as the blessed apostle Paul warns: Giving no offence to anyone, so that our ministry may not be blamed.

So that nothing might escape your piety about how grave an offence against the decrees of the fathers would be incurred if they were received in this way, which God forbid, I thought it right to append the rules themselves. These specifically decreed that none of such persons, once reconciled, should either be raised by advancement in ecclesiastical rank or desire to keep any longer honours which he must no longer doubt he acquired culpably. From them your piety will be better able to judge whether it can in any way be lawful to break such plain synodal decrees of the apostolic see, when the apostle's words cry out: If I build up again the very things I tore down, I prove myself a transgressor. And so I declare with confidence, in the words of the same apostle, that I trust in you in the Lord that you will think nothing otherwise; for, as the same teacher declared, I myself am also convinced of you that you are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, so that you are able to admonish one another.

If, then, the men you have told us about are eager to come to the right faith, let them not refuse to follow the rules of our faith, as the Lord says: If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and follow me. But if they are still driven by blameworthy ambition for honour, and are afraid to suffer losses to human glory for the gain of the holy faith, they themselves declare that they have not yet turned away from vice and error, and rather wish to entangle us in their own transgressions. Of such men the apostle says: They court you, but not for good; they want to shut you out, so that you may court them.

This being so, do not believe that your holy zeal, by which you desire the Catholic Church to be enlarged, is diminished in any way if such men are not received into the clergy, for the apostle forewarns: What then? If some of them did not believe, has their unbelief made the faith of God void? Far from it! For although the blessed Peter, doorkeeper of the heavenly kingdom, was drawn by a like zeal of charity for the increase of the faithful, and in order to win more of the Jews had stepped down from the rule of doctrine and its proper path by not rejecting all Judaism, yet Paul, the younger, the prisoner in the Lord, relates that he opposed him, saying: But when I saw that they were not walking straight toward the truth of the gospel, I said to Peter in front of everyone, 'If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?

' Weighing all these things carefully, with God at your heart's side, you will be able to see that we are not looking for a pretext to excuse ourselves, but humbly making known to you those things which, by reason of our office, we cannot overstep, as the apostle says: For we can do nothing against the truth, but only for the truth. Likewise, concerning both the person and the case of Bishop Stephen, do not believe that we are driven by zeal to defend anyone (far be it from any Christian mind, in the case of any person whatever, either to condemn innocence or to acquit crime). Rather, everything the apostolic see has arranged in this matter has always sprung from the same zeal by which you too desire the primacy of blessed Peter to be preserved in all things: namely, that in the case of those who have asked for a hearing before his see, his see should not be slighted and someone else's judgment be pronounced instead.

And therefore, since your clemency has wisely deigned to offer that the whole affair be re-examined by our legates, we entrust this task, God being its author, to those whom we are sending at once, on this condition, however: that the religious man Achilles may already now rejoice in our communion, in accordance with your command; but as for his enjoyment of the episcopate, once everything our legates have learned has been brought to us in their full report, what is to be followed will be decided more firmly after we have considered the rules of the holy canons, which you command to be observed.

As for your clemency having deigned to excuse our brother and fellow bishop Epiphanius, on the ground that the consecration of the said Achilles was the effect of your command rather than of his ordaining, we believe that he too knows he is rightly blamed. Besides the other things he neglected, he will scarcely be able to excuse this: that he did not point out, whether in season or out of season, to so pious and so clement a prince, who also defends the privileges of blessed Peter, what was owed in this matter to the reverence due to the apostolic see.

Concerning this business, and also concerning Justiniana, the city that witnessed your glorious birth, and likewise the assigning of our see's vicariate: whatever may be more fully decided, while preserving the primacy of blessed Peter, whom you love, and with regard for your piety's wishes, we will, God willing, quickly make known to you through the legates whom we are sending you.
It remains that, as we unceasingly beg of blessed Peter, we may always rejoice in the health and prosperity of your empire. Given on the Ides of October.

Copy of the statement of faith given by our most pious lord the Emperor Justinian to Pope Agapetus at Constantinople. In the name of the Lord [?] our God Jesus Christ, the Emperor Caesar Flavius Justinian, Alamannicus, Gothicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus, pious, fortunate, renowned, victor and triumphant, ever Augustus, to Agapetus, most holy and most blessed archbishop and patriarch of the fair city of Rome. The first condition of salvation is to keep the rule of right faith and in no way to stray from the tradition of the fathers, for the saying of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be passed over: You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church. What was said is proved by the course of events, since in the apostolic see the Catholic religion has always been kept inviolate.

Desiring, therefore, not to fall away from this faith, and following in all things the decrees of the fathers—that is, of the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers who assembled at Nicaea and set forth the holy teaching, or creed of the faith; of the hundred and fifty holy fathers who met in the city of Constantinople and clarified and made plain that same holy teaching; of the holy fathers who assembled at Ephesus in the first synod; and of the holy fathers who met at Chalcedon—and following the doctrines on the faith contained in each of them, by which every heresy that assails the holy and apostolic Church is done away with,

and approving in every respect and embracing all the letters on the Christian faith written by Leo of blessed memory, and confessing that one and the same Christ the Lord, the only-begotten Son, is to be acknowledged in two natures, that is, in divinity and humanity, without confusion, without change, without separation, the difference of the natures being in no way removed by the union, but rather the property of each nature being preserved and coming together into one person and subsistence, not parted or divided into two persons, but one and the same only-begotten Son, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ, as the prophets of old taught concerning him, as Jesus Christ himself taught us, and as the creed of the holy fathers has handed down to us:

we anathematize every heretic who has held or holds anything beyond what has been stated, especially the heretic Nestorius, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, who was condemned at the synod of Ephesus by Celestine of blessed memory, pope of the city of Rome, and by Saint Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria. With him we anathematize Eutyches, and Dioscorus, formerly bishop of the city of Alexandria, who was condemned at the holy synod of Chalcedon, which we embrace and follow. To these we join Timothy the parricide, surnamed Aelurus, and likewise condemn his disciple and follower in all things, Peter of Alexandria.

We also reject Acacius, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, who became their fellow heretic and follower, and also those who persist in communion and fellowship with them. For whoever embraces someone's communion incurs the same sentence of condemnation as they. In the same way we also condemn Peter of Antioch, together with his followers and all those named above.

Wherefore, as we said before, following the apostolic see in all things, we proclaim what it has decreed, and we profess that these things are to be kept unshaken, and we will compel all bishops to do likewise according to the terms of this statement: the most holy patriarchs are to make it to your holiness, the metropolitans to the patriarchs, and the others to their own metropolitans, so that our holy Catholic Church may stand firm in all things.

AND IN ANOTHER HAND: May the Godhead preserve you for many years, holy and most religious father. Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April at Constantinople, after the consulship of the most distinguished Belisarius.

AND IN ANOTHER HAND: I, Menas, by the mercy of God presbyter and warden of the hospice, accept the four holy synods named above and all the doctrines contained in them, and the letters of Pope Leo which he wrote on behalf of the faith. I confess that Christ our God is to be acknowledged in two natures, that is, in divinity and humanity, without confusion and without division, and I anathematize all who hold otherwise, together with all who have been condemned, as was stated above. I have signed.

BISHOP AGAPETUS TO JUSTINIAN AUGUSTUS. Venerable emperor, we rejoice that you burn with such zeal for the catholic faith. Throughout the whole of your most devout life you graciously give your devout care to keeping and increasing harmony among the churches, and you desire one faith to be preached to all Christian peoples, the same in every respect and equally firm.

Nor is it surprising that your clemency holds steadily to a purpose so pleasing to God, since nothing advances your empire more happily than the growth of religion. So I will gladly sing this in the prophet's words: "Our mouth is filled with joy and our tongue with rejoicing," because every day we see your most flourishing reign adorned with divine blessings.

For you ask, venerable emperor, that we too confirm by our authority the letter of your piety setting out your faith. You recently sent it through the bishops Hypatius and Demetrius to our predecessor of blessed memory, John, bishop of the Roman see, and that prelate ratified it. We praise it and we embrace it. This is not because we grant laymen authority to preach. It is because we confirm and ratify the zeal of your faith, which agrees with the rules of our fathers. Through it the unity of the church has already been achieved, and we trust that the remaining members of the catholic church [?] will return to its body through the constancy of your Christianity.

We append below the text of this confession, that is, of your letter, and by our authority we confirm the zeal you show so wholeheartedly toward God. We declare that this faith agrees with all the rules of our fathers and is in harmony with the teachings of the apostolic see. By the present decision we confirm it as consonant with the rules of the fathers, in order to remove any suspicion of heresy. And we decree that anyone who attempts to oppose this catholic faith of ours shall be cut off from holy communion.

Therefore Cyrus and his followers were suspended from the communion of the catholic church some time ago for this madness, and they have persisted in their faithlessness until now. Unless they make canonical satisfaction and come to follow the apostolic teaching, we will by no means allow them to be restored to holy communion. Indeed, we also place them under anathema as heretics. For we judge it right that whoever has scorned to obey our decrees should not defile the state and purity of the church. The text of the letter is as follows:

IN THE NAME OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST, GOD. THE EMPEROR CAESAR FLAVIUS JUSTINIAN, ALAMANNICUS, GOTHICUS, FRANCICUS, GERMANICUS, ANTICUS, ALANICUS, VANDALICUS, AFRICANUS, PIOUS, FORTUNATE, RENOWNED, VICTOR AND TRIUMPHATOR, EVER AUGUSTUS, TO AGAPETUS, MOST HOLY AND MOST BLESSED ARCHBISHOP OF THE NURTURING CITY OF ROME AND PATRIARCH. Some time ago a sickly dispute over the faith arose among certain persons in this royal city of ours. We rightly rejected it and suppressed it by issuing an edict.

Since it is our practice to refer such questions to the judgment of your apostolic see when they arise, we sent an embassy to your predecessor of blessed memory, John, through the venerable bishops Hypatius and Demetrius. With it went our letter, which set out the faith we had resolved to follow. Your predecessor gladly received it with thanks for the integrity of its faith, and he confirmed it with his own assent and that of the whole Roman church. The text of that letter of ours is as follows:

VICTOR JUSTINIAN, PIOUS, FORTUNATE, RENOWNED, TRIUMPHATOR, EVER AUGUSTUS, TO JOHN, MOST HOLY ARCHBISHOP OF THE NURTURING CITY OF ROME AND PATRIARCH. It has always been our wish, and still is, to give honor to the apostolic see and to your holiness. As is fitting, we honor your beatitude as a father, and so we hasten to bring to your holiness's attention everything that concerns the state of the churches. We have always been very eager to see the unity of your apostolic see preserved, together with the state of God's holy churches. That state has held until now and remains unshaken, with nothing opposing it. For this reason we have made haste to bring all the bishops of the whole East under the see of your holiness and to unite them with it.

So at present there has been some disturbance here. The matters in question are clear and beyond doubt, and all bishops have always firmly kept and preached them according to the teaching of your apostolic see. Even so, we thought it necessary that they be brought to your holiness's attention. Whatever is stirred up concerning the state of the churches, however clear and beyond doubt it may be, we do not allow it to remain unknown to your holiness, because you are the head of all the holy churches. For, as we have said, we are eager in every way to increase the honor and authority of your see.

We therefore make known to your holiness that a few unbelievers, strangers to God's holy catholic and apostolic church, have dared in Jewish fashion to speak against what all the bishops rightly hold according to your teaching,

and glorify and preach. They deny that our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God and our God, who was made flesh of the Holy Spirit and of the holy and glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God, who became man and was crucified, is one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. They deny that he is consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity and, the very same one, consubstantial with us according to his humanity, capable of suffering in the flesh and, the very same one, incapable of suffering in his Godhead.

By refusing to confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God and our God, is one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, they plainly follow the evil teaching of Nestorius. They say that he is Son of God by grace, and they say that God the Word is one and Christ another.

But all the bishops of the holy catholic and apostolic church, and the most reverend archimandrites of the holy monasteries, follow your holiness. They keep the state and unity of God's holy churches that they have with the apostolic see of your holiness, and they change nothing at all in the church's state, which has held until now

and still holds. With one consent they confess, glorify and preach our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son and Word of God and our God. He was born of the Father before the ages and outside time. In the last days he came down from heaven, was made flesh of the Holy Spirit, was born of the holy and glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God, became man and was crucified. They confess that he is one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

For we do not recognize God the Word as one and Christ as another. He is one and the same: consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity and, the very same one, consubstantial with us according to his humanity, capable of suffering in the flesh and, the very same one, incapable of suffering in his Godhead. Just as he is perfect in divinity, so the very same one is perfect in humanity too. For we accept and confess the union in one subsistence, which the Greeks express as "we confess the union according to hypostasis."

The only-begotten Son and Word of God was born of the Father before the ages and outside time. The very same one came down from heaven in the last days, was made flesh of the Holy Spirit and of the holy and glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and became man. He is our Lord Jesus Christ, properly and truly God. For this reason we also call the holy and glorious Virgin Mary properly and truly the Mother of God. This is not because God the Word took his beginning from her. It is because in the last days he came down from heaven, was made flesh of her, became man and was born.

We confess and believe, as has been said, that he is consubstantial with the Father according to his Godhead and, the very same one, consubstantial with us according to his humanity. And we acknowledge that the miracles are his, and so are the sufferings he willingly endured in the flesh.

We accept the four holy councils: that of the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers who assembled at Nicaea; that of the one hundred and fifty holy fathers who met in this royal city; that of the holy fathers who first assembled at Ephesus; and that of the holy fathers who met at Chalcedon. We accept them as your apostolic see teaches and preaches.

All the bishops, then, follow the teaching of your apostolic see, and so they believe, confess and preach. We have therefore hastened to bring these matters to your holiness's attention through the most blessed bishops Hypatius and Demetrius, so that your holiness may not be unaware of what a few monks have wickedly denied, in Jewish fashion, following the faithlessness of Nestorius.

We therefore ask your fatherly affection to send letters to us, and also to the most holy bishop and patriarch of this nurturing city, your brother. He too has written to your holiness through the same men, eager to follow the apostolic see of your beatitude in all things. In these letters, make it plain to us that your holiness accepts all who rightly confess what has been stated above, and that you condemn the faithlessness of those who have dared, in Jewish fashion, to deny the right faith.

In this way everyone's love for you will grow all the more, and so will the authority of your see. The unity of the holy churches that we have here will also be kept undisturbed, once all the most blessed bishops have learned through you the true teaching of your holiness on the matters reported to you. We ask your beatitude to pray for us and to win God's providence for us.

COPY OF THE SUBSCRIPTION: May the Godhead keep you for many years, holy and most religious father. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of June at Constantinople, in the third consulship of our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus.

For this reason we ask your holiness to confirm this letter by your authority, and to hold Cyrus and those like him outside communion until they obey the decrees of your holiness. COPY OF THE SUBSCRIPTION: May the Godhead keep you for many years, holy and most religious father. Given on the day before the Ides of March at Constantinople, after the consulship of the most distinguished Belisarius.

Therefore, as has been said, anyone who presumes to contradict this confession and this faith should know that he is cut off from catholic communion. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April at Constantinople, after the consulship of the most distinguished Belisarius.

TO HIS MOST GLORIOUS AND MOST CLEMENT SON JUSTINIAN AUGUSTUS, VIGILIUS, BISHOP. We received with our customary reverence the letter of your Clemency, delivered by the glorious man our son Dominicus, former consul and patrician. With manifold delight we saw that the universal Church has cause to rejoice, because you do not allow the Christian faith, by which the divine Trinity is honoured and worshipped, to be unlike itself or at variance with itself in anything. [?] By tireless works you heap up for your most clement rule the grace of God, whom you serve by reigning and by serving you reign. So in the gifts that the Lord has granted to your singular piety for the integrity and devotion of your faith, it can be seen that the apostle's teaching is justly and fittingly fulfilled: the saints through faith conquered kingdoms. The vast number of nations brought under your rule shows what kingdoms you have conquered more by the arms of faith than by bodily strength. The greater their numbers when they rise up, the more surely they are overcome by the perfect working of a single mystical miracle.

So we have every reason to glory in the Lord, because in his mercy he has deigned to grant you not only an imperial mind but a priestly one as well. All of us bishops, following ancient tradition, pray when we offer the sacrifice that the Lord may deign to unite, rule and guard the catholic faith throughout the whole world. Your Piety may be seen to have accomplished this with all your strength. Throughout every part of your realm and to all the ends of the earth, you order that faith to be preserved in unshaken peace which the venerable synods have plainly established beyond reproach: Nicaea, Constantinople, the first Council of Ephesus, and Chalcedon too, synods that the judgement of Christian confession must always embrace. You call no one by the name of Christian who separates himself from the unity of these synods. Whoever does not defend their faith with all his strength and every effort, you regard not as someone still to be judged but as someone already judged.

What priest, then, would not feel delightful exultation and boundless joy that the light of gospel truth, implanted in your heart by the grace of our God, has scattered the night of pernicious and heretical doctrines and now shines upon the universal Church? We declare that this brings joy to all our brothers and fellow bishops. Far be it from us, then, that our own joy should fail either to mingle with theirs or, as is more fitting, to stand out above them all.

For this reason, venerable emperor, we received with devoted thanks the pious words that you, kindled by the ardour of faith and stirred by a gentle anger, also addressed to us. In them you recalled with praiseworthy affection Celestine and Leo of blessed memory, prelates of the apostolic see. Condemning one heresy after another in synodal assembly, according to the divine stewardship entrusted to them, they established by a law that will last forever what all Christians everywhere must follow. Our predecessors of holy memory, Hormisdas and John the elder, and Agapetus too, preserved their commendable decrees in every respect, and struck all followers of the Nestorian and Eutychian heresy with the sword of a just sentence.

Let your Piety's clemency know without any doubt that we follow these decrees with all our strength and defend them with all our effort. We also wholly embrace, and defend with fitting love, the letters of blessed Leo sent to Flavian of holy memory, then bishop of the city of Constantinople, and to the Emperor Leo of most clement memory. In those letters, by God's inspiration, he confounded with reasoned argument the perfidy of the heretics, namely Nestorius and Eutyches. With God guarding it, the sincerity of our mind and faith will by no means allow us to go against them. Yet your Piety, in your admirable prudence, ought to consider that bishops who have failed to keep the decrees of these prelates of the apostolic see inviolate are not considered worthy of their office.

We follow in every respect, therefore, all that has been venerably defined concerning the faith by the fathers of the four holy synods, in the letters of Pope Leo of blessed memory named above, and in the decrees of our predecessors mentioned above. By the commendable authority of the apostolic see we condemn those who oppose their teaching. We anathematize whoever attempts either to dispute perversely or to doubt faithlessly the exposition or rightness of that faith. And those who hold views contrary to what was taught concerning the faith in the most holy synods of Nicaea, Constantinople, the first of Ephesus and Chalcedon, and also in the letters of our predecessor Leo of blessed memory

that we have mentioned, or contrary to anything contained in all that his authority sanctioned, we cut off from the unity of the catholic faith. We embrace and approve in every respect the statement of your faith which your Piety, with orthodox devotion, handed at that time through our own service to our predecessor Agapetus of blessed memory. In it you declared in writing what you hold in your mind, for the instruction of future ages. Deviating in nothing, on any pretext, from the faith of our oft-mentioned predecessors, we maintain this sentence. The only exception is if perhaps, once the darkness of the heresy

in which they wallow has been cut away, they are willing to follow the truth of the faith set out above, correcting themselves by fitting penance. They must condemn everything that certain people have said with most depraved impiety against what we have stated above, and reject all the errors of the heretics by their own signatures and with their own voices, being converted under the strictness of the canons. Then, once they have fulfilled with canonical and apostolic strictness all that we have stated, they may be found worthy of the mystery of holy communion. For it is not fitting for us to shut off the opportunity for penance from anyone who corrects himself.

Your Piety informed us about our brother and fellow bishop Menas. He was mindful of the statement of faith which he had presented, with your Clemency's consent, to our predecessor Agapetus of blessed memory at the time of his ordination, and he truly followed the discipline of the apostolic see. Accordingly he pronounced anathema on the heretics listed below: Severus of Antioch; Peter of Apamea; Anthimus, who had also invaded the church of Constantinople out of depraved ambition; Zooras; Theodosius of Alexandria; Constantine of Laodicea; and Antoninus of Versetum [?]. He also anathematized the defenders and followers of the Eutychian heresy, and of Dioscorus, who is recorded as having been condemned among others at the synod of Chalcedon.

We are in no way displeased by the condemnation pronounced against the heretics by our aforesaid brother or by anyone else. On the contrary, we gladly embrace it and confirm it by the authority of the apostolic see, and we strike the accomplices of the condemned with the same penalty of anathema. We do so on this understanding: as we mentioned above, and in accordance with the decrees of the prelates of the apostolic see, we open the way to penance and communion for those who come to their senses and accept the decrees of the earlier synods and of the pontiffs of the apostolic see named above.

We know that those who destroy heretical perfidy do more good to themselves by avoiding the company of those in error than they do by adding any firmness to the sentence of the fathers named above. That sentence has already been confirmed in many ways, and it plainly stands firm by its own strength, with God as its author. Until now, therefore, we did not think that a condemnation which was not newly pronounced needed any new response. Those found to be followers of the heresies we mentioned above, or of any others condemned by apostolic definition and decree, have been struck down not merely by a new law but by the condemnation passed long ago on their own founders.

A malicious interpreter may have wished your Piety to suspect or understand our silence otherwise. Yet the blessed apostle Peter, by pious tradition, appointed us to give an account to everyone who asks, and so we have judged that we must willingly satisfy your Christian Majesty. We humbly hope that in your most Christian times you will not allow the privileges of the see of the blessed apostle Peter to be diminished in any way through the snares of anyone who creeps in. If those privileges are disturbed or diminished in anything, which we do not believe will happen, it is a sign that the faith has been violated. For your Wisdom, in your singular piety, knows that the blessed apostle himself will reward you in every way for the authority which, with God inspiring you, you preserve, whether in his privileges or in the person of me, your humble servant.

Nevertheless, so that your Piety may be fully informed, and nothing may be left in doubt any longer through the cunning of a crafty plotter, we have attached the decrees of our predecessor Pope Leo of blessed memory that were sent to the East at various times. From the many, we have selected as many as we believed necessary at present. We ask you, by him whose cause you are eager to conduct wholly and desire to advance with Christian affection, that your Piety deign to read them all, leaving nothing unread. For I know that if God gives you the will to read them, you will weigh everything with the wisdom God has singularly granted you. You will then so arrange matters that none of the faithful priests can be troubled anywhere, either concerning religion or by any prejudgement.

Let it suffice, then, that we have given an account as far as we could, as the merit of your Christian Majesty demanded. No one, however cunning and subtle, will find that we have committed or attempted anything against the decrees of the synods or those of our predecessors, the prelates of the apostolic see. But I will not fail to recommend what benefits the catholic faith and your soul. As your Piety knows, I have more reason than others to be concerned for your soul, both because of my priestly office and because of the many favours your Clemency has shown me:

First of all, we beseech you, and ask through the intercession of the blessed apostle Peter himself, whom you love, that you always deign to send here to the apostolic see, to manage the interests of your state, men who are orthodox and pleasing to God, having no wrinkle or stain in their faith. Through them, matters concerning your public affairs may be wholesomely ordered, and the integrity of catholic discipline may in no way be disturbed, to the reward of your soul. Then everyone will truly recognize that your Piety already has, as we too believe, that gift of heavenly grace which Solomon once asked of the Lord when he said: Give your servant a heart to listen and to judge your people with justice, and to discern between evil and good.

We have also entrusted certain matters to be conveyed by word of mouth through our son Dominicus, the bearer of this letter. We hope that, with the Lord inspiring you, you will deign to listen to them willingly, and that with your accustomed Christian spirit and foresight you will arrange them, especially those that will serve the peace of the Church and, after that, the tranquillity of all.

TO HIS MOST BELOVED BROTHER MENAS, VIGILIUS. In our message to our lord and son, the most serene and most Christian emperor, we have set out everything concerning ecclesiastical matters, as far as we were able with God's help and believed it expedient. Nevertheless, we judged it necessary to send a letter to your Charity as well, through our most Christian son the patrician Dominicus.

Know that we received your letter with great exultation and joy. In it you declare that you inviolably keep the most holy synods of Nicaea, Constantinople, the first of Ephesus, and Chalcedon, in which the foundations of the orthodox and apostolic faith are set out. This is attested by the text of the pledge you gave at that time to our predecessor Agapetus of holy memory. Above all, you declare that you follow in everything the decrees of our predecessor blessed Leo. For what could be more worthy of your Charity and more befitting your office than not to depart from the teaching of the Roman prelates? And what could be more delightful or more welcome to us than to embrace in the love of Christ our Lord and Saviour those who keep to the acts of our forebears and predecessors?

Therefore we greet you in the spirit, and with the affection that befits us we exhort and unceasingly urge you to follow in everything his rule, his admonition, and, as you have both promised and declared, his decrees. For the archives of your Fraternity are full of the writings of our aforesaid predecessor Leo of holy and venerable memory, which that same pontiff is recorded as having sent to your predecessors. Likewise, what your predecessors promised to our predecessors may also be read there.

But let it suffice to have said this much, for the apostle's words are before our eyes: We speak wisdom among the perfect. We have learned that you were mindful of the statement of faith you had handed to our predecessor mentioned above, and that, following the decrees of apostolic teaching, you pronounced anathema on the heretics listed below: Severus of Antioch; Peter of Apamea; Anthimus too, the invader of the church of Constantinople; Zooras; Theodosius of the city of Alexandria; and also Constantine and Antoninus Bessentanus [?]. You also anathematized the defenders and followers of the Eutychian heresy, and of Dioscorus, who is recorded as having been condemned among others at the synod of Chalcedon. In doing so you added nothing to the sentence decreed long ago by the fathers. [?] Nor did the sentence given by such prelates, the vicars of blessed Peter, against the very founders of these heresies stand in any need of it, since whoever is known to follow a condemned heresy is struck down not merely by a new law but by the condemnation already passed on its founder. Nevertheless, we gratefully and gladly embrace your condemnation and confirm it by interposing the authority of the apostolic see, over which God has willed us to preside. All their accomplices, and all heretics, shall be subject to the same sentence of condemnation.

In all this, as befits apostolic moderation, we reserve only the following. Suppose that one of them, or anyone else in error, acknowledges the truth of the catholic faith and wishes to do penance and return. He must recognize the error of the heresy in which he wallows and condemn in a written profession the whole depravity of his own errors and those of his accomplices. Following the institutions of apostolic teaching, he must also pronounce anathema on anyone who does not follow the four synods named above in matters of faith, or who does not confess in everything the venerable decrees of our predecessor Leo of blessed memory and follow them with all his strength and complete purity of mind. Then he shall by all means be admitted to our communion, after apostolic and canonical satisfaction, as we said above. It is not fitting for us to deny communion to any penitent, for our Redeemer did not come to destroy anyone but in his mercy to save all.

AND IN THE LORD POPE'S OWN HAND: By God's help and through his grace, I, Vigilius, bishop of the holy catholic Church of the city of Rome, have reviewed with his assistance and signed these sheets containing the letters written above, which I dictated with God's help.

AND ANOTHER SIGNATURE, IN THE HAND OF THE PATRICIAN DOMINICUS: I, Flavius Dominicus, of clarissimus rank, count of the domestics, former consul and patrician, have signed these sheets, composed by the most blessed and apostolic Pope Vigilius in the cause of the faith and addressed to our lord Justinian, the most pious and most Christian emperor, and also to Menas, the most blessed archbishop of the city of Constantinople. I read them through, compared them, and agreed with them. Signed on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the consulship of Justin, of clarissimus rank.
POPE GELASIUS, AGAINST THE PELAGIAN HERESY.

GELASIUS, BISHOP, TO ALL THE BISHOPS THROUGHOUT PICENUM, GREETING IN THE LORD. Until now we have been grieving that barbarian incursions and the savage storm of war were laying waste the provinces, especially those nearest the City. But amid the burning dangers of these recent calamities we have learned that the devil has inflicted a more pernicious ruin on the minds of Christians than the savagery of the enemy has on their bodies. This evil chiefly concerns the priests of those regions. Overcome by such sluggishness and such neglect of their ministry, they ignore the guidance of the souls entrusted to them, and they let those souls be torn with impunity, before their very eyes, even by every petty little beast.
