Indeed, by fostering the wickedness that creeps in and giving way to those who corrupt the faithful, they not only fail to draw them back but, by their own example, actually feed their ruin.

But what would such bishops do if, God forbid, some new plague, unknown until now, were to break out, or if men of sharper wit and cunning minds, or men skilled in some secular learning, were to put forward sacrilegious blasphemies? For they neither recall nor refute the worn-out fabrications of so ancient an error, refuted both by the great teachers of the churches and in our own day as well, and they do not reject them even when ignorant and foolish men put them forward.

Thanks be to almighty God, for he tests the hearts of his own through people of this kind, who do not even understand the very poison they speak. What would the leaders of the peoples do against more cunning enemies, when they readily submit themselves to the unlearned? Even if the rulers of the Lord's flock were so utterly sluggish that they could neither understand nor restrain so vile and dull a person, they surely ought, out of pastoral care, to have sought from us what needed to be known, rather than thoughtlessly hand over a pliant will to absurd persuasions.

For a wretched old man named Seneca has been brought before us. He is not only a stranger to all learning but wholly lacking even in common understanding. Like one of the frogs, as we read of certain ones in the Apocalypse, he has heedlessly plunged into the mire of the Pelagian whirlpool and wallows horribly in its filth, finding no way at all to climb out. Having abandoned the purity of catholic truth, the more he tries to lift himself up along the slippery path of falsehood, the more he is hemmed in and swallowed by its muddy pits. He is one of those of whom the apostle Peter says: "But these, like irrational beasts, born by nature to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming in matters of which they are ignorant, will perish in their own corruption, receiving the wages of unrighteousness."

Truly his mind is so stupid and dull that he can neither take in nor give any account at all of the poisons he has wickedly swallowed and vomited up. Hardened by diabolical blindness and already given over to himself, he stands condemned by the deadly obstinacy of his own heart. Nothing remains for him except that our God, who said that what seems impossible to men is easy for him, should pierce such a mind with powerful compunction, so that, as the blessed apostle Paul says, he may come to his senses and escape the snares of the devil, by whom he is held captive [?].

We brought to light and laid open many points of the Pelagian views that had never so much as occurred to him even in his dreams, and we showed that they had long since been refuted. As for the very things he appeared to be putting forward, we showed that the Pelagian heretics had raised them long ago and that catholic preachers had duly crushed them. We proved that Pelagius, Caelestius, Julian and many others, men of oratorical eloquence, had been refuted on this very assertion and struck down by both ecclesiastical decrees and imperial ordinances. We therefore declared that he could not hold his ground on points where such men as these had been overthrown [?], since he can neither grasp with his understanding nor support with comparable eloquence the very arguments they had argued. But, as has been said, a mind possessed by diabolical inspiration, once it has sunk into the depth of evils, consents to no remedy.

Therefore, out of the countless kinds of blasphemy that the authors of the Pelagian heresy produced, we judged that we should not pass over in silence three which this lamentable old man has especially made his own. Once uncovered, they would be more plainly exposed, and once overturned by God's demolition, they would be more easily avoided. Infants, they say, are created in their mothers' wombs by the work of God:

and so they do not think it just that God's handiwork, without any acts of its own, should be born bound to any sin, and they make God unjust if people are made guilty before they are born. This they put forward as the sharpest argument of their teaching. They fail to notice that the first parents of the human race, who were produced from no parents at all but from the harmless material of clay, and who were powerfully, purely and soundly fashioned and made rational by divine craft, followed the devil, their seducer, by their own will, and were infected with depraved desires through the excess of their transgression. In them human nature certainly sinned, and human nature was made faulty, open beyond doubt to the evil it had not known before. That in falling away from the good and upright it sank back into an inclination toward evil and depravity is plain from the very course of what followed.

Having become such, then, the founders of our substance made themselves subject to suffering and corruption. They violated the gifts of their divine creation so far that they were punished with the penalty of death, for there is no doubt that they died on the day they were made mortal. Accordingly, whatever these parents brought forth from their seed is indeed the work of God according to the order of nature, but not without the contagion of the evil that they contracted by their transgression; and this, that is, the contagion of that evil, is certainly not the work of God.

So the fault that nature contracted by a movement of its own will does not come from God's creation. Even from a nature corrupted by its own doing, God still carries out the ordinance of his creation; but the creature brings forth a fault that it did not receive from the Creator's ordinance, but took upon itself through the fall of its transgression. For if the first human beings themselves, born, as was said, of no parents and formed without any contagion, could deprave themselves through the ambition of unlawful presumption and attach the work of diabolical fraud to the work of God, what wonder is it if, once depraved, they produced depraved offspring?

Again, although God certainly created human substance free, does not slavery, coming upon it from outside even under human laws, make it naturally bound and liable? People are begotten liable by their origin, they are born bound by servile condition, and in being born they are obligated before they are even begotten. If this happens in matters lying outside nature, how much less surprising is it that it should happen in those things by which human substance itself is known to be depraved? And so, just as human substance, from its pure original state, made itself guilty of reprobate acts and polluted in will, so it produced offspring and progeny of its nature stained by the guilty will behind its acts. It begot offspring such as it had made itself by the excess of its transgression; and therefore it brings forth from itself not only what God rightly established, but also what it wrongly and incongruously added.

That an inner quality of desire can change nature is confirmed by the authority of divine Scripture. Thus the flock of sheep entrusted to Jacob as he pastured it, when rods of varied colors were set in the watering troughs, was enticed while drinking by the delight of what it felt, conceived what it did not have in its nature, and passed on to its offspring what had become ingrained in its senses but had not been received in creation. What was then done figuratively signified that this would happen in the flocks of the Church as well; and God, foreseeing that the calumnies of the Pelagians would be stirred up, prepared for his faithful the understanding of a surer proof.

The divine testimonies, the very sacraments of the Church, and the tradition of the catholic teachers handed down from the Lord and Savior himself all teach that the beginnings of human generation are tarnished. Hence the prophet cries out: "Who will boast that he has a chaste heart, or that he is clean from sins? Not even an infant whose life upon the earth is a single day." Hence Scripture likewise says: "Who can make clean one conceived of unclean seed? Is it not you, who alone are?" And elsewhere it says: "For the seed was accursed." The prophet David also testifies: "In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother bore me." And if he says this, who would claim that he was begotten in any other way? The blessed apostle Paul also declares:

"We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest." Of this wrath it says in the Gospel: "Whoever believes and is baptized has eternal life; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, and the wrath of God remains upon him"—that very wrath of which it was said: "You shall surely die." The Lord Jesus Christ himself declares with heavenly voice: "Whoever does not eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood will not have life in himself." Here we see that no one at all is excepted, nor has anyone dared to say that a little child can be brought to eternal life without this saving sacrament; and without that life there is no doubt that he will be in everlasting death.

Why, then, is an infant shut up in this lot if he has no sin at all? Would not God, far be it, seem unjust instead, if punishment were inflicted where there is no fault? Since the infant is bound by no guilt from acts of his own, the only possibility left is that he is defiled solely by a faulty birth; and unless he has been cleansed by sharing in the Christian mystery, he cannot attain eternal life. This is why infants are exsufflated and catechized: because a work of diabolical malice has been added to the work of God, in which their Author established them well, they must be rescued from the power of darkness, as the apostle teaches, and transferred to the inheritance of the Son of God and to lawful cleansing.

Had the first generation, which God established good, not fallen into guilt through transgression and become worthy of rejection, there would have been no need to put a second generation in its place. That is why the blessed apostle Paul says: "As through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so it passed to all men, in whom all sinned"; and a little later: "Therefore, as through the trespass of one it came to all men unto condemnation, so also through the righteousness of one it came to all men unto justification of life." When he says "all unto condemnation," he certainly means those begotten of Adam their parent; just so, when he says "all unto justification of life," he includes only those who have been reborn in the mystery of Christ.

With countless proofs of this kind the deadly teaching of the Pelagian heresy was both refuted by our forefathers and can now be refuted by their abundant learning. Nor should these things trouble simple souls: for them it will be enough to believe, according to the Church's rule, what they do not understand, or, if anyone wishes to know more, he should ask.

As for his assertion that little children cannot be damned without holy baptism for original sin alone, that is a thoroughly impious and thoroughly profane proposition. No Christian is unaware that those fresh from their mothers' wombs are baptized for the remission of sins, and the catholic Church certainly does this not falsely but truly, lest, God forbid, she should seem to lie in the heavenly sacraments. Since they have no sins of their own, it is clear that what is remitted to them is original sin alone. And so, since by the remission of that alone they obtain eternal life through baptism, it follows that if that alone is not remitted, they cannot attain eternal life.

Hence the Lord too, as we said above, speaks words that can apply only to the baptized: "Whoever does not eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood will not have life in himself." But what is it to be without eternal life, if not to be placed in everlasting death? Although "the kingdom of heaven" is the same as "eternal life," yet, so that God's providence might cut away all the wickedness of the Pelagians, it was not only said: "Whoever has not been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit will not enter the kingdom of heaven," but it was equally said: "Whoever does not eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood will not have life in himself." No one doubts that this was said of eternal life, since many who do not eat this sacrament evidently have the present life.

They have no ground, then, for saying that unregenerate infants are merely unable to enter the kingdom of heaven but are not punished with everlasting damnation. Without baptism they can neither eat the body nor drink the blood of Christ; without this they cannot have life in themselves; and without life they can only be dead. Let them say, then, whether those placed in everlasting death are not to be considered damned. Let them do away with that third place, whatever it is, which they invent to deceive little children. Since we read of nothing but a right side and a left, let them not make these children remain unbaptized in the region on the left, but let them allow them to be baptized and carried over by holy regeneration to the saving right hand.

In the third chapter he peddles those ravings of the Pelagians, already known and refuted throughout the whole world, in which they say that man becomes blessed through free will, which he corrupted, defiled and lost, with the support of the good of his nature. Yet human nature, established good in the blessedness of paradise, could never have been driven out of it unless it had lost its good. It was made mortal because it had passed by transgression from good to evil and had turned from sharing in the divine to diabolical crimes. That is why it was justly handed over to its deceiver, to whom it had willingly consented; that is why it was shut out from the happiness so dear to it and condemned by the heavenly voice to thorns and thistles and manifold miseries. So heavy and harsh a penalty of just judgment would never have been inflicted on one who persevered in good, and it is shown to be fittingly imposed only on evil.

See, then: without divine help, which we never read that man sought while he was placed in that blessedness, his natural good not only could not profit him and did not make him blessed, but, when he trusted in it alone and did not turn back to its Giver, he lost blessedness instead and took up the beginning of all evils.

And as for their claim that people attain blessedness by free will—the free will which man used badly and so fell into perpetual slavery, as it is written: "Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin," and "by whatever a person is overcome, to that he is also bound as a slave"—is this not that natural presumption which sank under the laws of a detestable captivity, of which Holy Scripture speaks thus: "A heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam from the day they come forth from their mother's womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all"?

From this yoke our Lord Jesus Christ alone redeemed the human race by the exchange of his passion, and rescued us by a changed birth. He alone came to seek and to save what was lost, so that liberty, which had been cast down by reckless pride, might be restored and repaired by grace; and so that, in turn, the choice of the human will, which by following the devil had earned everlasting captivity, might by following the author of its renewed liberty return to the reward it had lost.

Hence the Lord himself says: "When the Son has set you free, then you will be free indeed"; and the blessed apostle Paul goes on: "When you were slaves of sin, you were free of righteousness" (that is, "strangers to righteousness"), "but now, freed from sin, you have become slaves of righteousness"; and again the same apostle speaks of "the freedom with which Christ has set you free." Does not the chosen vessel himself affirm: "It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will"—so that God should not be thought to work both the willing and the accomplishing in an evil will too?

But this is the peculiar poison of the Pelagians, long since worn threadbare: they think that God's grace can be bestowed according to human merits. Far be that from Christian minds! For the apostle already mentioned testifies: "Grace is what is given freely; otherwise, if it comes from works, grace is no longer grace," because then it is paid back as wages and not bestowed freely, which is where the word "grace" comes from.

What Christian would dare to say that he has anything good without grace, when the teacher of the Gentiles cries out, briefly summing up all the gifts within himself: "By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not in vain"? He says this to show that he did not go before the gift of grace but followed after it. And to show that he worked together with grace by following it, he says: "But I labored more than all of them"; and then, fearing that he might seem to presume on himself, he added: "Not I, but the grace of God with me." He did not say, "I and the grace of God with me," but put grace first, as going before, and placed himself after it.

What can anyone have without grace, when faith itself comes through grace, as the same apostle teaches us: "I obtained mercy so that I might be faithful"? And divine mercy is nothing other than grace. Let us hear too how he instructs the Church: "By grace," he says, "you have been saved through faith," to show that the beginning of salvation and of faith starts from grace; and so he goes on to add: "and this is not from yourselves, but it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may be puffed up." Elsewhere the same apostle declares universally and absolutely: "For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?"

Who could list one by one all the passages that plainly show that the choice of natural liberty does not earn grace, but rather receives it through grace, being mercifully released from the slavery it had earned by sinning? Through the redemption of this mystery, prepared by eternal providence before the beginning of the world, the ancient origin of all holy men and holy women was cleansed by figurative signs and sacrifices, whether before the law had been given or under the observance of the law; and to all the righteous, through the Spirit of grace, by adoring this mystery from afar, came the remedies of eternal salvation. Its fullness, now made manifest in Christ to the nations, cleanses and renews the world and makes people truly partakers of everlasting blessedness.

For this reason we strongly rebuke our brothers and fellow bishops, especially those governing the Lord's church throughout the provinces of Picenum, who not only failed to stop the perverse talk of a most foolish old man and an abject person, but even fostered it by their consent. Who could hear of it, who could bear it, that bishops allowed some unworthy corpse or other to dare to deprive of communion a presbyter who would not agree with him?

How could such a man be received by anyone or patiently heard, when on top of all this he laid down rules, gladly accepted, that servants of God should be mingled with consecrated virgins in a most shameful community? Spiritual minds are assailed by imagined allurements even when such company is absent; how could they not be aroused far more violently by the sight of the other sex, which entices even the unwilling? A still greater crime is added: in the sight and presence of priests, a dying fly, as it is written, spoiling the sweet-smelling oil, strove to tear apart Jerome and Augustine of blessed memory, the lights of the Church's teachers.

But why should we wonder that the leaders of the churches neglect these things, when, as we have heard from many, it is plain that they do everything contrary to the canons and throw everything into confusion everywhere against apostolic discipline? They ordain without keeping the rules, and it is permitted not only for monks but even for ministers of the church to travel abroad with women and come back again, and to be promoted into the clerical ranks by other bishops. Since not one of these things is to be tolerated, who could endure so many such crimes being committed? By them they offer a spectacle, not undeservedly, to Gentiles, Jews and heretics, and seem to be aiming, God forbid, at the very destruction of religion. To those who do such things the apostle's sentence will rightly apply: "For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you."

Let it suffice, then, that these things have been committed up to now; and, so that God may be appeased, let divine matters be attended to more carefully than human ones. Let the champion of this plague find no place anywhere, no access at all to the church, and no share anywhere in catholic communion, since he prefers by his wicked profession to follow the fellowship of heretics. As for those who are proven to have formed a harmful association with him before, unless they come to their senses and withdraw from his company, let them be removed from ecclesiastical service and punished with due penalty, so that the rest may be given an example of caution.

Let him approach no one, and let him never again be allowed to speak the blasphemies condemned long ago. Let men and women practice their devotion with circumspection, separated in their own dwellings, as befits a holy commitment. Let no one be admitted to ecclesiastical office contrary to the decrees of the canons. And let the rulers of each province know that they will find no pardon even for past errors if from now on they fail to avoid errors that have been exposed.

From now on no occasion for excuse will be left if, after these present instructions, which we have decided to send by Romulus the deacon, whose skill on behalf of the catholic faith and vigilance for religion we most gratefully commend, any bishop is found to be contemptuous or negligent in any of these matters. For just as it belongs to the governance of the apostolic see to provide due care fittingly to all the churches, so it must not neglect to use against the contumacious and the slothful the power divinely entrusted to it. Given on the Kalends of November, in the consulship of the most illustrious Albinus.
Letter of Gelasius, Bishop of the City of Rome, to the Dardanians.

We were greatly surprised that your Love wishes to know, as though it were a new and difficult question and something never heard of before, what the communicants of the Eutychian plague keep muttering in their wretched quarrelling. They have no answer to give in defence of their stubborn persistence in their own ruin, and they have already been refuted by argument many times. They mutter, not because their chatter carries any weight, but because they can find nothing at all to say.

In this matter we are more surprised that those who were trained in catholic understanding still hesitate than that those who have fallen away from the truth and strayed from the ancient tradition of the Church put forward profane novelties of words and the inanities of a perishing perversity. Your charity has reported that they boast that they do not think Acacius was justly condemned, because he does not appear to have been deposed by a special synod. And they pile still more on the madness of their vanity by childishly adding, "especially as he was bishop of the royal city."

Therefore, rejecting the folly of these empty complaints, you must go back over the record from the blessed apostles themselves and consider wisely how our fathers, the catholic and learned bishops, dealt with every heresy that arose at any time. Whatever they had once decreed in an assembled council for the faith, for the truth, and for catholic and apostolic communion, in accordance with the path of the Scriptures and the preaching of our forebears, they wished to stand thereafter unshaken and firm. Nor did they

permit what had been laid down in the same cause to be reopened through any fresh presumption. In this they saw most wisely that if anyone were allowed to repeat decrees soundly made, no settled ruling of the Church against any error whatever would remain stable, and every sound definition would be forever disturbed by the same frenzies breaking out again. For if, even when the boundaries of synodal rules have once been fixed and laid down, the plagues that were crushed do not cease to take up the fight again, to rise up against the foundation of the truth, and to strike [?] every simple heart, what would happen if the faithless were free to convene a council whenever they liked? For however manifest the truth may be, pernicious falsehood never lacks something to bring forward; even when it fails in reason and authority, it still refuses to yield out of sheer stubbornness.

Our forebears, perceiving this by divine inspiration, took the necessary precaution that whatever a synod held against any heresy had decreed for the faith, for communion, and for catholic and apostolic truth, they would not allow to be mutilated afterwards by new reconsiderations, lest the wicked be given occasion to assail what had been established as a remedy. Instead, once the author of any madness had been condemned together with his error, they judged it sufficient that anyone who at any time became a sharer in that error should be bound by the original sentence of his condemnation, since anyone could plainly be recognized by his profession or by his communion.

To pass over earlier cases, which a diligent inquirer can easily trace, a synod condemned Sabellius; and in order that his followers be condemned afterwards, it was not necessary to hold separate synods for each individual. Rather, in accordance with the tenor of the ancient decree, the universal Church held that all who had shared either in his depravity or in his communion were to be rejected.

So too, because of the blasphemies of Arius, the rule of faith and of catholic communion set forth at the Council of Nicaea includes, without any reconsideration, all Arians and anyone who has fallen into this plague, whether in belief or in communion.

So too the synod, once it had been held and had condemned Eunomius, Macedonius, and Nestorius, did not allow further recourse to new councils. Rather, the Church rejected all who in any way fell back into fellowship with them by the synodal boundary handed down to it. And it is evident that the Church never rightly yielded to new audacities under the pressure of any necessity, so as

to violate what had been soundly established. For this reason, even in the storm of the Arian persecution, many catholic bishops, breathing again on their return from exile once peace was restored, settled the troubled churches together with their catholic brethren in such a way that they did not alter anything that the synod of Nicaea had defined concerning the faith and catholic and apostolic communion. Nor did they strike anyone with a new condemnation for having lapsed; rather, they judged that those who did not come to their senses stood condemned by the tenor of that decree.

Having duly weighed these things from the tradition of the fathers, as has been said, we are confident that no true Christian is now unaware that the decree of any synod which the assent of the universal Church has approved ought to be carried out by no see more than by the first, which both confirms every synod by its authority and guards it by its continued governance. It does so by reason of its primacy, which the blessed apostle Peter received from the Lord's own word, and which, with the Church nonetheless following, it has always held and still retains.

When this see learned from sure evidence that Acacius had strayed from catholic and apostolic communion, it was for a long time unwilling to believe it, since it knew that he had often been the executor of its necessary measures against heretics. For nearly three years it did not cease to admonish him by letters sent to him, as the writings frequently dispatched by various messengers testify.

When he resolved for a long time to give no reply, keeping an improper silence, an episcopal legation was also sent to him, together with a letter. This warned him to remember his earlier deeds and to look back on what he had once labored for on behalf of the catholic faith, and it adjured him, with coaxing and threats alike, not to cut himself off from the body of catholic unity. At the same time, since John, bishop of the second see, was assailing him with grave charges, it urged him either to come or to send someone to a hearing before the first see.

For although the synod was not to be repeated, it was nevertheless fitting that the bishop of any city should not avoid the judgment of the first see, to which the bishop of the second see had appealed, since he could be heard by no one but the first see. This was especially so because John had been excluded by the Greeks, with their minds already made up, without any synod; he neither could nor ought to plead his cause before them at all. For one of higher rank could not be tried by inferior bishops, nor, if reason so required, condemned, except by the first see, as has been said. Moreover, since all the Eastern bishops, together with Acacius himself, were falling into the communion of Peter, the catholic bishop of the second see was in no way to be judged by men of an outside communion.

But Acacius not only disdained to satisfy these demands; he even deceived the very legation of the apostolic see with flatteries, bribes, and perjuries, promising, together with the emperor, that the whole case in all its parts would be reserved for the apostolic prelate. Thus he caused the legation to return polluted by the communion of Peter. He so despised the authority of the apostolic see that he not only refused to submit to it but even strove, through its own legates, to draw it into the fellowship of an outside communion. The apostolic see was therefore compelled to deprive the very bishops it had sent of both their rank and their communion, lest it appear to be infected by such contagion. It thereby showed clearly that it did not hate the person of Acacius in particular, but rejected the compacts of the lost, which it rightly abhorred

even in its own bishops. Meanwhile, Acacius declared in his own letters that he had most readily gone back into communion with Peter of Alexandria, whom he himself, as executor, had also condemned after seeking the authority of the apostolic see, and this without consulting that same apostolic see; and in his own words he conveyed an accusation against John and praises of Peter. If he was really confident about these things, he should rather have come or sent someone, so that he could refute John to his face regarding the lies he alleged, and present with sound reasons the commendations of Peter he had set out.

Since he did nothing of the kind, he showed quite plainly that he could neither convict John nor had confidence that he could demonstrate that Peter had been lawfully received. He showed that his only purpose was to tear down catholics and praise heretics, and he proved himself to be a partner of those he praised rather than a companion of the catholics he was trying to discredit. He passed judgment on himself, for when he was polluted by communion with a condemned man, he became a sharer in that man's condemnation.

Thus the apostolic see omitted nothing that pertained to necessary diligence, while Acacius, in accordance with the form of the synod of Chalcedon, by which the error he communicated with had been struck down, was shown to be condemned by his own judgment, as is written of the heretical man. And the apostolic see, which certainly remembered that it had condemned Peter of Alexandria and had not absolved him, justly and fittingly removed Acacius himself from its communion, lest through its former communion with Acacius it should also fall into fellowship with Peter, with whom Acacius had communicated.

Why, then, was there any need for a new inquiry to determine whether Acacius had communicated with error or prevarication, when he had already confessed it himself in his own letters, and, as it is written, "By your mouth you will be justified, and by your mouth you will be condemned," he was held guilty by the bonds of his own words and was rightly to be punished?

Why, in a new case that no synod had dealt with before, did he disdain to refute John, whom he was attacking in his letters, whatever sort of bishop of the second see he may have been, before the judgment of the first see of the blessed apostle Peter? Why did he scorn either to come or to send someone, so as to plead his cause in person or through a lawful representative of his own choosing? He thought it beneath him, the bishop of an ordinary city, to come to the judgment of the first see, to which he saw the bishop of the second see had come, even though Anatolius, bishop of the city of Constantinople, is shown to have done just that on his own behalf by sending legations.

See, in this respect too he has no grounds for complaint. See, I say, he was summoned to a lawful examination, where he ought either to have refuted the man he was attacking or to have defended his own side with just arguments. If he fled from the examination of the apostolic see when the case of John, a catholic bishop, was to be investigated, how was the apostolic see to follow the judgment of Acacius concerning the reception of Peter, a heretic condemned by its own sentence and not released by its own authority?

Or was it fitting for the apostolic see to await the judgment of the diocese of the church of Heraclea, that is, of the bishop of Constantinople, or of any others who were to be assembled with him or on his account, when the bishop of Constantinople was avoiding a hearing before the apostolic, that is, the first see? Even if he was supported by the rights of a metropolitan, even if he held a place among the sees, he still had no right to reject the jurisdiction of the first see, to which he was summoned to answer when the bishop of the second see appealed to it according to the canons. Did he not by this very act sufficiently show that he confessed himself guilty, when, summoned to a lawful trial, he scorned to appear?

Nor could the matter be put off any longer, lest, as has been said, if the old communion with him continued after he had joined himself to an outside one, the apostolic see too should be polluted through him by the contagion of the faithless. It was right that one who was either a prevaricator or a despiser of a competent tribunal, plainly despairing of his own case, should be shut out from catholic and apostolic integrity and communion.

Here, if an examination is asked for, there was no further need of a trial, since he had both confessed in his own letters and, when summoned, was afraid to come before a lawful tribunal. If the weight of authority is asked for, we find the tenor of the synod of Chalcedon in agreement with the apostolic see, and the execution of its definition. Having become a sharer in the error condemned there, he likewise appeared as a sharer in the condemnation laid down there; for the same error that has once been condemned together with its author carries both its curse and its penalty in anyone who becomes a partner in that wicked communion.

On this same principle, Timothy the Cat and Peter of Alexandria himself, who certainly appeared to have held the second see in some fashion, are shown to have been condemned not by a repeated synod but solely by the authority of the apostolic see, at the request of Acacius himself, who also carried out the sentence.

So let them now show that Peter was lawfully and truly cleared and duly separated from all contagion of heretics when Acacius communicated with him, if they think that Acacius, as his partner in communion, can be excused to any extent. Or if, as is closer to the truth, they cannot properly and lawfully prove that Peter was cleansed (which is why Acacius did not dare either to come or to send someone to the judgment of the apostolic see), it follows that the one who communicated with him was also infected by his uncleansed state.

Nor do we pass over in silence what the Church throughout the world knows: that the see of the blessed apostle Peter has the right to loose what has been bound by the sentences of any bishops whatever, since it has the right to judge concerning the whole Church, and no one may judge its judgment. For the canons have willed that appeal be made to it from any part of the world, but that no one be permitted to appeal from it. It is therefore quite clear that Acacius had no authority to undo a sentence of the apostolic see without any hearing by it.

Let them tell us, then: by what synod did he presume to do this, which even with a synod he would have had no right to do without the apostolic see? Bishop of what see was he? Prelate of what metropolitan city? Was he not of the diocese of the church of Heraclea? If he was allowed, without a synod, to break a sentence of the apostolic see without seeking its counsel at all, was the first see, then, not allowed, while duly carrying out the decrees of the synod of Chalcedon, to cast out such a prevaricator by its own authority?

Nor do we pass over the fact that the apostolic see, as has been said, has frequently, following the custom of our forebears, had the power both to absolve, even without any preceding synod, those whom a synod had unjustly condemned, and to condemn, without any synod, those who deserved it. Athanasius of holy memory, for instance, had been condemned by an Eastern synod; yet the apostolic see took him under its protection and absolved him, because it did not consent to the condemnation of the Greeks.

Likewise, John of Constantinople, of holy memory, had certainly been condemned by a synod, even one of catholic prelates; and in the same way the apostolic see absolved him, acting alone, because it did not consent. In the same manner it absolved Flavian of holy memory, who had been condemned by an assembly of Greek bishops, because the apostolic see alone did not consent. Rather, by its own authority it condemned Dioscorus, the prelate of the second see, who had been received there; by withholding its consent it alone set aside that impious synod; and it alone decreed, for the sake of the truth, that the synod of Chalcedon should take place. At that synod, to the countless bishops

who had fallen in the Robber Council of Ephesus and asked for pardon, it alone granted it, and those who persisted in their faithlessness it likewise struck down by its own authority. The assembly gathered there to restore the truth followed it; for just as what the first see had not approved could not stand, so what it judged should be decided, the whole Church accepted.

Here it is also shown as a consequence that a badly conducted synod, that is, one held contrary to the holy Scriptures, contrary to the teaching of the fathers, and contrary to the rules of the Church, which the whole Church rightly did not accept and the apostolic see above all did not approve, both ought to have been and could be overturned by a well-conducted synod, that is, one held in accordance with the holy Scriptures, the tradition of the fathers, and the rules of the Church, set forth for the catholic faith and communion, which the whole Church accepted and the apostolic see above all approved. But a well-conducted synod, in the manner described above, is in no way to be altered by a new synod.

Accordingly, if they admit that Eutyches is a heretic, they will likewise admit that the synod at Ephesus, by which he was received, was badly conducted, and, whether they like it or not, they will agree that the synod of Chalcedon, by which Eutyches and those who share his views were cast out, was very well conducted. Let them therefore recognize that it was not permissible to reopen a well-conducted synod with new disturbances.

And if perhaps they say that on the same principle the synod of Ephesus could not be changed either, let them weigh again these same points we set out above, now restated more plainly. A synod wrongly conducted against the faith, against the truth, and against catholic, apostolic, and truly Christian communion must by all means be shut out by a lawful synod held for the faith, the truth, and catholic and truly Christian communion; an unjust synod must be removed by a just synod. But a good and truly Christian synod, once held for the faith, the truth, and catholic and apostolic communion, neither can nor should be overthrown by repeating it in a new synod. Rather, if anyone strays from the path of a well-conducted and rightly settled synod, he is consequently and sufficiently to be punished by its definition, and he is deservedly subject to its decrees.

Nor is there any need to bring in new synods again for each individual who strays and deserves punishment. For according to the course laid down by the synod that condemned the author together with his error, whoever has in any way and under any title become an accomplice in that same error and has polluted himself by its contagion or communion fittingly becomes a sharer in the same condemnation and is held bound by the penalty of the one whose fellowship he chose to join.

I ask them, therefore, what they think of Eutyches: do they assert that he was a heretic or that he was not? If they contend that he was not, why do they deal in evasions? Why do they cover themselves with roundabout talk and tricks? Let them openly declare themselves Eutychians, so that, convicted in his sacrilegious frenzy, they may be crushed under the weight of the truth and plainly recognize not only how hostile this Eutychian plague itself is shown to be to Christian doctrine, but also how many other heresies, and those most grievous, it contains in its depravity. Then they will understand in what pits they are wallowing and into what precipice and abyss they are plunging.

At the same time, if they deny that Eutyches was a heretic, it becomes entirely public that the reason they argue about the names of those who communicate with the Eutychian plague, while keeping that error itself as it were out of sight, is that they are trying, through the snares and captious traps of such names, to lead us (God forbid!) into the madness of Eutyches. And even if they do not deny it, they are shown to be doing this, whether knowingly or unknowingly.

But if they do not dare to deny that Eutyches was a heretic, it remains for them to agree that what took place at Ephesus against the catholic faith should not be called a synod but rather a conspiracy of the lost. When Eutyches had been restored there, it struck down Flavian of holy memory and compelled all the bishops who were present, by military terror, to give their consent to so great a crime. And so they must necessarily agree with us that the proceedings of that conspiracy were depraved, perverse, and the work of robbers, and that they had to be abolished by every means. They must therefore acknowledge that the synod of Chalcedon proceeded justly, well, and in a truly Christian way in the measures by which it expelled Eutyches and, together with his supporter Dioscorus, condemned their heresy and error.

Let them not doubt, then, as has been said, that this synod, through which that harmful one was removed, is good, true, just, and Christian. Let them therefore see and at last concede that whoever strays from the faith, communion, and truth of this just, Christian, and true synod, or mixes in communion with those who stray from it, is sufficiently and fittingly bound according to its own definitions. For a bad synod had to be removed by a good one, but there is no reason why a good synod should be reconsidered by another synod, lest that very reconsideration take away the firmness of its decrees.

Accordingly, why do those who are attached to the assembly of Ephesus still hold up only the name of Acacius, and not openly profess themselves followers of Eutyches, who had been received there? But if they shrink from this and declare that they abhor Eutyches, then they will agree at the same time that the conspiracy of Ephesus, by which he was wrongly received, was rightly annulled, and that the synod of Chalcedon, by which he was rejected, was deservedly held. And so they will see that a synod established for the faith, communion, and catholic and apostolic truth could not, according to the pattern of the ancients, as has been said, be tossed about by novel questions; rather, according to its tenor, once lawfully and justly set forth, those who follow what is right are rightly approved and those who hold the contrary are rejected.

The apostolic see, guarding this ancient tradition as was fitting, did not consider that the synod should be repeated, but rather that this same synod should be carried out by expelling the one who had transgressed it.

Therefore, if anyone still finds fault with what the apostolic see has done in accordance with the synod of Chalcedon, then, besides the fact that he can be refuted both by the argument we have built up above and by many others, he will have to admit all the more that Acacius had no right to attempt these things. Let him say, then, by what synod Acacius decided that John, bishop of the second see, whatever sort of man he was, but certainly a catholic, ordained by catholics, and in no way accused regarding the catholic faith and communion, should be shut out; and by what synod he allowed Peter, a manifest heretic, condemned with Acacius himself carrying out the sentence, to be put in the place of a catholic bishop. For even if John had been manifestly guilty, it would at least have been proper for a catholic bishop to be appointed after him, just as the emperor himself is read to have promised in his sacred letters to Timothy of holy memory, the catholic bishop in Alexandria, that he would do.

By what synod did the same Acacius have Calendion, bishop of the third see, expelled, and then allow Peter to be put in his place by his own arrangement, though Peter was so plainly a heretic that Acacius did not even pretend to be in communion with him openly? By what synod, finally, did he throw out orthodox bishops stained by no crime throughout the whole East, and by his own provision put in their places every depraved man entangled in crimes? By what synod did this abominable plunderer seize so many privileges that belonged to others? But books would not be enough if we tried to write out one by one the tragedies he staged in the churches of the whole East.

Or do they think we should be confronted with that argument of his by which he has tried to shift his crimes onto the person of the emperor? Why then, when he wished, did he stand up to Basiliscus, who was certainly a tyrant, a heretic and fiercely hostile? Why, in refusing to communicate openly with Peter of Antioch, did he not subordinate his will to the emperor Zeno himself? See, he could have resisted in other matters too, had he wished.

But to pass over matters that would need fuller explanation, what of the fact that the emperor Zeno himself declares in his letters that he did everything on Acacius's advice? Acacius himself likewise testifies in his own letters that the emperor is not mistaken in this, for he wrote that the emperor had done everything rightly, and did not conceal that these same things had been done on his advice.

As if Acacius had proved a transgressor only by his communion with Peter of Alexandria, and not also with all those whom, after the catholic bishops had been driven out, he either had set over various churches like a tyrant or, once they had been so set over them, joined in perverse communion! By the canons, these men ought to have been driven from the communion of the Church for the very fact that they allowed themselves to be installed as successors while the bishops were still alive.

What Christian does not see that when catholic bishops had been thrown out of their own sees, only heretics could have been brought in? Yet Acacius either was responsible for installing all of them or joined in communion with them once they had been installed—men, at any rate, who differed in no way from the communion of the heretics.

Why then, when Acacius saw these things being done, did he not take care to refer them to the apostolic see, as he had already done under Basiliscus, so that, if he could not do it alone, what was fitting for religion might be pleaded before the emperor through joint counsel and deliberation with that see? For if Basiliscus, a tyrant and a heretic, as has been said, was powerfully broken by the letters of the apostolic see and called back from very many

of his excesses, how much more could a lawful emperor, who wished to be seen as catholic, have been softened by the moderate counsel of the apostolic see together with all the bishops—especially since he was a particular patron and admirer of this same Acacius, and is shown in his letters to have extolled with great praise both Acacius himself and Pope Simplicius of holy memory for having resisted the heretics most steadfastly? Why did Acacius keep silent so long amid all this, unless because he did not want anything to hinder what he wished to see accomplished for the heretics?

Let us suppose, however, that no synod had gone before, of which the apostolic see could rightly be the executor: with whom was a synod to be held about Acacius? With those who were already held to be Acacius's partners, and who, after catholic bishops throughout the whole East had been violently excluded and banished into various places of exile, were plainly sharers in an alien communion, having gone over to these associations before consulting the decrees of the apostolic see?

With whom, then, was a synod to be held? The catholic bishops had already been driven out everywhere, and only the associates of the faithless remained, with whom it was not even permissible to meet, since it was utterly contrary to the custom of the Church to join in any council with those who held a polluted communion mingled with the faithless, as the prophet also says: “I have not sat in the council of vanity, and I will not go in with those who do iniquity; I have hated the assembly of the wicked, and I will not sit with the ungodly.”

Rightly, therefore, was such transgression repelled according to the form of the synod of Chalcedon, rather than brought before a council, which was neither needed after the first synod nor permissible to hold with such men. For had they wished to understand, they could not have been ignorant of what was at stake for the catholic faith, when they saw catholic bishops being driven out of the whole East without any synodal examination, without any council—especially since they recognized that these were new cases; and the rest could have learned what to beware of from the character of those men.

It remains, then, that they clearly belonged to the party to which they gave themselves up after so many proofs, and rightly were they no longer to be consulted by the apostolic see and the other catholics, but rather censured.

We laughed, moreover, that they want a prerogative secured for Acacius because he was bishop of the royal city. Has the emperor not often resided for long periods at Ravenna, at Milan, at Sirmium, at Trier? Did the bishops of these cities ever usurp for their dignities anything beyond the measure anciently assigned to them? When Acacius excluded John from Alexandria—whatever sort of man John was, he was a catholic ordained by catholics—and received Peter, who had already been exposed and condemned for heresy, without consulting the apostolic see, did he boldly seize upon this with at least some synod held there? When he drove Calendion from Antioch and readmitted the heretic Peter, whom he too had condemned, without the knowledge of the apostolic see, is it shown that he did it by any synod?

If it is indeed a question of the dignity of cities, the dignity of the bishops of the second and third sees is greater than that of the bishop of this city, which not only is not counted among the sees at all, but is not even reckoned among those with metropolitan rights. As for what you call “the royal city”: the power of the secular realm is one thing, the distribution of ecclesiastical dignities another. Just as a city, however small, does not diminish the prerogative of the reigning emperor's presence, so the imperial presence does not change the measure of the religious order. Let that city be illustrious for the power of the reigning empire; religion under it stands firm, free and advanced only when, rather, in the emperor's presence it keeps its own measure without any disturbance.

Finally, if they flatter themselves about the emperor's presence and think that the bishop of Constantinople can thereby become a more powerful figure, let them hear how Marcian, emperor of that same city, after he had come forward as intercessor for the aggrandizement of that city's bishop and could obtain nothing contrary to the rules, praised Pope Leo of holy memory in the highest terms because he would on no account allow the rules of the canons to be violated;

let them hear Anatolius, bishop of that same see, confessing that it was the clergy of Constantinople rather than he himself who had attempted such things, and saying that everything lay in the power of the apostolic prelate; and let them hear how blessed Pope Leo himself, prelate of the apostolic see, by whose authority the synod of Chalcedon was confirmed, by a fitting refutation made void whatever was seen to have been attempted by a new proceeding, on the occasion of that assembly and contrary to the Nicene canons, beyond what was clearly delegated by him to be dealt with there on behalf of the catholic and apostolic faith and communion;

and how likewise, under Pope Simplicius of holy memory, the legate of the apostolic see, Probus of holy memory, bishop of the city of Canusium, taught in the presence of the emperor Leo, who was then requesting it, that these things could in no way be attempted, and gave them no consent whatever. Let them therefore not look to the rank of any city, but duly observe the order of the Church's dispensation established by the tradition of the fathers.

But it may be said that, concerning the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch, for certain reasons it was the emperor rather than Acacius who ordered what was done. Yet it was the bishop's duty to suggest to a Christian emperor—especially one whose familiarity and favor he enjoyed—that his vengeance for injury and insult to himself would remain intact, provided only that, as a Christian emperor, he allowed the rules of the Church to be kept; for in the case of each bishop a new matter had arisen and consequently required a new examination; and, as had always been done and as divine and human laws alike decree, judgments on bishops ought to come from a council of bishops, so that bishops of whatever sort—who, even if some human error had befallen them, had in no way departed from religion—should not be seen to be struck down by secular

power. Or was he, exalted by the honor of the royal city, not to suggest these things to the emperor on just grounds? If he had been made more exalted by that royal city, so much the more steadfast ought he to have been in suggesting these things; but if in matters that should have been put forward on behalf of religion he proved contemptible and despised, either sluggish or lacking the confidence to speak, in what respect was he made greater through the royal city? Was it so that through it he might exercise the tyranny of his transgression rather than lawfully attend to the causes of religion?

The prophet Nathan openly and publicly, to his face, declared to King David the error that had been committed, did not conceal that David himself had committed it, and then, when he had been corrected by confession, absolved him. Ambrose of blessed memory, bishop of the church of Milan, publicly and openly suspended the elder Theodosius from communion and brought royal power to penance. Pope Leo of blessed memory, as we read, freely rebuked the emperor Theodosius the younger when he overstepped his bounds in the Robber Synod of Ephesus.

Pope Hilarus of holy memory also, when Philotheus the Macedonian, relying on his familiarity with the emperor Anthemius, wished to bring new conventicles of various sects into the City, openly and in a loud voice at the shrine of blessed Peter the apostle bound the emperor not to let it happen, so much so that the emperor promised under oath that it would not be done.

Likewise Pope Simplicius of holy memory, and after him Pope Felix of holy memory, are known to have rebuked repeatedly and with free authority not only the tyrant Basiliscus but also the emperor Zeno for these very excesses; and Zeno could have been swayed, had he not been inflamed at the instigation of the bishop of Constantinople, who, having become a participant in an alien communion, was by now of necessity fostering what he had fallen into, preferring to persist in the obstinacy of his transgression rather than to be cured and return to wholesome ways, as the outcome of events has itself proved.

See, recently Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, a great man and an outstanding bishop, and many catholic bishops with him, steadfastly resisted Huneric, king of the Vandal nation, in his rage, and, enduring every extremity, do not cease even today to resist their persecutors. We too, it is well known, by God's help in no way obeyed Odoacer, a barbarian heretic who then held the kingdom of Italy, when he commanded certain things that ought not to be done.

But this good man Acacius, this exceptional bishop, so plainly showed that he could have spoken up, revealed that he would not, and indeed disclosed that he favored these things, that the emperor did not conceal that he had done everything on his advice, while Acacius himself extolled with great praises the emperor who did them and betrayed himself as a partner in carrying them out.

But grant that Calendion removed the emperor's name, and suppose it is claimed that John lied to the emperor: still, since these were new cases, a new ecclesiastical examination ought to have taken place. Or were those who were said to have sinned against a man, the emperor, to be thrown out without any synod intervening, while Acacius, who offended against God, the supreme and true emperor, and was eager to mingle the pure communion of the divine sacrament with the faithless, ought not to have been expelled in accordance with the synod by which this faithlessness was condemned?

What of the countless catholic bishops throughout the whole East driven from their own sees, and undoubted heretics brought in? These were certainly new cases, and consequently a new synod was owed them. Why did it not then occur to anyone to ask the emperor that in such cases at least some sort of synod be held, so that the bishops being thrown out everywhere—not only the bishops of ordinary cities but, without the least hesitation, metropolitans—might at least appear to have been excluded by some judgment of church tradition, however specious?

Since he did not resist all these things by such counsel as he could, Acacius consented to them by communicating with all the heretics who had been put in place of catholics. And the apostle says that not only those who do such things but also those who consent to the doers are undoubtedly counted guilty. Or was it lawful for the secular power, with Acacius consenting to such acts, to carry these things out without any synod, which the very newness of the matters demanded, and without consulting the apostolic see; and was it not lawful for the apostolic see, according to the tenor of the synod of Chalcedon, in an old case condemned by a just definition under an old decree, to drive from its communion Acacius, who was in communion with the enemies of the synod of Chalcedon?

But, they say, Acacius could not oppose the emperor. Why then did he oppose Basiliscus, because he wished to? Why did he refuse his assent to Zeno himself, so as not to be seen communicating openly with Peter of Antioch, though he did so secretly? See, the emperor did not press him when he resisted; see, he used no force on him when he was unwilling; see, he excused him when he shrank from manifest contagion.

Finally, why for so long, while these things were being done or when he knew they were going to be done, did he not hasten to refer them to the apostolic see, by which he knew the care of those regions had been delegated to him? Why instead did he himself become a praiser of these deeds before either warning that such things were being attempted or resisting their being attempted, as he had already done under Basiliscus? Why did he consent to communicate with those others who, as undoubted heretics, had been installed in the various cities after the catholic bishops were driven out? Finally, if he failed in his part and disdained to do what befitted a catholic bishop, could or should the apostolic see on that account neglect what belonged to it?

However one views it, therefore, the apostolic see repudiated the accomplice of heretics and removed from its communion the partner of an alien communion; and there was no need for a new synod, since the form of the old decree sufficiently prescribed this. Nor was there any need to inform the bishops of the East that this was to be done, since it is clear both that they were not ignorant of what was being done in the cause of the faith through the expulsion of the catholics, and that by communicating with the heretics installed in their place they consented to such an act.

There is no doubt, too, that the decrees of the apostolic see neither could nor should have been discussed with those who had become members of an alien communion. See, they recognized in the profession of those who persevered most steadfastly what was owed to the catholic faith and communion. See, they recognized how Acacius, by withdrawing from such men, and indeed by working against such men, strayed from the catholic faith and communion, and how they too, together with him, gave themselves over to error.

See, they recognized for what just reasons Acacius was removed by the authority of the apostolic see on behalf of the catholic and apostolic faith and communion—with which those who had persisted in it agreed, and from which those who opposed the persevering were shown to be estranged. (He was specially summoned to the see's examination, yet took no trouble either to come or to send anyone to clear himself of all these charges, if he had any confidence.) Likewise all who were his accomplices were removed; and he was rightly cut off, together with them, from that communion from which he himself is known to have first separated himself, with his partners, by breaking with the catholic bishops. And rightly he received the sentence of condemnation that was to be promulgated to his other partners, since he alone, on behalf of all his partners, professed in letters sent to the apostolic see that he had fallen back into communion with faithlessness.

If the Eastern bishops had been in communion with this Acacius before he reported here, they were without doubt shown to be involved in equal guilt, and rightly received through him the sentence for transgression, as having become partners with him in an alien communion; and they surely ought no longer to have been consulted as men of our communion, but repudiated as belonging to a contrary fellowship. But if they had not been in communion with him before Acacius reported here, they ought both to have censured him for communicating, and themselves to have reported here about him instead, and to have approved his being rightly struck down by the vigor of the apostolic see, and rather to have kept concord with that apostolic see and with those great catholic bishops.

But because they had broken away from the fellowship of those bishops and chosen to communicate with their successors, they were therefore by no means in agreement with the apostolic see. Because they had fallen into the same lot as the transgressor Acacius and clearly saw that they were consequently bound by his sentence, they did not want him to be seen as condemned, for they knew that they themselves stood condemned in the same transgression—in which they still persist today.

But just as these men, bound by the same condition, cannot judge their accomplice not to have been rightly condemned, nor can the guilty properly acquit the guilty, so, now that the transgressor has been justly condemned, they too lie prostrate under the same condemnation and can by no means be absolved from it unless they come to their senses. For just as the transgression of all who had fallen into the same act of faithlessness was made public through the writing of one man, so, when the transgression was punished in that one and the same man who had written on behalf of all, or by writing had betrayed the wishes of all, the transgression of all his accomplices was likewise punished together with him, or in him.

This sentence directed against Acacius is shown to have been lawfully issued in the name of the apostolic prelate alone, to whose power it certainly belonged—especially since it seemed that it had to be sent secretly, lest, with guards posted everywhere, this salutary measure be hindered by difficulties of one kind or another and be unable to take its necessary effect. Nevertheless, because the orthodox had been thrown out everywhere and only heretics and their partners were left in the East, so that catholic bishops either did not remain at all or enjoyed no freedom, an assembly of very many catholic bishops in Italy recognized that the sentence against Acacius had been reasonably pronounced.

This assembly of bishops did not meet against Chalcedon, nor as a new synod against the old and first one; rather, in accordance with the tenor of the old decree, it became a sharer in the apostolic execution. Thus it is plain enough that the catholic Church and the apostolic see, since it could no longer do so elsewhere at all, omitted absolutely nothing, where it could and with whom it could, that belonged to fraternal deliberation on behalf of an undefiled faith and a pure communion.

Though those who now appear to preside over the Eastern churches know all these things, they shun the restoration of Christian unity by lawful remedy precisely because they now refuse to give up this occasion of dissension, which serves their ambitions and allows them to throw the rights of all the churches into confusion everywhere without the authority of the apostolic see. They choose rather to persist in error than to lose the opportunity for their presumptions, loving the license of their usurpations more than they hold in their hearts any regard for divine judgment. In this it is necessary, whether they will or not,

that they receive what they deserve, both for neglecting the purity of the catholic and apostolic faith and communion and for plainly breaking the canons of the fathers—unless, while time here still allows, they strive with amended minds to avoid these perils of eternal damnation, so that they may not remain among those against whom an indissoluble sentence has been passed, but, by withdrawing from such men, may not be bound by that same sentence. Just as it has been fixed never to be loosed for those who persist in error, so it will not touch those who prove free of the depravity that deserves punishment.

We judge that these things are more than enough for the instruction of your charity, although, if the Lord grants opportunity, we shall endeavor to set them out more fully, so that every one of the faithful may know that the apostolic see decided nothing overhastily—God forbid—and so that perverse impudence may be shown that it has nothing it can justly object.

Your charity will do well to make what we write known both to catholics and to those who think otherwise, so that the sound may be given the firmness they need and the unsound a fitting medicine. Given on the Kalends of February, after the consulship of the most distinguished Viator.
(96.) Letter of Pope Gelasius to Bishop Honorius.

Gelasius to his most beloved brother Honorius. We are surprised that your Charity was surprised that the care of the apostolic see, which by the custom of our forebears is owed to all the churches throughout the world, was concerned for the faith of your region as well. When it was reported to the see that certain persons in Dalmatia were trying to corrupt catholic integrity and to bring in once more the poison of the Pelagian plague, long since condemned by divine and human laws, we thought there should be no delay at all. By looking into these matters more carefully, we hoped either that the errors, if they had perhaps crept in, would be promptly healed, or that our anxiety would be relieved if the reports proved false. We judged it better to be seen as too impatient in tracking down such things than to let the harm grow by ignoring it.

For we ought neither to suppress cases of this kind by silence nor to encourage them by delay. The teacher of the Gentiles says, "not slothful in diligence," and again, "he who presides, with diligence"; these words would surely convict us if we did not inquire at once, even if the reports were groundless. Nor would it matter through whom these things had reached our ears. Whoever reported them, and however they did so, once they had come to our knowledge the pastoral watch could not be neglectful in investigating them truthfully. In this way the hungry wolves could be met immediately, or, if there were no wild beasts, the flock could continue in safe keeping.

The apostle testifies that he learned of the dissensions of the Corinthians from Chloe's people, and he did not fail to write at once. He did so in order that, as a loving physician, he might either deal with the quarrels as they arose or soon rejoice on learning that the Corinthians were safe. We remember that we indicated the same in the letter we sent on this matter: namely, that we would either resist the follies creeping in or, if nothing of the kind had happened at all, rejoice in the integrity of catholic truth.

Therefore your Charity should not be disturbed by our vigilance. Rather, having received the greeting of this present address, you should join the efforts of your own diligence to ours. In this way, if such things have been attempted, they may be corrected at once; or, so that they may not be attempted by some kind of stealth, they may be prevented from slipping in by more careful precaution. As for the matters on which those whom your Charity sent wished to be more fully instructed, the following headings with their answers will make them known.

Those men declared that they accepted these points to the extent of affirming that they had held them from the beginning; but since some people had called them into question, they wished them to be set out more clearly. So, as far as was possible amid the business that scarcely lets us breathe, we have taken care, by the Lord's gift, not to be silent, following in the footsteps of the fathers in what we have received concerning such matters. Whoever follows this rule of sober belief with a faithful heart should rightly be counted among the orthodox; but whoever thinks it should be rejected should be in no doubt that he is exiling himself from the apostolic teachings.

Of course, if there is anything that may trouble your mind, let your Fraternity not fail to consult us with confidence, so that, with the grace of the Lord assisting, our brotherly exchange may clear away every obscurity and doubt.
(97.) Statements of the same against the Pelagian heresy.

There is a great deal of material on the Pelagian notions and sacrilegious blasphemies, which among our forebears were justly examined and condemned by both divine and human laws. Their destructive perversity takes many forms, and it is all the more harmful for being made subtle by a show of plausibility. Having begun with a wicked and deadly fabrication about the very first parent of the human race, a fabrication wrongly conceived, they wove the rest out of the falsehoods that follow from it. (For whoever has gone astray at the start, and wanders everywhere off the straight path, must stray the further the faster he thinks he is running.) Refuting these errors properly calls for a lengthy treatment, since the practice of sound medicine is first to understand or uncover the origin of a disease, and once it is laid bare, to prepare a fitting remedy.

If the Lord grants us life and the means, we will try to set all this out on another occasion, so far as we are able when refreshed by heavenly dew. For now, however, we have thought it enough to deal with this one point, which is said to trouble some people, so that once it has been properly examined they may weigh, with the help of the Lord our God, what they must guard against in the rest.

Some people suppose, then, that in this life a person can stand in such perfection as to be wholly untouched by the passions of human frailty and unshaken by the enticements of the body. Anyone who thinks he can attain this by his own strength and the resolve of his own will deceives himself, and the truth is not in him. The first human beings put too much trust in their own happiness and received so great a grace of God in vain. They did not pray (and nowhere are they said to have done so), they gave no thanks for what they had received, and they did not humbly beg that it might remain unspoiled; and so they could not remain unharmed. If they could not hold firm even when whole without God's help, how much less can people stand by their own strength, now that they are sick, after the ruin of the transgression into which they fell to their death through a wicked self-confidence that never sought out the Creator?

But suppose someone asserts that this can be granted in this life to some of the saints, not through the power of human ability but by grace alone. He does well, of course, to think so confidently of the gift of God, to whom all things are possible, and to hope for it in faith. Yet whether any have existed who reached this perfection in the present life is nowhere clearly established, and so it is not fitting for us lightly either to affirm or to deny it. It is more sober to learn how we ought to measure progress in this life from the words of the holy prophets and apostles themselves. Plainly there has never been, and is not now, anyone in this world more excellent than they in the conduct of a holy life.

Even if, by a more abundant gift of God, they were assailed by the passions of the human condition only rarely or very slightly, and by a richer grace of God easily overcame the faults of mortality, they still do not testify that they were so free of them as to be without sin altogether. That belongs to the spotless Lamb alone, for to have had no sin at all is his alone, and it would seem not to be his alone if any other saint were believed to have been free of fault. Let us be content, then, with what the saints profess, and listen to what they themselves declare about themselves, rather than pursue, without sure authority, what might be rashly imagined or tossed about in our own opinions.

After the mystery of humanity's restoration, almighty God could have granted us this as well, that we should be wholly free from every fault. Why, then, did he prefer that his faithful should be saved and wait for the security of perfect blessedness, so that what we desire in hope we may attain in reality? And why did he judge it better to perfect strength in weakness now, rather than remove our weaknesses and let the human condition be shaken by no disturbance of sickness? This will be discussed, as is fitting, so far as the Lord provides.

We should be instructed on these matters by the testimony of the Scriptures, against whose sense nothing should be rashly professed. It is established that Christ and the Church were prefigured in the first man himself, as the blessed apostle Paul teaches us when he speaks of the covenant of holy marriage: "This is a great mystery, and I say it refers to Christ and the Church." So from then on, every saint who came forth was counted within the figure of this mystery, and from Abel onward all the saints enacted this mystery in their sacrifices and deeds.

So it was in Christ and in the Church, in which the forgiveness of sins was prepared beforehand for all, that every one of the faithful lived for God and in holiness. And up to the time of the Law given through Moses, they were cleansed by particular sacrifices in the power of this mystery. If all of them needed to be continually atoned for by mystical offerings, there is no doubt that they were assailed by the faults of the human condition, from which they had to be continually absolved through those remedies of the sacrament to come. Moreover, the venerable reading of Scripture testifies that in the time of the Law there was no saint who did not offer a victim for sin. Indeed, the high priests themselves, when they pleaded before God the cause of the people who were then faithful, also sacrificed victims for their own sins, and all the prophets everywhere cry out, asking pardon for their sins.

That is why holy Job says: "No one is clean from filth, not even an infant whose life on earth is but a day," and elsewhere: "The stars are not clean in your sight." A clear pronouncement of the prophet David about the saints in general is also known, in which he says: "Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no one living will be justified in your sight." Here he plainly made no exception for any human being at all, as he shows more plainly and openly when he says the same thing: "I said, 'I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord,' and you forgave the wickedness of my heart. For this every saint will pray to you at the proper time." He [?] could not [mean] only the saints under the Law, but also those who would come afterward, of a higher calling, in the future grace of God; so when he added "at the proper time," he did not say it without knowledge of things to come. And the most wise Solomon in his prayer: "There is no one who has not sinned," and again: "Who will boast that he has a chaste heart, or that he is clean

from sin?" But it might be thought that the saints of those times should perhaps be excepted from this question of freedom from passion, because they made use of the wives God permitted them (although the blessed Elijah is recorded as having been subject to passions, as what follows will show, and the holy prophet Daniel is said to have prayed not only for the sins of the people but also for his own, as he himself says: "While I was praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people to the Lord my God"). So let us at last come to the blessed apostles. Let the blessed James speak. Although all the apostles were certainly just, we read that he obtained, properly and in a special way, the distinction of being called "the Just."
