He says: "Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him." And again, a little later: "But each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire. Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin, and sin, when it is complete, brings forth death." And the same writer again: "For we all stumble in many ways." And he went on to add: "Elijah too was a man like us, subject to passions."

Let the blessed apostle Peter speak: "Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and strangers to abstain from bodily pleasures, which wage war against the soul." And again: "Do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal that comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you." And later: "Be sober and watchful, for your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in the faith, knowing that the same sufferings are being experienced by your whole brotherhood throughout the world." From this brotherhood the apostles clearly do not set themselves apart: they often call themselves brothers of all the faithful, and they are shown not to have made an exception of themselves.

Let the blessed John the Evangelist speak, the one who reclined on the Savior's breast: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." And again: "If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word will not be in us." Let the same apostle say: "I write these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only but for those of the whole world." And again he says: "All that is in the world is the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes and worldly ambition, which is not from the Father but from the world. And the world is passing away along with its desire, but whoever does the will of the Lord abides forever."

Let the least of the apostles come forward, who is yet God's chosen vessel. Let Paul come, the teacher of the Gentiles, the unrivaled preacher of divine grace and the rich expounder of the heavenly mystery. He was caught up to the third heaven, not knowing whether in the body or out of the body, and heard inexpressible words. He overflowed with such grace that, though he was the last of all, he labored more than all of them. Let this teacher of free truth declare not only what he urges the faithful to think on this matter, but also what he says about himself. And since it would take too long to go back over everything said on this subject, let a few things out of many be set down. From them it will be shown to us quite sufficiently that we ought rather to be weak with Paul, so that Christ may dwell in us, than to seem strong by thinking otherwise than Paul, as though (God forbid) we no longer needed Christ's remedies.

He says, then: "For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For the will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish the good. For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want is what I do. Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me." And again: "For I delight in the law of God in my inner self, but I see another law in my members waging war against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin that is in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord."

Why, then, does he call himself a wretched man? Why does he rejoice to be delivered from the body of death through the grace of Christ, if he was troubled by no passions of human misery, and harassed by no assaults from which he needed to be delivered? Again he says: "The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other, so that you do not do the things you want." For the spirit does not accomplish what it wants, so that it may not grow proud of its perfection. And again, the flesh does not accomplish what it wants, so that it may in this way remind us of the human condition, yet not wholly overwhelm the resolve of faith.

Some, as is their habit, may suppose in their idle opinions that the blessed apostle Paul says these things in the person of someone else, whoever that might be, rather than confessing them about himself. Yet nothing of the kind can be shown there at all, and when he says, "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ," it can be proved that the person of a Gentile, or of a Jew, is ruled out. Still, let us hear him elsewhere pointing to himself, as it were, with his own hand and indicating himself specifically: "I myself with my mind serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin." And again about himself: "I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, so that after preaching to others I myself may not be disqualified." Who, then, would fail to notice that there would have been no point in his curbing his members by discipline so as not to be disqualified, if he was troubled by none of those goads which, had he neglected them and not subdued them by disciplining his body, could have led to his disqualification?

Therefore, since it is shown that the apostles also professed these things about themselves — and even if they had not disclosed them at all, there is no doubt that all of them would both have had to preach the Lord's Prayer and say it with a sincere heart. In it they prayed daily that their debts might be forgiven, and they are shown to have prayed not to be led into temptation and to have humbly begged to be delivered from evil.

That is why the blessed apostle John, as was said above, is understood to have written: "If we say we have no sin, we make him a liar" — that is, Christ. For he would not have given his disciples this form of prayer, in which daily debts are forgiven and they ask not to fall into temptation and beg to be delivered from evil, if there were nothing at all to weigh on them as an unforgiven debt, no temptation to sin that could be brought upon them, and no evil whatsoever from which they needed to be delivered.

Some people are troubled by the delusion that steals upon those who are asleep, as if the desire of those who are awake were not reckoned more serious. Bodily unruliness should indeed be curbed quite often, either by the discipline of fasting or by eating frugally, so as not to give the human senses material by which they may be deceived through the imaginings of illusory pleasure; or God's mercy should be implored with earnest prayers that minds lulled in sleep may be kept free from enticing visions. Still, whether these things happen to those who live without restraint or to those who live continently, the guilt of those who do not know what is happening, if there is any guilt, is certainly less than that of those who desire a carnal act openly and plainly. In short, though whoever is assailed by no such snares, if that is possible, or very rarely, enjoys no small gift of God, we nowhere read that the illusions of dreams are counted as guilt.

But we know very well that the Lord himself said that whoever looks at a woman with desire has committed adultery with her in his heart. There guilt is clearly present, and so it must be atoned for by constant prayer as well as by almsgiving and other good works. For it is not without purpose that it is said that all things can be cleansed by almsgiving, as when the Lord, speaking figuratively about inward and outward purifications, said: "But give as alms what is left over, and behold, everything is clean for you." So too it is said that love covers a multitude of sins, so that whatever is contracted through impurity of body and mind may be blotted out by the practice of reasonable devotion.

As for the blessed apostles, as we said above, we ought to know only what they themselves made known in their own words about how their way of life should be regarded. What they passed over in silence we will have no license to search into.

But let us now examine more carefully why, even after the restoration of the human race and the renewal of nature that takes place through the sacrament of baptism, these faults were not only not taken away, but do not cease to harass even those who have committed themselves to great continence, more or less according to the progress each has made as divine grace dispenses. Why were things left for the devout mind to fight against? And why, though we have already been saved through faith and have received the hope of redemption, is the redemption of our body, as the apostle says, still awaited? And though the pledge of adoption has been implanted in those already reborn through the heavenly mysteries, why must the completion of that adoption still be

waited for? It is so that, when these faults against which we now fight continually have come to an end, we may be freed from this necessity and attain, in the longed-for reality itself, what we received by faith and what we have waited for in the hope set before us. Then, wholly stripped of this plague of assaults, we may live always in tranquil holiness. This is promised to be fulfilled in that future blessedness when, as the apostle says, this corruptible body puts on incorruption and this mortal body puts on immortality, and the natural body takes on spiritual dignity.

There is no doubt, then, that pride is above every sin, since it is written of it: "Pride is the beginning of all sin." It is so great an evil that, while each wicked deed is judged worthy of condemnation simply because it is wicked, pride alone is shown to be dangerous even in good deeds. It is pride that not only kept the rational creature placed on earth from standing firm, but in its hostility also cast down the nature of the angels.

Almighty God, who made all things very good, created everything established in its own manner and fitting order, and granted that each could remain or advance in its proper measure. But here a disposition crept into the rational creature. Because it had been made more excellent, this disposition led it to trust more in its own dignity than in the very giver of that dignity, as its proper measure required. So, by seeking the security of its own eminence otherwise than its fitting and proper rule demanded, it made the creature break out of the natural order in its craving for the summit of a higher rank.

This overreaching brought guilt upon the one who overreached, and it also offended the [?] of the Creator, against whose order it was directed. And when the creature abandoned the course by which alone it could advance to everlasting fellowship with the highest good, failure consequently followed, since it could not attain a stable share in that good, as befitted the condition of a rational creature. That the angels were created for progress, so that they might earn eternal stability, is shown by this fact: if they had been made in such a way that they needed nothing further, no part of them could have suffered any failure. Nor should it be said that there was a different nature in them, lest the angel who fell by his own will be excused, as if it was not the choice of his own insolence that brought this on him, but the necessity of the condition given him that seems to have imposed it.

So the blessed and exalted angels, grateful for what they had received, rendered the service of devout piety, and fittingly preferred not themselves but their Author to themselves; and for this they were found worthy to advance and be raised up into his everlasting life. The reprobate angels, by contrast, were consequently ungrateful for what they had received. They disregarded the obedience they owed, and strove to prefer themselves to the one who had created a being of such dignity. Enticed by delight in their own creation, they ceased to honor the Creator. The more arrogantly they were puffed up, the more, by failing through irreverence to follow the uprightness of eternity, they were drawn away both from his favor and from sharing in him. And departing from what is everlasting, they were brought down into what is always failing.

We trust that with the help of our God we will treat this more fully on another occasion; for now, enough for the present purpose. This is that cause, this is that evil, through which the angel, moved by a kind of spiritual fornication even without bodily vice, fell from the divine grace by which he was enlightened and from his share in it. Degraded in this way and shut out of his heavenly seat because of this tarnishing of himself, he was inflamed with envy and overthrew the image of God in the second creation. He attacked man, who was living in security, with the same impulses by which he himself, in his wicked self-confidence, had fallen from the heights to the depths. That is why the happiness of paradise could not last for the first human beings. That is why the integrity of the first condition failed. It trusted in itself as though it had no need of the one who had made it. It gave no thanks for what it had received (nowhere is it said to have done so). It did not ask for help to keep what it had been given. Even when assailed by the approach of the tempter, it did not run devoutly to him and seek his counsel, but in prosperity trusted itself to its own will. And so, without the Creator's protection, it lay easily open to the deceiver's snares. Drawn into transgression, it consequently met the death that had been set as the penalty for what was forbidden, and was deservedly subjected to fitting punishment. For it had not been devout in keeping the good things it had, nor had it guarded against the evil foretold to it beforehand. Presuming, through ambition for greater power, that it would become a god, it fell into the pits dug by the enemy's persuasion. Had it kept its proper order and remained grateful to its Maker, it could have attained everlasting communion with the supreme Godhead. But since it failed in the service it owed to the supreme Divinity, it was fittingly cheated by a deceitful promise and could not attain to divinity.

So it was without the guiding love of that first and highest Reason, which always remains undefiled in holding fast to good things and rejecting their opposites. The rational creature had been made in the likeness of this Reason, so that by imitating it in fitting actions, according to its own measure, by keeping reverence for it and following its grace, it might truly remain its likeness and image. It might then have become worthy of fellowship with the divine Reason as its parent and author, and in this way, as a sharer in eternity, it too would have remained eternal. But it trusted in the dignity in which it had been created and thought that what it had been made was enough for it, and it did not worship its maker with humble devotion. So it both withdrew from sharing in him and could not stand by itself apart from him, in whom alone it had the power to subsist. Thus, overstepping the order of rightful reason, it was led off into the abyss of unreason by the plausible-seeming argument through which it believed it would become God. Deprived of him who is eternal life, it fell back into this life, which, cut off from the fountain of life, could not keep perpetual life.

Although it deserved punishment for these transgressions, God the just judge corrected this creature by the fairness of the law he had laid down. The creature that, amid its happiness, had scorned to follow the divine path he left to itself, weighed in a deserved balance. Yet it had also been deceived by the assault of a more powerful creature. That creature raged that the earthly substance might advance to the very place from which it, a spiritual being, had fallen, and it longed to take a kind of comfort from the ruin of another creature. Or else it wanted to claim that it was not alone to blame, since another had transgressed too, and so to lay its own fall at the door of the Creator's workmanship, as if another of his works had also been quite unable to stand. Because of this, God with unspeakable mercy took thought for the creature that had been ensnared. In this way he showed that both creatures had been rightly made. For the fallen angels are refuted by the blessedness of the holy angels. By the very means by which the holy angels

(that is, by the duty of due devotion and by praising their Creator with due proclamation) gained, through the increase of his favor and progress in fitting reverence, a share in the good parent and the lasting stability of everlasting glory, the fallen angels too could have come to a like blessedness if they had striven with the same constancy. But they grew slack in praising their maker and failed to show fitting reverence, and they were drawn back from the desire to share in him. So they could not receive the increase and perfection of their own dignity. Held fast by the splendor of their own creation, they presumed that they needed nothing further and could be sufficient for themselves. They trusted that they could obtain by themselves whatever they could have attained only through the grace of their Creator, something they could by no means possess in their own changeable condition —;

and man too is refuted by plain proofs drawn from himself, as having been rightly made. Since he can rise after his fall through divine grace, it is shown that he would have been far more able to remain whole if he had followed that same grace with a devoted mind. How powerful that grace is can be seen all the more from this: even while unharmed he could not stand without it, and yet through it he is able to return to that same soundness after his fall.

God, then, is a good craftsman. His goodness is his being, eternal and supreme, and so he never feels any desire to grow further, since there is nothing above what is always the eternal and supreme good. Nor can he be lessened by any decline from what he is, the supreme and eternal good. Hence it is also said that he who certainly had this by nature did not count it robbery to be in the form of God. That spirit was different. What it was, it held in no way as eternal or supreme, yet it chose to seize by robbery rather than to gain a lasting dignity through the grace of the author from whom it had received the substance of angelic brightness. The blessed angels, by contrast, remained in divine grace and attained the firmness of eternal blessedness. But the wicked spirit could not obtain what it had wrongly tried to seize, and by overstepping the bounds of its condition it could not even keep what it had been made.

So the good author, to prove that he had made a good work, one that would have stood if it had persisted in its original condition, took pity on the offense of his lower creature. The spiritual substance, which had become the deceiver both of itself and of another and persisted in its wickedness, had by no means been worthy of what he now did: in his mercy he took up both the nature and the cause of the earthly creature, the substance deceived by fraud. To explain it briefly now, he purposed to restore the fallen by a fitting plan, so that in himself this same nature, which through disobedience <was subject to> death, might return to life:

he alone knew no sin, in the substance which he had mercifully taken up to be restored after sin. He did this so that he might pay an undeserved death, which he certainly did not owe since he was without sin, to the account of those who had become debtors to death through sin. At the same time he dealt with the devil, the deceiver of man, who by right, through the divine sentence, held as his subject the man who had consented to him. Now owing him nothing any longer in justice [?]. And since the devil had killed one over whom, as he was without sin, he had no right, the devil would deservedly be handed over and made subject to him in turn. He who boasted that he was lord and god of human nature as his captive would in his turn be subjected to one who was both just and true God.

For boundless fairness required that the devil be overcome not abruptly by divine power but also by the justice of the very man whom he boasted he had laid low. Yet the exalted restorer was not content to win this triumph over the enemy of the human race alone, in the nature he had taken on. For what would be gained for our whole creation if Christ alone were the devil's conqueror? So in his boundless mercy he graciously granted fellowship to his faithful. Through his grace and the faith he bestowed, he granted that thousands of people should gain a share in him by the short way of an unspeakable sacrament. Made like their Savior in the nature renewed in him, they too would reverse their lot and become victors over their deceiver.

So, against the proud spirit that persists in its pride, this cure was provided for those who are to be saved. By fitting means they were to advance to the wholeness of their condition and to heavenly dignity, turning away as by medicine, through the necessary humility [?], from the deadly passion of pride which, as has been said, had earlier laid low not only human nature but angelic nature itself. In this way wholeness would be restored. For after the fall human nature had to be free of the evil that had kept it from standing firm while it was whole.

It was fitting, moreover, that the rational human creature, by God's grace, should recover by its own will what it had lost by its own will. What was healed in it without merit was to be granted in such a way that it might also go on to follow from merit. For this reason that unique Savior chose that strength be made perfect in weakness, rather than that human nature, made secure and free of all weakness, should either trust in itself or neglect its author.

Hence it is that blessed Paul, who set out more fully than the others both the ruin of the human condition and its restoration, also cries out about himself: "So that the greatness of the revelations might not exalt me, a thorn was given me in my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me. Because of this I asked the Lord three times that it might leave me, and he said to me, 'My grace is sufficient for you, for strength is made perfect in weakness.' Gladly, then, will I glory in my weaknesses, so that the strength of Christ may dwell in me." And again he says: "For the creation was subjected to futility":

still subject to futility, certainly, so long as it is still entangled in worldly senses and weighed down by its corruptible condition. This is the creation of which he says elsewhere: "If then anyone is a new creation, the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new." He also says of it elsewhere: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ for good works." And again he says of the same: "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but a new creation." This is the creation in which we have been remade in Christ, not the one in which we were made at the beginning.

Of this the blessed apostle James also speaks: "Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth, so that we might be a kind of firstfruits of his creation." He does not mean the creation that was formed in Adam. He means the creation that was begotten by the will of the Father of lights, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift, and that took its beginning in Christ through the word of truth. This was so that human nature might not trust in any good things of its own. Whatever it recognized as right in itself it should regard as coming down from above, from that unchanging light, always boundless and without any shadow of change. Changeable itself and darkened by the shadow of change, human nature would then feel that the gift of the true light was being bestowed on it by that light.

This, then, is the creation which lives a spiritual life and yet unwillingly endures the passions that assail our mortal nature. It fights against them without ceasing, and would rather have nothing to conquer than be locked in constant conflict with a hostile foe. It is subject to vain desires unwillingly, then, as to things that will surely perish. Hence the apostle says: "The flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do what you want." "But because of him," he says, "who subjected it in hope." This is so that no one in this life may again grow arrogant as if happiness were already complete, and again so that it may not perhaps sink into despair. So he subjected it to bearing these troubles in such a way that it might still be comforted and lifted up by hope.

This, then, beyond doubt, is the creation of which he says: "because the creation itself will also be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God." By saying "into the freedom of the children of God," he made clear which creation he wanted to be understood. In this world it is now in bondage in that part of it which is assailed by human vices. But then it will come to the freedom of the children of God in perfect security, when this corruptible body has put on incorruption and this mortal body has put on immortality, so that the saying that is written may come true: "Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting?" Now the sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore the blessed apostle, as one through whom Christ spoke, wanted to show more plainly which creation he was dealing with, and what bondage and what freedom of that creation he was discussing. So he presses the point further and says: "For we know that the whole creation groans and is in labor." This can only be the rational creation, and in particular that rational creation which, already reborn, knows why it groans and what it is laboring to bring forth. It weeps over its weakness and awaits the promise of everlasting peace.

We must consider more carefully how far the distinguished teacher takes this. "Not only it," he says (that is, the creation that is the Christian people), "but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit." He means the apostles themselves, the very leaders and parents of the church, who first received the gifts of the Holy Spirit so as to serve the church's growth in the Spirit. Here, beyond dispute, he places himself and the other apostles, though endowed with a greater measure of one and the same grace, in one and the same general condition as the whole church. That greater measure is why he says "who have the firstfruits of the Spirit," as if they were the foremost in the grace of God. So by saying "even we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves," he revealed whose groaning it was that he had spoken of above, and he plainly explained what it groaned for: "awaiting adoption."

Surely he has already received the pledge of adoption in the sacrament of rebirth. What, then, is this adoption that is still awaited after adoption has begun, and what is the redemption of our body that is set before us as still to come? Have you not received, then, what you say you are awaiting? "I have received it," he says, "but I have been renewed and initiated in heavenly mysteries. As they do their proper work in me, I, who survive and still remain in this mortal state, may come to their fullness and perfection, and the victory of those who fight here may be completed there, where it will be said: 'Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting?' For now we have been saved in hope. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience."

He has shown in a clear enough light what the state of the faithful is in this life: what they hold by faith, what they endure in hope, what they long for with all their love. All this certainly happens for the reason a teacher of the church wisely explained when he said: "The stuff of struggle has been kept for the great benefit of the faithful, so that holiness may not grow proud while weakness is under attack." Warned at least by its own frailty after the fall, our nature is not to trust in itself but to run back without ceasing to his mercy to be made anew. Because it did not seek his grace, it could not stand even in the unspoiled happiness of paradise. It is to learn that it fell from there for lack of the very protection through which it is now being taught to return, after its hardships, to everlasting joy, and that with this help it could have remained unharmed far more surely. By this it is not only brought back to what it was created to be, but is also prepared for a dwelling in heaven.

Let no one think that this discussion is contradicted by what the blessed John, apostle and evangelist, set out in his epistle: "Whoever is born of God does not sin," as if this meant that those who have been reborn should be believed not to sin. If that great man had promised this in the sense that some who judge wrongly suppose, then everyone without exception who had been reborn would no longer be able to sin.

Moreover, anyone who claims that John laid this down is shown to hold a view contrary to that same apostle. For he says elsewhere: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us." And again: "If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar and his word is not in us." It was an apostle so great and so worthy who said this. If anyone strives to consider himself his superior in merit, let him look to it and beware lest he fall headlong over a deadly precipice. For surely the very man who said these things had been born of God, and yet he taught and preached: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves," and the rest that was quoted above.

But let that man full of God himself explain in what way one who is born of God cannot sin. "If we say," he says, "that we have not sinned, we make him a liar; but if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just and will forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness." He has shown how one who is born of God cannot sin. Each of the faithful, after being born of God, must not declare that he has no sin. But the sin he has incurred by committing it is taken away by the forgiveness granted to one who confesses, and so it cannot remain in him. As he went on to add: "I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, the righteous one, and he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but for those of the whole world." What has been briefly pointed out here the careful reader will be able to find throughout the whole body of Scripture in abundant testimonies. He will be able to prove more clearly that the remedy for our salvation has been so balanced that, with all insolence laid aside, "whoever glories" should glory not in himself but "in the Lord."

Besides this, we must also look more carefully at something we have seen troubling some people. When the apostle was speaking to believing and unbelieving spouses, he said that an unbelieving husband or wife is sanctified through partnership with a believer, whether the believer is a man or a woman.

First of all, what is said of the marriage covenant comes to mind quite fittingly: "The two shall be one flesh." From this it can be understood that the body of a believing spouse, whether husband or wife, is a temple of God, cleansed by rebirth and sanctified through the purification of the divine mystery. So in a certain way, through the unity of flesh in marriage, sanctification also reaches the body of the unbelieving spouse. Such a partnership is very different from a union in which both spouses are enslaved to idols and defiled by the indwelling of an unclean spirit. In the first kind of marriage, through the law and covenant of wedlock, the divine blessing comes to one partner, perhaps unknowing and even unwilling, through the faith of the other, whose flesh is united with theirs. In the second, both that chief fornication by which the soul is estranged from God and the contagion of the evil spirit leave each spouse as stained with detestable defilement as they are estranged from that faith in the supreme Godhead which purifies hearts.

Next, and not unreasonably, I think, there is this further point: through the prayer of the believing spouse some measure of mercy is granted even to the unbeliever, at the very least the mercy that concerns well-being in this present life. In this mercy the unbeliever gains no small share of God's kindness, and so is said in a certain way to have become a sharer in the divine favor. The apostle testifies that foods described as unclean in the sacred law are sanctified by the word of God (hence the saying, "What God has cleansed, you must not call common"). If that is so, it will be neither absurd nor unfitting that the unbelieving spouse should gain something of sanctification through the prayer of the believing spouse, which is certainly offered for them out of married love, and through the divine mercy which that prayer implores. As has been said, this differs greatly from a marriage in which both spouses are strangers to the purity of the true Godhead and cut off from its visitation, and in which both call on unclean spirits and are filled with the same uncleanness.

For when lighter sins are compared with graver ones, the one involved in lesser guilt is said to be justified by the one entangled in greater vices. So it was said to Jerusalem, which was then seething with monstrous crimes and transgressions: "You have justified your sister Sodom." How much more fittingly, then, can we speak of justification or sanctification, even if not full and complete but in a certain way, where the believing spouse not only sins less but also begs the supreme Godhead for a remedy for the sinning spouse, than where both spouses sin?

These very words of the apostle testify that this sanctification reaches the unbelieving spouse through the believing one only in a certain way. He does not affirm that the unbelieving spouse has received full and rightful sanctification simply because they gain something of sanctification through the believing spouse. Indeed, he went on to add how such a person is to be regarded: "But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart." He thereby indicates that such a person is not to be received as a believer just because something of divine sanctification and grace reaches them in the ways described, whether through partnership with the believing spouse or through that spouse's prayer. Unless they themselves also become believers, they must without doubt be judged unbelievers.

There is also another way in which the believing spouse imparts sanctification to the unbelieving one. The believer may urge the other to turn to God and to believe in the supreme Godhead, impress on them his majesty and power, and through married affection more easily shape and incline them toward faith. The believer may also show them what hope there is for those who believe in the one God, both in the course of this life and in the rest to come after it has passed. When the believing spouse, with the confidence that marriage gives, often instills these things, knocking at the other's heart with holy words and a persistent voice, they pass on to them, in mind and body alike, the working of divine sanctification. As the blessed apostle Peter says: "Likewise, let wives be subject to their husbands, so that if any do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives, when they see your chaste conduct in the fear of God."

If the unbelieving spouse accepts this through the intimacy of marriage, and does not receive in vain and reject the grace of God ministered to him through conjugal affection, then the unbelieving spouse is sanctified through the believing spouse, since by these means he is drawn out of unbelief into a share in sanctification. But suppose he does not accept the grace offered to him even through conjugal affection. Receiving it in vain, and forgetting both God's gracious condescension and a singular human affection, he decides it must be refused, and for that reason he strives to renounce even his spouse's affection and to depart from the law of that devout partnership. Then he is rightly granted leave to depart, because he is not worthy of a marriage of which he has judged himself unworthy. Let the believing spouse patiently bear the loss of that marriage, which commits fornication away from God. By cleaving to God, the believing spouse keeps the chief chastity, that owed to God, and is thus rid both of an adulterer and of one who refuses truly to become one flesh with a spouse who now believes. Let the believer not consider lawful a union with one who scorned to be joined to him by divine law, but rather willingly accept that one who is separated from God in soul has also been divided from him in body.

It is in this same way, then, that we must also understand what is said about the children of such people. This is stated as a consequence in the passage where the apostle says that if this sanctification did not take place between spouses of this kind, their children would be unclean, but as it is they are holy. They are holy in a certain sense, by comparison with those born of two parents who are both enslaved to and defiled by diabolical uncleanness. For insofar as these children have sprung from the holy flesh of a believing parent, who is a temple of God and carries the one God in his heart, they have drawn something of the divine blessing. And holiness is certainly contained in that blessing, so that those touched by its favour are not undeservedly called holy.

Through this blessing they take up the grace of sanctification, and in order that they may duly attain it, they already receive its first rudiments through the believing parent and come to know the fragrance of holy knowledge. Sanctification is certainly already granted through the prayers of a Christian parent, in which God's mercy is undoubtedly implored for them. Often, too, through the zeal of the believing parent, the little ones are either brought to venerable places, or are reborn in the font of baptism even without knowing it and receive full sanctification; or else, once they have become capable of reason, it is instilled in them by the exhortation and instruction of the devout parent.

All these are clearly instruments of sanctification. Through them the children either come to a firm hold on it, or, if they despise them, strip themselves of sanctification and plainly make void the grace of God brought to them through the parent's affection. Cut off in this way from holy things, that is, from the teachings of holiness, they are reduced to the profane company of the unholy. Of them, too, let it be said just as was enjoined about their unbelieving parents: "If the unbeliever wishes to depart, let him depart."

Are these kinds of holiness or sanctification ever ascribed to children born of two profane parents? See the difference between the offspring of the one marriage and of the other. See how these children are intimate with and close to those who are sanctified, and are therefore not undeservedly declared holy. Divine mercy is accordingly implored for them by the believing parent's prayers; they are steeped in a holy upbringing and initiated into the love of sacred religion. If they come to stand firm in it, they attain through the sacrament the fullness of that sanctification whose rudiments they received through the believing parent even before the sacrament. Because of these rudiments, those who were being prepared by holy instruction have not unfittingly been called holy already.

When it was said that the unbelieving spouse is sanctified through the believing one, was it meant that he no longer needs the sanctification of his own faith? Was it not meant rather that, through that intimacy with the believing spouse, he has been brought near and close to receiving sanctification? For if he were said to be already sanctified, in the sense that he had no need of sanctification at all, the apostle would not go on to say of him: "If the unbeliever wishes to depart, let him depart."

So too their children have been called holy because, through the affection of a holy parent, they are close to receiving holiness. It is not that they no longer need sanctification of their own, for, as no Christian doubts, that sanctification is neither received nor possessed without the mystery of sacred regeneration. In the same way their unbelieving parent is said to be sanctified through the believing one, yet if he has not accepted as he should the effect of the sanctification brought to him through the believing spouse, he is called an unbeliever.

The apostle first says that this person has been sanctified through the believing spouse, and afterwards calls him an unbeliever, because he or she did not personally believe. The same is true of the children. They have been called holy because they were sanctified through the believing parent in the same way as the spouse was; but unless they too believe personally, they are consequently unbelievers. It is quite clear that this sanctification of the spouse, who is afterwards declared an unbeliever, was so called only in a certain sense, and the same must therefore be understood of the children.

The question must often be repeated: are the offspring of the profane touched by any portion of holiness of this kind from either parent? Do they receive any share in holiness, or knowledge of it, or hearing about it, or instruction in it, through disciplines, prayers or exhortations of this kind from anyone? Living under the dominion of unclean spirits and enslaved to diabolical transgressions and contagions, they are always unclean in the same way as their parents, for as long as they remain in the same perversity.

Often, too, something that is still in the future is said to be already, by way of anticipation, as is found very frequently in the text of holy Scripture. So we read in the Gospel that "Jesus was to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but to gather into one the children of God who were scattered." Here he certainly calls them children of God already, though they were still scattered throughout the world under grace's call, yet to be renewed by the sacred mysteries and adopted as children of God. Or again, when it is said, "Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed," those are already called blessed who were going to be blessed in the future, when they came to believe what they had not seen. In the same way, things still to be done are often reported as already done, as in: "They have pierced my hands and my feet."

Likewise, something is sometimes stated as going to be done which, through some intervening cause, is not done. Thus the blessed apostle, out of devotion to the preaching entrusted to him, declares that he will go to Spain, yet by a sure dispensation of God this did not come to pass. Another way is when something is called by a name that it has ceased to deserve, or is going to cease to deserve. So it was with the apostle Judas, who by his transgression lost what he was called. He was likewise called a disciple, though he was not a disciple of Christ but rather of the devil, as was said of him: "One of you is a devil," because he was the devil's agent. Yet he was called a disciple, even though he was not a true one and was going to cease being called one.

There is also the way in which something is often said generally and without qualification, though it plainly does not apply to all without exception. So it is said to Abraham: "In your seed all nations shall be blessed." All nations will indeed be blessed, and there will be no nation under heaven to which the gospel is not preached, "and then the end will come"; but the nations themselves will not all be blessed in their entirety, because not all have faith. Or again: "Let every tongue confess to God." Connected with this usage is the frequent practice of naming the whole after a part, just as at that time the phrase "man of Judah" was used when it undoubtedly meant the whole nation.

In the same way those children can be seen to have been called holy because many of them, or most, will be made holy through the means described above, once they have been steeped in the heavenly mysteries; so they are rightly said to be already what they will be. Or they have been called holy because of the portion of holiness they shared through their devout parent, as though they were already wholly so. Or again, because many such children were going to be heirs of full sanctification, these too were named from what they were going to be; and even if most of them perhaps would not become so, the whole group has been called holy in general terms from the part of them that is holy.

Concerning the nature of the resurrection, and the form that will be ours after the resurrection, let us hear the apostle's preaching, where he says: "But someone will ask: How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come?" Rebuking the distrust of the human mind, he rightly calls it foolish for judging anything impossible for God. Then the illustrious teacher fittingly brings in a magnificent likeness and comparison drawn from visible things and the familiar dealings of human life, saying: "Fool!" (you who think these things impossible for God, or doubt that they will be done) "what you sow does not come to life unless it first dies."

He fittingly applied this likeness to the resurrection of the body that is to take place after death. Then he went on to add: "And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain, of wheat perhaps or of something else; but God gives it a body as he has willed." With this he took care to apply a kind of comparison to the nature and form that will be ours after the resurrection. "As he has willed," he says. What more do you ask? As God wills, so he will give each one a body raised up by his ineffable power.

But perhaps you will think that this rather means that each person's own body will not be re-formed for him, since it is asserted that the body will be restored as God wills. If you are trying to learn what kind of body God will give back to each person "as he wills," then pay careful attention to the full meaning of the one who deals with these things, and weigh the words of the apostle as though he were already answering you on these very points. You wish to know what kind of body God will give, as he wills, to those raised from the dead? Recognize it wisely: "and to each of the seeds its own body." Surely the man full of God added this for no other reason than to drive away future doubts of this kind among men. Listen, I say, to what he wisely added, and from the likeness recognize the very thing to which it is compared.

"And to each of the seeds," he says, "its own body." If in the likeness each has its own body, then it is certain that in the reality of which it is the likeness, each will be given back its own body. For beyond dispute he compared these seeds to human beings, since it was their death and resurrection he was speaking of. So, matching each point to its counterpart, he explained wonderfully, through the remarkable comparison of the grain that does not come to life unless it first dies, all that concerns the bringing of bodies to life after death.

Next, with what kind of body each person should be thought to come after the resurrection, that is, whether in the condition he bore when he died or in one far better, he likewise revealed by that likeness, which he went on to set out: "And what you sow, you sow a bare grain, of wheat perhaps or of something else, and God gives it a body as he wills." In this form, then, he plainly expressed that God gives a body more beautiful than the one that died, as is said in what follows: "It is sown in corruption, it rises in incorruption; it is sown in dishonour, it rises in glory; it is sown in weakness, it rises in power; it is sown a natural body, it rises a spiritual body."

See how what is sown when a man dies is not the body that is to be. See how we are to understand that God re-forms after death, as he wills, the body of those who are to rise. By the immeasurable will of his mercy, what had been sown in corruption he restores in incorruptible nobility. What had been laid to sleep in dishonour, in its earthly condition, he raises in heavenly glory. What had been dissolved in the weakness of mortality he makes whole again, clothed in the beauty of immortality. Finally, what had died a natural body he restores and re-forms as a spiritual body.

All these things concern the state of improvement and exaltation. But the remaining part of the comparison he attached is firmly established as referring specifically to each person's being given back the distinctive character of his own body. That is the part where he goes on to say, "and to each of the seeds its own body." Here it is quite clear that, whatever the glory of those who rise, the distinctive character of the body will remain.

Nor is it idle that the blessed apostle did this. He was speaking only of the human race, since that alone is to be raised, and no other substance is to be adorned with this gift. It would therefore have been enough to apply one kind of seed by way of comparison to the one race of human beings, and by it he could have taught both that what is sown does not come to life unless it first dies, and that the body rises more honourable than it was sown. But he wished to assert that the distinctive body of each sex is to be renewed, and one kind of seed could not supply a likeness for this. So, lest he be thought by this to mean that there would be only one kind of risen body, with all distinctions removed, he carefully and fittingly decided to apply different kinds of seeds in his comparison,

so that, as has been said, the variety of seeds might indicate the distinctive character of bodies, which one kind could not distinguish. In this way the comparison would be fully equipped to say, most fittingly, in order to mark out the particular character of bodies, "and to each of the seeds its own body." Since a single kind of grain has no distinct sex, it could not convey this; so, as has often been said already, the variety of seeds would supply the understanding needed to express the distinctive character of bodies.

This comparison, then, contains three things: a proposition, an argument and a definition. As regards understanding the bodily resurrection, a fitting and sufficient likeness has been drawn from the grain that does not come to life unless it first dies. As regards the statement that what is sown is not the body that is to be, but God gives it a body as he wills, the reason is necessarily disclosed within the same passage: why the corruptible body that is sown is declared to return incorruptible, along with the other points shown to belong to this sense. And as regards teaching the distinctive character of bodies, it is made perfectly clear. The blessed apostle was by no means content with the comparison of a single seed, by which he could not show the distinctive character of bodies, since, as mentioned above, a single kind of seed does not have this. So he took care to show, from the variety of seeds, that to each of those who rise, who are certainly compared to the seeds,

his own body will be given back. Human beings, then, will rise, brought to life after death, for they have been compared to seeds that first die and are afterwards brought to life. And what dies, that is, what is as it were sown, is not what rises; rather God gives them a body as he wills, so that the corruptible becomes incorruptible, the mortal immortal, the natural spiritual, and what had been disfigured by the condition of death is restored, made beautiful with immortal wholeness. And without doubt they will each receive their own body, just as each of the seeds does. Because the different sexes could not be compared to a single seed, the comparison was made from the variety of seeds, so that the distinctive character of bodies might be signified by that variety. Now if each person raised from the dead will receive his own body, it follows beyond doubt that each sex will have its own body re-formed. For, as has been said, each of the seeds is also given back its own body. And if each of the seeds is given back its own body, and these seeds certainly signify the whole human race in both sexes, it follows that the whole human race, signified by these seeds in both sexes, will have its own body.

This much it is right for us to measure out from the apostle's words with sober consideration; to burst beyond it with reckless curiosity is the mark of transgressors. That is why we are also warned: "Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not search into what is beyond your strength," and: "Do not set your mind on lofty things, but associate with the humble." Finally, let us attend to what has been confirmed by the apostle's preaching as well: "What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, God has prepared for those who fear him." Whoever is not content with the understanding or the comparison of the apostle's meaning set out above is certainly forced, whether he likes it or not, to this conclusion: he dares to construct for himself, by some meditation of his own, the things that eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man.

As if some members of the human body had been created blameworthy, unseemly or open to reproach, when God made all things very good, and set each kind within its own class with fitting beauty! The only thing is that the excess of primordial concupiscence had disfigured those parts which have been called our unseemly parts. They had certainly been so ordained that they would serve at the bidding of the human mind and perform their functions only by the choice of the rational soul, for the purpose of begetting offspring. Apart from this purpose they would do nothing against the mind's command, neither insolently forestalling the will nor offering any rebellion when the will desired their use. But once the soul did not remain subject to what was above it, its pride was punished within itself by a like law of rebellious nature. So the services subject to the soul's dominion in turn resisted it, and the disobedient appetite of the human mind displayed what it had incurred by presuming on what was forbidden in that part of the body through which the vicious generation of a degenerate, disfigured and proud root was undoubtedly to be propagated.

Had these parts not been defiled by this deviation, they could have remained here, even in an undoubtedly earthly body, as seemly as they were restrained, serving only for the propagation of the human race. How much more must we believe that they can exist with inexpressibly greater seemliness in a spiritual body, especially since in that everlasting glory they will no longer perform any function of generation! They will lack nothing of their form and shape only so that what is raised may not be judged to be any form other than the human one to which resurrection is promised. Nothing is to be absent that would not remain in the perfect resurrection of the flesh, nor is any form to seem raised other than the one which the lineaments of whole human flesh delineate. Whoever is perhaps unwilling to weigh these things with moderate reason will, whether he likes it or not, as has been said, either return to the point made above, and not think that what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man is to be searched out; or, if he tries to break out further, let him look to the precipice of his own rashness.

How seemly the members of human substance were created is also shown to us by this fact: when our first parents were naked in paradise, they had no shame in them. It was only after sin, when the poison of concupiscence entered, that they were put to shame by the disordered disturbance of their bodies. So it is quite clear that if these parts could be seen without shame by those placed in that felicity of paradise, though still in an earthly body, much more can they be so in a spiritual body and in that sublime blessedness which will bear the likeness of the angels. Thus, so that man may lack nothing in the resurrection of the flesh, he will be re-formed whole; and lest the Creator seem to have created something unseemly, if anything were taken away from the risen body, his work will rather be proved good by this too, in that what he created remains even in the beauty of that glory.

Unless perhaps these people think that bodily impulses will still arise there, where, as the Lord himself says, "they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels." Certainly, if all were to be raised in one form of body and one sex, there would have been no reason at all to say this. Rather, since being given in marriage belongs more to the female sex, the saying indicates that this sex will not be absent there, but will wholly cease from marriage. Moreover, since it is also written, "that each may receive what is due for the things done in the body, whether good or evil," how will this come about unless each sex, in the distinctive character of its own body, either undergoes judgement or receives the reward of the blessed resurrection?

Those are mistaken, however, who think that the apostle's testimony supports them, by which they appear to claim that all human beings will be raised in male form, where he says, "until we all meet in one perfect man." What then will they do when the same apostle says in turn, "I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ"? This will undoubtedly contradict their opinion, unless, after examining the mystery as they should, they recognize with a modest mind how both statements agree.

So what is meant by the church being described in terms of both sexes, we will now explain, as far as we understand it with the Lord's help. Holy Scripture testifies that from the beginning Christ and the church were signified in human flesh by the likeness of marriage. So when the church is counted with the female sex, this shows the weakness of the human condition, which is fittingly expressed in the church as the bride of Christ. But by the name of virginity or continence, her holy resolve, or the integrity of her faith, is indicated, and the blessed apostle himself also speaks of this. But when it is said:

"until we all come to the perfect man," this is neither different nor divided. For whatever is contained in the body of the church, which is one flesh with Christ, is by the law of sacred marriage also his own flesh [?] in every way to come about in both sexes, as was said: whether "a chaste virgin" in the one place or "a perfect man" in the other. So they are both: they live in the inviolate faith of the catholic church and are continent by holy resolve. Although they are still placed in the weakness of the human condition, through the one flesh of the church and Christ, that is, of wife and husband, they also receive in him a man's firmness and perfect vigour. Through the virginal chastity of faith of the church, which is one flesh with him, they also become perfect members of that man.

Here we must also consider those words of the blessed apostle Paul in which he says: "We have all been baptized into one body in Christ." As regards the unity of the sacrament, we are certainly one body in Christ. As regards the difference of the sexes, he says elsewhere: "Whether man or woman, we are all one in Christ." For Christ is perfect together with his whole body, which is his fullness. And so, because through one and the same mystery we are received as his one body, though of different sexes, Christ is made perfect through the fullness of that body. Since, then, Christ as husband is the head, the strength and the perfection of the church as his wife, the whole church is rightly said to come to this one perfect man, whose one flesh it is.
(98.) LETTER OF POPE GELASIUS TO BISHOP HONORIUS.

To his most beloved brother Honorius, Gelasius. Caught up in constant business amid the many difficulties of the times, we can scarcely draw breath. Yet because we govern the apostolic see, we attend without ceasing to the care of the Lord's whole sheepfold, which was entrusted to blessed Peter by the voice of our Saviour himself: "And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers," and again: "Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep!" We therefore neither can nor should keep silent about the matter that weighs on our concern. We feel and say with the blessed apostle Paul: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?"

For a grim, horrifying and scarcely credible report has suddenly so overwhelmed us that it has confounded, wounded and stricken our mind. We have been told that in the regions of Dalmatia certain people have sown again the tares of the Pelagian plague, and that their blasphemy has gained such a hold there that they are deceiving all the simple by insinuating their deadly madness.

This wicked error is indeed all the more dangerous in stealing upon people because it is so cunning in deceiving them with an appearance of truth. Yet by the Lord's gift the pure truth of the catholic faith is at hand, drawn from the harmonious teaching of all the fathers. It exposes the subtle venom of this deadly depravity and brings to the human race, for its salvation, a medicine compounded from the Scriptures. Let it in no way, then, trouble hearts not yet rich in discernment, until both the hidden wound is brought to light and the one salvation shines forth. For however much the spirit of perdition arms itself with the art of deceit, it is both exposed and slain by the holy sword of the sovereign Spirit.

Therefore, through you, beloved, we admonish with brotherly affection all the priests of the Lord there. As you fight, with the Lord instructing you, against new errors, you ought not even to lend your ears to a perversity long since condemned throughout the whole world. For if it is rashly thought that this may be done, what heresy rightly extinguished by our forebears would not dare to challenge us again, and with renewed strength fight us openly and in public?

Is it lawful for us to undo what the venerable fathers condemned, and to reopen wicked doctrines that they cut away? What, then, is the point of our taking such great care that no heresy, once cast down, should strive to come up for examination anew, if we set about restoring what our forebears long ago recognized, examined and refuted? Would we not ourselves (God forbid, and the catholic Church will never allow it) be setting before all the enemies of the truth an example of how to rise up again against us?

Where is what is written: "You shall not move the boundaries of your fathers," and: "Ask your fathers and they will declare it to you, your elders and they will tell you"? Why, then, do we strain beyond what our forebears defined? If in our ignorance we wish to learn something, why is it not enough for us to learn how the orthodox fathers and elders laid down each and every point, either to be shunned or to be fitted to catholic truth? Why are these things not acknowledged as settled decrees? Are we wiser than they? Or shall we be able to stand firm and steady if we undermine what they established?

Or perhaps you do not know that this heresy of which we speak was long ago laid low by the apostolic see, in continuous and unceasing sentences, through Innocent of blessed memory and then Zosimus, Boniface, Celestine, Sixtus and Leo? Or that it was condemned not only by the laws of the catholic Church but also by those of the Roman emperors, so effectively that its followers were not permitted a place to live anywhere on earth? All this is shown both by the church records drawn up concerning their depravity in every region, and by the sanctions of public law.

Look at those whose ears delight to hear catholic doctrine, yet who take up these questions, handle these snares and patiently admit these blasphemies. Oh, if only they would take pains to learn the books and replies that our forebears wrote against these people! There they would see in every way that there is absolutely nothing these men have aired that the fathers have not crushed with magnificent truth. Thus all the faithful would be so well equipped to refute all their wickedness that nothing more would need to be sought.

But perhaps certain propositions drawn from their opinions have unsettled untaught minds. Even so, the teachings of the venerable fathers so thoroughly lay bare all their madness, and so clearly show the remedies by which it may be cured, that, from what has thus been provided beforehand by God's gift, everything they have woven together in their chain of arguments appears dangerous to those who follow it and foolish to those who see through it. So if anyone thinks he should resist, he shows himself not so much an opponent of the judgements of the ancients as an open and avowed enemy of human salvation and of catholic doctrine. All the more attentively, therefore, the watchful [?]

care of the shepherds ought to keep the savagery of wolves away from the sacred flocks. For whatever harm befalls the holy sheep condemns (God forbid) the negligence of the bishops, just as driving the harmful beasts away from the reborn flocks will secure an everlasting increase in the guardians' rewards. Certainly, if, as we would much prefer, these reports are false rumours, we wish to know it as soon as possible, so that we who tremble at the harassment of Christ's members may rejoice all the more at their steadfastness. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Faustus, vir clarissimus.

In the matter of the Christian faith, which has clearly never lacked enemies from its beginning, Nestorius and Eutyches have arisen in our own age, though at some interval of time from each other. They brought forth no new doctrines of perversity, only new names for them.

For about fifty-eight years ago Nestorius, following the error of Photinus and Paul of Samosata, was deservedly banished into exile in the Oasis. He had said, as he learned from his teachers, that Christ our Lord was born of the Virgin Mary as a mere man.

Many years later Eutyches, thinking he ought to argue against him, did not know how to keep to the right path. He fell into the madness of Apollinaris and burst out with words asserting that Christ was not a true man, and that two natures are not to be believed in him but only one, that of God the Word, though incarnate. He maintained that this incarnate nature was not that of a man but only something human, so that what was urged was the likeness of a human body rather than its reality. The catholic faith, by contrast, confesses that Christ the Son of God is true God and true man, not of one nature but of one subsistence and person.

Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, found this Eutyches, a priest and abbot in the city of Constantinople, urging such ideas. Eusebius had shown his zeal for the faith even while he was an agens in rebus, for at that time he had also rebuked Nestorius when he was preaching sacrilegious things in church. Out of this zeal he reported Eutyches to Bishop Flavian and summoned him to trial. The case was heard.

When this priest Eutyches saw his side being hard pressed, he sought the protection of the emperor Theodosius through Chrysaphius the spatharius. By the emperor's command the illustrious Florentius, a former consul, was required to be present at the examination of Eutyches, and in his very presence Eutyches was convicted and condemned.

The emperor took offence and ordered a synod to be assembled at the city of Ephesus. About three hundred and sixty bishops attended, led by Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, Juvenal of Jerusalem, Thalassius of Caesarea, Eustathius of Berytus, Eusebius of Ancyra and Basil of Isauria. Also present were the legates sent by the apostolic see, Julius, bishop of Puteoli, and Hilarus, archdeacon of the City, since the priest Renatus had been overtaken by death on the island of Delos. Dulcitius, notary of the church, was also present.

At this assembly the doctrinal letters of Pope Leo addressed to the synod and to Flavian were rejected and were not allowed to be read at all. The whole day, the sixth before the Ides of August, was spent reading nothing but the acts concerning Nestorius, long since condemned, that is, the acts of the earlier synod of Ephesus. At the same time, once all the documents had been read, the judgement of Flavian of holy memory concerning Eutyches was examined. Meanwhile, when Eutyches' blasphemies were read out, everyone acclaimed this as the true faith, this as the orthodox one. Over the objections of the Roman legates, Flavian was deposed and Eutyches received back. Bishop Eusebius, who had accused that same priest, was also condemned as a Nestorian, though earlier, while still a layman, he had been the accuser of Nestorius.

For these Eutychianists hold that there is no middle ground between themselves and Nestorius, so that anyone who is not a Eutychianist in their eyes is counted an outright Nestorian. Yet catholic doctrine unites the two natures in Christ and does not divide them as Nestorius did. And these men are found to babble even worse things. With the utmost confidence they assert something absurd, something even fools would abhor: that before the union, that is, the incarnation, one should speak of two natures, but after it of one, that of God the Word, though incarnate. It is as if we were to speak of something waxed, or pitched, or tinned, or coloured with some other kind of coating.

On the third day after the session of the synod at which Flavian of holy memory was deposed, Domnus of Antioch was deposed as well. Dioscorus departed suddenly, and the assembly was dissolved. Flavian was led into exile and died at Hypaepa, a city of Lydia, whether death came upon him naturally or was inflicted on him.

At that time a certain Anatolius, a priest of Alexandria, was staying at Constantinople, for it is the custom of that church to send clergy to the court in turn, in case some business or need should arise. So this Anatolius, a man of Dioscorus' party, was made bishop of Constantinople.

After a year had passed, the emperor Theodosius died, Chrysaphius was punished, and Marcian became emperor. Deeply grieved by the injury done to the faith, he summoned a synod at Nicaea, at which he himself and Pulcheria sat, together with the senate and all the secular powers. He later transferred this synod to Chalcedon because it was near the palace.

More than five hundred bishops of the whole East and of Egypt assembled. Dioscorus was brought forward so that he might give the council an account of what he had done. The emperor himself also attended the assembly, as did all the judges, the senate and all the officials of the court. Eusebius, the bishop of Dorylaeum mentioned earlier, had escaped from exile about a year before and come to Rome, and now he hurried to attend the synod of Chalcedon. He too accused Dioscorus, as did other Alexandrians. In short, Dioscorus was condemned. The body of Flavian of holy memory was brought back to Constantinople with the greatest honour, and at Alexandria Proterius, a catholic, was made bishop.

A certain priest Timothy, surnamed Aelurus, and the deacon Peter, who has now seized the episcopate of the church of Alexandria, were followers of Dioscorus and had separated themselves from the church of Alexandria. When their bishop Proterius could not recall them to their proper ministry, he condemned them both.

When the emperor Marcian died, Timothy and Peter gathered crowds of heretics and came to Alexandria, and Timothy was ordained bishop by heretics. So there came to be two bishops at Alexandria. Three days before Easter, on the day when the Lord's Supper is celebrated, they hired desperate men and seized the church in which Proterius of holy memory had taken refuge in fear. There, on that same day, he was killed in the baptistery, torn to pieces and thrown out; his corpse was burned and his ashes scattered to the winds.

Leo took up the imperial power, and the catholics' complaint about so great a crime reached him. The heretics petitioned against the catholics, asking that the synod of Chalcedon be abolished, while the catholics demanded that the crime be punished.

The emperor considered it too great a hardship to trouble the bishops with so long a journey, since age, illness or even poverty kept most of them from undertaking such a labour. So he sent magistriani throughout the whole East, and Bishop Anatolius also sent his deacon Asclepiades. Through them all the bishops who had assembled at Chalcedon learned what had happened at Alexandria. When consulted, they wrote back that the synod of Chalcedon must be defended even to the shedding of blood, because it had established no other faith than the synod of Nicaea had; and that Timothy was not only not to be regarded as a bishop but was even stripped of the name of Christian. After this another Timothy, a catholic, became bishop of Alexandria. The first Timothy was driven out only with difficulty. Peter fled, and Timothy was sent into exile at Cherson, a remote place on the Black Sea.

As long as the emperor Leo lived, Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, lived in peace. But when Basiliscus seized the empire, he began to condemn the synod of Chalcedon and drive out the catholics. Then at last the condemned Timothy, having gained his freedom, came to Constantinople and restored the condemned heretics to their places. He went to Alexandria; the catholic Timothy fled and hid in a monastery. Peter once again joined himself to Timothy, with whom he had earlier been condemned.

The emperor Zeno returned to his throne, and Basiliscus was overthrown. Orders were sent to Alexandria that the usurper Timothy should be driven out and the catholic Timothy restored to the church. But the condemned Timothy was overtaken by death, and his partner Peter was ordained bishop for the Alexandrians by a single heretic. The most Christian emperor nevertheless ordered him deposed and the catholic Timothy brought back, as is stated in the letters of Acacius, bishop of Constantinople. When certain bishops, clerics, monks and laymen refused to come into communion with the catholic bishop Timothy, the most clement emperor intimidated them with various imperial rescripts.

Timothy wrote to Pope Simplicius, saying that Peter had long ago been condemned while still a deacon and was now also cut off from Christian fellowship. Through Bishop Isaiah he asked that the emperor be written to about sending Peter farther away into exile, since he was lurking in the city of Alexandria and plotting against the church.

For about three years or more Pope Simplicius of holy memory never ceased writing to Bishop Acacius, asking that what Bishop Timothy requested be done about Peter. The emperor too was written to, but no reply ever came.

After all this, Timothy sent John, his priest and steward, to the emperor, asking that, should anything befall him in the course of human life, his Piety would order a catholic to be ordained by catholics. A reply was given to this request, written both to Timothy himself and to the clergy. In those same rescripts the steward John was highly praised, so that almost everyone at Alexandria now regarded him as the candidate for the office of bishop.

When Bishop Timothy died, the steward John, of whom the most clement emperor had written that he laboured for the church and the faith, was ordained bishop, a catholic by catholics. In keeping with the custom of our forebears, he sent synodical letters to the apostolic see through the priest Isidore and the deacon Peter. But Uranius, a subadiuva, arrived bearing an imperial rescript against Bishop John, and the pope suspended his confirmation of John's episcopate. And because the same rescript mentioned restoring Peter, whom the pope himself had condemned, that part was refused outright. This, it seems, is what offended the most clement emperor.

The letters that Pope Simplicius of holy memory had sent to Acacius so many times for the peace of the church of Alexandria and the integrity of the catholic faith had achieved nothing. Then the same holy bishop John arrived as a fugitive and was received by the apostolic see, as was fitting; for his predecessors too had likewise sought refuge with the Roman church in times of persecution. His arrival brought everything more fully to light.

As we read to him the letters Acacius had sent concerning Peter and John, Acacius' excesses, very grave in this matter too, were uncovered. For at the time when he reported on the condemned Peter of Alexandria, he had also written as follows about

Peter and John of Antioch. Peter, he wrote, had governed a monastery at Constantinople but had abandoned it because of his crimes and fled to Antioch. There, after the catholic bishop Martyrius had been driven out by the basest rabble and by heretics, Peter seized his see; he was at once condemned by the bishops and deported to the Oasis by the emperor Leo. He slipped away from there, returned to Constantinople and gave his word that he would never again dare to stir up any disturbance. But, as was said above, in the time of Basiliscus he was sent back to Antioch by the condemned Timothy who had come to Constantinople, so that he might hold the episcopate there again. After this the same Peter ordained a certain priest John, the one we said Acacius reported on, as bishop of Apamea. When the people of Apamea would not receive him, John returned to Antioch, drove out Peter, the very man who had made him a bishop, and seized his church. Acacius says that both were condemned together again. He asked the apostolic see that, if they should perhaps take refuge with it, it should not judge them worthy even to be seen; and that if they had perhaps already obtained some pardon, it should be void and their penance should not be accepted.

When the aforesaid holy John, bishop of Alexandria, read this, he could not keep silent. Acacius had condemned that John together with Peter and had had him condemned by the apostolic see without the remedy of penance; yet after so many condemnations, Acacius had sent him to preside over the church of Tyre.

So holy Pope Felix learned not only that his predecessor's letters had achieved nothing, but also that Acacius was making a mockery of things to the overthrow of the faith and of all church discipline.
