He therefore chose Vitalis, bishop of Truentum in the region of Picenum, and Misenus, bishop of the church of Cumae in the region of Campania, and sent them with these instructions: that Peter be driven out of the church of Alexandria; that Acacius reply to the petition of holy John, bishop of Alexandria; and that Acacius himself be ordered to pronounce anathema on Peter of Alexandria.

These legates, however, were thrown into custody like enemies and lost their documents. Even so, they ought not to have yielded to faithless and condemned heretics the one thing that could still be withheld: their will. Not only did they fail to do what they had been ordered, or whatever they could have accomplished; they even entered into communion with the heretics. They brought back confirmation of the episcopate of Peter, whom they had been sent to drive out, and carried Acacius' reply full of insults against Bishop John.

Moved by this, the most blessed pope held a synod, suspended Vitalis and Misenus from office and communion, and then condemned Acacius. Afterwards Acacius, in his audacity, committed still worse deeds: he even sent that Peter of Antioch, ordained by him, to the church of Antioch after the catholic Calendion had been expelled.

After Bishop John arrived and the Roman church received him as was fitting, holy Pope Felix appointed a legation, as has been said. At the hands of depraved minds it met with every kind of hostility. It was thrown into custody and lost its documents, and it barely returned, in great disgrace, bringing back a confirmation of the episcopate of Peter, whom it had been sent to expel. The Roman church had anathematized this Peter as follows:

Pope Felix to the bishops established throughout Egypt, the Thebaid, Libya and the Pentapolis, after other matters: "As for Peter, who separated himself from the unity of the church under Proterius of blessed memory and, to bring about his death, joined the parricide Timothy in persecuting the orthodox, we allow him to enjoy no share in so great a name or honour, since in those who made him, who are no different from him, what he thinks himself to be is found to be worthless from its very beginning [?]. The aforesaid man is therefore anathema to all. Let no one ever believe that he will be received by the catholic church, since he has persisted in his perversity despite repeated correction and over the course of so many years, and has thus lost the opportunity to make satisfaction."
(100.) BY THE SAME POPE GELASIUS, AGAINST ANDROMACHUS AND THE OTHER ROMANS WHO MAINTAIN THAT THE LUPERCALIA SHOULD BE CELEBRATED ACCORDING TO THE ANCIENT CUSTOM.

There are certain people who sit in their own houses, not knowing what they are saying or what they are asserting. They strive to judge others when they do not judge themselves. They want to accuse before they know, and to teach before they learn. With matters undiscussed, causes uninvestigated and no inquiry made into the facts, they thoughtlessly pour out and headlong vomit forth whatever comes into their mouths. They pass judgement not by stating the truth but out of a passion for evil-speaking, condemning what they do not understand. They have gone so far that they strive with malicious intent to tear apart even things rightly done. If they were wise, they would not rush to judgement at all, but would first examine matters thoroughly and only then bring out what ought to be said.

But since they charge us with being sluggish censors in restraining the vices of the church, let them in turn learn from us that bodily adultery is not the only sin which ought to be examined and justly punished. There is a far greater kind of fornication and adultery, which ought rightly to be punished in any Christian whatever, since every Christian is a member of the church. For the crime of sacrilege is as much greater as the fornication of the soul is worse than that of the body. Through the fornication of the soul one departs from union with God himself and passes over to unclean spirits by a kind of spiritual adultery.

And how does a man not fall into this category if he wishes to be seen as a Christian, professes it and says so, and yet does not shrink, does not recoil, does not fear to proclaim openly and publicly that diseases arise because demons are not worshipped and sacrifice is not offered to the god Februarius? To that god! [?] Where did he discover these ravings? How is he not a transgressor who runs into these profane blasphemies? How should he not be thought sacrilegious who abjures the providence and power of the one God, which he had confessed, and is led astray to monstrous superstitions and empty fictions?

According to the apostle, it is far worse, and rightly to be condemned, to abandon the truth one has confessed than never to have believed in it at all. For although the fictions he puts forward are ridiculous, the very disposition and will are criminal, and the profession and the preaching are rightly to be condemned. Therefore whoever wants sentence of condemnation to be pronounced against another without delay should recognize that in judging another he condemns himself.

For must the bishop punish those who commit bodily adultery, and not punish those who commit sacrilege, that is, spiritual fornication and adultery? When an adulteress was brought to the Lord himself, did he not say to her accusers: "Let whoever among you is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her"? He did not say, "whoever among you is not an adulterer in the same way," but "whoever is without sin." Therefore let no one who is bound by any sin at all dare to throw a stone at someone guilty of another sin. And when they went away because of their consciences, the Saviour of the world added: "Woman, where are your accusers? No one has condemned you, nor will I condemn you. But go, and from now on sin no more." You hold, and you are held; you press, and you are pressed; you bind, and you are bound. You demand an inquiry from the bishop and call for punishment: remember that the same must be brought forward against every crime.

Do not even human laws say that one defendant cannot accuse another? Do you see the speck in your brother's eye and not see the beam in your own? You who accuse adulterers, do you commit adultery yourself, and do you, a spiritual adulterer, attack bodily adulterers? You certainly demand an inquiry, you careful, mature and religious man. You do not want anyone in the church to sin; you want the sinner to be examined and then handed over to punishment. But whatever you bring forward against another, you will be compelled to bring forward against yourself too. You do this, you say, so that the bishop may not be accused of sloth and the church may not be stained. Then the bishop must not fail to show vigilance and severity towards all evil deeds, and the church's reputation must be cleansed of all of them. But perhaps you will say that you are

a layman while he is a minister of the church, and that this makes his crime the more serious. You speak truly, and I do not deny it. He must be examined all the more carefully the closer he is, and he is all the more guilty because he was placed in that ministry and ought by no means to have done these things. See, censure is not lacking: he is being heard, and if he is convicted, he will be handed over to punishment. Now then, what do you want done about yourself? Because you are not in the sacred ministry, are you therefore not among the holy people? Do you not know that you too are a member of the High Priest? Are you unaware that the whole church is called a priesthood?

Finally, if he is guilty who has entered the ministry of the church and then transgresses, are you not guilty too? After confessing the truth you are led back to the depraved, perverse, profane and devilish fictions which you professed to renounce.

Therefore you too, after blasphemies poured out openly and publicly, must by every means be kept away from the sacred Body. For you cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons, nor drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot be the temple of God and the temple of the devil; light and darkness cannot meet together in you. Whether you are urging and pressing for wrongdoing to be punished in another is something I shall look into. Nevertheless, you cannot evade the weight of your own crime. The less you will allow a crime in another to pass unpunished, the more clearly you show what we ought, in all reason, to do in your case too.

Yet in these very blasphemies of yours, for which you are rightly punishable, plainly recognize your ignorance. As the saying goes, you have the will to lie but not the skill to invent. You can see that you have an evil disposition and a perverse intention to apostatize, yet no material at all for that empty notion of yours is at hand, nor can you establish

what you conceive in your heart and bring forth with your mouth. Tell me this. In the Roman histories, in the orator Livy, one reads again and again that pestilence broke out in this city very frequently and countless thousands of people perished. Things often came to such a point that in those warlike times there was scarcely anyone left from whom an army could be enrolled. Was no sacrifice being offered to your god Februarius at that time? Or did this worship do no good at all? Were the Lupercalia not being celebrated then? You will not say that these rites had not yet begun at that time, since they are said to have been brought into Italy by Evander before Romulus.

As to why the Lupercalia were instituted, so far as the inventions of that superstition itself are concerned, Livy speaks of it in his second decade. He records that they were instituted not to check diseases but, as he thinks, to drive away a barrenness among women that had occurred at that time. Accordingly, if this rite had any power even for that very purpose, its discontinuation would not have brought disease, since the Lupercalia were not devised against disease. Rather, women ought to have stopped bearing children altogether, since these inventions are chanted for their fertility.

What will you say about plague [?], about barrenness, about the continual storm of wars? Did these things also happen because the Lupercalia were abolished? But if the Lupercalia were not established either to prevent or to cure these things, why are you tossed about in idle turmoil? What did any offence to the Lupercalia do to Tuscany, to Aemilia and the other provinces, where scarcely anyone remains, so that they were consumed by the necessities of war? Those provinces were laid waste long before the Lupercalia were abolished. When the emperor Anthemius came to Rome, the Lupercalia were certainly being held, and yet so great a pestilence crept in that it could scarcely be endured. Were the Lupercalia held throughout Campania, so that their abolition should produce diseases and pestilence there?

But you will say that everything relates to Rome as to its head, and that what was not done here has harmed the various provinces that belong to it. Why then did these provinces flourish with their own wealth, without the Lupercalia, before they belonged to Rome? Was it the abolition of the Lupercalia that caused the land's continued barrenness, or what our sins deserved? Of these sins it was said long ago: "And whatever Roman morals deserved to lose." Certainly it ought to have been barrenness of women that came, since the Lupercalia are boasted of as having been instituted to remove that, not barrenness of the land, which the Lupercalia were never instituted to remove. What about Africa? Where does its barrenness come from?

What about the Gauls? Did these Lupercalia do it, or our own morals? Thefts, murders, adulteries, injustices, iniquities, ambitions, greed, perjuries, false testimonies, oppression of the poor, attacks on good causes and defence of bad ones, and unheard-of perversity in everything; and finally, what is worst of all, minds false to God, sacrileges and magic arts that horrify even pagans. See, these are the things that make everything adverse and hostile to us, not the Lupercalia, which were abolished for your salvation.

But what do you yourselves have to say, you who defend the Lupercalia and propose that they be held? It is you who cheapen them; you make their worship and celebration vile and common. If offence to the Lupercalia has brought adversity on us, the fault is yours. You think this rite is uniquely beneficial to you, yet you see to its celebration most negligently, with worship and devotion far below that of the ancestors of your profanity. Among them the nobles themselves ran, and matrons were whipped with their bodies publicly bared. So it was you who first offended against the Lupercalia. It would have been better not to hold them at all than to celebrate them insultingly. But you have handed down this worship, which you hold venerable and think brings salvation, to vile and common persons, to the outcast and the lowest.

If, then, you truly profess that this rite, or rather this abomination, brings you salvation, celebrate it yourselves after the custom of your ancestors. Run about naked yourselves with the little thong, so that you may duly perform the mockeries of your salvation. If these things are great, if they are divine, if they bring salvation, if the soundness of your life depends on them, why are you ashamed to celebrate them in person? If it is shameful and a disgrace, can something be saving, divine and beneficial which you yourselves confess is a disgrace? No one professes a religion which he utterly blushes to perform himself and shrinks from. Let your very shame teach you that this is a public crime, not salvation, and not the worship of the divine, of which no wise man is ashamed. These are instruments of depravity. Your mind bears witness against itself: it professes that the rite must be performed, and blushes to carry it out.

Your Castors, certainly, whose worship you have refused to give up: why did they not grant you favourable seas, so that ships with grain might come here in winter and the city not suffer from want? Or is this to happen in the coming days of summer? This is a benefit established by God, not the empty belief in the Castors.

Tell us, you who are neither Christians nor pagans, everywhere faithless and nowhere faithful, everywhere corrupt and nowhere whole, who can no more hold both than the two can be reconciled with each other. Tell us, I say, you patrons of the Lupercalia! You are truly worthy defenders of such a mockery and of shameful songs, worthy masters of madness, who not without reason lack sound heads, worthy of this religion which is celebrated with cries of obscenity and outrage. See for yourselves what salvation can be bestowed on you by something that brings such a stain and ruin upon morals.

Nor can you say that doing these things and broadcasting each person's misdeeds rather deters minds from such acts and restrains them by shame, for fear of being sung about in public. As someone has said, these mockeries seem not so much to deter minds as to prompt them. As he also said, they draw anger and boldness from the crime. They become all the more shameless because, once the crime is published and modesty exposed, nothing at all is left to be ashamed of, and there is nothing left that they fear to have published. Instead, whoever has been sung about in the open, not by way of correction but amid a kind of rejoicing and festival of the gods, now boldly flaunts himself. He is even confident that he is doing religion a service by providing material for celebrating the solemnities of the gods, which are not observed except by singing of crimes.

Tell us, then, you who have the will for profanity but cannot give grounds for it, who set out to uphold a falsehood that you cannot defend: what will you say about drought, hail, whirlwinds, storms and the various disasters that come in accordance with the character of our morals? Did all these things happen because the Lupercalia were abolished? Or are they inflicted as deserved retribution to chastise evil morals?

But it is no wonder that people want these things to happen not by divine judgement but through the onset of vain superstition. To cover their own crimes and misdeeds, they claim that the stars of heaven exercise authority, and they bring in the error of fate and a necessity of sinning. They say that their misdeeds do not proceed from the perversity of their own hearts but depend on heaven as their author. State, then, what evils your Lupercalia were instituted to remove or what goods they were meant to win. Then let us see what goods came about while the Lupercalia were held, and what evils followed when the Lupercalia were seen to be abolished.

Stand your ground: what disaster of yours do you say these portents were devised to avert, you who are fit to celebrate some monster or other made of a mixture of beast and man, whether truly or falsely reported? If it was to remove pestilence, then, to pass over older times, see: before they were abolished in my own time, there was beyond doubt a severe pestilence among men and beasts, both in the city and in the countryside. If you put it forward on account of barrenness, why do these things happen in Africa or the Gauls, where there never were Lupercalia, and where nobody can say they were abolished? Why does the East now overflow and abound with plenty of everything, when it never celebrated the Lupercalia and does not celebrate them now?

Or do you say that they do harm only where they had been celebrated for very many centuries and were then suddenly abolished? Let us see, then, whether in the times when, as you say, they were performed duly and completed with full devotion, as you think, there was never any famine or pestilence at all. But if these disasters often brought things to the extreme of danger, it is clear that the Lupercalia were of no use in removing these evils, even at the time when, as you think, they were carried out in proper order. The same holds for each of the needs which you will say they were established to meet: if it turns out that those needs did not cease even then, this supposed remedy is proven to be an empty presumption. But why not test even now whether they have any power when properly celebrated? Run about yourselves in these mockeries after the custom of your ancestors! Then, by celebrating more devoutly a thing that is, as you say, divine and saving for you, you may provide for your salvation more and more. When these rites were being celebrated, was not

Rome captured by the Gauls, and did it not often come to the very brink? Did it not fall in civil wars while this festival was being held? Were the Lupercalia lacking when Alaric overthrew the city? And recently, when it was overturned by the civil fury of Anthemius and Ricimer, where were the Lupercalia? Why were they of no benefit to them? Surely, if the rite is divine, if it brings you salvation, why do you not perform it in person, as your ancestors did? Why do you diminish the means of your own salvation? Why do you tarnish them, why crush them, why reduce them to everything vile? Why do you blame us, when you yourselves trample on your own remedies?

It is better not even to attempt it than to perform it insultingly. Certainly, if your ancestors had celebrated some rite faultily, as it seemed to them, they thought it had to be repeated. You have reduced this worship to a faulty form by having it performed by all sorts of unworthy persons. Why do you not repair it by a fitting renewal, so that you may handle the means of your salvation more fully and perfectly? Why should you be ashamed to do it, if it brings salvation? If it is divine,

why should it be a disgrace to have performed it? But, you say, at least the image of the thing itself ought not to be removed. If it is beneficial, if it brings salvation, why should you have an image rather than the reality itself? Or if it certainly did no good even then, when it was performed with the rite intact, as you say, why do you seek the image of something whose reality, as you can see, did no good?

But you say that a thing practised for so many centuries ought not to be shut out. The superstition of paganism, however, was also kept going for many ages. Then let sacrifice be offered in the temples of demons, and let profane vanity be celebrated on the Capitol! Why do you defend a part and pass over the greater things? If very many kinds of vanity practised for many centuries have demonstrably been abolished, why can a part not be removed, however long it has been kept going? If you plead the prescription of time, blame your ancestors. They did not avail themselves of this prescription of time, and by removing more and greater things they showed that what is superfluous can and should be removed.

But you say that these things existed even in Christian times. But those other things too were celebrated for some time even in Christian times. Because they were not abolished under the first leaders of the Christian religion, does it follow that they ought not to have been removed under their successors? There are many things that individual bishops have abolished or cast out at different times as harmful. For medicine does not cure all the ailments of a body at once, but treats what it sees as the most dangerous threat, lest either the body's substance should not be equal to the treatment, or, given our mortal condition, it should be unable to ward off everything at once. Consider what kind of thing it is that you are pleading for. If it is good, if divine, if wholesome, then rightly it ought never to have been abolished at any time. If it is neither wholesome nor divine, you should rather complain that it is being removed so late, since it is agreed to be superstitious and vain, and it is clearly incompatible with the Christian profession. Finally, as far as I am concerned:

let no baptized person, no Christian, celebrate this; let the pagans alone, whose rite it is, carry it out. It is my duty to declare that these things are without doubt pernicious and deadly for Christians. Why do you accuse me if I declare that what is hostile to the very heart of the Christian profession must be kept away from those who share that profession? I at least will clear my conscience; let those who have neglected to obey just admonitions see to theirs.

I do not doubt that my predecessors perhaps did this too, and tried to persuade the emperors that these things should be removed. Since it is clear that they were not heard, and these evils persist even today, that is why these empires have failed, and why even the Roman name, the Lupercalia not having been removed, has come to the very extremity. Therefore I now urge that these things be removed. I know that they have done no good, and I declare that, being contrary to true religion, they have rather been harmful.

Finally, if you think my predecessors' conduct should be held up against me as a precedent, each of us will render an account of his own administration, as you see happens in public offices too. I do not dare accuse my predecessors of negligence. I rather believe that they perhaps tried to have this depravity abolished, and that certain causes and opposing wills hindered their intentions, just as you see that even now you yourselves are unwilling to give up your insane efforts.

BISHOP GELASIUS TO ALL THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT DARDANIA AND ILLYRICUM. We have heard of your love's orthodox steadfastness in Christ, and that you cling so firmly to the traditions of the ancient faith and of sincere communion that the contagion of the transgressors close at hand has in no way infected minds devoted to Christian truth. We glorified the Lord for this, and with all the eagerness of our hearts we have sent a letter to address your charity through those religious men, our sons the deacons Cyprian and Macarius.

We have taken care to do this because, by virtue of the primacy of the apostolic see, whose care, divinely entrusted to it, is owed to all the churches, we live if you stand fast in the Lord. And we triumph with great joy when we learn that everywhere on earth the Lord of Sabaoth has left a seed of pure confession. This seed did not fall on rocky ground and wither in the heat of temptation, nor fall beside the path, exposed to roaming enemies, nor land among thorns to be choked. Instead, scattered by heavenly sowing in the good soil of your pious devotion, it has yielded fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold and a hundredfold, which in mystical language signifies the perfection of the Lord's grain.

Therefore, with rejoicing hearts, we urge you all the more confidently to keep your hearts wisely undefiled against the onslaught of the Eutychian plague, since whoever perseveres to the end will be saved. The Lord is near: do not be anxious about anything. For he who is in us is greater than he who is in this world, and it is certain, as scripture testifies, that the kingdom of the Lord is within us.

So that you may guard against harmful fellowship with those who are set in error, do not let anyone who is in communion with such people slip into your fellowship by any stealth. In every heresy, once the author of the depravity has been condemned, Catholic integrity must avoid his successors, his accomplices and followers of that kind, who are mingled with him in polluted communion. In the same way, together with Eutyches, Dioscorus must be utterly rejected, along with Timothy Aelurus and Peter of Alexandria and Acacius, who was in communion with him, and also Peter of Antioch, together with all who share with them. Nor is anyone to be allowed in any way to enter the spotless folds of the sacred flock if he consents to the reciting of the names of the lost, or does not separate himself from communion with those who recite them, even if he promises to lay aside the depravity. In this way the church of our God, which tolerates no spot or wrinkle, may remain inviolate. Let the dreadful dealings of the viper's head, then, be far from Christ's faithful, and let deadly poisons be driven far from the heavenly pastures, so that the saving nourishment of that bread which came down from heaven may lead those who faithfully receive it to eternal life.

So that we may provide for these things by mutual exhortation, let your love take pains not to cease sending us frequent reports of your charity's well-being, which we long to hear, and of your zeal for our common faith. Then, rousing one another with mutual instruction, we may be able to win the reward of the Lord's lawful priests. Let your charity also be vigilant in making these same things known throughout the neighbouring provinces, so that those who stand firm in the sincerity of Catholic communion may be strengthened by fitting words, and those who have perhaps strayed from its uprightness may be brought back by wholesome admonitions to the integrity of Christian doctrine.

Let your fraternity know, moreover, that the bishop of the church of Thessalonica, though often urged by our exhortations, has never been willing to shun the contagion of communion with outsiders. Nor has he, by a fitting profession made before us, condemned the name of Acacius, or of the other faithless men like him and those in communion with them. It is therefore clear that he has not been received into the communion of the apostolic see, since we neither can nor should grant the heavenly fellowship of the blessed apostle Peter except to minds that are pure and cleansed of every plague of wicked association. Greater caution must therefore be used with this man, so that he does not steal upon Catholic minds by pretending to be reconciled with the apostolic see. Just as he cannot deceive and outwit that see by deceitful arts, so he cannot obtain its communion by guile.

We have also thought it right to send to you our authoritative letter that was addressed to the bishops of Dalmatia, so that you may know that everywhere we hold one consistent judgement in Catholic truth, according to the pattern of ancient tradition. If you learn of any new disturbances arising, you should report them to us with brotherly solicitude, so that we may then, with the Lord's help, provide remedies in keeping with the rules of the fathers.

And let no one at all persuade us that Acacius's crime of transgression was forgiven. He relapsed into fellowship with depravity and so justly deserved to be cut off from apostolic communion, and he died persisting in that same condemnation. Now that he is dead, therefore, he cannot obtain the absolution which he neither sought at all nor deserved while he was alive. For it was to the apostles themselves that the voice of Christ entrusted the words: "Whatever you bind on earth, and whatever you loose on earth."

Furthermore, concerning one who now stands under divine judgement, it is not lawful for us to decree anything other than the state in which his last day found him. Therefore, unless his name and those of the other partners in this error are rejected, you must not share with any of them at all the purity of the Lord's table, which our forebears always took great care to keep separate from heretical pollution.

And let no one try to outwit you by saying that the dispute is not about religion but about names, or that the apostolic see is not concerned with the cause of Catholic communion and faith, but is aggrieved by an insult, because it seems to have been treated with contempt by Acacius. Those who are set in error never stop spreading these and similar claims in order to deceive the simple.

For you see, as was said above, that if the names of the transgressors are thought fit to be recited in church (God forbid!), the contagion of their transgression is brought in along with them. The apostolic see, however, is so far from grieving over an insult, and so intent on defending the faith and sincere communion, that even today it would receive, with all the affection of its heart and with full charity, all who are seen to have broken out into contempt for it, if they return to the integrity of the faith and of Catholic communion and come in accordance with the path laid down by the fathers' rules. Given on the third day before the Nones of August, in the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius.

THE PETITION WHICH THE APOCRISIARII OF THE CHURCH OF ALEXANDRIA GAVE TO THE LEGATES SENT FROM THE CITY OF ROME TO CONSTANTINOPLE. To the most glorious and most excellent patrician Festus, and to the venerable bishops Cresconius and Germanus, sent together with his Excellency on an embassy from the city of Rome to our most clement and Christ-loving emperor Anastasius: from Dioscorus, priest, and Chaeremon, reader, of the venerable church of Alexandria, who serve as that church's representatives.

The venerable holy churches of the city of Rome and of Alexandria have always preserved not only a right and spotless faith, ever since the word of salvation was preached in them, but also harmony in the divine ministry. The foundation of the faith was laid in both by one man (we mean the blessed apostle Peter, whom the holy evangelist Mark imitated in all things). So if it ever happened that councils of bishops were held on doubtful matters, the most holy man who presided over the Roman church would delegate the most reverend archbishop of the city of Alexandria to take charge in his place.

But the enemy of the human race, who hates what is good and who always rages with impious fury for our ruin, did not shrink from sowing tares between the two churches through his own henchmen, so as to bring discord into so great a unity. For when the most impious Eutyches held views contrary to the faith preached by the most blessed apostles and tried to teach them, it happened that at that same time Leo, then bishop of the apostolic see, sent a letter to the Council of Chalcedon.

The translators of this letter were men who, together with Theodoret, bishop of the city of Cyrrhus, had at that time been followers of the Nestorian heresy. The letter was shown to be contrary to the faith set forth by the venerable three hundred and eighteen fathers, and it gave no small opening to those who champion the blasphemies of that most wicked Nestorius, so that they asserted all the more freely that Nestorius had held no perverse views at all.

For these reasons our God-loving people took offence. They judged from the Greek translation that the Latin text too contained a similar meaning, and they separated themselves from unity with the Roman church. The Roman bishop, for his part, thinking that we had leaned against the faith handed down by the most blessed apostles, withdrew from communion with us.

Nevertheless, wishing to satisfy his holiness that we hold the faith which the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and his disciple Mark handed down, and which the three hundred and eighteen venerable bishops later set forth, our church took care to send legates to the city of Rome. But there a certain man from our city was found who dissented from the right faith and was estranged from it for various other reasons as well, and he strove to ensure that no opportunity would be given for the legates to be received. They were not admitted even to greet him face to face, and they returned without achieving anything.

Not long ago, however, Photinus, the religious deacon of the holy church of Thessalonica, conversed with us about the peace of the holy churches. He said that a short time before he had been sent by the most holy archbishop Andrew of the church of Thessalonica to the Roman pontiff Anastasius. Regarding the things in the translation of the letter that so gravely offend us, he affirmed that he had been given satisfaction by the aforesaid bishop of the Roman church: namely, that errors are indeed found in the translation of the letter, but that the Latin letter itself had been composed in accordance with the faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers. Moreover, he reported that the same bishop had personally said certain things which served to censure what had been inserted in the translation and those [?] who had tried to fabricate it, but to satisfy those who do not neglect to keep the right and spotless faith.

We were amply healed by this, and, desiring that our former harmony be restored, we wished to learn from you as well whether what the religious deacon Photinus had reported to us was true. We desired to meet your holiness and to confer about all these matters. And indeed your holiness deigned to inform us, not once but often, that the errors inserted in the translation of the letter were not contained in the Latin text.

We therefore begged you to accept the confession of our faith, on whose behalf we are carrying out the embassy of our venerable church. This faith our most holy archbishop has also made known everywhere, and he has received replies from all approving it. If you see that your holy church too agrees with this faith, order that satisfaction be given to us, so that, with the stumbling-blocks removed, the venerable churches of both Rome and Alexandria may return to their former unity.

This confession of our faith, which we presented to you, contains the following: the only true and right faith, drawn by divine inspiration from the proclamations of the gospels and the apostles, < as > the three hundred and eighteen venerable fathers assembled at the Synod of Nicaea set it forth. The hundred and fifty equally venerable bishops who met in the imperial city also followed it. Carrying it through, the fathers gathered at Ephesus, with the assent also of Celestine, the most holy pope of the apostolic see, condemned the sacrilegious Nestorius and laid down a penalty for those who should try to establish another faith. We too condemn this Nestorius, together with Eutyches, with the punishment of anathema, since they held views contrary to what has been said above, and we accept those twelve chapters which Cyril of venerable memory, formerly archbishop of the church of Alexandria, wrote.

We confess the only-begotten Son of God, and God, who truly became man, our Lord Jesus Christ, consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity, and the same consubstantial with us according to his humanity; who came down and was incarnate of the Holy Spirit and of the Virgin Mary, the Theotokos, that is, the Mother of God; existing as one Son, not two. For we say that both the miracles and the sufferings which he willingly endured for us in the flesh belong to the one only-begotten Son of God. Those who divide or confuse, or who introduce some kind of phantasm, we in no way accept, because the incarnation which the Mother of God truly brought forth from herself added nothing to the Son. For the Trinity remained a Trinity even when God the Word, who is one of the Trinity, became incarnate.

We have written these things not to introduce anything new into the faith, but because we wish to satisfy you for the sake of harmony. Everyone who thinks or has thought otherwise, whether now or at any time, in any place or in any council, we strike with the penalty of anathema, and above all Nestorius and Eutyches and all who agree with them.

Your reverence, then, accepting this faith of ours, declared that you would report it to Anastasius, bishop of the Roman church, and mentioned that he was ready to give satisfaction to any persons we might send for this purpose. You also asserted that Dioscorus, Timothy and Peter, former archbishops of our city, had held views contrary to this faith, and that their names ought not to be read out in the diptychs. We, on the other hand, asked either that people be produced against them who would make and prove this charge, or, if none could be found able to convict them, that he should accept our satisfaction on their behalf, as we showed and proved that our aforesaid fathers and archbishops Timothy, Dioscorus and Peter held this faith, taught it and handed it on to all whom they instructed. But your holiness refused, saying that you had not been instructed by the bishop of the apostolic see to make any inquiry into these matters.

For this reason we adjure you before our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, who was incarnate and born of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and who gladly approves and accepts the harmonious praise and service of the faithful; before his holy angels; and by this same spotless faith concerning him: when, by the Lord's favour, you come to the city of Rome, present this document to Anastasius, bishop of the apostolic see,

which has been delivered to you in the name of the holy church of Alexandria, so that his holiness, after reading it through, may deign to make known his pleasure, either by a letter addressed to our most holy archbishop or through some intermediary. For once his holiness has upheld the confession of the right faith established by the blessed fathers, we declare that we are ready to send legates to the city of Rome to act for the unity of God's holy churches.

We trust in our Lord Jesus Christ that his beatitude will agree with this faith, in accordance with what is set down in the reply, and will regard our peoples too as his own and take care for their governance, desiring to prove himself useful to all according to God.

We have kept a copy of this document with us. If any delay arises that prevents the unity of the holy churches from being achieved, we hold it necessary to appear with it at the glorious coming of our Lord Jesus Christ from heaven, when he comes to judge the living and the dead, before his tribunal, where there is no favouritism, in order to refute those who have neglected the unity of the holy churches. HERE IT ENDS. I, DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS, TRANSLATED THIS FROM THE GREEK AT ROME.
(103.) COPY OF THE PROCEEDINGS CONCERNING THE ABSOLUTION OF MISENUS, IN THE CONSULSHIP OF FLAVIUS VIATOR, VIR CLARISSIMUS, ON THE THIRD DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF MAY, IN THE BASILICA OF BLESSED PETER.

The synod was in session under the venerable Pope Gelasius, together with Boniface, Maximinus, Epiphanius, Basil, Vitalis, Clarus, Irenaeus, Decius, Asellus, Euplus, Valentine, Martinian, Bassus, Benignus, Primitivus, Palladius, Vindemius, Constantius, Martyrius, Candidus, Laurence, Deodatus, Mercurius, Stephen, Dulcitius, Fortunatus, Paschasius, Sanctulus, Innocent, Chrysogonus, Colonicus, Viator, Sallust, Lucian, Molensis [?], Maximian, Valentine, Constantius, Gaudentius, Felix, Vitalian, Peter, Serenus, Aucupius, Timothy,

Stephen, Laurence and Probus, bishops. Also seated were Castinus, Laurence, Canusius, Eugene, Januarius, Marcian, Gordian, Peter, Urbicus, Paulinus, Valens, Peter, Asterius, Smaragdus, Boniface, Maxentius, Epiphanius, Justin, Felix, Redemptus, Projectitius, Jovinus, Bonus, Paschasius, Laurence, Callistus, John, Valentine, Sebastian, Martin, Epiphanius, Andrew, Servusdei, Apellio, Peter, Servandus, Romanus, Marcellinus, Domninus, Agapitus, Abundantius, Marcellinus, Litorius, Laurence, Agatho, Sebastian, Valentine, Anastasius, Genesius, Dionysius, Epiphanius, Acontius, Paulinus, Agapitus, Adeodatus, Benedict, Dominic, Redemptus, Severus, Julian, Stephen, Crescentio, Septiminus, Cyprian and Epiphanius, presbyters, together with Amandianus, a man of illustrious rank, and Diogenianus, a man of distinguished rank. With the deacons also standing by, Gelasius, bishop of the catholic church of the city of Rome, said:

"Your Love will remember that at our previous meeting a petition presented to us by Misenus was read out in your presence. If it please Your Love, let this same petition be reviewed again, so that our acts may contain it. He states that he also has another petition in hand, <by which> we may learn what it contains as well." And he added: "Let Misenus's petition be read again."

Anastasius the deacon read: "Presented by your servant Misenus on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of the most distinguished Viator. As regards the abyss of my misfortune, I declare that my error, however it was contracted, ought not to be spared, since I ought not to escape punishment for this very reason: that I deserved, by whatever chance, to be brought into a case that carries a penalty.

"But as regards the help of a remedy, there are two things that compel me to come and implore it as a suppliant: first, lest through despair I should rather deserve to be consigned to everlasting torments after the example of Judas the traitor; and second, because so great is that ineffable clemency which, through the apostolic power, can absolve every crime.

"Therefore, venerable pope, in my case I, a wretched man, pour out this one cry: 'Spare the one who lies prostrate; stretch out your hand to the fallen!' I rely on no excuse of ignorance, I plead no snares of deception, nor do I seek to shift onto anyone the blame for my calamity, since I, who ask to be mercifully absolved, ought not to accuse others. It is enough for me that, although I bring nothing in my own defence, I do not doubt that all these matters are to be dealt with by your judgment.

"I only beg this: following the heavenly mercy which declares through the prophet, 'I do not desire the death of the dying man, but that he turn back and live,' weigh rather with kindly consideration everything that has been done concerning me, and do not deny the viaticum to an old man worn out by continual sickness and wasting, lest I be snatched away without the church's gift. See in another man's fall the proof of what I fear: he could not obtain help even though you were willing to give it. And that I was entangled in this disaster rather through lack of experience is graciously shown by this very fact: that I have survived to be able to attain the grace of reception by the church."

When this had been read, Bishop Gelasius said: "The minutes will retain the petition," and he added: "Now let Misenus himself come in, and let the petition he presented be read in his presence." When he had come in, Misenus, lying prostrate on the ground, presented another petition and asked that it be accepted. When it had been accepted, Bishop Gelasius said: "Let both petitions that he has presented be read, with him also present."

Again Anastasius the deacon read: "Presented by your servant Misenus on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of the most distinguished Flavius Viator. As regards the abyss of my misfortune, I declare that my error, however it was contracted, ought not to be spared, since I ought not to escape punishment, because I deserved, by whatever chance, to be brought into a case that carries a penalty. But as regards the help of a remedy, there are two things that compel me to come and implore it as a suppliant: first, lest through despair I should rather deserve to be consigned to everlasting torments after the example of Judas the traitor," and the rest, as contained above.

Likewise the other petition: "Presented by your servant Misenus on the third day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of the most distinguished Flavius Viator. When I first presented my petition, I begged as a suppliant for nothing else than that the mercy of the apostolic see should not be denied me for ever.

"Since I now feel the hope of that mercy shining upon me, through the boundless goodness of God by which the see is governed, I declare ever more firmly that my conscience is free and cleansed of the contagion of the faithless, into which I had fallen through misfortune and entrapment rather than by intent. With my whole heart and mouth I solemnly attest, in the sight of God, that I readily reject all heresies and whatever is hostile to the catholic and apostolic faith and to true communion; and above all that I spurn, condemn and anathematize for ever the Eutychian heresy, together with its author Eutyches and his follower Dioscorus, and his successors and communicants Timothy Aelurus, Peter of Alexandria, Acacius of Constantinople and Peter of Antioch, and all their accomplices and communicants; and that I hold all these and their like in horror and execration. I profess that I will never in any way have any fellowship with such men, but will remain entirely estranged from them all.

"Although I never willingly accepted their depravity, yet because I appear, driven by my calamity, to have fallen into it through lack of caution, in the sight of God, of blessed Peter the apostle and his vicar, and of the whole church, I condemn, detest and abhor it by my confession and my voice, as I have said, affirming that I will always continue in the catholic and apostolic faith and communion alone. I have signed this petition of mine with my own hand on the third day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of the most distinguished Viator, and I have resolved to present it with my own hands to Your Beatitude in the assembly of the venerable fathers." And in another hand: "I, Misenus, have signed this petition of mine, presented by me, on the day and in the consulship written above."

Bishop Gelasius said: "Let what has been read be copied into the record," and he added: "We wish also to learn, by sharing in your counsel, what Your Fraternity thinks should be decided." All the bishops and presbyters rose, entreating and saying: "Hear us, Christ: long life to Gelasius!" This was said twenty times. "What God has placed in your power, grant it!" This was said twelve times. "Do what the lord Peter does!" This was said ten times. "We ask you to pardon him!" This was said nine times.

When they had sat down again, Bishop Gelasius said: "The apostolic see, which by the delegation of Christ the Lord holds the primacy of the whole church, acting in its general stewardship and care, which it always exercises with the necessary circumspection on behalf both of the catholic faith and of the canons of the fathers and the rules of our forebears, had some time ago, under my predecessor of holy memory, sent Misenus and Vitalis to the East, supported by a legation of its authority, against the followers of the Eutychian plague and against those who had polluted themselves by communion with such men. When synodal proceedings, after investigation of the matter, had made it plain how they had turned aside from the apostolic instructions and in one way or another had fallen back into fellowship with the very people against whom they had been sent, the see rightly and justly removed them from communion and from office alike.

"Yet, mindful of the heavenly goodness, it kept a place for mercy open to them in keeping with its own moderation. While it laid down the terms of punishment, it did not wish the hope of pardon to be cut off, and it so tempered its sentence that it preferred their pardon to come about together with the salvation of those whose fellowship had led them astray. In this way they would rather offer those whom they had confirmed in depravity by their own consent both a wholesome fear of correction and a share in an amendment worth imitating.

"Indeed, the very words of the censure were so balanced that those others would perceive that they had been struck together with these men, and, given the condition laid down for them, would not despair of being saved. In this way the path of return was certainly not wholly closed to these men, and to those others, if they wished, correction was offered through them, and an opportunity held out by which, with a better effort, they could make up for their past lapses, if they turned the favour they had so readily shown to the transgressors toward the restoration of catholic bishops instead. For it was declared that these men would remain suspended until, by God's authority and through the efforts of the catholic emperors or of the Christian people, the church of Alexandria had received a catholic bishop.

"For it was believed, to our joy, that the Greeks could in no way fail to reject what they saw had been condemned by the apostolic see, and that they could easily be moved by these men's punishment to learn what to avoid and consequently what to seek, and that they would wish to be seen coming to their senses and agreeing with the upright rather than erring continually with the faithless. And it was long awaited that, spurred on by these reasons, they would put away the wicked contagion and agree with the apostolic see, as had been hoped of their good will, and would rather devote their efforts to recalling catholic bishops, so that they themselves might return to orthodox unity and might secure for these men, who had shared in their error, the reception that had been promised. Nor was any opportunity that could be found neglected by which, suitably admonished and sufficiently instructed, they might both recognize the dangers to be avoided and perceive that the door of apostolic communion stood open to them if they sought it with sincere minds.

"But since matters have come to this, that even to healing exhortations, though they had nothing to say against them, they have so far put off giving their consent, we owe a father's feeling of devout grief to their stubbornness, praying to the omnipotence of our God, which alone can turn wills, however astray, into the way of truth, that by the wonderful working of his mercy he may graciously pour into them a spirit of repentance and the power to amend.

"Until this comes about through God's favour, as we trust in his power that it will, let us meanwhile by no means allow this man, who supplicates and earnestly seeks it, to perish. Thus the Easterners, who were not frightened by his deposition out of persisting in error, may at least be moved by his healing to return to salvation; especially since the very wording of what was said goes hand in hand with the clemency of the apostolic see's decision, and the decree that was issued will not be judged to contradict itself.

"For it was laid down, as has already been said above, that those of whom we are speaking should remain suspended until, by God's authority and through the efforts of the aforesaid, the church of Alexandria should receive a catholic bishop. This was not stated absolutely and without qualification, but was expressed in such terms that the sentence would not appear fixed regardless of whether those persons made the effort or not. Therefore, when the term on which the condition was balanced is absent, it releases the obligation of its own declaration. For what was declared to be done with the efforts of the aforesaid plainly cannot be done when those efforts are not forthcoming; and since it is stated that it is to be done by their efforts too, it is shown clearly enough that it cannot be accomplished without them. Therefore, although those whose effort is shown to be lacking are to be pitied for their obstinacy, yet because it is lacking — just as what was presumed could be achieved with it cannot be achieved without it — so, when the causes through which this clause was to reach its conclusion fall away, it does not keep the one it bound bound indissolubly.

"Consequently, since the means by which the sentence passed could hold to its appointed measure until its fulfilment do not exist, it grants freedom to provide for those who were previously held by it. And indeed the apostolic see, as must often be repeated, judging that the Easterners could in no way fail to reject what the apostolic see had refuted, and that they could not prefer any person to their own salvation and to apostolic communion, had thought better of their minds than this. But — and this again must not be passed over in silence — this lamentable ruin cannot so much convict the opinion of the apostolic see of being improvident in thinking well of the Easterners as it must be ascribed rather to their own obstinacy, in that they did not follow the path to their own restoration that was offered to them. Nor ought their obstinacy on that account to deprive others who desire healing of the opportunity for it.

"For at that time things were said confidently about the Greeks' agreement, because they seemed capable of placing fellowship with blessed Peter above any persons whatever, and, since they had formerly been catholics, they were thought likely to assent readily to the truth, and therefore unable to set attachment to any man above the desire for apostolic communion. Since they have not yet adopted the dispositions through which this course was to run, what was presumed could be done through them is seen to be dissolved; for when those who should bring something about are lacking, no result can follow — and all the more when the very persons through whom it was judged it should be done resist its being done.

"If — God forbid — they are to remain in this obstinacy, the condition attached to the thing that was confidently expected to be fulfilled through their efforts is dissolved. But if, as we would rather hope, they are converted to better things, then in the meantime, lest the man who asks for mercy should be cut off by age or by the sickness that frequently assails him, provision must be made for him while he is alive, so that it may not happen that no remedy can be supplied once he is dead. For it was not said 'whether they make the effort or perhaps even against their will,' but rather that what had been promulgated could stand with their effort. So, then, when they make [no?] effort, the conditions laid down in no way remain in force.

"On the same principle the blessed apostle Paul is not to be thought — God forbid — to have deceived anyone or contradicted himself because, having promised that he would go to Spain, he was occupied by divine disposition with weightier matters and could not fulfil what he had promised. As far as his own will was concerned, he declared what he truly wished to do; as far as the secrets of the divine counsel were concerned, which as a man he could not fully know, though he was full of the Spirit of God, he gave it up, forestalled by the heavenly disposition.

"Nor, because the blessed apostle Peter, out of reverence for the divine, answered the Lord himself, 'You shall never wash my feet,' will he be thought — God forbid — to have deceived anyone or to have failed to stand by his word; for he soon yielded to that same divine will, so that what he had said he would not let be done, he readily asked to have done, constrained by the needs of human salvation.

"Therefore, since the way by which the reconciliation of the accused had been arranged has not succeeded, it is permissible to take up another by which help may be brought to those whom it was decreed should be helped; especially since, whatever Misenus's excess or transgression, his punishment is sufficient, having been drawn out so far that it is now relaxed only out of regard for the human condition and its final end; and a punishment that has no further room to grow ought to be remitted. For since almighty and merciful God wills that no soul seeking a remedy through the compassion of the church should be denied it, there is no doubt that it comes about by God's own authority and through divine compunction that his reception is being considered at a time when a necessity that brooks no delay compels it to be granted.

"Moreover, since our Saviour entrusted to the blessed apostle Peter above the others the words 'Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven too, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven too,' then, just as nothing is excepted in these words, so through the office of the apostolic stewardship everything without exception can be bound and likewise everything loosed. This holds especially since by this act an example of apostolic mercy ought rather to be set before all, so that through the absolution of one who was condemned, all, if they repent, withdraw from error and return to the sincere purity of apostolic communion, may have no doubt that they will be freed from the bonds of that condemnation which they had incurred one and all through their transgression. For we who strive to bring those far away to the wholeness of the faith ought not to reject suppliants who return here before us. In this we must take careful heed lest — God forbid — by denying mercy to the very end to one who asks for it, we in any way incur harm to our conscience, and the severity of censure, persisting without end even toward suppliants, should turn into guilt.

"Accordingly, let us offer remedies to one who desires them, as far as human capacity allows with the Lord's permission, leaving to divine judgment everything that lies beyond the measure of our power. Those who demand that we grant pardon even to the dead — which is plainly not possible for us — will not be able to reproach us for remitting the offence of transgression to the living, which by God's gift is possible for the church. For since it was said, 'Whatever you bind on earth,' those who are known to be no longer on earth he has reserved not to human judgment but to his own; and the church does not dare to claim for itself what it sees was not granted even to the blessed apostles themselves, for the case of the living is one thing and that of the dead another.

"Vitalis has met the lot of divine judgment; he could not be helped, though we greatly wished it. Let the example of the other, so suddenly taken away, at least profit this man in obtaining remedies while the opportunity of life allows. And since we know that it is written, 'One will be taken and one left,' the peril of the one cut off urges us not to delay the aids of healing for the survivor, who is shown by God to be fit for reception by the very fact that he has outlived the one who did not deserve to reach this point. A kind of verdict of heavenly judgment shines out concerning the two, and it is shown to us all the more clearly in these two men, in which of them the case was beyond pardon and in which there is one that ought not to lack indulgence. Therefore, what even Acacius himself could have obtained had he duly sought it while still alive — for although it was laid down concerning him that the sentence would be indissoluble, it was not said 'even if perhaps he should amend' — much more is it fitting for apostolic compassion not to deny it to this man, who was infected by communion with him and now implores it with tears.

"Therefore, since Misenus has professed in due form that he detests all heresies, especially the Eutychian, together with Eutyches, Dioscorus, Timothy Aelurus and Peter of Alexandria, Acacius of Constantinople and Peter of Antioch, and all their successors, followers and communicants, and strikes them with perpetual anathema, he shall receive the grace of apostolic communion and of the priestly dignity which he received through catholic tradition."

All the bishops and presbyters rose in the synod and acclaimed: "Hear us, Christ: long life to Gelasius!" This was said fifteen times. "Lord Peter, preserve him!" This was said twelve times. "You hold his see — may you have his years!" This was said seven times. "We see in you the vicar of Christ!" This was said eleven times. "We see in you the apostle Peter!" This was said six times. "You hold his see — may you have his years!" This was said thirty-seven [?] times.

I, Sixtus, notary of the holy Roman church, by order of my lord the most blessed Pope Gelasius, issued this from the archive on the third day before the Ides of May, in the consulship of the most distinguished Flavius Viator.

Symmachus to his most beloved brothers, all the bishops, priests, deacons and archimandrites, and to the whole clergy and people throughout Illyricum, Dardania and both Dacias. This we long to see fully accomplished! If what we write is carried out, let no one be surprised that we have now broken the silence we kept until this time, since the voice of the most wise Solomon rings out: "A time to speak and a time to keep silent." For the present time puts silence to rout: amid what is now happening, to keep silent and not be roused by the goads of faith is plainly a sign of great indifference.

For where reverence for religion, and its very summit, is being shaken, it is fitting to say, as divine Scripture does, that those who are meek must become fighters. There is indeed a kind of spiritual combat that is acceptable to God; and so all things are endured, and endured to our credit, so that no one may be separated from the love of God. To teach you what is fitting lays a heavy burden on our modesty, but it is necessary to remind you of what is profitable. Nor is it appropriate to set out the doctrines of religious discipline for those from whom the full perfection of that very teaching is expected. So we touch only briefly on matters that are clear.

Who does not know with what contagion of Nestorius the church of Constantinople was afflicted, of Nestorius, I say, who was cut off like a rotten limb of the body from the fellowship of catholic communion? Where on earth is the holy assembly of the Council of Chalcedon not proclaimed, which with one undivided sentence condemned Eutyches and Dioscorus, two names notorious for great faithlessness, accomplices in iniquity who belched out with one spirit things contrary to the divine doctrines?

Who has not known Peter and Timothy, the house-slaves of those just named, champions of a condemned cause, who outdid their own authors and masters in perverse error? We mean that Timothy the parricide who, while Proterius of holy memory was still alive, not only seized the church through irreligious backers but also added the shedding of holy blood to the crime of usurpation. Indeed the voice of the universal church pronounced his condemnation, stripping him even of the name and honour of a Christian. His follower Peter was made known by the many sufferings of the orthodox, in which he delighted to display his strength of mind. Ephesus knew him, together with the whole party of Dioscorus, where, along with the author of his own sin, he became notorious for bringing about the death of the holy Flavian. Must [?]

the evils of Antioch be passed over in silence, where the revered name of the priesthood was held up to ridicule through the abominable mockeries of another Peter? Who could fittingly lament the groans of Apamea and Tyre, which bear comparison with the crimes of tragedy, even if he had leisure for them alone? And what of Acacius?

As though his good deeds, those he had done earlier in the reign of Basiliscus, had been weighed down by some evil spell, he has been caught in a new kind of punishment, pronouncing sentence against himself. With a change of will he defends those whom he once thought it glorious to condemn, and labours to join to the faithful those whom he had long ago shown to be heretics guilty of open betrayal. On their account above all he must be shunned and ranked with the condemned band named above, for he has undone the very things by which he had been proved faithful and has mingled with those through whom general injury has come upon the church.

If reason urges that the doctrines of the fathers must be upheld against these men, consider whether they could be trampled with greater transgression than they are now by those who in your regions are bringing the doctrines of Eutyches back to life. But if they are neglected without danger, as though they were weakly established decisions, then the whole of our belief stands without any strength, with new things forever coming along to dissolve the old decrees.

For when what the rules of the fathers laid down is despised, and the firmness of what was well established is not defended, such impiety must always befall the faith. Where a reasonable decree is easily undone, every form of holiness is corrupted, Christ is attacked, and (what believer could bear this patiently?) the revered institutions of the fathers are trampled underfoot. And (who would not rightly choose death over life?) where then is the adorable reverence of the catholic faith?

Where are the doctrines established by the abundant blood of the saints? Where is the faithful authority of the ancient teachers? Where is that astonishing endurance of devout minds, content to be stripped of their own goods so as not to fall away from the hope of an eternal inheritance, and seeking out any sufferings so as not to be judged unworthy of that incorruptible good?

For there are no greater proofs of faith than when the circumstances of the time urge us to submit our life to suffering; and so whoever has been found worthy to undergo the danger of persecution for the faith shows himself worthy of the heavenly army. Christ purchased us at the holy price of his blood and granted us the freedom of grace, when human works could find nothing worthy to give for so great a reward; and therefore, where religion is wronged, love of the faith must surpass every other affection.

Let each one, then, regard exile and wandering as his home and fatherland, lest, held back by human desires, he be deprived of fellowship with Christ. Behold the time when the faith calls back its soldiers and cries out to those who have received the fervour of grace to come to its defence! Let us imagine the faith itself saying: "Behold the time to be longed for, behold the harvest of the faithful so much desired, when for small sufferings they may gain great rewards!"

We would gladly exhort your charity at greater length, in keeping with the stewardship entrusted to us; but what need is there for the goads of our voice, when we are taught by the examples of the apostles and the fathers to bear sufferings for Christ with greatness of soul? Those examples have shown us that through the loss of human things come increases of heavenly virtue.

Let us therefore proclaim fearlessly, with great confidence, the clear teachings of the church; far from us be the word of the prophet who says, "And the priests have hidden the truth." For who does not know that teachers will be held to account for the knowledge of their disciples, and that what harms the followers by not being proclaimed is perilous for those who keep silent? Truth must needs struggle among those with whom falsehood, not being exposed, lies hidden under the colour of truth; and those who attack the faith gain great strength so long as the judgments issued against them are not manfully upheld.

But of you I wish to speak better things: that what has been thrown into confusion by the wicked may obtain through you the remedy of correction. It is not so hard for someone to be deceived as for one who has been deceived to persist in error. This evil is graver than all others, when the members disagree with their own body; for even if weakness does not seize every part one by one, still, as the apostle says, the whole body must be weighed down by the part.

Communion with the condemned must therefore be shunned. As the blessed apostle says, let no one be ashamed of the proclamation of the faith, for it is power to everyone who believes. Let us turn away from the sacrilegious error of Eutyches, which agrees with the malice of the Manichees; and let us with equal resolve avoid communion with those who have been brought up by such men, which is now trying to creep into the churches of your regions like a diseased contagion. Let no one pretend that he is not being swept along by the same storm as those just named, until, separated from their communion, he enters the harbour of the true faith.

I give these warnings out of love; I do not accuse with the hatred of a persecutor. For whoever censures what is blameworthy without supplying what is useful shows the zeal of a fault-finder rather than the affection of one who loves; but whoever urges others toward what will profit them displays more vividly the image of a good purpose, inviting them to seek what is useful more fervently. Therefore, brothers, longing for that good unity of the church and looking forward to the blessed beauty of holy concord, let us say with holy David: "How good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity," so that the apostle Paul may have said of us as well: "But you are all brothers, one in Christ." For until this unity returns, let no one doubt that the same things will come about as recently happened in the church of Constantinople, things over which I must both groan and keep silent; for those who believed that the admonition of the apostolic see could be neglected have deservedly fallen into what usually befalls those left without support.

If anyone, then, mindful of his own salvation, wishes to keep the judgments of the apostolic see, let him know that once he has separated himself from the taint of those named above, he is without doubt a sharer in our communion. But whoever does not withdraw from fellowship with those whom the apostolic see has condemned should know that by no pretext, no fabrication and no cunning can he slip past the vigilance of the church. For just as we gladly embrace those who separate themselves from the poisons of the men written above, that is, Eutyches, Dioscorus, Timothy, Peter and Acacius, so our care and concern is ever watchful regarding their followers, lest they slip in by stealth. And in another hand: May God keep you safe, dearest brothers. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of October, after the consulship of Felix, vir clarissimus.

Dorotheus to the holy and most blessed father and fellow minister Hormisdas, greeting in the Lord. Solomon, most blessed, who brings forth all the wonders of the divine precepts, says in one place: "As cold water is sweet to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country"; and holy David, plucking the spiritual lyre, sings: "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good tidings!" And indeed you too will all say [?].

What is so sweet to a man's soul, or what so fattens the bones, as to learn by good report that a nurturer of true peace and an unerring champion of right faith has taken the helm of the holy churches; that, as from a citadel, he calls what was scattered to agreement; that the members of the church which Christ our God entrusted to you, granting the prayers of the venerable father, who once scorned concord, are now coming to unity and hastening at once to the primacy of his see; that the former division and envy have been destroyed by the mere vote of your ordination; and that now every region of that holy church stands firm in concord and serenity?

We learned these things not long ago, and knowing the ancient custom of the church and hearing of your friendly and blameless character, I hoped to learn them more firmly and clearly from your own letter. But since I judged that you were kept from doing so by the winter season, and since it was fitting and right for a full and God-loving charity to pass over even scruples, I am writing to address the blessed head of your holiness, to let you know that I rejoice with the blessed see of the most holy apostle Peter that it is governed by such a hand, that it has received a leader who did not seize the honour but was seized by it, and, as many reports relate and as we believe to be so, a nurturer of peace and a contender for right faith, crowned as with precious stones by kindness of mind and by charity toward all.

For I wish you to know everything, venerable father. Having received from the ancient holy and venerable fathers an affection for that blessed see, and guarding it as a paternal inheritance, I wish and hasten to add this: that this endeavour may come to a useful end, through the kindness of our Lord and God Jesus Christ and the intercessions in all things of the most blessed apostle Peter and of the most wise Paul; that the honour justly due to their venerable see and to your blessedness may be preserved and rendered; that in your times the apostolic see may receive the honour befitting its primacy; and that all discord may depart from the church by the catholic will of all of us, and of our Lord and God Jesus Christ. We always anathematize the impious Nestorius and Eutyches, those who keep their doctrines, those who were or are their followers, and every heresy; we hold the right and undefiled faith unshaken as a sure and firm anchor; and we are ready for peace, with nothing, God forbid, standing in the way. This is especially so since your venerable head, as we have learned, abhors contentious men, whose life and food is the division of God's priests quarrelling among themselves, so that, quickly recognized by all as wolves in sheep's clothing, they may easily be driven away from the apostolic church.

I have now written this to your blessed head through the honourable Patricius, our common son. In doing so I have let the affection of long habit outweigh strict reckoning, being bound by charity to that blessed see and longing every day to see the fitting and due veneration preserved for it.

Write, then, you who are blessed in all things, as to one who is of one mind with you and who wishes even to offer his life for the orthodox faith and the peace of the holy churches, and to see what befits the venerable see of blessed Peter preserved in all things. This will easily be done once the unity of all is set in order and all hasten to you as to a secure harbour; for divisions are accustomed to despise other things as well and do not keep what befits good order.

I and those who are with me warmly greet in the Lord all the brotherhood joined to your holiness. And in another hand: Pray that I may be saved in the Lord, most holy and most blessed fathers! Received: the letter of Dorotheus, bishop of the church of Thessalonica, sent through Patricius, vir spectabilis, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Florentius, vir clarissimus.

Hormisdas to his most beloved brother Dorotheus. Where it matters to keep the precepts of charity, even if something should happen that might stir anyone's feelings, it ought nevertheless to be passed over calmly, so that what we said earlier about preserving concord may be upheld; for surely, if anything of the kind arises from ignorance, its very simplicity may serve as its excuse. Our God established his church by his own ordering, and what is known to have been arranged by divine precepts can in no way be set aside.

I do not take you to be ignorant of this, or unaware of it; for in doing, good things win praise, and fine words are adorned only when they are duly joined to what befits them. We received your charity's letter through our son Patricius, vir spectabilis, in which we had hoped to find a complete and commendable work, so that nothing would remain to separate anyone from the integrity of unity.

But since in that very letter you profess a disposition that could especially move us toward what we spoke of earlier, we pour out prayers to our Lord, that he, whose cause is at stake, may wipe away or cut off all scandals from his church and bind them together in one consent and in equal faith; and that he may not allow anything to be found in his priests that springs from anyone's private hatreds or empty designs, or from a wish, wicked as it is, to please men to the injury of God, rather than that each, despising all worldly things as the blessed apostle teaches, may not stray from the hope to come.

I exhort you for the sake of the common remedy, I invite you for the salvation of the faithful, I urge you for the sake of the healing of all. For who could be content to see divided those in whose unity he might glory? There is need, therefore, of common labour, so that, preserving what we have received from our fathers, we may stand secure concerning these things at that divine judgment.

The victor Anastasius, pious, fortunate, renowned, triumphant, ever Augustus, to Hormisdas, most holy and devout archbishop and patriarch. We do not think it unknown to your blessedness that the divine Scriptures, with provident admonition, have laid down that one should speak or keep silent according to the nature of the times. Now that the time for silence has run its course, we have been given occasion to speak, and so we have judged it opportune to bring to your hearing the disturbances that are arising among us under the guise of religion.

Before this, the harshness of those to whom the care of the episcopate you now hold had been entrusted made us refrain from sending letters; but now the pleasant report spreading about you has brought to our mind the goodness of paternal affection, so that we seek those things which God our Saviour taught the holy apostles by his divine word, and above all the blessed Peter, in whom he established the strength of his church.

Having made this beginning, therefore, we urge your apostleship to make yourself a mediator in the matters that have been stirred up in the regions of Scythia, for which we have judged it fitting that a council be held, so that, with contentions cut away, unity may be restored to the holy church.

All that we desire will be granted us if you remember us in your prayers and in frequent letters. Given the day before the Ides of January at Constantinople, and received in the consulship of Anthemius and Florentius, viri clarissimi, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, through Patricius.

Hormisdas to Anastasius Augustus.
