Thanks be to the power on high, which has deigned through your Piety's address to end a long silence, granting such a beginning to our correspondence that we may both rejoice in the prosperity of your Clemency and trust that, by God's gift, the holy church can return to unity.

This is the work of the heavenly clemency; this was also always the prayer of our predecessors, whom their very deeds show to have been ministers of the tradition of the fathers and guardians of the right faith.

For peace is the beginning of all goodness; as far as the practice of the catholic faith is concerned, nothing should be thought stronger, nothing loftier. For its sake, clearly, whoever wishes to be an approved disciple of the holy Scriptures ought to do and to bear all things. It is well known that Christ our Lord commended this mother and nurse of all good things to his disciples, saying: "My peace I give you, my peace I leave you."

With the care that belongs to our religious calling, and by the Lord's inspiration, we watch over this peace, [?] you are taking thought for the concord of the orthodox church, while we keep the divine precepts especially in reverence for the blessed apostle Peter. This secures for your empire a greater defence of heavenly favour; for veneration rightly offered to God grants devout minds an impregnable wall of defence.

We therefore pour out our prayers to almighty God that he who has granted you the zeal to seek the peace of the churches may also, under the hallowing of the catholic faith, bring your desire in this matter to fulfilment.

Moreover, in the sacred letter sent to us your Piety has deigned to mention a holy council. On this matter we shall be able to give a very full answer once you have been pleased to let us know clearly the reason for the gathering. For now, however, since by the gift of our Lord the opportunity for correspondence has been granted, we shall render with fitting veneration the duty of the reply we owe. Given the day before the Nones of April, in the consulship of Florentius, vir clarissimus. Through Patricius.

Anastasius Augustus to Pope Hormisdas. Divine matters must be placed before all other business; for we trust that with the favour of almighty God the commonwealth is both to be preserved and to be improved.

Since, then, certain doubts concerning the orthodox religion seem to have been stirred up in the regions of Scythia, it has especially pleased our Clemency that a venerable synod be held in the city of Heraclea in the province of Europa, so that with minds in agreement and every truth thoroughly examined, our true faith may become more clearly known to the whole world, and there may henceforth be no doubt or discord.

Therefore let your holiness deign to come to the aforesaid city of Heraclea by the Kalends of July, with whatever most reverend bishops you please, whom you have found to be suitable and well instructed in the orthodox religion from among the churches placed under the care of your priesthood. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of January at Constantinople, in the consulship of Senator, vir clarissimus. Received the day before the Ides of May, in the consulship of Florentius, vir clarissimus.

Hormisdas to Anastasius Augustus. Through Severianus. Your Clemency rightly trusts, as you indicated in the glorious letter sent to me, that it will especially profit your commonwealth if the cause of the orthodox faith is placed before all other business. For this, venerable emperor, is the most wholesome care a ruler can have in the government he has taken up: to win for himself, by good works, the favour of him who both grants and will rule every empire.

It is fitting, therefore, that I too should pray to our Lord Jesus Christ that he who willed your Piety to take thought for the concord of his church may deign to grant fulfilment in this matter, so that in your times the whole world may rejoice, endowed with the orthodox faith. As for what you have ordered concerning the gathering of a synod, I have instructed my brothers and fellow bishops, who will follow shortly, to set before your Glory what ought to be done; from their account, if divine favour attends my prayers, you will be able to learn everything more fittingly. Given on the eighth day before the Ides of July, in the consulship of Florentius.

THE EMPEROR ANASTASIUS AUGUSTUS TO POPE HORMISDAS. BY THEOPOMPUS AND SEVERIANUS, MEN MOST DISTINGUISHED. Everything that kindness has conceived is carried forward by the mind's sweet striving and by a praiseworthy haste. Such purposes believe no rest can be granted them until they have brought what they desire to a most wholesome outcome. Then the haste itself finds a kind of rest, once the hope of their prayers has been fulfilled.
We have borne this in the present case for good reason, until heavenly favour should open the way to our petition and grant a serene fulfilment to your promise.

The very great length of the journey, or the harshness of a winter beyond its usual custom, made what we hoped for uncertain. Meanwhile, therefore, we held our desires back within our minds, waiting for the divine favours that decide by their intervention whether a matter turns out well.

Recognizing, then, that His goodness had granted us the first favour, namely that the embassy sent to Your Beatitude returned safely, we went on to the second: that we should send the promised embassy. Through it, a report might be made of the matters we discussed at length with most holy men. Likewise, under God's auspices, the serene light of both our petition and your grace might shine forth in full, and the long-awaited joys might be granted to the whole world.

And so, to make this report and to render the honour of a greeting, we have sent to Your Holiness the illustrious Theopompus, count of the domestics, who commands a school of our sacred palace. He is faithful to us both for his character and for his affection for our native province. With him we send the most distinguished Severianus, count of our sacred consistory. Confirming the content of this letter in their own words, they are to press for the swift fulfilment of what is awaited, which we believe has also pleased the heavenly mercy. Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, at Constantinople, in the consulship of the most distinguished Peter.

HORMISDAS TO ANASTASIUS AUGUSTUS. BY THEOPOMPUS AND SEVERIANUS. Most clement emperor, you tell us that your mind is troubled by an eager longing until the hoped-for unity is restored as you wish. Good are the desires for salvation, and praiseworthy is the intention that commends itself to God in this way. It is a special proof of prudence when someone impatiently seeks what he believes will benefit him.

If in bodily diseases a slow cure is harmful, how much more serious is a belated desire for faithful remedies where the salvation of the soul is concerned? Let us take warning from spiritual teachings and not put off until a later day what can do us good. The most wise Solomon cries out: "Do not delay to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day." The span of life is uncertain, and so the soul's remedies ought to be made secure. Then he may enter into the joy of his Lord whom the Lord, at his coming, finds doing what pleases him.

So I confess I wondered why the promised embassy delayed so long, since force must be used if the kingdom of heaven is to be seized. Yet the very prompting that Your Clemency's address reveals holds out the hope of heavenly mercy, for even the will to do good comes from above. And I am confident that he who began a good work in you will carry it through to the end.

Press on, then, along the way you have begun. Spurn the slippery paths of those who go astray, and keep your footsteps firm with us upon the rock. The holy Church grew through such concord, as the history of the Acts of the Apostles testifies in these words: "The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul." How can people be bound together by the bonds of grace when their hearts differ in what they believe?

Lord emperor, let what you do prove the good faith of your words. Men's hearts are known by their fruits, not by their speeches. Even our father Abraham pleased God not by bare faith but by works that commended his faith.

I have weighed the stewardship entrusted to me and Your Piety's kindness toward me. Therefore, lord son, I urge and beseech you to direct the zeal for peace that you show in your letters toward settling with us, with God's help, the matters that trouble the churches. As the prophet says, "Great peace have those who love your name, and for them there is no stumbling block."

Your Clemency knows what separates us from the unity we long to restore. Take care that what you profess and praise is fulfilled in deed. Follow with all your strength the discipline of the apostle whose communion you believe should be sought. Shun completely the ruinous contagion of the guilty, knowing that the impious have no share with the devout and that faith has no fellowship with faithlessness.

It follows that whoever detests the founders of errors should hate their followers too. What is condemned in the seed must be held accursed in the flower. Offer this gift to God; offer it, I pray, for the sake of your reign. Christ has long been waiting for this sacrifice from you in return for all the blessings he has given you.

Why should one need to plead with a man who is himself pleading? You charge the senate of the city of Rome to urge me toward peace. I not only join them in turning words of supplication to you, but with the universal Church I throw myself at your feet.

Hear me, for I act as an ambassador for Christ. Do not allow Christ's members to be torn apart by wicked dogs. Cut off what you see is incurable, and heal what is sick. Why should what is sound be shaken by being joined to what is diseased? Keep the order that truth itself has laid down, and you will have given back to the world the peace you ask for.

I ask these things on this present occasion, and I will take care to plead again and often. I hope that this persistence of mine will please God, and that with you too it will not be in vain, through constant petitions, since the Lord taught us to pray in this way. Given...
(113.) ANASTASIUS AUGUSTUS TO THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME. BY THEOPOMPUS AND SEVERIANUS, MEN MOST DISTINGUISHED.

THE EMPEROR CAESAR FLAVIUS ANASTASIUS, PONTIFF, RENOWNED CONQUEROR OF THE GERMANS, RENOWNED CONQUEROR OF THE ALAMANNI, RENOWNED CONQUEROR OF THE FRANKS, RENOWNED CONQUEROR OF THE SARMATIANS, IN THE TWENTY-FIFTH YEAR OF HIS TRIBUNICIAN POWER, CONSUL FOR THE THIRD TIME, PIOUS, FORTUNATE, VICTOR AND TRIUMPHANT, EVER AUGUSTUS, FATHER OF THE FATHERLAND, SENDS GREETINGS TO THE PROCONSULS, CONSULS, PRAETORS, TRIBUNES OF THE PLEBS, AND HIS SENATE. If you and your children are well, it is good; I and my army are well.

Whenever the good of both commonwealths is pursued with favourable will, not only exhortation but also request is thought fitting. In this way two causes converge into one, and the mind, once stirred, may be able to attain what is fortunate and good for both parties.

Christ, our God and Lord, called us back to himself through his most gentle will and by a kind of entreaty belonging to his dispensation [?]. Having redeemed us with his own blood, he restored us to freedom in order to grant salvation to mortals. It does not seem unreasonable, then, to hope that the conscript fathers of the bountiful city of Rome will join the imperial petition and seek, both from the most glorious king and from the most blessed pope, what may profit both us and them in common, God willing. Namely: that they should not listen to the contrived speeches of fugitives, made up of nothing but lies. Rather, they should accept the satisfaction that has been made plain both by the truth and by the inquiry of the envoys who were sent, and come together toward the desired peace with a will acceptable to God.

It is beyond doubt that over a long series of years your steadfastness has been the defender of a great part of the commonwealth. Your most holy assembly ought therefore to strive with skilful zeal and careful labour. Approach both the exalted king, to whom the power and care of ruling you has been entrusted, and the venerable pope, to whom the faculty of interceding with God has been granted. Ask that they deign to apply their goodwill to the matter in which the members of both commonwealths may be saved by the healing we hope for.

You will be keeping your ancient custom, one well known for your wise counsel, if by deliberating, hoping and requesting you bring about, under God's auspices, what serves the public good. Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, at Chalcedon, in the consulship of Peter.
(114.) REPLY OF THE SENATE OF THE CITY OF ROME TO ANASTASIUS AUGUSTUS. BY THEOPOMPUS AND SEVERIANUS, MEN MOST DISTINGUISHED.

Unconquered emperor, rulers always look first for the devotion of those who petition them, and the favour of lords is won by obedience alone. If so, you will surely recognize with what rejoicing your senate received the oracles of your sacred command. This was especially so because the will of our lord, the most unconquered King Theoderic, your son, was added to it, for he commanded obedience to your instructions. And we know that, above all your benefits, we are raised up most when you consider us worthy to receive your commands.

At once, therefore, in our zeal to carry out the sacred command, we decided that the most blessed Pope Hormisdas should be entreated. It is too little to say of him that in his kindness he anticipated the prayers of those who petitioned him. He also joined his prayers to ours, so that what you urge might come about, and he supported his will with testimonies from the Gospel. He showed that the world is weighed down even more by scandals than by the multitude of its sins, since the Lord says, "Woe to the world because of scandals." He also showed that people must cut off the part of their members that causes scandal, rather than be cast into eternal fire for refusing to renounce scandals.

After this he showed from examples in the divine readings how good the fruits of peace are. He said that the apostle Paul, though full of the grace of God, found nothing better to wish for those he cared for than that the peace of God, which surpasses all excellence, should abound in their minds. He also noted that in the Gospel the Lord says: "For the peacemakers shall be called sons of God."

Returning again to that teacher of all the scriptures, he showed how much greater love is even than faith, by which we confidently look for the kingdom of heaven and by believing are saved from the torments of sin. He added this testimony: "Hope, faith, love; but the greatest of all is love." By the gift of divine grace, the same Spirit makes all virtues void in those who lack love.

So we shun scandals because of the punishment, and we pursue peace for the goods that peace brings, and Christ, who is love, urges us toward love. What, then, holds back those who are hastening with Catholic ardour? Why should the person of the sinner Acacius stand in the way of those who wish to see Christ? Why should those who are free of error of their own be burdened by someone else's?

These points have been set out more fully in the venerable pope's reply. Even so, we thought they should be included as a mark of our devoted obedience. Otherwise, if we kept back the answer we received to our petition, we might be thought not to have made the request at all.

Accordingly, most pious emperor, the senate, encouraged by the clemency of Your Serenity, has added these things in its own name. We hope you will be known to be as dutiful in restoring the unity of the Church as you were kindly disposed in bringing harmony to both commonwealths. The peace between kingdoms is known to benefit only the subjects, but this peace of religion profits the ruler together with his people.

Who would not think that the followers of faithless heresies have sinned more than their founders? Who would not condemn those who divide the members of Christ again, after the gibbet of the cross? If only this affair had begun under your reign, so that the evils could more easily have been checked as they arose rather than once they had grown! For who could doubt that [?] could not have existed in the reign of one under whom he saw the error being corrected?

HORMISDAS TO ANASTASIUS AUGUSTUS. BY THE BISHOPS ENNODIUS AND FORTUNATUS, THE PRESBYTER VENANTIUS, THE DEACON VITALIS, AND THE NOTARY HILARUS. Your Serenity acts well and profitably in applying the care of your princely acumen not only to the duty of governing the commonwealth. You also ennoble that care with better purposes, and through your concern to restore unity you win the favour of the author of your venerable empire. Rulers can be sure of protection if, while they preside, the chastity of the Church is not stained by any insolent admixture from the devil.

How can the Church direct pure prayers to our God on behalf of princes if the people is mortally corrupted by faithlessness? In emperors, wisdom made perfect according to God comes before all other goods. In the same way, supplication for them ought to come from the sanctuary of clean hearts and from souls rich in faith. Most sublime lord, no material for triumph could please you more than the subjugation of faithlessness. By the prerogative of the office entrusted to us, we also put this to you with confidence: a ruler who could, by God's gift, remove the darkness of errors from his subjects, but allows it to remain, comes close to letting his own splendour be darkened by another's cloud.

In your most sacred letter, Your Clemency has announced a coming synod. In the same pages you have reminded us, at God's bidding as we believe, that we ought to attend it. We rejoice at this, knowing that it is the mark of upright minds to seek out the teachers of the venerable Church. Only those who do not hold to what is just shun the examination of conscience. A person who wishes, through the apostolic and spotless faith and through competent preachers, either to be confirmed or to be corrected proclaims with a joyful mouth the splendour of his good will.

There is no precedent for this from a former age, and no older instance of the kind is recorded in books or preserved in memory. Yet that does not matter to us. By God's favour and at your piety's invitation, it is sweet to us to begin better things and to take upon ourselves the undertaking of so glorious a work, which we did not inherit from our forebears.

For we gladly undertake to do everything for the restoration of the faith and the peace of the churches, on these conditions. The definition of our elders and of the holy fathers must remain unshaken to its roots. Nestorius must be anathematized with his partners. He empties the sacraments of the divine nature and falsely claims that the blessed Virgin Mary is the mother of a mere man. He forgets the angel's annunciation, by which it was made known to the world that the one to be born of her would be called holy, the Son of God.

Away with so insulting an "honouring" of God by the impious! The Godhead so worked in the Virgin's womb that from her came forth a substance united to itself, made of flesh and a human soul, joined in a union undivided yet unconfused. Thus, out of love for our redemption, the person of our Christ Jesus is one in both natures, the mystery building up [?] ... by restoration he could undergo death [?] ... might be able to repair the frailty of nature by the power of the heavenly rule. Or thus, because of the unity of the person, the Lord of majesty is believed to have been crucified, and the Son of Man is believed to have come down from heaven.

Let the dullness of Eutyches, ignorant [?] ... of all good things, be renounced too, together with his companions; its very name is already detestable. He testified that our God and Lord Jesus Christ had only the appearance of flesh and not the reality of our substance. He did not know of whom it was promised that his persecutors would look on the one they had pierced. Both natures so persist in one and the same person that one Son of God, Jesus Christ, God and man, appears to the hearts of the faithful.

After his resurrection the Lord lived and ate with men for forty days. What did his presence accomplish, if not to show, by these acts, that the healing was older than the wound, against those who would deny the reality of his flesh? For he said to the disciples: "Why are you thinking [?]? Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have." Nor would it have been a mystery that he came in to them when the doors were shut if he had not had a complete human body.

By this gift of the Word we could carry our discourse further. Yet we think it enough, through our God, to entreat Your Clemency, who is well instructed, with these brief suggestions. We hope that, following the example of your venerable predecessors Marcian and Leo, you will also support the labour and care of the pastoral office by sharing your princely power with it. By God's favour your hope of victories will not be cast down, if you strengthen the bishops' struggle against the devil's stealthy attacks with a peaceful ordering of the contest.

Let the commemoration of Dioscorus, partner of Eutyches, and of the parricides Timothy and Peter never revive in the memory of the holy churches. Let the definition of the revered synod of Chalcedon be kept by all, as God works through you. Let Acacius, polluted by communion with Peter, the son of darkness, have as his partners those he chose. Among his other excesses, he did not keep himself clean even where Peter of Antioch and his accomplices were concerned. Let the curses heaped on the holy teachings of Pope Leo of holy memory cease. While Leo remains among his own, these curses punish only those who utter them.

In the matters we have set out above, we call on the care of your imperial rule. By guarding this, Your Piety will be able, after many years, to possess your crown and sceptre carried over into the other world.

Receive our prayers, sent out of love for you through Ennodius and Fortunatus, our brothers and fellow bishops, and through our sons Venantius the presbyter, Vitalis the deacon and Hilarus the notary. Their faith in the fear of God and their zeal have shone out clearly among us. Lend a gracious mind to those who come to you as suppliants in our place!

We hope, and trusting in God we promise, that the efforts you devote to the true religion will not go without recompense and reward. Given on the third day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of the most distinguished Florentius.
(116.) MEMORANDUM GIVEN TO THE BISHOPS ENNODIUS AND FORTUNATUS, THE PRESBYTER VENANTIUS, THE DEACON VITALIS, AND THE NOTARY HILARUS.

When, with God's help and through the prayers of the apostles, you come into the regions of Greece, if the bishops wish to come to meet you, receive them with the respect that befits them. If they wish to provide you with lodging, do not refuse it, so that the laity cannot claim that you want no harmony with them.

But if they wish to invite you to a banquet, decline with a polite excuse, saying: 'Pray that we may first be found worthy to share that mystical table in common, and then this one will be more pleasant for you.'

Do not accept provisions or anything else they wish to offer, except transport if the situation requires it. Excuse yourselves by saying that you lack nothing, and hope instead that they will incline their hearts to you, for in that are gifts and riches and charity and unity and whatever surely belongs to religious joy.

When, by God's favour, you reach Constantinople with these instructions, lodge wherever the most clement emperor directs. Before you see him, give no one leave to come to you except those whom His Piety sends. After you have seen the prince, however, if any who are orthodox and of our communion wish to see you out of zeal for unity, receive them with every caution. Through them you may perhaps also be able to find out what is going on.

So when you have been presented, hand the emperor the letter with this address: 'Your father greets you. Every day he prays to God and commends your reign to the shrines of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, asking that God, who gave you the desire to send to his Beatitude and consult him on behalf of the church, may himself also reward your good will by bringing it to fulfilment.'

If they wish to learn the plan of the embassy before he accepts the documents, use these words: 'Please order the letter to be received.' If he says, 'What do the documents contain?' answer: 'They contain greetings to Your Piety, and he gives thanks to God because he knows you are concerned for the unity of the church. Read it and you will learn.' Make no mention whatever of any matter until the letter has first been received and read.

After the letter has been received and read, add: 'He has also sent a letter to your servant Vitalian, because Vitalian, as he himself wrote, sent his men to your father the holy pope after receiving permission from Your Piety. But since it was right that he should first address Your Clemency, he has done this, so that at your command and direction we may, with God's favour, deliver to Vitalian the letter we have brought.'

If the emperor asks for the letter addressed by us to Vitalian, answer thus: 'Your father the holy pope did not instruct us to do this, nor can we do anything without his order. Yet so that you may know how simple the letter is, and that it contains nothing but entreaties addressed to Your Piety to incline your mind to the unity of the church, assign someone to accompany us, and in his presence let the letter we deliver be read.' But if the emperor says that he must read it himself, answer that you have already explained that the holy pope did not instruct you to allow this.

If he says, 'That is only what is contained in the letter; other things could be conveyed by verbal instructions,' then answer: 'Far be that from our conscience! That is not our custom. We have come for God's cause; are we then to sin against God? The holy pope's embassy is simple, and his petition, his very prayers, are known to all: that the decrees of the fathers not be corrupted and that heretics be removed from the churches. Apart from this our embassy contains nothing.'

If he says, 'That is why I invited the holy pope to a synod, so that if anything is in doubt it might be removed,' answer: 'We give thanks to God and to Your Piety, because we see that you have the disposition and the mind that the whole body of bishops should keep what the fathers established. For true and holy unity can exist among the churches of Christ only if you, with God's help, choose to keep what your predecessors Marcian and Leo upheld.' If he says, 'And what are these things you speak of?
answer: 'That the Synod of Chalcedon and the letters of the holy Pope Leo, which were written against the heretics Nestorius, Eutyches and Dioscorus, be in no way corrupted.'

If he says, 'We both accept and hold the Synod of Chalcedon and the letters of Pope Leo,' at once give thanks and kiss His Clemency's breast, saying: 'Now we know that God is gracious to us, since you hasten to grant such things. For this is the catholic faith; this is what the apostles preached, without which no one can be orthodox; this is what the whole body of bishops ought to hold and preserve by their preaching.'

If he says, 'The bishops are orthodox; they do not depart from the decrees of the fathers,' answer: 'Then if the decrees of the fathers are kept, and what was confirmed at the holy Council of Chalcedon is corrupted in nothing, why is there so much discord among the churches of these regions? What causes the bishops of the East not to be

of one mind?' If he says, 'The bishops were at peace and there was no discord among them; the holy pope's predecessor stirred up their minds by sending letters and, by agitating them, threw them into confusion,' answer: 'We have in our hands the letters that Pope Symmachus of holy memory sent. If, beyond what Your Piety has said, namely "I follow the Council of Chalcedon, I accept the letters of Pope Leo," they contain anything other than an exhortation to keep these things, then it is true that the confusion arose through him. But if the letters contain what your father hopes for and what Your Piety agrees to, what did he do that could seem blame-

worthy in him?' To these words add entreaties and tears, pleading: 'Lord Emperor, consider God! Set his coming judgment before your eyes! The holy fathers who established these things followed the faith of the blessed apostle Peter, on which the church of Christ was built.'

If the emperor says, 'What you want me to do by persecution [?], I already hold: see, communicate with me, for I accept the Synod of Chalcedon and embrace the letters of Pope Leo. Now communicate with me!', answer: 'In what way does Your Piety wish us to communicate with you? We do not shun Your Piety when you proclaim these things, for we know that you fear God, and we rejoice that you are glad to keep the decrees of the fathers. We therefore ask with confidence that through you the church may return to unity. Let all the bishops know your will, and that you keep the Synod of Chalcedon, the letters of Pope Leo and the decrees of the apostolic see.'

If he says that he must know how these things are to be done, again entreat him humbly, saying: 'Your father has written to the bishops generally. Attach your sacred letters to his, declaring that you uphold what the apostolic see also preaches. Then those who are orthodox will in no way be separated from the unity of the apostolic see, and those who oppose them will be revealed. Once this has been arranged, your father is ready, if need be, to come in person, and, provided the decrees of the fathers are kept, not to refuse whatever serves the integrity of the church.'

If the emperor says, 'Very well; now receive the bishop of our city back into communion!', again add entreaties, saying humbly: 'Lord Emperor, with God's help, and with your effort and support, we have come to make peace and to settle the dispute in your city. The dispute concerns two persons, and that matter has its own course. Let the body of bishops be set in order first; let there be one catholic communion; and then, in the next place, the case of these men, or of any others who are outside their churches, can be examined more carefully.'

If the emperor says, 'You are speaking of Macedonius. I understand your subtlety: he is a heretic, and on no account can he be recalled,' answer: 'Lord Emperor, we champion no one personally. If Your Piety considers it, we are speaking rather for the sake of your soul and your reputation: let there be an inquiry, and if he is a heretic, let that be established by a judgment, so that it may not be said that a man reputed orthodox was unjustly crushed.' If the emperor says, 'What do you want? Tell me now!

Will you talk about the Synod of Chalcedon and the letters of Pope Leo? See, the man who is bishop of the city agrees to these things,' answer: 'If he keeps them, they will be all the more able to help him when his case is examined. And since you gave your servant Vitalian, master of the soldiers, such permission that he might hope from the most blessed pope [?] that for such matters an examination of the case be held before him, let everything be preserved intact for those persons who may be in dispute over the see.'

If the emperor says, 'Is my city to be without a bishop? Does it please you that there should be no bishop where I reside?' answer: 'We have already said that there is a dispute between two persons in this city. As for the canons, we have already explained that to break the canons is to sin against religion. There are many remedies and many expedients by which Your Piety need not be without communion and the proper form of judicial process may be preserved intact.'

If he says, 'What are these remedies?' answer: 'They are not newly devised by us. While the case is suspended, let someone from among the other bishops who agrees with Your Piety's confession and with the decrees of the apostolic see hold the place of bishop of Constantinople in the meantime, until the outcome of the inquiry.'

If, with God's help, the bishops are willing to conform to the apostolic see, you have the text of the libellus issued from the church's archive, according to which they are to make their profession. If, however, catholics submit petitions against other bishops, by all means receive the petitions against those who shamelessly anathematize the Synod of Chalcedon and do not accept the letters of the holy Pope Leo. But reserve the case for the judgment of the apostolic see, so that you give hope of a hearing while the authority due to us is nonetheless reserved.

If, however, the most serene emperor promises to do everything, provided only that we come in person, by all means first send his sacred letter through the provinces by means of the bishops, or our letter carried by one of you, together with persons appointed by the emperor, so that it may thus become known to all that he keeps the Council of Chalcedon and the letters of the holy Pope Leo. When matters have gone forward in this way, send us a letter, in the sign of Christ, so that we may arrange our coming.

Moreover, it is the custom for all bishops to be presented to the emperor by the bishop of Constantinople. If their crafty scheming, in the wish to learn the form of the embassy, contrives that you see the emperor together with Timothy, who now appears to govern the church of Constantinople, act as follows. If you learn before you go in to the emperor that some people are arranging this, send word while you have not yet been presented: 'The father of Your Piety has instructed us to see Your Clemency without any of the bishops present.'

Persist in this until the emperor himself sets the custom aside. But if he absolutely refuses, or if it happens by some trick that you unexpectedly find Timothy with the emperor, put it this way: 'Let Your Piety order that we be granted a private audience, so that we may set out the matters for which we were sent.' If he says, 'Speak, here in front of him!

answer: 'We mean him no insult; we are only making known what concerns the matter. Our embassy also concerns him personally, and so he cannot be present when we make our representations.' On no account set forth anything while he is present, but once he has left, lay out the business of the embassy.
(116a) LIKEWISE THE HEADINGS OF THE PARTICULAR MATTERS.

That the holy Synod of Chalcedon and the letters of the holy Pope Leo be kept. The most clement emperor, in agreement, should send general sacred letters from His Piety to all the bishops, declaring that he both believes and upholds the above. The bishops who agree should also proclaim in church, before the Christian people, that they embrace the holy Synod of Chalcedon and the letters of the most holy Pope Leo, which he wrote against the heretics Nestorius, Eutyches and Dioscorus. They should anathematize also their followers Timothy Aelurus and Peter, and those held guilty in that same cause, and at the same time Acacius, formerly bishop of the church of Constantinople, and also Peter of Antioch, together with their associates. They are to do this by writing with their own hand, in the presence of chosen venerable men, according to the text of the libellus that we have issued through our notaries.

Those deported into exile on account of church matters are to be recalled for a hearing before the apostolic see, so that a judgment and a true examination may be held concerning them, with their case reserved intact for inquiry. But if any who are in communion with the apostolic see, preaching and following the catholic faith, have been driven out or are held in exile, it is right that these be recalled before all else.

Further, among other things we enjoined on the legates that if libelli happen to be submitted against bishops who have persecuted catholics, judgment of them should be reserved to the apostolic see, so that the decrees of the venerable fathers may be observed in their regard, for the edification of all.
(116b) COPY OF THE LIBELLUS SENT THROUGH THE BISHOPS ENNODIUS AND FORTUNATUS, THE PRESBYTER VENANTIUS, THE DEACON VITALIS AND THE NOTARY HILARUS.

The first condition of salvation is to keep the rule of right faith and never to stray from the decrees of the fathers. And since the saying of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be passed over, when he says, 'You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church,' what was said is proved by the course of events, for in the apostolic see the catholic religion has always been kept unblemished.

Desiring, then, never to be separated from this hope and faith, and following the decrees of the fathers in all things, we anathematize all heresies, and especially the heretic Nestorius, once bishop of the city of Constantinople, who was condemned at the Council of Ephesus by Celestine, pope of the city of Rome, and by Saint Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria. Together with him we anathematize Eutyches and Dioscorus of Alexandria, condemned at the holy Synod of Chalcedon, which we follow and embrace;

to these we add the parricide Timothy, surnamed Aelurus, and also his disciple and follower in all things, Peter of Alexandria. Likewise we condemn and anathematize Acacius, formerly bishop of Constantinople, who was condemned by the apostolic see as their accomplice and follower, and those who have remained in fellowship and communion with them; for whoever joins himself to the communion of such men deserves a sentence of condemnation like theirs. We likewise condemn Peter of Antioch, with his followers and the followers of all those named above.

Accordingly we accept and approve all the letters of the blessed Pope Leo that he wrote concerning the Christian religion. Hence, as we have said, following the apostolic see in all things and proclaiming all its decrees, I hope to be found worthy to be with you in the one communion that the apostolic see proclaims, in which is the complete and true solidity of the Christian religion. We promise also that the names of those cut off from the communion of the catholic church, that is, those who do not agree with the apostolic see, are not to be recited during the sacred mysteries.

I have signed this profession of mine with my own hand and presented it to you, Hormisdas, holy and venerable pope of the city of Rome, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the most illustrious Agapitus.
(117) COPY OF THE REPORT OF JOHN, BISHOP OF NICOPOLIS, SENT THROUGH RUFINUS, HIS DEACON.
TO MY LORD, MOST HOLY AND MOST BLESSED IN ALL THINGS, FATHER OF FATHERS, FELLOW MINISTER AND CHIEF OF BISHOPS, HORMISDAS: JOHN SENDS GREETING IN THE LORD.

It has always been my concern to seek nothing more than to attend to my own affairs and to give my private way of life over to anxious care. But since God's judgments are a great abyss, as I know Your Beatitude also teaches, when our late father and archbishop Alcison was called by Christ, the chief of shepherds, to the heavenly mansions, for a reason known to him who is Lord of all that is possible, the holy synod, which is given to good works, and the clergy passed the shepherd's lot to me.

Referring everything to God, who sets free the tongues of those who stammer, I fittingly have recourse to your prayers, asking that, according to the custom of your apostolic see, you deign to take care of the Nicopolitans as of all the churches, in keeping with your ancient spiritual ordering.

For as I ask that words be given me when I open my mouth, as the blessed apostle taught and the Lord himself commanded, ask the giver of these things together with me, seek together with me as I seek, and receive me with your spiritual hand as I knock. If you do this, most holy one, I shall be able both to receive and to find, and, as Christ opens the door, to walk rightly by the word of truth.

There are some who pretend to share our belief and to follow the holy synods assembled at Nicaea, Constantinople and Ephesus, at which the most holy bishops of blessed memory Celestine of your apostolic see and Cyril of Alexandria were the leaders, and also the synod assembled at Chalcedon against the impious Eutyches, which confirmed in itself all the aforesaid by the reasoning of truth and orthodoxy. Yet these people dare to attack us, as though we shunned the bond of concord without reason.

It is my desire to follow your teaching, as my predecessor Alcison, now among the saints, had done. I anathematize Dioscorus, and Timothy called Aelurus, and Peter their successor, and Acacius, who joined himself to them through communion with Peter, and Peter who threw the church of Antioch into turmoil; and I follow in all things the synodical and truly apostolic letters written by Leo, the true prelate of the Roman church. And I ask this:

admonish me more fully and completely about what ought to be kept, and make known in your protective letters what I ought to abstain from. Then, even if, being perhaps still inexperienced, I have been appointed to the order of readings [?], or have said or done anything at variance with your apostolic teachings, I may, schooled by your words, be able to resist the devices of the heretics. For if you do this, most holy ones, you will find the bishops of our holy synod firmer, and you will strengthen the clergy and the people in good works, making the holy church of the Nicopolitans truly your own household.

We ask you to receive kindly, as befits you, the venerable deacon Rufinus, who has been sent on so necessary a matter. Give him your confidence, and deign to grant him a swift return to us, bearing spiritual and apostolic decrees, O most holy in all things.
I and those who are with me send our warmest greetings in the Lord to all the brotherhood in Christ of Your Beatitude.

HORMISDAS TO JOHN, BISHOP OF NICOPOLIS. CARRIED BY THE DEACON RUFINUS. We rejoiced greatly in the Lord, dearest brother, when we received your letter, in which you state that by the grace of God you have taken up the priesthood. This is sure faith, and this is hope secure and free of doubt: the belief that the cause of everything good lies in the dispensation from above.

Knowing this, dearest brother, you devoutly give thanks for the benefits you have received from our God. Yet this too comes down from the same fountain of mercy: that human humility submits itself to its author. For he says: "Upon whom does my spirit rest, if not upon the one who is humble and quiet and trembles at my words?"

In these things, then, in which proving [?] such a disposition, you will shine out all the more clearly as an example of this virtue to others too, since God has so ordered things that the church of the catholics may also glory in you.

For as one taught by the divine testimonies and, as the apostle says, formed by instruction in the sacred writings, you made this the auspicious beginning of your ordination: that you stood with the judgments of the apostolic see against those who go astray. Nor could you repay the giver of such great benefits in any other way than by showing plain zeal for the apostolic confession against his enemies.

For it is well known that those people stand outside the fold of religion who themselves profess the knowledge of the faith, the confidence [?] * * and therefore the equal share in holy communion is fruitless for them, even though it matches that of the devout, because there is no doubt that whoever does not use the freedom he has earned confesses himself subject to iniquity. Why should we glory in teachings that we do not follow? He who does not prove himself a disciple of someone's teaching calls that person master falsely.

But since your confession is now in every point like ours, and you have taken up again the love of your own freedom, desiring once more to share in your fathers' inheritance, embrace the grace of the ancient tradition and stand firm on that unshaken foundation. Do not change your hearts with the times. Such changeableness usually marks an unsteady purpose, and so we must hold fast to what is well founded, since divine mercy knows how to foster such efforts. Then the firmness of your faith will bear fruit for you in the salvation of others, and the fervour of your zeal will be able to kindle in others too the desire to recover what is rightly theirs. In this way the holy apostle may be believed to have said of you as well: "Your zeal has stirred up very many."

Therefore, having condemned the impieties of Nestorius and Eutyches according to the decrees of the synods, and execrating their followers likewise, let us say with exultation: "'Come out from their midst and be separate, and touch nothing unclean,' says the Lord." For how can anyone detest the originators of evil inventions if he does not shun their followers? Or how does he hate the root who does not execrate the offshoot as well? The fame of teachers is proclaimed in their disciples, and as long as the root of seeds wickedly sown keeps flourishing under the care of successors, the memory of their authors will not perish.

Let Acacius also be added to the lost teachings of Eutyches, since under the communion of Peter he was mixed in with the error of all the condemned. Your love stated this clearly in your letter when you affirmed your faith.

For the fuller instruction of your faith regarding the procedure by which those who return should be received into our communion, we have appended a memorandum below. We hope in God, the giver of all good things, that through your love's praiseworthy earnestness for the faith this will benefit the salvation not only of your neighbours but also of all those whom the swift report of your faith and devout will may reach.

We have received in the love of Christ the deacon Rufinus, who delivered your letter to us. Commending him to the prayers of the apostles, we have sent him back in peace, and we urge you to read aloud to the people the letters we have addressed both to your charity and to the synod. Know that we have done this too as a commendation of your faith. Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Peter.
(119.) COPY OF THE REPORT OF THE SYNOD OF OLD EPIRUS.

TO OUR LORD HORMISDAS, MOST HOLY AND MOST BLESSED IN ALL THINGS, FATHER OF FATHERS, FELLOW MINISTER AND CHIEF OF BISHOPS, THE SYNOD OF OLD EPIRUS: JOHN, MATTHEW, CONSTANTINE, CHRISTODORUS, HILARY, PHILIP, JULIAN AND CHRYSIPPUS. If we attempt to open with a fitting preface, we must deliver it with many tears.

For a great many of us were in the imperial city of Constantinople while your most holy representatives were staying there: the bishops Ennodius and Fortunatus, the presbyter Venantius, the deacon Vitalis and the notary Hilarus, who were carrying on the contest of piety they had undertaken. With us also was our father and archbishop Alcison, now numbered among the saints. He submitted petitions of supplication with full confidence and was deemed worthy by your beatitude to enter communion with your apostolic see together with us.

But since he who holds power over all suddenly called him to himself, we came back to our homeland held fast by unrestrained weeping. Yet by God's grace we in no way tolerated error, but everywhere followed your decrees.

And as we wept and lamented, together with the fellow ministers left with us in the province, over who among the orthodox could rightly shepherd Christ's sheep, he who comforts the humble comforted us too through your prayers. He showed the metropolitan city the most holy John, who in all things was raised in the church from boyhood without fault, indeed lived in it so commendably that no one in it surpasses him in conduct, and who yields to no one at all in zeal for orthodoxy according to your apostolic admonitions.

By God's providence, then, we have ordained him prelate of the most holy church of the Nicopolitans. We ask that, according to ancient custom, you embrace him too with your fatherly heart. By God's grace, may your admonitions and teachings make you an invincible armour for us and for him. Incline your ear to our prayers and devise the means of godly concord, according to the apostolic foresight divinely inspired in you, so that in the peace that is dear to him all the most holy churches may be fitted together, weave an unfading crown for you, and be held together in Christ in all piety and humility.
We ask you to receive kindly the venerable deacon Rufinus, sent for this most necessary cause, and to send him back to us speedily, bearing your apostolic teachings.

AND IN ANOTHER HAND: Pray for my well-being, most holy father of fathers. I, John, bishop of Euroea, have submitted this. Pray for my well-being in the Lord, most holy and most blessed father of fathers. I, Matthew, bishop of Buthrotum, have submitted this. I, Constantine, bishop of Hadrianopolis, have submitted this. Pray for my well-being in the Lord, most holy and most blessed father of fathers. I, Christodorus, bishop of Anchiasmus, have submitted this. I, Hilary, bishop of Photice, have submitted this. I, Philip, bishop of Phoenice, have submitted this. I, Julian, bishop of Dodona, have submitted this. I, Chrysippus, bishop of Corcyra, have submitted this.
(120.) HORMISDAS TO THE SYNOD OF OLD EPIRUS. CARRIED BY THE DEACON RUFINUS.

Blessed be God, who joins together the members of his church! Blessed be God, who unites those divided at the instigation of the evil one in the same solid unity they once had! For although the enemy has long cried out like the partridge and, as the prophet declared, gathered those he did not hatch, he will without doubt be left desolate by them. The Lord's sheep do not follow a stranger or listen to the voice of another shepherd.

So we are not surprised that you have returned to the way of salvation, though we rather find fault with your slowness in this restoration. In the stability we seek, dearest brothers, we ought to make use of examples from our own household.

For at that time Timothy of Chersonesus, harmful as a pupil and more harmful as a teacher (he was a follower of Dioscorus and also the teacher of Peter), unleashed his reckless savagery against Proterius of blessed memory. He went beyond every limit of cruelty by murdering that devout man at the very altar, and he could scarcely hold back his own jaws from that holy blood.

Then the universal church, roused to hatred of the parricide, [cut off] the perpetrator of so great a crime not only from communion but also from the very [name] of Christian * * the minds of all were stunned with a strange new amazement at the audacity of such presumption. Then the blessed Eugenius, who held the primacy of your province, together with the holy synod under him, showed a zeal like that by which Phinehas commended himself to God. Not only can time not hide the memory of this; its fame grows greater day by day among the orthodox. To neglect the efforts of these men, so well proven, and not to cherish their judgments, is to fail in the very confession of our Lord.

And now, after your profession and your letter, all the doctrines of the faith are the same for us, since God joins his own together. We must pray that your will, which has lifted our spirits, may remain steadfast in that confession. But it is necessary, without regard for fear, to pursue the madness of those who strive against the faith. The more the error of the unbelievers boils over, the more our steadfastness commends itself if it resists. These things must not be overlooked out of forbearance, since this evil, fed by the vice of bad custom, has grown up among many under a certain colour of law, while wicked efforts band together and right ones hold back.

For, to speak of the matter at hand: Eutyches, as the inventor of an abominable heresy, is excluded even by those who love his doctrines. Among those very people he is so hated and shunned that they hate even the mention of his name. Yet these perverse ministers of the church's institutions, by another route, embrace as truly orthodox the very man they detest as a true heretic. For at the holy synod of Chalcedon Dioscorus, who held the same views, was condemned on the same grounds. Since one sentence struck both of them, let someone explain how a person who follows or loves either of them can exempt himself from the sentence that condemned those it named. Those whom equal transgression or impiety links together are undoubtedly bound by one chain of condemnation as well.

Timothy and Peter, their followers, are men corrupt in mind and a detestable plague upon the catholic name. Acacius embraced their communion in the person of Peter and likewise deserved to incur their sentence. Thinking so great an evil a small matter and never turning his purpose toward better things, he did not hold back even from the deeds at Antioch that we detest. There too he joined in communion with the transgressor Peter. He acted no less as an enemy toward the church of Apamea, and he did not order the church of Tyre with the integrity he should have.

For these reasons, beloved brothers, let us free ourselves from entanglement with them and keep the apostolic discipline, as if leaving some pestilent region. Let us look to our salvation with all diligence and care, and shun the errors of the abominable Nestorius as carefully as we pursue the impious inventions of Eutyches. For now especially, the doctrines of the faith are assailed from opposite directions by the snares of the men we have named. These wicked men weave their arguments to suit the times, in the hope of somehow slipping the fraud of their impiety into the paths of the innocent. So, like skilled and prudently trained money-changers who separate the approved from the rejected, you will be able to multiply the substance of the talent entrusted to you.

We have written these things, beloved brothers, moved by full charity. We have conceived hope for your faith, first from the gift of God and then also from the profession of our brother John, who presides over you, in which he declared that he holds execrable, by name, all whom the apostolic and universal church of the catholics condemns.

You too ought to have stated this clearly in your letter. You should not have thought it could suffice, especially amid such great snares laid by cunning men, to lump under some general condemnation those whom it is right to pursue and condemn one by one and individually. Old wounds need careful treatment, and nothing applied for the integrity of the faith and the stability of religion is thought to be excessive.

We have therefore sent a libellus with this letter, to which you must add your own signatures, so that your faith, attested by the writings sent through the deacon Rufinus, may become still clearer to us by the addition of this repetition. Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Peter.

HORMISDAS TO JOHN, BISHOP OF NICOPOLIS. CARRIED BY THE SUBDEACON PULLIO. The contents of the letter you sent, and the statement of your faith, which agrees with the judgments of the apostolic see, have lifted our spirits. Though stirred by so many joys, we were not content until we could learn more fully, through Pullio, subdeacon of the Roman church, what was happening among you. This is chiefly because the report of the bishops under your charity's jurisdiction does not state clearly everything that pertains to the church's decrees, as yours does.

Therefore, out of our solicitude and for their complete union with us, we have sent a libellus that they ought to sign, since all the bishops of your regions who have returned to the communion of the apostolic see have signed this same profession.

This charity, this eagerness for the common salvation, has prompted us. I believe your fraternity will welcome it gladly, for where the salvation of souls is at stake you ought to lend the effort of your zeal and attention, so that by leading the way you may reap the fruit of such praise.

With God's help, send the aforesaid Pullio back to us speedily with your charity's reply, so that our desires may not be kept long in suspense. Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Peter.
(122.) MEMORANDUM. CARRIED BY THE SUBDEACON PULLIO.

When, with God's help and the prayers of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, you arrive at Nicopolis, you are to proceed as follows. After the bishop of Nicopolis has received our letter, he should gather the bishops of his province and have them sign the libellus attached to the letters addressed to them.
If, however, the said bishop says it is too difficult to gather the bishops, let him send persons with you to each bishop, so that they may sign the said libellus in your presence.

With God's mercy, you must do this in such a way that the letters we have sent are read publicly. Or if you see that the bishops are unwilling to do this out of fear, let them at least read them to their clergy. Leave this to their discretion, however, and with God's mercy bring back to us the signed documents of the bishops and of that bishop, namely John the metropolitan.
Once this is done, we want you to make no delay there, because of the snares and cunning of our enemies.

HORMISDAS TO JOHN, BISHOP OF NICOPOLIS, WITH THE SYNOD, AS ABOVE. CARRIED BY HIS DEACON JOHN. We would wish, beloved brothers, that you might be free of all the waves of trouble and spend your life in secure tranquillity, and [serve] our God with a mind removed from the turmoil of worldly storms * * have moved [?], because what we do not wish to happen, we cannot help grieving over once it has happened.

But the world abounds in troubles, and this age in which we live as pilgrims lies open on every side to temptations. As great structures are battered by storms of wind, so the minds of the faithful are battered by the devil's snares, and, as it is written, those who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution.

But we are consoled by the hope promised by the just rewarder, for blessed is the one who is not scandalized in the Lord. Let not frail and fleeting assaults cast down the soldiers of God. He who stands by the valiant takes no delight in cowards. Passing things are easily despised if we consider the things that will endure. The occasion of testing is to be embraced, because though the burdens of toil are hard, the rewards of virtue are greater.

How will anyone be worthy of the reward who shows himself unequal to the test? Let us not be sluggish in brave deeds if we desire to attain what is promised. Who would wait for a human voice on this, when the sentence of truth rings in our ears every day: "Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake"?

But do not think, dearest brothers, that I am comforting you only with spiritual encouragement, great as that is among the faithful. As far as lay in human power, I have not rested from seeking remedies for your tribulation. Through the legates sent to the ruler of the East and to the bishop of Thessalonica I warned that he should cease persecuting you, and I issued further letters directing that a petition be made to the emperor.

These are the provisions made for the present; but it is rather the things that concern our future hope that we should contemplate in our minds. Indeed, I confess I was astonished that, amid your account of your hardships, this concern could creep into your devout prudence: that under the guise of seeking advice you should ask my permission to send the customary letters to the bishop of Thessalonica. Should I be the author of something I would condemn if I learned it had been done without my knowledge? Far be such perversity from me!

Hear the apostle's words, but applied fittingly to my own person: "If I build up again what I have torn down, I make myself a transgressor." Do not, I beg you, return to the contagion you have barely escaped, nor let feet pulled free from the mud that held them be wickedly plunged into it again. Let what is past remain forgotten. "No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God."

Those who turn their eyes back to look at what they are leaving are hindered from advancing on the road they have set out on. The church's discipline does not love those in whom any memory of faithlessness remains; they must cut themselves off entirely from those who err. Those who return to what they once rejected are judged so detestable that the blessed apostle Peter declared it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, having known it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. It is plain how tenaciously constancy in the faith handed down must be guarded, if it is more tolerable to remain in error than to become entangled again in the defilements one has fled. Given on the day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Agapitus.

HORMISDAS TO JOHN, BISHOP OF NICOPOLIS. CARRIED BY THE SUBDEACON PULLIO. On the return of our subdeacon Pullio we received your charity's letter, and we rejoiced at the constancy of your faith and your commitment to communion with the apostolic see. But we were saddened to hear that you are enduring some troubles. Yet these cannot last long, for where God is worshipped purely, even if adversities occur, they are turned into prosperity, as the apostle says: "Hope does not disappoint."

The prince of the apostles, doubting as he walked on the sea, was in distress; yet as soon as he called on his Lord he found him ready, and with an outstretched hand the Lord would not let him come to harm. So let us follow the examples of our forebears, remain in their faith, and ask for the help of him of whom it is written that he does not let us be tempted beyond what we are able to bear.

Therefore, as we greet your charity, we urge you, as we said before, to persevere in what has been well begun, because the one who perseveres to the end will be saved. Do not stop relieving our anxiety with frequent letters. Strengthen also the bishops of your province with suitable exhortation, for by doing this you will be able to multiply every day the talent entrusted to you.

We are also giving thought to the request your love makes, that our petitions should reach the most clement emperor for the peace of the whole church. It is your part not to cease supporting our wish and efforts with fitting prayers, for we will by no means be able to rest until, with God as author, these things are accomplished. Given on the fifth day before the Nones of March, in the consulship of Agapitus.
(125.) COPY OF THE IMPERIAL LETTER OF THE EMPEROR ANASTASIUS TO POPE HORMISDAS. CARRIED BY THE BISHOPS ENNODIUS AND FORTUNATUS, THE PRESBYTER VENANTIUS, THE DEACON VITALIS AND THE NOTARY HILARUS.

We give thanks to almighty God that your holiness, formed in heavenly teaching, has sent, as we asked, envoys of the faith: the venerable bishops Ennodius and Fortunatus, and also the religious men Venantius the priest, Vitalis the deacon and Hilarus the notary, such men as the loftiness of the cause required. They are able to carry through a matter of this magnitude by the light of the Church's teaching. With God at work, they examined closely everything that belongs to the right and true faith of Christians. They declared it themselves, as was fitting, and they learned from us, as was proper, that the Church of God is one, established everywhere on the teachings of the apostles.

Who, then, would dare to think otherwise about the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ than truth itself holds? Who would not confess that the Son, equal and consubstantial with the Father, for the sake of our salvation, according to the archangel's annunciation, took flesh from the Virgin in her womb and became man, and, as the Apostle says, took the form of a slave, so that in the flesh he might undergo the cross for us? Of him the blessed apostle Peter says to the Jews: "You asked that a murderer be released to you, but you killed the author of life." Of him we also read in the apostle Paul: "He became obedient unto death, even death on a cross."

For we confess that the blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God, bore for us God the Saviour in true flesh, with a rational and intelligent soul. We believe and affirm that he who before the ages is homoousios with God the Father and the Holy Spirit was also born at the end of time homoousios with us, except for our sins, as the prophet David says: "From my mother's womb you are my God."

Yet our substance was so assumed, without loss or confusion of our body, that the Son of God will come in that same flesh to judge the world, showing before the eyes of all the marks of the wounds and the nails, as it is written: "And they shall look on him whom they pierced."

Together with all the orthodox we likewise shun and abhor the most impious Nestorius and Eutyches. We condemn and anathematize both their persons and their doctrines, which are to be ranked with abominable sacrileges. Both men either chose not to know the divine dispensation and the remedies for human weakness, or blasphemed them once they knew them.
Such, then, is the resolve concerning the faith that the most high God has placed in the mind of our Clemency from the beginning of our life, and by it, we believe, our empire is also preserved.

We are surprised, however, that you chose to write to us about the most blessed fathers who met at Chalcedon. What they decreed is shown to have been confirmed by many decrees of our predecessors. No other synod has been held to weaken what that synod ordained, and no law has come from us whose novelty would undo the statutes of that episcopal council. Above all, the synod itself declared that anyone who should wish to teach or alter any faith other than the one laid down at Nicaea by the three hundred and eighteen venerable fathers ought to be anathema.

Moreover, that synod condemned those whom we named above, namely Nestorius and Eutyches, whom we too condemn. In this matter our sacred letters bear witness for us, sent to Alexandria not once but many times. In them we rebuked the Alexandrians for not considering the plain teaching of the faith sufficient for them, and urged them to give up their anathema against the synod of Chalcedon and against Bishop Leo of venerable memory.
For this reason we still apply no small effort and attention, so that we may draw them away from this needless anathema and join them to the holy universal Church.

As for the one point that seems to remain, our will might perhaps have agreed with your request for the sake of the unity of the churches, had we not believed that other scandals would arise from it in the venerable churches.

Now weigh carefully everything that must be done. Our Clemency judges it a grave thing for the living to be expelled from the venerable Church on account of the dead. We also know that what you write about this cannot be carried out without much shedding of human blood. But if you hope for everything from God, you will be able to take better counsel than those men who run through the provinces because of their errors and want discord, the enemy of the holy Gospels and of the churches.

Therefore see to it that the unity of the churches may please the heavenly Majesty, for we do not know whether the one who opposes us in the matters we have mentioned reproaches us rightly. In everything, however, you will be able to learn the sincerity of our will from the report of your envoys.

We ask that your apostolic office may be pleased to pray for us. We shall know that you do this willingly chiefly in this way: if God is pleased, through your arrangements, to grant us the perfect unity of the churches. For that voice of God commanded and bestowed a great blessing on those who love him when it declared: "My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you."
(126.) HORMISDAS TO ANASTASIUS AUGUSTUS. BY ENNODIUS AND PEREGRINUS,

BISHOPS. Some time ago, when your Gentleness's envoys were returning, I replied to your letters and instructions. I did not deal fully with everything, as the magnitude of the matter demanded, but for the time being I touched briefly on certain points. Yet even if I had managed to set everything out sufficiently, could I, while pleading the cause of the faith before your Clemency, be charged with importunity for repeating my petitions?

Let those fear the stigma of such unpleasantness who care only to apply their zeal to worldly business! He does not fulfil the work of the Gospel who thinks he may be excused for ceasing to preach it. Shepherds must keep a sleepless watch, their loins girded without slackening. Just as it is plain that the fruit of good admonition is sweet, so it ought not to be met with distaste.

Besides, why should anyone call my frequent petitions burdensome to your Gentleness, when the things done in the course of my office, the remedies of the faith, serve the welfare of your empire? The care that weighs on me relieves you; it lies on me but will profit you; though the seed is different, the fruit of both is one. For just as there is punishment for not speaking what is acceptable to God and for not doing it, so there is a sure reward both for the one who has preached spiritual things and for the one who has not scorned what he heard.

Your Clemency has indeed given, as it were, a hostage for your resolve by the testimony of your imperial address, and has bound yourself by a kind of pledge of good will. But what has been begun needs to be made firm. Let the foundations that have been laid receive their full beauty; let the hands that fight for God's churches not drop. The enemy of Israel fell as often as Moses did not lower his arms. Completion [?] the work; the end commends the beginning. It is no use to have begun if one abandons the task, for only perseverance in the faith brings salvation.

We bless God, by whose zeal your Piety declares that you wish to hate and pursue the impious transgressors Nestorius and Eutyches together with their wicked and sacrilegious doctrines. He proves that he hates vices who condemns those who err, and he leaves himself no room for straying who has not spared the one who went astray.

The first step of innocence is to hate what deserves blame. But it concerns the truth, my lord son, and catholic discipline, that you should also hate the followers and partners of those whose leaders you judge accursed. Crimes must be pursued not only in particular names that are to be condemned, but also in those who follow the condemned. In vain does a man claim to turn away from many if he makes an exception of one of those judged worthy of detestation, for what is weighed is not the number of people in error but the guilt of the errors.

I say this so that your Clemency may not readily think that the person of Acacius can be passed over. Is this not the Acacius who, by joining himself to Peter, polluted by the doctrine and communion of Dioscorus and Eutyches, was plunged into his filth, and who bears the punishment in the condemnation of the man whose fellowship he chose in communion? Whoever hates each of these men one by one for their impieties must also hate Acacius among them, and will love none of them in Acacius.

From him the leaven of abominable error grew up throughout the Eastern churches. From that source the pride of Alexandrian perfidy has been fed to such a degree that, as you wrote, it does not comply with the salutary commands of the one whose rule it serves, and in turning from error it does not follow the admonition of one whose power it finds useful to itself in the conduct of its affairs.

Men of this kind must therefore be shunned with all the greater detestation, because what they ought to have taught they do not accept even when others instruct them. They spurn the admonitions of their ruler in the very matters in which alone they are told that commands need not be feared, and, forgetful of their duty, they are stubborn against the salvation of the soul, when they ought to have been stubborn for its sake.

These outrages of lost minds were fostered by Acacius's communion with the perfidious, and so he must be reckoned in the place of an author, since sin is graver when it follows his example. Nothing feeds vices more than imitation, when things are believed not to deserve condemnation because others too are seen to take part in them. Mortal nature is frail and prone to fall; wicked thoughts scarcely die out even when they are suppressed. A harmful seed often lies hidden under fear and does not perish. Whoever adds his consent to depravity opens a wide door to wrongdoers.

Would that, most clement emperor, at the very beginning of apostolic severity the Eastern churches had shunned the abominable contagion of Acacius! That error would not have spread its noxious poison through many. Perhaps even the necks of Alexandria, now held so high, would then have bowed, when it recognised its own perfidy struck down in the condemnation of its imitator and saw itself displeasing in its accomplices. But while errors are fostered by evil nurture, and the consent of the wicked, which ought to have been corrected, is passed over with useless leniency, the impunity of the followers has multiplied the evil doctrines of the authors.

You indeed, if you effectively command what pleases God, commend your own resolve even through another's error. But one must consider, most clement emperor, whether it is enough before God merely to have blamed errors for one to whom he has given the power to correct them. The cure must not be put off; let healing hands be applied to the deep wounds! Before Acacius, Alexandria alone was befouled by the filth of its perfidy. See how many regions neglected correction has now polluted!

How long, my lord son, will you allow the Church of God to mourn the division of her members? Let your benefactions anticipate the sighs that would otherwise reach God. Take up the care of the faith, raise the banner of salvation, and rise up like a second Hezekiah to remove errors from Israel. It is right for you to match the glories of the ancients with the praise of new works. He destroyed the high places; you bring down the pride of exalted impiety. He crushed the idols; you break the hard hearts of the unbelievers. He destroyed the memorial of the bronze serpent; you pour out the venom of the present one. Offer to God the right deeds he did, and hope for the gifts he earned. For the Lord is faithful, who renders to each according to his works.

It is plain how great is the expectation of the faithful and how great the alarm of the perfidious. The former long to rejoice with the angels over those restored; the latter fear that, abandoned by those they had deceived, they will be left to the punishments prepared for them. Everyone's heart hangs in anxious suspense. An embassy sent to us from farthest Gaul, following the report, has asked whether our solicitude has made any progress in restoring unity.

Nor is the task difficult for your Clemency: God knows how to come to the aid of his own in their labours. It is customary for subjects to turn their hearts toward their rulers. The recent example of the emperor Marcian, of religious memory, gives the clearest proof. What did the common crowd or the people do then? There is no need to rehearse what is known: this perfidy grew up through those who went astray and was laid to rest through the just. Imitate in the integrity of his religious resolve the man whom you have equalled in your devotion to good government.

To press these matters with our tears and our prayers, and also to offer our respectful greeting, we have sent in our place Ennodius and Peregrinus, our brothers and fellow bishops. We have laid the charge of this second embassy above all on the man we designated, so that he who brought us the beginning of good hope may now, with God's help, bring back its full accomplishment. Heed, we beg you, the faithful admonitions of the one in whose teachings we long ago read that you took delight. Given on the third day before the Nones of April, in the consulship of Agapitus.

HORMISDAS TO ANASTASIUS AUGUSTUS. BY THE BISHOPS ENNODIUS AND PEREGRINUS. When I consider the depths of your wisdom, most clement emperor, I do not suppose that those who provide for their own salvation displease you. Neither divine admonitions nor human institutions hold that one who looks to a good hope should be blamed with any reproach, especially since your Piety too confesses that it burns with love for unity and peace. This has compelled me, both from confidence in your conscience and from the duty of the stewardship entrusted to me, not to hold back from the matter that has now arisen.

John, my brother and fellow bishop, prelate of the city of Nicopolis, following the example of his predecessor Alcison of holy memory, has sought communion with the blessed apostle Peter together with his synod, having condemned those whom the Church detests. He is now harassed by grievous plots. I beseech your Gentleness: oppose those who scheme wickedly, remove these troubles, and support the man who has corrected himself, though he ought to have been pressed to correct himself. Those who delay will know that they will be held guilty when they see those who have already returned supported by you.

I confess, most clement emperor, I am amazed at the obstinacy of these plotters, who are moved by regard neither for God nor for you. For those who hate in a man the zeal of good desire attack it, because they think it passes judgement on themselves. Those brought back to the right would deservedly be blamed if they did not turn back those who go astray; and there will be clear proofs of your faith if you stand by those brought back to unity. Consider how this may be accomplished by every encouragement.

HORMISDAS TO TIMOTHY, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE. Your Charity will not wonder at the reason for my past silence if you consider everything that went before; nor will you wonder at my present address if you weigh the power of love. For we have learned from the teacher of the Gentiles that love bears all things. And if love, as that same teaching holds, does not seek its own, it is not unfitting that I waive my privilege and offer what may rather be of benefit to you.

It would have been proper for me to wait until you were free from union with those in error, and then love you as one corrected; to see you separated from those who deserve condemnation, and then embrace you in a letter. But why should one delay calling the laggard whom one wishes to see return? Why should moderation not be given room, when nothing is taken away from justice? What helps those who are struggling should be offered, so long as it does not pollute us with the contagion of fellowship.
