This was the reason for the present letter: to urge and to warn that we should not carelessly allow our soil to lie barren. A diligent farmer does not long allow an unfruitful tree to take up ground. He waits patiently, but does he go on waiting forever?

You are called to what brings salvation; do not delay. He who returns to innocence without delay does not stray far from it. Be moved by the admonitions of the fathers, and, keeping to their faithful footsteps without slipping or erring, wash away what is past by what is to come.

It lies with you, now by urging the people to what is right, now by entreating at the emperor's feet on behalf of the faith, to set straight what has gone astray and to make firm what is in doubt. You must take great pains to ensure that the diligence of right action covers the faults of time past. He who confers some benefit on the universal Church does a service to his own soul, and the matter stands thus: if you press on zealously and tirelessly, the common cause will become profitable to you. Given as above.

HORMISDAS TO ALL THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED IN THE REGIONS OF THE EAST. Even if my care in admonishing you were to cease, it would still befit you, mindful of your own office, not to neglect carelessly what all should earnestly keep for the salvation of their souls, so that it might be clear that the discipline of the heavenly commandments dwells in you not through another's zeal but by your own resolve. For although one who follows good counsel is not without praise, he who anticipates what is right ranks as much higher in the honour of wisdom than he who follows what has been prescribed, as teaching is more illustrious than learning.

Let each one remember the calling with which he was called by the Lord, and consider what is expected of him. It is a miserable thing to fall short of the worth of one's profession, when what is displayed in name is not shown in action. We have received great things, if only we fulfil what the gifts bestowed demand.

Whoever rejoices that he has been chosen to feed the sheep of the Lord's flock should think of the judgement on the governance entrusted to him. A sleepless guard must be kept and the watch maintained without break. No room must be given to ravening wolves, nothing left to chance, for the neglected straying of the sheep is the fault of the shepherds. He will come who will examine the accounts of the stewardship entrusted to us.

It is certain that justice applies to all, and that no one is granted licence to sin unpunished. But who does not know that there are degrees of desert, and that just as rewards are not equal, so punishments also differ? For those who know, the stripes are multiplied; we read of few lashes for ignorance.

If this is so, as there is no doubt that it must be judged to be, what kind of conduct befits one to whom the errors of others must also be imputed? The Holy Spirit cries out through the prophet: "O shepherds of Israel, do the shepherds feed themselves? Do not the shepherds feed the sheep?" It is certain that more is to be required of the one to whom more is entrusted, and that we are made the more answerable the more lavish the grace with which we have been honoured.

The good Master, who teaches light through dark sayings and truth through the riddles of parables, did not accuse as faithless the servant who kept the talent he had been given without increase; he condemned him as useless. Hence it is plain how afraid one should be who has lost the Lord's coin, if the one who kept what he received without loss was blamed. Let no one be content with his own innocence, for to our God, who sees all things, we owe an account through constant preaching of the conduct of others as well.

Teachers' knowledge should be generous. The Christian faith does not love secrecy: whatever of it anyone does not pour out for increase, he hides. The preaching of the word to all nations was commanded to the apostles; how then can anyone to whom this has been entrusted excuse himself for keeping silent? What good is it to anyone to preserve reverence for the rules of the fathers, if he patiently accepts that others shake them and treat them without honour?

He shows a weak love who does not defend what he loves. The holy decrees are assailed everywhere by the perfidious, and wickedness, revived, repeatedly rises again from excesses once suppressed. How, I ask, does one prove his devotion to God who passes over such abominations?

Let us remember with what a throng of catholic bishops, as we have learned, those councils on which we rely were celebrated! How many were neither hindered by infirmity nor slowed by burdensome old age? The distances between far-flung regions seemed slight, and the very labours were welcome as a kind of consolation, so that, with the Spirit guiding the holy assemblies, a later [?] age might receive wisdom to preserve.

And when the impious attack these things after their perfidy has been condemned at the root, is he silent who knows that he has been commanded: "Lift up your voice, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem; lift it up, do not fear"? Was it not with this before his eyes that the teacher of the Gentiles instructed his disciple not to cease preaching the Gospel in season and out of season, warning him: "Take heed to yourself and to your teaching; persist in these things, for by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you"?

Therefore, whether roused by the goads of the prophets or instructed by the rules of apostolic teaching, take up the care of saving preaching. Love and defend the judgements approved by the pious and hostile to unbelievers, and, returning to the rock on which the Church is founded, clear yourselves also before the spirits of those fathers whose venerable decrees are being wickedly undermined. Consider, when the Lord comes to the judgement that is awaited, he who was entrusted to the apostles, who was made known through the doubt of some who tested him, who was promised by the angel's announcement, whether it is better to be accused by those fathers or to be joined to their company; whether to confess the Lord as he will be seen, or as the impious deny him.

Let nothing hold you back from salvation; return to the way with swift steps. A fall does not weigh down the one who falls, if he rises again. The teaching of the Lord's mercy is generous; the chains of error are harmful as long as they hold. Justice hates the obstinate; mercy cherishes those who amend. Given on the third day before the Nones of April, in the consulship of Agapitus.

HORMISDAS TO THE ORTHODOX BISHOPS. God is indeed the special comfort of the faithful, and those who have turned to him with the whole devotion of their mind never falter, whatever hardships they meet. Yet I confess that I owe your resolve this prayer: that just as I rejoice at the sincerity of your faith, so I may be granted to rejoice at the firmness of your constancy.

So, beholding you with the inward eye, I rise readily to my desire of speaking with you, that I may repay your love for God with a written word, strengthen your hope with exhortation on the page, and so give a glad testimony of charity to those with whom I share the fellowship of holy communion. For it is not enough for my mind to be at ease about you unless I also show the affection with which I embrace you. Indeed, whoever can fail to love those who are joined to him shows that his hatred of those cut off from the love of God does not come from judgment.

I therefore bless God when I consider the fervour of your faith amid various storms and the adversities of tempests. I urge you too, with fuller joy, to glorify his goodness in these things. To make the minds of his elect more acceptable to himself, he examines them, and though they are known to him, he still tests them with certain difficulties, so as to show that justice too is present in the gift he bestows. It is therefore fitting that you hold persistently to your good purpose and do not falter on the road that leads to the kingdom of heaven.

Whoever looks upon the priceless gifts of the Lord's promise can give no thought to any danger. For the thought of present evils does not break us unless forgetfulness of the good things to come overcomes us, since whoever has taken in the sweetness of the hope he awaits shuts out all the bitterness of toil. For what difficulty can equal blessedness, or what sufferings are worthy of the rewards, that is, of the glory to come, which, as the apostle declares, will be revealed in us?

Far be it that anything should separate us from the love of Christ! How great is a tribulation, if it gives birth to glory? What is thought to be adversity is the raw material of prosperity. When we are bowed down, we are lifted up. No one would have a reward to come unless he endured the hardships of the present. See how much labour it takes to make men's earthly harvest grow: how much toil, then, must we spend to ensure that heavenly gifts do not perish?

The life of the negligent is quiet, but its substance is not rich. The labourer is worthy to receive the fruit of his wages. Piety would languish everywhere, indistinguishable from impiety, if there were no testing to divide the good from the wicked. The contest of the righteous is a most pleasing spectacle to the Lord, and nothing wins heavenly grace for a person so much as the onslaughts of adversity patiently borne. Who would admire soldiers in the security of peace?

It is no hard thing to plant one's feet securely on dry ground, and a calm sea does not show the helmsman's skill. What counts is to advance undaunted in war, not to slip where the ground is slippery, and to scorn the waves in a storm. Let worldly temptation rage and stir up its commotions, so long as those who are being tested are plainly revealed.

Knowing these things, dearest brothers, hold fast to the constancy of your faith, and if dangers befall you, love them too, since they fight on behalf of your merits. Proclaim what you worship, and share the gospel commandments that you hold throughout the whole world. Over and above your own pay, let the correction of others also be credited to you.

Among the acknowledgments of sin by which the prophet, full of the Spirit of God, wins divine grace for himself, and among the things by which he begs for the mercy that may preserve him, he declares that he will teach the wicked the ways of the Lord and that through him the ungodly will be converted. Blessed are those whom a life lived in innocence rewards; blessed are those through whom an example is also given to others.

For our part, as far as lies in us, we do not cease from care or labour. Imitating the humility that our Lord taught us, we ask for what serves their salvation, so that, as my care for the stewardship entrusted to me is recognized, my discharge of its duties may also be approved. For a second time we have sent our brothers and fellow bishops Ennodius and Peregrinus on an embassy with instructions, pressing upon them reason, exhortations, prayers and tears, so that, separated from the contagion of the ungodly, they may come over to the true faith and the apostolic decrees by the same means as you did; or at least so that the world may recognize that it was not we who failed in preaching but they who failed their own salvation.

HORMISDAS TO BISHOP POSSESSOR. Hearing of the excellent earnestness of your charity and learning of the path of right faith that you uphold without clamour, we give thanks unceasingly to our God, praying that you may persist in that disposition and be able to give others an example to follow. These are heavenly gifts, these are the signs of divine bounty, these are the judgments of God, which would not allow you to be separated from the catholic fellowship of bishops.

Therefore, dearest brother, we exhort you in this present letter to persevere in the constancy for which you were chosen and to add growth to your commendable beginnings, because a good work, especially one that concerns the teaching of the faith, seems to diminish unless it keeps on growing. And if worldly tribulation should come, let us set the future rewards before our eyes and console ourselves with the apostle's admonition, saying: The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which will be revealed in us.

Yet we hope for better things, because God, who said through the blessed apostle that he does not let you be tempted beyond what you are able, will in his goodness rescue those whom he has chosen to be his own from the snares of their adversaries, as he always has.

We have received, through our returning legates, your beloved self's statement confessing the right faith, and in it we recognized the sincerity of your brotherhood, since you did not delay to proclaim with public attestation what you rightly believe. Dated the third day before the Nones of April, in the consulship of Agapitus.

HORMISDAS TO THE ORTHODOX CLERGY, PEOPLE AND MONKS RESIDING AT CONSTANTINOPLE. If he who, following the gospel commandments, offers a cup of cold water receives the reward of his good intention, repaid by the very Lord who taught these things, does not he who has put off proclaiming the truth to so great a people of the faithful justly incur the penalty of condemnation?

Hence, fleeing the threat of the heavenly command, which teaches that in matters that concern God one must speak and not keep silent, and caring also for your salvation, I have undertaken the admonition that the present need demands. I solemnly charge all who are concerned to keep the Christian religion with an undamaged faith to turn away and flee with all their strength from those who reject the holy synod of Chalcedon and the letters of blessed Leo written on the catholic faith. For it is they who, polluted by the contagion of Eutyches and Dioscorus of Alexandria, or rather by the abominable contagion of the Manichaeans, seem in word to be contending against the decrees of the fathers, but in fact plainly rise up against the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Remember, dearest ones, what was attempted when Basiliscus was squatting in the palace citadel, and the deeds of those times, which some of you saw and others heard of. Recall how wicked, how shameless and monstrous was the presumption of Timothy surnamed Aelurus at that time, and how great a fervour of your faith then showed itself to the whole world.

The people of Constantinople proved then how purely believers ought to keep the Christian mysteries. Would that those struggles were over and done with, and that the times did not now demand the same again! For the same heretics are once more lifting their wicked head out of the depths in which they had been held submerged.

And so I ask, exhort and admonish you, beloved: separate yourselves from their councils and their communion. Remember your former zeal and show that the light, the spark of spiritual fire, still lives in you, so that the cunning of the lost may not rejoice at having overcome your simple love of the truth.

What I have said about the present need and the precautions to be taken against the ungodly will suffice. I hope that if this admonition bears fruit, it will benefit both me and you, since God will be glorified in your salvation and the fruit of our care will be seen. Dated the third day before the Nones of April, in the consulship of Agapitus.

HORMISDAS TO DOROTHEUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA. John, my brother and fellow bishop, prelate of the city of Nicopolis, together with his synod, complains that he is being grievously afflicted with various extortions and losses because, having separated himself from the fellowship of transgressors and obtained the communion of the apostolic see, he did not send notice of his ordination to the church of Thessalonica.

This neglect could have been blameworthy if there were a single mystery of charity shared by all. But when many have cut themselves off from the solid rock that is Christ, who would not wish to be set apart from union with those who err, so as to be found worthy of union with those who stand in the truth? It is not, then, a custom that has been neglected but a contagion that has been avoided. Can anyone, then, call it an error when he understands it to be a precaution wisely taken?

We believed that what you ought to have taken up first, you could at least have followed after the example of others. Is it not enough that you linger in your lapses, without adding to the heap of reproach ill will toward those who are returning to the way? What else do those who pursue the people who take refuge at the altars of that see hate but the very name that the Lord gave to blessed Peter — a thing that cannot be said without impiety?

With what shame, I ask, do you want to keep for yourself the privileges of those whose commands you do not obey, and want to be shown, under ecclesiastical authority, the reverence that you do not show to the faith? Even if you stood in the same footsteps on which the catholics rely, you ought still to avoid persecuting your neighbour, knowing from the teachings of our Lord and Saviour, which we revere, that whoever causes one of the least to stumble is guilty of great sin.

Where, Lord, is the humility you taught when your disciples were arguing about rank? You show that he is greatest who strives to show himself least. Look down from heaven and see; visit the vine planted by you as its husbandman; look upon those who are least in regard to your commandments and puffed up in pursuit of honour!

Why do you desire new things and abandon the old, careless about the greatest matters and concerned with petty ones? Is this not to tithe cheap things and despise the precepts of the law? Keep what befits God, and what comes from men will easily follow.

Rather, take care for your salvation, and lament with feeling that another has gone before you in the truth, lest, if you persist in persecuting those who are returning to the members of the church, you too be joined with those whom the catholic sentence condemns by name. Dated the day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Agapitus.

HORMISDAS TO BISHOPS ENNODIUS AND PEREGRINUS. After your charity had set out, a deacon from Nicopolis, who also met you on the road, came to Rome. We saw him without delay, considering whether there might be something we ought to add to the instructions for the embassy entrusted to you. The matter itself clearly shows that this was reasonably done.

For he brought us a letter from his bishop John and another from the synod subject to the church of Nicopolis, in which they complain that the bishop of Thessalonica has stirred up both the imperial and the judicial authorities against them, and that they are being severely afflicted with extortions and losses because John did not send that bishop a report of his ordination according to ancient precedent. For this reason they hoped we would consider a remedy, and they also asked us whether we would give them leave to send the report to the designated bishop according to custom.

We therefore deliberated, and we admonished the bishop of Nicopolis not to dare attempt any such thing if he wishes to remain in communion with us, lest, had he sought confirmation from one who is estranged from our communion, our communion too should be contaminated through him.

We have told you these things so that you may know everything. What you are to do in this case, with God's favour, is set out below. Dated the day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Agapitus.

HORMISDAS TO BISHOPS ENNODIUS AND PEREGRINUS. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, with the saints interceding and helping, the case of the church of Nicopolis is to be handled as follows.

First, when with God's help you reach Thessalonica, deliver to the bishop of Thessalonica the letters we have sent in this case. In greeting him, observe the procedure that you know we have prescribed for those who are not in communion with the apostolic see, that is, with the catholic church.

Once you have delivered the letters, you must press him urgently to refrain from harassing that church. Give him the reason: one who had returned to communion and to the body of the church could have nothing in common with those who have not yet returned. Tell him that we are not abolishing the privileges granted by our predecessors, provided he himself does not abandon the ordinances of the church. Indeed, let him return to unity, and we will join him in insisting that all the privileges his church has obtained from the apostolic see be kept inviolate.
Tell him openly, too, that he shows himself an enemy of the faith if he persecutes those whom he sees returning to catholic communion.

If, with God's favour, you are able to settle the case there, write to the bishop of Nicopolis about what your efforts have achieved. But if he remains obstinate and refuses to stop persecuting him, then, in line with the letter we have sent to the most clement emperor, plead the case of the church of Nicopolis before the sovereign in these terms:

'Bishop Alcison made satisfaction to the catholic church at Constantinople; he was received and brought back to communion. His successor, Bishop John, having God before his eyes, mindful of his own salvation and following the good example of his predecessor, condemned the heretics and transgressors, sent to the see of the blessed apostle Peter, and was received. Now the bishop of Thessalonica is plotting against him and harassing him, seeking to demand of him the opposite of what he has done.'

'Therefore your father and all the orthodox ask that by your command this vexation be removed from him, lest it appear to men that he is suffering persecution because he returned to the communion of the apostolic see, and lest those who expect unity to come about through you begin to believe otherwise, if they see Your Piety overlook this and treat it carelessly.'

We have judged it expedient that your prudence should have the letters we sent to the bishop of Thessalonica in the case of the bishop of Nicopolis made public among various people in whatever way you can, but especially in the city of Thessalonica. By doing so the persecution of our people may be stopped, and we believe it will also contribute to his own salvation, if he mends his ways.
(136.) COPY OF THE REPORT OF AVITUS, A BISHOP OF GAUL.

TO THE HOLY LORD, MOST EXCELLENT IN MERITS, MOST GLORIOUS IN CHRIST AND MOST WORTHY OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE, POPE HORMISDAS, FROM AVITUS. You perceive that it accords with the state of religion and with the full rules of the catholic faith that the watchful care of your exhortation should instruct the flock entrusted to you throughout all the members of the universal church. So last year, if you will deign to remember, you visited the province of Vienne with a letter addressed to my humble self. It reached me through clerics of the church of Arles, as the opportunity that offered itself allowed, and it was indeed full of pastoral care. In it, just as you invite us to share your joy at the conversion of the provinces, namely Dardania, Illyricum and Scythia, so with most careful admonition you instruct us, lest anything should catch us unawares through ignorance.

The condemnation of Eutyches and Nestorius, whom the authority of your holy see long ago trampled underfoot through your most blessed predecessors, was brought to our knowledge long since by the provident diligence of the apostolic see toward us. But what now leaves us very much in suspense and anxious is this: although you bade us wait with eager expectation for the outcome of the embassy sent a second time to Constantinople, you have told us neither what your son, my holy brother Ennodius, reported, nor whether the embassy returned successful. You keep your promise in suspense through so long a silence that the silence of the preacher now leaves us no less dismayed than the delay of the embassy had earlier made us apprehensive.

For this reason alone I have sent your servants, my sons the priest Alethius and the deacon Viventius, with this letter of present service, in the name of the whole province of Vienne, which all your predecessors and the apostolic see have entrusted to the church in my charge. Through them I hope to learn, by the oracle of your most blessed reply, whether the fever of the aforesaid schisms — which had blazed up in the city of Constantinople through the vice of pernicious obstinacy, and in which, more grievous still, you say the churches of Alexandria and Antioch are entangled — has been quenched by fitting correction through your teaching, with Christ's favour; or whether the returning embassy brought documents plain enough to be read as straightforward, or perhaps instead reported by word of mouth something that leaves you with some suspicion on this matter. For we fear that the pontiff's judgment, in not reporting good news, may have perceived bad news.

To this is added that we have learned from the trustworthy reports of various people that the Greeks are boasting of reconciliation and concord with the Roman church. Just as this is to be welcomed if it is truly said, so it is to be feared that it may be a cunning pretence.

We all therefore ask, through my service, that you instruct us what answer should be given to your sons, my brothers, that is, the bishops of Gaul, if they consult me. For I promise confidently, not only for the devotion of Vienne but for that of all Gaul, that all seek your judgment on the state of the faith; so pray that the counterfeit profession of the lost may not deceive us, just as the truth we have found does not separate us from the unity over which you preside. Received on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Agapitus, through the priest Alethius and the deacon Viventius.

HORMISDAS TO BISHOP AVITUS, AND TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF VIENNE WHO ARE UNDER YOUR JURISDICTION. Anyone who already knows a great deal yet still wants to be instructed in matters of catholic discipline shows plainly how devoted he is to the divine commandments. Such care cannot exist except where faith is unfeigned. We therefore rejoice at the sincerity of your purpose, dearest brother. The letter you sent through the presbyter Alethius and the deacon Viventius shows you recalling what the apostolic see has decreed about the impious transgressors Eutyches and Nestorius, and asking whether our admonition has achieved anything against those who are throwing the Eastern churches into confusion.

This is a concern clearly worthy of the faithful: to groan over the falls of the wretched, and to take care that they themselves are not polluted by another's contagion. But do not suppose that we neglected to send you proper information if anything had been done. Let us briefly account for our silence, which has stung your love. If our admonitions do not come to you more often, it is because we are confident in the steadfastness of your conscience and your faith. Care may need to be spent on the doubtful; for the perfect it is enough to have pointed out what must be avoided.

As for our embassy, which we sent once and not twice, as you write: had it met with the outcome we hoped for, we would at once have eagerly shared the longed-for news with you. We know that it accords with reason and with our purpose that those whom we made sharers in our anxiety should also share with us the joys of restored unity.

But as for the Greeks, they express their wishes for peace with the mouth rather than the heart, and they speak what is just more than they do it. In words they boast that they are willing; by their deeds they declare that they are unwilling. They do not love what they have professed, and they follow what they have condemned.

Through our brother and fellow bishop Ennodius they promised to send men of priestly rank to confirm what the apostolic see had demanded, and they also promised many of the things we had asked for the correction of their depravity. How is it, then, that, contrary to their own undertaking, they not only failed to send religious men from whom full information on the case could be obtained, but dispatched laymen, strangers to the body of the church, as if some trifling matter were in hand? And how is it that they not only made no effort to drag themselves out of the mire in which they are held fast, but even believed (God forbid!) that they could darken with their own dryness [?] those who shine with the brightness of the catholic faith?

This was the reason for our silence, and you too have seen it, as your spiritual prudence revealed it to you. What could I have told you by letter about this affair, when I saw it stubbornly holding fast to its hard faithlessness, exactly as before? New developments call for careful and diligent reports. Whoever reports nothing about things already known declares plainly enough that matters remain as they were.

Therefore, dearest brother, we exhort you by this present letter, and through you, since the opportunity has arisen, we also admonish the others throughout Gaul who embrace the same faith with us. Keep the constancy of faith that you have promised and that is dear to God. Shun the fellowship of transgressors, and present your constancy as a chaste virgin to one husband, Christ, as you have pledged. Beware lest, as the serpent seduced Eve by his cunning, the minds of some should be corrupted and led away from the simplicity and chastity that is in Christ Jesus.

The flatteries of the harmful are deadly, so you must keep watch, for the adversary of human salvation, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour: resist him, firm in the faith. Those who follow and love the footsteps of their father, who was cast down from the citadel of heaven, have this peculiar trait: being deprived of the light of truth, they rejoice when others are darkened by their own darkness. Knowing that they will pay the penalty for their perversity, they exult if they can join the wretched to themselves in their condemnation.

For their neighbours, the Thracians, Dardanians and Illyrians, have recognized their perversity, and for the most part have deserted them. Why else, then, do they strive by frauds and various tricks to lure people far away, hoping that they are ignorant, unless they want to stain with their impious contagion in others too the light that they themselves do not possess?

So that you may know how people are disposed in those regions: many of the Thracians, though worn down by the attacks of their persecutors, nevertheless remain in our communion, knowing that faith becomes more glorious through adversity. Dardania and Illyricum, which border on Pannonia, have asked us to have bishops ordained for them, and we have already done this where it was necessary. They are so glad to separate themselves from the fellowship of the lost that they have sought remedies, provided only that they have nothing in common with the transgressors. The metropolitan of Epirus, that is, the bishop of Nicopolis, has recently separated himself and his synod from the impious and has come over to apostolic communion, producing a profession of faith to that effect.

We thought these things should be included in the present letter for two reasons. Just as we must grieve over the lot of those who are perishing, we should equally rejoice over the salvation of those who are returning. And the faithful who live far from those people should learn with what care they must flee the poison of men whom they see shunned, with such just loathing, even by their own neighbours.

We, for our part, mindful of our stewardship, must approach them once again through the office of an embassy. If they are not moved by regard for God or by the consideration of reason, perhaps out of desire for their own salvation they will at least yield to those who knock importunately and persistently. Then they will either turn from their errors and return to the right way, or else, because of their impenitent hearts, they will be shown before all to be without excuse, since even after so many warnings they persist in obstinate faithlessness.

Pray, and join your prayers and vows to ours before God, that through the help of his mercy our efforts on behalf of the stability of the catholic faith may make progress. Keep yourselves spotless and whole from all fellowship with transgressors, so that we may either unite our minds and hearts with them once they are corrected, or be found worthy to remain untouched by their poisons. We know, as you too testify is not hidden from your conscience, that Eutyches and Nestorius were condemned by the authority of the apostolic, that is, the catholic, sentence. How then could we be saved if we cling in any measure of communion to their followers and successors, since Belial can have no portion with our Christ?

We thought it would help to inform you if we let you read the documents themselves, so that you would know what was transacted here with the people of Nicopolis and the Dardanians, and the manner in which they were received into communion. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of Agapitus.

THE EMPEROR ANASTASIUS TO POPE HORMISDAS. Although silence is held to be a great thing, those who marvel at God's mercy must nevertheless speak of it constantly. And no one is unaware that forgiveness of sins stands first among the foundations of the faith that our Lord and God, the Saviour Jesus Christ, taught us.

For by his own passion he cleansed all the sins of Adam. This was the work of his humility: to free both Adam and all the fathers from the slavery of sin, willingly taking on the person of old age [?]. For the blessed apostle Paul taught us, writing to the Romans: Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned.

From this it has in some way been declared to everyone that particular examples should also be drawn from the general dispensation, or from the miracles, now that such things have once been established by the command of the great law and by such loving goodness. All the teaching that he handed down to his disciples rests on this foundation. By his own sickness he put to flight manifold kinds of suffering; by his own passion, as has been said, he untied the knot of sin; and, striving to have them accomplish similar things, he instructed his disciples by deeds and words.

But if, as some are trying to show, certain men from among the apostles themselves disobediently neglect to carry out such loving teaching, we do not know where the teaching of the merciful Lord and great God can still reach us.

We do not, however, believe this in such a way as to think that those who have learned mercy are themselves unmerciful. But from now on we suppress our request in silence, for we judge it unreasonable to offer the kindness of entreaty to those who stubbornly refuse to be asked. We can endure being insulted and treated as nothing; we cannot endure being commanded. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of July at Constantinople, in the consulship of Anastasius and Agapitus, men of clarissimus rank.
(139.) COPY OF THE PETITION OF THE MOST HUMBLE ARCHIMANDRITES AND OTHER MONKS OF SYRIA SECUNDA.

TO THE MOST HOLY AND MOST BLESSED HORMISDAS, PATRIARCH OF THE WHOLE WORLD, WHO HOLDS THE SEE OF PETER, PRINCE OF THE APOSTLES: THE ENTREATY AND SUPPLICATION OF THE MOST HUMBLE ARCHIMANDRITES AND OTHER MONKS OF YOUR PROVINCE OF SYRIA SECUNDA.

The grace of Christ, the Saviour of us all, has moved us to take refuge with your blessedness, as if fleeing from winter and storm into a calm harbour. Having been so counselled, we believe that we are no longer held fast by the calamities that surround us. For although we suffer, we endure it rejoicing, knowing that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come that will be revealed in us.

Since Christ our God has appointed you prince of shepherds, teacher and physician of souls, it is right for us to set before your holy angel the sufferings that have befallen us, and to expose the merciless wolves who are scattering Christ's flock. Then you may drive them out from among the sheep with the staff of authority, heal the soul with the word of teaching, and soothe it with the medicines of prayer.

Who these men are, and who has armed them against us, you have surely heard, most blessed ones. They are that Severus and that Peter, who were never counted among Christians. Every day they assail the holy synod of Chalcedon and our most holy and most blessed father Leo with public anathemas. They count the judgment of God as nothing and trample on the venerable canons of the holy fathers. With the backing of the imperial power they have bishops brought forward, and they afflict us with immeasurable tortures to force us to mock the aforesaid holy synod.

Some of our men could not bear the blows inflicted on them and departed this life, and no small number of ours were slaughtered. We were going to the enclosure of the lord Simeon on the church's business when those defiled men lay in ambush for us on the road. Falling upon us, they killed three hundred and fifty of our men and wounded others. Those who managed to take refuge at the venerable altars they slew on the spot. They also burned the monasteries, sending in by night a mob of unruly men and hirelings, and through such pestilent men they consumed all the poor substance of the church.

The documents carried by our venerable brothers John and Sergius will inform your blessedness on each point. We had sent them to Constantinople, thinking that vengeance would be taken for what had been committed. But he not only did not deign to speak a word to them; he drove them out with great insult and threatened those who might present such petitions. From this we have learned, though late, that all the depravity and audacity of these evils committed against the churches was set in motion at his instigation.

We therefore entreat you, most blessed ones, supplicating and begging you to rise up with fervour and zeal, to grieve as is right for the mangled body (for you are the head of all), and to avenge the faith that has been despised, the canons that have been trampled, the fathers who have been blasphemed, and so great a synod that has been assailed with anathema.

To you God has given the power and authority to bind and to loose. Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. Rise up, holy fathers, and come to save us! Be imitators of the Lord Christ, who came down from heaven to earth to seek the straying sheep. Imitate Peter, the prince of the apostles, whose see you adorn, and Paul, the chosen vessel, who travelled around the world and enlightened it. For great wounds need greater remedies.

Hired shepherds, when they see wolves coming against the sheep, abandon them to be scattered by the wolves. But to you, the true shepherds and teachers, who are entrusted with the care of the sheep's salvation, the flock itself comes running. It recognizes its shepherd, is freed from the most savage beasts, and follows the shepherd's voice, as the Lord says: My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. Do not, then, despise us, most holy ones, for we are wounded daily by ferocious beasts.

So that your holy angel may be fully informed, in this same entreaty of ours, which also has the force of a formal declaration of faith, we anathematize all those whom your apostolic see has cast out and excommunicated. We mean Nestorius, who was bishop of Constantinople; Eutyches; Dioscorus; Peter of Alexandria, surnamed the Stammerer; Peter of Antioch, called the Fuller; and likewise Acacius, who was bishop of Constantinople and shared communion with them; and all who defend any one of those heretics.

(140.) HORMISDAS TO THE PRESBYTERS, DEACONS AND ARCHIMANDRITES OF SYRIA SECUNDA.

I have read your loving letter. It laid bare the madness of God's enemies and gave a sorrowful account of the stubborn fury of the unbelievers, who hate the Lord with a revived spirit and impiously persecute his members. As for what it showed me of your constancy, I blessed God, who keeps the faith of his soldiers safe amid adversity.

But when I considered, in turn, how the churches are shaken and how the servants of God are troubled and burdened, I cried out with the prophet to help my groaning: "Arise, O Lord; judge your cause; remember the insults against you, those that come from the fool all day long!" And I gladly add the words that follow: "Do not forget the voice of those who seek you; the pride of those who hate you rises up to you continually." For just as we must guard the steadfastness of our faith, so it is not right for us to doubt the justice of God's judgment.

This hardship of the church is nothing new, brothers. Yet while the church is humbled, it is raised up, and it is enriched by the very losses that are thought to wear it down. It is the custom of God's faithful to gain the life of their souls through the death of their bodies. They lose what is perishable, but they purchase what is eternal; and while persecution opens the way to testing, testing becomes the ground of merit. The foolish, raging in their blindness, do not know that those whom they believe they can remove from human society they are leading into the kingdom of God.

Hence there is joy in the very midst of dangers and an eagerness for suffering, for the one who gives great rewards is watching the contests of his own. Who would not be broken by evils unless adversity were consoled by the thought of rewards? It is hope that does not let us fail in despair, for it shuts out the bitterness of tribulation with the sweet taste of virtue. Who would think much of the present if he knows how to value what is to come? Who would refuse to suffer losses in this life if he considers what is to be received?

Stand firm, my dearest ones. Keep your faith unshaken with a steady strength of mind, and lay hold in advance of the praise that perseverance earns, for in it lies salvation and the palm of good works. Great are the things to which we, unworthy as we are, are called. Let weakness not hold us back, for the one who calls us is a faithful rewarder and a strong helper. Let us not be deceived by the hope of prosperity or ease, nor set our sights on what is easy. Our Lord did not promise us delights or pleasant things; he promised rewards, not leisure. Praise and repose do not go together. What place will there be for reward if no one cares for virtue? The gate is narrow, but the kingdom is wide; few may enter, but those few are the proven.

Were not these the first words he spoke to those he taught: "They will persecute you and flog you in their synagogues"? As it is written, let us possess our souls through patience, so that we do not grieve to have lost them through impatience. First the Lord [Greek text, badly garbled:] [?] for the faithful of God to gain the life of their souls through the death of their bodies. They cast away present things but purchase eternal ones, and while persecution paves the way for testing, testing becomes the cause [?] of merit. The foolish, raging in their blindness, do not know that those whom they think they can separate from human society they are leading into the kingdom of God. Hence there are joys in the very dangers and eagerness for suffering, for the one who repays great gifts [?] the contests of his own. For who would not be broken by evils if adversities were not consoled by the prizes? It is hope that does not let us grow faint in despair; the sweet taste of virtues shuts out the bitterness of tribulations. For who would think the present great if he knows what is to come? Who refuses death if he considers the recompense of what is to come? Stand firm, my beloved. Guard the faith unshaken with steadfast reasoning, and reap the praise of patience, in which lies salvation and the prize of good works. Great are the things to which we unworthy ones are called. Let weakness not slow us down, for the one who calls is a faithful rewarder and a powerful helper. Let us not be deceived by the hope of what we desire or of what is pleasant, nor prefer what is easy. Our Lord did not promise us luxuries [?], nor did he promise flattering things; he promised prizes, not idleness. Praise and slackness do not go together. What place will there be for recompense if no one cares for virtue? The gate is narrow, but the kingdom is wide; few may enter, but those few are the proven. Are these not the first words he spoke to those he taught: "They will persecute you and flog you in the synagogues"? As it is written, let us gain our own souls by patience, so that we do not grieve to have lost them through impatience. [The Latin resumes:] our Lord, the teacher of patience itself, went up to the cross, to shape by his own example those whom he was going to help. He himself holds the scales between virtues and labours. He stands against the poison of those who rage, so that in proportion to the fury of persecution he himself may give the crowns of the eternal kingdom.

Recall the praise with which the ancient history follows the steadfast deaths of the Maccabees, the honour of death with which Judas and that phalanx of faithful brothers are remembered, and how widely the steadfast people who were destroyed on the mountain are spoken of. All these acts of courage were performed to keep the law, and they were only a figure and shadow of things to come, yet they earned the right to be such great examples. In the fathers we have seen, touched and tested the one we are to follow.

What should not be yielded to such a cause? What may be denied to the truth? What is not owed to the Redeemer? We gladly share these teachings with you, for the most wise Solomon says: "Blessed is he who speaks a word into the ear of one who listens." It is a joy to address those who are willing and to urge onto the right path those who do not resist. We hold the constancy professed in your letter as a pledge of your faith. By it you have separated yourselves from the contagion of transgressors and are returning to the teachings and commands of the apostolic see. You have entered the way of truth late, it is true, but blessed be God. He does not forget forever; he rebukes and heals. He does not allow the sheep of his flock to be torn apart continually by the greed of wolves lying in wait. Through a tempered severity he neglects neither the correction of his own nor their salvation.

But what [Greek text, badly garbled:] First our Lord, the teacher of his own patience, went up to the cross, to shape by his example those whom he was going to help. He himself holds the scales between virtues and labours. He stands against the poisons of those who rage, so that in proportion to the anger of the persecution he himself may provide the crowns of the eternal kingdom. With what praise the ancient history follows the steadfast deaths of the Maccabees! With what honour of death Judas and that phalanx of faithful brothers are proclaimed! On what lips is the people who were destroyed on the mountain! All these acts of courage, done to keep the law and being likenesses and shadows of things to come, were found worthy of such examples. We have seen, touched and tested in the fathers the one we shall follow. What does not suit the matter? What is out of tune with the truth? What is not owed to the Redeemer? We gladly share these teachings, for the most wise Solomon says: "Blessed is he who proclaims a word into an obedient ear." It is a joy, then, to converse with the willing and to urge onto the right road those who do not resist. We hold the constancy confessed in your letter as a pledge of your faith. Through it you have been separated from the defilement of transgressors and are returning to the teachings and commands of the apostolic see, though you set out late on the road of truth. But blessed is God, who does not forget to the end. He chastens and heals, and he does not allow the sheep of the united flock to be torn apart by the plundering of plotting wolves. Through a tempered severity he overlooks neither the safety of his own nor their salvation. [The Latin resumes:] is so surprising, then, if sheep that left that one true shepherd and were scattered have been thrown into confusion by the snares of the cunning, bloodthirsty and greedy one? Those who abandon their protector expose themselves to the dangers that tear them apart.

So now, at least, walk with firm steps on the way of the fathers, to which you have returned. God's mercy will be able to credit to your reward the correction of others as well, if you lead them back to what is right. But tear yourselves away completely from the mire in which the heretics are held fast, and shake off the filth of the dust that clings to you. With religious abhorrence condemn all who turn aside from the apostolic teachings, without exception. Darkness has no fellowship with light, and those who walk on straight paths do not join their footsteps to the wanderings of those who stray.

We must hold fast to the bond of faith and avoid the contagion of faithless company. As the Apostle says, just as anyone who joins himself to the Lord becomes one spirit with him, so anyone who clings to a harlot becomes one body with her. Virtues love their own company, and impiety drags those who cling to it down with it into the depths. [In sight,] before our eyes, on our lips, in our very hands are the teachings of the fathers, which we command you to keep. Every day the venerable councils bind us to preserve them.

It would take too many words to go over everything one item at a time. The Synod of Chalcedon, which embraces what all the councils hold in reverence, and the decrees of the venerable Leo, drawn from the very heart of the apostles, are what we ought both to know and to defend. In them is the standard of the faith, in them the bulwarks of truth; in them Christ is recognized, and in them the hope and the cause of our redemption are kept safe. This is the foundation we read of in the Apostle: whoever tries to build wood, hay and straw on it, to be consumed by fire, deceives himself.

By these councils the poisons of Eutyches and Nestorius were destroyed. These two strive against the saving mystery of the Lord's incarnation with arguments that contradict each other, yet they agree in a kind of equal sacrilege, unlike in their opinions and united in their impiety. One of them refuses to call the Virgin Mary the Mother of God and so divides in our Lord what has been united. The other confuses the distinct properties of the natures that come together and so extinguishes the mystery of our redemption. By an impious kinship, the one touches the sect of Photinus, the other the madness of Mani.

Against these men, dearest brothers, defend the remedies that have been provided with the same strength of mind with which you see the heretics fighting impiously to overthrow them. Let the assertion of truth not be sluggish. When you see deadly perdition loved so much, with what zeal ought salvation to be loved? Let us be ashamed to assert the laws of truth lazily when errors are defended so stubbornly.

The synodal decrees, it is true, pursue with just condemnations the authors of the evil inventions we have mentioned. But we also warn you to shun their followers. The apostolic see has found these to be equal to their authors and has joined them to the condemned: Dioscorus, and Timothy the parricide, Peter of Alexandria, Acacius of Constantinople with his followers, and also Peter of Antioch, like the Peter already named in error as in name, and Severus too, of the same see and no less of the same poison, Xenaias of Hierapolis, Cyrus of Edessa and Peter of Apamea. They are to be condemned not only for their own ruin but also for the ruin of others, for while they ceaselessly wrap themselves in the filth of their opinions, they have also polluted others by teaching what they wrongly learned.

I give you a general instruction for your welfare: reject whatever is put forward against the rules of the fathers, from any writings whatever. Let no one move you with unfitting precepts or new ordinances. If those who issue them are laymen, they cannot govern the churches, since it befits them to learn rather than to teach. It is wicked to bring foreign offerings to holy altars, for at the very beginnings of his worship God set fixed boundaries for religious observance. He divided the duties between the Levites and the rest of his people; the power of men is one thing, the ministry of priests another. The one who profaned sacred things by bringing strange fire into the divine sanctuary provoked the Lord rather than appeased him.

Who can claim the authority to give commands in an office that belongs to others, when there is no doubt that a man who offered the honour that was due was punished merely for presuming to take on that office? Uzziah would have kept his royal dignity and rule if, warned by an example of such severity, he had held back from religious rites and judged it better to fear them than to take them upon himself. But he was a stubborn profaner and would not desist even when the ministers of the temple forbade him. So he was struck with the abomination of leprosy right among the altars, and he lost the duties of kingship by usurping the ministry of the priest. Let them know, then, that when presumptuous men take upon themselves what God has commanded, it is not acceptable to him. He kept one offender alive so that his living disgrace would display the sentence; swift flame consumed the others.

And if there are things devised under some colour of religion, they can have no force when they oppose such great authorities. The Apostle Paul cries out: "Even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel other than the one we preached to you, let him be anathema." It was not enough for him to say this once; he repeats the wholesome command: "As we said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel other than the one you received, let him be anathema." Whoever follows the apostolic discipline must therefore keep the sentence pronounced to preserve the faith.

Our concern has certainly not been lacking. Through the office of two embassies we brought every humble entreaty, every reasonable argument and every wholesome command. But must the way of justice be neglected because faithlessness obstinately loves its errors? We must not fall along with those who are falling. Let those who do not turn from their impieties, even when their error has been rebuked, perish without defiling us. Given on the fourth day before the Ides of February, after the consulship of Agapitus, vir clarissimus.

Justin Augustus to Pope Hormisdas. God's benefits should be made known to many, but it is most fitting to announce them to the supreme pontiffs. We therefore declare to Your Holiness by this sacred letter that we have been chosen and confirmed as emperor, although we were unwilling and refused. This came about first by the favour of the inseparable Trinity, and then by the choice of the most eminent nobles of our sacred palace, of the most holy senate, and also of the most valiant army.

We therefore ask that you entreat the divine power with your holy prayers, so that the beginnings of our reign may be strengthened. It is fitting for us to hope for this and for you to bring it about. Given on the Kalends of August at Constantinople, in the consulship of Magnus, vir clarissimus.

Hormisdas to Justin Augustus. Most glorious son, in place of a gift the catholic church sends its congratulations on the first days of your venerable reign, for it trusts that through them it will find the rest of peace after its long weariness from discord. Nor is there any doubt that heavenly providence brought you to supreme power precisely so that the injury inflicted on religion in the regions of the East for so long might be abolished.

You have rendered to the blessed apostle Peter the first fruits of your reign that were due to him. We have received them devoutly because we believe without doubt that through you the concord of the churches will soon come. God, who moved Your Piety to wish to write to us, will himself grant, as we desire, devotion to the sincere worship of his religion.

You have told us that the burden of empire was laid on you although you were unwilling and refused. This makes it clear that you were chosen by heavenly judgment, as the Apostle says: "There is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordained by God." Since you have been chosen by God, as we indeed believe, it remains for you to stretch out your hand to comfort the church, which you see is struggling.

Let those who oppose its peace cease, and let those who try to scatter Christ's flock under the guise of shepherds be still! Their correction will strengthen the power of your empire, for where God is rightly worshipped, adversity will have no effect. This letter of congratulation, by the distinguished Alexander,
we have not failed to send. We hope, with the help of our God, to give Your Clemency an answer, through our son the distinguished Gratus, on each of the matters that concern the unity of the church.

Justin Augustus to Pope Hormisdas. John, a most blessed man and bishop of this royal city, and the other religious men, bishops from various places and cities who are here, have informed Our Serenity that they have composed a letter to be presented to Your Holiness. It concerns the concord of those who hold the true and orthodox faith and the unity of its venerable churches. They have earnestly asked that we too send you a letter on this matter.

We have always loved unity, so we gladly embraced their petitions and decided to send this divine letter to Your Beatitude. Having received it, may you be pleased to fulfil the wishes of the aforesaid most reverend bishops, and by your prayers to win the favour of the supreme majesty for us and for the state, whose government has been entrusted to Our Piety [?] from heaven.

So that the terms of peace, unity and concord may be more fully made known to Your Holiness, please arrange for certain most religious bishops who embrace and desire peace to come to our most sacred court. For this purpose we have sent the distinguished Gratus, count of our sacred consistory and master of the bureau of the memoria, whose excellent reputation has long been known to us. Given on the seventh day before the Ides of September at Constantinople, in the consulship of Magnus, vir clarissimus.

Hormisdas to Justin Augustus. Through Gratus. We took joy in the beginning of your reign; that joy was already strong among us on its own merits, and your earlier letter doubled it. We expressed it in return with matching devotion, and even then we foresaw what would follow: what you have now made known, by the inspiration of heavenly grace, about your desire for the unity of the church.

You already have glory now, most clement emperor, from such a desire; but expect everlasting glory from its fulfilment. These are the strongest foundations of your empire, which at the very beginning of your new reign, by a holy disposition, set the worship of God before all things. Hold fast, then, to this pious care, and press on for the peace of the catholics as you have begun, for our God, who gave you this intention, has also chosen those through whom he will bring it to fulfilment.

We also gladly welcome the wishes and prayers that the bishops have poured out to you. At last, prompted by the consideration of their own position, they desire what the apostolic see has long and frequently urged them to be willing to follow.

We have learned that Your Clemency desires this and that they too are asking for it. And the thing that has kept the peace of the churches divided until now through contentious obstinacy has not escaped the notice of Your Piety or of them, as if its cause were hidden.

What they must do is set out in our letter and in the text of the statement of faith we have sent. If, with the help of our God and of Your Clemency, they accept it and follow it, it will be possible to reach the concord we long for with the greatest ardour.

In addition, our son the distinguished Gratus, count of the sacred consistory and master of the bureau of the memoria, has shown your good judgment in himself by the maturity with which he presented his case. He will report to you himself and so explain more fully the reason for his delay.

HORMISDAS TO JOHN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE. In the letter you sent, your charity has told us of a spiritual joy: that with the help of our God the discipline of the catholic religion has recovered its proper order in your regions.

Who would doubt that these are gifts of heavenly mercy? Who would hesitate to add them to the trophies of the venerable prince? For he wins a greater triumph from this peace than from any battles. The glory of this labour knows no setting, because where God is rightly worshipped, the wickedness of adversaries never grows.

We have gladly received the confession of your Beloved, in which the holy synods are approved. Among them, in restoring all that had been decreed, you proclaimed the Council of Chalcedon, and, desiring to be joined to the number of the catholics, you declare that the name of the holy Pope Leo has been written in the diptychs.

These things are praiseworthy, provided that a will to see them through to completion follows. For to receive the Council of Chalcedon and follow the letters of holy Leo while still defending the name of Acacius is to uphold things that contradict one another. Who, while condemning Dioscorus and Eutyches, could show Acacius to be innocent? Who, while turning away, as we have said, from Timothy and Peter of Alexandria and the other Peter, of Antioch, and [?] their followers, would not abhor Acacius, who followed them in communion?

From your charity, indeed, we expect better things with the help of almighty God, since we have the hope given by your excellent promise. For in what you sent us you said that you think as we do in truth and defend these very things, hoping to be saved through them at that judgment.

After this, what remains but that you should also follow without hesitation the judgments of the apostolic see, whose faith you say you embrace? Show the Eastern regions, then, in your own person the example they should follow, so that the praise of all who are set right may be credited to your labours.

Since, therefore, you make great declarations and indicate that you embrace the faith of the blessed apostle Peter, rightly believing that our salvation can rest secure in it, send us the libellus, whose text is appended below, signed by your charity, so that without fear of conscience we may have one communion, as we pray.

For the person of our son Gratus too, vir spectabilis, we give unceasing thanks to our God. His faith and right belief have stirred our affection for him: he is truly worthy to have undertaken the care of so great an affair and to bring us the commands of the greatest prince.

COPY OF THE REPORT OF JOHN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE. TO MY LORD, IN ALL THINGS BELOVED OF GOD, MY MOST HOLY BROTHER AND FELLOW MINISTER HORMISDAS, JOHN SENDS GREETING IN THE LORD. I greet your holiness, dearest brother in Christ, and in greeting you I proclaim that the right faith is safe and the charity of brotherhood has been made firm. God, who alone is mighty, has willed this to come about through the zeal of Christians and of the most pious emperors. Deign, therefore, for the love of God, to write in apostolic fashion and to receive replies in brotherly fashion.

For, holding beyond all question the teaching of the holy apostles according to the tradition of the holy fathers, I likewise offer honour to the consubstantial and in all things holy Trinity, as the assembly of the three hundred and eighteen promulgated at Nicaea, as the gathering of the one hundred and fifty confirmed at Constantinople, as the meeting of the <two hundred> confirmed at Ephesus, and as the catholic assembly sealed at Chalcedon.

Keeping this faith by grace, then, to my last breath, I embrace in my heart with spiritual embraces both your holiness and the orthodox churches, thinking as you do in truth and hoping together with you to be saved on that day through this faith, by the good will of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. For to the consubstantial Trinity all glory is due, now and to the ages of ages. I and those with me send our warmest greetings in the Lord to all the brotherhood in Christ who are with your holiness.

We have written this much by way of satisfaction: that the venerable name of Leo of holy memory, formerly archbishop of the city of Rome, has been entered in the sacred diptychs at the time of the consecration for the sake of concord, and that your blessed name is likewise proclaimed in the diptychs.

But so that your holiness may be satisfied on every point, since we embrace your peace and are concerned for the unity of God's holy churches, we ask you to send men of peace, worthy of your apostolic see, who may give satisfaction and receive ours, so that in this matter too Christ our God may be glorified, who through you has preserved this peace for the world. Received on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, after the consulship of Agapitus.

COPY OF THE LETTER OF JUSTINIAN. The longed-for time, which we desired with our deepest prayers, divine clemency, looking upon the sorrows of the human race, has deigned to grant: a time in which all catholics and those perfectly faithful to God may commend themselves to his majesty. For this reason I have sent this letter to your apostleship, with the free leave now granted me by heavenly favour.

For our lord the most invincible emperor, who has always embraced the orthodox religion with most ardent faith and longed to recall the holy churches to concord, as soon as he had obtained the imperial insignia by heavenly judgment, declared to the bishops here that the churches were to be united in accordance with the apostolic rules.

And indeed a great part of the matter of faith has been settled, God being its author; only on the name of Acacius is it fitting that the consent of your beatitude should lead the way. For this reason our lord the most serene prince has sent to your holiness Gratus, a man of exalted rank and a friend of one mind with me, with the imperial letters, so that you may deign by all means to come to Constantinople to settle what remains for concord. We await your coming without any delay; but if some hindrance, which ought not to happen, should perhaps hold it back, at least make haste in the meantime to send suitable bishops, because the whole world of our regions, now turned toward unity, cannot bear delays.

Hasten, then, most holy lord, lest things that ought to be ordered in your presence be done in your absence. For we know what the letters of your beatitude and of your predecessors sent to the East contain on this very matter.

So that nothing may be left undone, however, the business of religion, on account of the matter so often mentioned, has also been entrusted to your son Gratus, a man of exalted rank, for his mission to the most invincible king, with the favour of our Lord Jesus Christ.

HORMISDAS TO JUSTINIAN. We received the contents of your letter, strong in the support of religion, with the joy that a most longed-for devotion brings, and we gave thanks to the Divinity, because you have given proof that what we might have urged you to do is readily done by you. Hence it is that, since you desire praiseworthy things of your own accord, the line of your family has deservedly reached the summit of rule.

Persist, therefore, and press on with spirits of religious vigour, so that, just as your family has merited the height of empire for a good will at the beginning, you may have the eternal glory of triumph for bringing it to completion.

See with what longing the world, so long mocked, yearns for the joys of peace; behold how the minds of all are lifted by confidence in your kindness to a sure hope of tranquillity! There is no room for doubt to creep in, no room for any uncertainty, since you testify, as we too know well, that the wishes of the religious prince are directed toward the concord of the churches.

Therefore, giving thanks to such magnanimity, we beseech you with all the entreaty we can that the name of Acacius with his followers, which hinders the joy of full unity among the churches, be removed by way of condemnation. For we have sent legates suited to the nature of the case, so that in their presence the beginning of joy that you have given may be brought to fulfilment in accordance with what is contained in their instructions.

HORMISDAS TO JUSTIN AUGUSTUS, BY THE BISHOPS GERMANUS AND JOHN, THE DEACONS FELIX AND DIOSCORUS, AND THE PRESBYTER BLANDUS. By the grace of the Divinity, the fame of your glory has spread so far, and, with the merit of your life supporting you, you have so laudably become known to the world as the report of the most esteemed men has spread it, that people believe the height of empire has been enlarged through you rather than that anyone could say you are known through the empire. It is certain indeed that such an advancement has added a crowning honour to your former splendour; but by your character you held the principate long ago.

Since a greatness that cannot endure to be hidden has thus spread you through the mouths of the nations, to us too, as we read in the mystic scriptures, the fragrance of your sweetness has come with its testimonies. And certainly, since the principles of your religious life had been spread widely by the judgment of wise men, we could not be unaware of whatever the world had made known about you by its witness. For just as things worthy of modest praise cannot claim boundless acclaim for themselves, so whatever has been adorned with a goodness that inspires admiration is swept out among the people to be proclaimed without end. Greatness claims for itself, by right of its own magnitude, the testimonies of fame, because wonderful things cannot lie hidden.

Hence it is that the laws of the state have entrusted the principate to you with glory. For since the marks of your merits have become the wishes of all, no one will prove so unjust a judge of affairs as to think that you received the titles of the glorious citadel [?] by chance, since it cannot be denied that you deservedly won those of empire, you whose integrity the world has recognised.

But it is a small thing to receive the right to reign as a reward, even by the judgment of all; this is more to be admired, that the empire receives you, shaped by the praise of men, in such a way that the judgments are divine. There is no doubt that you, whom the proofs of sincere faith surround, were chosen by the venerable predestination of the Divinity for the honours of such great power. Truly we may say that the words of the prophetic spirit fit you: Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you.

To this glory, by the incomprehensible ordering of the heavenly majesty, the service of nature brought you forth into the world; the integrity of a life spent under the guardianship of faith trained you; and divine clemency carried you to empire. This was surely so that at last, once those who divide the Lord's body had been checked by the carrying out of your faith, the concord of the churches might cut away the devil's obstacles and the whole world rejoice in its union. This office is specially entrusted from heaven to your religion, your faith, your serenity, to whom we see it granted both to be able to do all things and to accomplish them.

Therefore, as you have resolved to do, carry out zealously the task of the work you have undertaken, which you see laid upon you by heavenly providence. And truly it was fitting that the peace which reverence for the Divinity demands should be made through the prince. Give to our God these offerings of the empire you have taken up, so that through you the fruit of peace may be brought to fulfilment. Without doubt, whatever such a deed secures for your soul will be reckoned by the world as a gift bestowed by you.

Great and beyond all reckoning, venerable emperor, is the purpose for which you were taken up by the judgment of the Divinity. See, the prayers of those who long for peace are drawn out; through the long passage of time the indivisible communion of the churches, torn apart, mourns; not without groaning is the brotherhood at variance, since wills differ concerning the dogmas of the fathers.

Gird your loins, then, with the strength of faith; see what King the Divinity wishes you to serve, and how great is the thing it is bringing about through you: it has appointed that the body of the venerable church, which our Christ founded by his own passion, should be united by the deeds of your glory. There is nothing by which the majesty of heavenly grace could shine more brightly upon you than if the body of the church, formed by the redemption of the Lord's blood, were restored through your service.

The calamity in this matter is indeed very old, but because of its enormity the grief is very fresh, and the groaning in Christian souls is the stronger the longer it has been drawn out. You must see how fiercely the madness of the ancient enemy rages every day: although the case was long ago settled by a final sentence, he delays the peace, and although the synod of Chalcedon and the decrees of blessed Pope Leo are accepted, through which we wish to return to charity, he does not give up the struggle.

They follow what is bound up with those dogmas, yet they do not withdraw from the followers of those whom they understand to have been condemned by that same authority. They still hold in their embrace the name of Acacius, who, as they see, has deservedly suffered the penalty of the condemned by the judgment of the apostolic see.

Who would not see that it is mere pretence to say: 'We follow the dogmas of the holy fathers but do not love their deeds; what was established by the holy synod of Chalcedon and what the letter of blessed Leo contains we cherish, venerate and embrace, but to Acacius, who followed the communion of the condemned, we offer our devotion'?

But what need is there to speak of matters already judged, when it befits us only to urge that those who say such things should lay aside the pretence described above and desire peace in all purity? With you lies the whole reason for my entreaty, excellent emperor: resist these and suchlike things with the vigour of religious work. It falls to you that, having desired ecclesiastical concord in private life, you should bring it to effect as ruler.

Nothing could add more to the fullness of your grace than what has been given you by God: that what you always wished to happen can be brought to completion through you. Nor has any slight sign of divine grace shone upon you, to whom it is given to be able to do what you have always desired. Therefore, since you see that the honour of so great a cause has been reserved for you, remove whatever is thought to remain doubtful, so that our joy may be complete.

For we, having received with fitting affection the letter of your principate through Gratus, vir spectabilis, on whom we saw that the office of embassy had been suitably laid because of his moderation, have sent men suited to the greatness of the cause: the bishops Germanus and John, the presbyter Blandus, and also the deacon Felix. Through them, if, as we presume, the favour of your serenity smiles on them, the wishes of all may be made firm by the union of the churches, in accordance with the instructions given.

HORMISDAS TO JOHN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE. We have indeed given your letter, brother, a fitting reply with ecclesiastical freedom, and we have stated clearly what we were glad to find in it and what had been passed over in silence. And although now frequent embassies, now the long experience of your own life in the church, have instilled everything into your mind, it is nonetheless good to set out our counsel still more fully by repeating our reasoning, because the firmness of the faith is well discussed when the desire to make peace is explained in simple words.

For we have always wished that those regions might share your desires, by which you testify that you are hastening toward ecclesiastical concord, and, not content with mere eager wishes, we have also used prayers. What we say is confirmed by your testimony and the world's: that to bring about the restoration of catholic unity we lower our authority, keeping the integrity of the faith unimpaired. May divine mercy incline its ear to our prayers, so that what you believe ought to be requested you may follow and love when it is offered.

We have one concern in this cause, one safeguard: to desire peace in such a way that the decrees of religion and of the venerable fathers are kept. For things that do not disagree but share a harmonious belief should rightly stand by a like observance.

But why linger any longer? You yourself know what the cause of unity demands; you yourself know by what road you must come to fellowship with the blessed apostle Peter. You have a guide for your journey, which you claim already to follow: the council held at Chalcedon for the sake of religion. Now the teaching of blessed Leo, which you have likewise declared that you embrace, will accompany you too on your return.

If these things please you, let the defence of the condemned Acacius not please you: it is this that holds back the wishes of good zeal from their completion. For those decrees were so framed by the assembly of the venerable fathers against the enemies of God and of his law that whoever followed them in communion would at once fall under the sentence passed in their condemnation. What we steadfastly pursue, then, is nothing new; we are keeping the just judgments made in those times by the decree of the fathers.

We urge you, therefore, brother, and with the help of our God's mercy we knock at your mind, that you separate yourself from all contagion of heretics by condemning Acacius with his followers, and be fed together with us by sharing in the Lord's body. If you proclaim everything with us, why do you not condemn everything with us? For you will embrace with us what we venerate only if you shudder with us at what we detest. Complete peace knows no gap, and the worship of the one God cannot be true except in unity of confession.

Therefore, greeting you with the affection of brotherly charity, we declare your request granted, having sent, as you hoped, the most religious men Germanus and John, bishops, Felix, deacon, Dioscorus, deacon, and Blandus, presbyter. With what instructions they have been furnished you will clearly recognise, if you reflect, even before they present their case. They will receive you into peace on the basis of the profession of which we have often written in reply.
Fulfil, then, dearest brother, our joy and yours, and send back to us through them the declaration of your right faith, so that through you an example may be given to all.

HORMISDAS TO JOHN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.
