We have taken note of what your charity indicated in the letter you sent, and we rejoice that signs of your faith have come to our knowledge, praying that our God may deign to grant full effect, with regard to the peace of the church, to your intention, which we desire to be upright. We have conceived this hope in our hearts from the heavenly majesty, because we judge that the most serene emperor has been chosen by divine providence for this purpose, that through him the restoration of the churches, desired for so long, may come about.

Therefore, although what must be done for the unity of the faith cannot be hidden from your charity's knowledge, we have nonetheless sent the legates whom the nature of the case required, so that at their urging both what we signified long ago and what we have recently repeated may, with our Lord as its author, be brought to effect.

HORMISDAS TO CELER AND PATRICIUS, IN THE SAME TERMS. Although, in view of our position, we could by no means keep silent on the cause of the catholic faith, the most serene prince has greatly spurred our zeal in this direction by the letter he sent, and in accordance with his wish we have sent legates.

And since a cause of this kind ought to be supported by the help of the sons of the church, we greet you with fitting respect and honour and ask that you support, before the mind of the most serene prince, the representations made for the peace of the church by those who have been sent. Indeed, no small reward follows the labour of your highness when you give us cause to render thanks to almighty God for your works.

HORMISDAS TO THE PRAETORIAN PREFECT OF THESSALONICA AND THE OTHER ILLUSTRIOUS MEN, IN THE SAME TERMS. Although our concern for the cause of the church has never ceased, we have been spurred all the more readily by the sacred letter of the most serene emperor, and with the favour of heavenly mercy we have sent legates, so that by their service the good things we expect from the prince's intentions may be fulfilled.

And so, greeting your amplitude with the respect and honour that are due, we ask that you lend your zeal to the restoration of the faith and not allow the prayers of the faithful to be delayed any longer after so much time, for there is no doubt that your highness will gain the fruit of great praise if, through you and by the working of our God's mercy, there comes about what all good men desire.

HORMISDAS TO THE ILLUSTRIOUS JUSTINIAN. We have received with love your Magnificence's letter, full of holy faith, in which you announced that God has given us an opportunity to establish firmly among you the apostolic preaching. We therefore cannot thank our Lord enough for giving you both the time and the will for such excellent remedies.

We recognize that these things are ordered from above, now that the divine majesty has conferred the empire on one who judges that he was appointed to restore peace to the churches. It remains, then, for all the bishops of the East to attest, according to the wording of the libellus, that they have truly been brought to correction.

The way to venerable concord lies open; the remedies for the health we long for have been set out: let the bishops who desire catholic peace not refuse the catholic profession. For error must not be corrected in parts but cut out by the roots. Press on, then, as you have begun, so that your reward with God, which began with the undertaking of a good work, may reach its fulfilment with its completion.

The letter you sent us testifies that your mind is such that you need little encouragement to bring your good purpose to completion. Yet the very ground that has given us hope kindles our desire more fiercely, and we long all the more eagerly for the fulfilment of the joys which we believe God is already bringing near. That is why we daily implore the blessed apostle Peter in supplication that God may grant you, through whom holy Church now hopes to have her members made whole again, both swift success and long life.

For our part, following your wishes, we have sent men to make concord firm under the arrangement laid down by the Apostolic See. It is for you, just as we did not wish to fail your good intention, to see that they bring back to us the outcome we desire.
The venerable shrines have received your gift; but you will do something more pleasing to the blessed apostle Peter if through you they receive the unity of the Church they long for.

HORMISDAS TO THEODOSIUS, ARCHDEACON OF CONSTANTINOPLE, AND TO ALL THE CATHOLICS, LIKEWISE. We offer fitting thanks to the divine mercy, which has not allowed your faith to labour long. For a time has come in which the catholic Church can recover her sons, her soldiers. What greater joy could fill our heart than to recall that evils have been driven away?

Let present joys make up for the hardships of your affliction, for our God, who was your remedy, did not wish your charity to be crushed by adversity but to be tested. For if you weigh the evils of the past against the present reward, which is beyond doubt divine, who can doubt that you have gained greater rewards than adversity could ever have done you harm?

And although our concern for the state of the catholic faith has never ceased, yet, prompted by the sacred letter of the most serene emperor, we have taken care to send legates, through whose service we do not doubt that, God willing, what we have often commanded will be accomplished.

Strive, therefore, as is fitting, so that you may offer the catholic Church this as the chief gift of your deliverance: that, with everything that has done harm until now driven away, we may give thanks and offer praise to our God without ceasing in the one communion we have always desired.

HORMISDAS TO THE EMPRESS EUPHEMIA. The peace of the churches is now being restored by heavenly ordering, since God has chosen for the empire those whose devotion to his religion he has always known to be sound. For just as in private life you always worshipped God with right doctrine, so now you take thought for concord in religion; and indeed much has been done in the very first days of your reign that promises us hope of complete correction.

Therefore, rejoicing that the love of the faith burns in you, we give thanks to God and daily pray to the blessed apostle Peter for you, that he may support your prayers before the Lord and bring the course of your good will to fulfilment. Nor is there any doubt that you are helped by divine aid, since you obey the heavenly commands with such zeal for religion.

Hence, since the holy purpose of you and your husband is well known, we confidently send this letter to your Clemency, so that through you your husband's piety may be spurred on still more to bring the peace of the Church to completion.

You have taken up a great work; a great cause has been entrusted to you. For through you Christ wishes to call back to the covenant of the Church the peoples whom he willed to redeem from death through himself. A great occasion for praise has also been prepared for your sex, if at your urging Christ joins together the members of his Church that had been divided.

Nor indeed is the glory greater of her who searched for the wood of human salvation and alone found the cross which the whole world venerates. Rather, you will surpass her merits, because the unity of the Church, which through her found its sign, will through you obtain its remedy.

Let your husband's devout Clemency see to it, then, that our brothers and fellow bishops consent to affirm their faith according to the wording of the libellus we sent some time ago, so that the correction that has been begun may be completed. For any confession in the worship of God that lacks the fullness of faith is void. What we ask of the rest has, as is well known, already been done by many bishops, and unity in communion cannot be just unless it is preserved in the manner of their return.

HORMISDAS TO ANASTASIA AND PALMATIA, LIKEWISE. Zeal of good will is always accompanied by the success God grants. By the providence of our God an opportunity has been offered in which you ought to exert yourselves for the reward of your faith.

Trusting first in the mercy from on high, and then in the conscience of the most clement emperor, we have sent legates on behalf of the cause of the catholic religion. Through them we greet your Eminence with the respect that is due, asking that you not withhold your labour and effort for the restoration of the Church's concord, so that, when those whom the authority of the Apostolic See has condemned have been rejected and removed and the Christian people has returned to the one right communion, you may have the blessed apostle Peter, for whose faith we strive, as helper in your undertakings.
(158.) MEMORANDUM WHICH OUR ABOVE-NAMED LEGATES RECEIVED.

When, with God's favour, you have entered the East, if any bishops come to meet you and wish to present the libellus, whose content you know, signed by themselves, accept them and grant them fellowship in holy communion.

But if the bishops who meet you refuse to make their profession in the manner stated above, treat them indeed with the affection due to bishops, but do not share a table with them, and do not take even provisions from them, except only transport, if need requires, and hospitality, so that they may not think themselves altogether scorned with disdain.

When, with God's help, you have come to Constantinople, take up residence in the lodging the emperor provides, and let no one come to greet you before you have seen the emperor himself, except those whom the emperor himself sends or those you know to be of our communion.

When you are presented to him, greet him and offer our letter, telling him that we have received great joy from his accession and rejoice exceedingly that almighty God has [?] him for this purpose, as his sacred letter says: that, in accordance with what has been laid down by the prelates of the Apostolic See, with God as author and his reign lending its efforts, the peace and unity of the churches, desired for so long, may come about.

If he urges you to see the bishop of Constantinople, inform him that you have instructions already fixed, which they too have often been told: namely, what profession must be made by all bishops who embrace catholic communion. If the bishop of Constantinople is ready to fulfil these, we gladly come to meet him; but if he scorns to follow the exhortation of the Apostolic See, what need is there for our greeting to become an occasion for strife, since we have no commission for dispute or contest?
If the emperor wishes to have it explained to him what you are asking the bishop to do, show him the text of the libellus that you are carrying.

If he agrees about the anathema of Acacius but says that his successors should be read out, on the ground that some of them were sent into exile for defending the Council of Chalcedon, you will point out that you can remove nothing from the text of the libellus, in which the followers of the condemned are included alike.

But if you cannot turn them from this aim, at least agree to this: that, once Acacius has been specifically anathematized through the libellus we gave you, silence be kept about the names of his successors, their names being erased from the inscription of the diptychs. When this has been done, receive the bishop of Constantinople into our communion.

As for the libellus of the bishop of Constantinople, or of others whom you may, God willing, come to receive, first see to it that it is read aloud in the presence of the people. If this cannot be done, let it at least be read in the sacristy in the presence of the clergy and the archimandrites.

If all these things have, God willing, been accomplished, ask the emperor to send sacred letters through the metropolitan bishops, with a letter of the bishop himself attached, announcing that the bishop of Constantinople, having with his own consent made the profession that the Apostolic See sent, has been received into the unity of communion. In these letters let him also urge them to make the same profession.

If the emperor raises any difficulty on this point, let the bishop of Constantinople send instructions to the bishops under his jurisdiction and to the other metropolitans, in the presence of those whom you likewise send, making known what he himself has done. You must demand this from him by every means, so that, as the testimony of this deed travels about, it cannot remain hidden from anyone, even those who live far away.
(159.) COPY OF THE LIBELLUS OF JOHN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.

TO MY LORD, IN ALL THINGS MOST HOLY AND MOST BLESSED BROTHER AND FELLOW MINISTER HORMISDAS, JOHN, GREETING IN THE LORD. When your Holiness's letter was delivered to me, most dear brother in Christ, through Gratus, the most distinguished count, and now through Germanus and John, the most reverend bishops, Felix and Dioscorus, the most holy deacons, and Blandus the presbyter, I rejoiced at your Holiness's spiritual charity, in that you seek the unity of God's most holy churches according to the ancient tradition of the fathers and are eager to drive off those who tear apart the rational flock of Christ.

Know for certain, then, most holy in all things, that, as I wrote to you, I agree with you in truth and, being myself a lover of peace, I reject all the heretics you have repudiated. For I hold that the most holy churches of God, that is, of your elder Rome and of this new Rome, are one; I define the see of the apostle Peter and that of this imperial city to be one. I assent to all that was enacted by the four holy councils, that is, Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon, concerning the confirmation of the faith and the state of the Church, and I allow nothing that was rightly judged to be shaken. Rather, I know that those who have tried or have striven to overturn their decrees even in a single point have fallen away from the holy, universal and apostolic Church of God. And, plainly making use of your own rightly

spoken words, I say this in the present writing: that the first condition of salvation is to keep the rule of right faith and in no way to depart from the tradition of the fathers, since the saying of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be passed over: "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church." These words are proved by the facts, for in the Apostolic See the catholic religion has always been kept inviolate.

Desiring, then, not to fall from this faith, and following in all things the decrees of the fathers, we anathematize all heresies, especially the heretic Nestorius, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, who was condemned at the Council of Ephesus by the blessed Celestine, pope of the city of Rome, and by the venerable Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria. Together with him we anathematize Eutyches and Dioscorus, bishop of the city of Alexandria, who were condemned at the holy Council of Chalcedon, which we venerate, follow and embrace, and which, following the holy Council of Nicaea, proclaimed the apostolic faith.

Joining to these Timothy the parricide, surnamed Aelurus, we anathematize him, and likewise condemn his disciple and follower in all things, Peter of Alexandria. We likewise anathematize Acacius, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, who became their accomplice and follower, and also those who persist in communion and fellowship with them; for whoever embraces someone's communion incurs a like sentence of condemnation with them. In the same way we also condemn and anathematize Peter of Antioch, with his followers and all those named above.

We therefore approve and embrace all the letters of the blessed Leo, pope of the city of Rome, which he wrote concerning the right faith. Accordingly, as we said before, following the Apostolic See in all things, we also proclaim everything that it has decreed; and therefore I hope to be in one communion with you, the communion which the Apostolic See proclaims, in which is the whole and perfect solidity of the Christian religion. I promise that in future the names of those separated from the communion of the catholic Church, that is, those who do not agree with the Apostolic See in all things, are not to be recited during the sacred mysteries. And if I attempt to depart in any way from my profession, I declare that by my own condemnation I make myself a partner of those whom I have condemned.

To this profession I have subscribed with my own hand, and I have sent it in reply to you, Hormisdas, holy and most blessed brother and pope of great Rome, through the above-named venerable bishops Germanus and John, the deacons Felix and Dioscorus, and the presbyter Blandus.

AND IN ANOTHER HAND: I, John, by the mercy of God bishop of Constantinople, the new Rome, agreeing with all that is stated above in this my profession, have subscribed, being sound in the Lord. Pray for us, most holy and most blessed brother. Dated in the month of March, on the twenty-eighth day, in the twelfth indiction, at Constantinople, in the consulship of our lord Justin, perpetual Augustus, and Eutharic, vir clarissimus.
(160.) JUSTIN AUGUSTUS TO HORMISDAS.

THE VICTOR JUSTIN, PIOUS, FORTUNATE, RENOWNED, TRIUMPHANT, EVER AUGUSTUS, TO HORMISDAS, MOST HOLY AND MOST BLESSED ARCHBISHOP AND PATRIARCH. Know, most religious father, that what was long sought with the greatest efforts has been accomplished for us. Be informed that, even before those you sent had arrived, it had become clear that John, the most blessed prelate of our new Rome, together with his clergy, agrees with you, wavering in no ambiguity and divided by no discord. Know that he has signed the libellus which you had judged should be presented, in keeping with the council of the most holy fathers.

All whom the shining splendour of truth illuminates run together with eager effort to take up the wishes both of your see and of the see of Constantinople; all whom the clear way delights hasten most willingly. They follow the most holy decrees of the fathers and their most approved laws; and, with the resolve of some who held to the right path strengthened, and others who were wandering uncertainly corrected, the matter is coming to this: that they too worship the unity of the undivided Trinity with unity of mind.

It has been forbidden that in future, according to the terms of the libellus we have mentioned, any commemoration be made during the divine mysteries of Acacius the transgressor, formerly bishop of this royal city, or of other bishops who either were the first to oppose the apostolic decrees or became successors to the error, unamended by any repentance up to their last day.

And since all our provinces must be admonished to imitate the example of the royal city, we have decided that imperial orders are to be sent everywhere. So greatly do we burn with devotion to religion, so earnestly do we seek the peace of the catholic faith, in order that heaven may reward our state with peace and win heavenly protection for my subjects. For what can be found more pleasing, more just, more glorious, than that those whom the same realm contains and the worship of the same faith illuminates should not contend for different things, but with minds gathered into one should revere ordinances laid down not by human thought but by the wisdom of the divine Spirit?

Let your Holiness's religion pray, then, that the help of divine grace may grant that what is being achieved with watchful zeal for the concord of the churches of the catholic faith may be preserved for ever. Dated ten days before the Kalends of May, at Constantinople.
(161.) COPY OF THE REPORT OF JOHN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.

TO MY LORD, IN ALL THINGS HOLY AND BELOVED OF GOD, BROTHER AND FELLOW MINISTER HORMISDAS, JOHN, GREETING IN THE LORD. When God works his own wonders among his people, then we must boldly cry out what is contained in the divine writings, in the very words of Scripture: "Who shall tell of the mighty deeds of the Lord, or make all his praises heard at every time?"

For behold, he has raised up for the Roman state such a pious emperor as the catholic Church had long needed and the whole human race longed to see. And so he has inclined the horn of grace upon him from heaven, so that mercy might be poured out abundantly on his sacred head; and at the time of his proclamation all glorified with a loud voice God, the ruler of all, because by my hands he adorned such a head with such a crown.

This greatest emperor, then, has plainly displayed the first palm of his contests in the defeat of the enemy; the second merit of his virtue is this: he has most wisely brought about union for the most holy churches; the third blessing of his reign: he has joined together what was scattered and most wisely secured the peace of the world.

Therefore, giving thanks in all things to the great God who governs all things most wisely, I have not delayed to announce peace to you, a son of peace, most beloved of God in all things, so that you may leap with that joy with which David, under the Law, exulted figuratively at the bringing back of the ark of God, and with which the apostles truly rejoiced through grace.

Rejoice, then, in the Lord with a joy befitting your Holiness, and write what becomes your kindly spirit, man of God! For what was divided has been joined, what was scattered has been gathered, and what was far apart has been united together. And, as I must say and have written before, clearly understanding that both churches, of the elder and of the new Rome, are one, and rightly defining that the see of both is one, I recognize, with integrity of judgement, an indivisible union and a harmonious confirmation on the part of us both.

I therefore pray God that it may always remain inseparable, by the prayers of the holy apostles and the intercessions of your Holiness, through which may it be granted to us and to the whole world that the most clement and most Christian emperor Justin and his most pious wife, our daughter Euphemia, be preserved in peace for many years, most blessed and dear brother in all things.

Rejoicing, then, at the presence of the most reverend bishops and also of your clergy, we give thanks that, in answer to our request, you sent such peaceable men, worthy of your Apostolic See, who keep the rule of the fathers without confusion and guard the faith undivided. Embracing their mind in all things, we have done everything through them to the satisfaction of your Holiness.
I and those with me send warmest greetings to all the brotherhood in Christ that is with your Holiness.
(162.) COPY OF THE LETTER OF JUSTINIAN.

TO MY MOST HOLY LORD HORMISDAS, FIRST CHIEF PONTIFF AND POPE OF THE CITY OF ROME, JUSTINIAN THE COUNT. Your venerable Holiness, proclaiming the rules, prays unceasingly to Christ God for the peace of the churches and the concord of the people; and whatever you have now agreed should be carried out through your most blessed priests has all, by the favour of the Godhead, been brought to fulfilment, the discord of certain persons proving wholly powerless.

Fortified, therefore, by your sacred prayers and by your instructions in the faith of the orthodox, we humbly ask that you deign to offer your customary, effectual prayers to the eternal King for our most holy Augustus, the promoter of the whole faith, and for his state, and also for us, the keepers of your commands; and that you deign to visit us, your faithful suppliants, with your saving letters.
(163.) COPY OF THE LETTER OF POMPEIUS.

POMPEIUS TO MY LORD, THE MOST BLESSED AND APOSTOLIC FATHER HORMISDAS, ARCHBISHOP OF THE UNIVERSAL CHURCH. Moved by the holy prayers of Your Beatitude, the goodness of almighty God has seen fit to give us a prince of such great faith that the restoration of the Church's peace, which all the faithful sought in their prayers, may rightly be seen as granted through His Clemency's most devout merits. In bringing this about, he has laid, by the working of the Holy Spirit, the firmest foundations for his reign; and these foundations have a strength of unconquerable stability as great as the excellence of this deed is judged unique and admirable.

Therefore, greeting the revered Beatitude of your pontificate with the courtesy of a letter in reply, we ask that you will pray more and more for the prosperity of our most clement and most unconquered lord prince, so that the ineffable goodness of almighty God may, with the help of his grace, justly preserve his gifts, in which the fruit of your own husbandry also abounds. We ask, too, that the supporting intercession of your pontifical holiness may stand by us, your sons, who are bound to you in spiritual affection and whom concern for this work has always gripped most of all.
(164.) COPY OF THE LETTER OF ANICIA JULIANA.

ANICIA JULIANA TO THE MOST BLESSED LORD FATHER HORMISDAS. Through the prayers of Your Beatitude, and by the arrival of the legates of the principal apostolic see, the errors of the heretics have been crushed, and we have come together in the unity of the Catholic faith, gathered together at the mother's breast of the Church on the day of the holy Resurrection.

Therefore, addressing Your Holiness with a pen of veneration, we urge you to instruct the most reverend men you have sent not to depart on any account until, as you see fit and as is proper, the things they have well arranged are made firm; so that, with every remnant of past error cut away, the unity strengthened by the efforts of Your Beatitude may be brought to lasting effect.
(165.) COPY OF THE LETTER OF ANASTASIA.

ANASTASIA TO THE HOLY LORD AND MOST BLESSED FATHER OF FATHERS HORMISDAS, ARCHBISHOP OF THE UNIVERSAL CHURCH. We rightly declare that the grace of a divine gift has shone upon us, since we learn from the assurance of your letter that the reverence of your apostolate keeps us in remembrance in your holy heart. For with true hope we trust that the favour of heavenly mercy rests upon your pontifical intercession, most blessed lord and father, to be received with apostolic honour.

The unsleeping vigils of your prayers, and the wondrous faith of our most victorious prince, ever shining with Catholic splendour, have restored to the holy churches the harmony of peace so long desired, a peace he rightly rejoices to have borne before all his firmly established triumphs as an unconquered standard. Therefore may the spotless holiness of Your Paternity persist with unceasing constancy in offering vows and prayers to almighty God for the safety and prosperity of our said lord Augustus, that God may deign to preserve the ineffable grace of such great blessings, which he himself inspired in his devout mind, for his advancement towards future blessedness as well.

May your pontificate also kindly offer prayer for my lord husband, your son, and for me, your devoted servant, together with the offspring the Lord has deigned to give us, so that through its support the protection of divine favour may graciously breathe upon us.
(166.) COPY OF THE LETTER OF THEODORITUS, BISHOP OF LYCHNIDUS.

TO THE HOLY, BLESSED, PRAISEWORTHY AND ADORABLE LORD, THE APOSTOLIC FATHER HORMISDAS, POPE OF THE CITY OF ROME, YOUR HUMBLE SERVANT THEODORITUS. It would not befit my littleness to presume so greatly as to send these present tiny pages, in the speech of a little man, to your holy and devout apostolate. But because, in your innate kindness and with a devout and gracious mind, being appointed to protect all things by the will of God, you have given back to the whole world a bright day filled with every festivity, and by your praiseworthy prayers have called all things back to their former state of unity, and by your praiseworthy and adorable merits have granted that they be brought into harmony as one, or be subjected to you:

therefore, although I am overwhelmed by my iniquities and oppressed by them on every side, yet, revived from the very depths, as my fellow servant the devout man Pullio was hastening back to your glorious feet, I have taken it upon myself to present myself at your praiseworthy and adorable feet, both through him and through these small and slight lines, imploring the divine favour with all my strength and singing with a clear voice together with absolutely everyone: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among men of good will,

who in his incomprehensible goodness, through your wonderful prayers, has enlightened and set free all things, and through your prayers, worthy of God, has granted throughout the whole world a bright day filled with every festivity, has driven out all iniquity, has loosed every knot of entanglement, and has opened every path.

Offering, then, this prayer full of rejoicing to your devout apostolate, I beseech you, holy, blessed, apostolic lord fathers, to deign to remember my lamentable littleness in your devout prayers. Received on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, through Pullio, in the consulship of Eutharic.
(167.) REPORT OF THE DEACON DIOSCORUS, SENT BY THE SUBDEACON PULLIO.

The ineffable mercy of almighty God, and the goodness he graciously pours out upon the human race, cannot be measured by human powers or set out in words; it is enough simply to marvel at his wonders with devout minds and to know that every good thing depends on the remedies of his grace alone.
This is proved every day; yet I boldly presume to say, my lord most blessed pope, that the present matter, which God has reserved for your times and merits, surpasses everything that has gone before.

What was done at Aulon, what at Scampa, and what followed at Lychnidus, I reported in an earlier account. We came to Thessalonica. What our dealings with the bishop of Thessalonica were, and what was said or even agreed, you will learn from the spoken account of the bearer of this letter; but there is one thing that should not be passed over in silence, and I do not delay to report it:

after many disputes, the said bishop, convinced by argument, was willing to sign the libellus. But because not all the bishops under his jurisdiction were present, it was agreed for the present, and he promised, that after the holy days, when one of us had been sent from the see of the city of Constantinople, the bishops of his diocese would be assembled and would sign the libellus. With God's help we believe this will be accomplished. This is what was settled at Thessalonica.

Commended by your prayers, we arrived at the city of Constantinople on the Monday of Holy Week. At the tenth milestone from that city, distinguished and magnificent men came out to meet us, among them the master of the soldiers Vitalian, Pompeius and Justinian; and other senators followed, and many people who burned with zeal for the Catholic faith and with longing for the restoration of peace. What more need I say? We entered the city amid the highest rejoicing of almost everyone.

The next day, Tuesday, we were presented before the most pious prince. The whole senate was present there, and in that assembly were also four bishops whom the bishop of Constantinople had sent to represent him. We presented the letter of Your Beatitude, which the most clement prince received with great reverence. Those things were said which had to be made known before the matter was examined; then the case was begun.

The most clement emperor urged us, saying: 'Go and see the bishop of this city, and give account to one another in a peaceable manner.' We replied: 'Why should we go to the bishop to engage in disputes? Our lord the most blessed Pope Hormisdas, who sent us, did not instruct us to dispute. But we have in our hands the libellus which all the bishops who wished to be reconciled to the apostolic see have made. If Your Piety so commands, let it be read; and if there is anything in it that is unknown, or not believed to be true, let them say so, and then we will show that nothing is written in this libellus outside the judgement of the Church; or if they can show that it does not accord with the Catholic religion, then it is up to us to prove it.'

The libellus was read out in the presence of the prince and the senate. We at once added: 'Let the four bishops present here on behalf of the bishop of Constantinople say whether the things read in the libellus are not contained in the acts of the Church!' They answered that everything was true.

After this we added: 'Lord emperor, the bishops have both spared us a great labour and done what befits them in speaking the truth.' Then the most clement emperor said to the bishops who were present: 'If these things are true, why do you not do it?' Likewise several of the senatorial order said: 'We are laymen. You say these things are true: do it, and we will follow.'

After Wednesday had passed, the bishop of Constantinople received the libellus from us in the palace, and at first he tried, as it were, to make it a letter rather than a libellus. But after not many disputes it was agreed that he should write a short preface and then append the libellus just as Your Beatitude had dictated it. He made a subscription in keeping with the libellus, and likewise a dating clause; we have sent copies of it to your apostolate in both Greek and Latin.

Once the libellus had been made, the name of Acacius was struck from the diptychs, and likewise those of Fravitta, Euphemius, Macedonius and Timothy; and we report that, with God's help, this was done with great care not only in the one church where the bishop resides but in all the churches. Likewise the names of Zeno and Anastasius were struck from the diptychs.

The bishops of various cities, as many as were found there, likewise presented the libellus, and we report that great care was taken that no bishop should communicate with us who had not first given the libellus. All the archimandrites did likewise. We report that we had disputes with these archimandrites too, as they said: 'It is enough that our archbishop has done it; we follow what he has done.' What more? After many disputes they too, convinced by argument, presented their libelli in full form.

After all this, with God's help, we went in procession in the church; but what rejoicing there was at the unity, how God was blessed, what praises too were offered to the blessed apostle Peter and to you, you can see from considering the event itself, for my tongue is unable to describe it.

Nothing followed of what our enemies had marked out: no sedition, no bloodshed, no uproar, as the enemies had earlier been predicting in order to frighten us. Even the clergy of Constantinople themselves, marvelling and giving thanks to God, say that they cannot remember so great a multitude of people ever having received communion at any time.

When these things were completed, the most clement emperor also sent his own letter to Your Beatitude, setting out the course of events, and so too did the most reverend man John, bishop of the city of Constantinople. You should know also that general imperial edicts have been issued, and we believe that, by God's favour and through your holy prayers, they will very soon be sent throughout all the provinces. This is what was done at Constantinople.

Now the church of Antioch is under discussion, and work on it is still in progress, because a suitable person has not yet been chosen. Let Your Beatitude therefore pray more earnestly that God, who, moved by your prayers, restored the church of Constantinople to the apostolic see, may himself also grant a worthy person to be ordained at Antioch, and may unite the churches without delay.

If it seems good to Your Beatitude to write back to the bishop of Constantinople, make mention of the condemnations of Severus and of those whom you named in the letter you wrote to Syria Secunda through the monks John and Sergius. If you do the same in writing back to the emperor, it seems to me necessary… [?]

HORMISDAS TO JUSTIN AUGUSTUS. On reading Your Clemency's letter announcing that the harmony of the faith has been restored, the mind of the whole Church burst out joyfully into the hymn of divine praise in which is sung: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will!

Trusting in this hymn, then, look forward to the glory and happiness that the merits of the faithful deserve. For it was not human agreement alone that raised you, a prince so pleasing to God, to the summit of empire: divine favour had formed you for itself beforehand and handed you the empire of the East, so that you might become the instrument of its works; and so you bring it about that this prophetic saying rightly applies to you: You will make them princes over all the earth; they will remember your name in every generation and generation. Indeed, since it is your purpose to preserve Christian peace, who could doubt that you have been chosen by Christ?

These are the first foundations of your reign: to have appeased God by justice and to have won for yourself the help of his most excellent majesty, while you crush his adversaries as though they were your own enemies. These, surely, are the greatest foundations of the state; this is its solid and unconquerable strength. For what is walled about by the firmness of divine grace cannot be pierced by human blows.

Prophetic Scripture bears witness to this, for it says: I have chosen David my servant, and with my holy oil I have anointed him; for my hand will help him, and my arm will strengthen him. On the other hand, whoever has been forsaken by heavenly grace seeks arms and forces for himself in vain; for it is truly written: Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain.

You will indeed wage war, most excellent prince, safe under divine protection, and you will bend the necks of the fiercest nations under the yoke of your state; but no victory can be more outstanding than your overthrowing of the enemy of the human race after he had sought out strongholds for so long a time.

For other battles are by nature divided by race, bounded by regions, and stained with blood; this one embraces the whole human race in its palm of victory. You will credit this triumph to every region, and, what comes closest to divine goodness, those who a little while ago were running riot under the devil's leadership are now conquered without bloodshed, to bring about their own salvation.

The triumph of this Christian victory will therefore endure for ever, for what is founded on the stability of the everlasting faith cannot be wiped out by the decay of time; the fame of your deeds will remain far and wide, and, as the divine words declare, their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.

In other wars you protect fields, cities and towns, or, last of all, the freedom of your subjects, things acquired for the use of mortals and destined one day to be dissolved by a like mortality; in this contest life itself is defended, and the battle is fought, as it were, for the citadel of everlasting blessedness.

For this reason the preparation for so great a work demands Your Clemency's unbroken attention. See to it that the most savage enemy finds absolutely no hiding-place from which he might emerge again; strip him of every defence, and if any trace of him remains anywhere, purge it all away with a merciful remedy. Let every seed of wickedness be torn out by the roots; let the stock that is hostile to God be cut back to the quick, lest, if it is less firmly suppressed, the poisonous root of iniquity should once again (God forbid) spread its shoots more widely.

Why do I say this? Because there still remains for you the correction of the churches of Alexandria and Antioch and of others, which must on no account be neglected. If Your Clemency's care is turned to this, there is hope that it will be swiftly completed with the help of him by whose authority we believe every good thing is begun.

We further commend to you the legates sent by the apostolic see, and we place them in the keeping of your faith and religion. May Your Piety dismiss them, when everything has been completed, in such a way that, through the divine favours and your own, they may bring back to the apostolic see full joy concerning the peace of all the churches.
We have sent this letter to be delivered by Paulinus, defensor of the Roman Church and servant of Your Piety. Given on the seventh day before the Ides of July, in the consulship of Eutharic.

HORMISDAS TO JOHN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE. As I consider the letter of Your Charity, in which you have professed that you hold one faith with the see of the blessed apostle Peter, I am moved to cry out with the freedom of the prophet: Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity! For it does not matter how great the distances that separate us, when by God's doing we are now joined in one dwelling of faith.

For now, by the provision of divine mercy, the members of Christ once scattered are coming together into the form of one body; the inheritance of our Lord, foretold by the voices of the prophets and plundered by most wicked robbers, is being restored; and truly the foundations of the Eastern Church are being made firm in the faith of this rock, that is, in the steadfastness of the prince of the apostles. Since your letter reports that these things have been done, we must say with timely rejoicing: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of peace, who bring good news of good things!

Thanks be, then, to the most excellent Trinity, who has granted that the rulers of Church and state be of one mind in Christ! For it is great well-being for the world whenever one mind unites priests and princes in the truth of the Catholic faith. This is the firm bond of peace; this is a fellowship sent down from heaven. For it is not right for subjects to think otherwise in a matter on which they see their superiors agree.

Can there be any doubt that one Providence has arranged all these things: first, that the prince was chosen who, when he saw that he had taken up rule over men, did not forget that he was subject to God; and then, that he gave Your Fraternity to his Church as a bishop of whom there could be no doubt that he would enter into sure and lasting harmony of faith with our see, that is, the apostolic see? For since you gladly accepted from us the libellus of faith, being eager for reunion in Christ, you are recognised as never having been estranged from us in the divine predestination.

So, dearest brother, press on with the blessings of our God, which come of their own accord; gather more fully the members of the flock once scattered, and guard those who have been gathered. Remember now that you are the helmsman of a ship graciously entrusted to you by Christ; be mindful of the spirits of diabolical defiance that disturb the security of a peaceful voyage, and do not let the waves of an uncertain storm escape your notice, but watch for them with a wakeful mind and calm them with reason lifted up towards God.

Let no negligence in the task entrusted to you wrench the helm of the Lord's ship from your hands; keep your gaze ever fixed on that one sign of the right course, so that you may the more surely disregard the turmoil stirred up by the devil's contrary winds and reach the calm of the promised harbour. For this is the arena of the Christian contest; to such service in Christ's army the palm of eternal life is offered.

If you think most rightly on these things, the protection of the commander will not fail his soldier; and the more the snares of the enemy multiply, the more the grace of the supreme Ruler turns the adversary's poisons into occasions for his mercy, as the word of apostolic truth has declared: Where iniquity abounded, grace has abounded all the more. Only hold fast to the divine and most upright ordinances, fostering the harmony of the Church, so that, marked as it were with the sign of a peaceable will, you may be proved a disciple of him who said: My peace I give to you, my peace I leave with you.

Urge also our son, the most clement prince Justin, divinely provided for this Christian age, although he already strives of his own accord towards what is right, to carry out what he deigned to promise in his royal letter: that by sending edicts to those whom wandering error even now leads away from the breasts of mother Church, he may restrain the devil's deceit both by the authority of religion and by the measured power of the empire, and may count it his greatest victory against the common enemy of all mankind if, with the help of heavenly divinity, he crushes the poisons of the ancient serpent.

Do not fail to be concerned also about the state of the churches of Antioch and Alexandria, and petition the most clement prince repeatedly to restore peace in these too by a religious settlement, so that he may add the crowning of full completion to his good beginnings. For a good work is begun in vain if its completion does not follow in full.

We further commend to you the legates sent by the apostolic see; may Your Love so arrange their return to us that they may bring us full joy at the peace restored to all the churches. Given on the seventh day before the Ides of July, in the consulship stated above.

HORMISDAS TO THE BISHOPS GERMANUS AND JOHN, THE DEACONS FELIX AND DIOSCORUS, AND THE PRIEST BLANDUS. For what has been done, as contained in Your Charity's report, we give thanks to our God, who deigned to assist your labour. And we urge you to attend upon the most clement prince and his most pious consort the Augusta with fitting services, and, with the help of our Christ, to work so that, once everything has been settled in accordance with ecclesiastical observance, all the churches situated in any part of the world may be called back to the communion of the apostolic see.

As for the churches of Alexandria and Antioch, strive to have them joined to our faith under a reasonable observance, because the completion of so great a matter will win the grace of divine favour both for the most clement prince and for you. Given on the same day as above, in the consulship stated above.

Hormisdas to John, Bishop of Constantinople, and to Dioscorus the deacon. We have learned that our brothers and fellow bishops Thomas and Nicostratus were not received at Constantinople as we wished and as they themselves always hoped. It is said not only that the places due to them were taken away, but we have also learned that they were suspended from communion.

We believe that your fraternity (your love) also judges how bitterly our mind bears this. So you must act without delay, with all the effectiveness that you see the importance of the matter demands, so that we ourselves do not appear to have been treated with contempt instead, among those with whom they stayed. For, contrary to what we all desired, the burden of distress has been unbecomingly laid on them, to such a degree that our brother and fellow bishop John is said to have made no arrangement about their property, which is said to have been seized, and is said not to have received the letters we sent through them.

We earnestly wish you to act in all these matters so that your charity may be able to write back to us quickly about the outcome of this case. Given on the day stated above, in the consulship written above.
Hormisdas to the bishops Thomas and Nicostratus. Do not think that our mind is idle or slack concerning your business, for we think about your weariness no differently than about our own.

For we have learned from Menas, notary of our church, that your charity is still enduring the troubles of waiting. So, that almighty God may deign to grant a remedy for these adversities, we have sent a letter to John, our brother and fellow bishop, and we have also charged our son Dioscorus the deacon in our letter to make known to our lord and son, the emperor Justin, the need and the case of your love, and to press it earnestly, so that our lord may deign to bring about an outcome fitting your wishes.

Your fraternity should speak with this Dioscorus the deacon, for he must support your purpose, whether out of regard for catholic communion or in consideration of our exhortation. Given on the day stated above, in the consulship written above.

Hormisdas to Dioscorus the deacon. We rejoice at the result of the labour you undertook with the help of almighty God, so far as it has been accomplished. We direct you to consider how those who condemned the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon in writing are to be brought back: whether such men should perhaps be regarded not as schismatics but rather as heretics, or whether the case is indeed the same for those who condemned them in speech and for those convicted of having condemned them in writing. For our son, the illustrious and religious Albinus, seems to be raising a question over this distinction. Consider also whether those who wrote against the Council of Chalcedon should be received only through that general libellus, or whether something more should be added.
As for the churches of Alexandria and Antioch, strive with the help of our God that, once everything has been rightly arranged, they may be joined to catholic communion.

The long waiting of our brothers and fellow bishops Thomas and Nicostratus also saddens us, and we wonder why bishops of the right faith seem to be in difficulty under a catholic emperor. Your charity ought to support their wishes by your action, so that the sorrow of those seeking what they desire may be turned into joy.

John, Bishop of Nicopolis, has written to us through Ammonius the deacon that certain malicious people are trying to stir up a false accusation against him before the emperor. We commend him to your love, urging you to work hard so that the scheming of his enemies cannot disturb his peace.

When this Ammonius the deacon came to us, we were unwilling to receive him into the communion of the apostolic see until we had consulted with Sergius the deacon and inquired what ought to be arranged. Our deliberation found this acceptable to the aforesaid deacon: that he should be joined to catholic communion through the testimony of a libellus. We inform you that he solemnly presented this libellus, offered it, and has been admitted to our communion. Given.

Hormisdas to Pompeius. We confess that our devoted mind has been so filled with joy at the concord that we believe no words are sufficient for us to do justice to the purity of your faith. You will surely pass to posterity with a great memory of happiness, since it is certain that you were bound up in concern for making peace. You have merit before God, to whose religion you pay your devotion. You have indeed fulfilled the desires of all, but your own prayers have been fulfilled as well; and while you have prepared a reward for your own soul, the whole world rejoices in the benefit bestowed on it.

Therefore, greeting you with due honour, we urge and ask you to bring to completion, with the same energy with which you began the peace of the Church, and, wherever you see that traces of any contention remain, to take care to pursue them by every means. Stand by the fullest tranquillity of the churches of God; press on with the labour that you have offered to the Lord as the gift of your faith. For you make us demand completion from you with greater confidence, since we rejoice that you laid the welcome foundations of the union so long desired. Given on the day stated above, in the consulship written above.

Hormisdas to Dioscorus the deacon. We rejoice at the result of the labour you undertook with the help of almighty God, so far as it has been accomplished. We inform you that all the peoples of Italy were pleased with what was done through you by God's doing, and we give thanks without ceasing to our God, who has made you recognize that you were sent not out of hatred but rather because of the importance of the cause.

Since, then, the mercy of divine favour has helped our humble and pure intention through you, we must consider a reward and recompense for your diligence and toil. For at a later time we intend to write to our lord and son the emperor that he should have you ordained Bishop of Alexandria. It is right that the church in which you served especially from the beginning of your life should be set right by your teaching and moderation.

For we were displeased that the most clement emperor was trying to set your charity over the church of Antioch. It is better for you to receive the dignity of so great a priesthood in your native land, so as to teach the Egyptian peoples, than to seem to wander among Syrians, strange and unknown people, having been born in another part of the world.

The long waiting of our brothers and fellow bishops Thomas and Nicostratus also saddens us, and we wonder why bishops of the right faith seem to be in difficulty under a catholic emperor. Your charity ought to support their wishes by your action, so that the sorrow of those seeking what they desire may be turned into joy.

John, Bishop of Nicopolis, has written to us through Ammonius the deacon that certain malicious people are trying to stir up a false accusation against him before the emperor. We commend him to your love, urging you to work hard so that the scheming of his enemies cannot disturb his peace.

When this Ammonius the deacon came to us, we were unwilling to receive him into the communion of the apostolic see until we had consulted with Sergius the deacon and inquired what ought to be arranged. Our deliberation found this acceptable to the aforesaid deacon: that he should be joined to catholic communion through the testimony of a libellus. We inform you that, once this libellus had been solemnly presented, he offered himself and has been admitted to our communion.

We commend Paulinus, defensor of the Roman church, and we urge you not to leave anything unsettled in your haste to return. For everything is better arranged with the help of our God when there is ample time, and it is preferable that the condition of all the churches be settled slowly than that something be left unfinished through haste, which would create work for us again and bring difficulty to our arrangements. Given on the day stated above, in the consulship written above.

Hormisdas to the illustrious Justinian. We bless the ineffable help of God, because we have learned that the desire of all for the peace of the churches has been peacefully fulfilled. This did not happen contrary to our expectation, for, judging from the character of the most religious Augustus, we always held out hope for peace and believed that what was longed for regarding union would come about under a Christian emperor.

The glorious emperor will therefore have from this cause titles of triumph, not ones that mortal forgetfulness can efface, but ones that God's grace confirms for ever. Nor will you lack the reward of heavenly recompense, for you aided the good emperor's undertaking and, by your obedience to this fitting desire, caused the horror of separation to be shut out. Blessed be the Lord our God, who has visited and brought about the redemption of his people!

It remains now, since it is certain that this kind of duty has been laid on you by divine providence, that you gird up your loins, as the saying goes, and with the strength of peaceful exhortation pursue those by whom you see that peace is not acknowledged; above all because your glory is diminished if anything in this cause is left less than complete. Look carefully at everything around you with the faith by which you live, and with the diligence for which you are strong, meet every attack by which you see the reverence of the Christian religion being harassed, so that, thanks to your perseverance, we good people may be able to say with exultation: "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord."

This being so, it is fitting that you, who made the beginning of the catholic Church's tranquillity, should bring it to completion. The favour of our Saviour, who inspired you to begin this work, will not be lacking for its accomplishment. Given on the day stated above, in the consulship written above.

Hormisdas to [?]. Since it was necessary to send a letter to our lord and son the most clement emperor, we could not pass over your greatness in silence. So, after first offering you an honourable greeting, we commend those who have been sent on this business, asking that, with our Lord's help and under your direction, they may quickly reach their destination, so that the most sacred and most religious emperor may learn without delay of the glory of his merits.

Hormisdas to Gratus, vir spectabilis. Your greatness's silence has saddened us, for amid whatever occupations you ought not to have forgotten us. So, lest we seem to fall into the fault for which we reproach you, it was necessary to take up the work of the present pen, through which we greet your nobility with honour, asking you not to cease keeping us informed of your prosperity, since we long to learn, by God's favour, of your well-being by whatever signs.

Hormisdas to Juliana Anicia. Having received your greatness's letter, we give thanks to our God for the restoration of the catholic faith, praying that he may deign to preserve in your mind for a long life the zeal for his religion that he has granted, so that, just as the line of imperial blood ennobles your person, so the awareness of good deeds may make you shine with light.

Therefore, greeting you with fitting respect and honour, we ask that you persist in the purpose you have begun, and strive that the effort in so great a cause may reach completion, so that no seed of this evil may remain for the future, from which any enemy of the faith might later, on whatever pretext, spring up again.

Hormisdas to Anastasia. You testify that you had long desired that our God should make firm the members of his Church as they returned to their former peace. Rejoicing that this has come to pass, we for our part unceasingly pray to the divine clemency that, just as he has gladly accepted these first fruits of the reign, so he may always assist the faith of the good emperor with every success and prosperity, and keep both him and all of you in sacred love of religion, so that those whose faith has cast off the error of a most wicked dissension may flourish in life on earth and may afterwards receive the reward of eternal salvation.

Now, therefore, join your prayers to ours and implore God with all your strength that all the churches may follow the example of this correction, so that the devil, whom our concord rejoices to see already almost entirely shut out, may have no cause to rejoice that anything has remained to him.

Justin Augustus to Pope Hormisdas. We are known to have made it plain long ago with what zeal we burn for gathering the most sacred churches into concord. From the beginning of our reign we thought it right to urge your Holiness to send trustworthy men, so that through their intervention some remedy might be found for these matters; and before those who were appointed arrived, we prepared everything so that what had to be arranged through this most flourishing city might be accomplished more easily.

But since petitions have been presented to our Majesty from various Eastern provinces, setting out certain points concerning the catholic faith and declaring the secret convictions of their minds, which they testify they hold regarding the undivided Trinity and which they show they will firmly retain; and since, when these were read, Dioscorus asserted that some things had been inserted in an improper order, we rightly thought that what we have been informed of should be disclosed to you.

Before long, therefore, someone will be sent by us to inform your Blessedness more fully about everything, to make known to you the petitions that were presented to us, and to bring back your Piety's reply, so that unfitting doubts may at last be cut away. Being therefore assured of our intention, deign by your earnest prayers to make the supreme Godhead [?] favourable to us. Given on 19 January at Constantinople, in the consulship of Vitalian and Rusticius.
(182.) Copy of the report of John, Bishop of Constantinople.

To my lord, in all things beloved of God, most holy brother and fellow minister Hormisdas, John sends greeting in the Lord. We judge that your Reverence has been satisfied by these deeds of how we hold you among ourselves, dearest brother, with a pure heart and spiritual love, and how we consider you worthy of veneration in all things. In this we obey the Lord's voice, which plainly cries out: "Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them"; and we embrace the apostolic teaching which teaches us: "Outdo one another in showing honour."

We hasten to show this in deeds, holding fast the union of the holy churches by the indissoluble bond of spiritual love, so that we may not be shaken either by the blows of hostile spirits or by the storms stirred up by the prince of evils and enemy of truth, with the help of the holy and consubstantial Trinity and by the intercession of the glorious Mary, truly the Mother of God.

Through these things above all, my most holy lord, let us pray that the state of our churches and of yours may remain unshaken, and also that the unity of the faith may be kept inseparable; for God is able to grant the palm of victory without a struggle to those who hope in him.

As for the date of the coming Passion of the Lord, contained in your letter, we inform you that it is correct according to the Easter tables kept by us. We knew this before, and now, having checked it more carefully, we hope without any doubt that you will celebrate the festival of the world in good health on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, which is properly the nineteenth day of the coming month of April.

Pray, then, most holy one, and may your mind deign not to forget us. I and those with me send our warmest greetings to all the brotherhood in Christ who are with your Holiness. And in another hand: Fare well in the Lord, and pray for us, beloved of God and most holy brother. Given at Constantinople on 19 January, in the consulship of Vitalian and Rusticius, viri clarissimi.
(183.) Copy of the report of John, Bishop of Constantinople.

To my lord, in all things beloved of God, most holy brother and fellow minister Hormisdas, John sends greeting in the Lord. The most pious and most Christian emperor has shown how much eagerness and how great a desire he has for the perfect union of all the churches, not only by his will but by his very deeds, to those who live in this royal city, even before he came to the kingship given him by God. To your Holiness he has made it most evident through the labours he has carried through from the beginning of his reign until now, by which he strives with a ready mind to join all the members of the catholic Church into the one body of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.

And what need is there for lengthy words? Although we can stand as true witnesses to the facts themselves, your Holiness also has the experience of what it has come to know for itself. What is now being added confirms this.

For certain people under his most powerful hand, from among the most religious priests of the regions of the East, have presented petitions informing him about things they did not want. Not wishing this to escape your Holiness, he wisely decided to announce to your Holiness at present what has already happened, and shortly afterwards to make it known more clearly through those [?], so that, by common counsel and with our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, the Lord of all, leading the way, the things that serve the common good and are irreproachable in every respect may shine forth in the corrections of the catholic faith.

Thinking it timely, therefore, we ask your Holiness by this brotherly letter and with most affectionate words to deign to pray more fully and more earnestly to God, the Lord of all, for our most pious emperor. I and those with me send our warmest greetings to all the brotherhood in Christ who are with your Holiness. And in another hand: Fare well in the Lord and pray for us, beloved of God and most holy brother.
(184.) Copy of the report of John, Bishop of Constantinople.

To my lord, in all things beloved of God, most holy brother and fellow minister Hormisdas, John sends greeting in the Lord. Paulinus, an honourable man and a defensor, who delivered your letter, displaying in himself the virtues of your Holiness, spent time with us with joy and contributed his diligence to our common counsels and actions. But since he was hastening back to you and ought not to be detained for a longer time, we address your Holiness in return and commend the aforesaid man to your protection, as one who is worthy of your love and remains your faithful servant.

He will be a trustworthy narrator to you of what we have done in accordance with your mind, and of the care that we watchfully exercise for the holy churches. For, through the prayers of your Holiness and with regard to the natural goodness of this matter, we have the most watchful zeal, and with God working with us the word of grace, running freely in many places without any opposition, brings our purpose to fulfilment.

But since some difficulties have arisen, the matters raised by them must certainly be set out fittingly, with careful guidance and gentle arrangement, as your Holiness knows above all, and as is fitting for those whose lot is to feed the flocks of God: to do and undertake everything for the glory of God, placing their hope of salvation in him, as it is written: "For those who love God, all things work together for good." For, as has been said, most holy one, we strive both to think and to do what pleases you.
I and those with me send our warmest greetings to all the brotherhood in Christ who are with your Holiness.
(185.) Suggestion of Bishop Germanus, the deacons Felix and Dioscorus, and the priest Blandus.

We have received with longed-for joy the reverend words of your apostleship through your sons Leo and Eulogius. The first of your instructions rebuked us for not reporting what had happened at Thessalonica. But long before his arrival, taking the opportunity, we took care to report whatever we had learned, whether from the rumours of those arriving, or from the writings of those who suffered (copies of which we have attached below), or from the account of the most pious emperor.
A promise of punishment followed, to the point that Dorotheus, Bishop of Thessalonica, was taken to the city of Heraclea until the case should reach a conclusion.

Meanwhile, in accordance with your instructions, we took care to make known to the emperor the authority of your apostleship, that the aforesaid Dorotheus, together with Aristides, should be sent to Rome to receive the teaching of catholic purity. He replied that there was no reason for them to be sent to Rome for a hearing, where they could excuse themselves more freely without dispute from their accusers. But suddenly, while this was going on, he was released, so far as we have learned, from the city of Heraclea, where he was being held. For what cause, on what grounds or terms, or through whose agency, we do not know.

Concerning the day of Easter, let your Blessedness know that the judgement of the Easterners agrees with the apostolic see, so that the festival is expected to be celebrated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May, as will also be clear from the report of John, Bishop of Constantinople.
It remains that, with the support of your Blessedness's prayers, we may be found worthy to be presented quickly at your feet, as we desire.
(186.) Memorandum sent from Thessalonica by Bishop John and the priest Epiphanius.

If, for our sins, the bishops who were taken from here should get into Constantinople, we will not say that they are certain to see the emperor and be restored to their sees, though they have taken so much money with them that they could blind not only men but angels. But if, God forbid, they do get in, they will tell as many lies in our absence as the devil can invent. For if here, in our presence, they attempted so much and were put to shame because the Lord stood with us, how much more will they do in our absence?

So that their malice may be undone, order that any hearing which, for our sins, may take place be held in our presence. Then it will be clear to all that we have faced death undeservedly and that they are relying on the protection of money. For we can prove against them on every point, before the senate, that they are thorough heretics. Only then can their deceit be exposed.

It should also be said: if they are not heretics, how is it that two weeks before we came all the bishops agreed together that no one should hold masses outside the city, but that everyone should do so here? The aim was to gather a crowd for the coming riot and to have it taught according to their errors. And once they realized that we were coming, they preached publicly that people must hurry with their little ones, so that when the persecution came the infants would not die as pagans. Then, as if it were a second Easter, they baptized so many [?] that they surpassed the usual festival.

It should also be said: if they are not heretics, how is it that they consecrated so many sacraments that they handed out full baskets to everyone, so that people would not be unable to receive communion during the persecution that, as they claimed, was coming? And again: if they are not heretics, then after they had been accused in the court of the prefects, in the proceedings brought by the honorable Candidus, deputy of the master of soldiers in attendance, and knew that danger was soon to fall on them, why did they once again, as though facing condemnation and as though wishing to help the little ones again, perform so many baptisms, even after they had been refuted, that they truly showed everyone they were heretics? At this the magnificent authority of the prefects was very gravely indignant.

And again: if they are not heretics, how is it that, when we were hiding in the baptistery, they took counsel among themselves and wanted to put us on a ship by night, as if wishing to rescue us from danger, so that they could use the occasion to throw us headlong into the sea? We answered through the deacons Demetrius and Andrew: 'Everyone knows that we are all with you. How can we sail by night? But if you are truly concerned for our safety, then tomorrow have five or six senators who fear for their property or their lives summoned in secret, together with Count Candidus, deputy of the master of soldiers. Let them also know where we are being taken, and we will do as they order. But if it is only you, in secret, we will not do it.' Then, unable to achieve their aim, they kept quiet for the moment, and the next day they stirred up another riot among the people, from which, by God's will, we barely escaped. How could they do all this if they are not heretics?
(187.) COPY OF A LETTER OF JUSTINIAN.

TO THE HOLY LORD, MOST BLESSED IN MERIT, OUR APOSTOLIC LORD AND FATHER, POPE HORMISDAS, FROM JUSTINIAN. By the favor of the Godhead, which always builds up the catholic church through the growth of faith, the unity of the holy churches has come about through the teaching and authority of your apostolate.

But we have learned that certain men, monks in name only, who care more for discord than for charity and the peace of God, have left here and set out for Your Angelic Grace, wishing to stir up trouble. Your Beatitude, learning from this letter the reason for their spite, will please receive them as they deserve and drive them far from you. These men are in a hurry to bring novelties into the church that neither the four venerable synods nor the letters of the holy Pope Leo are known to contain, and their idle talk is clearly causing disturbances everywhere.

For this reason also, may Your Angelic Grace please send to us by the most reverend men, the bishops and deacons sent by your apostolate, [?], and order that these monks be struck with due correction and driven away, as said above. We therefore ask that you give strict orders for such a letter to be sent to us by the same bearer, as said above. Their names are Achilles, John, Leontius and Maurice.

Our greatest concern is that the unity which your labor and prayer have brought about should not be broken up by restless men. We hope in God that if anything still stands apart from the peace of the whole world, it too may be joined by your prayers to the communion of the apostolic see.

Relying, moreover, on your Beatitude's kindness, we earnestly ask your fatherly love to grant generously to us relics of the holy apostles, to honor and illumine both us and the basilica built here in our house under the name of those venerable apostles. Know that you could give us no greater gift or favor, most blessed lord and father, than to grant this request of ours.

Since the aforesaid agent is setting out suddenly, we have also sent two pure silk palls to adorn the altar of the holy apostles. Please accept them and have us remembered continually in your most effective prayers.
(188.) ANOTHER COPY OF A LETTER OF JUSTINIAN.

So that the fullest perfection of faith may come to us from your Beatitude's teaching, we have again sent Eulogius, an energetic man and an imperial agent, for this purpose among other matters. Through him we earnestly ask that we be confirmed on every point in the confession of the catholic faith by a careful and most cautious reply from your apostolate.

For after the unity granted once and for all to the catholic church by divine mercy, some now claim that Christ, the Son of God and our Lord, who was crucified in the flesh for our salvation, ought to be proclaimed as one of the Trinity. Whether this is to be accepted, may your Reverence, with fatherly foresight, please tell us in a most careful written reply what we should follow and what we should avoid on this point. For it seems to be words that create the dissension, since the meaning is shown to be one and the same among all catholics.

Take up again, then, the labor you have already undertaken, holy and venerable father, following your predecessors in this too, whose memory you cherish and whom you honor by sharing their pontificate, and hasten to set us free and secure on this question. For we believe that whatever your religious reply makes known to us is catholic.

It has been said that the Scythian monks have come to your see for this reason. Give them a reply in keeping with the tradition of the fathers and the order of the canons, and have them sent back to us with your letter, with nothing to fear. Order also that sealed copies of the letter be given to the aforesaid energetic man Eulogius. We ask you to arrange all this with particular care so that no room is given to lies or plots, since we embrace the catholic faith with the greatest desire and ask that unity be granted to the whole world through your teaching.

HORMISDAS TO JUSTINIAN, VIR ILLUSTRIS. We have received your Highness's letter, brought by our son Eulogius, vir clarissimus. Now that he is returning, we offer you the greeting we owe and inform you that the Scythian monks have put forward many claims that we cannot leave unexamined. But we are awaiting, with God's help, the arrival of our legates.

For this reason we think the monks should be kept in the city, and they themselves do not object to this arrangement. Still, we trust that your Magnificence remembers what you wrote to us about them in an earlier letter. As for their claims, once our returning legates have properly informed us, if our inquiry finds anything in them that deserves censure, we must apply church discipline to them.

Moreover, Victor, who is said to hold the office of deacon and whose faith these same monks accuse vehemently, and any others who may be raising perverse questions, should be sent to the city at our request by order of our lord and son, the most clement emperor, so that we may hear all the claims they are disputing.

HORMISDAS TO JUSTINIAN, VIR ILLUSTRIS. We know that your Magnificence's mind is so strong in devotion to religion that you would rather we demanded of you, than asked of you, the service of bringing the peace of the church to completion. For you judge that what we are moved to offer, out of desire for the common good, adds to the merits of your Excellence. So we too ask of you with confidence, as though

it were owed, what we know will add to your merits. Therefore, lord son, as we greet you with all charity, we hope that you will press on with the work which you founded with the Lord's help, mindful of the divine testimony: 'Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.'

As for the monks who, as you wrote, have come to Rome, we wanted them to return home at once. But since they declared, calling divine power to witness, that ambushes laid on the road might put their lives in danger, we did not allow them to be expelled by force when they were unwilling to return to Constantinople. So when our legates arrive we shall have to inquire into the true cause that has stirred up discord among them.

As you asked with the most religious devotion, we have sent the relics of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, with all veneration, by the bearer of this letter. We pray that through their prayers the offering and desires of your heart may be acceptable to the grace of God.
We also ask that you send a letter quickly to gladden our anxious heart with news both of what is being done for concord and of your good health. Given on 2 September, in the consulship of Eutharic.
(191.) COPY OF A LETTER OF JUSTINIAN, SENT BY THE BROTHER OF PROEMPTOR.

We want whatever is most cautious and most secure to be done for the holy faith and for concord among the holy churches. For this reason our most glorious brother Vitalian has written in reply to your Beatitude through Paulinus, vir spectabilis, defensor of your church, and through the same man we have taken care to tell your Beatitude that you ought to carry out whatever will grant peace and concord to the holy churches.

Soon afterwards, however, we sent someone with a letter from our most pious emperor to bring back a more definite reply from your Holiness. The religious defensor mentioned above can also inform your Holiness how serious a question has arisen in our parts.

We therefore ask that, if possible, you give a very swift reply, satisfy the religious monks John and Leontius, and send them back to us. For unless this question is settled by your prayers and diligence, we fear that peace among the holy churches cannot come about.

Knowing, then, that both the reward and the risk of this matter rest with you, deal with it diligently and send us back a very firm reply by the religious monks named above, if possible before our envoy reaches your Beatitude. For everything we are striving for depends on this alone.

JUSTIN AUGUSTUS TO POPE HORMISDAS. BY OUR LEGATES, THAT IS, THE BISHOPS GERMANUS AND JOHN, THE DEACONS FELIX AND DIOSCORUS, AND THE PRIEST BLANDUS. We owe you the greatest thanks for not hesitating to devote eager effort to gathering and uniting the venerable churches. But your consummate skill shines out above all in this: you choose men who can serve your Holiness's benevolent wish with a sincere and wholehearted mind.
