For the most reverend bishop Germanus, and Felix, Dioscorus and Blandus, most religious men, were so attentive and diligent and acted with such wisdom that, as far as their office was concerned, everything was carried through and fully worked out, and no further dispute remained.

But mortal frailty is so constituted that it wants to be treated somewhat gently and to have its questions given a plain answer, especially when a matter has spread among a vast multitude of people. So it has come about that in this most flourishing city everything that was ordained, in the time of John of most religious memory when he held the priesthood of this royal city, concerning the cause of religion and the celebration of unity with the apostolic see, is being kept unshaken, by God's favor. Your ordinance has also been approved and accepted in many other cities. The rest, however, need somewhat gentler handling in the matter of the names of bishops: not those specifically listed in the letter that your Holiness is known to have sent us, but others whose memory those cities especially cherish, because they are known to have flourished there in their lifetime.

For this reason your Holiness's legates had no licence to go beyond the terms of the mandate with which they were sent. The whole outcome of the matter now depends on your judgment alone, so that he who first set the affair in motion should be the only one to conclude the peace.

These matters, and certain others, will be explained more openly by our envoy, who will be sent shortly. For the present, as the most religious men return, we have thought it right both to address your Reverence and to urge you to offer your prayers for our empire and for the safety of the state. Given on 9 July at Constantinople, in the consulship of Vitalian and Rusticius.

JUSTIN AUGUSTUS TO POPE HORMISDAS. Since it is our intention, most religious father, that in every matter our counsels should agree, we believe that in the case of Elias too, most reverend bishop, we should decide, at the urging of your legates, whatever has been seen to be most expedient after weighing the various considerations on both sides. For at present the bishop of the city of Caesarea is protected by the favor of everyone. Because of his most admirable conduct, not only do the inhabitants think he must by all means be kept, but almost the entire East undoubtedly reveres him. Meanwhile the man who held the same priesthood before him complains that he was removed unjustly.

It has therefore seemed fitting that we should neither go against the wishes of countless multitudes, nor have a man distinguished for his integrity thrown out of a see of which he shows himself worthy, nor allow his predecessor to lose all hope of reclaiming the place which he affirms he was stripped of without cause. Instead, in a doubtful matter, we should proceed with moderation. For the present, then, this same Elias, most reverend bishop, should remain in retirement; but after his successor has died, he should at last return to the see he left. First, however, everything required by the most sacred canons for obtaining permission to return must be carried out, and the consent must also be obtained both of your apostolic see and of this most flourishing city, as well as of the other churches concerned.

As for Thomas and Nicostratus, most religious bishops, everything will be put into effect once the other venerable churches have also been joined to you in unity. We have decided that these matters should be settled, with heavenly protection going before us, likewise in accordance with the order of the most sacred canons.

Since our decision ought also to be made known to your Holiness, so that it too may show our desire, for which we are bending every effort to curb and calm controversies and to extend the longed-for concord to all, we have thought fit to send this present letter as well. Above all we urge that the heavenly Godhead be entreated by your prayers for the safety of the state. Given on 7 June at Constantinople, in the consulship of Vitalian and Rusticius.

EUPHEMIA AUGUSTA TO POPE HORMISDAS. We have received your Beatitude's letter with a grateful and joyful heart. For who would not listen most gladly to the words of one who is made renowned by the authority of the apostolic see and commended by the integrity of his life and his zealous care for the right faith?

We therefore ask and urge that my name, and above all that of our most serene husband, never drop out of your prayers, but that your prayers may win heaven's protection for each of us and for the state.
(195.) COPY OF THE REPORT OF EPIPHANIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.

TO MY MOST HOLY AND MOST BLESSED LORD, BROTHER AND FELLOW MINISTER HORMISDAS, EPIPHANIUS SENDS GREETING IN THE LORD. God, who dwells on high and looks upon the lowly and provides all things abundantly for human salvation, has in his goodness and mercy looked upon my littleness. After the death of the late archbishop and patriarch John of holy memory, he has deigned to confer on me the priestly see of the holy catholic church of the royal city. This came about by the judgment and choice of our most Christian and most just prince Justin, and of the most pious empress, who shares with him in every devotion to God, and of their followers, who are people of good life and exalted by royal honors; and with them the consent of the clergy, the monks and the most faithful people
was given. I have therefore thought it necessary to put this news first in my letter, to show what disposition I have toward your apostolic see.

It is my great prayer, most blessed one, to be united with you, to embrace the divine doctrines handed down to your holy see from God's blessed and holy disciples and apostles, especially Peter, the chief of the apostles, and to value nothing more highly than these. I am no outsider coming from elsewhere, ignorant of the ordinances of the holy church. By God's will I was brought up from my earliest years in the holy catholic church, and throughout that time I obeyed most holy bishops and patriarchs. Many times I was put in charge of those who put off their sins in the most sacred and ineffable rite of baptism, and I taught them the right and true faith in the Trinity of one essence. As I have said, that faith comes from the disciples of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, and the whole assembly of bishops and fathers embraces it.

For I revere and proclaim the truly divine and holy creed, given by God, of the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers who assembled at Nicaea, and I declare it to be the manifest sign of Christian splendor. I also hold the venerable synod of the one hundred and fifty holy bishops held in this royal city, likewise the assembly of the two hundred God-loving fathers held at Ephesus, and the synod of the six hundred and thirty most reverend fathers and bishops held at Chalcedon. That this last synod is one with the aforesaid holy councils, in agreement and closely joined with them, I myself have learned, and I know that I have taught it to others.

In these four holy and sacred synods, then, the great mystery of godliness was proclaimed, and the salvation of all people has been laid up. Those who held or hold the same view I receive and embrace, and I gladly unite myself with them. On the other hand, those who think or preach anything beyond these synods, or who have attempted anything in the past, I consider banished from the company of the orthodox. Likewise I embrace and receive the truly right and most religious letters of the venerable Pope Leo, written for the right faith.

Let your Beatitude's holy brotherhood, therefore, think of me in this way. I have made it plain to you, and I preach it to the churches under me, hastening in every way to have them joined by the bond of charity both to me and to your Beatitude. For they must be entirely united and inviolable, forming one body of the common apostolic church and keeping it forever.

Please consider how great is my love for your venerable brotherhood in all things: those whom your apostolic see condemned and ordered not to be read out in the sacred diptychs, I too do not allow to be named during the sacred mysteries. This is known also to the most reverend men you sent, namely the most holy bishop Germanus, the deacons Felix and Dioscorus and the priest Blandus, who effectively carried out what you had charged them to do.

May your Holiness pray, therefore, both for me and for the bishops under me, that we may be kept forever holding the right confession of God, and likewise for our most serene prince and for the most Christian Augusta, since their well-being will be a firm support for the holy churches everywhere.

Since this is our intention, by the grace of the Holy Spirit and the intercession of the holy and glorious Mother of God, the Virgin Mary, it will no longer be possible in any way for God's holy church to be torn apart.

I and those with me send our warmest greetings to all the brotherhood that is with your Holiness. AND IN ANOTHER HAND: Keep well in the Lord and pray for us, most holy brother and lover of God. Received on 17 September, in the consulship of Rusticius, vir clarissimus.
(196.) COPY OF A LETTER OF JUSTINIAN, VIR ILLUSTRIS.

With our Lord Jesus Christ's favour, that man reigns in this world who founds his empire on holy religion, since he who has first won the favour of heaven governs human affairs well. We rejoice that this has come to pass in our own times.

For your son, the most clement emperor, received the sceptre by the gift of the Eternal One and took up the task of settling the questions of faith. We sent an embassy to your holiness and obtained bishops of the apostolic see. Their arrival did much to increase the concord of the most holy churches, as we pressed the matter forward, as was fitting. The name of Acacius, which had caused the schism, was cut off at the root, in accordance with the terms of the libelli you sent, and the longed-for unity came about in this royal city and in many other cities. A unity found through the greatest labours ought to be revered for ever and must be guarded. No one will allow what the eternal Majesty has duly settled to be reopened by any argument whatever.

But the enemy of the human race is quick to obstruct a favourable course, and part of the Easterners cannot be compelled, by exile or by sword and fire, to condemn the names of the bishops who died after Acacius. This difficulty entangles the general concord in delays.

Let your holiness, therefore, inspired from heaven, consider the nature of the circumstances and the times. Once the authors of this error have been condemned, namely Acacius of Constantinople, Peter, Timothy Aelurus and Dioscorus of Alexandria, and Peter of Antioch, may you deign to end the long-standing dispute by laying the question of the other names to rest. In this way you may redeem from bloodshed the people whom our God has entrusted to you to rule, and you may reconcile the people to our Lord through priestly patience rather than through persecution and bloodshed. Otherwise, while we seek to win souls, we may lose the bodies and the souls of many.

For long-standing errors ought to be corrected with gentleness and clemency, especially since the predecessors of your beatitude very often wished to recall the bishops of our commonwealth to their communion on the sole condition that Acacius and the others mentioned be passed over in silence. It is therefore no hardship for your see to grant what it once urged itself.

We ask still more earnestly that your holiness, having received heavenly grace, deign to consider what the Eastern bishops put forward and give fitting assent to their faith. For it seems to us that our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, born of the Virgin Mary, whom the chief of the apostles proclaims to have suffered in the flesh, is rightly said to reign as one in the Trinity with the Father and the Holy Spirit. It seems ambiguous to say simply "one of the Trinity" without first putting the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Even so, we do not doubt that his person is in the Trinity together with the persons of the Father and the Holy Spirit. For without the person of Christ [?] the Trinity can neither be believed in piously nor worshipped faithfully, as Saint Augustine says: "or [?] some person of the Trinity"; and in another place: "he alone in the Trinity took a body"; and again: "one [?] of the three."

We therefore ask you, greeting you most reverently, to keep the judgment to come in mind and to settle the matter so that no doubt remains for the future. When every scruple of discord has been removed, the bonds of the desired peace may be renewed throughout the whole world, the concord of the venerable churches may flourish, and the members of the one body may be gathered back into their proper state. For that physician is rightly praised who hastens to heal old illnesses in such a way that no new wounds arise from them. Let your apostleship know in particular that once these two chapters are settled, all the bishops of this commonwealth will gladly embrace our communion. Received 17 September, in the consulship of Rusticius, vir clarissimus.
(197.) Copy of the letter of the illustrious Celer.
To the most blessed lord and apostolic father, Pope Hormisdas, from Celer. Whenever an opportunity arises to write to your apostleship, we are given the greatest cause for rejoicing.

Now, therefore, the most blessed bishop Germanus and the most reverend men whom you sent to unite the holy churches are returning, and we have thought it necessary to pay due reverence to your holiness. We report that these men were indeed eager for your will to be carried out in full. But the whole body was sick, and so for the present the head, which is judged the first necessity, has been healed by the application of your remedy. The dissension between the venerable churches of Rome and Constantinople has been buried by the coming of unity, and other members of no small importance have, by a like grace of God, been cleansed and joined.

We all cherish this hope as well: that the grace of God, which has always remained and still remains with your see, may inspire such goodness in you that the rest of the body, which as we said above is still held to be sick, may recover unity through your gentleness, your prudent management and your remedy, and so be joined.
In particular we beseech your pontificate to be pleased to pray for us with a father's kindly heart.
(198.) Copy of the letter of Anicia Juliana.

To the most blessed lord, most approved pontiff of the apostolic see, Pope Hormisdas, our father, from Anicia Juliana. First of all we pay your beatitude the homage of our greeting. We pray that God may cause this page to come before your venerable eyes, and that for the strength of his church he may deign to sustain your life with saving increase, so that through your constant watchfulness the state of the church may be defended against hostile and rabid dogs. For, venerable father, your care for the integrity of our faith befits the vicars of the glorious apostle Peter, to whom the Lord entrusted the office of feeding the sheep.

Let your holy solicitude on our behalf know, then, that we hold ever more firmly to the unshakable steadfastness of the right faith. We have resisted until now so as not to violate its sanctity. Your apostleship instructed us to take care in a cause of such piety, and as far as we were able, with all our strength, we have not ceased to admonish its opponents in a spirit of gentleness, with God's grace working with us.
(199.) Copy of the sacred letter of Justin Augustus.

Justin Augustus to Pope Hormisdas. When we dismissed from this royal city the most blessed bishop Germanus and those whom you had sent with him, we gave them instructions to this effect: we would afterwards make known to your apostleship, through the most reverend bishop John, the chapters concerning the perfect unity of the churches. These had, however, already been explained to them while they were present here.

But it has happened that the aforesaid bishop John is detained by a long illness. We do not want your reverence to form an unfavourable opinion, as though we were failing to carry out our promises through some wilful negligence. We have therefore judged it necessary to explain the reason for the delay through Eulogius, vir spectabilis, tribune and notary, whom we have sent to the most exalted king Theodoric on certain business. We add this as well: as soon as the gracious majesty of our Lord and God is pleased to restore that most religious man John to his former health, we will send him to your holiness at once, as we promised.

It remains for your holiness to deign to win divine protection for us by your prayers. Given on 31 August at Constantinople. Received at Rome on 1 October, in the consulship of Rusticius, vir clarissimus.
(200.) Copy of the letter of Justinian.

To the most blessed lord and apostolic father, Hormisdas, pope of the city of Rome, from Justinian. You know from many letters, ever since the most serene emperor, your son, began to reign, how great is the reverence with which we venerate your beatitude.

Now too, greeting your holiness with due respect, we earnestly ask you to labour with constant and very frequent prayers for the concord of the venerable churches. As we wrote after all these events through your legates as well, we ask your apostleship to deign to send us, through Eulogius, vir spectabilis, tribune and notary, a complete and unambiguous reply. It should cover both the expression on which the controversy turns and the names of the bishops who died under Acacius. Everything that was settled in the presence of your legates will, of course, remain firmly in force for ever. For the religious man bishop John, who is to come to Rome, is detained by bodily illness.

Nothing prevents concord from being reached even before he arrives, once the doubt concerning religion has been removed (although we will send him soon, God willing, for he is already better). The matters that have fallen into doubt are not difficult, and it is not expedient to draw out any longer a cause that concerns eternal life, lest delay give rise to something still more uncertain.

Let your holiness, therefore, mindful of heavenly eternity and of the dreadful judgment, hasten to carry out what has been entrusted to you, so that all may understand that you have rightly received the primacy of the apostolic see. With a father's affection, then, give orders that what your sons write to you be fulfilled as quickly as possible. For you know how admirable a glory it is for the errors of so many years to be rooted out in the time of your pontificate.

Hormisdas to Justin Augustus. Blessed be the Trinity, our God, who has entrusted to you the helm of earthly empire! Veneration is due to you not only by right of rule but also for the glorious moderation and integrity of your purpose.

Truly we glorified God when we read your Piety's letter. In it you excused the delay of the promised embassy by the illness of the man who was to be sent, and so you made clearer than daylight how much care you have for faith and for honour. You showed that for those who govern the world, the power they hold is not enough for the summit of dominion unless the adornments of character make their rule more precious. Most clement emperor, may our God preserve his benefits toward you, look upon your good deeds, and grant you eternal blessings!

Yet no suspicion troubled us, and we did not believe that the delay in fulfilling the promise came from any change of plan. It would have been wrong to doubt anxiously the words of one whose good faith we have been allowed to see so clearly in great matters.

Therefore, as our son Eulogius, vir spectabilis, tribune and notary, returns, we pay you the homage of due greeting. We beseech great God with continual prayers that he who, through your zeal, healed the wounds inflicted by unbelievers may lengthen your life over many years and make the unity restored to the church secure on every side as well. Given 29 October, in the consulship of Rusticius.

Hormisdas to Justin Augustus. The beginnings of the church's concord and the longed-for tranquillity of a pacified world answer the glorious labours of your Clemency with universal praise. This makes and keeps our words of thanks sparing. Yet we do not keep silent about this: we pour out prayers to our Lord for you without ceasing. For the affection in our prayers is boundless, whereas praise can express only a limited judgment.

But amid these benefits of your Piety one care does not leave us, and it has distressed us greatly. Elias, Thomas and Nicostratus, my brothers and fellow bishops, were the first to embrace the church's concord with eager devotion. Yet they are not only cheated of the palm that so great a beginning deserves; they are even dogged by the misery of an evil precedent.

We therefore beseech your Clemency, with tears mingled with our prayers, not to let the intolerable rejection of these men disturb the joys you give us daily through the conversion of heretics. It is not only the cause of these persons that troubles us, for the glory of a good deed and of merit together might be enough for them. We are troubled because the decrees of the venerable canons are being scorned, and because their rejection does no small injury to the apostolic see. Your sincere Christianity lends great patronage to the ancient decrees and has recently ratified the primacy of the apostolic see by acts of veneration. Let it not leave to posterity an insoluble question in this one matter.

Hormisdas to Euphemia Augusta. Together with the assembly of catholic bishops, we pray without ceasing and pay our vows to our God for your safety. Your earnest request does not prompt this; our devoted and steadfast purpose in the reconciliation of the church spurs us on.

For who that has been separated from the heretical conspiracy could hold back? Who could begin his prayer in any other way than by asking that you and the most serene prince, your husband, may have a longer life and draw ever nearer to divine grace for the increase of your prosperity? For you consecrated the beginnings of a happy reign by cursing an error that deserved punishment, and with peaceful intent you drove out discord, the devil's friend.

It is therefore fitting that you now press on with your praiseworthy undertakings and spread the perfect remedy throughout the whole world, since a larger flock offered to Christ may confidently claim a larger reward. Among these concerns, let it be your care that no wound afflict persons who were healed long ago, and that the unity of communion be a strong support for obtaining justice.

For we ask that at last, by your decree, what the authority of the most sacred canons requires be carried out regarding our venerable brothers and fellow bishops Elias, Thomas and Nicostratus. Otherwise they will seem, as if they were the authors of some evil, to have deserved to be struck down alone amid the common joy of all, simply because they were the first to hasten to unity with the apostolic see. And justice will seem to have given way in a praiseworthy cause, defeated by personal hatred.
Join your prayers to ours, then, before the most clement Augustus, so that hostile evasion may not take from them the fruit that the rules of the fathers command to be granted and preserved to them.

Hormisdas to Epiphanius, bishop of Constantinople. Out of regard for the divine judgment and for our charity, your fraternity ought to have done two things once we had received Elias, Thomas and Nicostratus, our brothers and fellow bishops, into the fellowship of our communion. You ought to have admitted them without hesitation to the divine mysteries with you. And for the fullness of our peace you ought to have recalled them to their churches, from which the error of discord had shut them out. Then the unity that God has restored to his churches throughout the whole world, after the passing of many years, would be harmed by no difference between our wills.

But a matter so welcome, and so consistent with the venerable statutes of the fathers, has been put off until now through certain delays; we remember writing about this to your fraternity's predecessor as well. We therefore urge you not to let discordant minds in any way sadden again the joy we have received from the condemnation of the past dissension. For no one will think that you are in communion with us with your whole heart if you separate from your fellowship those who are in communion with us.

Surely those who put off fulfilling the precepts of peace seem to receive peace in vain. For however long you delay receiving these men into communion, you take something away from our reconciliation. Care must be taken, dearest brother, that the concord of our churches, granted at last from above, does not begin with such examples. If it did, both the venerable rule of religion and the authority of the apostolic see would seem throughout the East to have been diminished, God forbid, rather than restored.

Hormisdas to Epiphanius, bishop of Constantinople. The news of the beginnings of your dignity long held us in suspense, and amid the rejoicing of our common gladness we were greatly surprised that the old custom had been neglected. The concord of the churches, restored with God's assent, called for the full duty of brotherly peace, especially since it was claimed not out of personal arrogance but in observance of the rules. For it would have been fitting, dearest brother, for you to send legates to the apostolic see at the very outset of your pontificate. You would then have come to know well the affection we owe you, and you would have duly fulfilled the form of ancient custom.

You omitted these things and judged that an exchange of letters, as occasion arose, would be enough. Nevertheless, impelled by grace, we have for the time being broken off our steady and just waiting and are returning words of mutual charity. Our own heart, impatient in its love, and the welcome report of our legates have together drawn us out of the silence the case required and into kindly offices. By these we show for the present the signs of our joy and pay, as it were, the tribute of private friendship.

Your embassy, however, we await with the same goodwill as before, and, relying on the ancient decrees, we require it. Then we may express more clearly how great a fruit of joy we gain from the honour of your pontificate, and what thanks are due to you for the services you have rendered in the work of spreading unity, as the account of our legates has abundantly attested.

Hormisdas to Justinian, vir illustris. In deigning to show me the goodwill of your heart, your Highness does something pleasing to God and in keeping with a right conscience. And the rewards of this purpose are not small for you: a greater fruit returns to you from such goodness, for the honour paid to a bishop is not empty.

It is beyond doubt that honour paid to the minister is worship of the Lord. Whoever holds a priest in high esteem will receive a greater reward from the one whom the priest serves, for the Lord Jesus says that those who receive prophets with honour will be given their reward. For my part, I value your favour greatly. Yet it is all the more precious because whatever favour you graciously bestow on me, you show in the defence of the churches.

But to turn our words to what your Highness desires: both the most clement emperor and you promise that an embassy will come, and it would be reasonable for us to await, above all, the arrival of those who are to be sent. Nevertheless, because the zeal for religion that you have declared is welcome to us, it is no burden to say this much in advance: those who follow their inclinations rather than reason must not confound the stability of your faith with an insolent novelty of words.

The Holy Trinity, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, is one God. This is what Israel was commanded to worship. Its substance is inseparable and undivided; it cannot be divided or separated by a sacrilegious distinction, while each person nevertheless keeps its own property. For the present we commend these things

to your faith. Bearing in mind the limits of a letter, we believe that a fitting brevity is enough. These matters will be set out more fully when, under the flourishing rule of the most clement prince and by God's favour, we receive the promised embassy and, having learned everything, send it back with a reply, given with the help of our God, for the instruction of all.

Hormisdas to Justinian, vir illustris. The results themselves confirm your zeal for the peace of the church and for the condemnation of the errors of heretical contention. A great and immeasurable reward for that work undoubtedly awaits you.

That is why, whatever we judge necessary for upholding the canons and for reverence toward the apostolic see, we at once entrust to your Magnificence to carry out, with confident assurance. Many examples of this kind testify that you take up such causes and the hopes placed in you with great joy. Therefore, without long and roundabout introductions, we turn the words of this letter to the matter itself.

The church grieves. At the great outset of the longed-for unity, it cannot enjoy the gladness granted to it because of the affliction in one case, and we implore you with earnest prayers that your good offices may remove this anxiety from us. We are distressed both by the present pain and by the occasion it has created for future disputes. Through it the rules of the venerable fathers are being neglected, and the authority of the apostolic see is thought to be something that can be despised.

By the favour of God and of the most clement prince, and by your effort as well, only those are now held to be bishops and to hold churches by right who agree to condemn their errors and return to our communion. Yet Elias, Thomas and Nicostratus, our brothers and fellow bishops, made a good beginning in this cause even under a hostile emperor, and their good efforts have done nothing to advance them. They cannot even hold the offices of the dignity the Lord conferred on them. Exiled from the flocks entrusted to them, they are forced to suffer the miseries of the condemned.

Wherefore we ask you, and we adjure you by the divine mercy, to give your utmost patronage and your well-proven energy to their cause, which is just. Keep close to the footsteps of the most pious prince, so that at last, out of regard for both piety and justice, he may restore them to their churches. For in the insult done to them, our enemies claim that the longed-for fellowship of our communion has met with disfavour.
(208.) Copy of the report of Dorotheus, bishop of Thessalonica.

To the most holy and most blessed father and fellow minister Hormisdas, Dorotheus sends greeting in the Lord. Most blessed and thrice-blessed father in all things, it is the chief aim of our purpose and our prayer to write to you, most holy ones, often and to be granted conversation in return, and it is fitting that I should never be without a share in such joy.

I have clearly learned that certain persons are disturbing your holy ears. I know beyond doubt that you are perfect in all things, that you can hear nothing without judgment, and that you do not incline your mind wholly to anyone. Still, I do not wish to seem, by keeping silent, to give more time to those who have suffered no harm from us but have armed themselves against us without cause and to no purpose.

So I nonetheless give satisfaction to God and to your holiness: on behalf of John, the most reverend bishop, who was sent a little while ago by your venerable crown, I exposed myself to dangers and endured death, and I know that I put my own life at risk for his. This is shown by the records, and by those very men, although through my absence they seem to have been most sharply examined [?].

And what need is there for a long speech, when our Lord God Jesus Christ can disclose everything to you and give you satisfaction? For when I learned that you had been called to preside over the apostolic see, I judged it a joy shared by the whole world. From that time on, writing this very thing to you, I have left nothing undone, as far as lay in me, that pertains to the honor and satisfaction of you and of the apostolic see, nor do I leave anything undone now.

Shortly, most venerable ones, you will learn, with the favor of the Lord Jesus Christ, that these things were devised by me from the beginning and that, when the Lord God granted the time, they were brought to completion. I and those with me also send our warmest greetings to all the brotherhood in Christ who are with your holiness.

Hormisdas to Dorotheus, bishop of Thessalonica. We considered that your fraternity's church, before the evils of the discord that is now passing away, was once joined to the apostolic see by an outstanding charity, and we believed that you would be a leader in the peace recently restored from above. But since you delay even to follow those whom you ought to have gone before, we groan not lightly over your fraternity's slowness and your postponed correction.

For you write that our ears have been disturbed by the atrocity of a certain crime. Would that so detestable a report had reached only us, and had not announced to Christian minds throughout the whole world a deed as lamentable as it is execrable, so that those who do not know you to be innocent believe that you have also strayed from the path of Christianity! For in what part of the world does the odium of this savagery not sadden the catholic churches and gladden the depraved wishes of the heretics?

We wish it to be shown that these things are foreign to the conscience of your love, as you state in your letter. For what better suits our wishes than that bishops who want to return to catholic peace should always be proved innocent of cruelty and crimes? We therefore expect, if your fraternity does not lack the support of the truth known to God, that you will both repel from yourself the odium of so great a crime and at last follow the example of those who have returned in the reconciliation of faith. Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of the most distinguished Rusticius.

Hormisdas to the bishops Elias, Thomas and Nicostratus. How wearied our mind is by sharing in your grief, it is superfluous to set out in words to those who know our mutual charity. But may he who, as the searcher who knows beforehand, beholds both our mind and your labors, turn our sorrow into joy through your prosperity.

So that we may never cease to act on your behalf with most just pleading and gentle intercession, know that we have sent letters dealing specifically with your case to the most clement emperor, to the most excellent Augusta, and also to the illustrious and magnificent men Justinian and Germanus, our sons. We have handed them to the sublime Eulogius on the understanding that he will first leave it to your judgment whether you choose to present them yourselves, or whether they should rather be delivered by the bearer himself, both to the emperor and to the other persons we named above.

Hormisdas to the most illustrious Germanus. You keep watch with a commendable purpose for the peace of the church and burn with such warmth of faith that thanks alone are not enough, for no prerogative of human praise entices you; rather, the expectation of divine reward sets you aflame.

What we chiefly owe, therefore, we have paid: every day we pray for your safety to our God, in whose causes you spend yourself, asking that your zeal for the unity of the church may burn so in every part that no opportunity for good service is left where the patronage of your defense does not support the rules of the fathers.

Above all, however, we are moved by the case of our brothers and fellow bishops Elias, Thomas and Nicostratus. They were the first to follow the concord the world needed, and they have been struck with the loss of their churches and are oppressed to the insult of the venerable canons as well. The glory of their own reconciliation becomes for them a cause of difficulty, as though they had resisted with a more stubborn mind and, while others were returning to the unity of the apostolic see, had themselves torn apart the members of the church.

Your prudence should judge how hard this is for us and how unworthy of the times of a most clement emperor, and at last provide a remedy that can relieve both their labors and our sadness with welcome consolation.

Justin Augustus to Pope Hormisdas. We received the illustrious man, the most reverend bishop, gladly, not only because of the honor due to priests but also out of affection for your holiness. For whoever has been approved by your judgment is judged most approved by us as well. As for the help and favor to be given to their holy churches, this will be settled more suitably once the envoys whom we are known to have sent recently to the magnificent king Thrasamund have returned, by divine favor, and brought us an answer.

May your blessedness deign to ask heavenly protection for us in unwearied prayers. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December at Constantinople, in the consulship of the Lord Justin, perpetual Augustus. Received on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Rusticius.
(213.) Copy of the report of the bishops Germanus and John, the deacons Felix and Dioscorus, and the priest Blandus.

In another letter we have told your blessedness how we arrived, with God's help, in the city of Aulon, how we were received by the bishop of that city, what was done and what answer they gave, and that he promised to submit the libellus when his metropolitan did so.

As for what happened in the city of Scampa, we have not failed to inform your prayers. Before we entered that city, the venerable bishop Troius came out with his clergy and people to meet us. We report to your apostleship how God was blessed on that day and what festivity followed through his devotion.

In our presence and that of his clergy and the noblemen of the city he wrote the libellus. He handed it over; we received it, and in the presence of all the clergy and people it was read out from the step by your servant Peter, notary of the holy Roman church.

The assembly was in the basilica of Saint Peter. We confess to your blessedness that we would hardly see such devotion, such praises to God, such tears and such joy among any other people. Nearly everyone, men and women alike, received us in the city with candles, and the soldiers with crosses. Masses were celebrated, and no name offensive to religion was recited, but only that of your blessedness. Our bishop, the venerable Germanus, celebrated mass, and they promised that from then on no names would be recited except those whom the apostolic see has received. May God graciously preserve for you all that has been accomplished for you.

We wrote this letter thirty miles from Lychnidus, hoping to arrive in that city the same day with God's help; and from what has reached us, we hope that the bishop of that city will do likewise. If this happens, we will write back when the opportunity arises.

While we were at Scampa, at dinner time after mass, Stephen and Leontius, men of rank sent by the emperor, came to meet us. They did not yet know that we were in the regions of Greece, since Count Stephen had been ordered to cross into Italy to meet us. (This Stephen, so it is said,

is a relative of your son Vitalian, the master of soldiers.) They told us that the senator Patricius had been proscribed and sent into exile; but for what reason we cannot say, except as it reached us, because it is not easy to judge such matters. It is said, however, that the apocrisiarii of the church of Thessalonica are also being held, and that letters are said to have been found on them; for what reason, we do not know. With them are also Philuminus, Demetrius the magistrianus, and other persons whose names we do not know. These are the things we have heard, as we said.

As for the church's cause, by God's mercy favorable news is reported. As for Cosmas the physician, we could not fully understand why he has come to Italy, except that he may perhaps have some complaint. You should be careful about him and find out why he has come there.
(214.) Another report of the same.
In another letter we are informing your blessedness about the city of Scampa and the venerable bishop Troius: how he gave the libellus and what festivity was celebrated in that city.

By God's mercy we have come to Lychnidus. Theodoritus, the venerable bishop of that city, likewise gave a libellus. The libellus was read out in church, and everything was done according to your directive.

Pray to God, and place your hope in his apostles, the most blessed Peter and Paul, that God, who granted such beginnings to your prayers, may likewise let prosperous things follow, so that the times of your crown may always be proclaimed for the correction of the churches. We sent this letter to your apostleship on the Nones of March.
(215.) Copy of the report of Andrew, bishop of Praevalis.

To the most blessed lord, ever my [?] own, to be preferred with inmost veneration in the apostolic see and equal in merit to the angels, father of fathers, Pope Hormisdas, from Andrew. Commending myself most humbly at your most holy feet, I report concerning the synod of Epirus Nova that they made a pretense of anathematizing certain persons among themselves. They used this device only to catch us in their malice. But the divine Trinity resisted them through your holy prayers. And when they had been caught in their malice, we could never persuade their archbishop to turn to the way of truth and to your precepts.

But now that the most blessed and most holy lord bishops and deacons sent by your holy crown have arrived, the bishop of Scampa, the most blessed Troius, went to meet them with all joy and with lights. Having presented the libellus according to your instruction, they were at once received into the peace of Christ and celebrated mass with him in the city of Scampa. And the people of Lychnidus, seeing what the bishop of Scampa had done, followed in the same way.

Indeed, while we were drafting this letter, a magistrianus arrived from the city of Constantinople and reported that, by God's favor and through your holy prayers, the people of Constantinople too have anathematized Acacius and celebrated Easter in peace. As for what follows, may your intercession labor with God that we may be found perfect servants of the apostolic see.
The letters which the most blessed bishops mentioned above sent to my humility I have forwarded to your piety, attached to this one. Received on the day given above.
(216.) Report of the deacon Dioscorus.
It is true that there are no joys, especially spiritual ones, against which tribulation is not wholly [?] prepared.
We rejoice at the unity of the church of Constantinople that has been achieved with the apostolic see; we are glad that every day libelli of satisfaction from various bishops are offered to us.

A small scandal occurred in the city of Ephesus, where the synod of Chalcedon was scorned and insulted. The most clement emperor has been called upon [?] to correct this, and you may hope that with God's help it will be done.

Now, though only after labors and after many disputes, the church of Antioch has been given a bishop. A certain Paul by name, a priest of the church of Constantinople, has been elected, whom the emperor's testimony has approved as most fit for this honor. They wished and tried to ordain him here; but I, not forgetting your command, objected, saying, 'Our lord the most blessed pope has ordered that, according to ancient custom, he be ordained bishop there.' What you commanded prevailed. Pray that God, at the prayers of the apostle Peter, may cause that city to receive its elected bishop in peace.

And because these things are being done and the catholic church is advancing in them every day, the ancient plotter has stirred up monks from Scythia who belong to the household of Vitalian, the master of soldiers. They oppose the wishes of all Christians, and their restlessness has caused no small delays to the unity of the churches, and especially to the ordination for the aforesaid church of Antioch.

These monks, among whom is also Leontius, who says he is a relative of the master of soldiers, are hurrying to Rome in the hope of having certain chapters confirmed by your blessedness. Among other things in them is one in which they want to say that one of the Trinity was crucified, which was not said in the holy synods, nor in the letters of the holy pope Leo, nor in the custom of the church. If this is allowed, it seems to me that no small dissensions and scandals will arise between the churches.

The emperor Anastasius strove hard to impose this on the catholics, and the disciples of Eutyches also proposed it at the synod of Chalcedon. Whenever the fathers discussed the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, they called the Son of God the Word consubstantial with the Father, homoousios with the Father. But the fathers never introduced this expression in the synods, precisely because it could undoubtedly in no way agree with the catholic faith.

If one examines closely the intent of this expression, how many heresies it lies open to, and what evils might be introduced through it into the church's debates, we will be able to explain it when we are with you, since it is a long matter. Hence it seems to me sound and useful and conducive to the peace of the churches to give no other answer than this: 'The holy council of Chalcedon is sufficient, in which the other synods are also contained; the letters of Pope Leo, which the synod confirmed, are sufficient. We neither wish nor ought to introduce novelty into the church.'

There is also this cunning point in their proposal, when they say: 'We have accepted the synod of Chalcedon; what we hope is that you will order it to be expounded for us, because as it is expounded it is not sufficient against the Nestorian heresy.' They do not say this because they fail to understand it, but because they are trying by subtlety to lead us into disputing about the synod of Chalcedon. If that happens, the synod is made to appear doubtful and weak, and it lies open to the error of all the heretics.

Moreover, if after the synod of Chalcedon, after the letters of Pope Leo, and after the libelli which the bishops have given and are giving, and through which they have satisfied the apostolic see, something new is added once again, it seems to me that whatever has been done is destroyed. Given on the third day before the Kalends of July, at Constantinople.
(217.) Another report of the bishops Germanus and John, the deacons Felix and Dioscorus, and the priest Blandus.

Your blessedness already knows, from other letters sent by your servant Pullio, how and with what caution we entered into communion in the church of Constantinople, by God's mercy. Likewise in other letters, not once but twice, we took care to report what men hostile to religion are attempting, so that nothing done or planned may be hidden from your blessedness. With God's help, whatever was settled in the church of Constantinople stands firm with us; the spiritual joys which the catholics celebrated and still celebrate do not waver.
The matter of the ordination for the church of Antioch has caused us not only labors but great tribulations, because men eager to obstruct general unity have raised various obstacles in various ways.

Our proposal was to ordain a bishop for the aforesaid church from among those who had kept themselves clear of the anathema. But they did not set the coming judgment before their eyes, and said openly, 'All who were in communion with the apostolic see are Nestorians,' and that those who now seem to have been brought back into the communion of the apostolic see deserved even less to be believed.

After many afflictions and contests drawn out by the parties for almost three months, the most pious emperor, by his own authority, chose a priest named Paul from the church of Constantinople to be made bishop in the church of Antioch. Among other things he gave this testimony about him: that during the two years he spent in Antioch he had resisted the heretic Severus in no small measure. All the catholics said the same with one voice. The emperor promised, however, to report all this concerning the said person to your blessedness.

Yet those who contrived and took part in these tribulations, and obstructed the unity of the churches, were the monks from Scythia. After they had failed here, marked out by everyone as intending nothing peaceable, they ran off to your blessedness, hoping to get in first by stealth and to confirm their aims through letters of your see.

They are accusing bishops of their province, among them Paternus, bishop of the city of Tomi. They presented petitions, and, compelled by the order of the most pious emperor and of lord Vitalian, master of soldiers, we met often for the hearing of the case. We did not do so because we wished to busy ourselves with these affairs, for we have before our eyes the precepts of your blessedness, by which you instructed us to attend only to the cause for which we had come and to involve ourselves in no other business; but we stooped to this in the hope that their aims could be calmed.

We labored long, and they accepted no reasoning, so that we made no progress toward what we were aiming at. Then the most clement emperor, in a public assembly at which he ordered us to be present as well, restored the aforesaid bishop Paternus and the magnificent Vitalian to friendship; he also commanded Paternus's accusers to make supplication to their bishop. But when the monks were likewise sought out for reconciliation, they slipped away in flight and preferred to leave the city rather than come to concord.

The aforesaid monks are coming to Italy above all to propose certain chapters, among which is also 'one of the Trinity was crucified', hoping to have them confirmed in this way by the authority of your blessedness. As we reported in other letters too, we say this now as well: no novelty should be written by the apostolic see. For we too declared this before the emperor and before the senate, saying:

'Beyond the four synods and beyond the letters of Pope Leo we neither say nor admit anything; whatever is not contained in the aforesaid synods or was not written by Pope Leo we do not accept. For if our lord should wish to write any novelty whatever, this beginning will be worse than the one made by Eutyches. What the church has endured for sixty years, from Eutyches until now, ought to be enough for it.'

We have written what seemed right to us; it is in your power to decide whatever God commands you. For this is what they are striving to assert, wishing to be satisfied in this way: that we should profess and say that one of the Trinity suffered, which neither the fathers nor the synods have said.

We have set these things out point by point so that their subtlety may not triumph over our simplicity. On account of these new aims of theirs they have stealthily won over the magnificent Vitalian, so that he champions such things and, for their sake, raises against us whatever obstacles he can. The whole church weeps with us over his change.

We therefore ask that, with your accustomed caution and the vigilance usual to our lord, you consider how those who have withdrawn from us in this way and been separated from our communion should be received, what answer should be given them, and how their chapters should be rejected, because the catholic church of Constantinople abhors all of them. Given on the third day before the Kalends of July, at Constantinople.
(218.) Another report of the same.

Your son, the magnificent Justinian, acting in a way that befits his faith, has built a basilica of the holy apostles, in which he also wishes to have relics of the blessed martyr Lawrence. Through our lowly persons he hopes that you will quickly grant him relics of these saints.

His request did indeed follow the custom of the Greeks, and we in turn explained the custom of the apostolic see to him. He accepted the reasoning. His faith is so fervent that it deserves whatever it asks of the apostolic see. What he hopes for is also of a kind that will help the salvation of his soul and the devotion of his faith to grow. So it is fitting not to refuse requests made with such desires.

Therefore, if it seems good to your Blessedness, order that contact relics of the blessed Peter and Paul be granted to him according to custom. It is for you to decide whether these relics may, if possible, be lowered as far as the second grating. He also asks, if it can be done, for something from the chains of the holy apostles and from the gridiron of the blessed martyr Lawrence.

These are the desires of this man, and these are what his faith has been stirred towards. For this reason he has sent the *spectabilis* Eulogius, a *magistrianus*, to your city. He judges that he will be satisfied if he may be found worthy to receive relics from the very fountain from which relics of the apostles have been given throughout the whole earth. And with God earnestly called as witness, you do well to entrust the church's cause to such a man, whose sincerity and integrity in the catholic religion are known to everyone.

They wanted to make silver caskets here and send them, but afterwards they decided that he should receive these too from your see, as a blessing. We suggest, however, that a separate casket should be made for the relics of each apostle. Given on the third day before the Kalends of July, at Constantinople.

HORMISDAS TO GERMANUS AND JOHN, BISHOPS, FELIX AND DIOSCORUS, DEACONS, AND BLANDUS, PRESBYTER. Conflicting reports have long made us anxious about your welfare and about how the business you undertook is going. This is especially so because in all this time no reply from you, our beloved, has told us anything certain. Still, since we have found someone to carry a letter, we have chosen to write this to you. So we greet you. Know that by the help of almighty God we are well, and we long to hear the same of you.

We want you to inform us more fully about everything that has been done. Tell us by whom and in what places you were well received, as we believe you were. Tell us where you, beloved, kept the feast of the Lord's resurrection, and what you have done since then. Explain all of this in prompt replies, so that you may relieve our anxiety about your welfare and the success of your mission. Then, if anything was lacking in the instructions you received for the matter, we can add it with the help of our God. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Eutharic.

HORMISDAS TO THE SAME AS ABOVE. Long waiting has made us anxious. You ought to have informed us quickly, especially since you were sent to so great an emperor. For we believed we would receive your letter before the day of the Lord's Ascension.

We wish to learn both whether you are safe and how the cause is progressing, which you undertook to carry through with the help of our God. We have therefore taken care to send Paulinus, defender of the Roman church, with this letter. We are also sending letters both to the emperor and to each of the others to whom it was proper to write.

So we pray our God with fitting prayers that in his kindness he may keep you safe and grant the cause the outcome we desire. For no title is greater for an excellent emperor than to deserve to be proclaimed by the church, now and in the future, as the author of peace. Given on the third day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Eutharic.

HORMISDAS TO OUR LEGATES, THE SAME AS ABOVE. We cannot help thinking about the state of the business entrusted to you and about your absence, beloved. Because of these things our concern does not allow us to pass up any chance to write.

Before this we sent a letter to you, dear brethren, by the *magistrianus* who returned to serve the patrician Symmachus. We urged you not to fail to inform us of everything that has been done or is being done in the church's cause. You ought to do this to relieve our anxiety. For we pray that almighty God may grant your labour the outcome we desire.
Stephen the merchant is delivering our words to you. Give him whatever help is fitting wherever need requires it, since you remember that he has always been one of ours. Given on the same day.
(222.) ALSO A REPORT OF THE DEACON DIOSCORUS.

We would have wished, and hoped, to send news in keeping with what we reported before: that John, bishop of the church of Constantinople, was still alive and that the confession set out in the *libellus* stood firm. There is no doubt that his merits are pleasing to God, since he was found worthy to leave this life for the next as a catholic and in communion with the apostolic see.

A certain Epiphanius, a presbyter who was formerly his *syncellus*, has succeeded him. His beginnings seem good, for he speaks reasonably. He promises to keep the rules of the fathers, and not to break up the peace and unity that have been established but rather to increase them.

This is what he promises, but we do not yet know what he can carry out in practice. We are sending this letter on the fourth day after his ordination, since we have found someone to carry it. We have not yet entered into communion with him. This is not because we are resisting, but because he has not yet invited us.

It remains for your Blessedness to keep praying that by the help of divine grace he may prove to be a man through whom we can rejoice in perfect unity. Received on the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Rusticius.
(223.) ALSO A REPORT OF GERMANUS AND JOHN, BISHOPS, FELIX AND DIOSCORUS, DEACONS, AND BLANDUS, PRESBYTER.

We are not surprised that through the prayers of your Apostleship everything has gone well for us, for we know that your prayer for us achieves more than our own ministry. The whole business of the church has turned out in such a way that no one can doubt that a miracle of blessed Peter was at work at every step. First, we found such zeal for religion among those who hold high office that Vitalian, Pompeius and Justinian came out ten miles to meet us. They did not think it beneath them to glory in our arrival and to give thanks to you. Then, the common people too were so devoted that most of the populace awaited our arrival with candles and with praises of you.

Amid such celebration we arrived at Constantinople, safe and joyful, on the Monday of Holy Week. The next day we were presented to the most pious emperor, and his warmth so encouraged us that his favour alone would have been enough to comfort us, even if nothing else had come before it.

But through your prayers greater things followed. That same day, in the presence of the whole senate, four bishops were also there, whom John, bishop of Constantinople, had sent to defend his side. We showed them the *libellus* of the apostolic see and proved that everything in it was properly canonical.

Finally, on Thursday, the day of the Lord's Supper, the bishop came to the palace for a general assembly. He read the *libellus* through, agreed to it, and signed it with the greatest devotion. Who could describe how great the joy of the emperor and the senate alike was there? Who could describe the tears that joy brought forth, or the cries that the whole gathering and the clergy raised in praise of the emperor or of your see? These things cannot be set out in a report. What we cannot put into words we leave to your imagination and to the bearer of this letter.

From the palace we went to the church amid the greatest celebration, so that communion too might strengthen the agreement of faith and of minds. One can scarcely believe how the joyful people wept, or how vast the crowds were that poured in. The crowd itself marvelled at its own joy. No one could doubt that the hand of heaven had been present to bring such unity to the world.

We report that in our sight the name of Acacius, the transgressor who was anathematized, was erased from the church's diptychs, along with the names of the other bishops who followed him in communion. The names of Anastasius and Zeno were likewise removed from the list read at the altar. Through your prayers peace has been restored to the minds of Christians. The whole church has one soul and one joy. Only the enemy of the human race mourns, crushed by the assault of your prayers.

Pray that a like happiness may also shine on the church of Antioch. The discussion about its bishop is still seen to waver there, since the people want different things and cannot agree on whom to choose. We believe, however, that through your Blessedness's prayers a worthy ordination will soon take place there too. Then the peace begun in your time may spread through the whole world. All parts will come together in apostolic communion and faith, and the church, made perfect, will be joined in all its members to its head, as it was before. Received [?]
(224.) ALSO A REPORT OF THE DEACON DIOSCORUS.

Through Eulogius, *vir clarissimus*, we received your Blessedness's letter. In it you told us what the Scythian monks were claiming, and how your Apostleship had decided to hand the case over to the bishop of Constantinople, so that he might hear it between them and those they are attacking. This did not displease me. Where, with God's help, a conscience is untroubled by fear, it ought to avoid no one. Rather, it should hurry on, so that what is true may be made clear to all through examination.

You told me that they had made a formal protest that heretics should not be associated with me. I do not know whom they call heretics, unless perhaps they mean those who accept the synod of Chalcedon, whom I call catholics. There is a deacon named Victor.

Before we entered Constantinople, certain people had a dispute with him about "one of the Trinity crucified", about "Christ composite", and about other points. Once we were here, they presented a *libellus* against him both to us and to the bishop of Constantinople. We met in the bishop's house to learn what the dispute between them was.

The bishop brought out the synod of Chalcedon. In front of everyone he read all that was laid down in that council, and said: "Let nothing beyond this be put to me. Whoever follows this can be counted among the catholics." Victor answered: "I likewise accept the letters of Pope Leo and the synodal letters of Saint Cyril that are cited in the council of Chalcedon. I sign with my own hand, and I confirm with oaths, that I accept these and preach nothing beyond them. If I am ever found preaching anything beyond them, I ask for no mercy." The Scythians, on the other hand, began to say: "Let 'one of the Trinity' be added too!" We replied: "What is not defined in the four councils or in the letters of the blessed Pope Leo, we can neither say nor add."

They did not like this statement. Yet who can know whether Victor said these things sincerely or deceitfully, except the one who knows hearts? We heard these words; it belongs to God to judge the mind.

Afterwards, without us, the magnificent Vitalian, master of the soldiers, and the bishop of Constantinople called Victor in between them and spoke with him. What they agreed among themselves we do not know.

After that Victor did not come to us, and the case was not argued. But your Blessedness should know that these Scythians call everyone who accepts the synod of Chalcedon a Nestorian. They say, "The synod is not enough against Nestorius," and that it must be accepted in the way they themselves have explained it. With God's help it has become plain to all catholics what kind of men they are, what they are aiming at, and what they want to bring into the catholic faith. The case does not need my labour, since God in his mercy has brought it to light.

I have neither kept silent about nor hidden what I learned from the fathers, which the catholic church has always kept. There is one God, of whom Moses speaks when he says, "Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God," and in another place, "The Lord alone led them." As I said before, we believe that the Trinity is of one substance: one Godhead, three persons. We do not speak of many gods, for we believe that there is one God, that is, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Nor do we deny three persons, so that we may not seem to follow the teaching of Sabellius. It is true that the person of the Son, that is, of the Word of God, is consubstantial with the Father. That person became flesh, dwelt in Mary's womb, and took on human nature without sin. In this way the Son of God became man and was born of the Virgin Mary.

For this reason we call her, and believe her to be, the Mother of God. The union of divinity and humanity began when the angel Gabriel announced to Mary, "Hail, Mary, full of grace," and "The Holy Spirit will come upon you," and the rest. That union was not divided in the womb, nor was it separated at the birth, in his nurture, in the passion, in the tomb, in the resurrection, or in heaven. For there is one Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, not divided in persons, not separated in natures, and not differing in power.

For it is the same one who also undergoes the passion. All the heresies have been cut off from the catholic faith: those that divide, like Nestorius; those that deny, like Eutyches; those that believe in a lesser incarnation, like Apollinaris; and those that bring in a phantom, like Mani. Their followers are workers of iniquity and enemies of the apostles' teaching. This is what I learned and what I heard from our elders. If there is perhaps something beyond this that we ought to follow and I do not know it, I must follow it once your Blessedness explains it.

As for Maxentius, who says he has a community under the title of abbot: if he is asked which monks he lived with, or in which monastery, or under which abbot he became a monk, he cannot say. Likewise, if I wanted to speak about Achilles, I would be wasting my effort. It is enough to say of him that he always stays in hiding, because his conscience has been condemned by all catholics. Given on the Ides of October, in the consulship of Eutharic. Received on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the same consulship.
(225.) ALSO A REPORT OF GERMANUS, BISHOP, FELIX AND DIOSCORUS, DEACONS, AND BLANDUS, PRESBYTER.

Great is the mercy of God and beyond measure are his judgments. He leaves nothing hidden, so that each person's conscience may be tested. Dorotheus of Thessalonica has not turned out to be anything new. He has shown himself to be just what true report long said he was. He has always been caught up in his evil desires. Given the opportunity, he committed the crime against the catholic faith that he had always been plotting.

In another letter we told your Blessedness why, as we passed through Thessalonica, we were unable to receive the *libelli*. It had been agreed, however, that once the holy church of Constantinople had been settled, we would send one of us to him. Dorotheus had hoped that, after the *libelli* were received, one of us would celebrate mass with him. This would serve as public testimony that he was joined to the unity of the apostolic see.

It happened late, but in the end we sent the venerable bishop John to him. By common choice the presbyter Epiphanius, brother of the venerable bishop Inlustris, was sent with him. Licinius, count of the *scholae*, also went with them by order of the most clement emperor.

This Licinius had earlier been sent to Thessalonica on another matter. A synod from the diocese of the church of Thessalonica had been gathered, and he was found there waiting, as promised, for one of us. They wanted to draw up the *libelli* and sign them in his presence. This was done: Licinius sealed the *libelli*, and when he came to Constantinople he reported what had happened. Dorotheus's *apocrisiarius* said to us, "Order someone to be sent to receive the *libelli*." It was decided, as we said above, that the venerable bishop John should go. So that he would have a witness to their signatures, we asked the most pious emperor to let Count Licinius go with him as well. And this was done.

When they reached the city, Count Licinius informed Dorotheus that our men were there. Dorotheus sent the presbyter Aristides with two other bishops to see our men. He alone knew that they were opposed to the business. Right at the start they wanted to pick quarrels with our men about the *libelli*, saying, "There are chapters that ought to be corrected." Our men said that they had no power to do this: "If you want to do it, thanks be to God. If you do not want to, we came, we have greeted you, and we are moving on." After these words they left.

The next day they met again and said the same things. Before any statement had been made, when no dispute had arisen and no insult had been given, a frenzied mob suddenly fell upon the bishop. They killed two of his servants, split his head open in two places, and injured his kidneys. If God's mercy and the protection of the basilica of Saint Mark had not rescued them from the mob's hands, they would have died there. But they were freed, so it is said, because the public authorities arrived and were able to rescue them.

Dorotheus's malice devised these things and the schemes behind them. Two days before our men reached Thessalonica, he baptized more than two thousand people. He handed out so many sacraments among the people that they might last them for some time, giving the people to understand that the true faith was being changed. How could such things not stir up the people? Whom would they not provoke to riot?

After this, in front of the people, he tore up the very *libellus* he had drawn up with the bishops, saying, "I will never do this as long as I live, nor will I agree with those who do." They also killed John, a venerable catholic, who had welcomed us into his house when we came. He had always kept apart from Dorotheus's communion because of the synod of Chalcedon. They put him to the same kind of death as those who killed Saint Proterius.

News of these things reached the most clement emperor, and throughout almost the whole city the catholics are mourning because of such crimes. His holy Clemency promises to punish Dorotheus and drive him out. For we solemnly declared to his Piety: "On no account can the most blessed pope receive Dorotheus among the bishops or into the communion of the apostolic see." We also declared that anyone who wants to receive him into their communion should know that they will be guilty under the authority of the church.

We have hurried to bring these things to your Blessedness's attention, so that nothing happening in these parts may escape your notice. Received on the fourth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Eutharic.
(226.) HORMISDAS TO GERMANUS AND JOHN, BISHOPS, FELIX AND DIOSCORUS

…to the deacons and to Blandus the priest. While the joys of the Church's prosperity were lifting our spirits, and we were gathering almost daily the full fruit of your labour, a report suddenly threw us into confusion, one hostile to everything that had turned out as we wished. Since you have not yet reported it to us, we suspect that the account behind this rumour is uncertain. Yet given the gravity of the matter, we thought we should not keep silent.

For word has reached us that our brother and fellow bishop John went to Thessalonica only to receive the statements of faith that had been promised. There he was so assailed by a senseless uprising of the people that first the man who had given him lodging on his arrival was killed. Then John himself was struck down in a similar assault, and he barely escaped, protected only by reverence for the holy font.

It is said that this uprising began with Aristides the priest, under the cover of a deceitful inquiry. If these things are clear, however, our complaint is not so much against the people. It will be in the power of the venerable emperor to cut back by his censure, as he sees fit, this injury done to his own reign and to a catholic bishop.

But as for what concerns us, we desire that it be carried out through you, God willing, with watchful care. For we want no one either to be converted without being given reasons, or to profess the right way of faith in such a way that he can claim something was imposed on him by the emperor without the remedy of teaching.

Therefore, through the representations you make in your petition, bring it about that the bishop of Thessalonica is sent by the emperor to the City. Under the pretext of asking questions he is striving to wreck the peace of the Church by dragging the business out at length. Let him receive from the apostolic see the teaching he refused to receive from you, and whatever he thinks doubtful, let him come here and learn it through inquiry in our presence. In this way he can prove that he is keeping the caution proper to the catholic profession, and is not maliciously pursuing quarrels of his own devising.

Let him know that we are ready both to instruct those who inquire in good faith and, with knowledge as our guide, to call back those who err to the right path of faith. But if a man in doubt will not try the teaching that is offered to him, nor yet accept in simplicity of heart what is commanded for the sake of peace and religion, it is plain in what spirit he resists the precepts of our God or despises the example of an orthodox emperor.

So let the whole effort of your representations be directed to this point. Those men cannot be saved by any other means, and the cause of the stirred-up people is better calmed under this arrangement. Let the most clement emperor also order Aristides the priest to come to us with him. For, as we said before, we desire that all those by whose equivocation the peace of the Church is divided should come together into our communion, be rid of the sickness of evil error, and feel the healing of catholic knowledge.

Moreover, as soon as you receive the present letter, you must send one of your company to us with a report covering everything, so that you may relieve our anxiety about what has been done or is being done. Also add a note of the date to your letters, so that the slowness of a courier cannot be blamed on you. Given on the third day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of Eutharic.

HORMISDAS TO THE BISHOPS GERMANUS AND JOHN AND TO BLANDUS THE PRIEST. We are deeply grieved by the death of John the catholic, who, you report, was killed by the madness of the heretic Dorotheus. We have learned that this same Dorotheus has been summoned to Constantinople by order of the emperor.

You must press our lord and son, the most clement emperor, against him, so that he does not return to that city again. Rather, let him be stripped of the honour of the episcopate, which he never exercised well, and banished from that place to a church far away, or at least sent here to the City under suitable escort.

You must also be watchful on this point: that Aristides, the instigator of the whole evil and party to it, is not ordained in his place by any underhand dealings. For it does no good to change the person if his shameful wickedness continues. You must choose a man such that the whole congregation of catholics rejoices at your judgement.

Once these things are attended to, your charity must apply itself vigorously to the cause of our brothers and fellow bishops Thomas and Nicostratus. For what use is it to have restored the Church if we see bishops shut out from its body? You know well that they were received into our communion carefully and with good reason. So it grieves us not a little if those who follow the preaching of the apostolic see neglect men who have been received in its faith and with its consent.

Therefore, as we have urged, press the most serene emperor hard for their communion and their sees. On this same matter we have sent letters to our lord and son, the most clement emperor, and to our son the illustrious Justinian, urging them to handle, together with your charity, everything that concerns the restoration of these men to their churches. We suspect you have forgotten this article of our instructions. For we said that the usurpers should be expelled and the men of whom we speak should return to their own churches, so that the others may be ordained elsewhere, provided they are of the right faith.

The illustrious Justinian has written to us about the Scythian monks, and we have sent copies of his letters to your fraternity. Since they were unwilling to wait for your charity's arrival, and said they could not bear the delays of being kept under watch, they tried to leave the City secretly. We had them guarded more carefully, however, because we wish to examine the things they have said against you, so that when you return, God willing, their error may be corrected by reasoned exhortation. Given on the third day before the Nones of December, in the consulship of Eutharic, a man of clarissimus rank.

HORMISDAS TO THE SAME AS ABOVE. Concern for your safety and your doings troubles us so much that we take every frequent opportunity to urge you to keep us informed, by letters sent to us, of what is happening around you. We have already sent you messages suited to our wishes by a man belonging to our son Agapitus, the illustrious and magnificent patrician. Now too we thought it would be some comfort to our anxiety to send you the present letter.

We ask only this: whenever a suitable courier is available, relieve us with letters about your doings and your health, and also about the delay by which, to our great sorrow, you are being held back. Given on the sixth day before the Ides of July, in the consulship of Rusticius, a man of clarissimus rank.

HORMISDAS TO BISHOP GERMANUS, TO THE DEACONS FELIX AND DIOSCORUS, AND TO BLANDUS THE PRIEST. Your charity's long silence saddens us as much as your absence over so long a time. This is all the more so because our sons, the magnificent patrician Symmachus and the illustrious Romanus, master of the soldiers, promised us that your charity would return without delay. We do not know whether it is the nature of the business that keeps you there, or some fraud disguised as necessity. We are ceaselessly anxious and question nearly everyone from those parts, and the reports we receive differ and contradict one another.

You are better placed to discover, understand and learn the causes of so long a delay, so you ought to have informed us of the things that torment our mind. Or if there is a proper reason for the delay, you should have sent one of your company to us, as was agreed.

So in case delays and obstacles are perhaps being contrived against you by cunning or some intrigue, write to us quickly. Then we can send a properly ordered request to our son, the most clement emperor, asking for your return.
