So write back to us fully and in detail about everything that is being done, both concerning persons and concerning the cause of the faith for which you have stayed so long. Once we know everything, we can consider, with God's favour, how mercy may come to the aid of you yourselves and of the cause at stake. Given on the Ides of July, in the consulship of Rusticius, a man of clarissimus rank.
(230.) COPY OF THE REPORT OF POSSESSOR, AN AFRICAN BISHOP, SENT BY HIS DEACON JUSTIN.

TO THE MOST BLESSED LORD, INEXPRESSIBLY ADMIRABLE AND PREEMINENT IN THE GRACE OF CHRIST, POPE HORMISDAS, POSSESSOR SENDS ETERNAL GREETINGS IN THE LORD. Whenever the health of the members is at stake, it is fitting and proper to turn to the remedy of the head. For who bears greater concern for those under him, or from whom should firmness for a wavering faith rather be sought, than from the one who presides over that see whose first ruler heard from Christ: "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church"?

I think your beatitude is not unaware of how many snares the Church in the city of Constantinople is struggling against, and how, in the manner of an old disease, a wound thought to be covered by a scar is again seeking to break out into pus. Some brothers were scandalized by a book of a certain Faustus, a Gaul by birth and bishop of the city of Riez, who appears to argue eloquently about various subjects, and most often about the grace of God. Others, as human interests go, took the opposite side, and they thought that I should be consulted about this dispute. I said that the things argued by commentators according to the capacity of their own

intellect are not to be received as canonical, nor kept as law in place of synodal decrees. Rather, we have fixed things, namely what is written in the Old or New Law and what has been decreed by the general judgements of the fathers, as the foundation of faith and the sound firmness of religion. But what various bishops have written is customarily judged on its own merits, without prejudice to the faith. But since this,

as we gathered from their repeated demands, seemed to them more of an evasion, I have ventured to send this letter of my lowliness to your apostleship through my deacon Justin, both because of their request and as an opportunity to pay you my respects. In it I ask above all for the protection of your prayers, and I beg that those who seek counsel may learn, by the authority of an apostolic reply, what is to be thought of the sayings of the aforesaid author. This is especially so because your sons Vitalian and Justinian, masters of the soldiers, particularly wish to be informed on this matter by a written reply from your beatitude.

I remember that I previously sent you, for review, a book containing commentaries on the epistles of the blessed apostle Paul, but I was not found worthy of the joy of a reply. So with a like prayer I beg that I may be granted the privilege of your blessing by a fitting reply. Received on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Rusticius.

HORMISDAS TO BISHOP POSSESSOR. Just as it is reasonable that those in doubt should seek counsel, so it is right that those consulted should reply. Whoever does not instruct the ignorant drives them into error. And nothing better befits one devoted to religion than the search for truth, since a man who asks the way he should walk more easily avoids going astray.

But before I take up the task of answering what your charity asks, I gladly confess that in your letter I found the fervour of your faith. Kindled by its warmth, you lament that the perversity of the unbelievers has revived and is flourishing in those parts. It is a most fitting grief, one that saddens hearts devoted to God. For among those who have a spark of charity no fall goes unlamented, since the single wish of spiritual men is the unshaken salvation of all.

But storms and tempests of this kind are neither unknown nor unfamiliar to the churches of God. Though the Church stands unshaken under the helm of her Pilot, she is still tossed and troubled by the various whirlwinds of rising waves.

Hence the voice of the prophet and psalmist, who, by the Spirit with which he was filled, took on the person of the Church herself and said: "Often have they fought against me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me." They shake her, but they will prevail in nothing. We are still on the threshing floor; the grain is mixed with the chaff; the good groan at the company of the wicked. But the flame awaits what is useless, and the barns stand ready for those already proven. Where on earth is there not this mixture?

It befits us to stand firm with our feet planted. We shall advance in our own good among our adversaries if we are not entangled in the errors of others. For a man proves the strong vigour of his virtue when he is pushed and does not move.

Where are the goads of various temptations not found? We endured such things for nearly this whole year from certain Scythians, who presented themselves as monks in appearance, not in truth, in profession, not in deed. We bore their tricks, hidden with subtle cunning, and their poisons, which served their hatreds under the cover of religion. We were eager to heal them of their inward wound by the restraint of a healing patience, and we did not keep silent the warning of blessed Paul: "Do not quarrel about words; it is useful for nothing but the ruin of those who listen."

But when is a poison that has entered the vitals drawn out? When do hearts that wrongly trust themselves obey the teachings of the truth? When does pride, walled in by its own opinions, put on the humility of obedience? When do men accustomed to the pursuit of quarrels, who love only to snatch at disputes about religion and neglect its commandments, consent to peace?

Among them there is never the charity commended by the new commandment, never the peace the Lord left behind at his departure. Their one concern is a stubborn purpose: to want to command reason, not yield to it. They scorn ancient authorities and crave new questions. They think the only right way of knowledge is any opinion formed on the spur of the moment. They are so puffed up that they think the judgement of both East and West must bend to their will, and they do not count among the faithful those who follow the tradition of the fathers if they see that they will not yield to their own opinion. They are skilled at sowing accusations and concocting the poisons of slander, at hating the sound body of the Church, organizing uprisings and stirring up ill will. And instead of the obedience that holds first place in the regular discipline of monasteries, they love the obstinacy of stubborn pride.

We could not restrain them by warnings, by gentleness, or by authority. They went so far as to come out into a public assembly to disturb the peace, shouting even around the statues of the emperors. Had the steadfastness of the faithful people not resisted them, they would have sown the wicked seeds of the devil's tares and stirred up dissension and discord among that very people through whom, with God's help, dissension had been driven from their regions. Too late we have learned by experience that the apostle spoke with a prophetic voice when he said that in the last days perilous times would come upon us, and men would be lovers only of themselves, having the form of godliness but denying its power, and that they were therefore to be avoided.

We thought your charity should be told these things on this occasion, so that if they happen to be brought there, they may not deceive, by some pretence of words, people who do not know how they behaved in the city of Rome. As for those who, as you indicated in your letter, consulted you about the sayings of a certain Faustus, a Gallic bishop, let them take this as their answer. Neither he nor anyone else whom examination has not received into the authority of the fathers can create doubt about the catholic faith or ecclesiastical discipline, or prejudice the faithful. The fathers have fixed the teachings that the faithful must follow. Whether it is an interpretation, a sermon, or a discourse composed to build up the people, if it agrees with the right faith and sound doctrine it is accepted; if it disagrees, it is rejected. There is one foundation; whatever building rises outside it is weak. Whoever builds upon it, let him consider whether he builds with cheap materials or precious ones. But he errs who strays from the way that the choice of the fathers has shown.

Yet it is not diligence ranging over many things that is condemned, but a mind turning away from the truth. Often these very writings provide the instruction needed to refute opponents, and it cannot be counted a fault to know what you should flee. So it is not those who read unsuitable things who incur blame, but those who follow them. If this were not so, that teacher of the Gentiles would never have agreed to tell the faithful: "Test all things; hold fast what is good."

It is not out of place to add a story which, though worldly, is not without reason. It is said that a certain man famous for his skill in painting, when he wished to depict a perfect horse with his brush, set a donkey in front of himself as he painted. He said this was not so that he might imitate the ungainly beast, but so that he might not slip into the likeness of some ugly feature.

Not without foresight did the venerable wisdom of the fathers define for faithful posterity which teachings are canonical, setting down, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, which books, even of the ancients, were to be received as authoritative, [?] so that a reader indulging his own opinion would not assert, not what suits the building up of the Church, but whatever his own will had conceived. What need, then, have slanderers to push questions beyond the established boundaries of the Church, and to stir up disputes about statements that carry no more authority than if they had never been made, when the Christian faith is bounded on a firm and unshaken path by the canonical books, the precepts of synods, and the regulations laid down by the fathers?

As for free will and the grace of God, what the Roman, that is, the catholic Church follows and holds can be learned in various books of blessed Augustine, and especially in those addressed to Hilary and Prosper. But specific chapters on the subject are also kept in the church archives. If these are lacking there and you consider them necessary, we will send them. Yet whoever carefully considers the words of the apostle will clearly recognize what he ought to follow.
Given on the Ides of August, in the consulship of Rusticius, a man of clarissimus rank.

EMPEROR JUSTIN AUGUSTUS TO POPE HORMISDAS. We are known to have shown openly the zeal we have always had, and still have, for reconciling the views of those who hold the catholic faith, so that all may with one mind venerate the undivided light of the Trinity. We showed it once when, of our own accord and for this very purpose, we sent to Your Beatitude as our envoy Gratus, the distinguished master of the bureau, so that a remedy might at last be found for the quarrels of those who dispute over various matters. We show it now by receiving with ready and glad affection the most religious men whom your apostolic see saw fit to send as mediators of unity.

Indeed, we looked upon them with joyful eyes as if they were peace itself, and judged that they should be embraced with outstretched arms. Moreover, we have arranged with all diligence that the venerable church of Constantinople, and many others besides, should accept your wishes, not only in other matters but also in removing from the sacred diptychs the names whose removal you especially demanded.

But there have been some cities and churches, in Pontus and in Asia and above all in the East, whose clergy or people have been tried with every kind of threat and persuasion and yet have by no means been brought to strike out and reject the names of bishops who enjoyed a high reputation among them. They think life harsher than death if they must condemn the dead in whose lives they gloried while those men lived. What, then, are we to do with obstinacy of this kind? It does not obey commands, and it so despises torments that it thinks it a grand and festive thing to give up the body before it gives up its religious resolve.

To us, at least, it seems necessary to act more gently and mercifully. If such gentleness and mercy cannot be found in Your Holiness, they will be found in no one else. For we did not take up the libellus out of a desire for blood and punishments, which is grievous even to say, nor so that the longed-for concord should be left unfinished over a small difference. We took it up in order to extend, by whatever means we can, the union of the members of the church. Which, then, will be better: for the sake of lesser things to have such great multitudes cut off from us entirely, or by conceding and remitting small matters to correct the greater ones, which must be pursued by every means, so that what could not be achieved in every respect may at least be secured in the essential parts?

We therefore ask indulgence regarding names. We do not ask it for Acacius, nor for either Peter, nor for Dioscorus or Timothy, whose names were contained in the letters Your Holiness sent us. We ask it for those whom episcopal reverence has honored in other cities, and even then excepting the cities where Your Beatitude's libellus has already been fully accepted, unless your goodwill decides that this part too should be corrected more gently.

Nor indeed does the matter lack the judgment of the apostolic see, so that it should be called not so much an indulgence as a ruling already deliberated and examined. For Anastasius of most religious memory, the summit of your church, laid down openly and plainly, when he wrote to our predecessor about this same business, that it was enough for those seeking peace if only the name of Acacius was passed over in silence. So whoever judges that not all memorials of the dead are to be scorned is following the earlier decrees of your see. It would therefore be thought unworthy and unfitting if your leniency, gentler toward all, both the departed and the living, were not proclaimed to every end of the earth.

And we would not doubt that this will please you so much that the world will at once be made more joyful by a peaceable reply. Your Holiness will remember, moreover, that we wrote some time ago that petitions had been sent to us from the East. They set out the wishes and decision of those people, and in them they show that they will hold firmly to this decision and believe they must on no account abandon it.

Accordingly, as we promised, we have rightly decided to send you this document now through John, a most reverend man and bishop. We hope that once your see has also accepted its contents, it may serve to gather and unite the venerable churches everywhere, and especially that of Jerusalem. All show that church such favor, as the mother of the Christian name, that no one dares to separate himself from it.

It is fitting, therefore, that Your Holiness should also declare your own consent in a letter, so that the world may be the more joyful once it has become known and clear to all that you too approve the contents of this document and hold firmly to them. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of September at Chalcedon, in the consulship of Rusticius. Received on the day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship stated above.
(232a.) COPY OF THE PETITION.

TO THE GOD-BELOVED AND MOST PIOUS EMPEROR JUSTIN, AUGUSTUS FROM GOD AND MOST CHRISTIAN PRINCE: A PETITION AND SUPPLICATION FROM THE CLERGY, ABBOTS AND LANDOWNERS OF JERUSALEM, OF ANTIOCH AND OF SYRIA SECUNDA, IN THE PROVINCE OF SYRIA.

'Draw water with joy from the springs of salvation,' cries the loud-voiced prophet Isaiah. By the springs of salvation he plainly means the preaching of the gospel truth. From these springs the blessed apostles, those who were their disciples in succession, and the wise teachers of the church drew the saving water of faith and watered the whole holy church of God. That church, founded on the rock of the chief of the apostles and keeping the right and unbending confession, cries out confidently with him at all times to the only-begotten Son of God: 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.'

We received this saving confession from the four holy synods, which are honored by the precepts of the gospel, and by Christ's grace we have never strayed from the right doctrines handed down to us. The proof of events bears witness to this, and our constancy of faith in a time of need demonstrates it.

If, then, most pious lord, as Christians we share in the reasoning of the faith and are hastening toward common peace and unity, we now make plain to Your Piety, through this statement, the faith we received from the beginning. Let it be known that we join in the peace and, with God's help, do not turn aside from the right faith, but execrate every heresy alike. We hate with our whole soul and anathematize not only the Eutychianists and the Acephali, but also the Nestorians and those who worship a man.

We, then, most Christian lord emperor, as was said above, were baptized from the beginning into the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and believing, we worship one essence of God in three subsistences. Following the teaching and creed of the holy fathers, we believe in one God the Father almighty, and in one Lord, our Jesus Christ, the only-begotten God the Word, and likewise in one Holy Spirit. In accordance with this divine teaching we also understand and receive the definition promulgated by the holy synod of Chalcedon, confessing and believing

that our Lord Jesus Christ, one substance or person, is one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity. This one person is what the holy synod itself proclaimed God the Word to be, in two natures, that is, in deity and humanity, without division and without confusion.

For if, as has been said, we accept one God in three subsistences, and neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit became incarnate, then it was God the Word, one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, who became incarnate and was made man, according to the property of sonship.

Believing thus according to the four holy synods already named, we do not refuse to confess also the second birth of God the Word according to the flesh. This is why the Virgin is believed to be in the proper sense the Mother of God, since in nature and in truth she gave birth to the Son consubstantial with the Father, God the Word, who without change in his nature became man from her. We confess two natures in Christ united by essence or substance, as in one person or substance. We do not take away their difference or their properties after the union, nor have we been taught to divide them into two persons and substances on account of the union,

and we acknowledge one and the same only-begotten Son of God both before his incarnation and after it. He is God and man together: passible in the flesh, impassible in the Godhead; circumscribed in body, uncircumscribed in spirit; that is, earthly and heavenly. The world received him as man and could not contain him as God; he is mortal and immortal. The difference of the natures is nowhere taken away, and we do not divide the union in essence.

For this is truly the great mystery of godliness: that one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, God the Word, incarnate and made man, is known and worshiped in both natures, deity and humanity, without division and without confusion. He undergoes no conversion or change, but preserves in himself, in one person, the properties of each nature.

For the sake of this faith, then, we receive and keep the holy synods already named, and we anathematize all who at any time or in any way have written anything against them. We anathematize especially John Aegeates, who as a Nestorian spewed out many blasphemies against the holy synod of Chalcedon, and we likewise condemn Timothy, surnamed Aelurus, who as a Eutychianist barked against it with his followers.

This, then, is what with God's help we have always held and hold now. We have therefore offered this statement to Your Piety, since you deigned to order us to set out our own understanding and our convictions about the sound faith. Certain heretics, in their haste to conceal their own bad faith, are trying to disparage our freedom in Christ and our right faith.

We therefore beseech Your Clemency to see to the perfect union of the holy churches. Let the unity that is achieved with God's help be <preserved>, so that from now on no spark of any occasion, reasonable or unreasonable, can disturb the peace. May the God of all fulfill your pious desire, for his own glory and for the good order of the state!
(233.) COPY OF THE REPORT OF EPIPHANIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.

TO HIS LORD HORMISDAS, HOLY IN ALL THINGS, MOST BLESSED BROTHER AND FELLOW MINISTER, EPIPHANIUS SENDS GREETING IN THE LORD. Both we and the most pious and most Christian emperor, together with his most faithful consort who flourishes in every good thing, have been very eager for the right and pure union of the holy churches. We received the holy bishops you sent with the love of God that befitted us, and we held the clergy in veneration. We believe that what has been done has already given Your Beatitude full assurance of all this.

We have believed, however, that if the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ our God brings these same most reverend fellow ministers of ours safely into your presence, everything that has been set in motion will become clear to you, most holy one. Through these very men you will learn more clearly the labor we were able to endure. You will learn how, by the grace of God and of our most faithful princes, our church of the city of Constantinople has been governed in peace. The names that we knew your see considers profane have not been recited during the sacred mysteries. Instead, the harmony of the four councils in defense of the right faith is proclaimed, and this is made plain to all by the reading of the sacred diptychs.

Let them report to you, then, that no small number of priests subject to us, and again no small multitude of bishops under their ordination, embrace the good of this union that has now begun. And let Your Holiness know that you have nonetheless been established as both the leader and the initiator of this general good.

Your Beatitude must therefore be roused by the spurs of praise to keep vigilant watch. Otherwise, what divine mercy had begun to arrange for your honor might seem not to reach its full completion as a common unity, as would be fitting.

Our most faithful and most pious princes, rejoicing in the unity and concord of God's holy churches, have written more fully about these matters to Your Beatitude. They have received petitions from a great many holy priests of Pontus, of the province of Asia and above all of the East. These priests find it difficult and even impossible to leave out the names of their former bishops, and their obstinacy is so great that they are ready to face any danger for such a deed.

We have considered all the causes set out above, which are necessary for the pursuit of peace, since only by this way of humility have we found union and salvation common to all. Therefore we ask, as has been said, that you settle the matter with the peaceable governance that befits you, once those whom we have sent on this business have given you full satisfaction. For since both are one church, there is no doubt that the good things brought about by vigilance will then win [?] the glory of common praise for both patriarchal sees, so that Christ our true God, the Lord and Maker of all, may be magnified, as is customary.

Concerning all these matters, may you be entreated with the greatest affection by John, the most holy bishop, who has shared many labors with us in the present struggle; by Heraclianus, the most reverend presbyter of our holy great church, who lives in our house; and by Constantine, the most reverend deacon of the same great church. Through them we have also sent our synodal letters to Your Beatitude, in accordance with the laws of the church.

Now, then, our most pious emperors, showing their zeal for the union of the holy churches, have written to Your Beatitude about these matters in peaceable [?] letters, and have sent you the petitions that the people of Jerusalem and of the East presented to them. We, wishing to find an occasion to greet you, have written you this letter, in which we make our entreaty, setting before you, most holy one, this divine word:

'Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation!' Behold, the Lord of all has entrusted us with a talent. It can be returned with increase through the fruit of good work. Through your praiseworthy stewardship it can save so many holy churches, so many of their priests and an innumerable multitude. That multitude is now indeed united to the holy church, but it will be in danger and go astray if Your Beatitude delays at the helm. This applies above all to those who live in the holy places of Christ our God, whom everyone is so attached to that their multitude ought not to be rejected. For at their prompting all persist so stubbornly in the evil of their obstinacy that they would rather depart from life than abandon what they have resolved. If God should ordain that they be united through Your Beatitude, the merit of the praise will be ascribed to you in both present and future times.

Let Your Holiness pray, then, both for our most pious and most Christian princes and for our littleness, and for universal union. May all things come together into undivided unity, and may the unshaken foundation of the catholic faith be made firm, by the grace of the holy and consubstantial Trinity and by the intercessions of our Lady, the holy and glorious Virgin Mary, Mother of God. Most holy brother in all things.

As tokens of our love in Christ our God we have sent through these most reverend men, for the ministry of divine worship in your holy and apostolic church, a gold chalice set with gems, a gold paten, a second chalice of silver, and two curtains of pure silk. We beg Your <Beatitude> to receive them with that love which we do not doubt you have according to God.

We, and those who are with us, warmly greet all the brotherhood in Christ that is with Your Holiness. Received on the day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of the most distinguished Rusticius.
(234.) COPY OF THE REPORT OF THE SYNOD OF CONSTANTINOPLE ON THE ORDINATION OF BISHOP EPIPHANIUS.

TO OUR LORD HORMISDAS, HOLY AND MOST BLESSED FATHER OF FATHERS, ARCHBISHOP AND PATRIARCH: FROM THEOPHILUS, BASILISCUS, ISAIAH, ANASTASIUS, PATERNUS, MARCIAN AND THE REST OF THE HOLY SYNOD ASSEMBLED IN THE CITY OF CONSTANTINOPLE.

We consider the countless and unsearchable wisdom of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, as far as human beings are given to understand it, and we rightly marvel at his immeasurable love. We cry with a loud voice: 'Who can tell the mighty acts of the Lord, or make all his praises heard?'

For behold, members that were once divided have been brought back by the grace of the Holy Spirit to unity and perfect love. This has come about through the good will of the holy and consubstantial Trinity and the intercessions of the glorious Virgin Mary, and through the zeal and vigilance of our most Christian and most faithful emperor and our most pious empress. Moses and Aaron, who are called leaders of Israel's true worship of God, once rejoiced, and now we too rejoice and cry out: 'Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored; he has become my helper and protector, for my salvation.' This is what we have been taught to believe and to proclaim with confidence.

We have also considered the love and the God-beloved life of Your Beatitude, as shown by the most reverend legates you sent, and likewise the peace of the holy churches of God of both the elder and the new Rome, in which we ourselves are shown to have shared. For all this we give thanks, as is our custom, to Christ our God, the good shepherd and prince of all.

For after the death of John of holy memory, the late archbishop and patriarch of the city of Constantinople, God gave us a holy shepherd and patriarch, Epiphanius. It is God who founded his own holy church, incorruptible, on the rock of the right faith and decreed that the gates of hell should not prevail against it. Epiphanius flourishes in virtues, in good discipline and in meditation on the divine scriptures. He holds the right faith and exercises a father's care for the bereaved, and, what more shall I say, he surpasses every fount of praise.

Rich in these virtues, he is known, and deservedly so, to have managed wisely and honorably the very great concerns of the church entrusted to him. He keeps in mind the words of the author of the sacred song: 'My mouth speaks wisdom, and the meditation of my heart understanding.'

Paul, the wondrous teacher of the whole church, declares that a bishop must be blameless, and that judgment has not been cheated in him. This is the right and approved judgment of our most faithful and most Christian prince, our most pious empress and the most glorious nobles of our common state, and it is confirmed by our testimony and now by that of everyone living in this city. So we see that our pontiff is crowned with virtues on every side.

Therefore, in fulfillment of the law of the church, we pay your apostleship the greeting we owe. We hope that Your Charity will deign to keep the bond of love and fatherly affection toward us still more firmly, and that you will carry matters through with wise governance, with the humility that befits a Christian, and with the gentleness that serves the salvation of the rational flock entrusted to you. Count it a common gain that through you and your brother and fellow minister, our lord and patriarch, peace has been secured for the churches of the whole world.

For we learn from the divine scriptures that a brother helped by a brother is, in spiritual terms, like impregnable walls and a fortified city. If through the intercessions of Your Beatitude general tranquility is restored to the churches of the orthodox, the angels will joyfully give glory in the highest to God, the Savior of all. Peace will be established on earth, and good will shall be rooted in the faithful servants of our common Lord and Savior Jesus Christ our God.

Whatever has been left unsaid will be added to our entreaties by three men. The first is John, the most holy bishop of the city of Claudiopolis, our fellow minister. The second is Heraclianus, the most reverend presbyter of the holy great church, who lives in the house of the most holy archbishop and patriarch Epiphanius named above. The third is Constantine, a most reverend man, deacon of the same holy church. They are known to have given proof of their right faith and good will some time ago to those who were sent from your apostolic see. They will show themselves worthy of Your Holiness, of the ministry of peace, of the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ our God, and of the union of the holy churches.

We hope that you will deign to send them back to us soon, instructed by your God-beloved counsel, rejoicing in the Lord and announcing the peace we have longed for. We too, and those who are with us, warmly greet all the brotherhood in Christ.

(235.) COPY OF A LETTER OF JUSTINIAN.

TO MY LORD, THE MOST BLESSED MAN AND HOLY FATHER HORMISDAS, PONTIFF OF THE CITY OF ROME, JUSTINIAN. How deep is our reverence for religion, and how anxious we have always been for the uniting of the holy churches, your Beatitude yourself can bear witness. For ever since our lord the illustrious emperor began to reign, we have sent letters by everyone travelling to Italy, petitioning your Apostleship as was fitting.

Now too, so that nothing that ought to be done may be left undone, John, a most reverend man and bishop, Heraclianus the presbyter and Constantine the deacon of the most holy church of this illustrious city have been dispatched to Rome (may it be with good fortune), to receive a complete reply on everything that your son, the most serene emperor, has written. May your Holiness therefore deign to receive these most religious men gladly, and, after prayers have been offered and the Godhead propitiated, so order everything reverently that nothing further remains in doubt.

For it seems to us that, since the Son of the living God, our Lord Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, whom the chief of the apostles proclaims to have suffered in the flesh, is rightly said to reign as one in the Trinity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, we are not unfaithful in believing that the person of his majesty is in the Trinity and of the Trinity.

As for the names of the deceased bishops, make your arrangements with clemency, as befits a father who makes peace; for your predecessor of blessed memory also wrote to Anastasius, of princely memory, that if only the name of Acacius were removed, we would have one communion. It is therefore no <heavy matter> for your see to grant what it has itself urged. For you ought to imitate the most holy Leo, the Roman pontiff, and, just as he wrote to Leo, so you too, setting aside all doubts, should write back to the most invincible prince, your son, complete and peacemaking pages [?] of the church, so that before the tribunal of the Judge who is to come you may share the lot of those whose see you hold by priestly right.

Let your Apostleship show, then, <that you have rightly> succeeded the apostle Peter, since the Lord will require from you, as the chief shepherds, the salvation of all, who will be able to be saved once concord has been made firm. For our part, once the chapters about which you have received our writings are settled, we will no longer allow anyone to stir up controversy about religion in our commonwealth, nor is it fitting for your Holiness to listen to people wrangling over superfluous matters.

HORMISDAS TO JUSTIN AUGUSTUS. Among the matters pertaining to the unity of the Church (the unity for whose sake God chose your Clemency to rule) that you set down in your letter, venerable emperor, your care for the faith, to which you declare yourself devoted in many ways, added this as well: that the petitions of certain persons should be enclosed and brought to the notice of my humility, so that from them I might learn what question had arisen, or might give a reply befitting religious knowledge to remove the uncertainty of the inquiry put forward.

I have read everything with due care, and although a full reply could have been given if I had simply written back what has been defined by the ancients, nevertheless, to repay the devotion of your religious purpose, I thought I should not withhold the service of my own words as well.

For what did the teaching of the fathers leave out when the poisons of Nestorius and Eutyches emerged? Synodal decrees, agreeing as one, crushed nearly every impiety together with the inventors of such abominable doctrines, and once such dreadful seeds of faithlessness had been cut away, no room was left any longer either to believe that Christ our Lord was without the reality of flesh, or that the same one did not come forth as both God and man from the undefiled fruitfulness of his mother's womb:

for the one, by his denial, made void, as far as lay in him, the dispensation by which we are saved, while the other, by an opposite opinion but a similar impiety, cut off the divine power in the same our Lord Jesus Christ from true humanity. The one did not remember that Christ showed his flesh to be touched; the other was not mindful of the Gospel, which says that the Word was made flesh, though the voice of the Lord ought to have sounded unceasingly in his ears, in which he said and taught: No one has ascended into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.

These things have often been set out in many judgments of those who went before us; yet your Clemency will not find them tedious to hear repeated, even though they have been said already, nor need we be ashamed to go over again what was proclaimed by our predecessors. For there cannot be diversity of preaching where there is one form of truth, nor will it be thought out of place if we agree in doctrine also with those with whom we are united in faith.

Let the synodal decrees and the ordinances of the blessed Pope Leo, which accord with the sacred faith, be read again to the pious ears of your Gentleness: you will find in them the same things you review in ours. What more, then, after that fountain of faithful statutes, could any inquirer, however curious, seek—provided he keeps within the bounds of the faith? What is full needs no addition, and what is perfect needs no further instruction, unless perhaps someone prefers to doubt rather than believe, to quarrel rather than know, to follow doubtful things rather than keep the decrees.

For if God is a Trinity, that is, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, and yet God is one, as the lawgiver expressly says, Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God, then whoever holds otherwise must either divide the Godhead into many or ascribe suffering specifically to the very essence of the Trinity; that is—may it be far from the minds of the faithful—either bring in many gods after the manner of profane paganism, or transfer sensible pain to that nature which is foreign to all suffering. The Holy Trinity is one.

It is not multiplied by number, does not grow by increase, and can neither be grasped by the understanding nor, in that it is God, be separated by division. Who, then, would attempt to force a profane division upon that secret of the eternal and impenetrable substance, which no nature, not even of the invisible creatures, has been able to search out, and to bring the hidden things of the divine mystery down to the reckoning of human custom? Let us adore the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, the substance of the Trinity, undivided yet distinct, incomprehensible and ineffable, in which, although the account of the persons admits number, the unity of essence does not; yet in such a way that we preserve what is proper to the divine nature and preserve what is proper to each person, so that neither is the oneness of the Godhead denied to the persons nor is what is proper to the names transferred to the essence.

Great and incomprehensible is the mystery of the Holy Trinity: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, an undivided Trinity; and yet it is known that it is proper to the Father to beget the Son, proper to the Son of God to be born of the Father, equal to the Father, and it is known too what is proper to the Holy Spirit.

And it is proper to the Son of God that, according to what is written, in the last times the Word should become flesh and dwell among us, within the womb of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, both natures being united without any confusion, so that he who was Son of God before all time became Son of Man and was born in time, after the manner of a man, opening his mother's womb at birth and yet, by the power of the Godhead, not undoing his mother's virginity.

A mystery plainly worthy of God being born: that he who made the conception to be without seed should keep the birth without corruption, preserving what he was from the Father and displaying what he took from his mother. For how else could it be that, lying in a manger, he was seen in heaven; wrapped in swaddling clothes, he was adored by the Magi; born among animals, he was announced by angels; scarcely past infancy, he proclaimed mystical doctrine without a teacher; and amid the first rudiments of boyhood he produced signs of heavenly powers?

For the same one is God and man—not, as the unbelievers say, by bringing in a fourth person, but the Son of God himself is God and man, the same one power and weakness, lowliness and majesty, redeeming and sold, nailed to the cross and bestowing the kingdom of heaven; of our weakness, so that he could be put to death, and of unbegotten power, so that he could not be consumed by death.

He was buried insofar as he willed to be born a man, and he rose again insofar as he was like the Father: suffering wounds and the healer of the sick, one of the dead and the giver of life to the dying, descending to the underworld and not leaving the bosom of the Father. Hence the soul which he laid down in accordance with our common condition he soon took up again by his singular power and wondrous might.

That these things are so and ought to admit no doubt—that is, lest our Lord Jesus Christ should be believed either not to be God amid the sufferings of the body, or to be God alone and not also man amid the astonishing works of his wondrous powers—he taught us by setting before us the example of two apostles, declaring Christ our Lord to be God through the faith of Peter and man through the doubt of Thomas.

For what purpose was there in his wishing to ask his disciples who men said he was, except that, when Peter answered, You are the Christ, the Son of the living God, he might make known that this had not been disclosed by flesh and blood but revealed by the inspiration of God the Father, and that through the testimony of that praised answer faith in the truth thus laid open might come about?

What purpose was there, when the Lord appeared after the resurrection, in Thomas alone being absent from the others or alone doubting, except that the world might believe what the doubting disciple had examined, so that, by allowing himself to be touched by the hands of one, he might be recognized for what he was by the whole body of the faithful? The doubt, then, was not put in to condemn the disciple but to provide instruction for posterity.

Or does it aim at anything else that the same Lord joined Cleopas and another disciple as they were on their way to Emmaus talking about him, and that, although they had learned of the Lord's resurrection from the women who had come first to the tomb, nevertheless, in order to give firmness of belief to future ages through their doubt, beginning from Moses and all the prophets he explained and showed that the Christ had to suffer and so enter into his glory—showing that the human nature was in him through the suffering and the divine through the glory?

These things are conveyed by many examples in the holy Scriptures, nor are they told to your religious conscience, venerable emperor, as though it did not know them. For the very faith which you steadfastly maintain repays you with this gift: it plants in your mind both love for itself and pours into it the knowledge by which it may be maintained more diligently. And yet it belongs to the stewardship entrusted to me that I too should not keep silent about known things even among those who know them, so that, as the preaching of catholic understanding is handed on from one age to the next,

what is unfailingly maintained may be believed without end. I could have discussed more fully, according to the definitions of the ancients, these matters concerning the Godhead and humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ and the two natures united in him without confusion, if it were necessary to argue against those who dissent from them. But since both the synodal ordinances and the teachings of the blessed Pope Leo are in everyone's hands, I thought it more fitting to touch briefly on a few points rather than to unfold everything.

For now it is enough to recognize, and to take care, that property and essence be so conceived that we know what we must ascribe to the person and what to the substance. Those who unbecomingly ignore these things, or conceal them with crafty impiety, lay snares for the threefold unity by leaving out what is proper to the Son. But if what has been said above is held fixed by strong roots, there is no departure from the tradition of the fathers, and questions are steadfastly met. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Valerius, of clarissimus rank.

HORMISDAS TO EPIPHANIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE. I am filled with great joy that I have learned, from the report of my legates as well, of such zeal for the peace of the Church on the part of both the most holy emperor and your Charity as you indicated in your letter. For clear proofs of heavenly mercy are thereby displayed, when the princes of the world join the cause of the faith to the ordering of the commonwealth, and the prelates of the churches, mindful of their office, carry out what belongs to their stewardship. After the storms of discord the Christian religion needed such rulers, who, having quelled the whirlwinds by provident arrangement and driven off the tempest, would bring back the peace that had long been in exile, and, extending the example of their purpose into the ages to come, would show beyond doubt that whatever posterity might do that is pleasing to God in imitation of them is to be credited to themselves.

Let us bless God, dearest brother, that this has been granted in our days, and let us strive with all the strength of our prayers and cares that what has been well begun by the help of our God may with his assistance be completed in every respect. For we may hope that the remaining members too, which are still divided, will hasten to rejoin the framework of their body, and that the lesser will not be at variance with the greater.

Since your Charity exhorts me to this out of zeal for Christian love, you ought to follow what you urge and embrace what you commend as worthy of love. For as we already bear a like care for the faith, we hope through religious patience for a like reward from the accomplishment of the good work. Nor must we give way to difficulties: faith is not wearied by hardships, no one presses on to the heights of heaven by a downhill path, and no one earns a reward without the exercise of toil.

Hence we are specially admonished not to grow weary in doing good; and, as the psalmist testifies, blessed are those who keep judgment and do justice at all times, because it is not the beginning of labour but its end that is wont to find the reward. Therefore, taking up an equal zeal of solicitude, since we share one fellowship in communion and belief, just as we rejoice together in the Lord over the church of Constantinople having been united to the apostolic see, so let us also take care, as you affectionately urge, for the restoration of the rest—first of all, that we keep our faith and integrity unstained by any contagion.

For you know, most holy brother, what bonds preserve ecclesiastical concord, what protect us from the snares of heretics, and through what the authority of the canons too is safeguarded. With these kept in full strength and with all circumspection, let remedies be granted to those who hope for them: for both the order of ecclesiastical rules and the very form of justice provide that reasonable medicine should not be denied, kindly and faithfully, to those who hope for it; nor is anyone so far removed from humanity that unwary simplicity would not move him from the rigour of strictness.

But so that this may be carried out carefully, without complaint or the stain of any error, dearest brother, you must take on my person in this matter, knowing in cases of this kind, as was said above, what is to be done and what is to be guarded against, providing for everything in such a way that you have no doubt that an account of this arrangement must be rendered to God; on condition, however, that your letters inform us of those who have been joined in communion with you, or through you with the apostolic see, and that the contents of the libelli they have presented be included in them. For in this way we shall both be clear of the error of Severus and his accomplices or the like, and not suffer the loss of those who could be healed.

We thought it right to lay this specially upon you, transferring our burdens to your diligence, because you have already given no small proofs in resisting heretics, and there ought to be no doubt about one who has been well tested. Take up at once the remedies of medicine; gird yourself at once with the authority of justice, and so soften with humanity toward suppliants that you exclude from those for whom counsel and provision are made for the restoration of the Church both those who persist in the contagion of heretics and those who feign innocence and agree with us only in word; for it is not expedient to relax ecclesiastical censure toward these. For the benefits of mercy will no longer serve the need of those who ought to be helped, if they are shared indiscriminately by good and bad alike.

And since your Charity thought fit also to mention the people of Jerusalem in your letter—a profession of theirs has also been brought to us—we thought it necessary both to review what was written and to reply as is fitting. If they keep the ordinances of the holy fathers, if they venerate those foundations of the faith, let them not depart from what was defined by the fathers under the prompting of the Holy Spirit. For these definitions are either perfect as they stand and need no addition, or are firmly valid and therefore not to be changed, since through them all the poisons of the heretics have been crushed.

Nor did the Synod of Chalcedon pass over anything useful that any diligence could have devised. It both set out more clearly the doctrines of those before it and confirmed them by repeating their authority, entering upon a special contest against Nestorius and Eutyches: the one separating the Godhead of our Lord Jesus Christ from the flesh and therefore shrinking from calling holy Mary the Mother of God, the other rejecting the reality of the flesh in the Lord. For our Lord Jesus Christ is the same Son of God and the same Son of Man, one person in two natures, of Godhead and of flesh, the natures not confused by their union; not as a fourth person added to the Trinity, but the Son of God himself emptying himself and taking the form of a servant.

For this reason we both profess one indivisible essence of the Trinity and yet know that each person has its own property. For we profess one person of the Father, one of the Son of God with the flesh he assumed, and one of the Holy Spirit, both distinguishing the persons by their properties and confessing the inseparable mystery of the Trinity through the unity of essence. Nor can it be doubted that the Word of God assumed human nature through flesh within his mother's womb, nor that, after the union of the natures within the womb, he was not thereafter divided from himself. For just as humanity was not brought forth in him without God, so on the cross the impassible Godhead was not divided from the suffering of the flesh, as is declared by the Virgin's childbearing and undefiled fruitfulness, by the unique resurrection from the dead and by the ascension into heaven.

If they keep these things as they were established by the fathers, let them believe them and not go beyond what has been defined; those who turn aside from this path pour a mist of doubt over themselves. But to the contentious we must give that apostolic answer: We have no such custom, nor do the churches of God.

I say this briefly, because it is not fitting to be in doubt about matters defined so often in accordance with the faith, and an argument offered to the well instructed is almost superfluous, especially since I have touched on not a few points concerning this matter in writing to the most clement prince, our son.

And since we have replied concerning the profession of the people of Jerusalem, we thought it fitting, for the sake of their salvation, to add this too: that if they desire the unity of apostolic communion, they should either send us through their own people their profession set down in writing, which they presented to our legates at Constantinople, or hand it over to your Fraternity—drawn up, however, in the same terms, as we have said—and by all means have it conveyed to us under your direction. As for the Thessalonians, whose legates came to us by arrangement of our most clement and most faithful prince, our son, lest we be thought to have omitted anything, we wish you to know that, according to what shall please our Lord Jesus Christ by his inspiration, the whole case is to be handled under our direction and, if they fulfil what they ought, settled.

Content to have written back these things pertaining to the matter through our brother and fellow bishop, the venerable John, and also through our sons Heraclianus the presbyter and Constantine the deacon, most worthy of ecclesiastical honour, we rejoiced to have found [?] in a man of our order equal merit and a religious purpose, together with wisdom and character befitting the embassy entrusted to him. For it is a thing much to be wished for and full of joy that those who come to be partners in communion and office should prove worthy by a just estimation. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Valerius.

Hormisdas to Justin Augustus. I know indeed, venerable emperor, that your clemency is content with the awareness of a good work alone, and that in the measures you take for the unity of the catholic church you have no need of human praise, lest the glory of great zeal be cheapened by an unworthy reward. For what does the whole of human acclaim amount to for one to whom it has fallen to be entrusted with the kingdoms of the earth, when the flatteries that lowly subjects offer to a ruler are open to the suspicion of adulation?

Besides, according to the teaching of the gospel, whoever looks for a reward of praise must necessarily go without the fruit of the heavenly reward. I therefore have no doubt that your gentleness, rich in every perfection of goodness, refers to God all the memorable things you do, and that, giving no thought to perishable things, you look for the reward of your deeds from him who is known to be the author of all good things.

And yet I comply with the divine ordinances I obey, so as not to pass over in silence the benefits of your religious conscience that have come to my knowledge, lest my silence, which only adds to your glory, should be turned (God forbid) into a fault of mine. For I know that of those ten whom our Lord and Savior in his mercy cleansed, nine were condemned with the mark of ingratitude, while the one who, once healed, gave thanks bore witness to his faith and to the healing he had deservedly received.

I follow the examples I have learned, and what I proclaim by virtue of the office entrusted to me I set forth on the occasion of this letter. I give thanks as great as I in my lowliness can, though not as great as I owe. But it is my consolation that the world rejoices with me over your benefits, and that the members of the church, torn apart until now, glory in being called back into one body. By pursuing error you have restored the faith to the peoples; the pride of the enemies of God's church has been bowed down, and the humble faithful have been raised up. A great thing has befallen you,

emperor; great advantages have joined with power in you. Understand what you merit: you have taken over no small share of that good work which our Lord Jesus Christ bestowed as he went to heaven; for the peace he gave his disciples the world has found through you. There is no doubt that the angels of heaven rejoice with you: for if, as the gospel declares, there is joy among them over one sinner saved, what joy must there be over a whole people?

Hail, Hezekiah of the present age! For although there were kings of Judah before him who did what was right in the sight of the Lord, none of them destroyed the high places. You too, destroyer of schisms and of pride and restorer of the ancient worship, may look for the course of your years to be lengthened like his, since you imitate the example of his deeds.

And all these things, which tend to the still greater increase of your glory, you undertake not spurred by another's urging nor roused by anyone's prayers: God alone is your counsel. There is no one who could try to claim a share in so great a work; the zeal for this undertaking you owe to yourself, and to yourself the accomplishment of this good deed. It is you,

venerable emperor, who encouraged me, grieving over the church's long-standing wounds, to hope that health would be restored; it is you who, after such unbroken turmoil, roused me to a new tranquillity when I was almost giving up in despair, by sending pious letters of your own accord. This too was beyond doubt granted by divine providence, so that at the very beginning of your reign you might dedicate the service of faith to him to whom you owed the empire you had received.

But I, who could not be the first to urge you to begin these things, am now, prompted by such great benefits, compelled with greater confidence to beg you not to let so good a work fall short in you, nor to withdraw the hands you raise to God from completing the work you have begun. I cannot deny that I ask these things out of love for our Lord and for unity; but I confess that I also owe these efforts to your salvation in return for the favor of such gentleness. For it is written that whoever perseveres will be saved.

Nor let the obstinacy of certain people make you slacker in your purpose. It is hard that the stubbornness of those who break the peace should prove more effective than that of those who uphold unity, that wounds should be cherished rather than remedies provided for health, and that it should be thought preferable to cut oneself off and join the dead rather than to cling to the living. Is it not right that those who are not moved by example should be made subject to the command of a religious prince? Not every sick man accepts what is good for him, and the effort to heal is often unwelcome to the very people to whom it is applied; and yet the constraint applied for the sake of health proves welcome, and those who are cured against their will are, once they have recovered, indebted for the benefit.

With great circumspection one must beware the craftiness of subtle men, who raise difficulties while they strive to undermine what has been settled. And who could allow that we should be thought to be led by peace to the very things to which we could not be forced by the pressure of discord, or that it should be considered fairer for a prince to follow the will of his subjects against salvation than for subjects to obey the prince's command for their own salvation?

Believe, venerable son, that the church of God herself joins me in imploring you to keep her without spot or wrinkle, as you know pleases the Lord, so that the ever-watchful eye may not see in her any blemish from which it would turn away. Love what you chose when God moved your heart, and keep undefiled that of which you wished to be a part. Formerly the concern was mine alone; now your clemency has made it a single cause for us both.

Let no one say that I am harsher than my predecessors, and let no one's exhortation be taken as carrying the authority of a decision: it is not a love of stubbornness but the scandals that followed that have made me more careful. Perhaps at the beginning there could have been room for leniency; but, as is well known, errors grew badly as earlier times went on. Do not think it a small thing, most holy son, that you have taken in hand!

Where have the holy Synod of Chalcedon and the most religious decrees of the venerable Pope Leo, who is among the saints, held any place of honor, and where has there not resounded against such great foundations of the faith something like a warlike army of the enemies of God? The more fiercely these have been attacked with darts, the more strongly they must be fortified with defenses. I beg you, most clement emperor, not to compel me either to abandon or to alter what has long been well approved. For that saying murmurs unceasingly in my ears, that no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God, since it is evident [?] that repentance belongs to evil works, not to good ones.

Yet although we are pressed by these difficulties, both out of regard for your gentleness and because we were moved by the not unkindly plea of the venerable legates, Bishop John, the priest Heraclianus and the deacon Constantine, who believed that remedies should be sought for those who are innocent or ignorant of the case,

we have sent letters to our brother and fellow bishop Epiphanius, so that, mindful of the faith and mindful of religion, he may admit to the fellowship of holy communion those whom he judges worthy of reception, or who are, as is asserted, innocent of the communion we have rejected, provided, however, that the terms of the libellus we have laid down are observed. For it is better and more pleasing to God that, with the faith kept intact, those who were cut off should be joined to the body of the church, than that those who have remained in the spotless communion of blessed Peter should go over to those who were cut off. Dated 26 March, in the consulship of Valerius.

Hormisdas to Epiphanius, bishop of Constantinople. With the affection of brotherly love we bless the Lord, because we have not only learned from the synodical report that you have worthily attained the episcopate, but see it confirmed by your deeds and conduct; and the rank you deserve has so revealed itself by its effects that we believed everything even before the testimony of our brothers and fellow bishops.

For what they promise you are able to accomplish by your conduct, we see that you have already fulfilled; and as though the grace of peace had been reserved for your faith, so the hopes of unity were put off until now. By divine foreordination of these events the name by which you are called came to your charity; and under it, now that the spirit of concord has appeared, it has come about that we may say: Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!

Therefore, offering you our greetings in Christ our Lord, we urge that the praiseworthy beginning of this good work be carried through in the course you have undertaken, according to the holy gospel, which warns us: whoever perseveres to the end will be saved. Exhort, then, the rest; invite them with admonitions, gather them in with gentle words, for the multiplied gains of the talent entrusted to us are sacrifices pleasing to God.

Moreover, it gave us the greatest pleasure to learn of your charity's promotion through the messengers, our brother and fellow bishop John and our sons the priest Heraclianus and Constantine; we think nothing could be sweeter than this. And since these men praised you, even if they did so out of the duty they had undertaken, yet not without reason [?], we are the happiest of all, because the messenger of a worthy matter proved a worthy reporter, so that the merits of the legates give you the most complete proof of your honor.

And in the pope's own hand [?]: We have received the golden chalice set with jewels, the silver paten, the other silver chalice and the two veils sent by your charity for use in the service of the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle. Dated 26 March, in the consulship of Valerius.

Hormisdas to the Synod of Constantinople. On the ordination of Bishop Epiphanius. We rejoice that, as your brotherhood reports, news has reached us that our brother and fellow bishop Epiphanius has, by God's favor, been raised to the office of bishop in most happy Constantinople. For tidings are in a way received more gladly when they are made known by a beloved person, and the joy that springs from the authority of the messenger is all the greater when there is nothing in the testimony to dispute.

So it was fitting, dearest brothers, so it was right that affection for a neighbor should show itself, that through you the apostolic see should learn that he shone in conduct and holiness, and that, as you too assert, he had long been so steeped in good principles that there is no stronger testimony to his merit than his being raised to the honor of the episcopate. For what can be held doubtful about a man in whom, as regards good conduct, with the concord achieved as proof, [?] the divine [gifts?] previously received [?] ...

Therefore you act in a holy, religious and pious way in willingly bearing witness to the truth and in not denying a reward to those who deserve it well: for it is the same error to keep silent about the truth as to support falsehoods, and the same injustice to deny honor to approved conduct as to grant it to the unworthy. It is certain, most beloved, that you share in the praises of the bishop whom you have made known to us, because what is praised in the one whom you chose from among yourselves is credited to the whole order of your brotherhood.

May almighty God, preserving the peace of his faith for ever, strengthen with great firmness your election and ordination, which you religiously thought should be made known to the apostolic see through our brother and fellow bishop John and our sons the priest Heraclianus and the deacon Constantine; and may he so scatter the struggles of all who are at variance and so restrain the hearts of the dissenters that, just as under our brother and fellow bishop Epiphanius a sign of reconciliation has been given, we may rejoice in its accomplishment. Dated 26 March, in the consulship of Valerius.
The proceedings in the case of Abundantius, bishop of Trajanopolis, we have in the archive.

Justin Augustus to Pope Hormisdas. We write so that your apostleship may learn what has happened in the case of the most reverend Paul. Holding the episcopate of the city of Antioch, he is said to have become so involved in many matters foreign to religious bishops that he is accused by the denunciation of his own clergy, of the inhabitants of that city, and of many others besides. This happened not only while the legates of your holiness were in this royal city (and we have decided to keep them here as well), but also after their departure. Overcome by the testimony of his bad conscience, and frightened besides that if an inquiry were held the matter might demand a graver outcome, he submitted a letter of resignation asking to be allowed to withdraw from the episcopal office he had taken up, as has been said.

Since, then, it is and always has been our heart's desire that the bishops of cities should always be held in the common love of all those whose souls they are believed to have received to govern, and since the most reverend Paul has of his own accord, as we have mentioned, abdicated his episcopate, we have thought it right to send the present letter, ... [?] be disclosed to you, and that you may deign by your own prayers to obtain heavenly protection for us. Dated 1 May at Constantinople, in the consulship of the most distinguished Justinian and Valerius.
(242.) Copy of the report of Epiphanius, bishop of Constantinople.

To the most holy and in all things most blessed lord, brother and fellow minister Hormisdas, Epiphanius. We would indeed like to write to your blessedness more often and to enjoy the affection of brotherly love; but now, wishing that what has happened should not escape your holiness, we have made use of the present letter.

For many disturbances, lasting no short time, have beset Antioch, that very great city, which is the first in the diocese of the East, on the ground that Paul, beloved of God, held the episcopate of that city; and many of the inhabitants of that city, as some have said, were separating themselves from the catholic church, pressing constant petitions on our most serene and most faithful prince, and begging that an inquiry into the charges brought should be held openly. (These things began long ago, as was known also to the God-beloved legates sent by your holiness, who learned all about these matters while they were staying in the royal city.)

The said Paul, beloved of God, therefore, thinking it to his advantage, chose by his own letter of resignation to give up the city assigned to him and the episcopate, and showed that he preferred general quiet and withdrawal from these affairs. We know that our Christ-loving prince has also made all these things known to your reverence.

But now what is more precious to all of us, and what we [pray for] most of all night and day, is good news concerning the God-beloved legates sent to your blessedness by our most loving prince and by us [?]: that you would deign to send them back to us as quickly as possible, joyfully announcing the peace that is dear to God and the unity of the holy churches, adorned with every beauty, so that in the present matter, as we have often written, there may be heavenly gain for those who are the prompt authors of a good correction, most blessed and most holy brother.
We and those who are with us greet for many years all the brotherhood that is with your blessedness in Christ.
(243.) Copy of the letter of Justinian, the illustrious.

Your apostleship knows well with what warmth of faith your son the most serene emperor and we ourselves have been filled from the beginning: we have never ceased to do whatever served to strengthen the divine religion.

For this reason we recently also sent most reverend bishops to Rome, so that full agreement might be reached on the chapters about which doubt had arisen. But we do not know what difficulty has arisen that matters which seem very slight have not yet been settled.

Greeting your reverence, therefore, we ask that no occasion be given [?] about which anyone could be in doubt, but that, keeping before your eyes the judgment of the heavenly majesty, you deign to make haste in every way.

TO MY LORD, VENERABLE BROTHER AND FELLOW PRIEST DIODORUS, MOST REVEREND BISHOP, EPIPHANIUS SENDS GREETING IN THE LORD. The Lord asked the Samaritan woman for a drink, conferring grace rather than receiving it, since he himself is the fountain of salvation. He sat by the well and was wearied by the toil of the journey, so that he would never depart from the consistent proof that his bodily presence was real. In this way he everywhere bestowed generously on human nature, which he had created, the gifts proper to it: at one time graciously taking it upon himself, at another truly claiming what belongs to it, and also exercising care and providence over it.

His disciples and his household too, from whomever they asked something, gave to them rather than received. Elijah also prefigured this very thing, going before in the likeness of his Lord. He fittingly asked for a measure of something necessary, but beyond what was necessary he imparted the abundance of the blessing that dwelt in him. He asked the widow for bread, but by occasion of this request he bestowed a wealth of blessing.

So too your Venerableness, in asking something of our littleness, is shown to give rather than to receive. For with your constant supplication to God working with us, a never-failing jar of oil will be supplied from a little, and from a scanty jar of flour an abundance beyond measure will be bestowed.

At the outset, then, venerable one, you asked in your letter about the stones that were commanded to be set in the breastplate of the high priest's ephod, at that time upon the breast of Aaron. You asked that I set out their names, colors and appearances, and also their places and the spiritual meanings they bear with reference to divine worship; and for which tribe each stone was set, or where it is found, or from what country it is shown to come.

For us, as I have said, as for the widow I mentioned, it was altogether difficult to find these things out, because of our poverty. But just as a wonderful thing happened to her through the blessing, and as the Samaritan woman was shown the gift of the Lord's mysteries in place of water that can be seen, so to us too, though we are very poorly furnished with wisdom, knowledge and speech, the means has been granted from every side. It is as if it came from many showers poured out with fruitful abundance at the prayers of Elijah and the other prophets. You are shown to be their son, disciple and successor, venerable one: you receive grace from the Lord just as they did, and you impart it to us through your prayers.
So I shall now begin to speak of these things. First I ask your pardon and make plain the eagerness of my purpose, though I can offer only the words of a feeble discourse.

First, then, it is written in four rows. The high priest's breastplate was divided into four parts, and was itself square, one span in both length and breadth. The order of the first row is: first the sardius, then the topaz, then the emerald. In the second row the first stone is the carbuncle, then the sapphire, then the jasper. In the third row the first stone is the ligure, then the agate, then the amethyst. In the fourth and last row the first stone is the chrysolite, then the beryl, then the onyx. These are the twelve stones that are known to have been set in the breastplate placed upon the high priest's ephod. We shall describe how they differ and where they are found.

The sardius, which is also called the Babylonian, looks like fire and has a blood-red color like that of the sardine fish. It was called sardius for this reason, taking its name from its appearance. It is produced in Babylon, which is in the land of the Assyrians. The stone is translucent and has healing power. Physicians smear its juice on swellings and festering sores and soothe them, as well as other wounds caused by cutting with iron.

There is also another, the sardonyx, which is called molochas and is able to reduce fat. In form it is somewhat greenish, and it is more potent around the beginning of spring, when the Passover is celebrated. And there is another, the sardachates, around which a white ring appears, as in the agate. Those who invent fables declare that it can drive away evils, and they call it 'the peaceful one'.

ON THE TOPAZ STONE. The topaz is red in appearance, second after the stone called the carbuncle. It was found at Topaze, a city of India, in the heart of a rock, by men who were quarrying stone there at the time. When the stonecutters saw how brilliant it was, they were delighted by its beauty, showed it to some Alabastrian merchants, and sold it for a small price. The Alabastrians in turn sold it to the Thebans for a higher price, and the Thebans offered it to the queen who was reigning at that time. She took it and set it in her diadem, in the middle

of her forehead. This stone has the following property. When it is ground on a physician's whetstone, it gives out a juice that is not red like its color but like milk. It fills many bowls, as many as those grinding it wish to fill, and afterward the stone is the same size as before, neither diminished in weight nor changed at all from its round measure. The juice drawn from it is excellent for ailments of the eyes. When drunk, it is also a powerful remedy for those gripped by the watery madness and for those driven violently insane by the sea grape. For skilled physicians give the juice of this stone to such people.

ON THE EMERALD STONE. The emerald, which is also called prasinus, is green in appearance. There are certain differences among emeralds: some are called Neronian, some Domitianic. The Neronian stone is bitter, very green in appearance, shining and flashing. They say it was called Neronian for this reason: they suppose that the emperor Nero ordered a mountain to be drenched with green Spanish oil, or Libyrtine [?] oil (others say almond oil, others lily oil);

but others say this was not so. They say instead that Nero, or Domitian, put the oil into bronze vessels from Nicaea, so that over time it would turn green from the verdigris of the bronze, and then drenched the mountain with it, and the rock that took in this oil bloomed all the more in greenness and clarity. Others deny this too, and recall that there was a certain Nero long ago, highly skilled in the art of [?] and very expert in knowledge of such stones, who discovered this desirable kind of emerald, and that it was first called Neronian after him.

What we have said about the Neronian emeralds should be understood in the same way of the Domitianic ones. For Domitian was emperor after Vespasian and his brother Titus, who laid Jerusalem waste. These princes, Nero and Domitian, were lovers of vain things.

There are also other emeralds: one in India, very similar to the Neronian, and another in Ethiopia, which is also found in the river Pishon. Divine Scripture also agrees with our account here when it says: 'Pishon: it is the one that flows around the whole land of Havilah. There the leek-green stone is found.' And it testifies that the carbuncle is there as well.

The Greeks call this Pishon the river Indus, while the barbarians and Havilites call it Barimanasi, and the Indians and Bugaeans call it the Ganges. Many Greek writers also call it by this name, the river Ganges, which flows through the whole land of Havilah; and they say that the Havilites are the inner Indians. It also flows around Ethiopia, the one called western, which is great Ethiopia, and from there it runs into the Ocean. This is why the carbuncle stone, carried along by the course of this river, is cast up in the regions around Libya, where the Ethiopians named above dwell.

But Aquila the translator, in Genesis, rendered the 'leek-green stone' neither as leek-green nor as emerald. He followed the surface of the Hebrew wording, and finding in the Hebrew the name of the stone, bodallin, where the Seventy said, 'There the leek-green stone is found,' Aquila said, 'There bdellium is found.' Bdellium is a kind of ointment or incense brought from India.
There are eight varieties of emerald, so far as each could be discovered. Although its nature is rather green and harsh, those from Ethiopia or India resemble hepar, that is, the liver.

It now remains for us to explain in what country that mountain lies which was once drenched with oil, whether by Nero, as the common story goes, or by Domitian. It lies far inward in what is called the Red Sea, at the very entrance to the region of the Indians. The divisions among those peoples are very numerous.

For in former times, as report has it, the Indians were divided into nine kingdoms: those of the Alabastrians, the Homerites, the Axumites with the Adulites, the Bugaeans, the Taianians, the Isabenians, the Libenians, the Dibenians with the Fish-eaters, and the Sirindibenians with the Havilites. But now there are many more, since they have broken away from the association they once had with one another: the Dibenians from the Fish-eaters, and the Sirindibenians from the Havilites. We shall give a historical account of these when we come back to their regions. The mountain of which we are now speaking was at that time subject to the Romans.

Smaragdinum, that is, the Emerald Island, is the natural name of a small island lying opposite Berenice.
