In Berenice is the harbor from India that leads to the Thebaid, and it is one day's sail from the Theban mainland in favorable weather, that is, eighty miles. Berenice, as it is called, borders on the region of Elephantine and also on that of Telmi, which is now held by the Blemmyes. The mines of this mountain have collapsed, but there are other mines in the mountains within the very barbarian territory of the Blemmyes, near the Telmeans, which the barbarians now dig, cutting out emeralds. The power of this stone is for seeing one's face reflected;
and those who invent fables also say that it foreknows the future.

ON THE CARBUNCLE STONE. The carbuncle has the appearance of a most intense red. It is produced near Carthage in Libya, which is called Africa. Others say this stone is found in the following way. It is not seen by day but by night. From afar it naturally gives out sparks like a lamp or a burning coal; at one moment it kindles like a live coal, at another it dies down. So those who seek this stone watch its brilliance from a distance and recognize it by this very fact, that it appears at intervals and goes out again; then they make their way toward its gleam and so find it. But whoever carries it cannot hide it, for whatever clothes he covers it with, its brilliance shines out through them. That is the reason it was called the carbuncle.

The stone called ceraunius seems somewhat similar to it. Some also call the ceraunius the 'wine stone', because it is the color of yellow wine. There is also the stone called Chalcedonian, which is itself close in appearance to these stones and is found in the same parts of that region.

Nor is it surprising that divine Scripture declares it to be in the river Pishon, although it can also be found in Africa. For the Pishon flows into the sea near the southern region and the western Ocean. The Ocean encircles the whole world, but the Pishon, as we have said, flows into its western part, and so this stone is carried to the regions of Libya. Divine Scripture says: 'A river goes out from Eden to water paradise, and from there it divides into four heads. The name of one is Pishon: it is the one that flows around the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold, and the gold of that land is excellent. There is the carbuncle, and the leek-green stone.'

ON THE SAPPHIRE STONE. The sapphire stone is said [?] to be like the purple they call blatta, but a deeper shade of it. There are many kinds of this stone. One of them sparkles with flecks of royal gold, but it is not so admirable

as the pure stone which shines throughout with the look of purple. This one is perhaps said to be found in India and Ethiopia because of the temple of Father Liber among the Indians, which is said, incredible as it may seem, to have 365 steps, all made of sapphire. Kings use it above all in their ornaments and necklaces, because it is wonderful, most beautiful and charming. For this reason some have called it the ornament of necklaces. It drives away pain: if it is ground with milk and smeared on places made rough by wounds, it becomes a remedy for those suffering from scabs and ulcers. And it is written in the Law that the vision given to Moses on the mountain appeared as if upon a sapphire stone.

ON THE JASPER STONE. The jasper is a stone that resembles the emerald in appearance. It is found at the mouths of the river Thermodon and at Amathus: not the Amathus in Cyprus, for the race of the Amathusians is naturally of many branches [?]. This stone looks like this: it is greenish, less so than the emerald, but duller and darker, and its inner body is green like the verdigris of bronze. Those who tell fables assert that phantasms, that is, apparitions, delight to settle on it.

There is also another jasper, paler than the sea, but deeper in bloom and tint. Another is found in the caves of Mount Ida in Phrygia, like the blood of the murex shellfish, but brighter, more like wine, and redder than amethyst. For they are not of one color and the same power. One is thinner and paler than smoky air, neither too brilliant nor uneven, with a bluish shimmer, as when in wintertime a vapor or mist rises from the ground as the south wind dies down. Another, which looks like ice, is said by those who invent fables to be a remedy against phantasms. It was discovered by the Iberians and the shepherds of the Hyrcanians, who live around the Caspian land and lake.

There is also another jasper, called opalius, like snow or the foam of the sea, or like blood mixed with milk, as the Massagetae are accustomed to drink it. Those who tell fables say that the wild beasts of the field fear this stone, and other portents fear it as well.

ON THE LIGURE STONE. We know nothing at all about where the ligure is found, either from the physiologists, that is, the investigators of nature, or from any of the ancients who are said to have concerned themselves with such matters. We have, however, found a stone called laggurium, which some, pronouncing it more narrowly, call liggurium, and I think perhaps this is the ligure, since the divine Scriptures have altered certain names: they called the emerald 'leek-green', for example, and named other things by other names.

And as for the liggurus, or laggurus, if it is indeed the ligure, again we do not know from what place it comes. Some have supposed that it comes from the upper Thebaid, because they affirm that certain stones of this kind are found in the temple called the Temple of Asclepius at Memphis in Egypt. In these there are flickering marks, as it were, not as in serpentine, but spots like those of the stone called cerinum. The spots are greenish, so that we may understand that deep inside this stone there is a most choice vein.

But this stone seems to have taken its name in a still clearer and more fitting way. For the liggurus is explained by reference to a certain animal called the liggium, which has the color of a young buffalo or a red heifer, and whose tail is short and has some greenish spots. For this reason the liggurus stone is also called 'liggus-tail'.

I wonder greatly why divine Scripture, which took care to use precious stones for the adornment and beauty of royal crowns and priestly vestments, and which mentions some that were very well known and familiar (I mean the carbuncle and the emerald, the amethyst and the agate, the beryl and the chrysolite), did not mention the hyacinth in its list of these stones. For this stone is most brilliant, and so precious and wonderful that we should consider whether divine Scripture perhaps calls it the ligure.

The hyacinth comes in different kinds, and the deeper in color a stone is found to be, the more it is prized above the others. The color purple is somewhat like the hyacinth, or the callainus; hence divine Scripture also says that the priestly vestments were adorned with hyacinth and purple. The finest hyacinth stone is called thalassites, because it resembles a calm sea. There is another called rhodiaeus, another opalius, and yet another perileucius. These stones are found in the inner barbarian lands of the Scythians.

The ancients used to call the whole northern region Scythia, where the Goths and the Dauni live, and the Venni and the Arii, as far as the region of the Germans and the Amazons. There, then, far inland in the desert of this great Scythia, is a very deep valley, completely impassable to men. It is walled in on both sides by rocky mountains, so that if anyone looks down from the mountain summits as from walls, he cannot see the valley floor; instead, a dark gloom rises from the depths to meet him like a kind of chaos.

So those who are sent by the kings who live nearby to search for these stones, following the procedure required by the task entrusted to them, slaughter lambs, flay them, and drop them from the rocks above into that immense chaos of the valley; and the stones, as they say, stick to the flesh of the flayed lambs. Then the eagles that live up among the rocks catch the smell of the flesh, swoop down, carry the flayed lambs up, and devour them, and the stones are left there on the mountaintops. So the condemned men who are sent to search for these stones by this kind of capture watch where the eagles have carried the lambs' flesh, go there, find the stones, and bring them back.

All these stones, whatever their variety of color, are precious, and they have this property: when placed on fiercely burning coals they are not harmed at all, but they at once put the coals out. Not only that, but if someone takes one of these stones, wraps it carefully in a handkerchief or some linen cloth, and holds it in his hand over burning coals, he himself will be tormented by the heat, but the linen in which the stone is wrapped

is in no way harmed or affected by any burning. This stone is also said to be useful to women, so that they may be delivered of the burden of childbirth without difficulty. It is likewise said to drive away phantasms.

ON THE AGATE STONE. The agate stone has been thought to be the perileucius, which is placed after the hyacinth stone. It is wonderful in appearance, blue in color, with a white ring around the outside. This too is found in the lands of the Scythians. Among these stones there is an agate of a lion's color which, when ground with water and smeared on places bitten by a viper, a scorpion or other serpents, drives out the poison. I mean the agate that has the look of a lion.

ON THE AMETHYST STONE. The amethyst stone has something fiery gleaming more deeply around its circle. Its brilliance is rather pale, and from the middle of its body it presents the appearance of yellow wine. It varies in form, and this one too, I think, is produced in the mountains of Libya. One kind is like the purest hyacinth, another like the amphicochlus [?]. It is found in a part of Libya along the seashore. Those who believe fables say that it cuts off storms and rains when the south winds blow.

ON THE CHRYSOLITE STONE. The chrysolite stone, which some have called chrysoberyl, displays the gleam of gold. It is found in the 'Well Rock', which is the name of a place on the shore of Achaemenid Babylon. They call both Babylon and that well of the rock Achaemenid because, they say, the father of King Cyrus was called Achaemenes, as some writers have reported. There is also the chrysoprase stone; ground and drunk, it is proven most healthful for those suffering from stomach complaints, colic and coeliac disorders.

ON THE BERYL STONE. The beryl stone is glaucous, that is, grey-blue, in color, like the tint of the sea and the air. It has the look of amethyst and of paederos, and of a more watery, that is, paler, hyacinth. It is found at the foot of the mountain called Taurus. If anyone holds it up against the sun, it seems to have tiny translucent particles inside, like bits of glass. Another beryl is like the pupils of a dragon's eyes. Yet another beryl looks more like coral. This beryl has been seen on the bank of the river Euphrates.

ON THE ONYX STONE. The onyx stone shows a very yellow color. They say that the wives of kings and of the rich delight in this stone, having it made into their cups. There are also other stones called onychites by an equivocal name, that is, not truly, which are like honey-colored wax. Some say these are formed from drops of water that harden. They call them onychites for a natural reason, because the nails of city-dwelling men are like marble, reddened by some admixture of blood. For this reason some falsely call the marble from the place Docimium 'onychite', because of its pure whiteness.

This, then, is what has been found out about the twelve stones that were at that time commanded to be fastened to the high priest's ephod, drawn from various authors who have written about the nature of these stones. So far as we have been able to investigate, we have noted briefly for the present their appearances, their places and the powers to be observed in them, and we have set out in order the names of each stone.

Here, then, the question now arises: by what means are we to establish the order of sequence that is most certain and fitting? For twelve stones were ordered to be set on for the twelve tribes, so that one stone would be fitted to one tribe and each stone would be assigned to the name of each tribe. And if the command had in fact declared which stone is to be fitted to which tribe, there would remain no inquiry at all to track down the divinely ordained arrangement; only the studious effort to explain to us the power of the stones would be left.

As it is, however, this is not determined; we must admit that the sequence of these stones and the form of their arrangement are recorded simply in two places: in the breastplate, which was placed on the high priest's breast, and in the ephod, by means of two gold rings arranged on it.

These rings held the breastplate in the middle by their ends, being in turn attached to the upper rings, which were fastened on the high priest's ephod on either shoulder. For the ephod too, since it was a single piece all the way round, was closed with just one opening. It had a band of blue interwoven with gold, and on the right one ring and on the left another, projecting over each shoulder, rings pointing toward the high priest's throat. These in turn were seen attached on either side of the breastplate, so that the two were thus connected and fitted to each other, namely by the two rings of the breastplate and the two rings of the ephod, where the gold chains hung down from above.

This breastplate, as I said, had twelve stones fittingly set into it and arranged in a square order; how they were interwoven is shown in what is appended below. The first and uppermost row, running from the high priest's left toward the right, had these stones set in it: sardius, topaz, emerald.

For this too must be noted more carefully, namely where the arrangement began and where again it ended; and it should be understood that these arrangements were made in accordance with the letters of Hebrew. For the Hebrews write, carrying the sequence of whatever is set down from left to right, while they themselves seem to have the hand that follows the letters moving from right to left [?]. So on the high priest's breast the rows ran from his left to the right.

The first row, as I have already said, was sardius, topaz, emerald; the second, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper; the third, ligure, agate, amethyst; the fourth, which was also the last, chrysolite, beryl, onyx.

Again, we find the same stones placed on the two parts of the ephod, on which two stones were seen set with gold chains, one on each side of the shoulders, no longer of different stones but of emerald alone; and on these two stones, again, the names of the sons of Israel were written and engraved according to the Lord's command.

It is not clearly shown, however, which name ought to be inscribed on the right-hand part of the green stone and which on the left, as he himself decreed. Nor is it likewise noted [?], except that it must certainly be understood that six names of the sons of Israel were written on the left part and six on the right. For one stone could not hold the names of twelve tribes because of its roundness. Nor did God command that the twelve tribes be inscribed twice, twelve on the right part and twelve on the left; he said simply: "with the engraving of a seal, the names of the sons of Israel," as the context of the passage itself has it, which we have now taken care to render word for word, and in which the office of the priesthood itself is also commanded to be established.

It says this: "And they made the ephod of gold and blue and purple and scarlet with twisted fine linen [?]. They made it a woven work, with shoulder pieces joined together on both sides, a woven work, clasping each other all the way round. From it they made it according to its workmanship, of gold and blue and purple and spun scarlet and twisted fine linen, as the Lord commanded Moses. They made both emerald stones, clasped and enclosed in gold, engraved with the engraving of a seal with the names of the sons of Israel, and they set them on the shoulders of the ephod, stones of remembrance for the sons of Israel, as Moses commanded [?]."

These are the two places for these stones and for their names, which were commanded to be recorded according to tribe: one place is in this breastplate, and the other in those which are called [?] in the hippodrome of Chabratha [?].

First, then, we must know this division and order of sequence, which follows the age of each: that is, Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah. But because of Rachel's quarrel, and because her maid Bilhah was given to Jacob, Dan is born next after Judah in order of age, and immediately a second son, Naphtali, is born of the same maid. Then, out of rivalry, Leah gave her husband her maid Zilpah, who conceived and bore Gad, then Asher. Again Leah his wife was granted to conceive, and she, in accordance with her knowledge [?], bore Issachar, and after him Zebulun. Last of all Joseph is born of Rachel, and then Benjamin. And this is the sequence: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher, Issachar and Zebulun, Joseph and Benjamin. This, then, is the first arrangement, according to the sequence of age.

When they came from Mesopotamia, as Jacob was returning to the land of Canaan, a second enumeration and division takes place. For Jacob made three companies, separating his own sons. He placed the two maids, Zilpah and Bilhah, as one company at the front, with their four sons, that is, Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher. In the second company he arranged Leah with her six sons, no longer according to age but according to their mother's affection: Reuben, I mean, and Simeon, Levi and Judah, Issachar and Zebulun. He himself remained last, with Rachel and Joseph, who was very small; Benjamin was still being carried in his mother's womb. And this is shown to be the second distinction in the arrangement of the same number.

The third number follows another arrangement of the division. For when Jacob was about to enter Egypt, as is appended above, the sons of Leah were gathered together, and with them in succession those of her maid Zilpah, as though born of the same mistress, and they are counted thus: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and from Zilpah Gad and Asher; then Rachel's sons, Joseph and Benjamin, and those from her maid, Dan and Naphtali.

The fourth division of arrangement and number is when Jacob blessed his sons as he was dying; for they must also be fitted into the numbers according to time. So this number and this time come next, when Jacob gave his blessing, that is: Reuben, then Simeon together with Levi, and Judah, and Zebulun and Issachar, Dan and Gad, Asher and Naphtali, Joseph and Benjamin.

Then follows the fifth division, from Exodus, when the sons of Israel went out of Egypt. For the divine word enumerated them, saying: "These are the names of the sons of Israel who went into Egypt with Jacob their father; each went in with his whole household: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun" (then the Lord commanded Moses:) "they made both stones" [?] (then Bilhah's:) "Dan and Naphtali" (and Zilpah's:) "Gad and Asher. But Joseph was in Egypt."

After this, the sixth division of number follows the encampment of the sons of Israel, as it is written in the book of Numbers by the Lord's command: in the first encampment Judah, Issachar, Zebulun; in the second Reuben, Simeon, Gad; in the third Ephraim and Manasseh and Benjamin; in the fourth Dan and Asher and Naphtali.

Again, the seventh division of number comes from the same book of Numbers, when it is declared, according to the Lord's command, who should be the leaders to offer gifts to the Lord. And he said: of Reuben, Elizur son of Shedeur; of Simeon, Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai; of Judah, Nahshon son of Amminadab; of Issachar, Nethanel son of Zuar; of Zebulun, Eliab son of Helon; of Ephraim, Elishama son of Ammihud; of Manasseh, Gamaliel son of Pedahzur; of Benjamin, Abidan son of Gideoni; of the tribe of Dan, Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai; of Asher, Pagiel son of Ochran; of Gad, Eliasaph son of Reuel; of Naphtali, Ahira son of Enan.

Likewise, after this follows the eighth division, from the same book of Numbers, when the Lord commanded and Moses sent the leaders of the tribes of Israel to survey the promised land. It says: of Reuben, Shammua son of Zaccur; of Simeon, Shaphat son of Suri; of Judah, Caleb son of Jephunneh; of Issachar, Sara son of Joseph; of Ephraim, Hoshea son of Nun; of Benjamin, Palti son of Raphu; of Zebulun, Gaddiel son of Suri; of the sons of Joseph, of Manasseh, Gelad son of Sudi; of Dan, Ammiel son of Gemalli; of Asher, Sachus son of [?]; of Naphtali, Hali son of Ulaphi; of Gad, Geuel son of Machi.

The ninth division of number is also given by the Lord's command, from the same book of Numbers, when the land is distributed by lot to the sons of Israel. "Of Judah," it says, "Caleb son of Jephunneh," and then the leaders of the tribes are listed in turn: of Simeon, of Benjamin, of Dan, of Manasseh, of Ephraim, of Zebulun, of Issachar, of Asher, of Naphtali.

Then again, the tenth division of number is when Moses blessed the sons of Israel, putting Reuben first and then adding Judah, Levi, Benjamin, Joseph, Zebulun, Issachar, Gad, <Dan>, Naphtali and Asher; and at the end he repeats what he says of Joseph: "These are the thousands of Ephraim, and these the thousands of Manasseh."

Likewise, the eleventh division of number appears when they are commanded, before they enter the land of Israel, that as soon as they have crossed the Jordan they should stand on the two mountains, Gerizim and Ebal, six on one side and six on the other, to bless those who keep the law and to curse those who scorn to observe the law's precepts. And this is the arrangement of the number: for the blessings were assigned Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph and Benjamin; for the curses, these: Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan and Naphtali.

The twelfth division of number, again, is when they receive by lot the land of their possession, and Reuben's lot falls beyond the Jordan, before the crossing into the land of Israel. And this is the distribution: Reuben, and beside him Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh; then, after the crossing of the Jordan, Judah receives first, then Benjamin, then Joseph through Manasseh, then Simeon, who is placed between Benjamin and Judah and, so to speak, squeezed in, because there was no room for them; then Zebulun obtains land, and Issachar, Asher, Naphtali and Dan. Levi, indeed, is scattered among all the tribes, receiving only cities and their outlying lands.

Again, the thirteenth division of number occurs in the prophet Zechariah, where he says: "On that day all the tribes of the land will mourn, the tribe of the house of David by itself and their women by themselves, the tribe of the house of Nathan by itself and their women by themselves, the tribe of the house of Levi by itself and their women by themselves, the tribe of the house of Simeon by itself and their women by themselves, and all the remaining tribes will mourn." He did not name which they were; but from the layout of the description of the land we have perceived that the sequence is this: the tribe of Benjamin, then Joseph, Reuben, Gad, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Naphtali and Dan.

Likewise, the fourteenth division of number is found in the Revelation of St John, who counted from each tribe twelve thousand of those sanctified by virginity. For he says: of Judah twelve thousand, of Reuben likewise, then of Gad, of Asher, of Naphtali, of Manasseh, of Simeon, of Levi, of Issachar, of Zebulun, of Joseph, of Benjamin. But nowhere in this passage does he mention Dan.

Perhaps the numbers may also be found recorded differently in other places; these, however, are the ones we were able to find. And these are the divisions which are evidently arranged in different ways according to number, sometimes according to the Lord's command, sometimes according to the will of the individual leaders, I mean Moses and Joshua son of Nun and those who afterward were found worthy to be their successors. Nor was this done without the Spirit; rather, as he willed, the same Holy Spirit enumerated and arranged each sequence according to his own will.

Returning to these again, I will set out briefly and in order, in one place, these same fourteen divisions and the choice among them. I shall not do it to no purpose, nor to be tiresome to Your Reverence as you go over these things, but so that you may know (and it is now for God to help us in this) how we may truly fit the stones mentioned to each tribe.

So, after much pondering, and treating the matter by testing this selection, our mind and the very sequence of the reading suggest to us how the square order of the breastplate may be discerned from the stones set in it according to the names mentioned. Let us now inquire of each number, as each division has been distinguished, which one agrees with the account and reading of these stones.

And wherever we examined the arrangement of the enumerated tribes in each place and weighed in our mind that it could not naturally be fitted to the names of these stones (for instance, where any of the numbers counted in a given division lacks one of the tribal names), we set it aside. So we at once duly set aside the second division, as one that could not agree with these stones, because it puts first Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher, that is, the sons of the maids, when Jacob, sending gifts to Esau, placed them in the first company, and after that made the sons of Leah another company, and then the sons of Rachel a third company. For since the more precious stones are at the beginning of the breastplate, while the sons of the maids are held to be lower and are here placed first, it is impossible for them to fit the scheme of the breastplate in this part of the number; and so it cannot be this way.

Likewise we examined the fourth division, the blessing of Jacob, when he blessed his sons as he was dying. For it has Reuben first, then Simeon and Levi joined together, so that this coupling of the two seems to stand in the way of agreement with these stones. Therefore we set this one aside too, since it can by no means be accommodated to these stones.

We also examined the fifth division, which contains the beginning of the departure of the sons of Israel from Egypt, and we found that it puts the sons of the free women first and places the sons of the maids after them in the order of arrangement, making the last <first> and the first last. And because Joseph, being in Egypt, was named last, we observed again that these stones could not be fitted to the names of the tribes mentioned:

both because the onyx stone cannot naturally be interpreted of the person of Joseph, and again because Joseph ought not to be set last in the arrangement of the breastplate, unless he was put out of his place only by necessity, so that, though he is reckoned eleventh, here he is counted twelfth by the compelling necessity of the arrangement of this number, which we found ordered in this way.

For in the Greek text, which was translated from the Hebrew, we find the onyx stone placed twelfth and last, so that it draws its symbolic meaning wholly to Benjamin; but we find the beryl eleventh, and we have accordingly fitted it to Joseph, the eleventh, both by number and by its symbolic meaning.

Examining also the Hebrew Exodus, in which the law is shown to be written as well, and reading about this breastplate in which these stones were enclosed, we found the onyx stone arranged differently: it was placed eleventh, and the beryl twelfth and last. From this an uncertainty very nearly arose for us, hindering our understanding, as though we had put forward an invented interpretation of these two stones, the beryl, I mean, and the onyx. And I kept asking, in supplication and continual prayer, how the error could have arisen; and I understood that this was so brought about by God's dispensation, so that the same Joseph, being eleventh among his brothers, should be found twelfth according to the arrangement of this number, which declared him twelfth when it said: "But Joseph was in Egypt."

Knowing, then, that by divine dispensation, for the sake of the true meanings that are fulfilled in Joseph himself, the beryl stone was to be fitted to him, it was so disposed that the beryl stone was placed twelfth and last. For Joseph too, though he is recorded as eleventh among his brothers, is nevertheless written twelfth and last in this arrangement of the number at the departure of the sons of Israel. So, entirely by divine illumination and dispensation, the onyx stone has very rightly been assigned to Benjamin, who in this arrangement is counted before Joseph, while the beryl has been fitted to Joseph because of the meanings that agree with him, even though that stone is counted last, since it happened that Joseph too was written last, as I have often asserted.

Passing beyond this division as well, we looked at the sixth arrangement, according to the sequence of the enumerated tribes, and found that, according to the encampment of Israel, the order of the square formation ought rather to correspond to the breastplate, three tribes and three tribes, just as one could see in that same breastplate, which is shown to be of square order. And this was very plain and symbolic, that is, meaningful, because of the arrangement of the ranks and its correspondence with the camps.

But among these, one tribe, set apart, stood in our way: the tribe of Levi. For Judah is placed with Issachar and Zebulun in one shared encampment, and is set first, toward the east, on account, I think, of its signifying royal power, and because Reuben fell from his own glory, since he defiled his father's bed, as is shown to be recorded in the divine scriptures.

In the second encampment Reuben is placed with Simeon and Gad toward the sea; to the west, Ephraim with Manasseh and Benjamin, who are all from Rachel and are placed in one encampment; but on account of Manasseh, Levi seems to be excluded. Then, to the north, the fourth encampment holds first Dan, then Asher, then Naphtali. And since we did not find Levi mingled among them, we recognized that this description too cannot be accommodated to the arrangement of the stones, lest one name of the sons of Israel appear to be missing from it.

Therefore, leaving this one aside as well, we turned to the seventh division, which we at once removed, because we did not find it agreeing with the arrangement of the stones. For it is evidently numbered according to the leaders of the tribes at the Lord's command: in it Reuben is placed first, then <Simeon, then Judah, then> Issachar and those that follow; but Joseph is counted twice, because Ephraim is placed in one number and Manasseh in another. And since Levi again is left out, we could not fit the number to the stones, because of the change regarding Levi and because of the addition of one tribe, which is shown to be divided in two.

Then we carefully examined the eighth division, from the book of Numbers, where God commanded and Moses sent the leaders of the tribes of Israel to survey the promised land; and we did not find this one agreeing with the arrangement of the stones mentioned either, because Reuben is counted first, then Simeon, then Judah, then Issachar and those that follow in turn, and nowhere is mention made of Levi.

Passing on, then, to the ninth division, we examined that one too, which was made at the Lord's command, as is contained in the book of Numbers, when the leaders of the tribes were sent to divide the promised land by lot among the sons of Israel; and we were likewise unable to fit this one to the sequence of the stones. For we found Judah placed first, then Simeon and afterward Benjamin, also Dan and Manasseh, and Ephraim as well, and Zebulun, and next Issachar, then Asher and last of all Naphtali; and finding again that the tribe of Levi was omitted and that Joseph was counted twice, in Ephraim and Manasseh,

we passed over this one too and turned our mind's attention to the tenth division; nor could we find it agreeing with the stones. For when Moses blessed the sons of Israel, he put Benjamin fourth, after Levi, and then Joseph; and since he made no mention of Simeon, it was impossible to fit it to the stones. It runs thus: Reuben, Judah, Levi, Benjamin, then Joseph, Zebulun and Issachar, then Gad, the son of the second maid, placed out of order, then Dan and Naphtali, then Asher last of all, who is likewise found to be a son of the second maid. Here too, since the number is diminished by the omission of Simeon, it was not possible for this division to correspond to the stones of the breastplate.

Passing over this one as well, we came with the most careful attention to the eleventh, and we found the place where Moses commanded that the twelve tribes should stand to bless and to curse, six on Mount Gerizim and six on Mount Ebal, as is shown to be written in Deuteronomy. Their division is as follows: "These shall stand," it says, "on Mount Gerizim to bless: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph and Benjamin; and these shall stand to curse on Mount Ebal: Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan and Naphtali." Here, apart from Reuben and Naphtali, the sons of the free women are shown to be given precedence; and since this division too appears inconsistent with the square order of the breastplate, it did not seem right to adopt it.

Nevertheless, looking carefully at this same eleventh division, since it appeared to be split into two parts, six on one mountain and six on the other, we judged that it matched the arrangement of the emerald stones. These were joined by little chains and set on each of the high priest's shoulders, fastened with gold and a blue band, so that the names of the sons of Israel were engraved on these two emeralds, because a single emerald, being round, could not hold twelve names. Even if it could have, however, the right and the left had to be distinguished. So the names were written on each stone, the one placed on the right and the other on the left, just as the tribes of the sons of Israel were arranged on the two mountains, Gerizim and Ebal.

These mountains can be seen facing each other in the eastern region, where Jericho lies, beyond the place called Gilgal. There, we are told, those who stood on Mount Gerizim blessed Israel, saying: "Blessed is he who does the will of the Lord." The voice was heard across the level plains where the people stood, and they were signalled to say: "So be it, so be it!" On the other side, Reuben and Gad and the rest with them, standing on Mount Ebal, said: "Cursed is he who does not do everything that is written in this book," and all the people answered: "So be it, so be it!" Now "so be it" is the meaning of "amen." These were the voices that rang out from the two mountains.

Gerizim also means "mountain of [?]" and "the cutting off of their sojourning." Some, however, who have not searched the divine scriptures carefully, especially those who come from among the Samaritans, have supposed that Gerizim might be the mountain that lies next to Shechem. This place is called both Sicima and Shechem, and facing it is Sychar, a city of the Samaritans, which the Lord entered, and from which that Samaritan woman came out and found him sitting by the well. Now Shechem is called Neapolis, the wealthiest city of the Palestinians. At that time, however, the region was called Samaria and Judea:

Samaria, because the mountain itself was originally named after a certain Somer. This man had a son, Somoron, and the mountain was called Somor, and from this the name came to be used. It was especially confirmed by the coming of those whom the king of Assyria sent to cultivate those lands.

For when the captivity of the Jews took place, the elders of Israel who were then in Babylon with Ezra the priest, those who were called counsellors, and other elders came together and begged the king of the Assyrians to send settlers into Judea, so that the fertile land would not go to ruin for lack of anyone to till it. He accepted their sound advice and sent four nations to live in those places, namely the Cudaeans, the Cuthaeans, the Sepharvites and the Anagogavaeans. When they went up, they brought with them their idols, which each nation had worshipped in its own land up to that time.

When they had come and settled in the land of Israel, they were called Samaritans, because "Samaritan" means "guardian": for they guarded the land of Israel. Later, however, lions, leopards and bears rose up against them and ravaged their numbers, so that they were being wiped out by them. For this reason the inhabitants and settlers sent envoys every day to the king

of Assyria, asking him to give them leave to depart from those places because of the savagery of the beasts. They wondered how Israel had been able to live there. When he learned this, the king of the Assyrians summoned the elders of the Jews and asked them how the people he had recently sent could remain in that place. They gave him sound advice without delay, saying that no nation could live there unless it kept the law of the Lord God. When he asked them for the law, they gave it to him at once. He had copies of the law made and kept the authentic originals with himself, and he sent the copies to the inhabitants and settlers

of the land, the Cudaeans, the Cuthaeans and the rest, by Ezra the priest (not the Ezra called Shealtiel, whose son was Zerubbabel, this Zerubbabel being the son of Jeconiah). So this Ezra of whom we have spoken went up to Jerusalem and brought them only the Pentateuch, that is, the five books of Moses from the Old Testament, books written in the script which the Lord gave on Mount Sinai. The Hebrews call this script deessinon, which means "engraved." For the letters the Hebrews use now are not the same, and their books are not written in the old script that was once engraved on the stone tablets. The script the Jews now use is called somahirenus. The Samaritans, however, keep deessenon, the script which, as we have said, was once impressed on the stone tablets.

But when Ezra went up from Babylon, he did not want Israel to be indistinguishable from the other nations, lest the race of Abraham should seem to be mixed with the inhabitants of the land, who do indeed hold the law but not the prophets. So he changed the original script and set aside deessenon, because that script had already been taken over by the Samaritans, so that in this way the seed of Abraham might be distinguished from the other nations. But having come to this point, we have been forced by the occasion of this subject to lengthen our discussion.

So those from the nations who remained in the land of Israel were called Samaritans for various reasons. First, from Somer, one of the sons of the Canaanites and Perizzites, before the patriarch Abraham came by divine guidance to that same land; both the mountain and everything that seemed to be near the mountain were called Somer and Somoron. Then again, the aforementioned nations sent by the king of the Assyrians were called Samaritans, which means "guardians."

There is also another way of looking at this name, namely with reference to the guarding of the law, since those who had been sent in were thought to guard the commandments of the law. For scripture says of them that they continued doing the law of God and worshipping their own idols. But since the law commands that idols are not to be worshipped at all, how could the law be kept by them?

Yet the following circumstance suggests how this is to be understood. The utterly profane priests of the four nations we have mentioned knew that Ezra the priest had been sent and had come, a man who abhorred idols in keeping with the divine commandments, and that anyone found serving idols was put to death by stoning, as the law commands. So they quickly took their own idols down from their high places and hid them on Mount Gerizim in a very remote and secret spot.

There were four idols, as ancient tradition holds. For the men of Babylon worshipped the goddess Succoth-benoth, the men of Cuth the goddess Nergal, the men of Hamath the goddess Ashima, and the Avvites the goddess Nibhaz Tartak, and Sepharvaim [?]. And they turned the hearts of the Samaritans, teaching them to pray toward Mount Gerizim. Therefore, wherever they are, they turn toward the mountain to pray: those in the east look toward the west, those in the west toward the east, those in the north likewise face south, and those in the south look north toward the mountain. So the scripture is fulfilled which says: "They continued doing the law of God and worshipping their own idols." For even though the worshippers themselves do not know of the idols hidden in the depths of the mountain, it is still impossible for divine scripture to speak falsely about this matter.

We were given the occasion for this explanation by the twelve tribes that were arranged on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, as the division of the ordered number itself shows. Those who do not read Deuteronomy with understanding have therefore been led astray, so that they have made up another scripture for themselves. For they have supposed that the mountain next to Neapolis, as we said above, is Gerizim; it is very high, and the one facing it, which they suppose to be Ebal, is also exceedingly lofty. Shechem lies in the valley between the two mountains, shut in on either side by the mountains that stand against it.

The Samaritans who live in that city have made steps up the mountain and built a kind of temple on the summit, so that, as we said, they may be seen to pray up on the mountain, which they call Gerizim out of a sort of careless forgetfulness, not according to the truth of faith and reason; for the book of the history says otherwise. But those who do not look carefully at what is actually the case are deceived.

In fact, these mountains are shown to be so lofty and so very high that no one in the valley could hear someone speaking up above. How then could the leaders of the tribes, who were up above, six men, make their voices heard by the people from such a height, so that those standing below could answer "amen"? For the height of the mountain rises a thousand paces or more, and it has a great many steps, more than fifteen hundred, as some say. Since, then, it is not possible for the voice of those above to be heard below, nor the voice of those below to be heard above, it is immediately proven that these are not the mountains that divine scripture means.

Then the sequence of the book of Joshua son of Nun makes this plain, when it records that those two mountains, Gerizim and Ebal, are in the region east of Jericho. Now the eastern region of Jericho lies next to Gilgal, the place called Gilgal, whereas Shechem lies to the north of Jericho, inclining toward the west, fifty-two miles distant from Jericho [?]
I. HERE BEGINS AN ACCOUNT SHOWING THAT ACACIUS WAS DULY CONDEMNED BY THE APOSTOLIC SEE.

GELASIUS TO HIS MOST BELOVED BROTHERS, ALL THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT DARDANIA. We are greatly surprised that your love wishes to be told, as though it were a new and difficult question, something never heard of before, about a matter on which the communicants of the Eutychian plague merely mutter out of contentiousness. They have nothing to answer in defense of the obstinacy that is ruining them, and they have often been refuted by argument already. They mutter not because their chatter carries any weight, and in fact they can find nothing at all to say.

What surprises us here is less that those who have fallen away from the truth and strayed from the ancient tradition of the church put forward profane novelties of words and the follies of a perishing perversity, than that those who have been trained in catholic understanding still hesitate. As your love has reported, these people keep boasting that Acacius was not, in their opinion, justly condemned, because he does not appear to have been deposed by a special synod. On top of this they heap up the madness of their vanity, childishly adding, "especially the bishop of the royal city."

Therefore you should reject the folly of these empty complaints, run through the record from the blessed apostles onward, and consider it carefully. Our fathers were catholic and learned bishops. Whenever a heresy arose, at whatever time, they assembled once and decreed what was needed for the faith, for the truth, and for catholic and apostolic communion, following the path of the Scriptures and the preaching of our forebears. They willed that whatever they had decreed should stand from then on unshaken and firm, and they did not allow what had been laid down in that same cause to be reopened by any fresh presumption

They saw very wisely that if anyone were allowed to reopen decrees that had been soundly made, no ordinance of the church would remain stable against any error whatever, and every sound definition would always be disturbed by the same recurring frenzies. For even when the boundaries of synodal rules have once been fixed, the plagues that were crushed do not stop renewing the struggle, raising themselves against the foundation of the truth and striking at simple hearts. What would happen, then, if the faithless were free to convene a council again and again? However plain the truth may be, pernicious falsehood never lacks something to bring forward. It may fail in reason or in authority, yet it refuses to yield out of sheer persistence.

Our forebears saw this by divine inspiration and took the necessary precaution. Whatever a synod held against a particular heresy had promulgated for the faith, for communion, and for catholic and apostolic truth, they would not allow to be mutilated afterward by fresh reconsiderations, so that the wicked would not be given an occasion to attack what had been established as a remedy. Instead, once the author of any madness had been condemned together with his error, they judged it sufficient that whoever at any time became a communicant of that error should be bound by the original sentence of his condemnation. Such a person could be plainly recognized, either by what he professed or by those he communicated with.

For the sake of brevity we pass over earlier cases, which a diligent inquirer can easily trace. A synod condemned Sabellius, and when his followers were later to be condemned, there was no need to hold a separate synod for each man. Instead, in keeping with the ancient ordinance, the universal church held that everyone who had shared either in his depravity or in his communion was to be rejected.

In the same way, the form of catholic faith and communion set forth at the assembly of Nicaea against the blasphemies of Arius includes, without any reconsideration, all Arians and anyone who has fallen into this plague, whether by belief or by communion.

In the same way, when a synod had once been held and had condemned Eunomius, Macedonius, and Nestorius, the church did not allow any further recourse to new councils. Instead, by the synodal boundary handed down to it, the church rejected all who in any way fell back into these blasphemies. And it is clear that the church never rightly gave way under pressure of any necessity so as to violate afresh what had been soundly established.

We are well aware that during the storm of the Arian persecution, when peace was restored and many bishops could breathe again after exile, they gathered their brethren in certain provinces and set troubled churches in order. But they did not change anything the synod of Nicaea had defined concerning the faith and catholic communion, nor did they strike anyone with a new condemnation for his lapse. Rather, they judged that by the terms of that decree such a person stood condemned unless he repented. It followed that unless he amended, he would without doubt remain under condemnation.

These things have been weighed, as we have said, in keeping with the tradition of the fathers. We are therefore confident that no true Christian is unaware of this: the ordinance of each synod that the assent of the universal church has approved ought to be carried out by no see more than by the first see. That see confirms each synod by its own authority and guards it by its continuing governance. It does so by reason of its primacy, which the blessed apostle Peter received by the Lord's word. With the church also following it, the see has always held this primacy and holds it still.

When this see learned from sure evidence that Acacius had strayed from the truth, it was slow to believe it, since it knew he had often been the executor of its necessary measures against the heretics. For almost three years it kept admonishing him in letters, as the writings sent to him in a friendly spirit by various messengers bear witness.

At first he resolved to reply to none of them, as though he had committed himself to silence. At last, however, he sent a letter declaring that he had entered into communion with Peter of Alexandria without the knowledge of the apostolic see. Yet Acacius himself, having requested the authority of the apostolic see, had also condemned this Peter as its executor. The see of blessed Peter knew that it had only condemned Peter of Alexandria and had never absolved him, so it did not accept this. Therefore, so as not to be drawn through Acacius into fellowship with Peter, it removed Acacius as well from its communion and cut off the transgressor, who had offended in many ways, from its fellowship.

If an examination is called for here, there was no further need of a trial once he had confessed in his own letter. If the weight of authority is asked for, the sentence is found to be the carrying out of the definition of the Council of Chalcedon. By that definition, anyone who became a communicant of the error condemned there would equally share in the condemnation already pronounced. For an error that has once been condemned together with its author brings both its curse and its penalty upon anyone who takes part in that wicked communion.

On this basis Timothy too, and Peter of Alexandria himself, who certainly appeared to hold the second see, are shown to have been condemned. They were condemned not by holding the synod again but by the authority of the apostolic see alone, at the request of Acacius himself, who also carried out the sentence.

Perhaps someone will say that it ought first to have been established whether Acacius had communicated with error or with transgression. We give a brief answer to this. If they think that Acacius, as Peter's communicant, can be excused in any way, let them show that Peter had been lawfully and truly purged and duly separated from all contagion of heretics when Acacius communicated with him. But if, as is nearer the truth, they cannot prove that Peter was fittingly and lawfully cleansed, it follows that the man who communicated with him was infected by the guilt that Peter had never expiated.

Nor do we keep silent about what the whole church throughout the world knows. The see of the blessed apostle Peter has the right to loose what has been bound by the sentences of any bishops whatever, since it has the right to judge concerning every church, and no one is permitted to pass judgment on its judgment. Indeed, the canons willed that appeal should be made to it from any part of the world, but that no one should be allowed to appeal from it. It is therefore clear enough that Acacius had no episcopal authority to loose the sentence of the apostolic see without its knowledge.

By what synod, indeed, did he presume to do this? Even with a synod he would have had no right to do it without the apostolic see. Bishop of what see was he? Prelate of what metropolitan city? Was he not under the jurisdiction of the church of Heraclea? He was certainly allowed, in their view, to break the sentence of the apostolic see without a synod and without consulting that see at all. Was the first see, then, not allowed to cast down such a transgressor by its own authority, while carrying out the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon as was fitting?

Nor do we pass over the fact that the apostolic see, as we have said, has frequently had the power, in keeping with the custom of our forebears, to absolve without any prior synod those whom an unjust synod had condemned, and also to condemn, without any synod, those who had to be condemned. Athanasius of holy memory, for instance, had been sentenced by an Eastern synod. Yet the apostolic see received him and absolved him, because it did not consent to his condemnation by the Greeks.

Likewise John of Constantinople, of holy memory, had certainly been condemned by a synod made up even of catholic prelates. In the same way the apostolic see absolved him, even acting alone, because it did not consent. Likewise holy Flavian had been condemned by an assembly of Greek bishops, and in the same manner the apostolic see absolved him, because it alone did not consent. Instead, by its own authority it condemned Dioscorus, prelate of the second see, who had been accepted at that assembly. By refusing its consent it alone set aside that impious synod, and it alone decreed, for the sake of the truth, that the Council of Chalcedon should be held.

In this matter, then, just as it alone had the right to absolve those whom synodal decrees had struck down, so too it is known to have condemned a great many, including metropolitans, without a synod in this same cause.

Someone may find fault with these acts of the apostolic see, or with what was done in accordance with a synod. Apart from being refuted by the long-established proof of the facts, he will have to admit all the more that Acacius had no such right. Let him say, then, by what synod Acacius decided to exclude the prelate of the second see. Whatever sort of man that prelate was, he was certainly a catholic, ordained by catholics, and never accused in any way concerning the catholic faith and communion. And by what synod did Acacius allow Peter, a manifest heretic whom Acacius himself had helped to condemn, to be put in the place of a catholic bishop?

By what synod did he have holy Calendion, bishop of the third see, expelled, and then allow, by his own arrangement, Peter to be put in his place, a heretic so manifest that Acacius did not even pretend to communicate with him openly? By what synod, finally, did he throw out orthodox men stained by no crime throughout the whole East and install in their place, by his own provision, every sort of wicked man entangled in crimes? By what synod did this abominable plunderer seize so many privileges belonging to others? But books would not be enough if we tried to describe one by one the tragedies he staged throughout the churches of the whole East.

Or do they think we should be confronted with that argument of his, by which he evidently tried to throw the blame for his misdeeds onto the person of the emperor? Why, then, did he resist Basiliscus when he wanted to, a usurper and certainly a heretic bitterly hostile to the church? Why did he not submit his will to the emperor Zeno himself when he refused to communicate openly with Peter of Antioch? Clearly he was able to stand firm in other matters when he did not want to comply. Does not the apostle say that not only those who do such things but also those who consent to those who do them are equally caught in guilt?

But let us leave aside matters that would need longer explanation. What of the fact that the emperor Zeno himself declares in his letters that he did everything on Acacius's advice? Acacius himself confirms in his own letters that the emperor is not misleading anyone in this, for he wrote that the emperor had done everything rightly, and he did not hide that these same things had been done on his advice.

As if Acacius had been a transgressor only in his communion with Peter of Alexandria, and not with all the others! Some of them he had set over various churches, like a tyrant, after driving out catholic bishops. With others, once they had been installed in this way, he joined in perverse communion. According to the canons, these men were to be driven from the church's communion for this very reason, that they had allowed themselves to be put in as successors while the rightful bishops were still living.

What Christian does not see that, once catholic bishops had been thrown out of their own sees, only heretics could be brought in to replace them? Yet Acacius either arranged for all of these to be put in or, once they had been put in, entered into communion with them, men who differed in no way from the communion of heretics.

Why, then, when he saw these things happening, did he not take care to refer them to the apostolic see, as he had already done under Basiliscus? Then, even if he could not succeed alone, by joint counsel and deliberation with that see what was fitting for religion could have been urged on the emperor. For if Basiliscus, a heretical usurper, as we have said, was greatly weakened by the letters of the apostolic see and called back from many excesses,

how much more could a legitimate emperor, who wished to be seen as catholic, have been softened by the moderate counsel of the apostolic see together with all the bishops? This is especially so since he was a particular patron and admirer of this same Acacius. In his letters he had highly praised both Acacius himself and the holy pope Simplicius for having most steadfastly resisted the heretic. Why did Acacius keep silent for so long amid all this, unless he did not want anything at all to hinder what he wished to see accomplished?

Yet let us suppose that no synod had gone before, of which the apostolic see would rightly be the executor. With whom was a synod about Acacius to be held? With those who were already counted as Acacius's partners? Throughout the whole East catholic priests had been violently thrown out and banished into various places of exile, and these men had plainly become associates in a foreign communion. They had gone over into these fellowships before consulting the decrees of the apostolic see. With whom, then, was a synod to be held?

The catholic bishops had by then been driven out on every side, and only the associates of the faithless remained. With these it was not even permissible to hold an assembly, as the psalm says: "I have not sat in the council of vanity, nor will I go in with those who do wicked things." Nor is it the custom of the church to sit in council with those whose communion is polluted and mingled with the faithless.

Rightly, therefore, was a transgression of this kind repelled by the rule of the Council of Chalcedon rather than brought before a council. After the first synod a council was not needed, and it was not permissible to hold one with such men. Besides, if they had been willing to understand, they could not have been unaware of what was being done regarding the catholic faith. They saw catholic bishops being driven out of the whole East without any synodal inquiry and without any council, even though they recognized that these were new cases. And the rest could have learned what to guard against from the character of those men.

It remains, then, clear that they belonged to the party to which they had given themselves after so many proofs. Rightly, therefore, the apostolic see and the other catholics were no longer to consult them, but rather to censure them.

We laughed, moreover, at their wanting a special prerogative to be granted to Acacius because he was bishop of the royal city. Did not the emperor reside for long periods at Milan, at Ravenna, at Sirmium, at Trier? Did the bishops of those cities ever claim anything for their dignity beyond the measure assigned to them from of old? When Acacius boldly undertook to exclude John from Alexandria, whatever sort of man John was, yet a catholic ordained by catholics, and to receive Peter, who had already been exposed in heresy and condemned, without consulting the apostolic see, did he at least hold some synod there? When he drove Calendion out of Antioch and admitted again the heretic Peter, whom he himself had condemned, without the knowledge of the apostolic see, can it be shown that he did this through any synod?

If the question is really one of the dignity of cities, the bishops of the second and third sees have a greater dignity than the bishop of that city, which is not counted among the sees at all, nor even reckoned among those with metropolitan rights. As for your phrase "the royal city," the power of the secular kingdom is one thing and the distribution of church dignities is another. Just as a city, however small, does not lessen the prerogative of the emperor who is present there, so the imperial presence does not change the measure of religious order. Let that city be illustrious for the power of the empire present in it. Religion under that emperor stands firm, free, and flourishing only if, in his presence, it keeps its own proper measure without any disturbance.

But perhaps it will be said that in the cases of Alexandria and Antioch it was the emperor, for certain reasons, rather than Acacius, who ordered what was done. Even so, it was the bishop's duty to advise the Christian prince, especially since he enjoyed his friendship and favor. He should have told him that his right to punish the injury and insult done to him would be preserved, provided only that, as a Christian prince, he allowed the rules of the church to be kept. A new cause had arisen in the case of both bishops, and so it called for a new inquiry. Judgments about bishops ought to come, as had always been done, from a council of bishops, so that bishops of whatever kind, who might have erred through human weakness but had in no way gone astray against religion, would not appear to be struck down by secular power.

Or was the man exalted by the honor of the royal city not obliged to put these things to the prince with sound reasoning? If he had been made more exalted by that royal city, then he ought to have been all the more steadfast in putting them forward. But if, in matters that had to be pressed on behalf of religion, he proved contemptible and despised, either sluggish or lacking the confidence to speak up, in what way had the royal city made him greater?

The prophet Nathan, openly and publicly, to King David's face, declared the wrong that had been done, did not keep silent that the king himself had done it, and then, when the king had been corrected by confession, absolved him. But this good man and excellent bishop showed that he could have spoken and made it clear that he did not want to. Indeed, he revealed that he supported what was done, so much so that the emperor did not conceal that he had done everything on his advice. Acacius himself extolled the emperor with high praise for doing these things and thereby exposed himself as a participant in them.

But suppose that Calendion did leave out the emperor's name, and suppose John is said to have lied to the prince. Since these were new causes, a new ecclesiastical inquiry ought to have taken place. Or ought those said to have sinned against a man, the emperor, to have been deposed without any synod, while Acacius, who offended against God, the supreme and true emperor, and who was striving to mingle the pure communion of the divine sacrament with the faithless, ought not to have been excluded according to the synod that had condemned this very faithlessness?

What of the catholic priests driven out of countless cities throughout the whole East, and the heretics put in their place? These were certainly new causes, and so a new synod was owed to them. Why did it not occur to anyone then to ask the prince in such causes for at least some kind of synod, so that the bishops being removed everywhere might seem to have been removed by some judgment of church tradition, however much for show? For not only the bishops of various cities but even metropolitan prelates were being removed without hesitation.

Since Acacius did not resist all this with such counsel as he could have given, he consented to it by communicating with all the heretics who had been put in place of the catholics. And the apostle says that not only those who do such things but also those who consent to those who do them are without doubt counted guilty. Was it permissible for the secular power, with Acacius consenting to such acts, to carry these things out without any synod, though the very novelty of the matters demanded one, and without consulting the apostolic see? And was it not permissible for the apostolic see, following the Council of Chalcedon, to drive from its communion Acacius, who communicated with the enemies of the Council of Chalcedon, in a cause that was old and had been condemned by a just definition under an old ordinance?

"But," they say, "Acacius could not oppose the emperors." Then why did he oppose Basiliscus when he wished to? Why did he not give his consent to Zeno himself, so as not to be seen communicating openly with Peter of Antioch, although he did so secretly? Clearly, when he pushed back, the emperor did not resist him. When he was unwilling, the emperor used no force on him. When he shrank from manifest contagion, the emperor let him avoid it.

Finally, why, for so long, while these things were being done or when he knew they were about to be done, did he not take care to report them to the apostolic see? He knew that the care of those regions had been delegated to him by that see. Instead he became a praiser of what was done before he either gave warning that such things were being attempted or resisted them so that they would not be attempted, as he had already done under Basiliscus. Why did he agree to communicate with all those others who had undoubtedly been put into the various cities as heretics after the catholic priests had been driven out? Finally, if he failed in his duty and did not care to do what befitted a catholic bishop, could or should the apostolic see therefore pass over what was its own duty?

In any case, the apostolic see rejected the accomplice of heretics and removed from its communion a partner in a foreign communion. There was no need of a new synod, since the rule of the old ordinance prescribed this clearly enough. Nor was there any need to inform the bishops of the East that this was to be done. It is clear that they knew about the expulsion of the catholics, which was carried out in a matter of faith, and that by communicating with the heretics put in their place they consented to it.

There is no doubt, too, that they had gone over to a foreign communion, and so the decrees of the apostolic see could not and should not be discussed with them any longer. They could see, in the profession of those who held out most steadfastly, what was owed to catholic faith and communion. They could see how Acacius, by turning away from such men, indeed by working against them, had strayed from catholic faith and communion, and how they themselves had submitted to error along with him.

See, they have recognized the just causes for which Acacius was removed by the authority of the apostolic see, together with all who were his accomplices. He was removed for the sake of the catholic and apostolic faith and communion. Those who had persevered in it were in agreement with that faith and communion, and those who opposed the ones who persevered were shown to be strangers to it. So he was rightly cut off, along with those men, from the communion from which he himself is known to have first separated himself by breaking with the catholic bishops who were his colleagues. And he rightly received the sentence of condemnation, which was to be made known to his other associates, since he alone, on behalf of all his associates, declared in a letter sent to the apostolic see that he had fallen back into the communion of unbelief.

If the Eastern bishops had already been in communion with him before he reported here, they were without doubt shown to be involved in the same guilt. Through him they rightly received the sentence passed on his transgression, since they had joined him in an outside communion. They certainly ought not to have been consulted as men of our communion but rejected as men who belonged to an opposing fellowship. But if they had not been in communion with him before Acacius reported here, they ought to have censured him for entering that communion and to have reported about him here themselves. They ought to have rightly approved his being struck down by the authority of the apostolic see, and to have kept concord instead with that apostolic see and with those many great catholic bishops.

But they had broken away from the fellowship of those men and had chosen to be in communion with their successors, and so they were in no way in agreement with the apostolic see. Because they had fallen into the same lot as Acacius the transgressor, they saw clearly that they were therefore bound by his sentence as well. That is why they did not want him to be seen as condemned: they knew that they themselves were condemned in the same transgression, in which they still persist in remaining today.

These men are bound by the same condition. They cannot judge that their accomplice was condemned unjustly, nor can the guilty properly acquit the guilty. So, since that transgressor was justly condemned, they too lie struck down under the same condemnation, and they cannot be absolved from it at all unless they repent. Through one man who wrote, the transgression of all who had fallen back into the same course of unbelief was made public. In the same way, when the transgression was punished in that one and the same man, who had written on behalf of all, or whose writing had revealed what all of them wanted, the transgression of all his accomplices was also punished along with him, or in him.

We judge that these things are quite enough for the instruction of your love. Still, if the Lord grants us the opportunity, we shall try to set out the same matters more fully, so that each of the faithful may know that the apostolic see did not, perish the thought, decide anything

too hastily. The sentence directed against Acacius is shown to have been lawfully issued in the name of the apostolic prelate alone, which was certainly within his power. This was all the more fitting because it seemed that it had to be sent secretly. Guards had been posted everywhere, and the danger was that this saving measure would be blocked by some difficulty and fail to have its necessary effect. Even so, the orthodox had been cast down everywhere, and only heretics and their associates were now left. In the East, catholic bishops either no longer remained at all or had no freedom. For this reason an assembly of many catholic bishops in Italy, with good reason, took formal notice that the sentence had been pronounced against Acacius.

This assembly of bishops did not meet against Chalcedon, nor as a new synod against the old and first one. Rather, in keeping with the tenor of the old decree, it became a participant in carrying out the apostolic sentence. So it is quite clear that the catholic church and the apostolic see, since they could no longer do so anywhere else, did so where they could and with whom they could. They left out nothing at all that belonged to brotherly deliberation on behalf of the unblemished faith and sincere communion. HERE ENDS THE ACCOUNT SHOWING THAT ACACIUS WAS PROPERLY CONDEMNED BY THE APOSTOLIC SEE, AND THAT NO ONE CAN SHARE IN HIS COMMUNION WITHOUT ENDANGERING HIS OWN SOUL.
II. AN ACCOUNT, IN ORDER, OF THE WICKEDNESS OF DIOSCORUS OF ALEXANDRIA.

Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, was condemned at Chalcedon for what he had done, namely for siding with the heretic Eutyches and condemning Flavian, the catholic bishop of Constantinople. He was condemned by the emperor Marcian of holy memory, by the officials of the court and by the whole synod. After this Proterius, a catholic, was made bishop.

Then the presbyter Timothy, surnamed Aelurus, and the deacon Peter, followers of Dioscorus, separated themselves from the church of Alexandria. When Bishop Proterius could not recall them to their own ministry, he condemned them both. After the emperor Marcian died, Timothy and Peter gathered crowds of heretics and came to Alexandria, and the heretics ordained Timothy bishop. So Alexandria began to have two bishops.

Three days before Easter, on the day when the Lord's Supper is celebrated, Proterius of holy memory was killed by men these depraved people had hired. He was killed in the church where he had taken refuge out of fear. There, on that same day, he was killed in the baptistery, torn to pieces and thrown out; his corpse was burned and his ashes scattered to the winds.

Meanwhile Leo took up the imperial power, and the complaint of the catholics about so great a crime reached him. The heretics petitioned against them, asking for the Synod of Chalcedon to be abolished, while the catholics for their part demanded that the crime be punished.

The emperor thought it too great a burden to trouble with so long a journey bishops whose age, infirmity or poverty kept them from undertaking such a labor. So he sent imperial agents throughout the whole East, and Bishop Anatolius also sent his deacon Asclepiades. Through them all the bishops who had been assembled at Chalcedon were to learn what had been done at Alexandria.

They wrote back that the Synod of Chalcedon must be defended even to the shedding of blood, because it held no other faith than the one the Synod of Nicaea had established, and that Timothy was not only not to be counted among the bishops but was even to be deprived of the name of Christian. When this was done, another Timothy was made bishop of Alexandria. That first Timothy was driven out only with difficulty and sent into exile at Cherson; the heretic Peter also fled.

As long as the emperor Leo lived, Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, lived in peace. But when Basiliscus seized the empire, he began to condemn the Synod of Chalcedon and to drive out the catholics. Then the condemned Timothy, having been granted his freedom, came to Constantinople and restored the condemned heretics to their places. He went to Alexandria; the catholic Timothy fled and hid in a monastery; and that Peter again joined Timothy, with whom he had earlier been condemned. The emperor Zeno returned to his throne, and Basiliscus was overthrown.

Orders were sent to Alexandria that the usurper Timothy should be driven out and the catholic Timothy restored to the church. But the condemned Timothy was overtaken by death, and a single heretic ordained Peter bishop for the Alexandrians. The emperor nevertheless ordered him to be deposed and the catholic Timothy to be brought back, as is also stated in the letters of Acacius.

Meanwhile the catholic Timothy wrote to Pope Simplicius of holy memory. He said that Peter had long ago been condemned while a deacon and was now also cut off from Christian fellowship, and he asked the pope to write to the emperor to have this Peter sent into a more distant exile, because he was hiding in the city of Alexandria and plotting against the church. For almost three years and more, Pope Simplicius of holy memory never stopped writing to Bishop Acacius asking that Bishop Timothy's request about Peter be carried out.

When Bishop Timothy died, the catholics ordained John as catholic bishop. Bishop John sent his synodical letter. But Uranius, an assistant official, also arrived, bringing a letter from the emperor against Bishop John, asking the pope to withhold his confirmation of that bishop. And because in the same letter the emperor had mentioned restoring Peter, whom he himself had condemned, this part was refused outright. The emperor appeared to be offended by this.

At the time when Acacius reported on the condemned Peter of Alexandria, he also added a report on Peter and John of Antioch. He wrote as follows: Peter had governed a monastery at Constantinople but had abandoned it because of his crimes and fled to Antioch; there, with the help of the lowest of the people and the heretics, he drove out the catholic bishop Martyrius and seized his see; and he was immediately condemned by the bishops and deported by the emperor Leo.

He is said to have fled back to Constantinople and given a pledge that he would never again dare to do anything with the help of the lowest mobs. But, as was said above, in the time of Basiliscus he was sent back to Antioch by that condemned Timothy who had come to Constantinople, so that he might hold the bishopric there once again. After this, Peter himself ordained John, whom we said Acacius had reported on, as bishop of the Apameans. When they would not receive him, he returned to Antioch, drove out Peter, the very man who had made him bishop, and seized his church.

Acacius says that both were condemned again, and he asked the apostolic see that, if they should happen to take refuge there, they should not be thought worthy even of being seen; that if they had perhaps already obtained some indulgence, it should be void; and that their repentance should not be accepted. What more is there to say? This very John, whom Acacius had condemned together with Peter and had caused to be condemned by the apostolic see without the remedy of repentance, Acacius himself sent, after so many condemnations, to preside over the church of Tyre.

As for Acacius' claim that Peter of Alexandria submitted a petition condemning the heresy of Eutyches or of Nestorius, this is clearly shown to be utterly false. For what led him, during his episcopate, to pronounce anathema on the Synod of Chalcedon and on the Tome of Pope Leo of holy memory? What led him to remove the names of Proterius and of the catholic Timothy and to write in the names of Dioscorus and the heretic Timothy? If he was a catholic, what led him to dig up from the ground the body of the catholic bishop Timothy, who had been buried among the catholic bishops, and throw it out? Is he not the same Peter who always clung to the condemned heretic Timothy? How is it that Acacius later heaps wonderful praises on the man about whom he remembered having earlier reported such great crimes?
AN EXTRACT FROM THE ACTS, IN WHICH ACACIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, IS SHOWN TO BE A HERETIC AND CONDEMNED BY POPE FELIX.

In the cause of the Christian faith, which has clearly never lacked enemies from its very beginning, there appeared in our own age, though at some interval of time from one another, Nestorius and Eutyches, who urged not new doctrines but only new names.

Nestorius, about one hundred and fifty-eight years later, followed the error of Photinus and Paul of Samosata and deserved to be banished into exile in the Oasis, for saying, as he had learned from his teachers, that Christ our Lord was born of the Virgin Mary as a mere man. Many years later Eutyches rose up against him, but in disputing he stumbled from [?] the right path and was swept away into the madness of Apollinaris.
