He broke out into statements asserting that Christ was not a true man, and that we must not believe there are two natures in him but only the one nature of God the Word, yet the Word incarnate.

This incarnate Word, he maintained, was not that of a man but of a human shape, so that what was urged was the likeness of a human body rather than its reality. The catholic faith, by contrast, confesses that Christ, the Son of God, is true God and true man, not of one nature but of one essence and person.

When Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, found that this Eutyches, a presbyter and abbot in the city of Constantinople, was teaching such things, he exposed him out of zeal for the faith. He had also, long before, rebuked Nestorius when he was preaching sacrilegious things in church,

and he likewise reported the absurdities of Eutyches to Flavian, the catholic bishop of the see of Constantinople, and summoned him to trial. The case was heard and Eutyches was condemned. The emperor Theodosius was offended, and at his command about three hundred and sixty bishops were assembled, among them the heretic Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria. Representatives sent by the apostolic see were also present, Julius, bishop of Puteoli, and the archdeacon Hilary, because the presbyter Renatus had been overtaken by death on the island of Abedus [?].

At this assembly the letters of Pope Leo that had been sent to the synod and to Bishop Flavian were rejected, and they were not allowed to be read at all for the whole day. Nothing else was read except certain acts concerning the condemned Nestorius, that is, of the earlier Synod of Ephesus. At the same time, with the documents set aside [?], the judgment of Flavian of holy memory against Eutyches was discussed. Meanwhile, when the blasphemy of Eutyches was read out, they acclaimed it as the true and orthodox faith.

So, over the objections of the representatives of the Roman see, Bishop Flavian was deposed and Eutyches was received back. Bishop Eusebius, the accuser of Eutyches, who while still a layman had been the accuser of Nestorius, was also condemned. Domnus of Antioch was deposed, and the aforesaid Flavian of holy memory was sent into exile, where he also died.

After the emperor Theodosius died, Marcian became emperor, and he was deeply grieved that the faith had been injured. At his religious command more than five hundred bishops from the whole East and Egypt assembled at Nicaea. He later moved this synod to Chalcedon because it was close to the palace. The emperor himself attended the assembly, as did the senate, all the judges and the officials of the court.

Eusebius, the bishop of Dorylaeum, who the year before had fled from exile and come to Rome, also hurried to take part in this synod. He accused Dioscorus and other Alexandrians. What more is there to say? Dioscorus was condemned, the body of Flavian of holy memory was brought back to Constantinople with the greatest honor, and at Alexandria Proterius, a catholic, was made bishop.

A certain presbyter Timothy and a deacon Peter, followers of Dioscorus, separated themselves from the church of Alexandria. When Bishop Proterius could not recall them to their ministries, he condemned them both. So after the emperor Marcian died, Timothy and Peter gathered crowds of heretics and came to Alexandria, and the heretics ordained Timothy bishop. They seized the church where Bishop Proterius of holy memory had taken refuge out of fear, and there in the baptistery he was killed, torn to pieces and thrown out; his corpse was burned and his ashes scattered to the winds.

Then Leo took up the imperial power, and the complaint about so great a crime reached him. The heretics petitioned for the Synod of Chalcedon to be abolished; the catholics, on the other side, demanded that so great a crime be punished. The emperor thought it too heavy a burden to trouble so many bishops a second time, most of whom were kept by age, infirmity or even poverty from undertaking such a labor. So he sent imperial agents [?] throughout the whole East, and Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, also sent his deacon Asclepiades to the bishops who had been assembled at Chalcedon.

They wrote back that the Synod of Chalcedon must be defended even to the shedding of blood, because it had established no other faith than the Synod of Nicaea, and that Timothy was not only not to be counted a bishop but was even to be deprived of the name of Christian. So another Timothy, a catholic, was made bishop at Alexandria; the heretic Timothy was sent into exile at Cherson, a place on the Black Sea; and Peter fled.

So as long as the emperor Leo lived, Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, also lived in peace. But when Basiliscus seized the empire, he began to condemn the Synod of Chalcedon and to persecute the catholics. Then the condemned Timothy came to Constantinople, restored the condemned heretics to their places, and soon came to Alexandria. Then the catholic Timothy fled and hid in a monastery. That Peter again joined Timothy, with whom he had been condemned.

Then the emperor Zeno returned to his throne, and Basiliscus was overthrown. At Alexandria too the usurper Timothy was driven out and the catholic Timothy restored to the church. But when this heretic Timothy was carried off by death, his associate Peter was ordained bishop of Alexandria by the heretics. The most Christian emperor nevertheless ordered him to be deposed and brought back the catholic Timothy.

Meanwhile, since a great many clergy, monks and wealthy laymen utterly refused to join in communion with the catholic bishop, the most merciful emperor frightened them all with various threats. Then Bishop Timothy wrote to Pope Simplicius asking him to write to the emperor

about Peter, who was hiding in Alexandria and plotting against the church, so that he might be deported into distant exile. And so for almost three years Pope Simplicius of holy memory did not stop writing to Bishop Acacius asking him to press the emperor to carry out Bishop Timothy's request about Peter, but he could achieve nothing whatever.

For when this Bishop Timothy died, John, the steward, a candidate of the office [?], who was highly praised by many, was ordained catholic bishop by the catholics. He sent his synodical letter to the apostolic see, but then a certain Uranius arrived, dispatched by Acacius, bringing certain false charges against John, who was already bishop, and also mentioning the restoration of Peter. At that point the pope held back from confirming John's episcopate, because the letters he had so often sent to Acacius for the peace of the church of Alexandria and the integrity of the catholic faith had achieved nothing at all.

While this was going on, Bishop John himself arrived and was received by the apostolic see, as was fitting. His arrival also brought everything more fully to light. What more is there to say? When we read the letters Acacius had sent to the pope about Peter and John of Antioch, Acacius' misconduct in this matter too was found to be very grave.

For the Peter we have mentioned ordained a certain presbyter John as bishop of the Apameans. When they would not receive him, he came to Antioch, drove out Peter, the very man who had made him bishop, and seized his church. Acacius says that both were condemned again, and he asked the apostolic see that, if they should happen to take refuge there, it should not consider them worthy even of being seen; that if they had perhaps already obtained some indulgence, it should be void; and that their repentance should not be accepted.

When the aforesaid John, bishop of Alexandria, had read this through, he could not keep silent about the fact that Acacius, after so many condemnations, had sent to preside over the church of Tyre that very John whom Acacius had condemned together with Peter and had caused to be condemned by the apostolic see without the remedy of repentance.

So when the holy Pope Felix learned that his predecessor's letters had achieved nothing, and that Acacius was making a mockery of things to overturn the faith, he sent Vitalis, bishop of Truentum in the region of Picenum, and Misenus, bishop of the church of Cumae in the region of Campania, to have Peter driven out of the church of Alexandria, to have Acacius answer the petition of the holy John, bishop of Alexandria, and to instruct Acacius in person to pronounce anathema on Peter of Alexandria. The legates then set out.

Although they were thrown into custody as if by an enemy and lost their documents, they still ought not to have given their consent to faithless and condemned heretics, which they could have refused of their own will. So not only did they fail to do what they had been ordered, but they even entered into communion with the heretics by confirming Bishop Peter, whom they had been sent to drive out. Acacius, for his part, directed insults at Bishop John.

When all this had been made fully known, Pope Felix, deeply moved, held a synod and suspended Vitalis and Misenus from their office and from communion. Acacius he condemned. Acacius, whose audacity drove him to commit still worse deeds, also sent that Peter to the church of Antioch after Calendion, the catholic whom he himself had ordained, had been thrown out.
HERE BEGINS THE FORMULA OF PROFESSION OF FAITH WHICH POPE HORMISDAS OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE DECREED SHOULD BE SUBMITTED BY EACH OF THE BISHOPS OF THE GREEK LANDS.

TO THE HOLY AND MOST REVEREND LORD HORMISDAS, POPE OF THE CITY OF ROME. The first condition of salvation is to keep the rule of the right faith and in no way to depart from the decrees of the fathers. And since the saying of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be passed over, when he says, "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church," these words are proved true by the facts, because in the apostolic see religion has always been kept unstained.

Therefore, not wishing in the least to be separated from this hope and faith, and following in all things the decrees of the fathers, we anathematize all heresies, especially Nestorius, once bishop of the city of Constantinople, who was condemned at the Council of Ephesus by Celestine, pope of the city of Rome, and by the holy Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria. Together with him we anathematize Eutyches and Dioscorus of Alexandria, who were condemned in the holy Synod of Chalcedon, which we follow and embrace.

To these we add Timothy the parricide, surnamed Aelurus, and also his disciple and follower in all things, Peter of Alexandria. We likewise condemn and anathematize Acacius of Constantinople, who became their accomplice and follower, as well as those who persist in fellowship and communion with them, because whoever has joined himself to their communion has earned the same sentence of condemnation as they. We also condemn Peter of Antioch, together with his followers and the followers of all those named above.

For this reason we accept and approve all the letters of the blessed Pope Leo which he wrote about the Christian religion. Therefore, as we said before, following the apostolic see and proclaiming all its decrees, I hope that I may be worthy to be in the one communion with you which the apostolic see proclaims, in which the Christian religion has its whole and true firmness. We also promise that the names of those who have been cut off from the communion of the catholic church, that is, who do not agree with the apostolic see, will not be read out during the sacred mysteries.

I have made this profession of mine and signed it with my own hand, and I have presented it to you, Hormisdas, holy and venerable pope of the city of Rome, through the most glorious magister Vitalian.
